## D138 — The UI is judged on click depth and focus latency; theming is a seam we ship or one they force

> **Revised by [D271](#d271--m5s-first-questions-answered-four-browsers-no-user-facing-theming-or-light-palette-and-guests-who-may-pause-and-seek-unless-the-host-withholds-it)** (2026-10-09): §4's theming seam is not shipped. There is no user-facing theming; what themes are used for is built in.

**Decided** (2026-09-21). Research: [ui-sentiment.md](../design/research/ui-sentiment.md), from
Plex's forum API, four Jellyfin trackers by reaction count, and GitHub repository search.

**Interface complaints are the majority of the conversation in this field, and they out-argue
money.** Of the 9,013 likes across the fifty most-liked Plex forum topics of the past year,
**4,557 — 51% — are about the interface**, against **938** for the lifetime-price thread. This
does not adjust [D108](#d108--the-interface-is-not-ours-to-change-out-from-under-people-and-an-old-client-stays-installable); it says D108 was under-weighted.

### 1. Nobody says it is ugly

Coded across ten threads, complaint density runs **remote/focus behaviour 45 > rollback
requests 29 > lost features 25 ≈ missing customisation 25 > click depth 23 > sluggishness 12**,
and **information density does not appear as an aesthetic complaint at all** — it appears as
navigation. Verbatim:

- *"…without having to hit up 1,000 times to get back to the menu or to be able to switch
  between library and collections with one click instead of 30."*
- *"30+ years of UI layout has categories on the left. The categories are still a drop down,
  now a nested drop down."*
- *"Scrolling between titles and the 'selection' lags by an entire second."* (4K Fire Stick)
- *"Can't find subtitles anymore since the menu pops up is only like 100 pixels and off to the
  side."*

**So the two numbers this project's clients are judged on are click depth to a chosen title and
focus latency on a television.** Not typography, not motion, not colour. Both are measurable,
so both get targets: they belong in
[performance-targets.md](../design/plans/performance-targets.md) beside time-to-first-frame,
and focus latency belongs in [device-lab.md](../design/plans/device-lab.md) because it is a
per-device number that a developer's laptop will never reproduce.

This sharpens [tv-client.md](../design/plans/tv-client.md)'s existing instruction to prototype
focus navigation before writing screens: the thing to measure in that prototype is **the delay
between a D-pad press and the selection moving**, on the worst device in the house.

### 2. The user arranges their own home

*"I prefer my own library folders/names on the sidebar as before. I could arrange the order.
Your categories are not arrangeable as the sidebar previously."*

**Row order on the home screen is user state, not a layout constant.** It rides
[D24](#d24--language-is-a-preference-axis-and-track-selections-stick-to-the-series)'s preference
machinery like any other per-user setting, and per
[principles §11](../principles/11-hot-path-values-are-cached.md) the rows themselves are maintained values. This is
cheap now and is a migration later, which is the only reason it needs deciding today.

### 3. A settings scope is a UI decision

The *"Discussions"* objection (441 likes) was not really about the feature. It was:

> *"This should not be a client side setting, buried in some submenu forcing you to find it to
> disable. It should be available via … your account settings."*

A preference conceptually about **a person** was implemented on **a device**, so opting out had
to be repeated per client and was hidden. That is exactly the distinction
[D103](#d103--a-device-scoped-preference-is-stored-a-device-capability-never-is) draws, and it
turns out to have a user-visible failure mode as well as an architectural one. **Recorded as a
rule: a preference's scope is chosen from what the preference is *about*, never from where it
happens to be convenient to store it** — and where the two disagree, the user experiences it as
the setting being hidden.

### 4. Theming: ship the seam, because it exists either way

Roughly **5,840 GitHub stars** sit on projects whose only purpose is changing how Jellyfin
looks — `ElegantFin` 2,163, `JellySkin` 1,026, `Ultrachromic` 994, `finimalism` 460,
`Jellyfin-Media-Bar` 207, and others. **The strongest single signal is
`jellyfin-plugin-skin-manager` at 660★: a plugin whose only job is installing other people's
CSS.** When a community builds a package manager for workarounds, the missing thing is a seam,
not polish.

Two details worth carrying:

- **`Jellyfin-Media-Bar` is a feature request written in CSS** — a hero row the product does
  not have. Themes are where unmet UI demand goes to be visible.
- **`ElegantFin` is *"inspired from Jellyseerr"*** — the *request* tool is the design people
  want their media server to look like.

**So we ship a theming seam deliberately.** The alternative is not "no theming", it is
unsupported CSS injection against an unversioned DOM, which breaks every release — which is
[D85](#d85--the-api-has-a-compatibility-contract-and-it-covers-three-protocols)'s compatibility
problem pointed at markup instead of JSON. A small, declared surface — tokens for colour,
density and poster shape — is cheaper to honour than an accidental one, and it can be versioned.

**What it is not:** a plugin API for the UI, and not arbitrary script. Themes are data
([D12](#d12--providers-are-sandboxed-wasm-plugins-no-in-process-plugin-code)'s reasoning applies —
third-party code in the client's origin is the last thing to allow unsandboxed).

### 5. The mod to fear is a client replacement, and it tells us what earns one

**PM4K / PlexMod for Kodi**: **5,312 likes, 6,494 posts, 203,921 views, running since
2019-10-25** — **4.7× the likes of the "roll back to Plex Classic" thread**, and the largest
thing on Plex's forum. It is not a skin. It is Plex's backend driven entirely through Kodi's
interface.

Its own list is headed **"Features (vs. official)"** and opens: **"Maintained. Very stable."**
Then *"Directplay anything"*, *"DirectStream support for every codec, not just AVC/MP3"*,
passthrough audio control, and *"correctly identify and display video/audio streams (Atmos, DV,
etc.)"*.

**Item for item that is [D2](#d2--playback-negotiation-the-client-decides-from-a-manifest),
[D4](#d4--three-playback-paths-direct-on-demand-segmented-background-prepared) and
[D17](#d17--direct-play-first-transcoding-additive-and-optional).** The most
successful community project in this field exists to deliver the thesis this project is built
on. That is the strongest external validation the design has received — and it is also a
warning, because the first two words are *maintained* and *stable*, which are not architecture.

### 6. Plexamp is the control group

The same company's music client is loved — *"the UI is probably the best music player I have
ever used"* — and two of its release threads sit warmly inside a top-50 otherwise full of
anger. Reviewers name the difference as **focus**: a dedicated player against a general
entertainment platform.

One company, one codebase family, two outcomes, separated by whether the app tries to be one
thing. That is [D10](#d10--clients-react-native-shell-native-player-modules-two-engines) with a
same-company control, and it supports [D1](#d1--scope-video-first-audio-second-photos-probably-never)'s
scope discipline from evidence rather than from principle.

### 7. Two concrete asks to design in now

- **A dense, titled list view** — `List view` (+30) and `show titles in poster view` (+28) on
  jellyfin-androidtv. A poster wall is every product's default and a measurable number of
  people want rows of text. It is the information-density complaint arriving as a feature
  request instead of as anger, and retrofitting a second layout is worse than allowing for two.
- **Track selection before playback starts** (+18), plus in-player **audio/subtitle sync
  adjustment** (+32) and **dual subtitles** (+33). The first is a manifest question, not a UI
  one: the tracks must be enumerable before a session exists, which
  [D23](#d23--axis-switching-is-mid-session-by-default-burn-in-is-the-one-thing-that-breaks-it) already requires for a different
  reason.

**Status:** Unresolved — what the theming surface actually contains. Tokens only, or slots? The
answer wants one real theme author, and guessing it now repeats the mistake
[D131](#d131--a-restriction-is-a-vector-not-a-ceiling-templates-are-seeds-and-they-say-what-they-hid)
avoided by deferring the template set. Also unmeasured: what click depth and focus latency
actually are on the incumbents, which would turn §1's targets from principles into numbers.

## D139 — Their worst complaint is one we cannot have; their redesign backlash is one we can, and reversibility is the only cure anyone has

**Decided** (2026-09-21). Research: [ui-sentiment.md](../design/research/ui-sentiment.md) §6,
from **2,205 App Store reviews** — 245 most-recent each for Netflix, Prime Video, Disney+,
Hulu, Apple TV, Roku, Peacock, Paramount+ and Plex, coded identically. The standing rule that
the large commercial operators get their own pass
([research/README.md](../design/research/README.md) §Method) applied to the interface.

| App | mean★ | 1★ | leading complaint |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Roku | 3.88 | 19% | navigation 3% |
| Netflix | 3.75 | 22% | price 14% |
| Apple TV | 3.05 | 35% | price 6% |
| Paramount+ | 2.63 | 47% | playback bugs 19% |
| Prime Video | 2.56 | 42% | **ads 26%** |
| Peacock | 2.44 | 51% | **ads 26%** |
| Disney+ | 2.17 | 54% | **ads 34%** |
| **Plex** | **2.04** | 58% | **redesign 20%** |
| Hulu | 1.49 | 70% | **ads 36%** |

**Star averages are weak evidence** — a subscription app's rating mixes catalogue and price
with interface — **and the theme mix is not.**

### 1. We cannot have the industry's worst complaint, and we get no credit for it

Advertising leads four of the nine and reaches **36% of Hulu's reviews**. It is a
business-model failure, and [D13](#d13--no-telemetry-no-account-no-upsell--as-a-stated-promise)
already forecloses it structurally rather than as a preference.

**The consequence is the useful part: we are not competing against their weaknesses.** The
thing that makes them hated is unavailable to us, so **we will be compared on everything else**
— navigation, resume, playback reliability — where they are strong and well-funded. Any plan
that leans on "we have no ads" as a differentiator is leaning on a floor, not a lead.

### 2. Plex is the only app whose leading complaint is its own redesign

At **20%**, and it rates **below every commercial service except Hulu**. An independent
instrument, a different population, and the same conclusion as
[D138](#d138--the-ui-is-judged-on-click-depth-and-focus-latency-theming-is-a-seam-we-ship-or-one-they-force)'s
forum analysis. Two sources that do not share a population agreeing this precisely is the
strongest form this project's sentiment evidence has taken.

### 3. Netflix got the identical backlash, and reports the opposite in testing

Netflix's 2025 TV redesign — **its first major layout change in 12 years** — drew Plex's
complaint set almost word for word: *"borderline unusable"*, larger artwork meaning **more
scrolling to see the same content**, **genre browsing buried deeper**. At the company with the
largest UX research budget in this field.

**And Netflix reports that in testing more users preferred the new design than the old.**

That has to be carried rather than filed away, because it contradicts the comfortable reading.
**Vocal backlash and measured preference can point in opposite directions**, so "users hated
our redesign" is not by itself evidence the redesign was wrong, and a project that treats
forum volume as a design oracle will be wrong in a different direction.

**The reconciliation, and it is what [D108](#d108--the-interface-is-not-ours-to-change-out-from-under-people-and-an-old-client-stays-installable) was already reaching for:** the two groups
answer different questions — *"which layout do you prefer?"* versus *"what happened to my
thing?"* — and **every service in this sample removes the old answer irreversibly**, so the
second question has no good answer anywhere in the industry.

**The anger is about lost agency more than about pixels.** Which means the remedy is not
conservatism — never redesigning is its own failure, and Netflix's testing says so. **The
remedy is reversibility**, and that is a capability rather than a taste: the old layout stays
reachable, the change is opt-in, and every client build stays installable. D108 is therefore
not a promise about restraint; it is a promise about **exits**, and it is the only cure anyone
in this sample offers.

### 3a. Telling "angry at change" apart from "angry at worse", which is the whole problem

Raised by the project owner: *"there tends to be backlash any time you redesign the UI of
something, so we need to somehow differentiate between those angry at change vs those angry at
something actually getting worse."* Exactly the right question, and treating the two as one is
how both mistakes get made — shipping a regression because "they always complain", and
freezing a bad layout because "they complained".

**Four discriminators, in order of how much they are worth.**

**1. Reversibility is not only a kindness — it is the instrument.** If the old layout is still
reachable, **usage is the referendum**, and it needs no survey: change-anger decays as people
relearn and they drift to the new one; degradation does not, and a stable population stays put.
*"What fraction is still on the old layout after 30 days"* is a number, it is attributable to
a cohort, and it arrives without asking anyone their opinion. **Nobody in this sample can run
that test**, because every one of them removed the old answer. So
[D108](#d108--the-interface-is-not-ours-to-change-out-from-under-people-and-an-old-client-stays-installable)
turns out to buy a measurement as well as a promise, which is the strongest argument for it
yet — and it is only available to a project that keeps the exit open **before** it needs it.

**2. Instrument the task, not the opinion.** *"I hate it"* is unfalsifiable; **clicks from home
to playing a chosen title** and **D-pad-press-to-selection latency** are not. If a redesign
moves the first from three to eight, that is not taste, and no amount of preference testing
redeems it. This is precisely why
[D138](#d138--the-ui-is-judged-on-click-depth-and-focus-latency-theming-is-a-seam-we-ship-or-one-they-force)
made those two targets rather than principles: **a regression gate is what separates the two
kinds of anger automatically**, before anyone posts anything. A layout change that holds both
numbers is a change; one that worsens either is a regression, whatever its reception.

**3. The complaint's shape tells you which it is.** Degradation reports **name a task and are
reproducible** — *"the subtitle menu is only like 100 pixels and off to the side"*, *"one click
instead of 30"*, *"no on-screen controls"*. Change-anger is **affective and unlocated** —
*"it's garbage", "I hate it"*. The Plex corpus contains overwhelmingly the first kind, which
is why [D138](#d138--the-ui-is-judged-on-click-depth-and-focus-latency-theming-is-a-seam-we-ship-or-one-they-force)
concluded what it did rather than dismissing it as novelty. Our feedback surface should
therefore **ask what the person was trying to do**, not how they feel about it — which
[bug-reports.md](../design/plans/bug-reports.md) is already shaped for.

**4. The gap between fresh preference and incumbent satisfaction is the transition cost, and
it is measurable.** Netflix's divergence is not a paradox: **their testing asked people with no
incumbency which layout they preferred; the field contains people who lost a familiar one.**
The difference between those two figures *is* the change-anger, separated out. A project that
measures only the first ships regressions; one that measures only the second never changes
anything.

**And one corollary worth stating, because it is where good intentions go wrong.** *"Users
resist all change"* is true and is **not a defence**. It predicts the *existence* of backlash,
never its *content*. The moment it is used to explain away a specific, reproducible,
task-naming complaint, it has stopped being an observation and become an excuse — which is,
read charitably, exactly what happened to everyone in the table above.

### 4. Four failures at well-funded companies that are reachable from here

Not business-model failures. Ordinary ones, at Disney, Apple and Amazon:

- **Resume is broken at scale.** Disney+: *"No automatic episode tracker … Every day, I have
  to scroll through MULTIPLE episodes to find where I left off."* Paramount+: *"when you scroll
  down, it defaults to the series very last episode."*
  [D81](#d81--play-state-is-an-append-only-event-log-plus-a-guarded-position-and-positions-are-edition-relative)'s
  subject, failing daily and visibly, at companies that can afford not to. **Treat play state
  as a headline feature, not plumbing.**
- **Each redesign buries things one level deeper.** Prime Video: *"You've moved the in-store
  code button several times recently. Each time, you bury it deeper in the app."* Depth is a
  ratchet unless something measures it — which is why
  [D138](#d138--the-ui-is-judged-on-click-depth-and-focus-latency-theming-is-a-seam-we-ship-or-one-they-force)
  made click depth a target rather than a principle.
- **The store outranks the library.** Apple TV: *"Essentially an entertainment store … It acts
  more like an App Store."* Prime Video mixes included, rental and third-party *"often without
  clear labeling"*. **Identical to what Plex users say about Discover** — so it is a failure
  of two different business models arriving at the same place, and the only structural defence
  is having nothing to sell.
- **The end-of-episode overlay steals the ending.** Hulu: *"Before the show ends the interface
  minimizes the show and you try to see the last 20 seconds and you can't."* **We have the
  means to do this properly**: [media-segments.md](../design/plans/media-segments.md)'s typed
  `outro`/`credits` boundary ([D82](#d82--media-segments-are-typed-attach-at-the-version-and-carry-provenance))
  says where the programme actually ends, so the next-episode prompt is placed on content
  rather than on a fixed timer. A segment model bought for skip-intro turns out to fix the
  complaint at the *other* end of the episode.

**Status:** Unmeasured, and it is the number that would make §3 actionable: what click depth
and focus latency actually *are* on Netflix, Apple TV and Roku. Roku rates highest in this
sample (3.88, navigation at 3%) and is the obvious benchmark to measure against rather than
admire. That belongs in [device-lab.md](../design/plans/device-lab.md), which already has the
hardware.

---

## D140 — Five gaps the sentiment corpus exposed, three declines, and one that undercuts a headline claim

**Decided** (2026-09-21). A deliberate sweep of the raw findings behind
[D138](#d138--the-ui-is-judged-on-click-depth-and-focus-latency-theming-is-a-seam-we-ship-or-one-they-force)
and [D139](#d139--their-worst-complaint-is-one-we-cannot-have-their-redesign-backlash-is-one-we-can-and-reversibility-is-the-only-cure-anyone-has)
for **features** rather than sentiment — every reacted issue across four Jellyfin repositories,
the Plex forum's yearly top fifty, and 2,205 App Store reviews — with each candidate grepped
against this tree. Looking for big gaps only.

**Most of it was already covered**, which is the useful baseline: deep links
([D88](#d88--casting-is-remote-control-of-another-client-which-is-watch-together-with-a-group-of-one)),
theme songs and backdrops ([D97](#d97--an-extra-is-a-typed-relation-not-an-edition-and-not-a-version)),
PIN protection ([D125](#d125--access-is-role-based-with-two-roles-a-watch-together-guest-is-not-a-principal)),
SyncPlay, offline downloads ([D87](#d87--a-download-is-a-rendition-plus-a-lease-and-it-is-self-contained)),
Chromecast ([D124](#d124--the-playback-role-may-be-a-cast-receiver-and-for-a-guest-that-is-the-best-path-the-phone-controls-it-does-not-relay)–[D137](#d137--the-cast-receiver-ships-no-subtitle-renderer-casts-own-is-the-statutory-one-and-the-cost-is-on-the-server)),
forcing direct play or transcode in both directions
([D4](#d4--three-playback-paths-direct-on-demand-segmented-background-prepared)), dual subtitles
(the schema already models the selection as a **set**), audio/subtitle sync offset
([D90](#d90--playback-presentation-is-a-persisted-per-user-preference-set-and-captions-have-a-statutory-floor)),
manual playlists and collections ([D79](#d79--four-levels-not-three-title--edition--version--file-with-collections-orthogonal)'s
*"explicit member list or a predicate"*), skip buttons
([D82](#d82--media-segments-are-typed-attach-at-the-version-and-carry-provenance)), and a `.srt`
dropped beside a film after the scan ([D24](#d24--language-is-a-preference-axis-and-track-selections-stick-to-the-series)).

**Five things were not.**

### 1. We do not read the sidecars already in the user's library — and this one is urgent

[D98](#d98--a-sidecar-carries-what-is-true-about-the-work-the-database-carries-what-is-true-about-a-person)'s
status line says *"NFO is the field's de-facto answer and **reading it is already planned**"*.
**It is not. No plan owns it.** `identification.md` covers *writing* overrides back;
`library-model.md` covers what is sidecar-*able*. Nothing covers **importing what is already
there**.

That is not a missing nicety, it is a **migration defect aimed at our own promise**. The user
this project is for arrives from Kodi, Emby or Jellyfin with **years of corrections sitting in
`.nfo` files beside their media** — and
[D7](#d7--the-files-are-the-source-of-truth-the-database-is-a-rebuildable-index) promises that
a user's corrections survive. A first scan that ignores them **destroys on import exactly what
the project promises to protect**, silently, at the moment of highest goodwill.

The demand is measured: *Plex NFO Agent Forum Preview* is **291 likes and 510 posts — the
most-replied thread on their forum this year**, already noted in
[sentiment.md](../design/research/sentiment.md) without anybody drawing this conclusion from it.

**So: reading NFO on import is [identification.md](../design/plans/identification.md)'s, it is
Phase 1, and it is a first-run concern rather than a feature.** Writing it stays the open
compatibility question D98 left.

### 2. Nothing answers "this film has no subtitles" — and that undercuts the headline

[D11](#d11--subtitles-are-a-subsystem-not-a-feature) makes subtitles **the** differentiator:
*"the single largest defect area in the field"*, *"the cheapest place to be visibly better"*.
Every subsequent decision — extraction at scan, font subsetting, libass correctness, the
overlay rendition, the statutory control set — handles **subtitles that exist**.

**Nothing in the tree handles a file that has none**, which is an ordinary situation and the
reason **Bazarr** exists. The requests are there: androidtv *On-Demand Subtitle Search* (+13),
*Downloadable Subtitles Like Plex in Jellyfin TV App* (+12).

The awkward part is that we have already researched the *constraint* and never the feature:
[tech-licensing.md](../design/research/tech-licensing.md) records OpenSubtitles at **5
downloads/day anonymous, 20/day with a free account, 1000/day VIP**, and *"must be the user's
account"*. So the hardest fact is known and unowned.

**A claim to be the best subtitle experience in the field, with no answer for the empty case,
is a claim with a hole in the middle of it.** New plan,
[subtitle-acquisition.md](../design/plans/subtitle-acquisition.md), `UNSPECIFIED` — it is
genuinely plan-sized (providers, per-user credentials, rate budgets, hash matching, and
verifying that a downloaded track is actually in sync), and per
[plans/README](../design/plans/README.md) an un-fleshed idea is a file, not a bullet.

> **Resolved 2026-09-21 by [D147](#d147--a-subtitle-is-chosen-by-measurement-not-by-filename-and-the-correction-runs-before-the-choice)
> and [D148](#d148--the-speech-map-is-a-scan-artefact-and-the-reference-is-a-subtitle-track-before-it-is-audio).**
> The crux this gap named — *"verifying that a downloaded track is actually in sync"* — turned
> out to be the whole feature rather than a detail of it, and it is measurable: a normalised
> score separated 64 correct candidates from 64 wrong ones at a fixed threshold, with no
> errors. The plan is `PLANNED`.

### 3. There is no watchlist

Zero occurrences in the tree. We have **favourite** (Title-level,
[play-state.md](../design/plans/play-state.md)), **Continue Watching**, **Next Up**,
collections and playlists — and nothing for *"I intend to watch this"*, which is a different
verb from *"I love this"* and the one a household uses most.

It is also the **top navigation complaint against Apple TV** in the App Store sample:
*"Finding your wish list or watchlist is a chore… you have to scroll through at least three
pages of the homepage just to find it"*, and *"I add it to the list, but I don't know where
this list is."*

Cheap: a per-user Title relation in the play-state family, riding the same change journal and
the same database-only rule ([D98](#d98--a-sidecar-carries-what-is-true-about-the-work-the-database-carries-what-is-true-about-a-person)). It lands in
[play-state.md](../design/plans/play-state.md) with favourites and ratings.

### 4. The metadata model is thorough and nobody can edit it

Provenance per field, manual identification overrides that survive rescans, user-chosen
artwork, sidecar write-back — and **no document says where a person actually does any of
this**. It is a UI gap behind a well-specified model, which is exactly the kind that survives
review.

Plex's *Metadata Editing on Mobile* sits at 66 likes. The surface belongs to
[web-client.md](../design/plans/web-client.md) (it is admin-shaped), and the rule it must
honour already exists: an edit is user-authored data about the work, so it goes to the change
journal and is never overwritten by a refresh.

### 5. No external-player handoff

*"Add option to play via external player directly from movie/episode screen"*, +28 on
androidtv. Small, cheap, and it is **the honest answer to
[D17](#d17--direct-play-first-transcoding-additive-and-optional)'s tail**: when we cannot play
a file and no transcoder is registered, hand it to something that can rather than showing a
failure. It is also a pressure valve — the alternative is the force-transcode arms race the
same tracker is full of.

### Three declines, stated so they are decisions rather than oversights

- **Request flows** (Overseerr/Jellyseerr-shaped). Companion-app territory, and
  [D20](#d20--plugin-architecture-constraints-and-four-things-the-catalogue-says-belong-in-the-core) already says the public
  API is the seam that makes them possible. Not ours to build; ours to be good enough to build
  against.
- **Voice assistants.** Plex dropping its Alexa skill drew 66 likes, so the want is real and
  small. Declined for now, and note the cast path
  ([D137](#d137--the-cast-receiver-ships-no-subtitle-renderer-casts-own-is-the-statutory-one-and-the-cost-is-on-the-server))
  already gives away the useful half, since Cast carries voice-originated load requests with a
  reserved `credentialsType`.
- **A separate desktop application.** *Are the Desktop Apps Dead?* is 186 likes on Plex's
  forum, which is a question we should answer before it is asked: **the web client is the
  desktop client**, and saying so is better than leaving a hole people read as neglect.

**Status:** Only the first two are urgent. NFO import is Phase 1 because the first scan is when
it matters and a later fix cannot recover what a user gave up on. Subtitle acquisition is
Phase 2-or-later work whose *plan* is due earlier, because per-user provider credentials touch
[auth.md](../design/plans/auth.md) and a per-user rate budget is schema.

## D141 — We write NFO too, and the lock markers are the part that matters

**Decided** (2026-09-21), by the project owner: *"we may also have to support exporting to
those nfo files as well if someone decides they'd rather go back to Kodi."* **Answers the half
[D98](#d98--a-sidecar-carries-what-is-true-about-the-work-the-database-carries-what-is-true-about-a-person)
deferred** — it settled *what* goes in a sidecar and left the format as *"a compatibility
question nobody has examined"*.

### It is not a new feature; it is a promise coming due

The README already says it, publicly:

> *"if you grant a writable path, **sidecar files beside your media** carrying your metadata
> corrections **in a format any other media server can read** … The second protects you from
> **us**."*

[Principles §2](../principles/02-the-users-files.md) says the same thing in the same words — sidecars are
*"**portability**, the part that means 'survive us'"*. **A portable format only we can read is
a contradiction**, so the commitment was always to somebody else's format; D98 simply had no
reason to pick one yet.

[D140](#d140--five-gaps-the-sentiment-corpus-exposed-three-declines-and-one-that-undercuts-a-headline-claim)
picked it. Once we read NFO, writing NFO stops being a decision and becomes the inverse of a
parser we already need. **Exit symmetry is the point of the feature, not a courtesy attached
to it**, and it is the same structural commitment
[D72](#d72--the-hosted-relay-has-no-free-tier-holds-no-data-and-has-no-accounts) makes about the relay:
leaving takes an afternoon and migrates nothing, because there is nothing to migrate.

### Write what is not re-derivable

Kodi's NFO files carry a full scrape. Ours should not, and the rule is one we already use:
**[D77](#d77--back-up-with-vacuum-into-back-up-only-the-irreplaceable-and-test-the-restore) backs
up only the irreplaceable, and this is that rule in a different medium.**

So a written sidecar carries **the user's corrections plus the provider identifiers needed to
re-find the work** — and not the plot summary TMDB will hand anyone who asks.
[D7](#d7--the-files-are-the-source-of-truth-the-database-is-a-rebuildable-index) already says
the rest is a rebuildable index *by definition*; writing it into someone's media tree asserts
provider data as fact, makes every file larger, and goes stale.

### The lock markers are the part that makes it work

`lockdata` and `lockedfields` are how the format records *"a human set this; do not overwrite
it on refresh"* — Jellyfin maps `lockdata` onto `item.IsLocked`.

**Without them the export is pointless.** A user who leaves for Kodi with unlocked NFO files
gets their corrections overwritten by Kodi's first scrape, and the sidecars we so carefully
wrote become the thing that quietly loses their work. **The correction has to survive as a
correction, not as a value.** This is the single detail most likely to be skipped by someone
implementing "write NFO" from the field list, and it is the whole of the feature.

### Preserve what we do not understand

We read, the user edits, we write back. **Anything in that file we have no model for must
survive verbatim** — elements written by tinyMediaManager, MediaElch, Kodi's own extensions or
a scraper nobody here has heard of. **A round trip through our server must not delete data
another tool wrote.**

Note this is the **third** appearance of one rule:
[D61](#d61--containment-now-detection-later-and-plugin-shaped-four-affordances-to-keep-open) has the
node protocol skipping unknown record kinds;
[D85](#d85--the-api-has-a-compatibility-contract-and-it-covers-three-protocols) has a client
ignoring fields it does not know; this is the same instruction pointed at a file on disk.
Three consumers is enough to call it what it is — **unknown content is preserved, never
dropped** — and it belongs in the sidecar format from the first line of the writer, because
retrofitting it means the damage is already done to real libraries.

### Our NFO is deliberately lossy, and we say so

[D98](#d98--a-sidecar-carries-what-is-true-about-the-work-the-database-carries-what-is-true-about-a-person)'s
split cuts across this format. NFO can carry `playcount`, `lastplayed`, `watched` and
`userrating` — Jellyfin's `NfoUserDataSaver` writes exactly those into the shared file beside
the media — and **we will not**, because the media tree is shared with the household and often
with a grantee.

So somebody leaving for Kodi takes their **corrections** and not their **watch history**. That
is a stated limitation following from a principle rather than an omission, and the two-ways-out
design already covers the other half: watch state leaves in the
[D77](#d77--back-up-with-vacuum-into-back-up-only-the-irreplaceable-and-test-the-restore) backup,
which is the *durability* half of the same split. An explicit, named
*"export my watch state into the sidecars"* is defensible as a deliberate act by one user about
themselves; doing it by default is not.

### When, and under what permission

- **On change, never on a schedule.** Three and a half thousand files rewritten periodically
  is disk churn in the user's media tree, and
  [D94](#d94--disk-spin-down-is-a-cost-of-the-snapshot-interval-and-archival-means-untouched)
  already prices what waking an array costs.
- **It needs the opt-in writable path**, which
  [principles §2](../principles/02-the-users-files.md) does not grant by default and
  [D89](#d89--deletion-is-opt-in-per-library-two-phase-and-names-every-file) made per-library.
  Reading requires nothing; writing requires permission. That asymmetry is correct and should
  be visible in the UI rather than discovered.
- **It happens in the node** ([D33](#d33--hub-and-spoke-a-core-that-never-touches-media-and-n-media-nodes-that-do)), like
  every other write near the media, and the core never touches the filesystem.

### Done when

**The test is a round trip, and it is the only one that proves the promise.** Import a Kodi
library, correct something, export, and **Kodi reads the correction back and does not
re-scrape over it**. Plus the internal case: rebuild-from-empty followed by sidecar import
reproduces every correction. And a file containing elements we do not model survives a
read-edit-write cycle byte-comparably in those elements.

**Status:** Unresolved — whether to offer *"write the full scrape"* as an option for people who
want genuinely self-contained archival trees, which is a real want and is the opposite of the
irreplaceable-only rule above. Also undesigned: the layout variants (`<filename>.nfo` beside
the file, `movie.nfo` in the folder, `tvshow.nfo` at series level) and which we emit — read
should accept all of them, write should pick one and say which.
