## D142 — Export names one user or none; writing to media restarts the node, and the file transport has no channel for it

**Decided** (2026-09-21), by the project owner, refining
[D141](#d141--we-write-nfo-too-and-the-lock-markers-are-the-part-that-matters): *"we could ask
them when exporting which user they want to base it on (or no user, and accept losing all
user-specific data)"*, and *"exporting this info could get tricky, depending on what kind of
transport we have to the node responsible for the particular files. We'd also need to handle
permissions and read-only filesystems."*

Both right. The first improves D141; the second exposes a hole in the node contract.

### 1. Whose watch state, asked once, at export

D141 said per-user state never reaches a sidecar, with an explicit export *"defensible"* as an
afterthought. **Make it the flow instead**: the export asks **which user to base it on, or
none**, and **none is the default**, because the safe answer should also be the cheap one.

**One user, never several.** The format has no user dimension — an NFO carries a single
`playcount`, a single `lastplayed`. *"Export everybody's"* is not expressible, and offering it
would be a lie about what the file can hold. Naming one user is the only honest shape.

**And the prompt discloses rather than merely asks.** *"Export Alice's watch history?"* is the
wrong question; the right one names the consequence:

> *This writes what Alice has watched into files beside your media. Everyone in the household
> — and anyone you share the library with — can read them.*

That is [D98](#d98--a-sidecar-carries-what-is-true-about-the-work-the-database-carries-what-is-true-about-a-person)'s
reasoning surfacing as a UI moment, and it is the same shape as
[D119](#d119--a-join-link-admits-membership-is-what-persists-rotation-is-seamless-ejection-is-owner-only-and-a-cap-bounds-the-leak)'s
ejection prompt: **ask about the consequence, not the mechanism.** A user who picks "none" and
migrates to Kodi loses their history to that tree and keeps it in the
[D77](#d77--back-up-with-vacuum-into-back-up-only-the-irreplaceable-and-test-the-restore) backup,
which is the split working as designed.

**Who may do it at all is a role capability** ([D130](#d130--a-role-is-a-named-policy-object-users-are-assigned-to-one-never-configured-individually)) — it writes into the media tree and it
discloses one person's viewing to the household.

### 2. Writing to media widens the node's ruleset, so it needs a restart

[media-nodes.md](../design/media-nodes.md)'s permission table says media roots are
**read-only** to the node. [D35](#d35--node-exchange-directory-progress-pair-config-generation-and-permissions-as-the-trust-boundary)
says that table **is** the node's Landlock ruleset. And
[D107](#d107--the-node-channel-is-mutually-authenticated-and-a-nodes-roots-are-local-and-never-remotely-settable)
says *"a Landlock ruleset is declared at startup and cannot be widened at runtime."*

**Therefore granting a library a writable path does not take effect until the node restarts.**
Not a flaw — it is the property doing its job, and the alternative is a node that can be talked
into write access while running. But it **must be in the interface**: *"this takes effect when
the node restarts"*, stated at the moment of granting. The failure to avoid is a user who
grants the path, presses export, and gets a permission error from a component that was never
going to be able to comply.

**And this is the second consumer of machinery that already exists.**
[D89](#d89--deletion-is-opt-in-per-library-two-phase-and-names-every-file) built the opt-in
writable path per library, two-phase confirmation, and the rule that it happens in the node —
for deletion. Export is the same shape: a permissioned write into the user's tree, named in
advance. **Reuse D89's flow rather than inventing a second one**, including the confirmation
that says how many files will be written and where.

### 3. Read-only is the normal case and must be probed, never discovered

Media may be read-only by our own default ([principles §2](../principles/02-the-users-files.md)), by the
mount options, by the NAS's own export configuration, by the filesystem, or by ordinary POSIX
permissions — and the user cannot be expected to know which.

So the node **probes writability per root at startup and reports it**
([principles §9](../principles/09-sensors-report.md), [D73](#d73--each-component-reports-according-to-its-own-visibility-blind-is-not-opaque)), and
the core knows before it offers the button.
[D35](#d35--node-exchange-directory-progress-pair-config-generation-and-permissions-as-the-trust-boundary)
already requires *"degraded modes, stated rather than discovered"*; this is that rule with a
new subject.

**Partial success is the normal outcome, not the error case.** A library spanning two roots
where one is a read-only archive mount will export half. That is fine and must be **reported
per root and per item** — the failure to design against is an export that stops at file 1,400
of 3,500 and reports a single boolean.

### 4. The file transport has no bulk core→node channel, and now something needs one

The exchange directory is asymmetric, and it was asymmetric for a good reason:

| | direction | size |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `config.json` | core → node | small, desired state |
| `state.json`, `reports/`, `log/` | node → core | **large** |

**There is no core→node bulk path.** That was correct while core→node carried only commands.
**Export inverts the flow**: the core becomes the producer of thousands of small documents that
the node must write to disk, and pushing them through `config.json` would be an abuse of a
desired-state file.

Two ways out. **Declare export unsupported on the file transport** — which fails precisely the
case that transport exists for, a NAS reached over a share, where the media and the `.nfo`
files actually live. Or **mirror the directory**, which is cheap and symmetric:

```
<exchange-dir>/<node-id>/
  config.json      ← core writes, node reads + watches
  payload/         ← core writes, node reads          (bulk; new)
  state.json       ← node writes, core reads
  reports/         ← node writes, core reads   (large)
  log/             ← node writes, core reads
```

**Mirror it.** Same permission split, same retention obligation, same "namespaced by node id"
rule, and it keeps D35's core insight — *the permissions split is the security model* — intact
rather than bolting content onto the command channel.

Note what this is: **[D127](#d127--the-node-dials-out-a-unix-socket-is-the-default-and-the-file-channel-is-the-fallback)'s
finding for the third time.** That decision listed acknowledgement and incremental delivery as
things the file channel makes you rebuild; **bulk transfer in the core→node direction is the
third**, and it was invisible until a feature needed it. Over HTTP or a Unix socket this is a
request body and costs nothing.

### 5. The write loop, which is the bug this will actually produce

The node writes several thousand sidecars **into a tree it is watching**. Its watcher sees
several thousand changes, journals them, and the core ingests them as observations. Not
infinite, but it is a scan storm immediately after an export, and it will be reported as a bug.

**The resolution keeps [principles §9](../principles/09-sensors-report.md) intact rather than bending it.**
The node **still reports the writes** — a sensor that suppresses its own output is exactly what
§9 forbids, and *"I did this"* is a memory a node should not need to keep. **The core knows
what it commanded and does not treat those paths as new information.**

That is §9's own test, applied literally: *could the node determine this from what it observed,
with no memory of previous observations?* No — so it is a judgement, and it belongs in the
core. The node saw a file change; only the core knows it asked for it.

**Status:** Undecided — whether an export is resumable. It should be, by
[D102](#d102--the-nodes-work-is-a-pipeline-of-independently-deferrable-passes)'s rule that every
pass is restartable and idempotent because a NAS gets switched off mid-pass, and an export is a
pass in everything but name. Also open: what happens if an export is requested while a scan is
running on the same root — they are both walking the same tree and one of them is writing.

---

## D143 — A lone user is not a household; an export ends the scan; and anything that deletes gets a trash

**Decided** (2026-09-21), by the project owner. Three refinements —
the first two to [D142](#d142--export-names-one-user-or-none-writing-to-media-restarts-the-node-and-the-file-transport-has-no-channel-for-it),
the third extending [D89](#d89--deletion-is-opt-in-per-library-two-phase-and-names-every-file).

### 1. The export default follows the number of accounts

D142 made **none** the default for whose watch state an export carries. The owner's correction:
*"'none' should be the default only when there are multiple user accounts. If there's only
one, then it's a single user who tried our product, didn't like it, and wants to go back to
Kodi."*

**Right, and it is not an exception to
[D98](#d98--a-sidecar-carries-what-is-true-about-the-work-the-database-carries-what-is-true-about-a-person) — it is D98's own scope.** That rule exists
*"because the media tree is shared with the household and often with a grantee."* **With one
account there is no household.** The precondition is absent, so the rule does not bite, and
defaulting to "none" there protects nobody from anybody while quietly throwing away the
user's history at the exact moment they are leaving.

It is also **checkable rather than guessed**, because
[D130](#d130--a-role-is-a-named-policy-object-users-are-assigned-to-one-never-configured-individually)
made a grantee *a user with a role*: one user account genuinely means nobody else can read
it. (A Watch Together guest is not a user —
[D125](#d125--access-is-role-based-with-two-roles-a-watch-together-guest-is-not-a-principal) —
and has no filesystem anyway.)

So: **one account → default to that user. More than one → default to none.** The question is
asked either way; only the pre-selected answer moves.

**One thing the prompt must say in the single-user case**, because it is the part that is easy
to get wrong: **the disclosure is permanent.** Adding a housemate next year does not retract
what is already on disk. One sentence, and it costs nothing:

> *These files stay readable if you add other people to this server later.*

### 2. An export ends the running scan, and the reasoning generalises

Closes D142's open question — *what happens if an export is requested while a scan is running
on the same root* — with the owner's answer: *"an export is a signal for someone exiting, so
we should stop any existing scan. If we guess wrong, it's one 'rescan' button away in the
admin panel."*

**Two reasons, and the second is the better one.**

It **removes the contention instead of making it safe**. A scan and an export walking the same
tree while one of them writes is a race we would otherwise have to design around — ordering,
locking, or teaching the scanner to ignore paths mid-flight. Stopping the scan deletes the
problem rather than solving it.

And **stopping costs almost nothing**, because
[D102](#d102--the-nodes-work-is-a-pipeline-of-independently-deferrable-passes) already makes
every pass restartable and idempotent and
[D118](#d118--the-scan-is-incremental-prioritised-and-steerable-and-playability-comes-first)
makes the scan incremental. A resumed scan picks up; it does not start over.

**The rule worth naming, because it will recur: when two readings of an action are possible,
take the one whose error is cheaper to reverse.** Reading an export as "this person is
leaving" costs one button if wrong. Reading it as "just another job" costs a partial export
and a race. The asymmetry decides it, and no amount of thinking about *which is more likely*
was needed.

### 3. If we can delete, there is a trash

The owner: *"I personally prefer keeping my library read-only… I don't trust Jellyfin or Plex
accidentally deleting or corrupting something… I don't know what the average user wants… we
should take write access very seriously and carefully. If we are going to offer delete or
write functionality, we should probably have a trash directory so that things can be undone."*

**The read-only posture is already the default and should be named as a supported choice**,
not a cautious user's workaround: [principles §2](../principles/02-the-users-files.md) mounts media
read-only, and [D89](#d89--deletion-is-opt-in-per-library-two-phase-and-names-every-file)
makes a writable path opt-in **per library**. Someone who never grants one has a fully
functional product.

**On whether people use delete, the honest answer is that we do not know** — and there is one
data point rather than none: Jellyfin's `UserPolicy` constructor sets
`EnableContentDeletion = false` explicitly, so **the field's own default answer is "assume
not."** Recorded as evidence about defaults, not as evidence about usage.

**But where it is offered, it goes to a trash first**, and five things follow that are easy to
get wrong:

- **Per library root, never global.** `rename(2)` does not cross filesystems, so a central
  trash turns every delete into a copy-and-delete: slow, needs the space twice, and can fail
  half way — the worst possible failure for the one destructive operation in the product. So
  the trash lives **at the root of each library root**, and a delete is a rename.
- **It is excluded from scanning**, or deleted items reappear as new ones on the next pass.
  The same class of bug as [D142](#d142--export-names-one-user-or-none-writing-to-media-restarts-the-node-and-the-file-transport-has-no-channel-for-it)'s
  write loop, and Jellyfin's `IgnorePatterns` — which already skips `sample`, `metadata/`,
  `ps3_update/` and friends — is the prior art for how such an exclusion is expressed.
- **It carries a manifest, not just files.** Undo needs the original path, the timestamp and
  who asked. That manifest lives **in the trash directory**, so it survives a database rebuild
  ([D7](#d7--the-files-are-the-source-of-truth-the-database-is-a-rebuildable-index)) and is
  readable by a human with a text editor if we are gone.
- **It never empties itself.** Automatic expiry would be the one place this product destroys
  something nobody asked it to destroy, and it contradicts
  [D89](#d89--deletion-is-opt-in-per-library-two-phase-and-names-every-file)'s rule that a
  retention policy may only ever *mark*. Show what is reclaimable, and let the user empty it.
  A user-set expiry may exist; it is **off by default**.
- **A read-only library has no trash and therefore no delete.** Consistent rather than
  awkward — and it is exactly the configuration the owner runs.

**And it makes the dangerous operation reversible, which changes the confirmation.**
D89's two phases were *confirm*, then *delete*. They become **confirm → trash → (separately,
deliberately) empty**. The confirmation can be less frightening precisely because the action
is now undoable, and the irreversible step is a second act on a screen that shows exactly what
it will destroy.

**One apparent inconsistency, resolved:** D98 rejected *"a dot-directory beside the media"* for
sidecars, because it breaks the *"any other media server can read it"* property that was the
whole point of sidecars. **Trash has no such property to break** — it is not for other servers
to read — so the objection does not transfer, and putting it inside the root is what makes the
rename atomic.

**Status:** Open — whether the trash is also where a *failed* or *interrupted* write lands, so
that a half-written sidecar never sits beside the media. Probably yes, and it would make the
trash the general undo surface for everything the node writes rather than only for deletion.

---

## D144 — Deletion is deferred, not designed away; the policy is the deliverable and the export already carries the danger

**Decided** (2026-09-21), by the project owner: *"if deletion is disabled by default in the
incumbents, then maybe it's not such an important feature. Maybe we just leave the possibility
and only add it if people ask?"* **Defers the build half of
[D89](#d89--deletion-is-opt-in-per-library-two-phase-and-names-every-file) and most of
[D143](#d143--a-lone-user-is-not-a-household-an-export-ends-the-scan-and-anything-that-deletes-gets-a-trash) §3.**

### The evidence is much stronger than the Jellyfin default

Measured across the three corpora gathered for
[D138](#d138--the-ui-is-judged-on-click-depth-and-focus-latency-theming-is-a-seam-we-ship-or-one-they-force)
and [D139](#d139--their-worst-complaint-is-one-we-cannot-have-their-redesign-backlash-is-one-we-can-and-reversibility-is-the-only-cure-anyone-has):

| Corpus | Mentions of deleting media |
| --- | --- |
| Top-reacted open issues, four Jellyfin repositories | **0 of 120** |
| Plex forum, yearly top 50 topics | **0 of 50** |
| App Store reviews, nine apps | **16 of 2,205 (0.7%)** — and see below |

**The sixteen do not say what they look like they say.** Read individually: three are about
removing an item from **Continue Watching**; four are about a service **deleting the user's
own downloads** — the opposite complaint; two are Netflix removing titles from its catalogue.

**Exactly one concerns deleting media at all**, and it is not a request for the feature:

> *"Deleted files still show — I delete videos but they remain on view."* (Plex)

That is a complaint that the server **failed to notice a deletion made outside it** — the
inverse of wanting a delete button, and something we already handle: tombstone only on a
positive report from a live node, never on silence, with
[D41](#d41--diagnose-the-failure-boundary-by-walking-up-and-guard-the-silent-case-which-is-worse)'s
shrinkage guard behind it.

### And D89 was never a demand finding, which is the part that makes deferring clean

D89 came from the audit's §11 — *"No deletion story at all. Zero occurrences in the tree."* Its
own justification is about **policy**, not product:

> *"Unstated, this ends with `os.Remove` in a handler and the read-only promise becomes a
> comment."*

**D89 asked "what is our policy?", not "should we build this?"** — and **"we don't" is a
complete answer to the question it asked.** So this defers D89's *build* and keeps D89's
*point*, which was always the more valuable half.

**The policy becomes an enforced absence**, and that is cheaper to maintain than the feature is
to build: **no code path removes a file beneath a media root**, asserted by a test rather than
by intention. [D75](#d75--one-predicate-language-three-bindings-a-typed-field-registry-is-the-schema-deliverable)'s
retention binding keeps *marking*; the user acts outside the product.

**Which is arguably where it belonged.** Radarr and Sonarr already delete and replace files —
that is their job, and they do upgrade-and-replace properly.
[D20](#d20--plugin-architecture-constraints-and-four-things-the-catalogue-says-belong-in-the-core)
says the public HTTP API matters more than the plugin API precisely because the community's
real extension mechanism is a separate program. **Deleting media is acquisition-layer work, and
we are the thing it drives.**

### But deferring deletion does not defer the danger

This is the part worth saying out loud, because it is easy to conclude the opposite.
**[D141](#d141--we-write-nfo-too-and-the-lock-markers-are-the-part-that-matters)'s sidecar
export already writes into the media tree.** So:

- **the per-library writable path gets built anyway** — export needs it, and with it the
  node-restart consequence [D143](#d143--a-lone-user-is-not-a-household-an-export-ends-the-scan-and-anything-that-deletes-gets-a-trash) recorded;
- **we can already destroy user data.** Overwriting an existing `.nfo` can lose somebody's
  hand-edited file — through a crash mid-write, or through a bug in the
  preserve-unknown-elements rule. *"We never delete"* does not make the media tree safe once
  we write to it at all.

**So one piece of the trash survives the deferral, and it is justified by export rather than by
deletion:**

- **Write atomically** — temp file plus rename, which is
  [D39](#d39--reports-are-jsonl-completeness-is-in-the-filename-and-is-scoped-not-global)'s own
  `.partial` pattern reused, so a crash leaves the original intact.
- **Retain the file we replaced**, once, beside it. That is the trash in embryo and it costs a
  rename.

### What stays recorded, and why that is the point

**[D143](#d143--a-lone-user-is-not-a-household-an-export-ends-the-scan-and-anything-that-deletes-gets-a-trash) §3's
trash design is not withdrawn — it becomes the precondition.** If deletion is ever asked for,
shipping it *without* a trash is the mistake, and the reasoning that makes the trash
non-obvious is already written down: per library **root** because `rename(2)` does not cross
filesystems; excluded from scanning or items reappear; a manifest inside the trash so undo
survives a rebuild-from-empty; and it never empties itself.

**This is the design working as intended rather than wasted effort.** The decision log's job is
to make the *next* decision cheap, and a deferred feature whose hard parts are already solved
is in a better state than one nobody has thought about — which is exactly what D89 found when
it discovered "delete" appeared nowhere in the tree.

### Two deletion-adjacent wants that are real, and are already covered

Worth naming so they are not mistaken for the deferred thing:

- **Noticing deletions made outside us** — the single genuine signal in 2,205 reviews.
  Covered.
- **Removing an item from Continue Watching** — three mentions, and
  [play-state.md](../design/plans/play-state.md) already requires *"remove this from my list
  possible without marking something watched"*.

**Status:** The trigger for revisiting is **a real request**, not another audit. And if it
comes, the first question is whether the asker wants to delete a file or to stop seeing an item
— because the corpus says those get conflated, and only one of them needs a writable path.

---

## D145 — The trash is one directory per event with a parallel tree inside, because our unit of undo is a bulk operation

**Decided** (2026-09-21), by the project owner, sketching: *"top-level directories named after
delete events, with a parallel directory structure to make recovery a simple `cp -a`… We'd of
course consider bulk operations like export to be a single delete event."*

**The sketch is right, and it is better than both prior arts for our workload.** Adopted with
four changes.

### It has been invented twice, which is reassuring and also instructive

**The freedesktop.org Trash Specification v1.0** stores `$trash/files` alongside `$trash/info`,
with a `.trashinfo` per item carrying **`Path`** (the original location) and **`DeletionDate`**
(RFC 3339). And it is **per volume** — `$topdir/.Trash/$uid`, or `$topdir/.Trash-$uid` when the
shared one fails its sticky-bit and not-a-symlink checks.

**That independently confirms [D143](#d143--a-lone-user-is-not-a-household-an-export-ends-the-scan-and-anything-that-deletes-gets-a-trash)'s
per-root rule from an external standard**, for our reason: a trash that is not on the same
volume cannot be reached by a rename.

**Syncthing's `.stversions`** is the closer analogue, because it versions files that were
**replaced**, which is exactly our case. Three strategies — *trashcan* (one copy, overwritten),
*simple* (N timestamped versions), *staggered* (age-based expiry) — and recovery is documented
as *"manually retrieving them from this directory"*, which is the owner's `cp -a` instinct
confirmed as the industry answer.

**But both are designed for one file at a time.** fd.o's trash is a file manager deleting a
document; Syncthing's is a sync client trickling changes. **Ours is 3,400 sidecars in one
export**, and that is the case neither was built for:

- restoring an export under fd.o's scheme means reading 3,400 `.trashinfo` files and moving
  3,400 items individually;
- under the owner's scheme it is **one command**:
  `cp -a .trash/2026-09-21T143205Z-export/. /media/films/`
- and **repeated replacement needs no versioning scheme at all** — the same relative path
  appears in several event directories, and the chronology is the directory name. Syncthing
  needs *simple* vs *staggered* precisely because it has nowhere else to put the ordering.

**The unit of undo should match the unit of action, and ours is a bulk operation.** That is the
whole argument, and it is why we depart from two working precedents.

### The shape

```
<library root>/.trash/
  2026-09-21T143205Z-export/
    manifest.json
    films/Glass Runner (1982)/Glass Runner (1982).nfo
    tv/Show/Season 01/Show - S01E01.nfo
    …
```

Hidden, because other media scanners generally skip dotfiles and we would rather **not have
somebody else's Jellyfin index our retained copies**. The path inside the event directory is
the path relative to the library root, so the parallel structure is exact and `cp -a` lands
where it came from. Excluded from our own enumeration
([D144](#d144--deletion-is-deferred-not-designed-away-the-policy-is-the-deliverable-and-the-export-already-carries-the-danger)).

### Four changes to the sketch

**1. One manifest per event, not a sidecar per file.** The parallel structure already records
*where*; a per-file JSON would double the inode count to restate the path. So `manifest.json`
at the event root carries what the path cannot: **when, which user, which operation, how many
files, and per-file size and hash.** The hash is what lets a restore notice that the current
file has changed since — fd.o has no equivalent because it never restores over a live file.

**2. Retain only when the bytes actually differ.** Without this, every export of a
3,500-item library trashes 3,400 sidecars, and two exports leave 6,800 retained files. Compare
the rendered sidecar against what is on disk; **identical means do not write and do not
retain**. Free, and it turns the trash from a growth problem into a change log.

**3. `cp -a` is the guarantee, not the recommended path.** Restoring an *old* version over a
*newer* current file silently destroys the newer one — and the newer one was never trashed,
because nothing replaced it. So: **we guarantee `cp -a` works**, because surviving us is the
point ([D141](#d141--we-write-nfo-too-and-the-lock-markers-are-the-part-that-matters)); and
**our own restore trashes the current file first**, as a new event. Both true, and the second
must exist or someone loses data by being clever with the first.

**4. No colons in the directory name.** `2026-09-21T143205Z-export` rather than RFC 3339's
`14:32:05`. Colons are legal on POSIX and **not on SMB or NTFS**, and this project explicitly
targets libraries on NAS shares. Sortable, self-describing, and `ls` is the index.

### The write sequence

~~write temp → **hardlink** the old copy into the trash → atomic rename.~~
**Superseded by [D146](#d146--copy-the-small-file-the-hardlink-was-an-optimisation-for-a-case-we-are-not-building)**:
the hardlink avoided copying bytes, and the files we retain are **kilobyte sidecars**, so it
bought a dependency on `link(2)` — unavailable on **exFAT** and variable over **SMB**, both of
which are squarely in our path — in exchange for saving nothing. **Copy the small file.**

```
write   <target>.partial            temp, same directory
copy    <target> → .trash/<event>/<relpath>
rename  <target>.partial → <target>   atomic
```

The hardlink returns only if deletion ships and we start retaining multi-gigabyte files, where
a copy costs time and double the space.

### One naming tension, recorded rather than resolved

With deletion deferred, **nothing in `.trash` was deleted** — it is all replaced files, and
calling it a trash is slightly wrong today and exactly right if deletion ever ships. The
manifest's `operation` field (`replaced`, and later `deleted`) carries the distinction, and
one mechanism serving both is worth more than an accurate name. Flagged so nobody
re-litigates it as a bug.

**Status:** Unmeasured — path depth. Nesting the original relative path under an event
directory adds roughly forty characters, which is nothing against Linux's 4096 and could
matter against a legacy 260-character limit over SMB on a deeply nested library. An
`assumptions/` test, not a redesign.

---

## D146 — Copy the small file; the hardlink was an optimisation for a case we are not building

**Decided** (2026-09-21), from the project owner's question *"does NTFS support hard links?"*
**Supersedes the write sequence in
[D145](#d145--the-trash-is-one-directory-per-event-with-a-parallel-tree-inside-because-our-unit-of-undo-is-a-bulk-operation).**

### The answer, and why it is not the useful part

**NTFS does support hard links** — `CreateHardLink` since Windows 2000, **files only, never
directories, same volume only, and a maximum of 1023 links per file** (ReFS raises that to a
million). So on the filesystem the question named, the answer is yes.

**But NTFS is not the variable that matters**, and asking about it makes that visible:

| Where the media actually lives | `link(2)` |
| --- | --- |
| ext4, btrfs, xfs, zfs | yes |
| NTFS — natively, or via `ntfs-3g`/`ntfs3` | yes, ≤ 1023 per file |
| **exFAT, FAT32** | **no, by design** — no reference counting |
| **SMB/CIFS mount** | **depends on the server**, and the Linux client needs working server inode numbers; *"hardlinks will not be recognized on this mount"* is a real reported condition |
| NFS | yes |

**The two hazards are exFAT and SMB, not NTFS** — and both are squarely in our path. exFAT is
what large USB drives ship formatted as, which is a very common home media disk. SMB is the
NAS case, which is [this project's stated topology](../design/media-nodes.md).

### The realisation: we are optimising a case we are not building

**A hardlink exists to avoid copying bytes.** The files we retain today are **sidecars, a few
kilobytes each**. Copying one costs nothing measurable.

So D145's sequence was engineered for a file size we do not have. **The correct rule is by
size, and today everything we retain is small:**

- **Small file → copy it into the trash, then rename the temp over the target.** No filesystem
  dependency, no 1023 limit, no SMB variance, no window where the target is absent, and it
  works on exFAT. **The entire compatibility problem disappears.**
- **Large file → hardlink**, because a copy of a 40 GB remux costs time and needs the free
  space twice. That case only exists if deletion ever ships
  ([D144](#d144--deletion-is-deferred-not-designed-away-the-policy-is-the-deliverable-and-the-export-already-carries-the-danger)),
  so **the hardlink question defers with it** — and when it arrives it arrives with a
  capability probe, because on exFAT there is no hardlink to fall back on and the honest
  answer there is that the trash costs a copy.

**So today's write sequence is:**

```
write   <target>.partial            temp, same directory
copy    <target> → .trash/<event>/<relpath>
rename  <target>.partial → <target>   atomic
```

### What this changes about the assumptions test

[D145](#d145--the-trash-is-one-directory-per-event-with-a-parallel-tree-inside-because-our-unit-of-undo-is-a-bulk-operation)
put *"does this filesystem support `link(2)`"* in
[`assumptions/`](../design/plans/testing-strategy.md). **It comes out** — nothing depends on it
any more. The **path-length** test stays, because nesting a library-relative path under an
event directory is a real cost against a legacy SMB limit regardless of how the bytes get
there.

**And the general lesson is worth more than the change.** The hardlink was chosen because it
was the *cleverest* correct answer, not the *simplest* one, and the cleverness bought
compatibility risk on exactly the filesystems this project targets in exchange for saving a
copy of five kilobytes. **A question about one filesystem's capabilities was enough to show
the capability was not needed** — which is the cheapest way this kind of thing ever gets
caught.

---

## D147 — A subtitle is chosen by measurement, not by filename, and the correction runs before the choice

**Decided** (2026-09-21). Research: [subtitle-sync.md](../design/research/subtitle-sync.md).
**Closes the crux question left open by**
[subtitle-acquisition.md](../design/plans/subtitle-acquisition.md), which
[D140](#d140--five-gaps-the-sentiment-corpus-exposed-three-declines-and-one-that-undercuts-a-headline-claim)
opened as the gap that *"undercuts a headline claim"*.

The project owner described the experience precisely: a list of candidates *"with some names
more similar to your exact filename than others (not that a normal user would know what the
original filename actually was)"*, about half failing to download, and the survivors *"either
out of sync right off the bat, or drifts over time, or maybe — just maybe — it actually
works."*

### The cause is a ranking function that does not measure the thing

Bazarr's vendored `subliminal` scores a candidate on `hash`, `title`, `year`, `source`,
`edition`, `release_group`, `audio_codec`, `resolution`, `video_codec`, `hearing_impaired`,
`streaming_service`. **Every term but `hash` is parsed out of the uploader's filename, and no
term measures sync.** When the hash matches, the answer is right and cheap; when it does not —
any re-encode, any differently-sized rip — the list is ordered by *filename resemblance*, and
the user is asked to do the search by hand against a **5–20 downloads/day** budget
([tech-licensing.md](../design/research/tech-licensing.md)).

**And the fix is already in the box, switched off.** Bazarr vendors the whole of `ffsubsync`
(MIT) at `libs/ffsubsync/`, and then ships `subsync.use_subsync = False`,
`subsync.no_fix_framerate = True` — the drift fix disabled separately from the offset fix —
and gates the whole thing on the *metadata* score being poor. Sync is wired in as **a repair
for a suspicious-looking match**, never as a check on every download, and **its result is
never fed back into which candidate to keep**.

There is a real reason nobody ranks by it, and `ffsubsync` states it in its own source:
*"The score's sign is meaningful even though its magnitude is not."* A raw convolution peak
compares two alignments of one pair; it cannot compare two candidates.

### So: a normalised score, computed on every candidate, after correction

- **The score is a normalised binary correlation** (a φ coefficient) between the subtitle-on
  indicator and a speech map, at 10 ms bins — bounded, comparable across candidates and across
  films, which is the property the field lacks and the only reason ranking is impossible today.
- **It is maximised over the correction, not over the raw file.** Offset in ±60 s and the
  discrete framerate set (`24/23.976`, `25/23.976`, `25/24`, and inverses) are searched before
  the score is taken. Measured on Tears of Steel: **inject a constant offset, a PAL framerate
  ratio, or both, and the worst cue in the corrected file lands 0.130 s from its true place —
  the same figure as a file that was never corrupted at all.** Correction is lossless.
- **Therefore desync is not a selection criterion.** This is the inversion. Once correction
  runs first, "is it in sync" has no discriminating power left, and the only question is
  **does this subtitle belong to this film** — which separates cleanly: over **128 candidate
  evaluations across two films, with half the correct candidates deliberately desynced, a
  fixed threshold of r ≥ 0.25 accepted 64/64 right-film candidates and 0/64 wrong-film
  candidates**, with a 3.4–3.6× margin. The top-scoring candidate for one of the two targets
  was a file that had been desynced by −10.9 s with a 0.959 ratio, and that is the right
  answer, not a flaw in the ranking.
- **A low score is an answer.** When the detector cannot separate, it scores everything low
  rather than scoring something wrongly high — measured on Sintel under a weak detector, where
  every candidate landed near 0.15. **The correct output there is "I could not verify this",
  not a silent guess.** That distinction is the whole difference between this and the button
  everyone already hates.

### What the user sees instead of the list

- **Nothing, in the ordinary case.** The fetch is a background job: candidates are scored,
  the best is corrected and written, and the subtitle is simply *there*. There is no list to
  pick from because picking was never a human judgement — it was a measurement the software
  declined to take.
- **When nothing clears the threshold**, say exactly that — *"no subtitle for this could be
  verified against the audio"* — and offer the unverified best as an explicit choice, labelled.
  Never present an unverified track as though it were checked.
- **The measured offset is shown, not hidden**, and D90's manual offset control
  ([D90](#d90--playback-presentation-is-a-persisted-per-user-preference-set-and-captions-have-a-statutory-floor))
  stays: it is the correction for the residual and for the piecewise case below.
- **A user nudge is ground truth.** If someone moves the offset and keeps watching, that value
  is persisted onto the track for everyone, and it is worth more than our score.

### What this does not solve

- **A structural break** — an ad-break-segmented broadcast rip, a different cut — is not an
  offset and not a ratio, and a single linear correction cannot fix it. `alass` and
  `ffsubsync --split-penalty` both implement piecewise alignment for this. **Out of scope for
  the first version**; the honest behaviour is that the score is mediocre, the track is
  labelled unverified, and the user gets the offset control. Recorded as an open item.
- **Download failure.** Half the complaint is transport, not sync: Bazarr maintains a typed
  back-off table with **3–6 hour** penalties for `DownloadLimitExceeded`. Nobody builds that
  for a rare event. The answer is
  [D148](#d148--the-speech-map-is-a-scan-artefact-and-the-reference-is-a-subtitle-track-before-it-is-audio)'s
  budget accounting plus surfacing the *reason* — "your daily quota is spent", not "failed".

### Consequences

- **`subtitle-acquisition.md` moves from UNSPECIFIED to SPECIFIED**, and its stated crux —
  *"is a downloaded track actually in sync? … is undecided and is the crux"* — is answered
  with a measurement rather than a fallback to the user's offset control.
- **A subtitle track carries provenance and a score.** `origin` (embedded, sidecar, fetched),
  `provider`, `verified_score`, `applied_offset`, `applied_ratio`, and whether a human
  overrode it. A track that was never verified must be distinguishable from one that scored
  0.6, everywhere it is offered.
- **The same measurement applies to subtitles we did not fetch.** An embedded track or a
  sidecar the user already had can be out of sync too, and scoring it costs the same 8 ms.
  **This is the part the incumbents cannot do at all**, because they have nothing to score
  against — see [D148](#d148--the-speech-map-is-a-scan-artefact-and-the-reference-is-a-subtitle-track-before-it-is-audio).
- **The provider hashes are free, which was an open cost question.** OpenSubtitles'
  `moviehash` and TheSubDB's hash are both computed over the **first and last 64 KiB plus the
  size** — a strict subset of the 1 MB head/tail window
  [D116](#d116--the-content-hash-is-a-sampling-hash-whole-file-hashing-is-opt-in-and-separate)'s
  sampling hash already reads. The node emits them from the same pass. That matters because a
  hash match is the one thing the field's ranking already gets right, and it is the cheapest
  way to skip the measurement entirely.
- **`ffsubsync` and `alass` are prior art we should read, not reimplement blindly.** Both are
  permissively licensed and both are better than a first attempt at the pieces they cover; the
  normalised score and the "score every candidate" policy are the parts that are ours.

**Status:** measured. What is unmeasured is the piecewise case and a real provider pool — our
negative controls are a second film, which is a clean separation but an easier one than two
different cuts of the *same* film.

---

## D148 — The speech map is a scan artefact, and the reference is a subtitle track before it is audio

**Decided** (2026-09-21). Research: [subtitle-sync.md](../design/research/subtitle-sync.md).
Implements the measurement [D147](#d147--a-subtitle-is-chosen-by-measurement-not-by-filename-and-the-correction-runs-before-the-choice)
requires. Adds a pass to
[D102](#d102--the-nodes-work-is-a-pipeline-of-independently-deferrable-passes).

[D147](#d147--a-subtitle-is-chosen-by-measurement-not-by-filename-and-the-correction-runs-before-the-choice)
needs a speech reference at the moment a subtitle is fetched, which may be months after the
scan and on a node that is asleep. Recomputing it per candidate would put a decode on an
interactive path. **It is not a computation; it is an artefact** —
[principles §11](../principles/11-hot-path-values-are-cached.md), a value on a hot path is maintained, not computed.

### Three references, in order, and the first one is free

| Reference | Separation measured | Cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **An existing correct subtitle track** in the file | **0.65** | none — no decode at all |
| **The centre channel** (`FC`) of the audio | 0.31 – 0.39 | one audio-only decode |
| The stereo downmix | 0.22 – 0.23 | same |

**A subtitle track beats the audio by a factor of two and costs nothing**, because dialogue
timings are dialogue timings whatever language they are in. Anything with embedded subtitles —
most of a real library — never needs the audio path at all.
[D11](#d11--subtitles-are-a-subsystem-not-a-feature) already extracts embedded tracks at scan,
so this reference exists the moment the pass that makes it does.
(`ffsubsync` reaches the same conclusion: its default detector is named `subs_then_webrtc`.)

**When audio is needed, take the centre channel.** Dialogue is mixed to `FC` on every 5.1
master, `-af "pan=mono|c0=FC"` costs nothing at decode, and it improved separation on both
films and both detectors.

### The detector has to be a real one

**A plain energy VAD is not a detector.** On Sintel it marked 42% of the film as speech and
every alignment ran to the rail. The proof is the control: Blender publishes a
**dialogue-free** music-and-effects master of the same film, and the energy detector reports
essentially the same speech fraction on it as on the full mix. It was measuring the orchestra.

**`webrtcvad` — the field's default — reports 31.5% speech on that dialogue-free track**, and
on Sintel its separation is **0.002**, which is none. It works on the easy half of the content.
**`silero` reports `0.000`**, and separation 0.309. At **233–387× realtime** on one CPU core it
is affordable, and it is the difference between the feature working and not.

### The pass, and what it costs

A **tenth pass** for [D102](#d102--the-nodes-work-is-a-pipeline-of-independently-deferrable-passes),
in the cheap class of [D114](#d114--a-pass-costs-what-it-costs-because-of-one-thing-whether-it-decodes-video)
because it never touches the video stream, and fusable with the existing audio decode that
[D83](#d83--loudness-is-measured-at-scan-and-applied-as-gain-downmix-has-one-default-and-a-dialogue-control-drc-is-per-device)'s
loudness and [D115](#d115--intro-detection-is-fingerprint-first-and-chromaprint-needs-a-stereo-downmix-or-it-fails-outright)'s
fingerprint already perform — D102's 38%/45% fusion saving applies directly.

| | Per 2-hour film | Whole reference library |
| --- | --- | --- |
| decode to mono 16 kHz (2,065× realtime) | 3.5 s | |
| silero pass (233–387× realtime) | ~29 s | **≈14 h on one core, ≈2.5 h on six** |
| *(compare)* trickplay | | **9.2 days** |

*(The library figure is sized the same way [D114](#d114--a-pass-costs-what-it-costs-because-of-one-thing-whether-it-decodes-video)
sized loudness: 31 hours at 102× realtime puts ≈3,160 hours of content in the reference
library, and decode plus detector compose to ≈223× realtime.)*

**And the artefact is trivially small.** Run-length encoded at 10 ms bins: **1.1–3.2 kB per
film, ≈7 MB for the whole reference library** — against trickplay's 5.7 GB and overlays'
42 GB.
It is the cheapest thing in the pipeline by three orders of magnitude.

With the map stored, **the full search — seven framerate ratios × ±60 s of offset at 10 ms
resolution, 84,007 evaluations — is 3–8 ms.** Scoring ten candidates is under a tenth of a
second, on the core, with the node asleep.

### Consequences

- **The map lives with the Version**, beside the other scan artefacts, and is invalidated by
  the same signal that invalidates them. It is **derived**, so
  [backup-restore.md](../design/plans/backup-restore.md) need not carry it.
- **Verification is available for subtitles we did not fetch.** Every embedded track and every
  user sidecar can be scored for 8 ms. A library-wide *"these 14 subtitle tracks do not match
  their audio"* report is a query, not a job — and no incumbent can produce it.
- **Deferrable like every other pass** ([D102](#d102--the-nodes-work-is-a-pipeline-of-independently-deferrable-passes)):
  a library that never fetches subtitles and has embedded tracks everywhere can skip it, and
  a first fetch can trigger it for one file on demand.
- **The parser is an adversarial-input parser.** **7 of 65 subtitle files in the two
  *official* Blender releases needed tolerant parsing** — one is an HTML page saved as
  `.srt`, several use `- >` instead of `-->`, several put the cue text on the timestamp line.
  A strict parser returns zero cues and the user sees "it failed". This is
  [threat-model.md](../design/plans/threat-model.md)'s hostile-data rule with a very ordinary
  subject.

**Status:** measured on two films. Unmeasured: the pass on NAS-class hardware, silero's cost
on ARM, and whether the centre-channel advantage survives on stereo-only sources, where there
is no `FC` to take.

## D149 — Eight gaps the source sweep found, six declines, and the one that is a hole in the business model

**Decided** (2026-09-21). Research:
[feature-sweep-2026-09-21.md](../design/research/feature-sweep-2026-09-21.md). From the project
owner: *"look at the source code of every competitor and associated product we can find to get
a list of functions and features we don't yet have in our design."*

[D140](#d140--five-gaps-the-sentiment-corpus-exposed-three-declines-and-one-that-undercuts-a-headline-claim)
swept the **complaint record**. This swept the **shipped surface** — 60 Jellyfin controllers and
their configuration schemas, Emby at the 2018 fork point, Kodi's JSON-RPC and settings tree,
Plex's object model via `python-plexapi`, Tautulli's triggers, Kometa's builders, Maintainerr's
rule vocabulary, 36 official plugins — then added two axes the first sweep did not have:
**what people install a second program to get**, and **what somebody built and withdrew**.

**Most of the tree survived the sweep**, which is the useful baseline: chapters are already
distinguished from segments, playlists and collections, favourites and user ratings, watchlist,
offline download, deep links, theme songs, pairing, duplicates and versions, and the
declines already on the record. What follows is what did not.

### The one that is not a feature gap but a business-model hole

**There is no per-user or per-role bandwidth or concurrent-stream limit anywhere in this
tree** — three incidental mentions, no design. Jellyfin has `RemoteClientBitrateLimit`; Plex
has per-user limits; a *Transcode Killer* plugin exists because the field's caps are not enough.

That is a nicety for a LAN server and it is **not** a nicety for us:
[D25](#d25--remote-access-is-tiered-and-the-promise-changes-from-no-accounts-to-we-only-charge-for-another-machine),
[D64](working-notes-archive.md#d64--watch-together-makes-the-remote-access-question-concrete-and-supplies-the-premium-tiers-first-honest-member) *(its relay argument withdrawn by [D68](#d68--turn-is-not-an-independent-requirement-the-media-server-is-already-the-relay))*
and [D86](#d86--adaptation-is-the-client-re-picking-on-a-buffer-signal-and-it-puts-bandwidth-transcoding-on-remote-accesss-critical-path)
put a **paid relay** on the critical path, and
[D72](#d72--the-hosted-relay-has-no-free-tier-holds-no-data-and-has-no-accounts) prices it.
**A relay with no ceiling is an unbounded bill**, and the ceiling has to exist in the schema
before anything meters against it. It belongs with [auth.md](../design/plans/auth.md)'s role
object ([D130](#d130--a-role-is-a-named-policy-object-users-are-assigned-to-one-never-configured-individually)),
because "how much of the shared pipe may this person take" is a policy attribute exactly like
the ones already there.

### Seven more gaps, ranked by demand over cost

1. **Show the play statistics we already store.** **9,196★** of companion applications —
   Tautulli 6,589, Jellystat 2,472, Playback Reporting 135 — exist because no server in this
   field shows a user their own history.
   [D81](#d81--play-state-is-an-append-only-event-log-plus-a-guarded-position-and-positions-are-edition-relative)
   already makes play state an **append-only event log**, so we hold the data and nothing reads
   it back. This is the best ratio in the sweep: a query and a page. It is also the one place
   [D13](#d13--no-telemetry-no-account-no-upsell--as-a-stated-promise) pays a visible dividend
   — the statistics are *yours*, computed locally, and were never sent anywhere.
2. > ~~**Outbound notifications.** Tautulli ships 22 triggers and 28 delivery agents … the four
   > worth having are the operational ones: buffering, the concurrent-stream ceiling being hit,
   > a new device, and the server unreachable from outside.~~
   >
   > **Withdrawn 2026-09-21 by [D151](#d151--withdrawn-notifications-a-media-server-has-nothing-you-are-waiting-for-and-its-ui-is-the-notification)**,
   > the day after it was written, on the project owner's question *"who would be the consumer
   > of these, and what is the utility?"* Measured demand is **8 reactions** across the ten
   > video repositories against subtitles' 479, and **zero** for the new-device trigger. I read
   > a rich surface as demand and double-counted Tautulli's stars into both this and the
   > statistics item. **Statistics is unaffected and stands.**
3. **External critic and audience scores are not in the field registry.** Zero mentions in this
   tree. Maintainerr carries **twelve** rating properties (IMDb, Rotten Tomatoes critic *and*
   audience, TMDb, Trakt, each with a vote count) and most of Kometa's 129 builders rest on
   them. `library-model.md:129` has *user* ratings and nothing external. **This is schema**, so
   it is due before [library-model.md](../design/plans/library-model.md) freezes, and it lands
   in [rules-engine.md](../design/plans/rules-engine.md)'s typed registry
   ([D75](#d75--one-predicate-language-three-bindings-a-typed-field-registry-is-the-schema-deliverable))
   with the same null-handling problem D75 already solved for play count.
4. **External list import.** Kometa is **3,414★** and assembles its builders from **22 external
   services**. [D79](#d79--four-levels-not-three-title--edition--version--file-with-collections-orthogonal)
   already says a Collection is *"an explicit member list or a predicate"*, so the model is
   there — what is missing is the loop that fetches a list, reconciles it against the library,
   refreshes it, and reports the members we do not have. Note this is **extensional** where
   D75 is intensional: a third axis alongside the explicit list and the predicate, because the
   membership is authored somewhere else.
5. **Admin-curated home rows, per role.** Plex models this as **`ManagedHub`** with
   `homeVisibility ∈ {none, all, admin, shared}`, `promotedToOwnHome`, `promotedToSharedHome`;
   the Jellyfin plugin is 513★. We have per-user row **order**
   ([D138](#d138--the-ui-is-judged-on-click-depth-and-focus-latency-theming-is-a-seam-we-ship-or-one-they-force))
   and no way for an owner to say *"this collection is a row on the kids' home screen."* Every
   part already exists —
   [D130](#d130--a-role-is-a-named-policy-object-users-are-assigned-to-one-never-configured-individually)'s
   roles, D75's predicates, and
   [D134](#d134--a-pending-item-discloses-nothing-a-rule-shows-its-coverage-and-the-home-page-computes-nothing)'s
   rule that a home-page value is maintained rather than computed, which is what makes a
   curated row affordable in the first place.
6. **Retention as a presented decision.** **3,301★** — Maintainerr 2,287, janitorr 753,
   media-cleaner 261. This looks like it collides with
   [D144](#d144--deletion-is-deferred-not-designed-away-the-policy-is-the-deliverable-and-the-export-already-carries-the-danger)
   and does not, because **Maintainerr's actual product is the grace period**: it gathers
   candidates into a *visible collection*, leaves them there while everyone catches up, and only
   then acts. The visible-collection half needs no deletion, is D75's retention binding with a
   surface on it, and is the part that does the work.
7. **The small client behaviours that are simply absent.** **Shuffle and random play score zero
   mentions in the entire tree**; so do folder browsing and poster overlays. Playback speed,
   sleep timer, picture-in-picture, bulk edit and manual re-identify are named once or twice
   and never designed. Individually trivial, collectively the difference between "complete" and
   "obviously unfinished" — and two of them are not free: **playback speed is shared state or
   explicitly local in Watch Together** (a participant at 1.25× is not drifting, and
   [D66](#d66--no-clock-synchronisation-monotonic-local-time-and-bounded-round-trips)'s
   reconciler must not fight them), and **manual re-identify is the escape hatch for every
   identification bug we will ever ship**.

### Six declines, on the record

MaxSilence reads as neglect, so these are stated rather than omitted. They join the table in
[overview.md](../design/overview.md).

| Declined | Why, with the number |
| --- | --- |
| **DLNA / UPnP** | Demand is 11 reactions. **Jellyfin moved it out of the core in 10.9** and the resulting plugin has **87★ against 84 open issues** — nearly as many open bugs as stars, which is the clearest "walking away" signal in the dataset. Cast ([D135](#d135--casting-on-your-own-is-a-device-delegation-not-an-invitation-the-credential-is-the-session-and-the-queue-is-next-up)) covers the useful half. |
| **3D / stereoscopic** | One issue, 23 reactions, and it needs a whole rendition axis. |
| **Sonos / multi-room audio** | Plex has it; nobody asks us for it; audio is already second ([D1](#d1--scope-video-first-audio-second-photos-probably-never)). |
| **Games, sports, music videos as a library type** | Emby shipped Games and Jellyfin did not carry it; Plex built an arcade and killed it (§D150). |
| **Multi-server federation** | Zero mentions here, three reactions there. |
| **Poster overlays baked into artwork** | Kometa's 24 overlay families are its most visible feature and it implements them by **rewriting the poster**, which is destructive to a file we do not own ([principles §2](../principles/02-the-users-files.md)). If we ever want badges they are a *client render* over an untouched image. |

### Two more worth naming without deciding

- **Common Sense Media.** Plex exposes `parentalAdvisoryTopics` (per-topic rating, with a
  `positive` flag so a topic can be a reason *to* watch), `parentsNeedToKnow` and
  `talkingPoints`, behind Plex Pass. It is a genuinely better parental layer than
  [D131](#d131--a-restriction-is-a-vector-not-a-ceiling-templates-are-seeds-and-they-say-what-they-hid)'s
  national-system descriptors, and it is licensed data — which puts it exactly where
  [D16](#d16--gplv3-no-nonfree-components-and-provider-keys-belong-to-the-user) puts every other
  provider: the user's key, or nothing.
- **Artwork has no type enumeration.** [artwork.md](../design/plans/artwork.md) covers sizes,
  languages, caching and provenance and never says *which kinds of image exist*. Kodi has
  `GetAvailableArtTypes`; Plex has Art, Poster, Logo, Theme, SquareArt. Clearlogo and banner
  are the ones televisions actually use.

**Status:** the gap list is evidence-backed; the *ordering* is a judgement and should be
re-read against the roadmap rather than treated as a schedule.
