## D150 — Read the withdrawals, not just the requests: five features the field built and took away

**Decided** (2026-09-21). Research:
[feature-sweep-2026-09-21.md](../design/research/feature-sweep-2026-09-21.md) §5. From the
project owner's question: *"…and if anyone abandoned them."*

Every previous sweep in this project measured **wanting**. This one measured **regret**, and it
is a better signal, because a withdrawal is a company paying a reputational cost to stop
carrying something. Five of them land on decisions we have already made.

### 1. Plex killed its plugin system at under 2% usage — and we have three plugin tiers

September 2018: *"Less than 2 percent of people were using Plugins."* The technology needed a
complete rebuild and Plex judged it unjustifiable.

**We have bet heavily here** —
[D12](#d12--providers-are-sandboxed-wasm-plugins-no-in-process-plugin-code),
[D15](#d15--two-plugin-tiers-in-process-wasm-and-out-of-process-adapters),
[D19](#d19--the-transcoder-is-a-plugin-we-happen-to-maintain-plugin-tiers-become-three) and
[D20](#d20--plugin-architecture-constraints-and-four-things-the-catalogue-says-belong-in-the-core).
The distinction that survives the finding is real but narrow, and it must be stated rather than
assumed: **Plex's plugins were content channels** — Pandora, CNN, Vimeo — a *content-source*
tier, competing with the streaming apps already on the television. **Ours are metadata
providers and protocol adapters**, and the evidence that *those* are used is on the other side
of the ledger: Jellyfin's third-party catalogue reaches 4,492★ for a single metadata plugin
([plugins-and-workarounds.md](../design/research/plugins-and-workarounds.md)).

Two things change anyway:

- **A content-source plugin tier is now explicitly declined**, with Plex's 2% attached. That is
  the tier that died, and it is the one nobody should propose without this number.
- **[D19](#d19--the-transcoder-is-a-plugin-we-happen-to-maintain-plugin-tiers-become-three)'s
  rule — the plugin API stays private and unstable until a first-party consumer has proven it —
  is upgraded from prudence to the lesson of the largest player's most expensive retraction.**

### 2. Plex withdrew Watch Together in February 2025 — and we call it a first-class feature

This is the uncomfortable one and it gets no softening.
[D62](#d62--watch-together-is-a-first-class-feature-and-the-per-client-surface-is-six-methods)
makes Watch Together first-class and
[D64](working-notes-archive.md#d64--watch-together-makes-the-remote-access-question-concrete-and-supplies-the-premium-tiers-first-honest-member)
made it the paid tier's first honest member *(withdrawn by [D68](#d68--turn-is-not-an-independent-requirement-the-media-server-is-already-the-relay))*. **On 25 February 2025 Plex ended support for
Watch Together on its new apps**, keeping it in the web app only, because the apps were
*"rebuilt from the ground up to boost our development speed"*.

Read precisely, it is a **maintenance-cost** verdict, not a demand verdict, and three facts cut
the other way:

- **Demand is the second-highest thing in the whole issue corpus** — 10 issues, **127
  reactions**, led by *Add support for Jellyfin SyncPlay* at +65.
- The coverage of Plex's removal pointed readers at **Jellyfin's SyncPlay as the replacement**,
  which is the demand relocating rather than evaporating.
- Plex's own stated reason is that it did not survive a **client rewrite**.

**So the finding is a cost warning aimed exactly where we are weakest.** Watch Together is
per-client work ([D62](#d62--watch-together-is-a-first-class-feature-and-the-per-client-surface-is-six-methods)
names six methods per client), and
[D28](#d28--keep-the-exit-from-react-native-cheap-and-designate-the-fallbacks) contemplates
precisely the client rewrite that killed it at Plex. Two consequences:

- **The six-method surface is now a hard budget, not a description.** If a client's Watch
  Together support cannot be carried through a rewrite in those six methods, the design is
  wrong — because that is the exact failure that just happened to the largest player.
- **[D67](#d67--tvos-never-gates-a-feature)'s "tvOS never gates a feature" gains a sibling: a
  rewrite never drops one.** Whatever is first-class must be cheap enough per client to survive
  being rebuilt.

### 3. Plex killed Watch Later for lack of use — and our watchlist is the same feature

*"Costly to maintain and hard to justify when only a handful of folks used it."* Our watchlist
went into [play-state.md](../design/plans/play-state.md) from
[D140](#d140--five-gaps-the-sentiment-corpus-exposed-three-declines-and-one-that-undercuts-a-headline-claim)'s
sweep. Its demand in this corpus is **one issue and three reactions** — the lowest score of
anything we have actually committed to build.

**It stays, and it stays for a reason that is not demand:** as a *row* it is a bookmark nobody
uses, but as a **stored predicate over items** it is one row in a table D75 already needs, and
[D149](#d149--eight-gaps-the-source-sweep-found-six-declines-and-the-one-that-is-a-hole-in-the-business-model)'s
external list import needs the same storage. It is nearly free *because* it is not a feature.
**What it must never become is a surface with its own screens and sync semantics** — that is
what Plex paid to remove. Recorded so nobody later reads its presence as evidence it was
wanted.

### 4. Jellyfin removed the PIN — and the PIN is the loudest single request in the corpus

*PIN protection for users* is **+56 on `jellyfin-androidtv`, the highest single-issue score in
the whole 932-issue corpus**. Jellyfin **removed** its PIN (`EasyPassword`) in 10.9 as *"a big
security risk especially for administrator accounts."*

Both are right, and the resolution is in the distinction they collapsed:

- **A PIN is not an authentication factor.** Jellyfin's was a *short password* that could log
  an administrator in, and four digits guarding a server is indefensible.
- **What people are asking for is a profile selector** — the living-room problem of a child
  picking their parent's tile on a shared, already-trusted television. That is a *switch
  between already-admitted identities on an already-authenticated device*, which is the
  same object as [D130](#d130--a-role-is-a-named-policy-object-users-are-assigned-to-one-never-configured-individually)'s
  role and [D120](#d120--a-participant-is-a-person-devices-attach-to-them-with-roles-and-the-cap-counts-people)'s
  person-plus-device.

**So: a PIN may gate a switch to a more-privileged profile on a device that is already
authenticated, and may never be a credential that authenticates a session, obtains a token, or
admits an administrator.** [parental-controls.md](../design/plans/parental-controls.md) carries
it, [threat-model.md](../design/plans/threat-model.md) carries the prohibition, and the
assertion is that no code path accepts a PIN as an authentication factor.

### 5. The companion that fills your gap is not a plan — it gets archived

Three of the field's most-installed companions are **archived**: `sct/overseerr` at 4,975★,
`9p4/jellyfin-plugin-sso` at **1,458★**, and `ConfusedPolarBear/Intro-Skipper` at 968★. The
live-TV-from-library idea has been rebuilt **three times** (pseudotv → dizqueTV → ErsatzTV) and
the M3U proxy twice (xTeVe → Threadfin).

Two conclusions, pointing in opposite directions and both true:

- **"A plugin exists" is not an answer to a gap.** The single most-starred authentication
  plugin in this field is unmaintained, which is the strongest available argument for
  SSO/OIDC/LDAP being in the core — where the roadmap already has it, now with a reason
  attached.
- **But the fork worked.** Jellyseerr is **2.5× Overseerr**; intro-skipper is 2.9× its archived
  predecessor. What made that possible was a **stable public API to build against**, which is
  [D20](#d20--plugin-architecture-constraints-and-four-things-the-catalogue-says-belong-in-the-core)'s
  seam and [D108](#d108--the-interface-is-not-ours-to-change-out-from-under-people-and-an-old-client-stays-installable)'s
  promise. Our obligation to the ecosystem is not to build the companions; it is to be the
  thing a dead companion's successor can be rebuilt against.

### And the reason this axis is worth keeping

**Emby's public repository has not moved since 2018-09-19.** Eight years of a product's
development are invisible from source, and we have been reading it as though it were current.
Every claim in this tree derived from the Emby repository is a claim about the fork point — a
statement of what Jellyfin inherited, not of what Emby is. Stated here because it is the kind
of quiet error that survives many readings.

**Status:** the withdrawals are documented from primary announcements and archived-repository
metadata. What is *not* measured is how many users each withdrawal actually affected — Plex
gave a percentage only for plugins.

---

## D151 — Withdrawn: notifications. A media server has nothing you are waiting for, and its UI is the notification

**Decided** (2026-09-21). **Withdraws item 2 of
[D149](#d149--eight-gaps-the-source-sweep-found-six-declines-and-the-one-that-is-a-hole-in-the-business-model)
and deletes `notifications.md`.** From the project owner, one day after it was written:

> *"I'm not sure I understand the appeal. Is this sending notifications to outside systems when
> things like new content are added? Who would be the consumer of these, and what is the
> utility? I could imagine maybe sending an update to clients about new content being
> available, but they could just as easily find out from the 'what's new' section of the
> UI."*

That is correct, and re-reading my own corpus says so plainly.

### The numbers I had, read properly

| | title hits | reactions |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Notifications / webhooks, **across the ten video server and client repos** | **5** | **8** |
| …of which actually about *sending* a notification | **1** — *Feature Request: Notification for added media* | **+3** |
| …the other four | Android **media-control** notifications in the shade — a different feature I mis-bucketed | 5 |
| New device / login alert / session security | **0** | **0** |
| Server down / unreachable / health check | 1, and it is an **IPv6 install bug** | 12 |
| Home automation / Home Assistant / MQTT | **0** | **0** |

Eight reactions, in the corpus where subtitles score 479. **It is close to the least-wanted
thing in the whole sweep**, and I listed it second.

### Where the demand actually is, and why that settles it

The 243 reactions notifications draw across all twenty-one repositories are **concentrated
almost entirely in the request and acquisition tools** — Overseerr *Allow users to subscribe to
TV episodes or Movie notifications* **+92**, *Custom notification support* **+53**, *Ntfy
Notifications* +11; Sonarr *Templates for Notifications* +20, *Download Decision Webhook* +7.

That is not a coincidence and it is the general rule the question exposed:

> **A notification is worth sending when the user is waiting on an asynchronous outcome they
> cannot see.** Sonarr, Radarr and Overseerr all have one — *you asked for a film that does not
> exist yet, and one day it will.* **A media server has no such outcome.** It serves what is
> already there, so every state change it could announce is already a row on a screen the user
> opens anyway.

Which is exactly the objection: *"they could just as easily find out from the 'what's new'
section."* The correct place for "new content" is
[D134](#d134--a-pending-item-discloses-nothing-a-rule-shows-its-coverage-and-the-home-page-computes-nothing)'s
maintained home-page value, which already exists and already costs nothing.

**And note it is the declined feature that has the demand.** Requests are
[D140](#d140--five-gaps-the-sentiment-corpus-exposed-three-declines-and-one-that-undercuts-a-headline-claim)'s
companion-app territory — so the notification demand sits downstream of a thing we deliberately
do not build, and belongs to whoever builds it against
[D20](#d20--plugin-architecture-constraints-and-four-things-the-catalogue-says-belong-in-the-core)'s
public API.

### The three triggers I claimed were operational, checked individually

- **Concurrent-stream ceiling hit** — I argued a household cannot tell a policy refusal from an
  outage. It can: [D92](#d92--a-failed-rendition-falls-to-the-next-one-and-the-client-remembers-the-server-still-has-no-device-database)
  already requires a refusal to name itself **at the point of refusal, to the person
  refused**, which is better than a message to the owner an hour later.
- **New device authenticated** — **zero demand**, and the control is a device list with
  revocation, which [threat-model.md](../design/plans/threat-model.md) already owns. An alert
  you read on Tuesday is not a security control.
- **Buffering** — an aggregate, and [observability.md](../design/plans/observability.md)
  already exposes it. One stall is not an event worth waking somebody for.

### The one residue, and our own architecture forbids it

> ~~**"Is my server reachable from outside?"** is the only question a UI genuinely cannot
> answer … the only component of ours positioned outside the house is the relay, and D72
> deliberately gives it no accounts and no data, so it holds no address to reach the owner at.
> **The single notification worth sending is the one D72 forbids.**~~
>
> **Wrong, and corrected the same day by
> [D152](#d152--reachability-is-three-questions-with-three-observers-and-all-three-are-already-in-place).**
> There is no blind spot: **the core holds the dial-out**
> ([D71](#d71--one-relay-artefact-three-jobs-and-the-core-dials-out-to-it)), so a dropped relay
> connection is a *local* fact needing no messenger; the relay reports its own view to the core
> like every other role ([D73](#d73--each-component-reports-according-to-its-own-visibility-blind-is-not-opaque));
> and only a client traverses the whole path, so the end-to-end check is a client action. I
> repeated the exact conflation D73 exists to correct — *no account to notify* is not *nothing
> to say* — one decision after citing D73 elsewhere. **The exception is withdrawn too**, which
> makes this decision's withdrawal complete rather than hedged.

### The method error, because it will recur

I read a **rich surface as demand**. Tautulli's 22 triggers × 28 delivery agents *look* like an
enormous feature, and a large surface in source means only that somebody built a lot, not that
anybody wanted it. The sweep's own §1 warns about exactly this and I did not apply it.

**And I double-counted.** I attributed Tautulli's **6,589★** to the statistics gap *and* used
its trigger list as the evidence for notifications. Tautulli's own README calls it
*"monitoring, analytics and notifications"* and lists notifications **third of twelve**
features. The honest artefact for notifications alone is **`jellyfin-plugin-webhook` at 251★**
— against intro-skipper 2,788, sso 1,458, home-sections 513, mergeversions 442 in the same
catalogue. Mid-table, not a core gap.

**The statistics finding is unaffected and survives** — it never rested on the trigger list, and
Jellystat's 2,472★ is an independent artefact for it.

**Status:** withdrawn. `notifications.md` is deleted rather than archived because it was never
designed — there is nothing to archive, and this entry is the record.

---

## D152 — Reachability is three questions with three observers, and all three are already in place

**Decided** (2026-09-21). **Corrects the residue
[D151](#d151--withdrawn-notifications-a-media-server-has-nothing-you-are-waiting-for-and-its-ui-is-the-notification)
left behind**, which claimed a blind spot that does not exist. From the project owner:

> *"If we want to know if we're reachable, the relay will know. If the connection between the
> relay and the core doesn't work, the core can find out easily. If we want to test the whole
> pipeline, the client app can do it."*

All three are right, and together they dissolve the problem rather than solve it.

### The error in D151

D151 kept one residue — *"is my server reachable from outside"* — and called it a genuine
tension with [D72](#d72--the-hosted-relay-has-no-free-tier-holds-no-data-and-has-no-accounts),
on the grounds that the only component outside the house is the relay and the relay holds no
address to reach the owner at.

**That is the same category error
[D73](#d73--each-component-reports-according-to-its-own-visibility-blind-is-not-opaque) was
written to correct**, made one decision after citing D73 elsewhere. D73 opens by saying of
D72: *"That conflated two different things and got the conclusion backwards"* — blindness is
about **custody**, not **sight**. D151 conflated a second pair the same way: the relay having
**no account to notify** is not the relay having **nothing to say**. It reports to the core,
as every role does.

And the framing was wrong before that even mattered, because **nobody needs to be told**.

### Three questions, and each already has an observer in the right place

| Question | Who knows, and how | Already decided by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Is the core connected to the relay?** | **the core** — it holds the dial-out socket, so a drop is a *local* fact needing no messenger | [D71](#d71--one-relay-artefact-three-jobs-and-the-core-dials-out-to-it), and [D37](#d37--the-core-judges-liveness-from-observation-not-from-a-node-declared-interval)'s rule that liveness is judged from observation |
| **Is the relay itself healthy and serving?** | **the relay** — throughput, connection state, RTT per leg, drops, error codes — reported to the core over the channel it already has | [D73](#d73--each-component-reports-according-to-its-own-visibility-blind-is-not-opaque), [D34](#d34--a-node-status-record-that-distinguishes-dead-from-wedged-from-idle) |
| **Does the whole path work end to end?** | **a client** — the only thing that traverses client → relay → core → node → bytes | [D73](#d73--each-component-reports-according-to-its-own-visibility-blind-is-not-opaque)'s client vantage, piped through the relay |

That is D73's own table, which already existed, applied to a question I failed to recognise as
the one it answers. **There is no blind spot and no tension with D72.** The information already
flows the right way; the only thing missing was noticing.

### What follows: the useful output is the hop, not the alarm

The person who discovers an outage is **someone holding a client, trying to watch something**.
They do not need an alert — they are already looking. What they need is **which hop failed**,
because each one has a different remedy and only one of them is theirs:

| What the client can distinguish | What the user should do |
| --- | --- |
| no network at all | fix your wifi |
| relay unreachable | nothing — it is ours, and saying so stops a support request |
| relay up, core not dialled in | the server at home is off or has lost its uplink |
| core up, media node unreachable | the NAS is asleep or gone ([D34](#d34--a-node-status-record-that-distinguishes-dead-from-wedged-from-idle)'s dead-versus-wedged, surfaced) |

This is [principles §3](../principles/03-explain-the-decision.md) and
[D92](#d92--a-failed-rendition-falls-to-the-next-one-and-the-client-remembers-the-server-still-has-no-device-database)'s
*a refusal names itself*, extended one step: **a connection failure names its hop too.** "Can't
connect" is the message every competitor ships and it is the one that generates the support
request; four sentences instead of one is the entire fix, and three of them end the
conversation.

### The one thing to build, and it is small

**On reconnect, the relay hands the core what it saw during the gap** — the count of connection
attempts and the window they fell in. Not who: counts and times, so
[D72](#d72--the-hosted-relay-has-no-free-tier-holds-no-data-and-has-no-accounts) is untouched
and there is still nothing to subpoena.

That turns *"was I unreachable last Tuesday?"* from a guess into a row in the core's own log,
and it is the shape
[D40](#d40--error-and-skip-records-and-why-the-error-record-carries-the-completeness-scope)
already established: **the record of a failure carries the scope of what was missed.** A gap
with no observations is ambiguous between "nothing happened" and "I was not there"; a gap
annotated on reconnect is not.

### And this is why D151's withdrawal was right rather than merely defensible

D151 withdrew notifications and kept one exception, which is the shape a bad decision usually
takes. **The exception is gone too**, and for a better reason than the original: not *"the
demand is small"* but *"the observation already exists, at the component best placed to make
it, and the person who cares is already holding a screen."* Nothing is pushed anywhere,
`observability.md` needs no push half, and the relay stays accountless.

**Status:** corrects D151's residue; adds one relay behaviour (gap annotation on reconnect) and
one client requirement (name the failing hop), both recorded in
[remote-access.md](../design/plans/remote-access.md).

---

## D153 — A ranked feature register, ordered by demand and annotated by retrofit cost, because those are different numbers

**Decided** (2026-09-21). From the project owner, closing the sweep:

> *"Some are essential to a working product, while others can definitely be deferred (possibly
> indefinitely). **The only thing I care about is that these features are kept in mind while
> designing the architecture so that it's possible to add them.** Let's keep a ranking of the
> features according to how essential and impactful they are … I may want to adjust this list
> or even remove things."*

Two different things were asked for and the second is the load-bearing one. A ranking answers
*what to build first*. **"Possible to add them" is not a ranking question at all** — it is a
question about which decisions foreclose which futures, and the answer does not correlate with
demand. So the register carries **two independent axes**, and the architecture only has to read
one of them.

### The two axes

- **Rank** — how essential, which is the ranking asked for: 0 no product without it · 1 its
  absence reads as broken · 2 deferred but owed something now · 3 deferred and free ·
  4 declined. Called *rank* rather than *tier* because this tree already has plugin tiers
  ([D15](#d15--two-plugin-tiers-in-process-wasm-and-out-of-process-adapters)) and corpus tiers
  ([D109](#d109--five-corpus-tiers-and-nobody-has-to-download-media-to-run-the-suite)), and
  they are unrelated.
- **Retrofit cost** — **free** (additive) · **seam** (needs an extension point) · **schema**
  (needs a migration) · **invariant** (needs a rule not to have been assumed) · **protocol**
  (breaks [D108](#d108--the-interface-is-not-ours-to-change-out-from-under-people-and-an-old-client-stays-installable)).

**They are uncorrelated, and that is the finding.** *Shuffle* has universal adoption and costs
nothing to add in year three. *An item must not be required to have a File* protects **live
TV — which we have declined** — and is unrecoverable once assumed. Ranking alone would have
put effort on the first and nothing on the second, and the second is the one that becomes
impossible.

### Ten obligations, which is the actual deliverable

The whole register distils to ten things the architecture must keep true, and they are the
list to read a design against rather than the 86 rows above them:

an item need not have a File · Collection membership is **three** kinds, not two · a rating is
`(source, kind, score, votes, as_of)` with critic ≠ audience · a content descriptor carries a
score **and a sign** · the track model is not exactly three axes · the playback role is
protocol-agnostic rather than Cast-shaped · the client **fetches** its home layout · playback
rate is shared session state or explicitly local, decided rather than discovered · a PIN never
authenticates and the session model never assumes one factor · Watch Together costs **six
methods per client, as a budget**.

Plus one that pays for three rows at once: **[D81](#d81--play-state-is-an-append-only-event-log-plus-a-guarded-position-and-positions-are-edition-relative)'s
play-event log is retained, not truncated.**

### A decline records what keeps its door open

The declined table has a fourth column for *what would make this possible again*. That is not
politeness. **Live TV is declined and still constrains the schema**; DLNA is declined and its
door is [D15](#d15--two-plugin-tiers-in-process-wasm-and-out-of-process-adapters)'s adapter
tier, already built for other reasons; poster overlays are declined as *baked images* and
remain possible as a client render. Without the column, a decline reads as a demolition and
somebody eventually assumes the opposite is safe.

### Where it lives, and the one rule that stops it rotting

[`docs/FEATURES.md`](../../FEATURES.md), beside `ROADMAP.md`, because it is the owner's
document rather than a finding. Four documents now answer four questions — **when**
(`ROADMAP.md`), **how** (`plans/`), **why** (this log), **whether and how much**
(`FEATURES.md`) — and a fourth index is a real rot risk, so:

**a row links to a decision and never restates it; where they disagree the decision wins.**
Every row carries a stable `F`-number so one can be struck without renumbering the rest, and
the tiers are explicitly a preference the owner may change at any time — unlike everything
else in this tree, that file is not evidence.

**And the general rule is now [principles §12](../principles/12-defer-the-work-never-the-seam.md) — *defer the work,
never the seam*** — because the failure it prevents is silent: keeping an invariant open looks
like doing nothing, costs nothing, and is the only kind of work that becomes impossible.

**Status:** the register is complete as of the 2026-09-21 sweep
([feature-sweep-2026-09-21.md](../design/research/feature-sweep-2026-09-21.md)) and is expected
to be edited. The **obligations** are the part that should be treated as binding, and each
needs to be checked against `library-model.md` before it freezes.

## D154 — One grant table, opaque and revocable; the session credential never appears in a URL

**Decided** (2026-09-21). Research: [token-model.md](../design/research/token-model.md).
**Closes [threat-model.md](../design/plans/threat-model.md)'s oldest open question**, carried
since 2026-09-18, which [D93](#d93--device-pairing-is-rfc-8628-shaped),
[D104](working-notes-archive.md#d104--a-watch-together-invite-is-a-capability-url-scoped-to-one-edition-the-group-is-never-a-grant),
[D105](#d105--a-protocol-adapter-acts-as-the-user-never-as-itself),
[D107](#d107--the-node-channel-is-mutually-authenticated-and-a-nodes-roots-are-local-and-never-remotely-settable)
and [D125](#d125--access-is-role-based-with-two-roles-a-watch-together-guest-is-not-a-principal)
all say they inherit, and which [auth.md](../design/plans/auth.md) says it settles the
principals but not their credentials. **`auth.md` is Phase 1**, so this was the most blocking
unanswered question in the tree.

### 1. One primitive, not ten

Ten things need a credential — an interactive session, a paired television, a stream URL, a
cast receiver, a Watch Together join link, a download lease, an API key for the `*arr` stack,
a protocol adapter, a media node, a relay. The temptation is ten mechanisms.

**They are one row.** What differs is scope, lifetime and who may revoke — *policy* — not
cryptography.

```
grant(hash, kind, subject, scope, issued_at, expires_at, last_seen, revoked_at, label, device_id)
```

- **Opaque and random**: 256 bits from a CSPRNG. Not a JWT, not signed, carrying nothing.
- **Hashed at rest** — SHA-256, and we look up *by the hash*, never storing or comparing the
  secret. **Jellyfin stores its tokens in plaintext**, so a single database read compromises
  every session in the household; ours yields nothing usable. A slow KDF (bcrypt, argon2) is
  the wrong tool and worth saying so: those defend a *low-entropy, guessable* secret, and there
  is nothing to guess in 256 random bits.
- **`kind` is a closed enum** and `scope` is drawn from a closed vocabulary — reusing
  [D130](#d130--a-role-is-a-named-policy-object-users-are-assigned-to-one-never-configured-individually)'s
  capability enum, plus a resource reference where the kind needs one. This is
  [D21](#d21--a-fixed-named-output-menu-negotiated-by-a-prioritised-client-list)'s rule again:
  **a fixed named set, never a grammar of conditions.** Jellyfin's `ApiKey` row is
  `(Id, DateCreated, DateLastActivity, Name, AccessToken)` — **no scope column exists**, which
  is why an API key there is admin-equivalent by construction.

**Measured, and it decides the shape** ([token-model.md](../design/research/token-model.md)):
an opaque token verifies in **4.23 µs** at 100,000 rows on the slower pure-Go driver, against
an authenticated request rate of about **5/second**. A signed token verifies in 0.57 µs *if
it is never revoked*, **4.61 µs if it is** — and **Ed25519 costs 32.6 µs**, making the
"so a relay can verify locally" argument the most expensive option on the list.
[D117](#d117--the-session-link-is-the-grant-revocation-is-the-control-and-the-creator-owns-what-plays)
and [D119](#d119--a-join-link-admits-membership-is-what-persists-rotation-is-seamless-ejection-is-owner-only-and-a-cap-bounds-the-leak)
already make **revocation the control**, so the signed token's only advantage was never
available to us. **Opaque wins on its merits, not by default.**

**And it protects [D108](#d108--the-interface-is-not-ours-to-change-out-from-under-people-and-an-old-client-stays-installable).**
A JWT's claims become a de-facto public contract the moment one client parses them. An opaque
string cannot be parsed, so its internals stay ours to change forever.

### 2. The rule that closes the Jellyfin bug: no credential in a URL

**The session credential never appears in a URL — not as a query parameter, not in a path, not
on any endpoint, ever.** Jellyfin accepts `?ApiKey=` and `?api_key=`
(`AuthorizationContext.cs:105,110`), which is precisely how *Copy Stream URL* hands out a
permanent admin-equivalent credential.

It turns out almost nothing forces a URL-borne credential:

| Surface | Carries the credential how |
| --- | --- |
| API calls, hls.js, ExoPlayer, AVPlayer, libmpv | an **`Authorization` header** |
| `<video>` with native HLS on Safari/iOS, `<img>` posters | a **cookie** — `Secure`, `HttpOnly`, `SameSite`, and **scoped to the media paths only** |
| Our Cast receiver — it is our own web app ([D124](#d124--the-playback-role-may-be-a-cast-receiver-and-for-a-guest-that-is-the-best-path-the-phone-controls-it-does-not-relay)) | **`LoadRequestData.credentials`** plus a request filter |
| A URL the user deliberately exports to VLC or mpv | **a `link` grant, minted on purpose** |

**The cookie/header split is the load-bearing detail.** The cookie is valid *only* on the byte
paths — `/stream`, `/image` — and never on the API, which takes the header and nothing else.
So the CSRF question answers itself: the only thing a forged cross-site request can do with
the cookie is fetch media the user was already entitled to fetch, by `GET`, changing nothing.
**Bytes take a cookie; the API takes a header.**

And the one irreducible case is **not a leak, it is a feature**: *"play via external player"*
is a **+63** request ([tv-client.md](../design/plans/tv-client.md), F59). A URL you meant to
export gets a grant minted for the purpose — one item, one rendition, minutes — so the thing
that is a vulnerability in Jellyfin is a supported action here.

### 3. The kinds, their scope and their lifetime

The rule across all of them: **the broader the scope, the more deliberate the act that creates
it; the narrower the scope, the shorter it lives.** No kind is both broad and casually minted.

| `kind` | Subject | Scope | Lifetime | Revoked by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `session` | a user + a device | the user's role, entire | **no absolute expiry; idle expiry on `last_seen`** | the user, any admin, or signing the device out |
| `link` | a user | **one item, one rendition** | minutes | expiry, or revoking the parent session |
| `cast` | a user + a receiver | one cast session's queue | the cast session ([D135](#d135--casting-on-your-own-is-a-device-delegation-not-an-invitation-the-credential-is-the-session-and-the-queue-is-next-up)) | the sender, or session end |
| `join` | **nobody — a guest is not a principal** ([D125](#d125--access-is-role-based-with-two-roles-a-watch-together-guest-is-not-a-principal)) | one Watch Together session | the session | rotation, ejection, cap ([D119](#d119--a-join-link-admits-membership-is-what-persists-rotation-is-seamless-ejection-is-owner-only-and-a-cap-bounds-the-leak)) |
| `api_key` | a user | **an explicit capability subset** | none by default, optional expiry | the user or an admin |
| `adapter` | an adapter + a user | that user's role ([D105](#d105--a-protocol-adapter-acts-as-the-user-never-as-itself)) | idle expiry | removing the adapter, or the user |
| `node` | a machine | the node protocol only | long; enrolment is a deliberate act ([D107](#d107--the-node-channel-is-mutually-authenticated-and-a-nodes-roots-are-local-and-never-remotely-settable)) | un-enrolling the node |
| `relay` | a machine | **forward bytes for sessions the core named** | long | un-enrolling the relay |

**On session lifetime specifically**, because it is where products annoy people: an **idle
expiry, not an absolute one.** A television in the living room that signs itself out every
thirty days is the behaviour users describe as broken; `last_seen` plus a long idle window
gives the security benefit — an abandoned device stops working — without the one that costs
goodwill. It is revocable at any moment, which is the actual control.

**Refresh tokens do not exist here**, and the reason is worth recording so nobody adds them:
they exist to renew *unrevocable* access tokens silently. Ours are revocable and cost 4.2 µs
to check. Remove the reason, remove the mechanism — and with it a second credential class, a
rotation protocol and a race.

### 4. Three consequences for decisions that were waiting

- **[D93](#d93--device-pairing-is-rfc-8628-shaped) is complete.** RFC 8628 was *"shape only"*;
  the device-authorization flow now terminates in a `session` grant bound to that `device_id`,
  which is what makes *"sign this television out"* a single row update.
- **[D105](#d105--a-protocol-adapter-acts-as-the-user-never-as-itself)'s awkward case
  resolves without weakening anything.** A Jellyfin client expects a non-expiring
  `X-Emby-Token`; we do not want to issue one. **We do not have to**: the adapter owns the
  Jellyfin-shaped credential *on its own side* and holds an ordinary revocable `adapter` grant
  against the core. Their model's weakness stays inside the adapter, where it is
  independently revocable, which is exactly what *"acts as the user, never as itself"* is for.
- **[D87](#d87--a-download-is-a-rendition-plus-a-lease-and-it-is-self-contained)'s lease needs
  an honest sentence.** There is no DRM ([D3](#d3--streaming-format-cmaffmp4-segments-hls-manifest-no-drm)),
  so **nothing enforces a lease on a file already on a device.** The grant governs
  *acquisition, renewal and re-download* — which is real and worth having — and playback of
  bytes already downloaded is a client-side courtesy. Say so in the product rather than
  implying otherwise.

### 5. The last admin, and recovery

[auth.md](../design/plans/auth.md)'s two smaller open questions, answered together:
**`administer` is revocable by another admin, and the last holder of it is not removable or
demotable** — a household with no administrator is unrecoverable, and the check belongs next
to the role assignment rather than in the UI.

**And the recovery path is the filesystem**, which is
[D35](#d35--node-exchange-directory-progress-pair-config-generation-and-permissions-as-the-trust-boundary)'s
*"the permissions split is the security model"* applied to people: a one-shot `session` grant
with `administer`, minted by a command on the server host, written to a file only the server
user can read, single-use and expiring in minutes. Anyone who can run that already owns the
machine, so it grants nothing they did not have — which is the property that makes a recovery
path safe rather than a back door.

### 6. What this must never become

- **No credential in a URL.** The assertion is mechanical: no endpoint reads a token from a
  query string or a path segment, and a test asserts it for every route.
- **No unscoped grant kind.** Every kind names its scope in the table above; adding one
  without a scope is the Jellyfin `ApiKey` bug.
- **No plaintext storage**, and no logging of a secret — including in
  [bug-reports.md](../design/plans/bug-reports.md)'s fan-in, where a URL could otherwise carry
  one into a report.
- **The relay never mints and never reads.** [D72](#d72--the-hosted-relay-has-no-free-tier-holds-no-data-and-has-no-accounts)
  holds: the grant is opaque bytes it forwards, and its own `relay` grant permits forwarding
  and nothing else.

**Status:** settles the model. Unsettled and deliberately so: the **idle-expiry window** is a
number wanting a real household rather than a guess, and **whether a `node` grant is mTLS or a
shared enrolment secret** is [D107](#d107--the-node-channel-is-mutually-authenticated-and-a-nodes-roots-are-local-and-never-remotely-settable)'s
open choice, which this decision constrains only by requiring that the node's credential be a
row here like every other.

---

## D155 — EIDR checked against its own schema: the levels are right, the citation was a proposal, and Edition must be optional

**Decided** (2026-09-22). **Corrects the EIDR account in
[D79](#d79--four-levels-not-three-title--edition--version--file-with-collections-orthogonal)
and [library-model-review.md](../design/research/library-model-review.md), and changes one
thing in the model.** From the project owner: *"if EIDR does it that way, we're going to run
into fewer problems if we do that too?"*

The premise is right and worth acting on, so I read **EIDR's published XSDs**
(`schema.eidr.org` — `eidr-base.xsd`, `doiavs.xsd`, `common.xsd`) rather than the secondary
summary the earlier review used. Three findings, one of which changes the schema.

### 1. What we cited was a proposal, not the model

[D79](#d79--four-levels-not-three-title--edition--version--file-with-collections-orthogonal)
says EIDR *"models audiovisual works as Abstraction → Edit → Manifestation, plus Collection as
an orthogonal container"*, presented as *"a tree of four record types"*. **There is no such
tree in the schema.** From the XSDs:

| Field | Type | Values |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `StructuralType` | `doiavs:creationStructuralType` | **`Abstraction` `Performance` `Digital` `Physical` `Restricted`** |
| `ReferentType` | `eidr:referentType` | **`Series` `Podcast` `Season` `TV` `Movie` `Short` `Web` `Compilation` `Interactive Material` `Supplemental`** |

**"Edit", "Manifestation" and "Collection" are not record types.** They come from EIDR's own
**2018 nomenclature proposal**, which would add a `RecordType` element mapping `Edit ←
Performance`, `Manifestation ← Digital + Physical`, and `Collection ← Series, Season,
Compilation`. Our earlier review read that proposal as the shipped model.

**The substance survives**, which is why this is a correction and not a reversal: `isEditOf`
and `isManifestationOf` are **real, first-class members of a closed relationship enum** in the
shipped schema. The chain is genuinely there; it is expressed as edges rather than as levels.

### 2. The real shape is a flat record set with eleven typed edges — and we should not copy it

```xml
<xs:complexType name="relationshipInfoType">
  <!-- a relationship is described with
       "<Relationship type="eidr:isSeasonOf">assetDOI</Relationship>" -->
  <xs:extension base="eidr:assetDOIType">
    <xs:attribute name="type" type="eidr:relationshipType" use="required"/>
```

A relationship is literally **`(type, target DOI)`**, with `type` drawn from eleven values —
`isSeasonOf` `isEpisodeOf` `isEditOf` `isManifestationOf` `isClipOf` `isCompositeOf`
`isCompilationOf` `isPackagingOf` `isPromotionFor` `isSupplementTo` `isAlternateContentFor` —
and **the schema constrains nothing about what the target is.** EIDR is a typed edge list over
a flat record set, not a hierarchy.

**Adopting that shape would be a mistake here, for a reason that is about us and not about
EIDR.** EIDR is a **registry** where any party may register any record independently, so it
*cannot* assume a parent exists or that one organisation owns the chain. We are a **local
index of files on a disk**, where a File always has a parent we can see. A fixed tree buys
foreign keys, cascade semantics, cheap joins, and a query planner that knows the shape — and
[D75](#d75--one-predicate-language-three-bindings-a-typed-field-registry-is-the-schema-deliverable)'s
field registry **requires a level per field**
([D79](#d79--four-levels-not-three-title--edition--version--file-with-collections-orthogonal)
cross-cut 2), which a flat graph makes meaningless. *Same problem, different institution,
different right answer.*

### 3. The change: Edition is optional, because EIDR lets a Manifestation hang off an Abstraction

This is the finding worth having. Because EIDR's edges are unconstrained, **`isManifestationOf`
may point straight at an Abstraction** — a manifestation whose *edit is unknown*.

**Our tree cannot express that.** Every Version hangs off an Edition, so a file identified as
*Glass Runner* whose cut we cannot determine — **which is the ordinary case**, since most rips
carry no edition marker in the filename — needs a synthetic *"unknown edition"* row. Then
identification improves ([identification.md](../design/plans/identification.md) is built to be
replayable for exactly that reason) and we have to **merge** a real Edition into a fake one,
carrying watch state across, which
[D79](#d79--four-levels-not-three-title--edition--version--file-with-collections-orthogonal)
puts at the Edition. That is the same class of bug D79 was written to remove, one level up.

**So: a Version's parent is an Edition, or — when the edition is unknown — the Title
directly.** One nullable foreign key.

**And we already had the principle and failed to apply it here.**
[D131](#d131--a-restriction-is-a-vector-not-a-ceiling-templates-are-seeds-and-they-say-what-they-hid)
makes every content descriptor **tri-valued** because *"no violence descriptor" means unknown,
never none*; [D132](#d132--authoring-a-role-is-a-preview-loop-and-an-item-the-rules-cannot-judge-is-denied-not-shown)
refuses to judge an item whose fields are unknown; [play-state.md](../design/plans/play-state.md)
refuses to mark an item watched when its runtime is unknown. **Unknown is a first-class state
everywhere in this tree except in the one place where the structure itself is unknown.**
A synthetic row is the structural form of the same mistake.

Consequences, all small:
- ~~**Watch state stays at the Edition** … when the Edition is unknown, state attaches to the
  Title.~~ **Wrong, and corrected the same week by
  [D156](#d156--a-position-is-stored-at-the-version-and-resolved-at-the-edition-the-title-never-holds-one).**
  Four unidentified cuts of one film would put four positions on one Title row, and D79 had
  already said a Title cannot hold a position. **A position is stored on the Version and
  resolved over the Edition's Versions when an Edition exists** — which also means naming a
  cut later moves nothing at all.
- **Two Versions under the same Title with no Edition are not known to be the same viewing**,
  which is correct and is the honest answer rather than a guess.
- The UI never shows *"Unknown Edition"* as though it were a cut.

### 4. Two alignments worth taking, free

- **Use EIDR's relationship names for [D97](#d97--an-extra-is-a-typed-relation-not-an-edition-and-not-a-version)'s
  typed extras** rather than inventing a vocabulary: `isClipOf`, `isPromotionFor`,
  `isSupplementTo`, `isAlternateContentFor`, `isCompositeOf`, `isPackagingOf`. D97 already
  chose the *shape* EIDR uses — a typed relation rather than a level, arrived at
  independently — so taking the names costs nothing and buys interop if anyone ever maps us
  to a registry.
- **`isEditOf` chains in EIDR** — an Edit of an Edit, e.g. the broadcast-censored version of
  the extended cut. Noted, not adopted: it is one more nullable parent and the case is rare.
  Recorded so the option is visible rather than rediscovered.

### 5. And one place where following EIDR would be a regression

`episodeInfoType` carries a single `Parent` and a single `SequenceInfo` (`minOccurs="0"`, so
`maxOccurs` defaults to **1**). **EIDR can express exactly one episode ordering.**
[D96](#d96--an-episodes-position-is-ordering-season-number-and-a-series-declares-its-orderings)
gives us `(ordering, season, number)` with several orderings per episode — aired, DVD,
absolute — because anime makes it unavoidable.

**We are deliberately ahead of EIDR here**, and this is recorded so that a later reading of
"align with EIDR" does not undo it. *An identifier registry needs one canonical sequence; a
player needs the sequence its user expects.*

**Status:** the model change (optional Edition) is schema and therefore **Phase 1**, due before
[library-model.md](../design/plans/library-model.md) freezes. The relationship-vocabulary
alignment is a naming choice with no migration. Read from the XSDs at `schema.eidr.org`, cached
at `/yoloai/cache/http/eidr/`; the 2018 nomenclature proposal is known only through EIDR's own
summary of it, since the document itself is no longer served.

---

## D156 — A position is stored at the Version and resolved at the Edition; the Title never holds one

> **Superseded 2026-09-22 by [D157](#d157--a-position-belongs-to-the-file-completion-rolls-up-the-position-never-does).**
> The diagnosis below is right and the fix did not go far enough. Resolving a position *over an
> Edition's Versions* still assumes they share a timeline — and **PAL speedup alone makes them
> differ by 4.27%, which is 98 seconds at the forty-minute mark**. The position belongs to the
> **File**; completion rolls up and the position never does. §"the machine groups, the human
> names" and the speech-map measurements below stand, demoted from load-bearing to advisory.

**Decided** (2026-09-22). **Corrects
[D155](#d155--eidr-checked-against-its-own-schema-the-levels-are-right-the-citation-was-a-proposal-and-edition-must-be-optional)
§3 and the watch-state half of
[D79](#d79--four-levels-not-three-title--edition--version--file-with-collections-orthogonal).**
Found by the project owner's worked example:

> *"if I have Glass Runner San Diego sneak preview, american theatrical release, international
> theatrical release, and director's cut but we didn't manage to figure out which cuts they
> were at ingestion, then they would all show up in the UI as an unknown cut, and if later the
> user specifies which as which, it doesn't affect existing view data, right?"*

**Four Editionless Versions under one Title breaks D155**, and the example is chosen well
enough to break it twice.

### The bug: four positions, one row

D155 said *"watch state attaches to the Edition when there is one and to the Title when there
is not."* That survives one unidentified Version and collapses on four: **all four positions
land on the same Title row and overwrite each other.** Watch forty minutes of the theatrical,
then ten of the director's cut, and the first is gone.

Worse, **D79 already said why that cannot work** — *"Not Title — the theatrical and director's
cuts have different runtimes, so a resume position across them is meaningless"* — and D155
contradicted it one paragraph after citing it. The Editionless case is not an exception to that
rule; it is the rule's own example, with the labels missing.

### The fix: store where you observed, resolve where you have evidence

**A position is stored on the Version.** Resume resolves at **the coarsest level there is
evidence is the same content**:

| What is known | Resume resolves over |
| --- | --- |
| the Version's Edition is known | **all Versions of that Edition** — most recent position wins |
| no Edition | **that Version alone** |
| — | **never the Title** |

This preserves D79's actual requirement — *"upgrading 1080p to 4K must not lose your place"* —
because two encodings of one cut share an Edition and therefore share a resume. It costs
nothing, because when the Edition *is* known, Edition-relative and Version-relative timelines
are the same timeline; that is what an Edition means.

**And it is [D59](#d59--a-node-publishes-a-snapshot-plus-a-journal-it-observes-it-does-not-interpret)'s
cross-cut, which D79 itself states and I failed to apply**: *store the observation, not the
interpretation.* A position is an observation about a Version. "These two Versions are one
viewing" is an interpretation, and interpretations belong at read time where they can be
revised.

### So: does labelling disturb existing view data? No — there is nothing to move

That is the answer to the second half of the question, and the fix makes it structural rather
than careful. **Naming a cut writes one column — `edition_id` on the Version. No position row
is touched.** What changes is only which positions are considered interchangeable when resume
next resolves.

- **Label all four differently** — the case in the question — and **nothing happens at all**.
  Each Version already had its own position and keeps it. Four cuts, four resumes, before and
  after.
- **Label two the same** (the 1080p and the 4K of one cut, each already watched) and resume
  now has two candidates: **the most recent wins, and neither is deleted.** The other remains
  that Version's own position, and [D81](#d81--play-state-is-an-append-only-event-log-plus-a-guarded-position-and-positions-are-edition-relative)'s
  event log holds the history regardless.
- **Mislabel, then correct it** — again nothing moves.

A design where the answer is *"we migrate it carefully"* is a design with a migration to get
wrong. This one has no migration.

### The UI half: four unknown cuts are four items, not one with a quality menu

The other half of the question — *"they would all show up as an unknown cut"* — is right about
the facts and points at a presentation bug.

**Versions sharing an Edition are interchangeable encodings** and belong behind one entry with
a quality menu. **Versions with no Edition are not known to be interchangeable**, so rendering
them as a quality menu tells the user that four different films are four bitrates of one. They
are **separate playable entries under the Title**, distinguished by what was actually observed
— runtime, resolution, container, and the verbatim filename
[D59](#d59--a-node-publishes-a-snapshot-plus-a-journal-it-observes-it-does-not-interpret)
already requires us to keep.

**Never a row called "Unknown Edition".** That names a cut that does not exist and implies the
four are one thing. The absence of a label is shown as an absence — with, per
[D133](#d133--the-pending-items-alert-which-is-how-the-queue-actually-drains)'s pattern, a
maintained count for the admin: *"4 versions of Glass Runner have unidentified cuts."*

### Why the obvious heuristic is unsafe, using the example given

Runtime looks like it should separate these. It does not, and *this particular film* is the
counter-example:

| Cut | Runtime |
| --- | --- |
| Workprint | 113 min |
| **San Diego Sneak Preview** | **115 min** |
| **US theatrical (Domestic)** | **116 min** *(some references say 117)* |
| **International theatrical** | **117 min** |
| **Director's Cut** | **116 min** |
| Final Cut | 117 min |

**The US theatrical and the Director's Cut are the same length** and are the two most different
films in the set — voice-over against none, studio ending against none, no unicorn against
unicorn. The International cut and the Final Cut collide too. And the reference sources
**disagree with each other** about which runtime belongs to which cut. Runtime is not an
identifier; it is a hint that fails exactly where it is needed.

### What *can* group them, and it is already on disk

[D148](#d148--the-speech-map-is-a-scan-artefact-and-the-reference-is-a-subtitle-track-before-it-is-audio)'s
**speech map** — 1–3 kB per Version, built for subtitle verification — answers the grouping
question directly, because a cut that adds a voice-over or removes a scene changes *where
people are speaking*. Measured, scoring synthetic variants against a real map with the same
normalised correlation the subtitle verifier uses:

| Candidate | r (ToS) | r (Sintel) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| **same cut, re-encoded** | **1.000** | **1.000** |
| same cut, one 60 s scene removed | 0.593 | 0.708 |
| same cut, three scenes removed | 0.363 | 0.700 |
| voice-over added to 30% of pauses | 0.413 | 0.191 |
| voice-over added to 60% of pauses | 0.281 | 0.193 |
| **a different film** (control) | **0.100** | **0.115** |

**The identical cut scores exactly 1.000 and nothing else comes close** — so *"these two
Versions are the same cut"* is answerable with certainty, which is the whole grouping question.
Everything that is a different cut lands in a broad 0.19–0.71 band: enough to say **"not the
same"**, and **nowhere near enough to say which cut it is.**

That is the right division of labour and it should be stated as a rule: **the machine groups,
the human names.** The scanner may *propose* that two Editionless Versions be merged under one
Edition when their speech maps match at 1.0 — [D132](#d132--authoring-a-role-is-a-preview-loop-and-an-item-the-rules-cannot-judge-is-denied-not-shown)'s
preview loop, showing what would change — and must never propose a *name* for a cut, because
nothing it can measure carries one.

**Status:** schema, and therefore Phase 1 with the rest of
[library-model.md](../design/plans/library-model.md). The 1.000 threshold is measured on
synthetic variants of two real films; what is unmeasured is **two genuinely different masters
of the same cut** — a remaster with different room tone could plausibly score below 1.0, and
the merge proposal should be tested against that before it is trusted.

## D157 — A position belongs to the File. Completion rolls up; the position never does

**Decided** (2026-09-22). **Supersedes
[D156](#d156--a-position-is-stored-at-the-version-and-resolved-at-the-edition-the-title-never-holds-one),
and overturns the watch-state half of
[D79](#d79--four-levels-not-three-title--edition--version--file-with-collections-orthogonal)
and [D81](#d81--play-state-is-an-append-only-event-log-plus-a-guarded-position-and-positions-are-edition-relative).**
From the project owner:

> *"I wonder if maybe we're trying to do too much here? … what if an edition was ripped from a
> DVD and included some extra studio intro in the now flat video? Also, if there's a 1080 and
> 4k version of the same cut, can we assume that the person really wants to just continue
> watching from the place they left off on the 1080 one…? Maybe we just tie view position to
> the file?"*

Yes. Three objections, and the middle one is fatal to the design as it stood.

### 1. "Same Edition" does not imply "same timeline", and this tree already proves it

D79's founding fixture was *"upgrading 1080p to 4K must not lose your place"*, which assumes
two Versions of one Edition share a timeline. **In a library of rips they routinely do not.**
The baked-in studio ident is one instance and the mild one. The severe one is **PAL speedup**,
and we know the number cold because
[D147](#d147--a-subtitle-is-chosen-by-measurement-not-by-filename-and-the-correction-runs-before-the-choice)'s
entire subtitle design is built on it: **25/23.976 = 4.27%**.

A 116-minute cut on a PAL transfer runs **111 minutes 15 seconds**, and the error is a *rate*,
not an offset:

| Position on the NTSC copy | Same moment on the PAL copy | Drift |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 10:00 | 9:35 | 25 s |
| 40:00 | 38:22 | **98 s** |
| 70:00 | 67:08 | 172 s |
| 100:00 | 95:54 | **246 s** |

**No offset transfers a position across that pair**, and there is nothing wrong with either
file — both are honest copies of the same cut. Add the studio ident, telecine pulldown, a
different part split and a stray black frame, and the premise is simply false for the
libraries this product exists to serve.

**And the refutation was already in the tree, in the adjacent bullet.**
[D82](#d82--media-segments-are-typed-attach-at-the-version-and-carry-provenance) puts media
segments at the Version and [library-model.md](../design/plans/library-model.md) gives the
reason in the line directly below the one about positions: *"a timecode indexes an encoding:
a 4K remux and a web-dl differ in lead-in, and a **PAL-speedup rip differs throughout**."*
Segments were placed correctly for exactly the reason positions were placed wrongly, two
lines apart, and nobody noticed. **That is what
[principles §13](../principles/13-state-attaches-to-what-you-observed.md) is for** — the rule is easy to state and easy to
violate while quoting it.

### 2. The scenario it buys is rare, and it is the user's call anyway

Even where the timelines *do* match, the question is a good one: having watched forty minutes
in 1080p and then acquired a 4K copy for a new screen, does anyone want to resume at 40:00 —
or to start again and actually see it? **We do not know, and it is not ours to decide.**
[principles §3](../principles/03-explain-the-decision.md) says explain the decision to the user; silently
seeking forty minutes into a film somebody bought a television for is the opposite.

And the case is *rare*: acquiring a better copy **during** a viewing is an uncommon event in a
narrow window. We were paying a schema-wide unsound assumption for it.

### 3. So: the position is stored on the File, and nothing else holds one

**A File is the only object in the model with an unambiguous timeline.** A Title has none. An
Edition has none — it is a *cut*, an editorial fact, not a duration. A Version has one only by
concatenating its parts. A File has exactly one, always, by construction.

It is also **the observation**
([D59](#d59--a-node-publishes-a-snapshot-plus-a-journal-it-observes-it-does-not-interpret)):
the player knows precisely one thing — *which file, and what timestamp*. Everything above that
is a conclusion, and conclusions must not own the user's data.

Three things get *simpler*, not just safer:

- **Multi-part stops needing arithmetic.** [D81](#d81--play-state-is-an-append-only-event-log-plus-a-guarded-position-and-positions-are-edition-relative)
  invented Edition-relative positions *because* of multi-part — *"12:30 into part 2 is not an
  Edition-level position"*. At the File, **"12:30 into part 2" simply is the position.** The
  part arithmetic moves to *display*, where it is done once, on read, and can be wrong without
  corrupting anything.
- **It is cheaper on the path that is hot.** Progress writes are every ~10 s
  ([D81](#d81--play-state-is-an-append-only-event-log-plus-a-guarded-position-and-positions-are-edition-relative),
  measured at ~2/s for a household); resumes are rare. A File position needs **no arithmetic
  at write time**.
- **The guarded row becomes `(user, file)`**, which is what the client was reporting all along.

### 4. What we keep: completion rolls up, because it has no timeline

This is the split D79 half-noticed and then did not act on — it said *"whether a watched flag
rolls up is a UI question; a resume position cannot roll up regardless"*, and then attached
both to the Edition.

- **A position is a fact about a timeline** → the File. Never rolls up.
- **Completion is a fact about the work** → rolls up freely. Finish the 1080p and the 4K shows
  as watched, the Edition shows as watched, the Title shows as watched. **No timeline is
  involved, so nothing can be wrong.**

That keeps the part of cross-version state people actually notice — *"have I seen this?"* —
and drops the part that cannot be made correct.

~~**And where continuation is genuinely wanted, offer it.** *"You're 40 minutes into the 1080p
version"* next to the 4K, as an explicit labelled choice.~~ **Withdrawn the same day by
[D158](#d158--we-group-files-for-browsing-and-never-relate-their-timelines-the-continuation-offer-is-withdrawn)**:
the hint is wrong in ordinary cases — it quotes a number that is 98 seconds out on a PAL pair,
it points at a **broken rip** as the place you left off, and on a hand-edited cut it invents a
correspondence only the user could know. Each file shows **its own** progress and the user
scrolls, which is one drag and always correct.

### 5. The payoff, and it is the answer to the first objection

*"Teasing out editions is already hard enough."* It is — and with positions at the File,
**it stops mattering.** The Edition becomes a **labelling and grouping concept with no runtime
semantics**:

| If we get the Edition wrong | Before | Now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Two cuts merged under one Edition | **positions collide and overwrite** | a misleading group in the UI |
| One cut split across two Editions | resume lost on switch | a duplicate entry |
| Relabelling it later | a migration carrying state | **one column, no state moves** |

**A hard inference stops propagating its difficulty into data the user cannot afford to
lose.** That is the right response to a problem we cannot fully solve: not to solve it harder,
but to remove what depends on it.

[D156](#d156--a-position-is-stored-at-the-version-and-resolved-at-the-edition-the-title-never-holds-one)'s
**speech-map grouping survives and is demoted** — it is still the honest way to propose *"these
two Versions are the same cut"* (measured at r = 1.000, and nothing else close), but it now
suggests a label rather than deciding where somebody's place in a film is kept. That is the
right job for a measurement with a threshold.

### What this gives up, stated plainly

Automatic resume across two encodings of one cut, and — after
[D158](#d158--we-group-files-for-browsing-and-never-relate-their-timelines-the-continuation-offer-is-withdrawn)
— any hint about it either. Each file shows its own progress; the user looks and scrolls.
That is the whole cost.

**And [principles §13](../principles/13-state-attaches-to-what-you-observed.md) generalises it**, because this is the second
time in three days the same mistake shipped — [D155](#d155--eidr-checked-against-its-own-schema-the-levels-are-right-the-citation-was-a-proposal-and-edition-must-be-optional)
put a position on the Title, [D156](#d156--a-position-is-stored-at-the-version-and-resolved-at-the-edition-the-title-never-holds-one)
moved it to an inferred Edition, and both were caught by someone describing an ordinary
library rather than by review.

**Status:** schema, Phase 1. Supersedes D156 and amends D79, D81 and
[play-state.md](../design/plans/play-state.md). Unmeasured and not worth measuring first: how
often two Versions of one Edition genuinely share a timeline — the point is that we no longer
need to know.

---

## D158 — We group files for browsing and never relate their timelines; the continuation offer is withdrawn

**Decided** (2026-09-22). **Withdraws the cross-version continuation offer added by
[D157](#d157--a-position-belongs-to-the-file-completion-rolls-up-the-position-never-does)**,
and states the general rule the last three corrections have been circling. From the project
owner:

> *"I think even putting the machinery to offer continuation is too much. It's no big deal for
> the user to look at where the 1080p version sits in playback and then scroll to the same
> position in the 4k edition. We also have issues with bad rips … Making assumptions and
> trying to fix is the wrong shape."*

### The trade, stated honestly, goes the other way

| | The user scrolls | We offer a hint |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Effort | one drag, once, rarely | a query, a UI element, a number |
| Correct? | **always** — they can see the picture | **often**, and confidently wrong in ordinary cases |

D157 kept the offer because it looked nearly free. It is not nearly free, because **a hint
that is sometimes wrong costs more than no hint** — the user must now evaluate it, and the
cases where it misleads are exactly the cases where they are already confused.

**Three ordinary situations, and two of them are the owner's:**

- **The PAL or studio-ident pair.** The hint says *"40 minutes into the 1080p"*; on the other
  file that moment is at 38:22. We hand over a number we already know is wrong by up to four
  minutes ([D157](#d157--a-position-belongs-to-the-file-completion-rolls-up-the-position-never-does)).
- **The bad rip.** *"The user gets 61 minutes in and suddenly the rip is broken, so the user
  tries ripping with a different app."* The offer now points at a **broken file** as the place
  you left off. The one thing the user is certain about — that file is rubbish — is the one
  thing our hint does not know.
- **The self-made cut.** *"I have the Wings extended edition but I HATE the early LV-426
  scenes … so I manually deleted them."* Two files whose timelines differ by an amount **only
  the user knows**, on a cut that exists in no database anywhere. Any correspondence we offer
  is invented.

**So it is withdrawn entirely**, and nothing replaces it. What remains is not a feature: each
file **shows its own progress**, which is simply not hiding the state we already hold, and is
what makes the owner's remedy — look, then scroll — possible.

### The rule, and a test for it

> **We group files for browsing. We never relate their timelines.**

The test is mechanical: **if a feature needs to know that a moment in file A corresponds to a
moment in file B, it is out of scope.** Grouping for presentation is cheap and its failures
are cosmetic; correspondence is expensive and its failures move or misstate the user's data.

**Multi-part is the only crossing, and it is not an inference.** The parts of one Version are
*declared* by that Version's ordering and their timelines are **concatenated, not
corresponded** — there is no claim that 12:30 in part 2 means anything in part 1. The rule
holds.

### Two things the examples say we owe

**1. A user-authored Edition is first-class, and identification never overwrites it.**
A hand-edited *Wings* is a cut matching no release, no runtime and no provider record. The
user may create an Edition and name it, that name is **their data**, and a rescan or a
metadata refresh must not correct it. The machinery exists and was written for exactly this
shape — [D141](#d141--we-write-nfo-too-and-the-lock-markers-are-the-part-that-matters)'s lock
markers, [D98](#d98--a-sidecar-carries-what-is-true-about-the-work-the-database-carries-what-is-true-about-a-person)'s
sidecar/database split, and [D7](#d7--the-files-are-the-source-of-truth-the-database-is-a-rebuildable-index)'s
rule that a full rescan must not destroy user-authored data. It simply had not been said about
**Editions**, and this is where it would have been discovered.

**2. A changed content hash is a new timeline, so the position does not carry.**
[D116](#d116--the-content-hash-is-a-sampling-hash-whole-file-hashing-is-opt-in-and-separate)'s
sampling hash answers *"is this the same file I saw before"*. Edit the file in place and the
answer is no — **and the position is discarded rather than carried, because the place it named
no longer exists.** That is the correct behaviour and it needs stating, because carrying it
forward would silently point somewhere wrong. The remedy is the owner's own: scroll.

### What the examples confirm is already right

Worth recording, because the same examples that killed a feature validate three others:

- **Subtitle verification survives a cut that exists nowhere.**
  [D147](#d147--a-subtitle-is-chosen-by-measurement-not-by-filename-and-the-correction-runs-before-the-choice)
  aligns against **the file's own audio**, so the hand-edited *Wings* still gets correct
  subtitles from its embedded track — and a *downloaded* one is **correctly refused**, scoring
  low because its timings genuinely do not match a cut the uploader never saw. Both outcomes
  are right, and no filename- or metadata-driven approach can produce either.
- **Speech map, media segments and loudness are all per-Version**
  ([D148](#d148--the-speech-map-is-a-scan-artefact-and-the-reference-is-a-subtitle-track-before-it-is-audio),
  [D82](#d82--media-segments-are-typed-attach-at-the-version-and-carry-provenance),
  [D83](#d83--loudness-is-measured-at-scan-and-applied-as-gain-downmix-has-one-default-and-a-dialogue-control-drc-is-per-device)),
  so every derived value describes **the file the user has**, not the film the database thinks
  it is.
- **Nothing is keyed on the Edition**
  ([D157](#d157--a-position-belongs-to-the-file-completion-rolls-up-the-position-never-does)),
  so being unable to identify a home-made cut costs exactly nothing.

### The pattern worth naming

**Three corrections in three days on one subject, each one subtraction.**
[D155](#d155--eidr-checked-against-its-own-schema-the-levels-are-right-the-citation-was-a-proposal-and-edition-must-be-optional)
moved a position to the Title,
[D156](#d156--a-position-is-stored-at-the-version-and-resolved-at-the-edition-the-title-never-holds-one)
to an inferred Edition,
[D157](#d157--a-position-belongs-to-the-file-completion-rolls-up-the-position-never-does)
to the File while keeping a hint, and this one removes the hint. Every round the design got
*smaller* and more correct, and every round the error was found by someone describing an
ordinary library rather than by review.

**The bias is worth stating so it can be watched for: faced with an inference we could not
make reliably, the instinct was repeatedly to make it cleverer rather than to make it
load-bearing for less.** [principles §2](../principles/02-the-users-files.md) now carries the general
form — the user's *arrangement* of their files is no more ours to correct than the bytes are.

**Status:** removes a feature; no schema change. The assertions in
[testing-strategy.md](../design/plans/testing-strategy.md) gain the negative case — **no
surface offers a position from one file against another** — because a withdrawn feature with
no test is a feature somebody re-adds.
