## D159 — D96 holds under the new lens, and reaches three things it did not: the ordering choice is a preference, an ordering may be authored, and a multi-episode file is a boundary

**Decided** (2026-09-22). Read at the project owner's suggestion that
[D96](#d96--an-episodes-position-is-ordering-season-number-and-a-series-declares-its-orderings)
*"feels like it touches on similar ideas"* to
[D157](#d157--a-position-belongs-to-the-file-completion-rolls-up-the-position-never-does)
and [D158](#d158--we-group-files-for-browsing-and-never-relate-their-timelines-the-continuation-offer-is-withdrawn).
It does, and the first finding is that **D96 already got the part the last four decisions kept
getting wrong.**

### Why D96 survives, and what that shows

An episode carrying `(aired, S01E05)` **and** `(dvd, S01E03)` looks like the correspondence
[D158](#d158--we-group-files-for-browsing-and-never-relate-their-timelines-the-continuation-offer-is-withdrawn)
forbids. It is not. Those are **two labels on one entity**, not a claim that a *moment* in one
file maps to a moment in another — and under
[D157](#d157--a-position-belongs-to-the-file-completion-rolls-up-the-position-never-does) the
position lives on the File, so **switching ordering moves nothing**: Next Up is a query, not a
stored value.

**D96 put the structure in a relation and left the user's state alone**, which is precisely
what [principles §13](../principles/13-state-attaches-to-what-you-observed.md) was extracted from D155–D158 to say. Worth
recording as the counter-example: the same author got this right in September and then got the
film version of it wrong three times running. The difference is that D96 was reasoning about
*coordinates* and D79 was reasoning about *containers*, and a container invites you to hang
things off it.

### 1. The open question closes on a table that already exists

D96's status: *"Whether the ordering choice is per series or per `(user, series)` is open — per
user is strictly more capable and the extra column is trivial, so the argument against it is
UI, not storage."*

**Neither — it is a preference**, and [D24](#d24--language-is-a-preference-axis-and-track-selections-stick-to-the-series)
already provides the table with **user, library and series** scopes. So:

| | Who owns it | Where it lives |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **which orderings exist** for this series | the providers — a fact about the work | one row per ordering, on the series |
| **which ordering I watch in** | the user | a [D24](#d24--language-is-a-preference-axis-and-track-selections-stick-to-the-series) preference at series scope |

That is the D157 split a third time: **the fact is stored where it was observed, the choice
belongs to the person, and neither owns the other.** It also answers D96's own objection —
there is no extra column *anywhere*, so the UI argument is the only one left, and two people
watching one anime in different orders costs nothing.

### 2. An ordering may be authored by a person, and a refresh never overwrites it

[D158](#d158--we-group-files-for-browsing-and-never-relate-their-timelines-the-continuation-offer-is-withdrawn)
made a **user-created Edition** first-class. The television analogue is a **user-created
ordering**, and D96 does not contemplate one — it lists *"aired, DVD, absolute and a
provider's alternate orders"*, all provider-sourced.

But **an ordering is an ordering whether TheTVDB supplied it or a person did.** Same table,
different provenance, and [D141](#d141--we-write-nfo-too-and-the-lock-markers-are-the-part-that-matters)'s
lock markers already say a refresh must not overwrite a human's answer. A household that
places a special between two episodes, or defines its own run through a series, has authored
one.

**And one distinction has to hold**, because the best-known example crosses it:

- An **ordering** is a coordinate system over **one series' episodes** — aired, DVD, absolute,
  or a person's.
- A watch order **spanning works** is an **ordered Collection**. The *Machete order* for Star
  Wars — **IV, V, II, III, VI**, omitting Episode I so that the prequels play as a flashback
  after the Vader reveal — is six films, not one series' episodes.

[D79](#d79--four-levels-not-three-title--edition--version--file-with-collections-orthogonal)
says *"a Collection is either an explicit member list or a predicate"* and **never says the
list is ordered.** It must be, and the Machete order shows why the ordering must also be
**partial**: it omits a member. D96 already got that right for episodes — *"an episode has one
position per ordering **it appears in**"* — and the Collection needs the same sentence.

### 3. A multi-episode file is a boundary, not a row — and it is missing entirely

**`multi-episode` appears nowhere in this tree.** Zero occurrences across 86 documents. It is
ordinary: anime and older television rips ship `S01E01-E02.mkv` constantly.

It is [D157](#d157--a-position-belongs-to-the-file-completion-rolls-up-the-position-never-does)
inverted, and the answer falls out of the same rule:

| | Shape | Position |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **multi-part** | one work across N files | on the File; parts **concatenated** for display |
| **multi-episode** | **N works in one file** | **one position; the episode boundary is a timecode inside that file** |

A timecode inside one file is not a correspondence between files, so
[D158](#d158--we-group-files-for-browsing-and-never-relate-their-timelines-the-continuation-offer-is-withdrawn)
is untouched — and it is exactly what
[D82](#d82--media-segments-are-typed-attach-at-the-version-and-carry-provenance) already
models. **Add `episode_boundary` to the segment type enum**: a seventh type in a table that has
six, with the same provenance and the same user override.

Then **"have I finished the first episode?" is derived** from the position against the
boundary and never stored — [principles §13](../principles/13-state-attaches-to-what-you-observed.md) — with the payoff that
follows: **if the boundary is wrong the position is still right**, and fixing the boundary
fixes the derived completion immediately. Nothing moves.

Two things fall out for free:

- **The detector already exists.** A mid-file episode boundary sits right after an `outro`,
  which [media-segments.md](../design/plans/media-segments.md) already detects and already
  uses to place the next-episode prompt.
- **"Next episode" becomes a seek, not a load** — no re-open, no re-buffer, and the
  next-episode prompt works mid-file where every incumbent shows one episode and stops.

### 4. And the thing not to build, in the same spirit

**Do not infer which ordering someone is watching in.** Watching S01E05 then S01E03 might be
DVD order, or might be somebody skipping about. Offering to switch their ordering on the
strength of it is the *"making assumptions and trying to fix"* shape
[D158](#d158--we-group-files-for-browsing-and-never-relate-their-timelines-the-continuation-offer-is-withdrawn)
just removed. **An ordering is chosen, never detected.** It is one setting, visible, on the
series.

### What must be asserted

- **Switching ordering moves no stored state**; Next Up recomputes and every position is
  byte-identical afterwards.
- **A user-authored ordering survives a full rescan and a provider refresh**, name included.
- **A multi-episode file holds one position**, and per-episode completion is derived from the
  boundary rather than stored.
- **Two files claiming the same episode keep separate positions**, and nothing bridges them —
  [D158](#d158--we-group-files-for-browsing-and-never-relate-their-timelines-the-continuation-offer-is-withdrawn)
  restated for television, because the film wording will not be found by someone reading the
  series code.

**Status:** schema, Phase 1 — the ordered-and-partial Collection and the `episode_boundary`
segment type both land in [library-model.md](../design/plans/library-model.md). The preference
resolution adds nothing. Unmeasured: how often multi-episode files actually occur in a real
library, which decides whether boundary detection is worth scheduling early or is a later
pass.

---

## D160 — There is no "series" concept: a sequence is what a Collection produces, and Next Up is a query over any of them

**Decided** (2026-09-22). **Generalises
[D159](#d159--d96-holds-under-the-new-lens-and-reaches-three-things-it-did-not-the-ordering-choice-is-a-preference-an-ordering-may-be-authored-and-a-multi-episode-file-is-a-boundary)'s
ordered Collection from a Metropolis curiosity into the ordinary case.** From the project
owner:

> *"It feels like we should have some kind of 'series'-like ordering for movies as well, and
> not just for the same movie series (Friday the 13th 1,2,3,4,5…) but also a mix (think wings
> and unknown franchise) … And even for tv series, someone might want to lump together
> Three's a Houseful and Three's a Crowd. Or Gruelstone with Lockfast."*

Right, and it is wider still: **the distinction between "a series" and "an ordered collection"
does not survive contact with those examples, and removing it deletes code rather than adding
any.**

### The four examples, and what each demands

| Example | Members | What it needs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *Friday the 13th* 1–5… | Titles | an ordered sequence of films |
| *Wing* + *Unknown* + the crossovers | Titles from **several franchises** | a sequence whose membership no provider will supply |
| *Three's Company* → *Three's a Crowd* | **two series** | a Collection **containing Collections** |
| *Gruelstone* → *Lockfast* | two series | the same |

The third and fourth are the load-bearing ones. *"Lump together Three's Company and Three's a
Crowd"* is not a list of episodes — it is **one thing made of two series**, and it has to stay
correct as new episodes are ripped. A flattened list of episodes authored once would not.

### So: one concept, and the series stops being special

> **A Collection produces a sequence. Next Up, progress and the binge affordances are queries
> over a sequence. Nothing asks whether the members are episodes or films.**

[play-state.md](../design/plans/play-state.md) currently defines Next Up as *"the earliest
unwatched **episode** after the latest completed one"*. **Delete the word "episode".** That is
the whole change to the query, and it is what makes a superfan's eleven-film run behave like a
season — not because we added a feature, but because we stopped having two.

Four things make it true, and three of them are already there:

1. **Members may be Titles or other Collections.** Required by *Three's Company + Three's a
   Crowd*. Flatten depth-first at read time; a nested Collection contributes its own ordered
   members. **The nesting composes for free**: [D159](#d159--d96-holds-under-the-new-lens-and-reaches-three-things-it-did-not-the-ordering-choice-is-a-preference-an-ordering-may-be-authored-and-a-multi-episode-file-is-a-boundary)
   made the ordering choice a [D24](#d24--language-is-a-preference-axis-and-track-selections-stick-to-the-series)
   preference at **series scope**, so somebody who watches *Three's Company* in DVD order gets
   DVD order inside the composed run too, without the composition knowing anything about it.
2. **A Collection may not contain itself, transitively.** One check at write time. Dull, and
   omitted it becomes an infinite flatten in a page render.
3. **Explicit means an authored order; a predicate means a sort.** This completes
   [D79](#d79--four-levels-not-three-title--edition--version--file-with-collections-orthogonal)'s
   *"explicit member list or a predicate"*, which never said what a predicate's sequence is.
   **And the predicate is the better answer to the owner's first example**: `franchise =
   Friday the 13th` sorted by release date **picks up part 12 the day it is ripped**, where a
   hand-ordered list silently would not. Hand-authoring is for the orders a rule cannot
   express — Machete, or a contested Wing/Unknown chronology.
4. **Progress is already free.** Completion rolls up
   ([D157](#d157--a-position-belongs-to-the-file-completion-rolls-up-the-position-never-does)),
   so *"3 of 11"* across a composed run is a count, and the run appears in Continue Watching
   for the same reason a series does.

### The apparent contradiction about seasons, resolved

[library-model.md](../design/plans/library-model.md) lists **season** as a Collection, and
[D96](#d96--an-episodes-position-is-ordering-season-number-and-a-series-declares-its-orderings)
makes `season` a component of the coordinate. That reads as redundancy and is not:

- **The season-as-Collection** is the browsable object — it has a name, artwork and a page.
- **The `season` in `(ordering, season, number)`** is a coordinate **within an ordering**, and
  it has to be, because *an episode's season can differ between orderings*: absolute numbering
  flattens season splits away entirely, and a DVD order can move an episode across a boundary.

One is a thing you look at; the other is where an episode sits in a particular reading. Both
are needed.

### What not to build, by the now-usual rule

- **Do not infer a franchise.** A provider collection (TMDB's `belongs_to_collection`) is a
  fine *source*, on exactly [D159](#d159--d96-holds-under-the-new-lens-and-reaches-three-things-it-did-not-the-ordering-choice-is-a-preference-an-ordering-may-be-authored-and-a-multi-episode-file-is-a-boundary)'s
  terms: a provider may supply one, a user may author one, they are the same row with
  different provenance, and **a refresh never overwrites the user's**
  ([D141](#d141--we-write-nfo-too-and-the-lock-markers-are-the-part-that-matters)).
- **Do not guess a cross-franchise order.** Where *Wing vs. Unknown* sits relative to
  *Alien³* is contested fan territory and not a fact. **Release date is the default sort
  because it is an observation**; anything else is authored.
- **Do not detect a binge.** Watching three *Friday the 13th* films in a row does not earn an
  offer to create a collection. Same shape as
  [D158](#d158--we-group-files-for-browsing-and-never-relate-their-timelines-the-continuation-offer-is-withdrawn).

### Why this is a deletion

Every incumbent has two systems: a series with seasons, episodes, Next Up and continue-watching,
and a *collection* that is a static grid of posters with none of it. That split is why nobody
can binge a franchise, and it exists because the series machinery was built first and the
collection was bolted beside it.

**We have not built either yet**, so the cost of having one is negative: one members table with
a position, one flatten, one Next Up query. A series is simply the Collection whose members are
the episodes of one work — which is what
[D79](#d79--four-levels-not-three-title--edition--version--file-with-collections-orthogonal)
said in September and what everything since has quietly treated as a special case anyway.

**Status:** schema, Phase 1 — self-referencing membership with a position, and the cycle check.
The Next Up generalisation is a deletion in [play-state.md](../design/plans/play-state.md).

> **Measured 2026-09-22**, and **the worry was aimed at the wrong thing.** The largest
> realistic collection is *every Star Wren in order* — **963 episodes across 52 seasons and 13
> series, plus 13 films**, so ~976 members and not the "thousands" written above.
>
> | at 976 members | computed | maintained |
> | --- | ---: | ---: |
> | flatten the sequence (recursive CTE) | **1.2–1.7 ms** | — |
> | Next Up | **14.8 ms** | **0.23 ms** |
> | progress (*n* of *N*) | 12.3 ms | — |
> | progress + Next Up as one row | — | **0.01 ms** |
> | materialise the sequence | — | 2.3 ms, once, on change |
>
> **Nesting is free**: the nested shape (66 collections, depth 4) and the flat one (1
> collection) flatten in the same time, so *"how deep does nesting go"* was never the
> variable. **The cost is the completion join**, and it is super-linear — 14.8 ms at 976
> members becomes 124 ms at 2,900.
>
> So the boundary is exactly where [D134](#d134--a-pending-item-discloses-nothing-a-rule-shows-its-coverage-and-the-home-page-computes-nothing)
> already put it, and nothing new is needed: **a collection's own page computes** (15 ms,
> inside `performance-targets.md`'s 50 ms), and **the home page reads a maintained row**
> (0.01 ms), because Continue Watching showing *"247 of 963"* is precisely the shape
> [principles §11](../principles/11-hot-path-values-are-cached.md) exists for. Harness:
> `/yoloai/cache/bench/collections/`.

---

## D161 — Cache and invalidate; do not incrementally maintain. A missed invalidation is stale, a missed update is wrong

**Decided** (2026-09-22). **Sharpens [principles §11](../principles/11-hot-path-values-are-cached.md)** and the
mechanism in [D134](#d134--a-pending-item-discloses-nothing-a-rule-shows-its-coverage-and-the-home-page-computes-nothing).
From the project owner:

> *"even if it were a performance issue, it costs little to cache the render of the data,
> contingent upon a scan changing the landscape."*

§11 has said *"maintained, not computed"* since 2026-09-21, and **"maintained" quietly implied
the wrong implementation** — including against the instruction it was derived from, which said
*"queries that can easily be **cached**"*. The word was right the first time and I changed it. Maintaining a value means updating it incrementally as things
happen; caching it means computing it lazily and throwing it away when something relevant
changes. They perform identically on read and differ completely when they break.

### The asymmetry that decides it

| | Cost of a miss | Cost of a bug |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Cache + invalidate** | one recompute — **43.6 ms**, once | a **stale** number until the next event, or a needless recompute |
| **Incremental maintenance** | — | a **wrong** number, permanently, with nothing to notice it |

Incremental maintenance requires enumerating *every* path that can change the value. The
pending-items count alone moves on a scan, a rule edit, a role edit, a tag edit, a
re-identification and a removal. **Miss one and a child's library silently stops growing** —
which is the exact failure [D132](#d132--authoring-a-role-is-a-preview-loop-and-an-item-the-rules-cannot-judge-is-denied-not-shown)
and [D134](#d134--a-pending-item-discloses-nothing-a-rule-shows-its-coverage-and-the-home-page-computes-nothing)
exist to prevent, reintroduced by the optimisation meant to serve them.

**Caching cannot drift.** The worst a wrong invalidation rule produces is a value that is
briefly old or an occasional 43 ms. And the invalidation signal already exists:
[D166](#d166--the-journal-is-an-accelerator-never-a-dependency-the-server-may-always-answer-with-state-and-that-is-the-ordinary-path-rather-than-the-error-path)'s change journal
says exactly what changed, which is the owner's *"contingent upon a scan changing the
landscape"*.

### So "maintained" splits into three mechanisms, and only one of them was ever intended

| Mechanism | When | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Cached result** — compute lazily, keep, drop on a known event | **the default** | recently added, the pending count, a collection's sequence and progress |
| **Derived column** — computed at write time beside the row | when the query takes a *parameter*, so there is no single result to cache | FTS `bm25` rank, [D47](#d47--sort-order-is-a-materialised-cldr-sort-key-per-item-per-locale)'s sort keys |
| **Stored artefact** — bytes derived from bytes | the source is a file | the speech map, trickplay, artwork |

**Incremental counters are not on the list.** They are the one shape that can be silently
wrong, and nothing in this project needs them: every invalidating event here is *rare* — a
scan, a rule change, a metadata refresh, somebody finishing an episode — against reads that
are constant. That ratio is what makes recompute-on-miss free.

### And it makes the collection measurement a non-question

[D160](#d160--there-is-no-series-concept-a-sequence-is-what-a-collection-produces-and-next-up-is-a-query-over-any-of-them)'s
Star Wren case measured **14.8 ms computed** at 976 members against **0.01 ms** from a stored
row. Under a cache that is not a design decision at all: the first read after a scan pays
15 ms, every other read is a lookup, and **no code has to know how a scan changes a
sequence** — only that it might have.

The key spaces are small enough to make this uninteresting, which is the point: a collection's
sequence keys on `(collection, ordering)`, its progress on `(user, collection)`, the pending
count on `(role)`. A household has tens of users and hundreds of collections, not millions.

**Status:** mechanism guidance, no schema. §11 is revised; D134's *"maintained counter"*
should be read as *"cached result"* throughout. Unmeasured and deliberately so: the cache's
own storage, because at these key spaces it is not a number worth producing.

---

## D162 — Containment makes an extra, a name only types it; a provider's trailer URL is not one

**Decided** (2026-09-22). Closes the two items
[D97](#d97--an-extra-is-a-typed-relation-not-an-edition-and-not-a-version) left open —
discovery, and the not-on-disk trailer — and adds four the three days since D97 have exposed.
Read from `Emby.Naming/Common/NamingOptions.cs`, `CoreResolutionIgnoreRule.cs`,
`IgnorePatterns.cs` and `MovieResolver.cs` at `/yoloai/cache/repos/jellyfin/`.

D97's shape was right and is untouched: **an extra is a typed relation from a Title or an
Edition to a work.** What follows is who may assert one, on what evidence, and what happens
when the evidence is wrong.

### 1. The evidence is containment. A name may only *type* what containment already found

Jellyfin carries **34 extra rules across 12 types** — **15 directory names**, **3 filenames**
and **18 filename suffixes** — and applies them wherever a file turns up. That is the wrong
shape, because the two ways of being wrong are not symmetric:

| Mistake | Consequence |
| --- | --- |
| an extra listed as a film | **visible clutter**, one action to file |
| a film classified as an extra | **it vanishes from the library**, and nothing says so |

The second is [D132](#d132--authoring-a-role-is-a-preview-loop-and-an-item-the-rules-cannot-judge-is-denied-not-shown)'s
failure class exactly: an item silently absent, with no surface that says it was removed. So
the rule is the narrow one.

**Two admissible evidences, both requiring containment in a title's own folder:**

1. a subdirectory whose name is in the closed vocabulary — `trailers`, `featurettes`,
   `deleted scenes`, `behind the scenes`, `interviews`, `scenes`, `shorts`, `clips`,
   `backdrops`, `theme-music`, `extras`, `extra`, `other`;
2. a file whose stem is the title's own name plus a vocabulary suffix —
   `Glass Runner (1982)-trailer.mkv` — which is the Plex and Kodi convention and has to work.

**Nothing at a library root is ever an extra.** A library *of* short films has a `shorts/`
folder that means the opposite of the vocabulary. Jellyfin needs an explicit carve-out for
this — `CoreResolutionIgnoreRule` reads *"Don't ignore top level folders"* and tests
`parent is not UserRootFolder` — and with containment as the rule the carve-out is not needed,
because the condition was never met.

A suffix or a bare filename **never creates** an extra; inside a folder that already is one,
it picks the type. Absent a match, the type is `Unknown` — the relation still holds, which is
the same shape as [D155](#d155--eidr-checked-against-its-own-schema-the-levels-are-right-the-citation-was-a-proposal-and-edition-must-be-optional)'s
unnamed cut: *filed, not named.*

### 2. `Sample` is not a type. It is debris, and it is skipped

Jellyfin's own source contradicts itself here: `IgnorePatterns` skips `sample.mkv`,
`*.sample.mkv` and `sample/`, while `VideoExtraRules` carries **five** `ExtraType.Sample`
rules. So `x.sample.mkv` disappears and `x-sample.mkv` becomes a library item — same 30-second
torrent fragment, opposite outcomes, decided by a hyphen.

A sample is not an extra of the work. It is a fragment of the release, it is nobody's
intention, and treating it as an extra means hashing it, probing it, generating trickplay for
it and showing it. It belongs in [scanner.md](../design/plans/scanner.md)'s skip list beside
`.trash/`, where it is **reported as skipped** rather than silently dropped. Eleven types, not
twelve.

### 3. The scanner may attach an extra to a Title. Only a person may attach one to an Edition

D97 allows the relation to point at either, and said nothing about who may say which. Disk
layout cannot tell you: `Wings (1986)/deleted scenes/` sits above the theatrical cut and the
special edition both, and the scenes belong to one of them.

So the inference stops at the Title, and an Edition attachment is a human act — the same
division [D158](#d158--we-group-files-for-browsing-and-never-relate-their-timelines-the-continuation-offer-is-withdrawn)
drew for merging: **the machine groups, the human names.** It also inherits D155's property
that naming a cut later moves nothing: the extra was never on the Edition to begin with.

### 4. An inferred relation is an index; an asserted one is a sidecar

[D98](#d98--a-sidecar-carries-what-is-true-about-the-work-the-database-carries-what-is-true-about-a-person)'s
test decides this and D97 never applied it. *Is it true about the work or about a person?*

- A relation the scanner inferred from the tree is **rebuildable from the tree** — database
  only, like any other index ([D7](#d7--the-files-are-the-source-of-truth-the-database-is-a-rebuildable-index)).
- A relation, a type correction or an Edition attachment a **person** made is true about the
  work and is not recoverable from anything. It **mirrors to a sidecar**, exactly like an
  identification override.

### 5. An extra is not always a video, and the pass set follows the item

`ThemeSong` is audio — `MediaType.Audio` on 2 of Jellyfin's 34 rules — and the ten-pass
pipeline ([D102](#d102--the-nodes-work-is-a-pipeline-of-independently-deferrable-passes),
[D114](#d114--a-pass-costs-what-it-costs-because-of-one-thing-whether-it-decodes-video))
assumes video throughout: trickplay, poster derivation, segment detection and the speech map
are meaningless on a 90-second `.mp3`. The passes are already independently deferrable *per
library*; this makes the gate **per item, on its media kind**, which costs a column and a
predicate. Extras also sit at the bottom of D102's user-value ordering, where a 90-second
featurette belongs.

### 6. Three exclusions, each a one-line predicate and each a field bug if unsaid

- **Extras never enter Continue Watching or Next Up.** A trailer you paused is not something
  you are partway through. The *position* is still kept — positions are per-File under
  [D157](#d157--a-position-belongs-to-the-file-completion-rolls-up-the-position-never-does)
  and cost nothing — so a 50-minute making-of resumes when you open it.
- **Extras never count toward a Collection's sequence or progress**
  ([D160](#d160--there-is-no-series-concept-a-sequence-is-what-a-collection-produces-and-next-up-is-a-query-over-any-of-them)).
- **Watching an extra never marks the Title watched.** Completion rolls up over the *work's*
  own Versions, and an extra is a different work.

### 7. A provider's trailer URL is not an extra, and it is not a row

D97 guessed *"probably not"*. Settling it: **no**, and for a reason stronger than taste.

Every property the relation buys — subtitles, loudness, segments, play state, identity under
[D116](#d116--the-content-hash-is-a-sampling-hash-whole-file-hashing-is-opt-in-and-separate) — is defined over
**bytes a node observed**. A URL has none of them, so the row would be a work-shaped hole: no
Version, no File, no hash, nothing to scan, and nothing for
[D7](#d7--the-files-are-the-source-of-truth-the-database-is-a-rebuildable-index)'s rebuild to
recover it from, because it was never in the files.
[D99](#d99--the-core-does-not-decode-an-image-either-and-community-uploaded-artwork-is-why)
is not the precedent it looks like: a provider poster becomes **bytes we hold**, not a live
link to a third party during playback.

So a provider's trailer link is **metadata about the work** — a field, of the same kind as a
poster URL before it is fetched — and following it is opening a link, not playback. The door
stays open in [FEATURES.md](../../FEATURES.md) rather than in the schema.

**Status:** closes D97. §1–§4 are schema and stay in Phase 1 with it; §5 is a column and a
predicate; §6 is three predicates; §7 is a decline. Unmeasured: the per-file overhead of a
disc rip with fifteen extras, which multiplies item count without meaningfully adding runtime.

## D163 — Every observed file carries a filing with a reason, and "what did the scanner pass on?" is the library browser with the filter off

**Decided** (2026-09-22), prompted by the project owner:

> *"I've had many issues where the Plex scanner messed up and an extras subdir remained
> forever hidden from the UI. Make an admin UI where I can browse everything the scanner
> passed on, and tell the system what it actually is."*

[D162](#d162--containment-makes-an-extra-a-name-only-types-it-a-providers-trailer-url-is-not-one)
argued three days' worth of caution about *classifying* a film as an extra because it would
vanish. It never said where you go to see what vanished. This is that surface, and it is
larger than extras: **it is every reason a file the node can see is not in the library.**

### 1. The field's bug is not the misclassification. It is that the skip is a branch

Read from `/yoloai/cache/repos/jellyfin/`:

```csharp
// LibraryManager.cs:1006
public bool IgnoreFile(FileSystemMetadata file, BaseItem? parent)
    => EntityResolutionIgnoreRules.Any(r => r.ShouldIgnore(file, parent));

// LibraryManager.cs:1044
var fileList = files.Where(i => !IgnoreFile(i, parent)).ToList();
```

A **LINQ filter**. The excluded files are dropped from an enumerable; nothing is written,
nothing is queryable, and `Any()` discards *which rule fired*. `MovieResolver.cs:427` does the
same thing to an extras directory with a bare `continue;`.

**You cannot build "show me what was skipped" over a `continue` statement.** That is why every
incumbent's answer to "where did my file go?" is reading a log, and why the owner's extras
directory stayed hidden forever: no component was ever in a position to mention it. The defect
is architectural and it is upstream of every individual scanner bug.

### 2. We are already most of the way there, and nothing consumes it

[D40](#d40--error-and-skip-records-and-why-the-error-record-carries-the-completeness-scope)
gave the node's report a **`skip` record "carrying the rule that caused it"** and an **`error`
record carrying a closed `code` and a `scope`**. The reasons are already on the wire, already
structured, already per-path — and **no document in this tree reads them into anything a
person can open.** This decision is mostly plumbing that was specified and then not connected.

### 3. The shape: a filing is a stored value, and the library view is a predicate over it

**Every file the node enumerated gets exactly one `filing`**, from a closed set, with a reason:

| `filing` | Meaning | Reason carries | Set by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `listed` | in the library | — | core |
| `extra` | filed as an extra of another work ([D97](#d97--an-extra-is-a-typed-relation-not-an-edition-and-not-a-version), [D162](#d162--containment-makes-an-extra-a-name-only-types-it-a-providers-trailer-url-is-not-one)) | the owning work, the type, and which evidence matched | core |
| `skipped` | an ignore rule or extension filter fired | **the rule**, verbatim (D40) | node |
| `errored` | enumerated but unreadable or unprobeable | D40's `code` and `scope`, plus the raw platform text | node |
| `unidentified` | probed, no provider match | what was tried | core |

The default library listing is `filing = listed`. **"Show me everything the scanner passed
on" is `filing != listed`**, and "show me everything" is no predicate at all — which is the
owner's *"this should also extend to the top level scanned items"*, answered by removing a
clause rather than by building a second screen.

**This is complete by construction.** A file the node enumerated cannot fail to have a filing,
so a reason invented in 2027 appears in this view with no UI work — which is what *"skipped for
whatever reason"* actually requires. A bespoke "skipped items" page would cover the classes
somebody remembered on the day, and the owner's Plex directory is precisely a class somebody
did not remember.

**And it is the same browser.**
[D132](#d132--authoring-a-role-is-a-preview-loop-and-an-item-the-rules-cannot-judge-is-denied-not-shown)
already settled this argument for a different axis — *"one predicate compiler, one query, a
different principal"* — because a preview that does not share the enforcement path diverges
from it and is worse than none. Same here: one browser, one query, a different filter. The
grid, the sort, the search and the detail pane are the ones that already exist.

**Two axes, kept apart.** A `filing` is a fact about the *file in the library*; whether a given
person may see a listed item is a *policy* question answered by their role and D132's pending
state. The admin view turns off the first filter; "browse as this role" turns off the second.
Conflating them would put one household member's policy into a library-wide value, which is
[D98](#d98--a-sidecar-carries-what-is-true-about-the-work-the-database-carries-what-is-true-about-a-person)'s
line in a new place.

### 4. You have to be able to look inside a subtree we never walked

A skipped *directory* is the owner's actual case, and nothing is enumerated beneath it — so
there is nothing to browse. The view must therefore be able to ask the node to
**enumerate a skipped path on demand, changing no rule and writing no library rows**: a
read-only peek, an ordinary entry in
[D38](#d38--three-tier-state-reporting-and-an-ordered-command-list-in-the-config)'s command
vocabulary. Deciding before looking is the thing the field forces on you.

**Bounded to paths under a configured library root**, or it is an arbitrary-filesystem-read
primitive exposed over the API wearing an admin button ([threat-model.md](../design/plans/threat-model.md)).
Browsing the disk to *add* a root is a different feature and must not be reached through this
one.

### 5. Playing it is how you tell what it is, so playback must address a File

You cannot say what something is without watching ten seconds of it, and an unfiled file has
no Title, no Edition and possibly no probe. So:

- **the playback path must be addressable by File**, not only by a library item — an
  **invariant to keep true now**, since it is free today and a rewrite once every endpoint
  takes an item id;
- **opening one probes it on demand**, which is [D102](#d102--the-nodes-work-is-a-pipeline-of-independently-deferrable-passes)'s
  *"the user can jump the queue"* with a different trigger, not new machinery.

### 6. Fix the rule, not the item — because the complaint is never one file

An extras directory is twenty files. Triaging twenty rows one at a time is not a fix, and a
tool that offers only that will be abandoned at file three. So the view **groups by reason**,
and the group is the unit of action:

> `**/sample.???` skipped **47 files** in *Films* — *unskip all · stop applying this rule here · confirm*

Five actions, closed: **make it a work** (into the ordinary identify flow) · **file it as an
extra of X**, with a type · **keep ignoring it** · **stop applying this rule here** ·
**retry**, which exists only for `errored`, because a failure is not a decision and the share
that was down may be up.

### 7. Where a correction lives — D98's test, three answers

- *"This is the 1982 theatrical cut"* — about the **work** → **sidecar**, which
  [identification.md](../design/plans/identification.md) already says.
- *"This is not media; keep ignoring it"* — about the **file**, not about a person → **mirrored
  to disk** so it survives a rebuild and so somebody else's scanner honours it too
  ([D7](#d7--the-files-are-the-source-of-truth-the-database-is-a-rebuildable-index)). Jellyfin's
  `DotIgnoreIgnoreRule` reads a gitignore-style `.ignore` per directory and is the right prior
  art for the format.
- *"This rule should not apply in this library"* — **configuration** → database, and therefore
  backup-critical ([D77](#d77--back-up-with-vacuum-into-back-up-only-the-irreplaceable-and-test-the-restore)).

### 8. Unreadable is the *loud* case, and the reason has to name the fix

The owner's second case is a different animal from the extras directory:

> *"So many times I've copied over a media file, only for it to not show up in Jellyfin no
> matter how many times I rescan or restart. Later I discover it's because the file is owned
> by root. But I had no easy way to see that the program had skipped it, or why. Meanwhile I'm
> pulling my hair out trying to debug."*

An ignored file is a decision, and going to look for it is reasonable. **An unreadable file is
a failure, and the user does not know there is anything to look for** — which is why the loop
is *rescan, restart, rescan*. Four consequences, each cheap:

- **A scan that could not read something did not succeed.** The summary must say
  *"complete — 3 files could not be read"* and link to them.
  [D40](#d40--error-and-skip-records-and-why-the-error-record-carries-the-completeness-scope)'s
  trailer record already carries the counts; reporting a clean scan over a non-zero error count
  is the specific lie that produces the hair-pulling.
- **The reason must name the fix, not the errno.** `permission_denied` is where the field stops
  and it is not an answer. The answer is *"owned by `root:root`, mode `0600` — and this node
  runs as uid 998 (`mediasvc`)"*, which diagnoses itself. That needs **two additions**: D40's
  optional raw field carries **owner, group and mode**, and the report **header** carries the
  node's **effective uid and gid**. One field each, on records that already exist, and the gap
  they close is the entire distance between *denied* and **denied to whom**.
- **An error is durable and counted, not a log line.** The row carries **first seen** and
  **last seen**, so *"failed on 6 consecutive scans since Tuesday"* is on screen — which
  separates a share that blipped from a file that will never be read, and makes the user's
  repeated rescan *informative* instead of futile.
- **A library root is checked for readability when it is configured**, not first discovered at
  3 a.m. two scans later. It is one `stat` and an `open`, and it catches the most common setup
  mistake at the moment the person is still looking at the screen.

And the rule that must not bend: an unreadable file **exists**. D40 already forbids it from
contributing to a removal — *"present-but-unprobed, never absent"* — and the inventory view is
where that distinction finally becomes visible to a person rather than merely honoured by the
core.

### 9. The honest limit, stated so it is not discovered

A file under **no library root** was never observed and cannot appear here; that is
configuration, and the root list is itself on screen. Everything else is covered: an unreadable
subtree appears as an `errored` row with D40's `subtree` scope rather than as silence — which is
the whole reason that field exists — and a tree changed since the last walk is covered by
showing **when each library last completed one**
([observability.md](../design/plans/observability.md)).

**Status:** `filing` and its reason are **schema**, and Phase 1, because retrofitting a value
onto every file after the fact means a full re-scan to populate it. The peek command is node
work; the surface is [web-client.md](../design/plans/web-client.md); the grouped query is a
[rules-engine.md](../design/plans/rules-engine.md) predicate like any other. The capability is
on the role ([D130](#d130--a-role-is-a-named-policy-object-users-are-assigned-to-one-never-configured-individually)).
Unmeasured: the row count of a `filing != listed` query on a library with a large ignored
subtree, which is the only place this could be slow and is a
[D161](#d161--cache-and-invalidate-do-not-incrementally-maintain-a-missed-invalidation-is-stale-a-missed-update-is-wrong)
cache if it is.

## D164 — The predicate language stopped being a feature and became the query layer; a restricting rule must fail closed, and the complexity budget is one number

> **Refined by [D193](#d193--the-audits-proposals-are-accepted-the-node-does-all-media-work-prepare-is-the-one-path-besides-direct-play-the-machinery-is-cut-and-cut-as-design-freezes)** (2026-09-23): the compiler is **deferred** to the first authored or restricting rule. Cut A's pages are fixed sqlc queries plus one hand-written filter builder for search, which the compiler replaces rather than joins.

**Decided** (2026-09-22). Closes the three items
[plans/rules-engine.md](../design/plans/rules-engine.md) left open and one security gap that
only exists because two correct decisions were composed. Measured at
`/yoloai/cache/bench/rules3/` on SQLite **3.53.4** via `modernc.org/sqlite`, over a
**3,500-item library with 25 tags each — 86,751 tag rows** — with a **10,000 × 100 (986,709
rows)** headroom point.

### 1. The shape: three authored bindings, and the rest of the product

[D75](#d75--one-predicate-language-three-bindings-a-typed-field-registry-is-the-schema-deliverable)
said three bindings; the plan says five. Counting what actually compiles a predicate today:

| | Binding | Written by | Evaluated |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Authored** | smart playlist | a person | on read / journal |
| | smart collection | a person | same |
| | retention | a person | on a schedule |
| **Restricting** | share ([D76](#d76--a-share-is-a-grantee-plus-a-predicate-and-it-fails-closed)) | a person | **every access path** |
| | profile restriction ([D84](#d84--certifications-are-system-code-with-a-per-system-order-a-kids-profile-is-a-grantee-plus-a-predicate)) | a person | **every access path** |
| **Structural** | the library listing — `filing = listed` ([D163](#d163--every-observed-file-carries-a-filing-with-a-reason-and-what-did-the-scanner-pass-on-is-the-library-browser-with-the-filter-off)) | us | every page |
| | Continue Watching, Next Up ([play-state.md](../design/plans/play-state.md)) | us | every page |
| | the admin inventory view ([D163](#d163--every-observed-file-carries-a-filing-with-a-reason-and-what-did-the-scanner-pass-on-is-the-library-browser-with-the-filter-off)) | us | on demand |

**D75 designed for the first family and the other two arrived by accretion.** That is not a
criticism of D75 — it is the sign that the abstraction was right — but it changes three things
it decided, because *"a user's saved query, evaluated occasionally, whose errors are the user's
problem"* and *"the WHERE clause of every page, whose errors are ours"* are not the same
artefact.

### 2. The bug: D75's invalid-rule rule is fail-**open** for the two bindings that must fail closed

D75, correctly for an authored rule:

> *a rule whose field no longer resolves is **kept, marked invalid, and surfaced** with the
> offending field named — never dropped, never silently emptied.*

D76 and D84, also correctly:

> share and profile restriction **fail closed**.

**Compose them and a child's restriction evaporates.** Rename a column, forget the alias, and
the `Kids` predicate no longer resolves. It is *kept and marked invalid*, so it is not
evaluated — and a predicate that *limits* visibility, not evaluated, **limits nothing**.
"Never silently emptied" is the safe direction for a selecting rule and the unsafe direction
for a restricting one. Surfacing does not save it: surfacing is to an admin who may not be
looking, while the child is looking tonight.

This is not the item-level case
[D132](#d132--authoring-a-role-is-a-preview-loop-and-an-item-the-rules-cannot-judge-is-denied-not-shown)
already solved — *"an uncovered item is denied and queued"* is about a **value** being unknown.
This is the **rule itself** failing to resolve, and nothing covers it.

**So, two changes:**

- **Validity is per binding.** An invalid **authored** rule is inert, kept and surfaced —
  D75 unchanged. An invalid **restricting** rule **matches nothing, denies everything, and is
  loud**: the role's users see an empty library with a message naming the field, which is
  alarming, correct, and fixed in a minute. An alarming failure beats a silent one.
- **Better: it never gets that far.** A migration that removes or renames a field referenced by
  a *restricting* rule, with no alias registered, **fails the migration**
  ([principles §7](../principles/07-migrations-are-safety.md) — migrations are a safety feature). D75's `alias`
  mechanism exists precisely to make this a non-event; this makes forgetting it impossible
  rather than merely regrettable.

### 3. The complexity bound is not term count or SQL size. It is one shared depth budget

D75 left this open — *"term count, depth, or generated-SQL size; needs a corpus"*. It needs no
corpus, because the database answers it directly. Measured:

| Construct | Maximum | Error at the next value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **`EXISTS` nesting depth** | **29** | *Expression tree is too large (maximum depth 1000)* |
| ANDed `EXISTS` terms | **932** | same |
| OR-chain terms | **997** | same |
| **`IN` list length** | **no failure below 2,097,152** | — |
| tables in a join | **63** | *at most 64 tables in a join* |

Three different constructs, **one error**: every one spends from the same
**expression-tree depth budget of 1000**. So the bound is **depth, tracked as a single pool**,
and the compiler prices each construct against it. Three consequences:

- **Prefer `IN (…)` to an OR chain, always.** 2,097,152 against 997 is not a tuning
  preference, it is a factor of two thousand for identical semantics. The generated SQL should
  contain an OR chain only where the terms differ in *field*, not in value.
- **Rule references get a real number.** D75 allowed rules referencing rules and said "bound
  the depth" without one. Nesting costs ~34 depth units a level, so **29 is the ceiling** and
  the practical limit is lower, because —
- **Composition spends from the same pool.** A page is `listing AND role AND share AND the
  user's collection`. Four rules individually within budget can exceed it together, so the
  budget is enforced **on the composed statement**, apportioned with the **structural and
  restricting bindings taking their share first** and the authored rule receiving the
  remainder. The error must then name *which* contributor overran, because the author of a
  perfectly small rule is otherwise told their rule is too complex.

### 4. Tags live in a join table, with a derived count column

D75 forced this question onto `library-model.md` and did not settle it, noting *"Navidrome's
JSON choice is what created their batching problem"*. Measured, at the reference library:

| Query | Join table | JSON (`json_each`) | JSON / join |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| single tag | **159 µs** | 7.96 ms | **50×** |
| 3-tag AND | **280 µs** | 8.37 ms | **30×** |
| NOT tag | **656 µs** | 7.22 ms | **11×** |
| `count(tags) > 20` | 4.72 ms | **2.75 ms** | 0.6× |

JSON wins exactly one shape, and it wins it because the join-table version asks a correlated
`count(*)` per row. **A `tag_count` derived column settles it: 66 µs** — 42× faster than the
JSON it lost to and 71× faster than the correlated count. That is
[D161](#d161--cache-and-invalidate-do-not-incrementally-maintain-a-missed-invalidation-is-stale-a-missed-update-is-wrong)'s
**derived column** mechanism, the second of its three, used exactly as described.

So: **normalised `tag` + `item_tag`, plus a `tag_count` column on the item.** The ratios hold
at the headroom point (40×, 43×, 24×) and the derived column stays flat at **101 µs against a
986,709-row tag table**.

### 5. A negative result worth more than the design it replaces

The obvious worry about §1 is cost: a restricting predicate ANDed into every page. The obvious
fix is D161 — cache each role's visible set and join against it. **Measured, it is not worth
doing.**

| Composed page (listing AND role AND collection, `ORDER BY`, `LIMIT 60`) | reference | headroom |
| --- | --- | --- |
| live, `NOT IN` form | 1.227 ms | 6.775 ms |
| role set cached per D161, `NOT IN` form | 1.142 ms | 5.428 ms |
| **live, `NOT EXISTS` form** | **506 µs** | **1.015 ms** |

The cache bought **7%**. Rewriting the negation as `NOT EXISTS` bought **2.4×** — and the
well-shaped live query is **twice as fast as the cached one**. Caching a result set here would
have been a table, an invalidation path and a class of staleness bug, bought with a 85 µs
saving that better SQL returns several times over.

**And the shape that wins standalone is not the shape that wins composed.** Standalone,
`NOT IN` beats `NOT EXISTS` (656 µs vs 1.61 ms); inside the page, `NOT EXISTS` wins by 2.4×,
because `LIMIT 60` over the `(filing, added_at DESC)` index lets SQLite stop early and evaluate
the negation on a few hundred rows, while `NOT IN` materialises the whole excluded set first.
**The compiler chooses the negation form by whether the query is bounded**, which is a rule it
can apply mechanically.

### 6. Provider-supplied fields are materialised columns with an `as_of`

The third open item — *"a field needing a network call cannot be in a `WHERE` clause"*. It
cannot, and it does not have to: a provider field is **materialised on refresh**, carries an
**`as_of`**, and is a registry entry flagged as such so the UI can say how old it is. That is
[D149](#d149--eight-gaps-the-source-sweep-found-six-declines-and-the-one-that-is-a-hole-in-the-business-model)'s
rating tuple `(source, kind, score, votes, as_of)` generalised, and it composes with everything
above: a never-refreshed provider value is **unknown**, and D132's coverage rule already denies
an uncovered item in the two restricting bindings. **No network call is ever reachable from a
predicate** — which is also what stops a rule evaluation from depending on a third party being
up.

**Status:** §2 is a **correctness and security fix** and is Phase 1 with the rest of the
engine; §3 is compiler behaviour and a constant; §4 is the `library-model.md` schema decision
D75 deferred, now made; §5 removes a planned mechanism; §6 is a registry flag and a column.
Unmeasured, and deliberately: a corpus of real Kometa-scale rules, because the ceiling turned
out to be a property of the database rather than of the corpus, and measuring the corpus would
not move the number.

---

## D165 — A heartbeat is not an event: the log records state changes and watched spans, there is no retention horizon, and an offline device must not be able to rewind you

**Decided** (2026-09-22). Closes
[D81](#d81--play-state-is-an-append-only-event-log-plus-a-guarded-position-and-positions-are-edition-relative)'s
stated open item, resolves a contradiction between it and
[FEATURES.md](../../FEATURES.md), repairs two places the document still contradicts
[D157](#d157--a-position-belongs-to-the-file-completion-rolls-up-the-position-never-does), and
closes a gap that puts the exact bug D81 exists to prevent back on the offline path. Measured
at `/yoloai/cache/bench/playlog/`.

### 1. The open item, and the contradiction it was in

D81: *"the log is the first table with an unbounded row count and wants a stated horizon."*
FEATURES.md, from the sweep: *"D81's play-event log **must be retained rather than
truncated**, because F39, F43 and most of F41's reconciliation read it."*

Both are right about their own concern and they cannot both be satisfied — **unless the log is
not actually big**, which is a measurement nobody had taken.

### 2. Taken: D81 as written costs 92.6 MB a year in heartbeats

A household of four, three hours each a day, over a 3,500-item library — **7,331 viewings a
year**:

| Representation | Rows, 1 yr | On disk | Rows, 5 yr | On disk |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **D81 as written** — `progress` every 10 s | **1,592,258** | **92.6 MB** | 7,967,990 | **470.1 MB** |
| **state changes + watched spans** | **54,543** | **2.5 MB** | 279,453 | **13.4 MB** |
| | **29× fewer** | **37× smaller** | 28.5× | 35× |

D81's instinct was right: half a gigabyte of heartbeats on a NAS is a real problem, and it
arrives in five quiet years. **But the horizon is the wrong instrument**, because the rows it
would delete are the ones carrying no information.

### 3. The fix is structural: `progress` is not a log event

D81 lists `progress` among `started · paused · seeked · completed · abandoned`. **It does not
belong there.** A heartbeat every 10 s is not something that *happened*; it is a restatement
of where you are, and the model already has a place for that — the guarded position row, which
is mutable by design. Three objects, each with one job:

| | Job | Written |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **the guarded position** | where you are now | every ~10 s, in place |
| **a state-change event** | `started`, `paused`, `seeked`, `completed`, `abandoned` | when one happens |
| **a watched span** | `(user, file, device, pos_from→pos_to, t_from→t_to)` | **appended when a state change closes it** |

A run of heartbeats with no intervening state change **is** one span, so collapsing them loses
nothing: *how much did I watch, when, and on what* is a span, exactly. This is
[D148](#d148--the-speech-map-is-a-scan-artefact-and-the-reference-is-a-subtitle-track-before-it-is-audio)'s speech-map
run-length encoding applied to a different stream of samples, for the same reason.

**And the log stays append-only**, which is the obvious objection and it does not land: spans
are *appended* on close, and the only thing mutated is the position row that was always
mutable. The open span simply *is* the position row.

**Every question gets faster, by a lot**, because the aggregate no longer counts heartbeats:

| Play-statistics query | D81 as written | spans | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| watch time last 30 days, per user | 86.0 ms | **1.2 ms** | 69× |
| most-watched titles, all time | 236.7 ms | **4.7 ms** | 50× |
| one user's last 50 viewings | 2.8 ms | **84 µs** | 33× |
| how much of this file did they see | 139 µs | **12 µs** | 12× |
| busiest device, per month | 788.3 ms | **6.5 ms** | **122×** |

At five years the worst case is **4.42 s against 42.7 ms** — the difference between a page that
works and one nobody ships.

### 4. So: no retention horizon. Keep everything

**13.4 MB for five years of a four-person household.** A horizon would be a migration, a
deletion path, a setting, and a class of *"where did my 2019 statistics go"* complaint, bought
to save single-digit megabytes. FEATURES.md's obligation is satisfied outright rather than
traded against, and `play-statistics.md`'s *"watch time in 2019"* question simply works.

One line survives from the old concern: a span table is still the largest table, so it is the
one that gets a **row count on the observability page**. Visible, not capped.

### 5. The gap: an offline device can rewind you, and that is the 29-comment bug

D81's guard is a **monotonic sequence** on the position row, and it is correct online because
the server issues it. Offline it inverts:

> Monday, on a plane: the tablet reaches **40:00**. Tuesday, at home: the television reaches
> **25:00**. Wednesday the tablet reconnects and its events arrive.

If the guard is assigned when events *arrive*, Monday's 40:00 lands after Tuesday's 25:00 and
wins. That is *"Media playback randomly starts over again or jumps back — **STILL**"* (29
comments), which is the tracker item D81 quotes — **reintroduced on the path D81 said the log
existed to make possible.** Both plans assert *"progress made offline merges without losing
either side"* in a *Done when*, and neither says how.

**The missing half of the mechanism is already half-specified.** D81 has events carry *"the
client's own monotonic clock"*, which orders a device's events against each other. To order
them against *another device's* you need absolute time, and the wall clock is exactly what
cannot be trusted. So:

- **Anchor the monotonic run at sync.** The device reports its current monotonic value with
  the batch; the server knows the true time of that instant, so every event converts:
  `true_t(e) = now_server − (mono_sync − mono_e)`. **Exact back to the last monotonic
  discontinuity, however wrong the device's calendar is.** One extra field on a sync request,
  not a new mechanism.
- **The position is the latest anchored event's. Recency, not maximum.** Furthest-position is
  the tempting rule and it is wrong: deliberately restarting a film would keep throwing you
  back to the end.
- **When a run cannot be anchored** — the device rebooted between watching and syncing — the
  events are ingested with their time marked **uncertain and they do not move the position**.
  They still count toward statistics. This fails toward *"your position did not move"*, which
  is one action to fix, rather than *"your position jumped back"*, which is the 29-comment
  bug.
- **And nothing is merged.** Two sessions on one file are two spans; the log holds both, and
  the most recent one is where you are. There is no arithmetic that could be wrong — the same
  discipline as [D158](#d158--we-group-files-for-browsing-and-never-relate-their-timelines-the-continuation-offer-is-withdrawn),
  arrived at from the other direction.

**A span with no closing event is left open and marked unterminated**, closed at the last known
position by the next sync or a timeout. A client that crashes is an ordinary case, not an
error.

### 6. Two places play-state.md still contradicts D157

Found while reading, both from before D157 landed and both stale in the same document that
states the correct rule twenty lines earlier:

- A table giving **resume position → Edition** and **played/play count → Edition**, with *"a
  1080p→4K switch must not lose it"* as the reason — the precise claim
  [D157](#d157--a-position-belongs-to-the-file-completion-rolls-up-the-position-never-does)
  refuted and [D158](#d158--we-group-files-for-browsing-and-never-relate-their-timelines-the-continuation-offer-is-withdrawn)
  withdrew. Position is at the **File**; completion rolls up freely because it involves no
  timeline.
- **Continue Watching described as a list of "editions"**. Positions are per File, so the
  question *what is a row* needed answering rather than inheriting: **a row is a work, showing
  the most recent position among its files, and it names the file when there is more than one
  candidate.** Not a merge and not an offer — the most recent viewing, labelled. The other
  file's position is still in the log and still on the item's own page.

**Status:** §3 is schema and changes a table before it exists rather than after; §4 removes a
planned mechanism; §5 is a field on the sync request plus a stated resolution rule, and is a
correctness fix on
[offline-download.md](../design/plans/offline-download.md)'s central promise; §6 is repair.
Unmeasured: the write cost of the position row at ~2 writes/second household-wide, which is
the one number this changes on the hot path and is almost certainly nothing.

## D166 — The journal is an accelerator, never a dependency: the server may always answer with state, and that is the ordinary path rather than the error path

**Decided** (2026-09-23), by the project owner, redirecting the framing this log had:

> *"A journal is indeed helpful to cheaply keep the client in sync with the server, but it's
> not something that breaks the client if it's unavailable (or at least it shouldn't). Caching
> is one of the hardest things to do in computer science, and network comms makes it even
> worse. We're going to have to assume that caching will break somewhere for a really dumb
> reason that we didn't consider. That's just Murphy's law. We should also keep in mind that
> the kind of data it's syncing isn't that big, and that there may be a point where it's
> better to just ingest the current state rather than grab a huge journal to walk through.
> Furthermore, we don't necessarily need the entirety of the datascape in sync before we allow
> user interaction. I'd rather keep this section simple, with easy escape hatches."*

[D8](working-notes-archive.md#d8--a-change-journal-and-delta-sync-cursor-exist-in-the-first-schema) has been
`Provisional` since the first week, no plan consumes it, and its own status concedes it is
*"unvalidated until a mobile client exists"*. The previous survey of it listed four open
questions and one hole. **Three of the four dissolve under this framing and the hole dissolves
with them** — which is the sign the framing is right rather than merely nicer.

### 1. The empirical claim, checked

"The kind of data it's syncing isn't that big" is the load-bearing assumption, so it was
measured (`/yoloai/cache/bench/sync/`). Everything a client needs to *browse* — id, kind,
title, sort key, year, artwork reference, parent, sequence, duration, and this user's position
and watched flag:

| | reference library (3,510 rows) | large household (20,000 rows) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| full state, raw JSON | 847 KB | 4.8 MB |
| **full state, gzipped** | **215 KB** | **1.2 MB** |
| on a 10 Mbit link | **0.2 s** | 1.0 s |
| on a 1 Mbit link | 1.8 s | 10.1 s |
| client decodes it in | 8 ms | 42 ms |
| client writes it to local SQLite in | 16 ms | 97 ms |
| first screen of 60 from the local copy | 109 µs | 151 µs |

**215 KB is one HTTP response.** The whole state of the reference library costs less than a
single poster image. So the fallback is not an emergency path that has to be justified — it is
cheap enough to be *the* path, with the journal as an optimisation on top.

### 2. The crossover is real, and the journal's useful band is narrow

A journal entry is **79 B raw, 23 B gzipped**. Walking a journal is only cheaper than taking
the state while:

| | reference library | large household |
| --- | --- | --- |
| entries alone, gzipped | 9,736 | 55,562 |
| **entries with the changed rows attached** — the honest comparison | **~2,600** | **~14,700** |

So the journal wins exactly where it should: **the ordinary case of a handful of changes since
this morning.** Past a couple of thousand changed items it is strictly worse than saying "take
everything", and the server knows both numbers and can simply compare them.

### 3. So: one response type, two shapes, and the server chooses

**There is no "your cursor is too old" error.** A client presents a cursor; the server replies
with *either* a delta *or* the full state, and which one is a **cost decision, not a failure**.
Consequences, all simplifying:

- **The resync path is exercised constantly** rather than being emergency code that has never
  run. That is the direct answer to Murphy: the escape hatch cannot rot, because it is load
  every day.
- **The journal is allowed to be lossy.** This is the largest simplification and it follows
  only from the fallback being free. A journal that must be authoritative needs durability,
  ordering guarantees, retention policy and a compaction bound. One that may be incomplete can
  be capped at a fixed size, truncated under pressure, dropped on restart, held in memory, or
  **not written at all** — and every one of those is answered by returning state instead.
- **One journal table, not N paired audit tables.** Immich's shape was copied on day one
  without asking whether it is ours. `(seq, entity_kind, entity_id, op, at)` is enough,
  because the client's response to any entry is to re-fetch the row — the journal says *what
  changed*, never *what it changed to*.

### 4. The visibility hole dissolves, and costs one line

The gap flagged the day before: **a role predicate changing makes items invisible with no row
having changed**, so a journal of row changes leaves a child's client showing what a parent
just excluded. That needed a mechanism when the journal was authoritative. It needs a sentence
now:

> **Anything that changes what a principal may see invalidates that principal's cursor.**

Their next request returns state, filtered for them by
[principles §10](../principles/10-only-what-a-client-may-use.md)'s per-principal construction, which already exists.
No visibility journal, no new table, no per-item recomputation — and
[D164](#d164--the-predicate-language-stopped-being-a-feature-and-became-the-query-layer-a-restricting-rule-must-fail-closed-and-the-complexity-budget-is-one-number)
already makes "the restricting predicate changed" a single observable event.

### 5. The local copy is a cache with a completeness marker, not a database

*"We don't necessarily need the entirety of the datascape in sync before we allow user
interaction."* So the client's rule is:

- **Anything the local copy cannot answer, the server can.** The local copy is an accelerator;
  nothing lives only in it. A screen renders from the server while the copy is still filling.
- **No "syncing, please wait".** The 10.1 s case above — 20,000 items over a 1 Mbit link — is
  precisely where this matters, and it is the only case where it does.
- **Therefore every cache failure is a performance event, never a correctness one**, which is
  the property that makes all of the above safe to be casual about.

### 6. And D8's urgency argument evaporates — honestly recorded

D8 was decided in the first week on the strength of *"retrofitting a change journal is a
migration over the whole schema"* and *"an `updatedAt` column cannot express a delete"*.

**Neither survives.** A full-state fetch expresses deletion perfectly — by absence — so the
delete argument only applies to a design that has no fallback. And what cannot be retrofitted
is not a journal; it is **a design that assumed the journal was authoritative**. One journal
table is additive and can be added in year three.

The journal stays, because 23 B against 215 KB is a real saving on the common case and it
costs one table. **But it stays as an optimisation we chose, not as a foundation we could not
defer** — and the difference is the whole of this decision.

### 7. The one genuine exception, stated so the two never merge

**An offline download is not this mechanism**
([D87](#d87--a-download-is-a-rendition-plus-a-lease-and-it-is-self-contained)). A download is
self-contained with a lease precisely because it must work with no server to ask. That is the
single case where the client cannot fall back, and it is handled by *carrying everything it
needs*, not by trusting a sync cache. **The sync cache must never become load-bearing for
offline**, or this decision's central property is quietly lost.

**Status:** Replaces D8's shape while keeping its table. Schema impact is now **one journal
table** rather than a paired audit table per syncable table, and the "which tables are
syncable" question is no longer load-bearing — an unjournalled table is simply one where the
client always takes state. Unmeasured: the state payload with artwork included, which is a
different and much larger question that [artwork.md](../design/plans/artwork.md) owns; every
figure above is metadata only, and artwork is fetched by reference.

## D167 — Absence is never a reason to destroy: a download whose server copy is gone is orphaned, not deleted, and entitlement is the only thing the lease may remove

**Decided** (2026-09-23), prompted by the project owner asking what happens when a video
downloaded to a device is deleted on the server.

[offline-download.md](../design/plans/offline-download.md)'s *Done when* answers it in eight
words — *"an item deleted on the server disappears from the device on next contact"* — and
that rule is wrong, contradicts the paragraph immediately above it, and would have become a
mass-deletion trigger the moment
[D166](#d166--the-journal-is-an-accelerator-never-a-dependency-the-server-may-always-answer-with-state-and-that-is-the-ordinary-path-rather-than-the-error-path)
landed.

### 1. "Deleted on the server" is four different events

| What actually happened | What the user wants |
| --- | --- |
| the owner deliberately deleted the media ([D89](#d89--deletion-is-opt-in-per-library-two-phase-and-names-every-file)) | keep my copy; it may be the only one left |
| the file vanished from disk — a drive died, somebody moved a folder | **keep my copy**, urgently |
| **a node is offline**, a mount is down, a share is unreachable | keep my copy; nothing happened |
| a mis-scan, a permission change, a path outside a library root ([D163](#d163--every-observed-file-carries-a-filing-with-a-reason-and-what-did-the-scanner-pass-on-is-the-library-browser-with-the-filter-off)) | keep my copy; *we* were wrong |
| **entitlement was revoked** — a housemate left, a role changed | remove it, and that is the point |

**Four of the five want the opposite of the stated rule**, and only the last is about
permission at all. The tree already holds this distinction one layer down and states it
plainly for nodes:

> Mark an absent node's items **unavailable, never deleted**. **Never tombstone on silence** —
> absence of a pulse is absence of information, not evidence of deletion.
> ([D34](#d34--a-node-status-record-that-distinguishes-dead-from-wedged-from-idle))

**This is that rule at the other end of the wire**, and it was not carried across.

### 2. The failure it produces is catastrophic and lands at the worst moment

A node goes down for maintenance on Friday. The phone checks in on Saturday, sees the item
gone, and deletes the holiday films. The user discovers this **on the plane**, where the
recovery path — re-download — is the one thing that cannot work.

A destructive action, on a device we do not own, triggered by an *inference*, at the precise
moment it is unrecoverable. Every clause of that is something this project has decided against
somewhere else.

### 3. And D166 made it far worse, one day later

D166 lets the server answer any sync request with **full state instead of a delta**, and a
full state expresses deletion by *absence*. But absence cannot distinguish **deleted** from
**unavailable** from **no longer visible to you** from **we mis-scanned** — so "absent ⇒ delete
my downloads" turns D166's ordinary, cheap, exercised-every-day fallback into a **mass deletion
trigger on every client**. Two decisions a day apart, each sound, composing into data loss.

So the rule has to be the strong form:

> **Absence is never evidence. Only a positive statement is.** Nothing on a device is destroyed
> because something was missing from a response.

### 4. Availability and entitlement are separate, and only one of them removes anything

- **Availability gone → the download is `orphaned`.** It stays on the device, it stays
  playable, and the client says so: *"no longer in the library — this may be the only copy."*
  The user decides. [principles §2](../principles/02-the-users-files.md) says the user's files are not ours
  to touch, and a download on someone's phone is **further** from ours than a library file is.
- **Entitlement gone → the lease is not renewed, and the client removes it on expiry.** This
  is the mechanism [D87](#d87--a-download-is-a-rendition-plus-a-lease-and-it-is-self-contained)
  already has, and it is the honest one: revocation is **eventual, bounded by the lease
  period**, because [D3](#d3--streaming-format-cmaffmp4-segments-hls-manifest-no-drm) declines
  DRM and **we cannot un-give bytes**. The plan says this already — *"nothing enforces a lease
  on bytes already sitting on a device… playback of an already-downloaded file is a client-side
  courtesy"* — which is exactly why the *Done when* two paragraphs later cannot be right.

**The server must tell them apart, because the client cannot.** The reconciliation reply
distinguishes *"this item is no longer available"* from *"you are no longer entitled to it"* —
a small protocol point with the whole behaviour hanging off it. MaxSilence is neither.

### 5. Three things that fall out, all cheap

- **The download may be the last copy, and both ends should say so.** D89's two-phase
  confirmation already *"names every file and its size"*; it gains **"and 2 devices hold a
  downloaded copy"**. Nobody in the field does this, and it is the sentence that prevents the
  regret.
- **Play state from a deleted item must still land.** A phone returning from a trip syncs
  spans for a file the server no longer has, and
  [D165](#d165--a-heartbeat-is-not-an-event-the-log-records-state-changes-and-watched-spans-there-is-no-retention-horizon-and-an-offline-device-must-not-be-able-to-rewind-you)
  keeps the log forever. So this is the first concrete consumer of the invariant the data
  survey named: **no row a user's history or authored data references is ever hard-deleted —
  it is tombstoned.** Decided here rather than left open. *(Mechanics specified by [D173](#d173--a-replaced-file-is-a-deletion-and-an-addition-what-is-in-a-files-timeline-dies-with-the-file-and-what-is-about-the-work-survives-at-the-title).)*
- **An orphaned download cannot be repaired.** If it was partial when the source went, it
  stays partial: say so, offer to remove it, and stop retrying. A client silently retrying a
  fetch that can never succeed is a battery bug wearing a progress bar.

**Storage is the user's call, not ours.** *"3 orphaned downloads, 12 GB"* is a screen with a
delete button on it, which is the whole of the reclamation policy for bytes we do not own.

**Status:** Corrects a *Done when* and adds one distinction to the reconciliation reply, both
before any client exists. The tombstone invariant is **schema** and is due with
`library-model.md`. No measurement needed: every quantity here is a policy choice, and the one
empirical question — how long a lease should be — is the same unmeasured household number as
[auth.md](../design/plans/auth.md)'s idle-expiry window and should be decided with it.
*(Narrowed the same day by [D169](#d169--a-lease-is-indefinite-by-default-expiry-is-a-property-of-a-conditional-relationship-and-the-servers-prepared-rendition-is-a-cache-rather-than-a-referent):
a lease is indefinite by default, so the question is only **how long a share's lease** should
be.)*
