## D168 — Entitlement is resolved at the point of use, never pushed: revocation needs no message, and the notification is a latency optimisation that may always be lost

**Decided** (2026-09-23), answering the project owner's question — *how do we manage
entitlement, and by what mechanism do we inform clients that it has ended?*

**The short answer is that we do not inform them, and that is the design rather than a
shortcut.**

### 1. Three different things are being called entitlement

| Question | Governed by | Ends when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Am I still a principal?** | the grant row ([D154](#d154--one-grant-table-opaque-and-revocable-the-session-credential-never-appears-in-a-url)) | `revoked_at` is set, or idle expiry passes |
| **May I still see *this*?** | the role or share predicate ([D130](#d130--a-role-is-a-named-policy-object-users-are-assigned-to-one-never-configured-individually), [D76](#d76--a-share-is-a-grantee-plus-a-predicate-and-it-fails-closed), [D164](#d164--the-predicate-language-stopped-being-a-feature-and-became-the-query-layer-a-restricting-rule-must-fail-closed-and-the-complexity-budget-is-one-number)) | the predicate changes, or the item does |
| **May I keep bytes I already hold?** | the lease ([D87](#d87--a-download-is-a-rendition-plus-a-lease-and-it-is-self-contained)) | the lease is not renewed |

They are usually conflated, and conflating them is how systems end up pushing a *"you are
revoked"* message and then trusting it.

### 2. The mechanism: nothing is ever pre-authorised

**Every request resolves entitlement at the point of use, against current state.** A client is
never holding a decision — it is holding *content it was already given*. So:

> **Revocation takes effect on the very next request, with no message sent to anybody.**

A grant revoked at 14:00 fails at 14:00:00.1. A role predicate narrowed at 14:00 stops
returning those items at 14:00. Nothing is in flight, nothing must arrive, nothing can be
missed.

### 3. Affordable, measured — and the one place it could have cost something is free

The objection to checking every request is cost, so it was measured
(`/yoloai/cache/bench/entitle/`, 3,500-item library, 200 live grants):

| | |
| --- | --- |
| grant is live — hash lookup, `revoked_at` and expiry checked | **3.26 µs** |
| may this principal see **this one item** — the role predicate | **3.78 µs** |
| **both, as one byte request does them** | **6.64 µs** (150,602/s) |
| revoke every grant one user holds | **145 µs**, one `UPDATE` |

A 6-second segment means one check per 6 seconds per stream:

| Concurrent streams | Cost |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | 0.00011% of one core |
| 20 | 0.0022% |
| **100** | **0.011%** |

**There is no performance argument for caching an authorisation decision.** There never was;
nobody had checked.

### 4. And D164 already made this true, by declining an optimisation

D164 measured caching a role's visible set and **declined it** — 7% against 2.4× from better
SQL. That read as a performance non-event. It is actually the security property: **because no
materialised entitlement exists on the server, there is nothing stale to invalidate.** Had the
cache been taken, this decision would have needed an invalidation protocol, and revocation
would have had a window.

### 5. So what *is* the notification for? Latency, and it may always be lost

A connected client sitting on a library grid does not re-request for minutes. Telling it
*"your entitlement changed, re-sync"* closes that window. That message is exactly
[principles §14](../principles/14-a-cache-may-always-be-wrong.md)'s shape and
[D166](#d166--the-journal-is-an-accelerator-never-a-dependency-the-server-may-always-answer-with-state-and-that-is-the-ordinary-path-rather-than-the-error-path)'s:
**an invalidation hint, never the mechanism.** Therefore:

- **No delivery guarantee, no ordering, no acknowledgement, no retry.** If it is lost, §2
  catches it on the next request. This is why it is cheap.
- **It carries no detail.** *"Your access changed"* — never *"you may no longer see Wing"*,
  because naming what was withdrawn **tells a child that Wing exists**, which is precisely the
  disclosure [D134](#d134--a-pending-item-discloses-nothing-a-rule-shows-its-coverage-and-the-home-page-computes-nothing)
  closed everywhere else.
- **It is the same event that invalidates the sync cursor** (D166 §4), so it is one signal with
  two consumers rather than a new channel.

### 6. Disconnected: time is the only mechanism, and we say so

You cannot inform a client that is not listening. For a device offline on a plane there is
**no mechanism but expiry**, and the honest statement is that revocation latency is bounded by
a *duration*, not by a network:

- the **session's idle expiry** ([D154](#d154--one-grant-table-opaque-and-revocable-the-session-credential-never-appears-in-a-url)),
- and the **download lease** ([D87](#d87--a-download-is-a-rendition-plus-a-lease-and-it-is-self-contained), [D167](#d167--absence-is-never-a-reason-to-destroy-a-download-whose-server-copy-is-gone-is-orphaned-not-deleted-and-entitlement-is-the-only-thing-the-lease-may-remove)).

Those two numbers **are** the revocation guarantee, and they should be stated in the product in
those terms. **Sharpened the same day by [D169](#d169--a-lease-is-indefinite-by-default-expiry-is-a-property-of-a-conditional-relationship-and-the-servers-prepared-rendition-is-a-cache-rather-than-a-referent)**,
because a lease is indefinite by default: *for your own devices there is no offline revocation
guarantee, and there should not be one; for a grantee there is, and it is exactly the lease the
owner set on the share.* An **idled-out session must not orphan a download** — tying playback
to a session timer produces the plane-mode failure
[D167](#d167--absence-is-never-a-reason-to-destroy-a-download-whose-server-copy-is-gone-is-orphaned-not-deleted-and-entitlement-is-the-only-thing-the-lease-may-remove)
exists to prevent. Anything stronger would require enforcing against bytes on hardware we do not
control, which is [D3](#d3--streaming-format-cmaffmp4-segments-hls-manifest-no-drm)'s declined
DRM wearing a different hat.

### 7. A stream in flight — and a misreading of D70 to head off

[stream-service.md](../design/plans/stream-service.md) says *"authorise the **session**, not
the segment"* ([D70](#d70--hosted-fan-out-is-the-right-shape-for-remote-party-viewing-and-the-cheap-part-is-keeping-it-possible)).
**That is a statement about cache keys, not about skipping checks** — it exists so identical
bytes keep one URL instead of one per viewer. The grant still rides on every segment request
(the path-scoped cookie) and is still checked at the 6.64 µs above.

**So a revoked viewer stops within one segment**, mid-film, which is the correct behaviour and
costs 0.011% of a core at a hundred streams.

### 8. Three places the rule is deliberately different, named so they are not "fixed"

- **Watch Together** ([D117](#d117--the-session-link-is-the-grant-revocation-is-the-control-and-the-creator-owns-what-plays)):
  the session link **is** the grant and is deliberately *not* predicate-governed. Revocation
  there means **ending the session**, not narrowing a predicate.
- **A cast receiver** ([D124](#d124--the-playback-role-may-be-a-cast-receiver-and-for-a-guest-that-is-the-best-path-the-phone-controls-it-does-not-relay)–[D137](#d137--the-cast-receiver-ships-no-subtitle-renderer-casts-own-is-the-statutory-one-and-the-cost-is-on-the-server))
  holds its own grant, so revoking the controlling user must revoke the receiver's with it —
  otherwise the television keeps playing for a person who has been removed.
- **A protocol adapter** ([D105](#d105--a-protocol-adapter-acts-as-the-user-never-as-itself))
  acts *as the user* and holds no standing privilege, so it inherits all of this for free. That
  is the whole reason for the rule.

**Status:** No new mechanism and no new table — this is a statement of where the check happens,
plus one detail-free invalidation message sharing D166's event. The cast-receiver revocation
coupling in §8 is the only implementation item. Unmeasured, and the same number as three other
open questions: **how long the idle window and the lease should be**, which is the household
figure [auth.md](../design/plans/auth.md) already flags and should be decided once for all of
them. *(Halved by [D169](#d169--a-lease-is-indefinite-by-default-expiry-is-a-property-of-a-conditional-relationship-and-the-servers-prepared-rendition-is-a-cache-rather-than-a-referent):
the lease is indefinite unless a share says otherwise, so only the idle window and a share's
lease remain.)*

---

## D169 — A lease is indefinite by default; expiry is a property of a conditional relationship, and the server's prepared rendition is a cache rather than a referent

**Decided** (2026-09-23), by the project owner, correcting the default this log had been
assuming:

> *"My guess is that most of the time the lease duration will be infinite. There would have to
> be a specific reason why it's only allowed for a short time."*

That is right, and following it exposes that
[D87](#d87--a-download-is-a-rendition-plus-a-lease-and-it-is-self-contained)'s lease was doing
**two unrelated jobs under one name** — which is why an expiry looked obligatory.

### 1. The two jobs, separated

| Job D87 gave the lease | Who it serves | Does it need an expiry? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *"a prepared rendition that nothing references must not be reaped"* | **the server's disk** | **no** — see §2 |
| a backstop that reaches a device nobody can contact | **revocation** | **only where there is something to revoke** |

They were bundled because both sounded like reference counting. They are not the same
mechanism and they do not want the same lifetime.

### 2. The server's prepared rendition is a cache, so it needs no referent at all

A download that is a **transcode** leaves a derived artefact on the server. D87 made the lease
the thing that keeps it alive. But once the bytes are on the device, **the server's copy has
no job except making a re-download cheap** — and that is a cache, governed by disk pressure,
evicted whenever the server likes.

[principles §14](../principles/14-a-cache-may-always-be-wrong.md) is the whole argument: losing it must be a
*performance* event, and it is — a re-download re-transcodes. **No lease, no reference count,
no reaping policy.** A direct-copy download leaves no artefact at all and never needed one.

That removes the job that made expiry look structural.

### 3. What remains is enforcement, and enforcement is a property of the *relationship*

[D168](#d168--entitlement-is-resolved-at-the-point-of-use-never-pushed-revocation-needs-no-message-and-the-notification-is-a-latency-optimisation-that-may-always-be-lost)
settled that entitlement online needs no message and costs **6.64 µs** at the point of use. So
a lease's only remaining job is the device nobody can reach — and **that job only exists where
somebody might need to take access away.**

| Whose device | Lease | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **the owner's own, on their own library** | **indefinite** | there is nothing to revoke; it is their media on their hardware |
| a household member under a role | **indefinite by default** | narrowing a child's rules is not usually *"confiscate what is on the phone"*; if it is, the owner says so explicitly |
| **a grantee** ([D76](#d76--a-share-is-a-grantee-plus-a-predicate-and-it-fails-closed)) | **finite, set with the share** | a share can end, and this is the only mechanism that reaches them offline |
| a Watch Together guest | **none — no download** | a guest is not a principal ([D125](#d125--access-is-role-based-with-two-roles-a-watch-together-guest-is-not-a-principal)), so there is nothing to hold one |

**So the rule is:** *indefinite unless someone deliberately attached an expiry to a share*, and
the expiry is authored where the share is, not where the download is. A finite lease is a
statement about a person, not about a file.

### 4. Which makes the honest guarantee more honest, not less

D168 said the idle window and the lease *are* the revocation guarantee. With this default that
sentence has to be said properly:

> **For your own devices there is no offline revocation guarantee, and there should not be
> one.** For a grantee there is, and its duration is exactly the lease the owner set on the
> share.

Claiming otherwise would mean pretending to enforce against bytes on hardware we do not
control, which [D3](#d3--streaming-format-cmaffmp4-segments-hls-manifest-no-drm) declines.

### 5. What the indefinite lease still is: a registration

Dropping the expiry does not drop the row. The server still needs to know **which devices hold
what**, for reasons that have nothing to do with enforcement:

- [D167](#d167--absence-is-never-a-reason-to-destroy-a-download-whose-server-copy-is-gone-is-orphaned-not-deleted-and-entitlement-is-the-only-thing-the-lease-may-remove)'s
  delete confirmation says *"2 devices hold a downloaded copy"*;
- the owner can see what is out there and **forget a device** — a phone that was lost, sold or
  wiped — which is the same act as signing it out
  ([D154](#d154--one-grant-table-opaque-and-revocable-the-session-credential-never-appears-in-a-url)) and needs no timer to
  discover.

**A stale registration is untidy, not dangerous**, so it is cleaned by a person noticing rather
than by an expiry firing. That is the correct trade for a value whose only failure mode is a
list with an old phone on it.

### 6. Two consequences worth stating

- **An idled-out session must not orphan a download.** D154 expires sessions on idle; a phone
  in a drawer for three months signs in again and its films are untouched. Playback of an
  already-downloaded file is a client-side courtesy either way, and tying it to a session
  timer would produce exactly the plane-mode failure
  [D167](#d167--absence-is-never-a-reason-to-destroy-a-download-whose-server-copy-is-gone-is-orphaned-not-deleted-and-entitlement-is-the-only-thing-the-lease-may-remove)
  exists to prevent.
- **Orphaned downloads become the ordinary case, not the edge case.** With indefinite leases a
  download routinely outlives the server's copy of the file, so D167's *orphaned* state is
  normal operation and its labelling has to read like it — *"no longer in the library"* as a
  neutral fact, never as a warning.

**Status:** Simplifies rather than adds — removes a reaping policy, removes a default expiry,
and moves the one remaining expiry onto the share where its owner can see it. No measurement:
every quantity here is a policy choice, and the number D168 flagged as wanted — *how long a
lease should be* — turns out to be **wanted only for shares**, which is a much smaller and more
answerable question than the household-wide one it was filed under.

---

## D170 — One source per title, fetched once: a user's correction is permanent, and every refetch is an act of the user

**Decided** (2026-09-23), by the project owner, after this log had been drifting towards
keeping every provider's value for every field and resolving between them:

> *"What I actually worry about is flooding data providers at scan time. If you're scanning a
> fresh library or a library that changed significantly, and grabbing 10 sources for the name
> on every title, that's going to cause problems if/when rate limiting bites for the user.*
>
> *A user being unhappy with the metadata is the exception, not the norm. When a user is
> unhappy, they select the video they don't like, and we provide options for them to fix it,
> be it checking a different source from the default, or just manually adding their own.*
>
> *When a user adds their own, they're unlikely to want it to ever be changed. If they want to
> go back to sourced metadata, they use the same UI flow to choose that. We keep track of which
> source they want so that we can update fixed data, but even that would be a manual 'rescan
> metadata' event, triggered explicitly by the user."*

**Closes** the question the data-architecture survey left open: *is a metadata field a column,
or a resolution over a set of sourced values?* **It is a column.** Provenance is two small
facts beside it, not a table of competing claims.

### 1. Why the claims model was wrong

The case for keeping every source's value — "reset to automatic" and "disable a provider"
become local recomputations — was real, but **every one of its advantages assumed the
alternatives were already on hand**, and the only way to have them on hand is to fetch them.
For every title, at scan time, from every source. That is the flood.

The limits make it concrete (published figures, 2026-09):

| Provider | Limit | Reference library, 3,500 films, one call per title |
| --- | --- | --- |
| TMDB | about 40–50 requests/s per IP; 429 beyond | **about 90 s** |
| OMDb (free key; IMDb, Rotten Tomatoes, Metacritic scores) | **1,000 requests/day** | **3.5 days** |
| OpenSubtitles | 20 downloads/day (D12) | — |

**One extra source turns a first scan measured in minutes into one measured in days**, and it
does so on the user's key ([D12](#d12--providers-are-sandboxed-wasm-plugins-no-in-process-plugin-code)),
so the ban lands on them. The claims model optimises the exception — somebody unhappy with a
title — by charging the ordinary case for it on every title.

### 2. The model

- **A library has a default source.** A scan reads the local sources, which cost nothing —
  the filename parse, embedded tags, an NFO sidecar — and fetches the default source **once
  per newly identified title**.
- **The fetch is a queue, not part of the scan.** A title is listed as soon as it is filed, on
  local data; its provider metadata fills in behind it. The queue honours `429` and
  `Retry-After`, keeps a per-provider budget, and shows its progress in the same place
  [D163](#d163--every-observed-file-carries-a-filing-with-a-reason-and-what-did-the-scanner-pass-on-is-the-library-browser-with-the-filter-off)'s
  scan status does. Rate limiting delays metadata; it never delays the library.
- **Per title, the user may choose a different source.** They open the title, pick a source,
  the server fetches *that one title* from it and shows what it found, and they accept it or
  not. One title, one call, on request.
- **Per field, the user may type their own value, and it is permanent.** Nothing changes a
  manual value except the user, through the same screen. There is no "lock" to set separately:
  a manual value is a lock.
- **Going back is the same screen.** Choosing a source for a field that has a manual value is
  how the manual value is removed.
- **A refetch happens only when the user asks.** Per title, or in bulk ("refresh metadata for
  this library"), through the same queue. It refetches the **selected** source and never
  touches a manual field. There is no TTL-driven background refresh.

**A newly added file is a first fetch, not a refresh.** A new episode of a series already in
the library is fetched when it is filed, like any new title. This matters because the obvious
misreading of "no automatic refresh" is "new episodes never get metadata".

### 3. What is stored

| Fact | Level | Authored by | Where it survives |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| the value of each field | column | whoever last set it | the database — derivable from the rest |
| **which source this title follows**, and its provider ID there | per title | the default, or the user | database, backup, **sidecar** |
| **which fields are manual** | per field | the user | database, backup, **sidecar** |
| the provider's raw response | cache | — | nowhere that matters |

The two middle rows are exactly what
[D141](#d141--we-write-nfo-too-and-the-lock-markers-are-the-part-that-matters) already writes: *"the
user's corrections plus the provider identifiers needed to re-find the work"*, with the manual
fields as `lockedfields`. **This decision is what D141's lock markers were a picture of.**

The raw response is kept because it is the input
([library-model-review.md](../design/research/library-model-review.md)'s *keep the input*): a
parser change that reads a new field out of it needs no refetch, and switching back to a
source already fetched is free. It is a cache under
[principles §14](../principles/14-a-cache-may-always-be-wrong.md): losing it costs one fetch, on the user's request.

**The source choice is per title and the manual value is per field**, deliberately. A source
choice takes the whole record from one provider, because a title whose name came from one
database and whose cast came from another is the kind of result nobody can explain later.
Individual fixes are what manual fields are for.

### 4. What this retires

- **[D12](#d12--providers-are-sandboxed-wasm-plugins-no-in-process-plugin-code)'s *"field-level
  provider ranking"*** and [tech-metadata.md](../design/research/tech-metadata.md)'s *"ranked
  and merged per field"*. There is no automatic merge across providers. What survives of the
  intent — "a provider change doesn't silently rewrite a user's library" — is now true by
  construction, because nothing refetches without being asked and nothing overwrites a manual
  field when it does.
- **The TTL in D12's *"cache everything, with a TTL and an explicit refresh"*.** The explicit
  refresh stays; the TTL goes.
- **Episode orderings are unaffected.**
  [D96](#d96--an-episodes-position-is-ordering-season-number-and-a-series-declares-its-orderings)
  already made the ordering a declared choice at the series, which is this decision's "which
  source" at series level rather than a per-field merge.
- **Artwork follows the same rule** — a default source, the user's choice permanent — and
  [artwork.md](../design/plans/artwork.md) already says so; only its phrase *"a background
  refresh"* was wrong.
- **Rebuild-from-empty** ([backup-restore.md](../design/plans/backup-restore.md)) costs one call per
  title to the selected source — the same as a first scan — because the source choices come
  back from the backup or the sidecars.

### 5. Open, and what I would do

- **External scores are the flood by definition.** `library-model.md`'s critic and audience
  scores come from several sources and go stale — OMDb alone is the 3.5 days above. **Each
  score source should be opt-in per library**, queued at low priority, never blocking anything
  else, and refreshed only on request like everything else, with `as_of` showing its age. A
  rule over a score that has not been fetched already treats it as unknown
  ([rules-engine.md](../design/plans/rules-engine.md)).
- **Thin metadata from an early fetch stays thin.** A title fetched the day it was released
  often has no overview and episodes named "TBA", and with no automatic refresh it stays like
  that. Within this decision the server may *notice* — "14 titles have incomplete metadata" —
  and offer a one-click refresh. It must not refetch unasked. **To confirm with the project
  owner.**
- **An ambiguous match** (identification.md lists it as unspecified) now has an obvious
  landing place: it is filed on local data, marked, and fixed through this same screen.

**Status:** Decided. Built in M2: one source per title, fetched once, and a refetch only a
person's act; the mechanism revised by D231 (work derived from state), the intent standing. The
screen is [web-client.md](../design/plans/web-client.md)'s metadata editing surface. **Layered by [D182](#d182--metadata-is-a-stack-of-layers-with-one-fetched-layer-re-derivation-reads-only-stored-input-a-new-config-requirement-is-a-default-a-derivation-or-a-question)**: user overrides over one source (an NFO *or* one provider) over local fallbacks. **External scores and the thin-metadata refresh answered by
[D171](#d171--external-scores-are-a-ranked-list-the-first-source-with-a-score-is-the-one-shown-named-and-the-detail-screen-may-show-several)** (2026-09-23).

---

## D171 — External scores are a ranked list: the first source with a score is the one shown, named, and the detail screen may show several

**Decided** (2026-09-23), by the project owner, answering the first open item of
[D170](#d170--one-source-per-title-fetched-once-a-users-correction-is-permanent-and-every-refetch-is-an-act-of-the-user):

> *"Give them a prioritized list. Whichever prioritized source has a score is the one we show
> (with an indicator of which source it's using). We may even want to allow multiple rating
> sources that get displayed on the detail screen for a video (IMDB logo + 7.5, tomato logo +
> 7.9, popcorn logo + 7.1)."*

And the second: **the one-click refresh for thin metadata is confirmed.** The server may count
titles whose metadata is incomplete and offer to refresh them; it never refetches unasked.

### 1. The shape

- **A library has an ordered list of score sources.** Wherever one score is shown — a poster
  tile, a list row — it is **the first source in the list that has a score for that title**,
  with that source's mark beside it. A score is never shown without saying whose it is.
- **The detail screen may show several**, each with its mark, in list order.
- Stored as `library-model.md` already has it: `(source, kind, score, vote_count, as_of)` at the
  Title. Critic and audience are separate rows — the tomato and the popcorn are two `kind`s of
  one source.

### 2. How it stays inside D170

- **Sources that come free are free.** TMDB's vote average arrives with the TMDB fetch; one
  OMDb call returns IMDb, Rotten Tomatoes' critic score and Metacritic together. Fetching is per
  *call*, not per score.
- **Only the list's first reachable source is fetched at scan time**, and only if the library
  opted into it (D170 §5). The rest are fetched **when someone opens the detail screen** — one
  title, a few calls, on a user's act, then kept. A library of 3,500 titles never fetches the
  third-ranked source for films nobody looked at.
- **Fallback is a display rule, not a fetch rule.** If IMDb has no score for a title, the tile
  shows the next source *already stored*; it does not go asking.

### 3. Three things the list must not do (recommendations)

- **Never mix scales in a sort or a rule.** A fallback list puts IMDb's 7.5 (a mean of votes out
  of 10) next to the Tomatometer's 79% (the share of critics who were positive) — different
  quantities, not different units. Displaying them side by side with their marks is honest;
  **sorting "by score" across them is not**. So a sort or a rule names **one source and kind**;
  the ranked list is for display only. Titles without that source's score sort last as unknown,
  as [rules-engine.md](../design/plans/rules-engine.md)'s coverage rule already treats them.
- **Show each score on its own scale.** 79% stays 79%, not 7.9; the mark tells the reader how to
  read it. (The owner's "tomato 7.9" is exactly the conversion to avoid.)
- ~~**A score with too few votes counts as absent.**~~ *Withdrawn by D172: shown with its count.* IMDb 9.6 from 11 votes is noise, and a
  fallback that skips it is better than one that shows it. The threshold is per source, stored
  with the list.

**Honest limit:** Rotten Tomatoes' audience score (the popcorn) is not in OMDb and Rotten
Tomatoes has no public API. It is available only through a provider that scrapes, which is a
plugin's business ([D12](#d12--providers-are-sandboxed-wasm-plugins-no-in-process-plugin-code)),
not a built-in.

**Status:** Decided. Schema already in `library-model.md`; the list is library configuration;
the tile and detail rendering belong to the clients. **Revised by [D172](#d172--a-low-vote-count-is-shown-not-hidden-an-ambiguous-match-is-never-guessed-and-selecting-it-asks-rather-than-plays)** (2026-09-23): the vote
threshold no longer hides a score — the count is shown beside it, and a low count means
"refresh on detail view"; the popcorn is out of scope.

---

## D172 — A low vote count is shown, not hidden; an ambiguous match is never guessed, and selecting it asks rather than plays

**Decided** (2026-09-23), by the project owner, revising
[D171](#d171--external-scores-are-a-ranked-list-the-first-source-with-a-score-is-the-one-shown-named-and-the-detail-screen-may-show-several)
and settling ambiguous matches:

> *"We won't worry about hard to fetch metadata. That can be a feature or plugin added later.
> I only care about the easy data for now.*
>
> *We should allow scores with too few votes, but show the number of votes: IMDB logo + 9.6
> (11), which later settles down to IMDB logo + 8.1 (914). For cases where there are too few
> samples for a stable result, it would make sense to fetch on detail page view.*
>
> *Ambiguity: … I have a number of items in my library that show up as the wrong thing, and
> it's worse than not finding it at all. What we can also do is put a big question mark over
> the entry in the video selection screen (posters), or some kind of indicator when they are in
> detailed listing mode. Selecting an ambiguous entry brings up the selector for them to confirm
> what it is rather than trying to enter/play it."*

### 1. Scope: easy data only

Built-in sources are the ones with a public API and a usable free tier — **TMDB, and OMDb for
IMDb, Rotten Tomatoes' critic score and Metacritic**. Anything that needs scraping (Rotten
Tomatoes' audience score among them) is a later feature or a plugin
([D12](#d12--providers-are-sandboxed-wasm-plugins-no-in-process-plugin-code)). D171's
"honest limit" becomes simply out of scope.

### 2. Scores: the vote count is shown, not used as a filter

- **D171's vote threshold is withdrawn.** A score is shown whatever its vote count, **with the
  count beside it**: *IMDb 9.6 (11)*, later *IMDb 8.1 (914)*. The reader judges; the server does
  not hide.
- **An unsettled score is refetched when its detail page is opened.** Below a per-source vote
  count the score is still moving, so opening the detail page refreshes that title's scores.
  This is the one refetch not requested by name, and it stays inside
  [D170](#d170--one-source-per-title-fetched-once-a-users-correction-is-permanent-and-every-refetch-is-an-act-of-the-user)'s
  intent: one title, triggered by a person looking at it, never a sweep. **Recommended:** at
  most once a day per title (by `as_of`), so a browsing session does not become a loop of calls.
- The vote-count threshold therefore survives with a different job: not "hide this" but "this
  is still worth refreshing on view".

### 3. Ambiguous matches: never guessed

A wrong match is worse than no match — it shows the wrong poster, synopsis and rating for a film
the user owns, and nothing says it is a guess. So:

1. **A provider ID in hand skips the search** — from an NFO, or in the name (`{tmdb-480631}`).
2. **A clear winner is accepted**: one result whose title and year both match the parse.
3. **Anything else is not guessed.** The title is listed on local data, marked **ambiguous**,
   and **the search results are kept**, so the choice costs no further call.
4. **The mark is visible where the title is**: a large question mark over the poster in the
   grid, an indicator in list view, and a library filter — *"12 titles need a choice"* — beside
   the thin-metadata count ([D171](#d171--external-scores-are-a-ranked-list-the-first-source-with-a-score-is-the-one-shown-named-and-the-detail-screen-may-show-several)).
5. **Selecting an ambiguous title opens the chooser**, not the title. The candidates are shown
   with poster, year and runtime beside the file's own duration; confirming one files it and
   makes the choice permanent (D170). "None of these" opens the same search-another-source
   screen as any correction.

**Recommended, for people who may not edit metadata:** they see the question mark and can play
the title normally — the file is theirs to watch; only the identification is uncertain. And
under a restricting rule an ambiguous title has **no rating**, which
[rules-engine.md](../design/plans/rules-engine.md)'s coverage rule already denies, so a child
never sees an unidentified film on the strength of a guess.

**Cheap because of earlier decisions:** watch state lives on the File
([D157](#d157--a-position-belongs-to-the-file-completion-rolls-up-the-position-never-does)),
so confirming or changing a match moves nothing a user would miss.

**Status:** Decided. Identification behaviour in `identification.md`; the grid, list and chooser
belong to the clients.

---

## D173 — A replaced file is a deletion and an addition; what is in a file's timeline dies with the file, and what is about the work survives at the Title

**Decided** (2026-09-23), by the project owner, rejecting a proposal to carry a resume position
across a Radarr-style upgrade:

> *"A 1080 file replaced with a 4k one is two things: the 1080 cut has been deleted; the 4k cut
> has been added. Even if it claims to be the same cut, we can't guarantee that everything will
> still line up.*
>
> *Also, if the user has Groundhog Day from one rip, deletes it, and gets the 'same' film from
> another source, we can't be sure that everything will still match up. What if the new rip,
> while still the same 'cut', had previews inserted?"*

**Extends [D167](#d167--absence-is-never-a-reason-to-destroy-a-download-whose-server-copy-is-gone-is-orphaned-not-deleted-and-entitlement-is-the-only-thing-the-lease-may-remove)'s
tombstone invariant with its mechanics, and applies
[D158](#d158--we-group-files-for-browsing-and-never-relate-their-timelines-the-continuation-offer-is-withdrawn)
to replacement.** D158 already says we never relate two files' timelines; an upgrade is two
files that happen not to coexist, and not coexisting does not make them relatable. Four minutes
of trailers at the front of a re-rip shifts every timestamp by four minutes, and "same cut" in
a filename or a provider ID is an assertion about the story, not about the byte timeline.

### 1. The split

| Bound to the **file's timeline** — dies with the File (tombstoned with it) | About the **work** — survives at the Title |
| --- | --- |
| resume position ([D157](#d157--a-position-belongs-to-the-file-completion-rolls-up-the-position-never-does)) | watched / completion |
| watched spans (kept as history, never re-pointed) | rating, favourite, tags |
| subtitle and audio sync offsets | the identification choice (D170) |
| media segments — intro, credits ([D82](#d82--media-segments-are-typed-attach-at-the-version-and-carry-provenance)) | extra relations between Titles |
| chapters, trickplay, a subtitle verified against this file | a user-authored Edition *and its name* — but see §3 |

The test is one question: **is it expressed in seconds of this file?** If so it belongs to the
file and cannot be moved. That is D157's split — the position is on the File, completion rolls
up — recognised as a general rule rather than a fact about positions.

### 2. Consequences

- **An upgrade is observed as a delete and an add**, including when Sonarr's or Radarr's
  "On File Upgrade" webhook names both paths. The webhook is a hint to scan now, not a claim of
  identity.
- **A half-watched film whose file was replaced leaves Continue Watching.** Its position
  belongs to a file that no longer exists, and resuming a different file at that time is the
  guess this decision declines. The new file starts at zero; the old position stays in the log.
  *(Recommended; the alternative — keep the row with "the file you were watching was removed" —
  is noise for the common upgrade case.)*
- **Watched survives, because it is about the work.** "I have seen Groundhog Day" is true of
  every rip.

### 3. Correction to what I told the owner

When explaining tombstones I said re-adding a film would bring back *"its watched mark, your
edition name and your extra links"*. Two of three. The Edition and its name survive on the
Title, but **the new file does not join it automatically** — that would be asserting it is the
same cut, which is §1's error. It arrives with no Edition
([D155](#d155--eidr-checked-against-its-own-schema-the-levels-are-right-the-citation-was-a-proposal-and-edition-must-be-optional)),
and the user may place it in their named Edition with one action.

### 4. The tombstone's mechanics, which D167 named but did not specify

1. **Enforced by the schema, not by care.** Every foreign key from history or authored data is
   `ON DELETE RESTRICT`, so a hard delete of a referenced row fails loudly — a
   [principles §10](../principles/10-only-what-a-client-may-use.md) alarm. It depends on `_foreign_keys=on`, which
   [D31](#d31--sqlite-with-a-pure-go-driver-supersedes-d5) already sets; SQLite ignores
   foreign keys on any connection that does not.
2. **Identifiers are never reused.** SQLite without `AUTOINCREMENT` issues the largest current
   rowid plus one, so deleting the newest row hands its number to the next file — and every
   span still pointing at it silently describes a different film. Tombstoning prevents this by
   keeping the row; `AUTOINCREMENT` on referenced tables makes it true even if something does
   delete.
3. **Uniqueness ignores the dead.** "One live File per path" is a partial unique index
   (`WHERE removed_at IS NULL`), or a re-rip at the same path collides with its own tombstone.
4. **Live is the default view.** Queries read views that exclude tombstones, so nobody has to
   remember to — the failure of tombstoning is dead films in the browser.
5. **A merge redirects rather than deletes.** When two Titles prove to be one (a corrected
   match, [D172](#d172--a-low-vote-count-is-shown-not-hidden-an-ambiguous-match-is-never-guessed-and-selecting-it-asks-rather-than-plays)),
   the loser records `merged_into`, and references resolve through it.
6. **Removing history on purpose is allowed.** The invariant protects what history points *at*,
   not history itself: a user deleting an entry from their own history deletes their spans;
   deleting a user purges theirs; and an explicit admin **purge** removes a tombstone together
   with everything that references it, behind a confirmation — never one without the other.

**Cost:** a File row is a few hundred bytes; a library replacing 1,000 files a year accumulates
well under a megabyte of tombstones in a decade.

**Status:** Decided. Schema, due with `library-model.md`; the Continue Watching consequence in
`play-state.md`.

## D174 — Sharing is an account from outside the house; a household behind a grantee is a "rebroadcast" grant, deferred, and it makes another server a source

**Decided** (2026-09-23), by the project owner, in the feature-register audit. The question was
what *sharing with another household* adds over adding accounts, and the answer in this design
is: very little, because [sharing-model.md](../design/plans/sharing-model.md) already made
*"a share is a role with one member"*
([D76](#d76--a-share-is-a-grantee-plus-a-predicate-and-it-fails-closed), [D130](#d130--a-role-is-a-named-policy-object-users-are-assigned-to-one-never-configured-individually)). Plex needs a distinct
feature because a friend sees your library **inside their own server's app**, which needs a
central identity and federation — both declined ([D13](#d13--no-telemetry-no-account-no-upsell--as-a-stated-promise), F77).

### 1. Now: invite someone outside the house

An account, a role, and two differences from a household member:

| | Household member | Invited from outside |
| --- | --- | --- |
| arrives by | the owner creating them | an **invite link**, redeemed on their own device |
| sees of the household | members, activity, shared state | **nothing** — no user list, no one else's activity |
| downloads | indefinite lease | finite, set on the invite ([D169](#d169--a-lease-is-indefinite-by-default-expiry-is-a-property-of-a-conditional-relationship-and-the-servers-prepared-rendition-is-a-cache-rather-than-a-referent)) |
| bandwidth and streams | role default | a ceiling that matters (F31) |
| edit, delete | per role | never |

The register's "sharing" becomes this row. It is small and almost entirely designed already.

### 2. Later: a rebroadcast grant

The owner's shape for the friend who has a household of his own:

> *"With a 'rebroadcast' grant, he can allow any member of his household to view my libraries as
> if it were his own, and also have an overlay database that allows him to override my tags for
> his own kids, or add his own. My library becomes just another source from his perspective,
> albeit prepopulated with metadata. Note that rebroadcast is not transitive. He can't share my
> libraries with others in this way; only his own. This isn't a feature that's needed soon."*

That is **server-to-server**: the grantee is his server, not a person, and his household are his
users under his roles. It reverses F77's decline in a narrow form — one hop, one grant, no
directory. The pieces map onto things already in the tree:

- **My library is a source to his server** — structurally a remote node whose observations
  arrive with assertions already attached. My identifications reach him the way a sidecar
  reaches a scan ([D141](#d141--we-write-nfo-too-and-the-lock-markers-are-the-part-that-matters)):
  as asserted values his side may override.
- **His overlay** is his own database: tags, corrections, roles and rules for his children,
  none of which ever reaches mine.
- **His household's play state lives on his server** — his users are his. My server sees one
  grantee's streams, counted against that grant's ceilings. This revises
  sharing-model.md's *"playback state lives with the media, keyed by the grantee"* for this
  case only.
- **Non-transitive by construction:** an item whose source is another server cannot be offered
  onward by a rebroadcast grant. As everywhere in sharing, this is intent, not enforcement —
  anyone who can play a file can re-transmit it.

### 3. What it owes the architecture now

Deferred, so only the doors:

1. **A grantee may be a server, not only a person.** The grant table
   ([D154](#d154--one-grant-table-opaque-and-revocable-the-session-credential-never-appears-in-a-url))
   must not assume a subject is a user.
2. **A Version's file need not be local.** Obligation #1 (*an item need not have a File*) already
   covers most of it; add that a file may be reached through another server.
3. **Every item carries its source**, so "was this given to me?" is a column, not an inference —
   which is what non-transitivity is checked against.

**Open for when it is built:** whether his household's streams come from my server directly,
with a token his server mints within my grant, or through his server — which doubles his
bandwidth. Measure before choosing.

**Status:** §1 decided and registered; §2 deferred (rank 2 for its obligations). **§2–§3 corrected by [D177](#d177--a-rebroadcaster-is-a-user-whose-core-treats-our-server-as-a-node-and-his-household-plays-on-derived-grants-that-only-his-core-can-mint)**: the grantee is a user, his core treats our server as a node, and his household plays on derived grants.

## D175 — Watch Together for two, remote, moves to directly after the web client; voice is there from the start

**Decided** (2026-09-23), by the project owner: *"I want Watch Together to have high priority
because my gf is going to be remote for a long time. The rest don't need high priority if it
doesn't help."*

This is the design's best case, not a stretch: [watch-together.md](../design/plans/watch-together.md)
already ranks **two** as priority 1, because echo is fully solvable there
([D65](#d65--playback-offset-is-per-participant-and-it-is-an-echo-control)), a stall has an obvious answer, and the relay is free. What moves is the
schedule, and three dependencies with it.

### 1. Voice is day one

> *"Either she's going to be playing the movie on her phone while talking to me, or she'll have it
> playing on a TV and talking through her phone, and then the echo problem creeps in. I can
> adapt on my side by playing through a laptop."*

The design already covers both configurations ([D63](#d63--voice-chat-is-webrtc-and-headphones-are-the-supported-configuration), [D65](#d65--playback-offset-is-per-participant-and-it-is-an-echo-control)):

| Her setup | His setup | Echo | Handled by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| film and voice on her phone, earbuds | laptop, any | none | tier 1 |
| film on her phone's speaker | laptop, headphones | her phone's platform AEC — if the film plays on the official media path it is a reference | tier 1, and to verify on her actual phone |
| **film on the TV, voice on her phone** | **laptop, headphones** | only her side leaks | **tier 2: she runs ahead by the one-way latency, her leak arrives aligned with his copy, and it fuses** |
| film on the TV, voice on her phone | laptop **speakers** | both sides leak | tier 3 (content-referenced AEC) — so he wears headphones |

**Headphones on his side turn every configuration of hers into a solved case.** That is the
supported setup, and tier 3 stays later. Voice uses [D68](#d68--turn-is-not-an-independent-requirement-the-media-server-is-already-the-relay)'s
server relay, which at two is free.

### 2. Reachability: port-forward if the ISP allows it, the relay if not

She is non-technical, but **reachability is the server's problem, not hers**: from her side it is
always an invite link (D174 §1). What differs is the owner's side:

- **If the ISP allows a port-forward** — plus TLS — it is the whole answer for now, and costs
  nothing to build beyond certificates.
- **If it does not** — usually carrier-grade NAT, recognisable when the router's WAN address is
  in `100.64.0.0/10` or differs from what an external "what is my IP" reports — then
  [D71](#d71--one-relay-artefact-three-jobs-and-the-core-dials-out-to-it)'s relay moves forward with Watch Together. **IPv6 is the check before that**:
  many CGNAT providers hand out global IPv6, and if both ends have it, direct connection works.

**The owner tests the ISP first; the answer decides whether the relay is on the critical path.**

### 3. Bandwidth: a prepared version, not live transcoding

watch-together.md gates a remote party on adaptive bitrate (Phase 4b). For two people watching a
film **they chose in advance**, the batch compatibility transcoder (Phase 4a) is enough: prepare
a ~8 Mbps 1080p Version ahead of time, and it direct-plays like any other. Live ABR stays late;
**4a moves forward** with Watch Together. A film not prepared still plays if her link carries the
original.

### 4. The resulting order

Web client (phone-good, D176) → Watch Together LAN half → **reachability** (port-forward, or
the relay) → **invite from outside** (D174) → **prepared versions** (4a) → **remote Watch
Together for two, with voice**. Everything else in cuts B–D keeps its place.

**Open:** what devices she has. It decides the path to her TV: from an Android phone the web
client can cast ([D124](#d124--the-playback-role-may-be-a-cast-receiver-and-for-a-guest-that-is-the-best-path-the-phone-controls-it-does-not-relay)); from an iPhone, Safari cannot use the Cast SDK and the route is
AirPlay to an Apple TV, or the TV watching the film on its own browser.

**Status:** Decided; ROADMAP reordered. Her devices and the path to her television: [D177](#d177--a-rebroadcaster-is-a-user-whose-core-treats-our-server-as-a-node-and-his-household-plays-on-derived-grants-that-only-his-core-can-mint).

## D176 — Register audit: phones are the web client for now, the file browser is the last resort, "now playing" is added, music awaits research

**Decided** (2026-09-23), by the project owner, reviewing the register
([D153](#d153--a-ranked-feature-register-ordered-by-demand-and-annotated-by-retrofit-cost-because-those-are-different-numbers)) against D160–D173.

- **Phones: web first.** *"We focus on web clients first until we get most of the UI sorted out,
  then we go into specific target clients well-armed with UI flows."* Consequence: **the web
  client must be good on a phone from the start** — touch, small screens, iPhone Safari's
  constraints — because it *is* the phone client until native ones exist. iOS has no native
  plan and does not need one yet.
- **F58, folder browsing, is the escape hatch of last resort** — an admin view of the tree
  where every file shows **what it is attached to and how**: its filing and reason, its place
  (Title → Edition → Version, or the work it is an extra of), and whether that came from
  inference, an asserted sidecar, or a person. F88 is the same data seen as a library; F58 is
  it seen as folders.
- **Now playing (new, F89, rank 1).** Admin sees every session; everyone else sees their own.
  Per stream: who, what, which device, where (LAN, remote, relay), direct play or transcode
  **with the stated reason**, bitrate against the ceiling, and **client-reported buffer
  health** — the field that answers "why is it buffering". Actions: **stop with a message**,
  and lower a stream's ceiling on the spot. Live only; history is play statistics' job.
- **Music: undecided, pending research** — competitor and sentiment research to the usual
  standard, commercial players first. The owner's concrete wish, *"my music collection playing
  through the TV"*, is recorded as the case to judge it by.
- **Stale rows corrected:** F39 (no retention horizon, D165), F40 (ranked display and easy
  sources, D171/D172), F46 and obligation #10 (met by D90: rate is local unless a group shares
  it), F26 (now includes the ambiguous-match chooser and the thin-metadata refresh), F50
  (designed by D89; tombstones by D167/D173).
- **Two tensions recorded:** F41's scheduled refresh is permitted under
  [D170](#d170--one-source-per-title-fetched-once-a-users-correction-is-permanent-and-every-refetch-is-an-act-of-the-user) because **subscribing to a list is the user's standing request** — one call
  per list, schedule visible on it. And F15's rank hides a chain: remote access over a bad link
  needs F31, F32 and bandwidth transcoding ([D86](#d86--adaptation-is-the-client-re-picking-on-a-buffer-signal-and-it-puts-bandwidth-transcoding-on-remote-accesss-critical-path)).

**Status:** Decided. Register and roadmap updated. The release-cut restructure proposed in the
same audit is **not** decided. *(Settled the same day by [D178](#d178--the-first-release-is-for-two-people-the-owner-at-home-and-one-person-remote-watching-together-with-subtitles): the first cut is
defined by its two users.)*

## D177 — A rebroadcaster is a user whose core treats our server as a node, and his household plays on derived grants that only his core can mint

**Decided** (2026-09-23), by the project owner, **correcting [D174](#d174--sharing-is-an-account-from-outside-the-house-a-household-behind-a-grantee-is-a-rebroadcast-grant-deferred-and-it-makes-another-server-a-source) §2–§3**, which had
made the grantee a server:

> *"A grantee is a user, like any other. When he's granted rebroadcast rights, he can plug his
> account on my server into his core, so my core or relay becomes just another node as far as
> his side is concerned … We would then need a way for him to grant playback rights on MY
> server to HIS household accounts, in a way that doesn't allow other third party users to also
> playback."*

### 1. What changes

- **No new kind of principal.** He is an ordinary user with one more capability on his role,
  `rebroadcast`. His core signs in *as him* — the same rule every adapter already obeys
  ([D105](#d105--a-protocol-adapter-acts-as-the-user-never-as-itself): an adapter acts as the
  user, never as itself).
- **To his core, our server is a node** — one that answers observations and serves media, with
  our metadata attached as assertions his side may override. The node's contract must not
  assume a local filesystem daemon; that is the door this keeps open.
- **D174's obligation *"a grantee may be a server"* is withdrawn**, replaced by §2's.

### 2. Derived grants: how his household plays without anyone else being able to

The grant table ([D154](#d154--one-grant-table-opaque-and-revocable-the-session-credential-never-appears-in-a-url))
gains one column, `parent`. A user holding `rebroadcast` may mint a **derived grant** under
his own:

| Property | Rule | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| scope | **within the parent's** — his predicate, never wider | his household sees at most what he does |
| lifetime | **short** — one playback session, minutes to start | a copied link is worth little |
| label | an opaque tag from his side naming the household member | so *now playing* (F89) can say "Ben (via Mark)" without us knowing Ben |
| may mint | **never** — a derived grant has no `rebroadcast` | non-transitive by construction |
| counted against | **the parent's** stream and bandwidth ceilings | his household is one grantee to us |
| revoked by | him, or us; **revoking him revokes all of it** | one `UPDATE`, and entitlement is checked at use ([D168](#d168--entitlement-is-resolved-at-the-point-of-use-never-pushed-revocation-needs-no-message-and-the-notification-is-a-latency-optimisation-that-may-always-be-lost)) |

**Only his core can mint**, because minting needs his credential and his core holds it. So the
set of people who can play is exactly the set of users on his server who his rules allow — which
is what "his household" means operationally. A third party would need to be a user on his
server. We cannot stop him adding a friend to his server; that is the same *intent, not
enforcement* line sharing already draws, and the parent's ceilings bound what it costs.

**Cost of the check:** entitlement already costs 6.64 µs per request; the parent's liveness is
one more hash lookup (≈3 µs), and depth is always one because a derived grant cannot mint.

### 3. Obligations, revised

- ~~A grantee may be a server~~ → **a grant may have a parent**: narrower, shorter-lived,
  never able to mint, dead when the parent is.
- **A node need not be a local filesystem daemon** — it may be another core, acting as a user.
- Unchanged: a file may be reached through another server; every item carries its source.

**Open for when it is built:** whether his household's bytes come from us directly on a derived
grant, or through his core. Through his core costs him nothing extra when they are at home — his
core fetches once and serves his LAN — and doubles his upload only when one of them is away.

**Status:** Decided in shape, deferred in schedule (F91).

**Also recorded here — the remote viewer's devices** ([D175](#d175--watch-together-for-two-remote-moves-to-directly-after-the-web-client-voice-is-there-from-the-start)'s open item): a MacBook Air,
an iPhone and a Samsung television with Google TV. The best first path is **Chrome on the MacBook
casting to the television** through our cast receiver
([D124](#d124--the-playback-role-may-be-a-cast-receiver-and-for-a-guest-that-is-the-best-path-the-phone-controls-it-does-not-relay)),
with **voice on the iPhone**. Safari on iOS and macOS cannot cast, so the iPhone is the voice
device, not the sender. The film on the MacBook alone, voice and all, is the simplest fallback.
The native Android TV client (Phase 3) later runs on that television directly.

## D178 — The first release is for two people: the owner at home and one person remote, watching together with subtitles

**Decided** (2026-09-23), by the project owner, settling D176's open restructure: *"I only care
about me and my gf for now. I'll need subtitles because so many movies have terrible audio when
played through my TV (too loud background with too quiet voice)."*

### 1. The rule

**The first cut is defined by its two users**, and a feature is in it only if one of them needs
it. Everything else keeps its rank in [FEATURES.md](../../FEATURES.md) and its place in the phases,
and is ordered later. **The schema still lands whole**: every table on the register's
obligations list exists from the first release even if nothing fills it yet — the retrofit
argument ([principles §12](../principles/12-defer-the-work-never-the-seam.md)) is about tables, not features, and it is
unchanged.

> **Narrowed by [D180](#d180--a-prepared-renditions-play-state-is-its-sources-additive-schema-comes-with-its-feature-mistakes-are-assumed-so-migration-needs-a-policy) §2** (2026-09-23): additive schema arrives with its feature; what
> lands in Cut A is only what a later schema could not add without reshaping — keys and
> identity, the four levels, position on File, tombstones and the rest of D180's list.

### 2. What is in it

| Need | Features |
| --- | --- |
| a library that is right | scan (F1), identify with the ambiguous-match chooser and manual fixes (F2, F26, D170–D172), the four levels and versions (F3, F20), extras (F19), NFO read, **what the scanner saw** (F88) |
| playing it in a browser | direct play (F4), negotiation (F9), **remux to fMP4 and audio transcoding** — mandatory rather than optional, because browsers and Chromecast refuse MKV and most of TrueHD, DTS and AC-3 |
| finding and resuming | browse and search (F5), play state and Continue Watching (F7), artwork (F10) |
| **subtitles** | embedded and sidecar tracks with fonts and libass rendering (F8); **a sync offset control** (D90); **acquisition on request** for a title that has none (F27's fetch half — per title, by a person, which is also the only thing OpenSubtitles' 20 downloads a day permits); a preference to have them on by default (the minimal part of F33) |
| **quiet dialogue** | [D83](#d83--loudness-is-measured-at-scan-and-applied-as-gain-downmix-has-one-default-and-a-dialogue-control-drc-is-per-device)'s **dialogue boost**, see §3 |
| two users | local accounts and sessions (F6), invite from outside (F90) |
| watching together | Watch Together for two with voice (F35, D175), reachability (port-forward or the relay), prepared ~8 Mbps versions (Phase 4a), the cast receiver for her television (F21, D177) |
| keeping it running | backup and restore (F12), now playing (F89) |
| the architecture | media nodes (F13), the web client good on a phone (F11, D176) |

### 3. The dialogue problem is a downmix problem, and the fix is already designed

*"Too loud background with too quiet voice"* on television speakers is almost always a **5.1 mix
folded down to stereo**. Dialogue lives in the centre channel; a standard downmix attenuates it
and sums the surrounds and effects on top. Jellyfin ships five downmix algorithms and its own
documentation records a quiet-dialogue complaint against nearly every one.
[D83](#d83--loudness-is-measured-at-scan-and-applied-as-gain-downmix-has-one-default-and-a-dialogue-control-drc-is-per-device) already chose one default matrix plus a **dialogue-boost** control — centre
gain in the downmix — as a per-user preference. It belongs in this cut, and it is cheap:

- **It needs the downmix, not the loudness scan.** Loudness normalisation needs a 31-hour
  measurement pass over the library; the dialogue boost needs only the audio transcode path this
  cut already requires. The measurement pass stays later.
- **It only works if we do the downmix.** If the television receives 5.1 and folds it down
  itself, our boost never runs. So the device declares *"my output is stereo speakers"* (the
  same per-device declaration D83 uses for dynamic range) and the server sends a boosted stereo
  mix to it.
- **Subtitles and boost are complements:** subtitles for the films where boost is not enough.

### 4. What is out, for now

Roles and parental controls (F16) — two adults; the `role` table still exists. Collections as
sequences (F17), orderings beyond aired (F18 — schema only), offline download (F22), segment
detection (F23), **loudness measurement** (F24's pass), trickplay (F25 — a 9.2-day pass),
**subtitle verification** (F27's speech map — a 31-hour pass; the offset control covers the
failures by hand meanwhile), NFO write (F29), TV pairing and the native TV client (F30, F34),
ceilings and adaptation (F31, F32), the Jellyfin adapter (F38), OIDC/LDAP, the rules engine's
authoring surfaces, play statistics (F39), and live bandwidth transcoding.

**Phase 0 narrows accordingly:** the survey question is now what fraction of the owner's
library direct-plays in Chrome, Safari and a Chromecast, and what the remainder needs — remux,
audio, or video.

**Status:** Decided. ROADMAP gains a "Cut A" section ahead of the phases; FEATURES marks the cut.

---

## D179 — A file's identity is a hash of its media payload, not its bytes; a rebuild restores the identity rows and runs an ordinary scan; duplicates are surfaced

**Decided** (2026-09-23), by the project owner, in the data-architecture critique.

### 1. What the critique found

The database is a rebuildable index ([D7](#d7--the-files-are-the-source-of-truth-the-database-is-a-rebuildable-index)),
and the backup deliberately omits the library index as regenerable
([backup-restore.md](../design/plans/backup-restore.md)). But everything the backup *does* keep
— watch state, spans, preferences, tags, shares — references library rows by id. **Rebuild the
index and those ids are reissued, and the restored history points at nothing, or at the wrong
film.** The index is rebuildable; its keys are not.

I proposed integer keys plus a public UUID. The owner asked what the UUID accomplishes, and the
answer is **nothing**: an id means "this row is that file" only through the evidence that binds
them, and whatever restores the evidence can restore the integer id itself. A UUID earns its
place when several parties mint ids without coordinating, and nothing here does — devices never
mint library rows, sidecars carry provider ids
([D141](#d141--we-write-nfo-too-and-the-lock-markers-are-the-part-that-matters)), and a
rebroadcaster references ours ([D177](#d177--a-rebroadcaster-is-a-user-whose-core-treats-our-server-as-a-node-and-his-household-plays-on-derived-grants-that-only-his-core-can-mint)). **Withdrawn; library-model.md's "UUID primary
keys" is replaced by integer keys that are never reissued ([D173](#d173--a-replaced-file-is-a-deletion-and-an-addition-what-is-in-a-files-timeline-dies-with-the-file-and-what-is-about-the-work-survives-at-the-title)).**

What survives: **anything outside the database that refers to a file carries its evidence, not
only its id** — a registered download records the source's identity hash, so it can reattach
even after a rebuild with no backup.

### 2. A rebuild is an ordinary scan

The core must already decide *"is this the same file as before?"* every day — scanner.md says
the core concludes a move from a disappearance and an appearance, and never said how. That
missing rule is the whole of the rebuild problem, so one procedure does both:

1. **Restore the identity rows** — every File's id, identity hash, payload length, mtime and
   last path, tombstones included — all marked **unconfirmed**. They are backed up although the
   rest of the index is not; about a megabyte for the reference library.
2. **Run a normal scan.** Each observation is matched against identities by the rules below.

No separate restore path: the rebuild is the ordinary path from an unusual starting state —
[principles §14](../principles/14-a-cache-may-always-be-wrong.md) applied to identity.

| Observed against an identity | Conclusion |
| --- | --- |
| same identity hash and path | **same file** |
| same identity hash, different path | **same file, moved or renamed** — history follows it |
| same path, different identity hash | **a different file at that path** — new row, the old one tombstoned (D173) |
| two observations match one identity | **duplicates** — the one at the recorded path keeps the identity; **both are surfaced in the admin area** |
| matches nothing | **new file** |

**Titles, Editions and Versions bind through their Files and provider ids**, Files first
because their evidence is strongest: a Version matches when its Files do, a Title through its
provider id and the user's corrections, a user-created Edition through its Versions.

**Drift and unreachable nodes:** an identity nobody reports on **stays unconfirmed** — history
attached, shown unavailable, never tombstoned on silence
([D34](#d34--a-node-status-record-that-distinguishes-dead-from-wedged-from-idle),
[D167](#d167--absence-is-never-a-reason-to-destroy-a-download-whose-server-copy-is-gone-is-orphaned-not-deleted-and-entitlement-is-the-only-thing-the-lease-may-remove)). It becomes a tombstone only when a live node completes a scan of its root
and the file is not there. A rebuilt database starts partial and converges.

### 3. Hash the payload, not the file — measured

The owner: *"We could hash from the end of the header."* Tested against the most common
in-place editor, **mkvpropedit** (MKVToolNix 102.0), on a 94 MB mkvmerge-authored file:

| Edit | Size | Where it wrote | D116 head+tail hash | **Payload hash** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| set title | same | header, into the Void | **changed** | same |
| set a 6 KB title | +6 KB | **moved Info to the end of the file** | **changed** (both ends) | same |
| add 300 global tags | +19 KB | Tags at the end | **changed** (both ends) | same |
| add a 300 KB attachment | +300 KB | appended at the end | **changed** (both ends) | same |
| rename and relabel a track | same | header | **changed** | same |
| `ffmpeg -c copy` remux | +37 KB | **everything** — 52 clusters where there were 70 | changed | **changed** |

**Every in-place tag edit broke [D116](#d116--the-content-hash-is-a-sampling-hash-whole-file-hashing-is-opt-in-and-separate)'s
hash**, and three of five also changed the size and the tail, because mkvpropedit relocates an
element that outgrows its slot to the end of the file rather than shifting 94 MB. The grey case
I had described was not grey: under D116 as written, **fixing a track title sends a film's
history to a tombstone.** mkvpropedit never touched a Cluster.

So **the identity hash is anchored on the media payload**: in Matroska, the first megabyte
from the first Cluster, the last megabyte before the last Cluster ends, and the payload length;
located from the SeekHead, so the cost is a few small reads and no walk over the clusters. In
MP4 the payload is `mdat`, which tag editors leave alone while rewriting `moov` — *not yet
measured*. Containers without a separable header (MPEG-TS, raw streams) keep D116's
head/tail/size.

**A remux is a new file**, as [D173](#d173--a-replaced-file-is-a-deletion-and-an-addition-what-is-in-a-files-timeline-dies-with-the-file-and-what-is-about-the-work-survives-at-the-title) already says of anything re-produced: the
payload is re-laid-out, and whether its timeline still lines up is exactly what we declined to
assume.

### 4. Duplicates are surfaced

Two observations with one identity hash are the same content in two places. That is shown in
the admin area — a filter beside *"needs a choice"* ([D172](#d172--a-low-vote-count-is-shown-not-hidden-an-ambiguous-match-is-never-guessed-and-selecting-it-asks-rather-than-plays)) in the file view (F58,
F88) — naming both paths. Nothing is merged or hidden automatically.

**Status:** Decided. Schema: identity rows are backup-critical. Node: reports the payload
hash. Measurements: `/yoloai/cache/bench/hash/` (not in the repo). **D116 amended; the change
journal is removed from backup's irreplaceable set ([D166](#d166--the-journal-is-an-accelerator-never-a-dependency-the-server-may-always-answer-with-state-and-that-is-the-ordinary-path-rather-than-the-error-path)).**
