## D180 — A prepared rendition's play state is its source's; additive schema comes with its feature; mistakes are assumed, so migration needs a policy

**Decided** (2026-09-23), by the project owner, answering the critique's two remaining points:

> *"Prepared versions: we can just track the source. Retrofit: I'm fine with adding things
> later. The purpose of the exercise was to make sure an earlier schema doesn't preclude adding
> a feature later. However, we must assume that mistakes will be made and we will have to
> migrate. So we need a migration policy, and I want it well-researched."*

### 1. A prepared rendition records against its source File

A server-prepared rendition ([D175](#d175--watch-together-for-two-remote-moves-to-directly-after-the-web-client-voice-is-there-from-the-start)) is produced from one File without cutting, so its
timeline **is** the source's, by construction — the one case
[D158](#d158--we-group-files-for-browsing-and-never-relate-their-timelines-the-continuation-offer-is-withdrawn)'s *"never relate two timelines"* does not reach, because we made it. Positions
and spans are recorded against the **source** File, so watching the 8 Mbps copy remotely and
resuming the original at home is one viewing. The rendition itself is a cache
([D169](#d169--a-lease-is-indefinite-by-default-expiry-is-a-property-of-a-conditional-relationship-and-the-servers-prepared-rendition-is-a-cache-rather-than-a-referent)): it has no play state, no identity row worth backing up, and losing it costs a
re-transcode.

### 2. The register's purpose is "does not preclude", not "exists now"

The retrofit exercise was never "build every table early"; it was **"make sure an earlier schema
does not preclude a later feature."** So:

- **Additive schema arrives with its feature.** A new table or column is cheap in SQLite and
  precludes nothing — loudness, segments, the speech map, certifications, descriptors, scores,
  home rows, artwork type, the rules field registry.
- **What Cut A must get right is what would preclude**: keys and identity
  ([D179](#d179--a-files-identity-is-a-hash-of-its-media-payload-not-its-bytes-a-rebuild-restores-the-identity-rows-and-runs-an-ordinary-scan-duplicates-are-surfaced)), the four levels with optional Edition, position on File, tombstones,
  the translation split, series as Collections with per-ordering positions, extras as a
  relation, tags as a join table, the span shape, grant parents, item source, "an item need not
  have a File", filing on every observation.
- **[D178](#d178--the-first-release-is-for-two-people-the-owner-at-home-and-one-person-remote-watching-together-with-subtitles)'s "the schema lands whole" is narrowed to that list.** The register's
  `schema` retrofit label is read the same way: *owed now* only where adding it later would
  mean reshaping what exists.

### 3. But mistakes are assumed

Getting the preclusion list right reduces migrations; it does not eliminate them. **Some
decision in Cut A will be wrong, and a real user's database will have to be reshaped.** So a
migration policy is required before the first release that stores anyone's data — researched to
the usual standard, commercial players first. *Research in progress; the policy follows as its
own decision.*

**Also corrected here:** D176 annotated F50 as *"designed: D89"*. Deletion is **deferred**
([D144](#d144--deletion-is-deferred-not-designed-away-the-policy-is-the-deliverable-and-the-export-already-carries-the-danger));
D89 is its precondition, not its design.

**Status:** §1–§2 decided; §3 pending research. *(Settled by [D181](#d181--the-migration-policy-two-integers-our-own-small-runner-a-snapshot-that-outlives-success-refuse-what-we-cannot-read-and-re-derive-rather-than-transform), which is §3's
migration policy.)*

---

## D181 — The migration policy: two integers, our own small runner, a snapshot that outlives success, refuse what we cannot read, and re-derive rather than transform

> **Suspended in part by [D228](#d228--until-migrations-are-live-librarydbs-schema-is-a-baseline-and-one-step-and-a-schema-change-folds-the-last-step-into-the-baseline)** until migrations are live: the
> steps are a baseline and one step after it, and a schema change folds the last step into the
> baseline rather than keeping every step forever.

**Decided** (2026-09-23), for the project owner's requirement in
[D180](#d180--a-prepared-renditions-play-state-is-its-sources-additive-schema-comes-with-its-feature-mistakes-are-assumed-so-migration-needs-a-policy) §3. Research: [migrations.md](../design/research/migrations.md) — Chromium,
Firefox, Android Room and Apple Core Data from source; Jellyfin, Plex, Home Assistant, Navidrome,
Sonarr/Radarr, Immich, Gitea and Grafana from source and their trackers; SQLite measured at the
reference scale. Plan: [migrations.md](../design/plans/migrations.md).

### 1. What the research changed

- **The mechanics are free at our scale; correctness is the whole risk.** The worst operation
  measured — a 12-step rebuild of 279,453 spans with indexes, views and a foreign-key check — is
  **1.0 s**; a `VACUUM INTO` snapshot of the 46 MB reference database is **177 ms**. So a snapshot
  before every migration costs nothing, and no migration needs to run online.
- **The ledger is the riskiest code, not the schema.** Jellyfin 10.11's largest incident (#15027,
  121 comments) was translating one migration ledger into another. Ours is **two integers** —
  `user_version` and a `compatible_version` — and never changes format.
- **Something will kill us mid-migration**: Docker healthchecks did it to Jellyfin *"30+ times"*.
  Each step commits on its own and resumes; the health endpoint reports *migrating*, not
  *unhealthy*; `migrate` is also a command.
- **The snapshot must outlive a successful migration.** Jellyfin deleted its pre-migration backup
  on success — exactly when users wanted to go back. Ours is kept, one per from-version, pruned
  with the other backups.
- **Downgrade is designed at upgrade time.** Nobody runs down-migrations in the field. Chromium's
  `compatible_version` — history at v70 still readable by v16 — lets an older release keep working
  whenever the newer one only added; otherwise the older release **refuses and names the snapshot**
  (Gitea, Home Assistant), and never runs anyway (Sonarr: *"Error parsing column 45"*).
- **Re-derive rather than transform.** Our database is mostly an index
  ([D7](#d7--the-files-are-the-source-of-truth-the-database-is-a-rebuildable-index),
  [D179](#d179--a-files-identity-is-a-hash-of-its-media-payload-not-its-bytes-a-rebuild-restores-the-identity-rows-and-runs-an-ordinary-scan-duplicates-are-surfaced)), so a migration of derived data is *drop and rescan* — Navidrome does it in
  23 of ~95 migrations. Careful migration is reserved for the irreplaceable set and the identity
  rows. **No migration touches the filesystem or the network**, the class behind Navidrome #3763,
  #3787 and Jellyfin #14602.
- **A migration error is never called corruption, and nothing is moved aside automatically.**
  Home Assistant #92650 moved a healthy database aside and started empty.

### 2. The choices, briefly

| Question | Answer | Declined |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bookkeeping | `user_version` in the step's transaction, `compatible_version` row, `application_id` | a tool's ledger table |
| Runner | ours, ~150 lines, owning the checks a SQL file cannot fail on | goose (version written outside a no-transaction step), golang-migrate (cannot run our rebuilds), Atlas (free edition mangles views, triggers, FTS5) |
| Step format | SQL files sqlc reads; Go only for data transforms that change no schema | Go-defined schema changes sqlc cannot see |
| Transaction | one per step, resume on interruption | one for the whole chain |
| Downgrade | `compatible_version`, then refuse naming the snapshot | down-migrations; Plex's stored rollback SQL; rewinding the version |
| Oldest upgrade-from | **every step kept, forever** | a floor, until a measured reason |
| Destructive fallback | none for irreplaceable data | Room's `fallbackToDestructiveMigration` |
| Patch releases | no schema steps | Jellyfin 10.11.7's security fix held behind a failing migration |
| Testing | a golden per released version, schema equality with a fresh install, interruption, refusal, restore, a reference-scale budget of 10 s a step | "model has no pending changes" (Jellyfin's only test) |

### 3. Beyond the database

The owner asked what data lives outside it, and the answer widened the policy. **Anything
changeable at runtime lives in the database**; files hold only what must exist before it opens.
Authored files carry a version, are read in every past version, and are **never rewritten by us
unasked**. Formats read by another version — node and core, a phone offline for months — carry a
version per message, readers ignore unknown fields, and the core and a node tolerate one minor
release of skew and **refuse outside it with a reason**. Disposable data (`cache/`, consumed
reports, logs) is **versioned by discard**. Backups restore and then migrate like any older
database.

### 4. What it amends

- **[Principles §7](../principles/07-migrations-are-safety.md)**, *"detect-and-refuse across a version gap rather
  than auto-converting"*, is sharpened: an **older** database is always converted — every step is
  kept — and a **newer** one is refused unless it declared itself compatible.
- **[backup-restore.md](../design/plans/backup-restore.md)**'s *"restore refuses a gap"* becomes:
  an older backup restores and migrates; a newer one is refused by the same rule.
- **[api-compatibility.md](../design/plans/api-compatibility.md)** is unchanged; it is this
  policy's third class.

**Status:** Decided. Due before Cut A stores anyone's data. **Refined by [D182](#d182--metadata-is-a-stack-of-layers-with-one-fetched-layer-re-derivation-reads-only-stored-input-a-new-config-requirement-is-a-default-a-derivation-or-a-question)**: re-derivation reads stored input only; fetched data is migrated, never refetched; config keys are a default, a derivation, a question, or a refusal with a remedy.

---

## D182 — Metadata is a stack of layers with one fetched layer; re-derivation reads only stored input; a new config requirement is a default, a derivation, or a question

> **Amended by [D200](#d200--every-opinionated-value-is-a-setting-row-seeded-with-its-starting-value-nothing-has-a-default-in-code-the-config-file-holds-only-what-must-exist-before-the-database-opens-and-all-of-it-is-required):** a config file key is never defaulted in code; every key is
> required.

**Decided** (2026-09-23), by the project owner, reviewing [D181](#d181--the-migration-policy-two-integers-our-own-small-runner-a-snapshot-that-outlives-success-refuse-what-we-cannot-read-and-re-derive-rather-than-transform):

> *"For re-deriving data, we need to be careful because we allow user-overriding of data, and
> also any derived data not derived from the files themselves could drift over time.*
>
> *When we allow user-overrides of metadata, it's actually an overlay on top of another source
> (NFO file, IMDB, etc). Would we end up with a situation where we have IMDB as a base 'layer',
> with some fields overridden by the NFO, and others by the user?*
>
> *What if we discover that an initial config file (created by the user) needs more info than we
> had in an older version?"*

### 1. Yes: metadata is a stack, and only one layer is ever fetched

Per field, the value shown is the highest layer that has one:

| Layer | Holds | Scope | Where it lives | Changes when |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **1. User override** | a value a person typed, or an NFO field marked `lockedfields` | per field | database, mirrored to the NFO ([D141](#d141--we-write-nfo-too-and-the-lock-markers-are-the-part-that-matters)) | only the person changes it |
| **2. The title's source** | **one** of: the NFO beside the file, or one provider | per title | the NFO file itself, or the provider's cached response | the NFO changes on disk, or the user refreshes ([D170](#d170--one-source-per-title-fetched-once-a-users-correction-is-permanent-and-every-refetch-is-an-act-of-the-user)) |
| **3. Local fallbacks** | embedded container tags, then the filename parse | per field | stored observations | a rescan or a parser improvement |

So the owner's example is exactly the shape: TMDB as the base, some fields from the NFO, some from
the user — **except that the NFO and a provider are not stacked on each other.** They are
alternatives for layer 2, which is what keeps D170's promise: **one fetched source per title, and
nothing merged across providers.**

- **An NFO beside the file is the title's default source**; without one, the library's default
  provider is. Choosing *"use TMDB for this title"* on the D170 screen switches layer 2 without
  touching layer 1.
- **This refines [identification.md](../design/plans/identification.md)'s import rule**, which
  read a whole NFO as a user override. A Kodi NFO is usually a **full scrape** — plot, cast,
  ratings — and treating every field as permanent would freeze it forever. Only the fields a
  person **locked** are layer 1; the rest is a source.
- **Fields missing from the source fall through to layer 3** — a title with no provider match
  still has the filename's year.
- **The layers are stored, and the column is a cache of the resolution**
  ([principles §14](../principles/14-a-cache-may-always-be-wrong.md)) — the column the rules engine and the poster grid
  read.

**One conflict needs a rule, because we both read and write the NFO.** We write a user's override
into the NFO; later another tool, or the user in a text editor, changes that field on disk. Both
are a person. **The later change wins, and the conflict is shown** — *"the NFO changed on disk
after you edited this"* — never resolved silently.

### 2. Re-derivation reads stored input, never the world

D181 said derived data is dropped and re-derived rather than transformed. The owner's correction:
some "derived" data was not derived from the files, and refetching it gets a **different** answer
— the provider changed, rate limits bite, and D170 forbids refetching unasked. So the classes are
three, not two:

| Data | A migration may |
| --- | --- |
| derived from **stored input** — raw probe output, verbatim filenames, cached provider responses, NFO files | **drop and re-derive** it |
| **fetched** from a third party, with no stored response | **migrate it in place**; never refetch |
| **authored** — layer 1, choices, corrections | migrate it in place, and **re-derivation never touches it**, because it sits above whatever is re-derived |

**Drift is honest, not avoided.** A parser improvement re-derives layer 3 and may change what an
item shows; that is the point of D59's replayability. It cannot change anything a person set,
because layer 1 is above it, and it cannot change a title's identification that a person
confirmed ([D172](#d172--a-low-vote-count-is-shown-not-hidden-an-ambiguous-match-is-never-guessed-and-selecting-it-asks-rather-than-plays)), because a confirmation is layer 1 too.

### 3. A config file that needs something new

*"Never rewritten unasked"* holds, and a new version needing more than an old file says is handled
in this order:

1. **A default.** Every new key has one where a default is safe — which is almost always, because
   the file holds only what must exist before the database opens (D181).
2. **A derivation from what is there.** If an old key is split or renamed, the new value is
   derived from the old one **in memory**, with a warning naming the new key. The file is not
   touched.
3. **A question.** If neither is safe, and the value does not have to exist before the database
   opens, **it is not a file key at all**: the server starts and asks for it in the admin UI, and
   it is stored in the database.
4. **A refusal with a remedy.** Only if the value must exist before the database opens and cannot
   be defaulted: the server refuses to start, names the key, shows an example, and offers
   `config upgrade`, which writes the new file **when run** and keeps the old one beside it.
   Running it is the asking.

**Rule for anyone adding a key:** it states which of the four it is. The fourth needs a reason.

**Status:** Decided. identification.md's import rule refined; migrations.md's classes split;
[D170](#d170--one-source-per-title-fetched-once-a-users-correction-is-permanent-and-every-refetch-is-an-act-of-the-user)'s "which fields are manual" is layer 1 of this stack. **Simplified by [D183](#d183--an-override-is-an-override-wherever-its-value-came-from-a-librarys-source-is-asked-not-defaulted-a-default-must-be-safe-to-be-wrong-and-visible-where-it-acts)**:
an override is an override whatever it was picked from (a frozen copy with its origin noted);
"an NFO is the default source" becomes a question at library creation; §3's step 1 applies only
to defaults that are safe to be wrong.

---

## D183 — An override is an override wherever its value came from; a library's source is asked, not defaulted; a default must be safe to be wrong and visible where it acts

> **Amended by [D200](#d200--every-opinionated-value-is-a-setting-row-seeded-with-its-starting-value-nothing-has-a-default-in-code-the-config-file-holds-only-what-must-exist-before-the-database-opens-and-all-of-it-is-required):** settings have no defaults in code. Every opinion is a
> row, seeded with its starting value and shown beside it; §3's *default* marking is replaced.

**Decided** (2026-09-23), by the project owner, simplifying [D182](#d182--metadata-is-a-stack-of-layers-with-one-fetched-layer-re-derivation-reads-only-stored-input-a-new-config-requirement-is-a-default-a-derivation-or-a-question):

> *"We could just treat any override as 'user override', regardless of where the user overrode
> from (the NFO, IMDB, TVDB, etc). Then the user can pick and choose where he gets his info from.
> This won't handle updates in online sources, but I'm not sure if that's such a big idea that we
> need to explode our data structures to support it.*
>
> *I worry about defaults. I've been bitten too many times with defaults that hide behavior the
> user didn't want."*

### 1. Two layers the user controls, one they do not

| Layer | Holds | Stored as |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Override** | any value a person chose for a field — typed, **or picked from** the NFO, TMDB, TheTVDB or any other source the fix screen can show | `(title, field, value, origin, set_at)` — `origin` says where it was picked from, for display only |
| **The title's source** | the NFO *or* one provider | as D170 |
| **Local fallbacks** | embedded tags, the filename | stored observations |

**An override is a frozen copy.** Picking TheTVDB's episode title for one field copies it; if
TheTVDB later corrects it, the override does not follow. The owner accepts that, and it is what
keeps the structure one table: **no per-field source bindings, no multi-provider claims.** A
person who wants the new value picks it again. An NFO's locked fields import as overrides with
`origin = nfo`.

**What this removes from D182:** nothing structural was built yet, so it removes a *concept* —
"per-field source" — before anyone implements it. The pick-and-choose the owner wants comes from
the fix screen fetching one alternative source for one title on request (D170), which already
existed.

### 2. A library's source is asked when the library is created

D182 made *"an NFO beside the file is the title's default source"* — precisely the kind of rule
the owner means: invisible, consequential, and discovered only when a title shows the wrong plot.
So it is **a question at library creation**, with the effect stated:

> *Where should this library's metadata come from?* — **NFO files where present, TMDB for the
> rest** · **TMDB only, ignore NFO files** · **NFO files only, never fetch**

and the answer is shown on the library's settings page and, per field, on every title's fix
screen ("from NFO", "from TMDB", "you set this — picked from TheTVDB").

### 3. The rule for defaults

The owner's concern generalises, and it belongs in the principles as
**[§15](../principles/15-safe-visible-defaults.md)**: a default is a decision made on someone's behalf without
asking, so **it must be safe to be wrong, and visible where it acts.** Where either fails, ask.

The field's example is Plex's *"Empty trash automatically after every scan"*: when a network share
drops, a scan flags its files as deleted and the trash is emptied, taking the entries' metadata
with it. It is safe only while the share never drops, and its effect is stated nowhere near the
switch. *(Plexopedia documents the failure; whether the option was ever on by default is not
verified here — Plex's support page refused the fetch.)* Home Assistant's backup-before-update,
**off by default** since 2025.2, is a verified default of the hiding kind. D34 and D167's *"absence is never evidence"* is this project's
answer to that failure; §15 is the rule behind it.

**Consequence for [D182](#d182--metadata-is-a-stack-of-layers-with-one-fetched-layer-re-derivation-reads-only-stored-input-a-new-config-requirement-is-a-default-a-derivation-or-a-question) §3** (a config file needing something new): step 1, *"a
default"*, now applies only when the default is **safe to be wrong**; otherwise the value is asked
(step 3) or refused with a remedy (step 4). ~~And a defaulted value is **visible**: the settings page
marks it *default*, and startup logs each defaulted key once.~~ [D200](#d200--every-opinionated-value-is-a-setting-row-seeded-with-its-starting-value-nothing-has-a-default-in-code-the-config-file-holds-only-what-must-exist-before-the-database-opens-and-all-of-it-is-required): there are no defaults in code; every
opinion is a setting row seeded with its starting value, shown beside it.

**Status:** Decided. [identification.md](../design/plans/identification.md) and D182 amended.
**An audit of the existing defaults against §15 is owed** — the log says "by default" 42 times.

---

## D184 — The defaults audit: four become questions, seven must be made visible, the rest pass

**Decided** (2026-09-23), at the project owner's request, auditing the log and plans against
[principles §15](../principles/15-safe-visible-defaults.md) ([D183](#d183--an-override-is-an-override-wherever-its-value-came-from-a-librarys-source-is-asked-not-defaulted-a-default-must-be-safe-to-be-wrong-and-visible-where-it-acts)): *a default must be safe to be
wrong and visible where it acts; otherwise, ask.*

### Method and scope

Every mention of "default" in the log (216 lines) and the user-facing plans was read in context.
§15 is about **decisions made on the user's behalf about their data, exposure, cost or
experience**. Engineering choices a user never observes — direct play before transcoding, the
platform engine before libmpv, AV1/Opus as output codecs, a Unix socket as the node transport,
the sampling hash, `BINARY` collation, zstd levels, test tooling, the pseudo-localised
development build — are out of scope and pass without comment.

### 1. Four become questions

| Default today | Why it fails §15 | Becomes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a library's metadata source, and with it **fetching posters from TMDB** ([D61](#d61--containment-now-detection-later-and-plugin-shaped-four-affordances-to-keep-open), [D99](#d99--the-core-does-not-decode-an-image-either-and-community-uploaded-artwork-is-why), [D170](#d170--one-source-per-title-fetched-once-a-users-correction-is-permanent-and-every-refetch-is-an-act-of-the-user)) | fetches from a third party; wrong source shows wrong data | **asked at library creation** — already decided by D183; artwork follows the same answer |
| **how often a library is checked for changes** — `snapshot_interval` ([D94](#d94--disk-spin-down-is-a-cost-of-the-snapshot-interval-and-archival-means-untouched)) | wakes the disks on a schedule the owner never chose — power, wear, noise; D94 itself calls the right value unmeasured | **asked at library creation**: *watch for changes · check every N hours · only when I ask (archival)*, with the disk consequence stated |
| **how a device plays sound** — downmix, DRC, and whether dialogue boost can act ([D83](#d83--loudness-is-measured-at-scan-and-applied-as-gain-downmix-has-one-default-and-a-dialogue-control-drc-is-per-device), [D178](#d178--the-first-release-is-for-two-people-the-owner-at-home-and-one-person-remote-watching-together-with-subtitles)) | the owner's own complaint is this failure: quiet dialogue from a mix nobody chose for TV speakers | **asked on a device's first playback**: *TV speakers · soundbar or receiver · headphones*, changeable in the player |
| **what an invited person can see** — the default share ([D76](#d76--a-share-is-a-grantee-plus-a-predicate-and-it-fails-closed), open) — and their ceilings ([D174](#d174--sharing-is-an-account-from-outside-the-house-a-household-behind-a-grantee-is-a-rebroadcast-grant-deferred-and-it-makes-another-server-a-source)) | exposure | **asked when the invite is made**, with the answer shown on the person's page; the lease is already set there (D169) |

**Library creation now asks three things, each with its effect stated:** where metadata comes
from, how changes are noticed, and whether we may write into the folder (read-only unless granted,
[principles §2](../principles/02-the-users-files.md)). Three questions once per library is the price of no
surprises for its lifetime.

### 2. Seven pass only if they are visible where they act

| Default | Safe because | Must be shown |
| --- | --- | --- |
| media **read-only** ([D7](#d7--the-files-are-the-source-of-truth-the-database-is-a-rebuildable-index), [D89](#d89--deletion-is-opt-in-per-library-two-phase-and-names-every-file)) | wrong costs a feature, never data | on the library page, and wherever a feature it disables would be offered: *"read-only — NFO export and deletion are unavailable here"* |
| **backups on**, in the data directory ([D77](#d77--back-up-with-vacuum-into-back-up-only-the-irreplaceable-and-test-the-restore)) | off would be the dangerous direction (Home Assistant's) | at setup and on the backup page: where, how many kept, and that **a backup on the same disk does not survive that disk** — with the option to move it |
| **downloads kept indefinitely** on household devices ([D169](#d169--a-lease-is-indefinite-by-default-expiry-is-a-property-of-a-conditional-relationship-and-the-servers-prepared-rendition-is-a-cache-rather-than-a-referent)) | the owner's decision | on the role's page |
| Watch Together **transport for everyone**, stall policy by size, a small cap ([D117](#d117--the-session-link-is-the-grant-revocation-is-the-control-and-the-creator-owns-what-plays), [D119](#d119--a-join-link-admits-membership-is-what-persists-rotation-is-seamless-ejection-is-owner-only-and-a-cap-bounds-the-leak), [D121](#d121--an-ability-is-a-row-in-a-closed-table-with-a-two-valued-grant-chosen-at-session-creation)) | wrong costs an interrupted film | pre-selected **on the session-creation screen**, not hidden |
| **trickplay deferred** in the scan ([D114](#d114--a-pass-costs-what-it-costs-because-of-one-thing-whether-it-decodes-video)) | wrong costs waiting | in scan status (F36) |
| **embedded fonts off** ([D56](#d56--embedded-fonts-are-off-by-default-the-client-must-ask-for-them)) | wrong costs a font | already shown: the client marks a track with embedded fonts ([D57](#d57--the-embedded-font-opt-in-is-per-user-sticky-per-series-and-the-client-may-still-refuse)) |
| **track selection** falling through to the file's own flag ([D24](#d24--language-is-a-preference-axis-and-track-selections-stick-to-the-series)) | wrong costs a menu tap | already shown: *"— the file marks this track default"* — **the model for every other row** |

### 3. The rest pass: they fail safe and cost nothing to be wrong

No telemetry ([D13](#d13--no-telemetry-no-account-no-upsell--as-a-stated-promise)); `/metrics` off and local ([D91](#d91--a-metrics-endpoint-off-by-default-and-local-when-on)); deletion off
([D144](#d144--deletion-is-deferred-not-designed-away-the-policy-is-the-deliverable-and-the-export-already-carries-the-danger));
the trash never empties itself (D143); an API key has no capabilities until given some
([D154](#d154--one-grant-table-opaque-and-revocable-the-session-credential-never-appears-in-a-url));
an unjudgeable item is denied to a restricted role
([D132](#d132--authoring-a-role-is-a-preview-loop-and-an-item-the-rules-cannot-judge-is-denied-not-shown)); no transitive re-sharing (D76); an adapter never
acts as the owner (D105); no score source fetched until opted into (D171). Every one of these errs
towards *less* — less exposure, less fetching, less destruction — which is what "safe to be
wrong" means.

### 4. A standing rule

A new setting is written down with **which of the three it is** — a question (and when it is
asked), a visible default (and where it is shown), or a fail-safe default (and why being wrong
costs nothing). The same test as D182's config keys, applied to everything.

**Status:** Decided. Plans amended: scanner (change detection asked), audio-presentation (device
question), sharing-model (default share asked), backup-restore (visible at setup), web-client (the
library-creation questions).

## D185 — The Cut A schema is written down as SQL that runs; the database is backed up whole; the watched-badge cache is measured out

**Decided** (2026-09-23), completing the data-architecture critique the project owner asked for.
The sketch: [schema.md](../design/plans/schema.md) — every Cut A table with its key, its class
(authored, identity, observed, fetched, cache), what references it and the decision behind it.
Its SQL blocks are loaded verbatim by a benchmark (`/yoloai/cache/bench/schema/`) on SQLite
3.53.4, so the sketch cannot silently stop being valid SQL.

### 1. What writing it down settled

- **The whole `library.db` is backed up**, revising
  [D77](#d77--back-up-with-vacuum-into-back-up-only-the-irreplaceable-and-test-the-restore)'s
  *"back up only the irreplaceable"* for the database file. D77's split made sense against
  gigabytes of thumbnails; the database itself is **32–46 MB and 130–180 ms** by `VACUUM INTO`.
  Backing it up whole carries [D179](#d179--a-files-identity-is-a-hash-of-its-media-payload-not-its-bytes-a-rebuild-restores-the-identity-rows-and-runs-an-ordinary-scan-duplicates-are-surfaced)'s identity rows without a special case and makes a
  restore a restore rather than a rebuild. **Fetched responses and working queues move to a
  separate `cache.db`**, never backed up and deletable at any time.
- **Every observation is a `file` row** with its filing ([D163](#d163--every-observed-file-carries-a-filing-with-a-reason-and-what-did-the-scanner-pass-on-is-the-library-browser-with-the-filter-off)), and a sixth filing,
  **`attached`**, for a subtitle or NFO beside a video.
- **A fetched subtitle lives in the database**, not the media tree: it cost a daily download, the
  library may be read-only, and in the database the ordinary backup carries it.
- **No series table and no season table**: a series is a Collection of episodes, a season is a
  number within an ordering plus optional text ([D160](#d160--there-is-no-series-concept-a-sequence-is-what-a-collection-produces-and-next-up-is-a-query-over-any-of-them)).
- **A sync offset is a preference at `file` scope**, because it is in seconds of one file
  ([D173](#d173--a-replaced-file-is-a-deletion-and-an-addition-what-is-in-a-files-timeline-dies-with-the-file-and-what-is-about-the-work-survives-at-the-title)).
- **`invite` is a ninth grant kind** ([D174](#d174--sharing-is-an-account-from-outside-the-house-a-household-behind-a-grantee-is-a-rebroadcast-grant-deferred-and-it-makes-another-server-a-source)), and `"grant".parent` carries
  [D177](#d177--a-rebroadcaster-is-a-user-whose-core-treats-our-server-as-a-node-and-his-household-plays-on-derived-grants-that-only-his-core-can-mint)'s derived grants.
- **The library row carries the three creation questions** ([D184](#d184--the-defaults-audit-four-become-questions-seven-must-be-made-visible-the-rest-pass)); the device row
  carries the first-playback sound question, NULL until asked.
- **Cut A reads cast and crew from the cached provider response**; people and credits arrive as
  tables with the feature that needs them.

### 2. The watched-badge cache, measured out

Reference scale — 3,500 titles, 10,000 files, 209,781 spans, 126,004 events, four users — for a
50-poster keyset page with watched badges rolled up File → Version → Title: **0.36 ms with a
`title_watch` cache, 0.84 ms computed live** (p95 1.49 ms), against a **50 ms** budget. Not
built — the verdict [D164](#d164--the-predicate-language-stopped-being-a-feature-and-became-the-query-layer-a-restricting-rule-must-fail-closed-and-the-complexity-budget-is-one-number) reached for the role cache. The measurement's real finding
is the other row: **the same rollup shaped as an `EXISTS` the planner turned into a scan took
7.2 ms**, ten times worse than the cache saves. Query shape is the risk, and it belongs in query
review.

### 3. Stale text corrected

library-model.md's *"guarded position per `(user, edition)`"*, its retention horizon, its
fixture *"resume position survives switching between the 1080p and the 4K"* — which would have
tested the rule [D157](#d157--a-position-belongs-to-the-file-completion-rolls-up-the-position-never-does)
and [D173](#d173--a-replaced-file-is-a-deletion-and-an-addition-what-is-in-a-files-timeline-dies-with-the-file-and-what-is-about-the-work-survives-at-the-title) reject — its *"two devices… one edition"*, and its score sources.

**Status:** Sketch. It becomes the first migration when Cut A's implementation starts, and
changes after that go through [migrations.md](../design/plans/migrations.md).

## D186 — Music would cost one reshape, and it is made now: things that are not titles share an item; plus four cheap renames

**Decided** (2026-09-23), at the project owner's request: *"Let's do an exploration of [audio] to
see what changes it would require to our schema. I'm fine with it requiring a migration later,
but I'd like to have a good idea of what we'd be in for (and whether there are cheap changes we
can make now)."* Research: [music.md](../design/research/music.md). **Music itself stays
undecided** (F92); this settles only what adding it would cost.

### 1. The one reshape, and it was already a video bug

Every table describing *a thing* — `artwork`, `favourite`, `user_rating`, `watchlist`,
`field_override`, tags, `sort_key`, the FTS index, provider ids, `user_deny` — was keyed on
`title`. Music exposes it at once: an album and an artist need all of them. **But so does a TV
series**, and a box set: Cut A had nowhere to put a series poster, no way to sort or search series
by name, to star one, to correct its name, or to deny a whole series to a user. Both research
agents and the benchmark found this independently.

**So a shared `item` table** — `title`, `collection` and a reserved `person` take their ids
from it, and every satellite table references `item`
([schema.md](../design/plans/schema.md)). Cost to video, measured on the reference library: the
poster grid goes from **0.84 ms to 0.91 ms**. Cost later, had it waited: a rebuild of every
satellite table and every query that touches them.

### 2. Four cheap changes

1. **`track` → `stream`.** In every music API "track" is the song on an album; our table is a
   container's audio, video and subtitle streams. The rules field registry would otherwise hold
   both meanings.
2. **Orderings are generic**: `ordering.collection_id`, `position(grp, number)`, `group_text` —
   season and episode for a series, disc and track for an album, the same tables.
3. **The sort key carries its listing** — measured: at 500,000 tracks one shared key made an
   album page walk every song and artist, **9.4 ms**; listing-first, **0.35 ms**.
4. **Several provider ids per provider** — a recording can have several ISRCs.

And one reservation: music credits must not name their column `role`, which here means a user's
permissions ([D130](#d130--a-role-is-a-named-policy-object-users-are-assigned-to-one-never-configured-individually)).

### 3. What we would be in for later — additive

People and credits (ordered, typed, credited-as, join phrase; groups as well as people), an album
side table, observed genre and mood joins beside the authored `tag`, `work` for classical,
playlist entries that may repeat a song, ReplayGain columns (nullable — Navidrome learned that 0.0
is a value), lyrics, and two `CHECK` lists widened. **The decisions that matter most to music
users are already this project's**: artists as entities rather than strings, per-user state that
survives rescans and retags ([D173](#d173--a-replaced-file-is-a-deletion-and-an-addition-what-is-in-a-files-timeline-dies-with-the-file-and-what-is-about-the-work-survives-at-the-title), [D179](#d179--a-files-identity-is-a-hash-of-its-media-payload-not-its-bytes-a-rebuild-restores-the-identity-rows-and-runs-an-ordinary-scan-duplicates-are-surfaced)), tags first with the user choosing
the rule ([D183](#d183--an-override-is-an-override-wherever-its-value-came-from-a-librarys-source-is-asked-not-defaulted-a-default-must-be-safe-to-be-wrong-and-visible-where-it-acts), [D184](#d184--the-defaults-audit-four-become-questions-seven-must-be-made-visible-the-rest-pass)). One question is new and belongs to §15 when music is
built: **what defines an album** is asked, not defaulted — MusicBrainz id when present, else a
stated tuple, or the folder — and an album's user state follows its member files when the rule
changes, so a regrouping never loses stars (Navidrome's 0.55 release notes: *"Artist favourites
and artist ratings will be lost after the upgrade"*).

### 4. Retagging must not change identity — measured

Music is retagged in bulk (Picard, beets). With mutagen on FLAC and MP3, **every retag changed the
whole-file head and four of six changed the size; the payload-anchored hash was unchanged in all
six.** [D179](#d179--a-files-identity-is-a-hash-of-its-media-payload-not-its-bytes-a-rebuild-restores-the-identity-rows-and-runs-an-ordinary-scan-duplicates-are-surfaced)'s anchor therefore covers FLAC (after the metadata blocks) and MP3
(between ID3v2 and ID3v1) as well as Matroska; Ogg must hash packet data, because a comment that
outgrows its pages renumbers every page after it.

### 5. Scale

Navidrome's telemetry across 154,673 installs: 84% have 20,000 tracks or fewer, 97.7% 100,000 or
fewer. At **500,000 tracks** our schema is **480 MB**; every browse query measured stays under
1 ms; a backup is ~460 MB and 1.4–3.4 s, so retention count becomes a real setting.

**Status:** Decided. schema.md revised and re-validated; the video benchmark re-run on it.

## D187 — Users are responsible for what they play; we never supply, locate, unlock or promote it — and the store and legal constraints that follow

**Decided** (2026-09-23), at the project owner's request:

> *"I don't want to be legally exposed as the author of this software if users are using it for
> piracy. We don't need to actively block them, but all features we add should be viewed through
> the lens of users being responsible for their own actions, and us not actively promoting piracy.
> This could also touch on rebroadcast, and how those rights work when dealing with private
> individuals (as opposed to a bar franchise using our software to rebroadcast to all their
> bars)… We should also look into client software on various platforms, and whether they have had
> gatekeeper issues."*

Research: [legal.md](../design/research/legal.md) and
[app-stores.md](../design/research/app-stores.md). **Not legal advice**; legal.md §6 lists what to
ask a lawyer before anything hosted ships.

### 1. The position the law supports

**A player for your own files is safe; what makes a tool's author liable is what the author says
and bundles.** *Cox v. Sony* (March 2026, 9–0) requires **intent** — inducement, or a product
"tailored to" infringement — and holds that mere knowledge is not enough. *Filmspeler* made a
media player infringing because it shipped **pre-installed add-ons pointing at pirate streams**
and was advertised for them. No core repository of Kodi, Jellyfin, the *arr tools or Navidrome
appears in GitHub's DMCA archive; takedowns hit the layers that supplied sources. **And blocking is
not required**: failing to filter is not evidence on its own, and monitoring would *create* the
knowledge liability rests on. So the owner's instinct — don't police users, don't promote — is also
the legally stronger position. It becomes **[principles §16](../principles/16-people-are-responsible-for-what-they-play.md)**.

### 2. What we never do

| Never | Because |
| --- | --- |
| **circumvent copy protection** — no decryption of DVD/Blu-ray/streaming DRM, no bundled or linked `libdvdcss`/`libaacs`, no instructions | §1201 is the one liability that lawful uses do not cure (*Corley* enjoined even linking); the German youtube-dl hosting case is final. An encrypted disc is **refused with its reason** ([principles §3](../principles/03-explain-the-decision.md)); unencrypted disc structures play |
| **supply or locate content** — no bundled or pre-configured indexers, trackers, debrid, IPTV playlists, add-on catalogues of sources, or "request → download" wiring | *Filmspeler*, Popcorn Time, TVAddons; and it is exactly what app stores remove (Kodi on Amazon, Stremio, 36 IPTV players) |
| **promote it** — no piracy-flavoured wording, comparisons to pirate apps, VPN/debrid/seedbox affiliate links, "fully loaded" anything | *Grokster*'s evidence was marketing; *Amstrad*'s warning counted for it |
| **show commercial content in what we publish** — screenshots, demos, store listings, test fixtures | Popcorn Time's notice cited screenshots; youtube-dl's cited test cases naming label videos; Play's policy names movie posters |
| **build for venues or resale** — no venue, kiosk or public-display mode, no payments between users, no public or open sign-up, no directory of servers | a bar is a public performance in every bar; paid access to someone's server is *"almost unequivocally piracy"* (Jellyfin's words) |

### 3. What we keep, and why it is fine

- **Integrations are generic.** A webhook saying "a file arrived" is dual-use, like Kodi's attitude
  to torrent clients; so the *arr stack remains welcome as a *sender*. **Documentation names it
  neutrally, among other tools that write files**, which amends
  [D32](#d32--being-told-beats-watching-the-no-agent-path-is-a-tiered-measured-self-reporting-walk)'s *"documented as a first-class
  setup step"* only in emphasis, not substance. Subtitle and metadata providers are fetched per
  title on a person's request with their own key ([D12](#d12--providers-are-sandboxed-wasm-plugins-no-in-process-plugin-code), [D170](#d170--one-source-per-title-fetched-once-a-users-correction-is-permanent-and-every-refetch-is-an-act-of-the-user)).
- **Sharing is designed for a household and a few named people** — invite-only accounts
  ([D174](#d174--sharing-is-an-account-from-outside-the-house-a-household-behind-a-grantee-is-a-rebroadcast-grant-deferred-and-it-makes-another-server-a-source)), caps ([D119](#d119--a-join-link-admits-membership-is-what-persists-rotation-is-seamless-ejection-is-owner-only-and-a-cap-bounds-the-leak)), ceilings — which is the "family and its social
  acquaintances" the US statute describes and the "personal relationship" German law asks for.
- **Plugins**: nothing pre-installed that supplies content; third-party repositories are added by
  hand; any official catalogue has written rules and removes on notice (and would need a DMCA
  agent — legal.md §4).
- **"Missing" is never an action.** Missing episodes (F66) and external lists (F41) may show what
  you do not have; nothing offers to get it — the README's *"no storefront"* already says so.

### 4. Sharing, rebroadcast and the bar

- **Household remote access is private** (*Fox v. Dish*). **A few invited people and Watch
  Together are probably private** — the relationship decides, not a number, and a screen in a
  public place is public there.
- **The owner sees how many people outside the household can play the library** — a display on
  the sharing page, **never an enforced threshold**, because no source gives a legal number.
- **The rebroadcast grant ([D177](#d177--a-rebroadcaster-is-a-user-whose-core-treats-our-server-as-a-node-and-his-household-plays-on-derived-grants-that-only-his-core-can-mint)) raises the stakes**: a second household the owner
  cannot see. So the grantee **accepts terms when the grant is made** (personal, non-commercial,
  never in a public place, never resold), the owner sees **how many people** each grant serves,
  and **non-transitivity stays a hard rule** — it is legally valuable, not just tidy.
- **The owner acknowledges too, when they grant rebroadcast** (added 2026-09-25, by the project
  owner: *"I do want family households to be able to share family videos with each other, but I
  don't want to be charged with encouraging piracy when some people share copyrighted content
  this way. We can't stop them, but we can bring up a nag screen whenever they do grant
  rebroadcast on a library to someone, and then show a nag screen to the receiver when he adds
  it as a source"*). Granting rebroadcast shows the owner a notice they accept: share only what
  you have the right to share, such as your own videos; the household it goes to uses it
  privately, never in a public place or for money. The receiver's acceptance above is shown when
  they add the library as a source. **Each is shown once per grant, not on every use, and kept
  with the grant**: who accepted, when, and which version of the wording — a record is evidence,
  and a screen that nags every time is clicked through and proves less. The wording speaks of
  the user's responsibility and leads with family videos; it never says or implies that we
  check what is shared (§1: monitoring would create the knowledge liability rests on). Its final
  text is legal.md §6's third question for a lawyer.
- **A bar franchise is a public performance in every bar**, which no feature of ours makes lawful
  and none is built for. What we can say, we say in the docs and in the relay's terms.

### 5. The hosted relay is the real exposure

[D71](#d71--one-relay-artefact-three-jobs-and-the-core-dials-out-to-it) already flagged that 1:N
fan-out "is the shape of a pirate streaming service". Before it ships: a **pure conduit**,
end-to-end encrypted and content-blind; **terms** (personal, non-commercial, no public places or
businesses, no charging for access); a **copyright contact**, a **published repeat-infringer
policy** (a precondition of every US safe harbour, conduit included), **DMCA agent** registration
where anything is hosted, the **DSA** contact points; **short published log retention**; a
per-account bandwidth ceiling.

**One tension with [D72](#d72--the-hosted-relay-has-no-free-tier-holds-no-data-and-has-no-accounts),
for the owner:** D72 charges for the relay. The research recommends pricing **flat and near cost,
never tied to bandwidth or volume**, because revenue that grows with use is the "direct financial
benefit" of vicarious liability and triggers *GS Media*'s profit presumption. A flat subscription
reconciles them; a per-GB price would not. **To confirm, and to put to a lawyer.**

### 6. Stores and platforms

**No store bans a client for your own server; they remove content-source features, and they reject
on operations.** So, from [app-stores.md](../design/research/app-stores.md): the web client served
**same-origin** by the server; against Safe Browsing's "Deceptive site" flags, **no project-branded
share tags on users' instances, an admin-customisable login page, no search indexing by default,
demos on a separate domain**; a **permanent reviewer demo server** of public-domain or Creative
Commons content; listings that say *requires your own server* first and show only the demo library;
clients that **open with no server reachable**, say why, and resume after reconnecting (Samsung's
blocking failure for Jellyfin); an **organisation** Play account (it avoids the 12-tester, 14-day closed test new personal
accounts need) and package names and signing keys **registered under** Google's developer
verification — which applies to every developer whenever they registered, from 30 September 2026
in four countries and globally in 2027; there is no grandfathering to get ahead of, and an
organisation account needs a legal entity and a D-U-N-S number; and the escape
hatches [D108](#d108--the-interface-is-not-ours-to-change-out-from-under-people-and-an-old-client-stays-installable) already promised
— signed APKs, F-Droid, `adb` — because sideloading is narrowing everywhere and any store may pull
us for a while. Clients are MPL-2.0 ([D80](#d80--licence-by-artefact-gplv3-for-the-server-mpl-20-for-the-clients-and-the-sdk)), so the licence that cost VLC the App Store does not reach us.

### 7. The notice

A short notice in the README, the documentation and the first-run screen — *Amstrad*'s warning
counted for it. Draft, **for a lawyer to finish**:

> *[Project] is a player for media you have the right to use. It does not provide, locate or
> download content, and it does not remove copy protection. You are responsible for complying with
> copyright law where you live, including when you share access with others.*

Community rules before launch, Kodi- and Jellyfin-style: no discussion of or links to pirated
content, no support for installs using pirate-source plugins, no selling or trading of server
access; filenames scrubbed from shared logs ([bug-reports.md](../design/plans/bug-reports.md)); a
moderation log. And **register the project's name as a trademark** once it has one — it is what
let Kodi act against "fully loaded" boxes.

**Status:** Decided as policy. Legal review owed before the relay, any terms of service, and the
final notice (legal.md §6).

## D188 — The interface is designed against the field's recorded failures; accessibility shapes the design but does not gate Cut A; her television plays and her phone talks

**Decided** (2026-09-23), by the project owner, on
[ui-competitors.md](../design/research/ui-competitors.md). Owner, on accessibility: *"We'll try
to get accessibility right, but I won't mind if it's not perfect before I start using the app.
We just need to make sure our design works for it."* On the television: *"I want to have
Apple's model for tv playback. If it can be done with a browser alone that would be ideal, but
I'm not against a prototype app. If it turns out to be too much trouble we can fall back to
laptop play."*

### 1. What the research confirmed, and what it added

Most of the field's largest traps are already closed:
- **direct play decided by the client**: [D2](#d2--playback-negotiation-the-client-decides-from-a-manifest), [D17](#d17--direct-play-first-transcoding-additive-and-optional)
- **track choices that stick per series**: [D24](#d24--language-is-a-preference-axis-and-track-selections-stick-to-the-series)
- **corrections that are permanent**: [D170](#d170--one-source-per-title-fetched-once-a-users-correction-is-permanent-and-every-refetch-is-an-act-of-the-user), [D183](#d183--an-override-is-an-override-wherever-its-value-came-from-a-librarys-source-is-asked-not-defaulted-a-default-must-be-safe-to-be-wrong-and-visible-where-it-acts)
- **a view of what the scanner understood instead of rename rules**: [D163](#d163--every-observed-file-carries-a-filing-with-a-reason-and-what-did-the-scanner-pass-on-is-the-library-browser-with-the-filter-off)
- **a home the user arranges**: [D138](#d138--the-ui-is-judged-on-click-depth-and-focus-latency-theming-is-a-seam-we-ship-or-one-they-force)
- **an old layout that stays available**: [D108](#d108--the-interface-is-not-ours-to-change-out-from-under-people-and-an-old-client-stays-installable)
- **restrictions on every access path**: [D76](#d76--a-share-is-a-grantee-plus-a-predicate-and-it-fails-closed)

The research adds these, each placed in the plan that owns it:

| Adopted | Evidence | Lands in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Continue Watching opens the home screen, by recency; selecting an item plays at once with no resume prompt, and "start over" is in the player** | Netflix's homepage paper; Roku certification; Apple HIG | [play-state.md](../design/plans/play-state.md) |
| **Any item can be hidden from Continue Watching, with undo, on every client; hiding is not "watched"** | Jellyfin's second most-wanted request (1,722); Netflix 2022, Disney+ 2025 | play-state.md |
| **Unattended playback is detected and is not viewing**: "still watching?" after three episodes and 90 minutes without input; plays after that point mark nothing watched | Netflix's TV rule | play-state.md |
| **Track menus name the track**: language, SDH, forced, commentary | Plex *show track names*, 417 votes | [web-client.md](../design/plans/web-client.md), [tv-client.md](../design/plans/tv-client.md) |
| **Left and right on a remote always seek from the current position**, 10 s steps, thumbnails over 15 minutes | Samsung focus bug; Plex skip length, 453; Apple, Roku | tv-client.md |
| **No pagination, no search cap, titles on posters by default, a list view** | 1,176 votes; caps of 24 and 30 | web-client.md |
| **Every effective setting shows where it came from** — person, library, series or device override | Emby *Server vs Device*; jellyfin-web #5456; 258 votes | web-client.md |
| **The transcode reason is on screen**, in the player's info panel and the admin's sessions view | Plex's largest admin topic, 3,069 likes | web-client.md (already a non-negotiable; now placed) |
| **Every error names the item, the cause and one next action** | 39% of Jellyfin's top troubleshooting threads get "send logs" early | web-client.md |
| **The web player's conventions and traps**: keyboard, subtitle layer, iPhone, autoplay, network drop, Media Session | ui-competitors.md §4 | web-client.md |
| **Watch Together**: named events, undo for a seek, subtitles and audio per person, film and partner volume separate, a reconnecting state | Syncplay; SharePlay; Hearo, Discord | [watch-together.md](../design/plans/watch-together.md) |
| **Each server release is tested against the previous client release** | Jellyfin 10.11 broke shipped clients | [testing-strategy.md](../design/plans/testing-strategy.md) |

**Declined: autoplaying previews and heroes.** Every service that shipped them ended up adding an
off switch, and a personal library has nothing to promote. If one is ever proposed, it arrives
with a single switch that every client obeys (Roku's rule since 2024).

### 2. Accessibility: the design must work for it; Cut A is not gated on it

The research's conclusion — *every project triages by votes, and a population that cannot use
the product does not vote* — is right, and it argues for building accessibility into the
design rather than scheduling it. It does not require holding back a release two people will
use. So the line falls here:

- **Design requirements, from the first screen:**
  - every focusable element has an **accessible name derived from what it is** (a card's name is
    its item's title, never a badge's count; Plex's Fire TV reader says *"1… 241… 36"*)
  - everything reachable by pointer is reachable by keyboard and by remote, and focus is always
    visible
  - no state is shown only by colour
  - text scales without breaking the layout, and reduced-motion is honoured
  - the caption controls of [accessibility.md](../design/plans/accessibility.md) are reachable
    during playback
- **Not a gate on Cut A.** Shortfalls found during Cut A are recorded, not blocking. Whether
  accessibility gates a release anyone else installs is decided before that release.

This is cheap because the structure is the same work: the TV client's focus model is what a
screen reader walks ([tv-client.md](../design/plans/tv-client.md)), and a web client built from
semantic elements is most of the way there.

### 3. Her television: Apple's model, paths tried in order

**The television plays the film; her phone carries the voice and the remote.** Apple's SharePlay
design, and what the top post (157 likes) in Plex's withdrawal thread asked for. It needs no new
model:
- [D120](#d120--a-participant-is-a-person-devices-attach-to-them-with-roles-and-the-cap-counts-people)
  already attaches devices to a person with roles: `playback`, `voice`, `control`
- [D124](#d124--the-playback-role-may-be-a-cast-receiver-and-for-a-guest-that-is-the-best-path-the-phone-controls-it-does-not-relay)
  already lets the `playback` device be a cast receiver

What is new is **how the playback device gets there**, tried in this order:

| # | Path | Needs | Known risk |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | **The television's own browser** opens the web client in a playback mode, ~~signed in by a code shown on the TV ([D93](#d93--device-pairing-is-rfc-8628-shaped))~~ **joining the session as a device of her membership, by link or short code** ([D191](#d191--watch-together-behaves-as-if-nobody-has-an-account-a-signed-in-participants-viewing-is-also-recorded-as-their-own)) | nothing installed | TV browsers' codec and HLS support; remote focus in a web page; a Google TV device has no browser by default |
| 2 | **Our cast receiver**, launched once from Chrome on her MacBook; it then holds `playback` and talks to the server itself, while her phone holds `voice` and `control` through the web page | Cast registration ($5), HTTPS | **the Cast web sender runs only in Chrome, so her iPhone cannot launch it**; the laptop does it once per session |
| 3 | **A prototype Android TV app**, sideloaded ([tv-client.md](../design/plans/tv-client.md)) | a Google TV or Android TV device; `adb` or a limited-distribution developer account (up to 20 devices) | the prototype is the start of Phase 3, early |
| 4 | **Fallback: the laptop plays** and her phone or laptop talks | nothing | not the living room |

**Which one is decided by her actual setup**, which the owner will learn in about two weeks.
"A Samsung television with Google TV" is ambiguous: Samsung's own sets run Tizen, whose browser
is path 1, while a Google TV streamer plugged into a Samsung is paths 2 and 3. The questions for
that conversation are in [device-lab.md](../design/plans/device-lab.md).

**Two voice consequences follow from putting the film on television speakers**:
- **Echo.** Her phone's microphone hears the TV, so the owner hears the film echoed back.
  Earbuds on her phone remove the path the owner would hear. Without them, this is
  [D65](#d65--playback-offset-is-per-participant-and-it-is-an-echo-control)'s tier 2, the offset
  alignment already planned.
- **iOS Safari with the microphone open** has sent call audio to the earpiece at low volume since
  iOS 15 (WebKit #230902). Earbuds also avoid this. Whether `navigator.audioSession` fixes it
  without earbuds is UNVERIFIED and goes on the device-lab list.

### 4. Closes one open question in watch-together.md

*Is the subtitle track group state or local?* **Local — per person**, along with the audio track
and the film's volume. SharePlay and Discord both do this, and the case that motivates the
feature needs it: one of the two needs subtitles. The inconsistency the plan worried about
(*"seek to the funny bit"* versus *"turn subtitles on"*) does not arise. A seek is shared
position; subtitles are presentation, and presentation was never shared.

**Status:** Decided. Plans amended as listed; [schema.md](../design/plans/schema.md) gains
`play_span.unattended` and a `progress_hide` table, both Cut A because Continue Watching is. The
television path waits on her setup; the voice-on-phone checks join the device lab.

## D189 — Focus adds to the focused item and takes nothing from it or its neighbours

**Decided** (2026-09-23), by the project owner: *"One thing I find incredibly annoying in tile
view selector UIs is when the selected item darkens or otherwise becomes harder to see the item
being selected. Another annoyance is enlarging to the point where it obscures neighbors."*

**Both are the same mistake: the focus effect costs legibility.** The focused tile is the one
being read ("is this the one I want?"), and its neighbours are the ones being read next ("where
do I go from here?"). An effect that darkens the first or covers the second makes focus harder
to use at exactly the moment it is being used. Apple's tvOS guidance points the same way
([ui-competitors.md](../design/research/ui-competitors.md) working notes, HIG *Focus and
selection*): a focused item stands out *"through elevation to the foreground, illumination, and
animation"*, and the designer must *"make sure the larger item doesn't crowd the surrounding
interface."*

### The rule

1. **Focus only adds.** It adds a ring, a lift (shadow or elevation) and at most a modest scale.
   It **never darkens, dims, desaturates, blurs or overlays the focused item**, and never
   covers its artwork or title with a gradient, a scrim or a button row. Anything shown on
   focus (a progress bar, a title that does not fit) goes **outside** the artwork or in a
   detail line below the row.
2. **The ring is visible on any artwork**: two colours, a light outer and a dark inner ring
   (WCAG technique C40). A single colour vanishes against a poster of the same colour, and
   scale alone is too subtle to find from across a room.
3. **Growth stays inside the gutter.** A focused tile may grow on each side by at most half
   the gutter, minus the ring width. Half, because during the move the tile losing focus is
   still shrinking while the new one grows. With 200 px posters and a 24 px gutter that is a
   scale of about 1.09. The layout sets the gutter from the scale, not the other way round.
   Vertically the same budget applies against the row header, the tile's own title and the
   row below.
4. **Neighbours are not dimmed either.** Android TV's row presenters dim unselected rows by
   default, which is the same cost moved onto the tiles you read next. Contrast between the
   focused tile and the rest comes from the ring and the lift, not from making the rest worse.
5. **The focused tile is always entirely on screen.** Rows scroll to keep it inside the safe
   area, and nothing (the player's controls, a toast, the on-screen keyboard) covers it. This
   is WCAG 2.2's *Focus Not Obscured* (2.4.11/2.4.12), which protects the focused item. Rule 3
   is its mirror for the neighbours.
6. **Pressed and selected states follow the same rule.** A press may briefly brighten or shrink
   by the same small amount; a selected (checked) item gets a mark, not a darker tile.

### Why it is cheap to enforce

These are geometry and pixel facts, so they are tested, not reviewed
([testing-strategy.md](../design/plans/testing-strategy.md)). For every tile component, in every
layout density:
- the focused tile's bounding box, ring included, intersects no neighbour's box and no row
  header or title
- the mean luminance and contrast of the focused tile's artwork are not lower than when
  unfocused

A theme ([D138](#d138--the-ui-is-judged-on-click-depth-and-focus-latency-theming-is-a-seam-we-ship-or-one-they-force)
§4) can restyle the ring and the lift. It **cannot** override rules 1, 3 and 5, because the
test runs against themes too.

**Status:** Decided. Applies to the web client's grids and the TV client's rows alike; amended
into [tv-client.md](../design/plans/tv-client.md),
[web-client.md](../design/plans/web-client.md),
[accessibility.md](../design/plans/accessibility.md) and testing-strategy.md.

## D190 — The testing strategy: devices report on themselves against numbers, a missing capability fails, every check first shows it can fail, and the lab is built from what is on the shelf

**Decided** (2026-09-23), on the owner's request for a testing strategy built on competitors'
practice, yoloAI's, and the home hardware. Research:
[device-testing.md](../design/research/device-testing.md). It refines
[D112](#d112--the-node-probes-its-confinement-and-reports-it-the-escape-test-asserts-what-is-in-force),
extends [D109](#d109--five-corpus-tiers-and-nobody-has-to-download-media-to-run-the-suite)–[D111](#d111--assumptions-is-a-test-directory)
and [device-lab.md](../design/plans/device-lab.md), and replaces none of them.

### 1. The device reports; the lab judges against numbers

Every mature project that tests playback at scale makes the player report its own state rather
than driving its UI: Shaka, Netflix, YouTube, the BBC.
[device-lab.md](../design/plans/device-lab.md) §3 already chose that. What was missing is
**numbers to fail against**, and other people have fixed them. They are the starting values; each
becomes a frozen baseline under
[D110](#d110--every-threshold-gate-compares-against-a-frozen-baseline-and-the-assertion-is-chosen-per-test)
once measured here:

| Check | Starting criterion | From |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Playback starts, direct play on the lab LAN | ≤ 8 s | Roku certification |
| Playback progresses, any path | within 15 s | dash.js |
| Dropped frames | **≤ 1% of total and ≤ 10 consecutive**; on failure re-run the mandatory baseline rendition, and report *device* or *our choice* accordingly | Media3 |
| A seek lands | within 0.5 s of its target | dash.js |
| Pause takes effect | within 3 s | dash.js |
| Remote key to focus moved | ≤ 250 ms (the D-pad gate's first ceiling) | Roku certification |
| Subtitle rendering | per-platform screenshot golden, image similarity with a per-test threshold | Shaka |

**A result with nothing in it is invalid, not good.** "0 dropped of 0 frames" means nothing
played; a probe must be seen to fail on a stream the device certainly cannot play before its
passes count.

### 2. A missing capability fails; only a named list may be absent

yoloAI's hardest-won rule. One of its test tiers skipped itself for months, and two of its
security tests had never run, because a missing prerequisite meant *skip*. So:

- A test whose prerequisite **could exist on this host and does not, fails.**
- Each CI step or lab job may name what is legitimately absent
  (`VP_TEST_UNCONTROLLED=nvenc,vaapi,landlock,cast`), and the run prints that list.
- A test that **cannot** run on this platform at all (tvOS on a Linux runner) is not scheduled
  there, and the run lists it as **uncovered**. Uncovered is shown, never silent.
- A gate check fails when code reads a `VP_TEST_*` variable that nothing (Makefile, CI, lab
  runner) sets.

[D112](#d112--the-node-probes-its-confinement-and-reports-it-the-escape-test-asserts-what-is-in-force)'s
"skip loudly" becomes **fail**, except where the step names Landlock as uncontrolled.

### 3. Every check first shows it can fail

A yoloAI run reported *"7 PASS / 0 FAIL"* and concluded the exact inverse of the truth, because
the sandbox lacked the capability under test. The rule: **before trusting a pass, observe the
same check fail on a case where failure is certain.**
- **The escape test** opens the forbidden path *without* our confinement and sees it succeed,
  then with it and sees the denial, and attributes the denial to our layer. A denial may
  otherwise be the container's mounts or file permissions (D112's correction of 2026-09-23).
- **Each device probe** carries a negative control, a stream that device cannot play.
- **Each gate script** has tests that make it fail, as `check_docs.py` does.
- **Each benchmark** stamps the harness version and lists what it did *not* try.

### 4. Taken from yoloAI, as each piece of code arrives

- **A fake `ffmpeg` fixture.** It asserts the arguments we pass (`-force_idr 1` reaching NVENC),
  the environment the worker receives, and that errors carry the tail of stderr.
- **Architecture claims as named tests** (`TestArch_…`), cited from the prose, with a gate that
  every cited test exists and every such test is cited. The first five:
  - the core never executes FFmpeg ([D26](#d26--no-ffmpeg-in-the-core-process-confine-it-with-landlock--seccomp))
  - nothing deletes under a media root except the trash writer ([D145](#d145--the-trash-is-one-directory-per-event-with-a-parallel-tree-inside-because-our-unit-of-undo-is-a-bulk-operation))
  - the playback decision never branches on client identity, only on declared capability ([D2](#d2--playback-negotiation-the-client-decides-from-a-manifest), [D103](#d103--a-device-scoped-preference-is-stored-a-device-capability-never-is))
  - the node imports nothing from the core
  - only the store package imports SQLite
- **Revert-and-require-red.** For each changed source file, the old version is restored in a
  throwaway worktree and some test must fail. A fix only a device can confirm carries a
  `Verified-By:` trailer naming a **verification-queue** item. A check confirms the item exists
  and is ticked, because yoloAI's unchecked trailer has been used zero times.
- **One conformance suite per contract, run against every implementation.** Each implementation
  declares what it cannot do, with a reason, as an explicit skip. The contracts are:
  - the client surface ([D62](#d62--watch-together-is-a-first-class-feature-and-the-per-client-surface-is-six-methods)'s
    six methods), across web, cast receiver and TV clients
  - the encoder ([D19](#d19--the-transcoder-is-a-plugin-we-happen-to-maintain-plugin-tiers-become-three)),
    across software, QSV, VAAPI and NVENC on the Proxmox hosts and the 3090
- **`make check`:**
  - builds the lab- and integration-tagged tests
  - cross-compiles for linux/amd64, linux/arm64 and darwin
  - pins tool versions, including FFmpeg's, and fails on a missing one
  - runs tests in a hermetic environment (time zone, locale, git config)
  - no gate is pull-request-only
  - govulncheck, with suppressions that fail once a fix ships
  - setup output is logged, never discarded
- **A Stop hook that runs the checks and blocks an agent's turn on failure**, and an
  `agent-failures.md` with a "Caught by" field, both from the first code commit. This project
  is agent-written, as yoloAI is.

**Not taken:**
- the rest of yoloAI's repo-hygiene suite (`check_docs.py` has the parts that matter here)
- frozen harness versions as separate files
- per-OS linting and a Docker-provider matrix
- transcript-parsing provenance hooks
- coverage targets
- a single release test needing every host at once

### 5. Watch Together and voice get tests nobody else wrote

Nobody publishes how they test watch-party sync, so it is designed here:
- **Sync:** two clients play a test clip with a burned-in frame counter and a flash-and-beep
  every ten seconds.
  - **Automated:** the lab server timestamps each client's position reports on arrival over a
    sub-millisecond LAN and computes the drift, within the RTT's bound.
  - **Ground truth:** a verification-queue item where a phone films both screens and the frame
    counters are compared. It calibrates the automated number and is re-run when the sync code
    changes.
- **Voice:** Playwright with Chrome's fake-media flags feeds a `.wav` as each microphone.
  `getStats` asserts audio arrives, with jitter and loss within bounds. A beep's round trip gives
  the mouth-to-ear latency that
  [D65](#d65--playback-offset-is-per-participant-and-it-is-an-echo-control)'s offset needs.
- **Both run across the simulated remote household** (§6), under netem profiles for a good
  home link, a congested one and a lossy mobile one. A real phone on mobile data remains the
  real carrier-grade-NAT client.

### 6. The lab, from the shelf

**Hosts.**
- **devnas (F2-422, J3455, 8 GB):** the low-end server floor. It must run the server, and its
  QSV decodes HEVC 10-bit but encodes HEVC 8-bit only and does no AV1.
- **nas (F4-424, N95) and nuc13 (NUC 13 Pro), both Proxmox:** they host the VMs:
  - the CI runner
  - the **remote-household simulator**: two VLANs, NAT between them, `tc netem` on both, and a
    `100.64.0.0/10` WAN address
  - distro VMs for the install matrix
  - a Windows VM when it is wanted
- **gpuhost:** NVENC encoder conformance and the 12-session limit.
- **MacBook:** Safari, Apple's HLS validators, Apple builds, and the Chrome sender for Cast.
- **stagehost is the owner's desktop and is not a lab host.** Its browsers are clients like any other.

**Network.**
- The Zyxel carries an **isolated lab VLAN** and a separate management VLAN.
- The MT6000 maps a lab SSID onto the lab VLAN.
- Port mirroring feeds packet capture.
- The MT3000 is the physical remote-household router when the radio matters, at the cost of its
  repeater role.
- The SFT1200 (vendor OpenWrt 18.06, no SQM) is a plain NAT box at most.

**Clients, reference tier** (always connected):

| Device | Why it is in the reference tier |
| --- | --- |
| Apple TV HD (tvOS 26.6, frozen) | the strictest client: H.264 and HEVC SDR at 1080p30 only; a device that will never update |
| Fire TV Stick 4K Max 2nd gen (Fire OS 8) | the modern ceiling: AV1, HEVC 4K60 10-bit, Dolby Vision |
| one Fire OS 7 stick (Lite, 3rd gen or HD) | the 1080p HDR rung with no AV1, the most common tier |
| Fire TV Stick 4K 1st gen (2018, Fire OS 6) | the oldest Android base present |
| Samsung S23, Chrome | modern Android and the Cast sender on a phone |
| a current iPhone, Safari | ManagedMediaSource, no element fullscreen, the voice path |
| the oldest iPhone on iOS 26/27 (iPhone 11 or SE 2nd gen) | the iOS floor |

- **Sweep tier** (rotated): the other sticks, phones and browsers.
- **Archive tier:** iPhones below the iOS floor, kept as frozen old-Safari clients in case the
  web client's floor is set lower.
- **Vega OS sticks, if any:** web only, since `adb` is not documented there.

**Operating habits** (Shaka, the BBC, yoloAI):
- a device roster in the repository, with a written reason for every disabled device
- a nightly run, plus on demand; runs from a change only after review
- one job per device at a time
- up to three retries, **each one recorded**, so the flake rate is a number
- a pre-flight: reachable, enough disk, running the build under test
- a recovery ladder: relaunch, then reboot (`adb`, `pyatv`), then power-cycle (`uhubctl` or a
  switched plug)
- failure signatures matched against a device-idiosyncrasies register
- each failed run diffed against the last good one

**One gap Cut A cannot close without buying something: no Cast device.** Cut A includes the
cast receiver
([D124](#d124--the-playback-role-may-be-a-cast-receiver-and-for-a-guest-that-is-the-best-path-the-phone-controls-it-does-not-relay)),
and it is path 2 for her television
([D188](#d188--the-interface-is-designed-against-the-fields-recorded-failures-accessibility-shapes-the-design-but-does-not-gate-cut-a-her-television-plays-and-her-phone-talks)).
test-hardware.md's rule was to buy a Google TV device when Cast is built, and Cast is now being
built. **Recommended: one Google TV Streamer** (or whatever Google currently sells), after her
setup is known, so that if she has one, the lab has the same model.

### 7. What Cut A needs from all this

**Needed:**
- the web client in Chrome and Firefox on Linux, Safari on the MacBook, Safari on the current
  and the oldest iPhone, and Chrome on the S23
- the Cast device
- the remote-household VM with its netem profiles
- the sync and voice tests of §5
- the §1 criteria on those clients
- the gates of §2–§4 as the first code lands

**Not needed yet:** the reference television tier beyond whatever path her setup chooses.

**Status:** Decided. Plans amended: [device-lab.md](../design/plans/device-lab.md) (§0c the lab,
the criteria, the habits, sync and voice) and
[testing-strategy.md](../design/plans/testing-strategy.md) (the gates). **To confirm on the
devices:**
- the staging host's model and its 64 GB
- the F2-422's CPU
- whether netem installs on the MT6000's kernel
- the 3090's session limit on the installed driver
- the S23's AV1 decode
- which Fire TV sticks run Vega OS
- whether a capture card sees HDCP-protected output

## D191 — Watch Together behaves as if nobody has an account; a signed-in participant's viewing is also recorded as their own

**Decided** (2026-09-23), by the project owner, answering the audit's P6
([audit-2026-09-23.md](../design/research/audit-2026-09-23.md) §1.4): *"For watch together, we
record user playback data if they have an account, but it's just an extra thing we do if the
user is logged in. The main functionality behaves like 'no account'."*

### 1. The rule

**The session never depends on an account.** Joining, syncing, voice, the transport and every
role work for a participant who holds only the link, exactly as
[D117](#d117--the-session-link-is-the-grant-revocation-is-the-control-and-the-creator-owns-what-plays)–[D122](#d122--the-session-is-the-object-what-plays-is-mutable-state-on-it-and-a-guest-sees-the-stream-rather-than-the-library)
designed. **Being signed in adds one thing: your viewing is recorded against your own account**,
as positions and spans on the File that played, the same records solo viewing makes. The
host's viewing is recorded as before.

So the audit's question — *whose play state advances when the two of them watch together?* —
has the obvious answer: **each signed-in person's own, and nobody else's.** An anonymous
participant still accrues nothing, which keeps
[D125](#d125--access-is-role-based-with-two-roles-a-watch-together-guest-is-not-a-principal)'s
reason intact: a link-holder never acquires a durable identity from the session.

### 2. What it changes

- **[D125](#d125--access-is-role-based-with-two-roles-a-watch-together-guest-is-not-a-principal)
  is refined in place.** *"A guest accrues no play state"* now reads *"a guest who is not
  signed in"*. The session still grants a signed-in participant nothing beyond the stream. If
  she can browse the library, that comes from her account, not from the session.
- **A device attached to a signed-in person records for that person.**
  [D120](#d120--a-participant-is-a-person-devices-attach-to-them-with-roles-and-the-cap-counts-people)
  already makes a participant a person with devices attached by role. Her television (playback
  role) and her phone (voice) are one membership, so the TV's viewing is recorded under her
  account when **either** device is signed in. The TV itself need not be.
- **Her television joins the session, not the server.**
  [D188](#d188--the-interface-is-designed-against-the-fields-recorded-failures-accessibility-shapes-the-design-but-does-not-gate-cut-a-her-television-plays-and-her-phone-talks)'s
  path 1 had the TV browser *"signed in by a code"* (D93). Under this rule it only needs to
  **join the session as a device of her membership**, by the session link or a short code shown
  by her phone. Device pairing (F30) therefore stays out of Cut A, which resolves the audit's
  contradiction between D178 §4 and D188. Pairing returns when she wants to watch on that
  television alone.
- **The audit's proposal is withdrawn.** P6 proposed admitting only signed-in users. The link
  stays, and so do rotation, the cap and ejection, the parts of D119 that protect an anonymous
  session.

**Status:** Decided. D125 and D188 refined in place;
[watch-together.md](../design/plans/watch-together.md) amended.
