## D192 — Built in a private repository, tested at home, released through public betas; standards follow the final stack

**Decided** (2026-09-23), by the project owner: *"The initial development time will be me (and
sometimes my gf) testing internally. I'll have a repo on github, but it will be private until
I'm satisfied that it's ready for public release. We'll do a series of betas like we do for
yoloai, until I'm satisfied that we've got a solid base."*

### 1. Three stages

| Stage | Who | What it means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Internal** | the owner and their partner | A private GitHub repository. Cut A ([D178](#d178--the-first-release-is-for-two-people-the-owner-at-home-and-one-person-remote-watching-together-with-subtitles)) is this stage's target. Nothing is published. |
| **Public betas** | anyone | The repository goes public. `0.x` releases, yoloAI's model: every breaking change is written in a `BREAKING-CHANGES` file, and the next version escalates the moment something breaking lands. |
| **Stable** | anyone | When the owner says the base is solid. The compatibility contract ([D85](#d85--the-api-has-a-compatibility-contract-and-it-covers-three-protocols)) and the migration policy's promises to strangers ([D181](#d181--the-migration-policy-two-integers-our-own-small-runner-a-snapshot-that-outlives-success-refuse-what-we-cannot-read-and-re-derive-rather-than-transform)) are binding from the first public beta, because a stranger's database is the thing that cannot be rebuilt. |

### 2. What the internal stage changes

- **Packaging is only what the lab needs.** The binary plus systemd units, or the `.deb`, on
  the host that runs Cut A. The audit's public channels ([audit-2026-09-23.md](../design/research/audit-2026-09-23.md)
  §6) — the image, the signed repository, NAS catalogues, the release feed — are **beta-stage
  work**. Their pipeline is built before the first public beta, not before Cut A.
- **The Cast receiver stays unpublished**, and her device is registered by serial number. A
  private repository cannot use free GitHub Pages hosting, so the receiver is served from the
  owner's own server under its public HTTPS name (audit §1.3). That is simpler anyway, and it
  has to exist for the microphone.
- **Nothing ties the internal stage to GitHub's public services.** No public release URLs and
  no public issue tracker. The Android APK, if a prototype is needed (D188 path 3), is installed
  from the owner's server or over `adb`.
- **The licence files ([D80](#d80--licence-by-artefact-gplv3-for-the-server-mpl-20-for-the-clients-and-the-sdk))
  go in at the first commit anyway.** They cost nothing, and a private repository that later
  goes public must not need a relicensing pass.

### 3. Standards follow the final stack

Once the technology set is settled (the audit's P7), **write the per-technology standards**,
modelled on yoloAI's `standards/`. Their four aims, in the owner's words:
- **Human readability.**
- **Low complexity, enforced by tooling**, as yoloAI enforces it.
- **Understandable without chasing definitions:** names that say what a thing is. yoloAI does
  this too.
- **Linting that catches LLM errors early.**

**At the same time:**
- review yoloAI's principles for any that transfer;
- study how yoloAI has used Go, the problems it hit, and how it solved them.

That is one research round, and its output is `standards/` plus any principles adopted.

**Status:** Decided. The standards round is scheduled after P7.
[ROADMAP.md](../../ROADMAP.md) notes the stages.

## D193 — The audit's proposals are accepted: the node does all media work, "prepare" is the one path besides direct play, the machinery is cut, and Cut A's design freezes

> **§2 narrowed by [D344](#d344--the-whole-film-prepare-is-retired-every-playback-the-device-cannot-play-as-it-is-plays-from-its-ladder-cut-on-time-where-its-keyframes-cannot-be-had)** (2026-10-26): prepare is retired; the one path besides direct play is the ladder of chunks (D247 §10, D260).

**Decided** (2026-09-23), by the project owner, answering
[audit-2026-09-23.md](../design/research/audit-2026-09-23.md) §9: *"P1: yes. P2: yes. P3: yes.
P4: yes. P5: I have a bunch of domains already that I can use. P7: yes. P8: devnas doesn't have
direct access to the media files (they're on nas). But for testing I could copy a corpus
across. P9: yes."* P6 was answered differently in
[D191](#d191--watch-together-behaves-as-if-nobody-has-an-account-a-signed-in-participants-viewing-is-also-recorded-as-their-own).

### 1. The node does every media read and every FFmpeg run (P1)

The core never opens a media file. **For direct play, the core authenticates the request and
reverse-proxies the byte range to the node** over its Unix socket. **For every other
playback**, the node runs FFmpeg and writes into its own cache, and the core proxies that the
same way. This settles the audit's §1.1:
- [D33](#d33--hub-and-spoke-a-core-that-never-touches-media-and-n-media-nodes-that-do) is now
  literally true;
- "the core serves the film" in
  [D128](#d128--the-artefact-channel-is-the-real-payload-and-the-node-keeps-what-it-makes)
  means "the core relays it";
- the overview's "the core encodes audio" was wrong.

A remote node later is the same proxy over TCP, or a redirect.

### 2. "Prepare" is Cut A's only playback path besides direct play (P2)

**What it is.** One node job per (File, profile) runs **one FFmpeg command**. It produces an HLS
rendition, in fMP4 segments, in the node's cache: video copied or encoded, audio converted,
text subtitles extracted. The playlist is written as an `EVENT` playlist that grows while the
job runs, so **playback starts once the first segments exist**, not when the job ends. It is
[D4](#d4--three-playback-paths-direct-on-demand-segmented-background-prepared)'s third path,
"background-prepared", now doing the second path's job for Cut A. The rendition is a cache
([D169](#d169--a-lease-is-indefinite-by-default-expiry-is-a-property-of-a-conditional-relationship-and-the-servers-prepared-rendition-is-a-cache-rather-than-a-referent)),
and its play state is recorded against the source File
([D180](#d180--a-prepared-renditions-play-state-is-its-sources-additive-schema-comes-with-its-feature-mistakes-are-assumed-so-migration-needs-a-policy)).

**How it is invoked.** Three ways, all ending in the same job:

1. **Pressing play.** The client sends its prioritised menu list
   ([D21](#d21--a-fixed-named-output-menu-negotiated-by-a-prioritised-client-list)), and the
   core resolves it per axis
   ([D22](#d22--video-audio-and-subtitles-negotiate-as-independent-axes)):
   - **The original is acceptable on every axis:** direct play.
   - **A matching prepared rendition exists:** its playlist.
   - **Neither:** the core queues a prepare job at the front of the node's queue and answers
     at once with the playlist URL and a reason for the transcode. The client shows
     *"Preparing — ready in a few seconds"* until the first segment exists.
2. **"Get this ready."** A button on a title, and automatically when a Watch Together session is
   created for a title, for each participant whose link or device needs a smaller copy. This is
   D175's "prepared in advance", now simply the same job started earlier.
3. **The admin view.** Lists the queue and each job's progress and reason, and can cancel a job.

**The profiles in Cut A**, each a combination from D21's menu:

| Profile | Video | Audio | Used when |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `remux` | copied | `aac-stereo`, plus `aac-stereo` with dialogue boost | the video plays but the container or the audio does not (MKV, TrueHD, DTS) — the common case |
| `h264-8m` | `h264-sdr` at ~8 Mbps, hardware encoder where present | the same two | the video codec does not play, or the link is remote and slow |

Both carry the text subtitle tracks, extracted as ASS for libass (JASSUB) and as WebVTT for the
cast receiver. Bitmap subtitles (PGS) are the audit's narrowed D78 question, and not in the first
build.

**Dialogue boost in Cut A is on or off.** D83 wanted a continuous control. A prepared rendition
is a shared cache, however, so it offers two stereo downmixes as two audio renditions: the
standard matrix, and one with the centre channel raised. The client picks by the user's
preference, and switching between them mid-film needs no new job. Finer steps can come later as
further renditions.

**Timing.** Measured remux runs thousands of times faster than real time, so in practice it is
bound by disk and network:
- **a remux is complete within a minute or two**, and a seek past the prepared point waits for
  seconds at most;
- **an encode runs at a few times real time** on Quick Sync, so a seek ahead of it waits. That
  is why remote viewing prepares in advance.

Live segment-addressed transcoding stays unbuilt until a measurement says first-play latency
hurts.

**Scheduling.** Nodes run at most one encode at a time, which matters on an N95. Remux jobs are
limited by the disk. A job that fails records the FFmpeg exit and its stderr tail as its reason,
shown to the user (principles §3). A crash restarts the job from zero, which is cheap because
the output is a cache.

### 3. The encoder is a node capability; two plugin tiers wait (P3)

A node advertises what it can produce: `remux`, `aac`, `h264_qsv`, `h264_nvenc`, `x264`. The
core sends a job to a node that can do it. The desktop's RTX 3090 becomes a second node later,
with no plugin API at all. **Plugin tier 3
([D19](#d19--the-transcoder-is-a-plugin-we-happen-to-maintain-plugin-tiers-become-three))
is retired** into the node. **Tier 1 (WASM, [D12](#d12--providers-are-sandboxed-wasm-plugins-no-in-process-plugin-code))
is deferred** until a third-party provider is asked for. TMDB and OpenSubtitles are Go packages
behind the provider interface, which is the future host-function list. Tier 2 (protocol adapters,
[D15](#d15--two-plugin-tiers-in-process-wasm-and-out-of-process-adapters)) needs nothing from us
but a stable API, and is unchanged.

### 4. The mechanism cut (P4)

Adopted as the audit's §2 table. In short:
- **The node:**
  - **One node transport:** HTTP+JSONL over a Unix socket, with dial-out TCP later. The file
    exchange channel and its signing, attribute-cache and torn-read handling are **deleted**.
  - **Node liveness** is an HTTP status endpoint plus the report stream.
  - **The first-scan scheduler** is a FIFO with "play this now" at the front.
- **FFmpeg:**
  - **FFmpeg is confined per invocation**, through a re-exec shim. The confinement is ranked:
    1. argument hardening, always;
    2. read-only mounts;
    3. a seccomp **denylist**;
    4. Landlock, where the kernel has it.
  - **The custom FFmpeg build is deferred.**
- **No predicate compiler until the first authored or restricting rule.** Cut A's pages are
  fixed sqlc queries, plus one small hand-written filter builder for search. The compiler
  replaces that builder when it arrives. It never sits beside it.
- **Voice** is browser WebRTC through a TURN server embedded in our binary (`pion/turn`), with
  signalling on the session WebSocket. The upgrade ladder and content-referenced echo cancellation
  are **deleted**.
- **Reachability:** no own relay role in Cut A. The order is a port-forward, then IPv6, then a
  standard tunnel (rathole, frp or WireGuard) to a VPS.
- **Subtitles:** stock JASSUB, with the custom libass build and the served variable-font set
  deferred until a user's language needs them. D78's overlay is narrowed to a later question.
- **Role ceilings and lease columns are dropped** from `schema.md`, because additive schema
  arrives with its feature (D180).

### 5. One public name (P5)

The owner already holds domains, so choosing one is a practical step that needs no decision.
Cut A serves everything under one name, `media.<domain>`:
- the web client;
- the cast receiver, unpublished and registered to her device (D192);
- the TURN service's TLS port.

The certificate comes from Let's Encrypt through a **DNS-01 challenge**, so it works with no
inbound port open. Inside the house, split-horizon DNS or the router's hairpin makes the same
name reach the same machine.

### 6. The stack (P7)

As the audit's §5:
- **Web and cast receiver:** plain React + TypeScript + Vite, in a pnpm workspace with the SDK
  as a React-free package.
- **The TV framework** is decided by building the same four screens in Compose for TV and in
  react-native-tvos when TV work starts.
- **Server libraries:** huma v2 for the API and its OpenAPI; `openapi-typescript` +
  `openapi-fetch` for the client; `oasdiff` for D85's gate; a pure-Go SQLite driver behind one
  `Open()` whose pragmas are read back at startup.
- **FFmpeg:** a pinned jellyfin-ffmpeg portable build, bundled and checked by hash, never
  downloaded at runtime.

This is the technology set whose standards [D192](#d192--built-in-a-private-repository-tested-at-home-released-through-public-betas-standards-follow-the-final-stack)
§3 schedules next.

### 7. Where it runs (P8)

Measured by the owner (`/sys/kernel/security/lsm`):

| Host | OS | Landlock | Media |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **nas** (F4-424, N95, Quick Sync) | Proxmox | **off** | **the library is here** |
| nuc13 | Proxmox | off | — |
| **devnas** (F2-422, J3455, Quick Sync) | Debian trixie | **on** | none |
| gpuhost | Mint | on | — |

- **Development runs on devnas, with a corpus copied across.** It has Landlock and Quick Sync, it
  is the low-end reference host of D190, and a copied corpus is also what the tests want.
- **The Cut A deployment belongs on nas, beside the library.** A node reads files, and a node
  that reads them over the network brings back NFS change detection and its attribute caches,
  which this design has kept away from Cut A. The
  recommended form is a Debian LXC container on nas with:
  - **Landlock turned on in nas's kernel:** add
    `lsm=lockdown,capability,landlock,yama,apparmor,ima,evm` to the kernel command line and
    reboot. An LXC shares the host kernel, so it inherits Landlock.
  - the media bind-mounted **read-only**;
  - `/dev/dri` passed through for Quick Sync.

  Until the owner makes that change, a node on nas runs and reports itself *unconfined*
  ([D112](#d112--the-node-probes-its-confinement-and-reports-it-the-escape-test-asserts-what-is-in-force)),
  which is the degraded mode that decision designed for.

### 8. The build contract, then a freeze (P9)

[plans/cut-a.md](../design/plans/cut-a.md) is written. It holds:
- the process topology and byte path;
- the repository layout;
- the API endpoints;
- the node and Watch Together message sets;
- the error enumeration and the job queue;
- milestones M0–M5 with acceptance tests.

**From then on, Cut A's design is frozen:** a new decision is made only when code or a
measurement forces one. Research into what comes after Cut A may continue, but it does not
reopen Cut A.

### 9. What it changes, marked in place

- **Refined:**
  - D4: prepare is Cut A's second path.
  - D10: the web client is plain React; the TV framework is decided later.
  - D12 and D15: tier 1 is deferred.
  - D26: confinement is re-ranked, and the custom build deferred.
  - D31: pragmas are read back at startup.
  - D43: confinement is per invocation.
  - D68: TURN is embedded, and the ladder deleted.
  - D71: our own relay role is deferred.
  - D118: the scheduler is simplified.
  - D128: the core relays.
  - D164: the compiler is deferred.
- **Superseded in part:**
  - D19: tier 3 is retired.
  - D127: the file channel is deleted.
- **Everything else stands.**

**Status:** Decided. The contradiction sweep of the audit's §3, the schema fixes of §3.1 and
`plans/cut-a.md` follow in the same change.

## D194 — Secrets: our users' passwords are hashed, third-party secrets are sealed with a key that never enters the database, and nothing reads a secret back out

> **Amended by [D198](#d198--m1s-four-open-points-secretkey-lives-in-the-state-directory-cachedb-waits-for-m2-the-agent-makes-a-golden-the-owner-approves-and-m1s-api-is-setup-sessions-settings-and-secrets):** `secret.key` lives in the state directory, which is what §4
> already described; §3's "beside the configuration file" is struck.

**Decided** (2026-09-23), by the project owner (*"Settle the API keys and passwords now"*),
closing the question [auth.md](../design/plans/auth.md) left open after
[D193](#d193--the-audits-proposals-are-accepted-the-node-does-all-media-work-prepare-is-the-one-path-besides-direct-play-the-machinery-is-cut-and-cut-as-design-freezes).

### 1. What the secrets are

| Secret | Whose | Can we verify it instead of storing it? | Treatment |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **A user's password for this server** | each user | **yes** | hashed (§2) |
| Session, invite, join and cast credentials | — | yes | already hashed ([D154](#d154--one-grant-table-opaque-and-revocable-the-session-credential-never-appears-in-a-url)) |
| **TMDB API key** | the server's admin ([D16](#d16--gplv3-no-nonfree-components-and-provider-keys-belong-to-the-user)) | no: we present it | sealed (§3) |
| **OpenSubtitles API key, username and password** | each user | no: we log in with them | sealed |
| **DNS provider token** for the certificate's DNS-01 challenge | the server | no | sealed |
| **TURN shared secret** | the server; we generate it | no: short-lived TURN credentials are derived from it | sealed; rotating it is free |
| TLS private key and ACME account key | the server | no | files in the state directory, mode 0600, never in the database. They are re-issuable, so losing them costs a new certificate |

**The rule is to store a verifier wherever we can, and a sealed secret only where we must
present the secret to someone else.**

### 2. Our users' passwords: argon2id

- **argon2id** from `golang.org/x/crypto/argon2`, with **RFC 9106's second recommended
  parameters**: 64 MiB, t = 3, p = 4. The hash is stored as a PHC string, so the parameters
  travel with it and can change later.
- **Measured:** 41 ms on an i3-1315U (`/yoloai/cache/bench/argon/`). The J3455 in devnas is
  several times slower, so M1 measures it there with a ceiling of **500 ms**; above that, the
  memory cost comes down to OWASP's 46 MiB, t = 1.
- **A login under older parameters is re-hashed** on success.
- **Failed logins are rate-limited** per account and per address, because 64 MiB per attempt is
  also a memory-exhaustion lever.
- **No password recovery by email.** There is no mail server and no account elsewhere (D13). An
  admin sets a temporary password that the user must change at first sign-in.

### 3. Third-party secrets: sealed, in a table of their own

- **The key.** On first start the server generates a 256-bit key and writes it to
  **`secret.key`** ~~beside the configuration file~~ in the state directory ([D198](#d198--m1s-four-open-points-secretkey-lives-in-the-state-directory-cachedb-waits-for-m2-the-agent-makes-a-golden-the-owner-approves-and-m1s-api-is-setup-sessions-settings-and-secrets)), mode
  0600. It is **never** written into the
  database.
- **The table.** Sealed secrets live in a **`secret`** table, separate from `setting`
  ([schema.md](../design/plans/schema.md)). Each row holds:
  - the XChaCha20-Poly1305 ciphertext (`golang.org/x/crypto/chacha20poly1305`);
  - its nonce and the id of the key that sealed it;
  - a **hint** (the last four characters of an API key; nothing for a password);
  - who set it, and when.
- **The associated data is the row's identity** (scope, user, name). A ciphertext copied into
  another row, or into another user's row, fails to open.
- **Why a table of its own.** Anything that dumps settings (a bug report, `doctor`, an admin
  export, a support copy of `setting`) then cannot carry a secret by accident. Only the
  `secrets` package may query this table, and the linter enforces that.

**What this protects, and what it does not.** It protects a database or backup file that leaves
the machine on its own, the realistic leaks:
- a backup synced to cloud storage;
- a database attached to a bug report;
- a copy handed to someone for help.

In each case the file holds ciphertext. **It does not protect against root on the server**,
because the server must decrypt a secret to use it, and nothing short of a hardware key store
changes that. Say so in the documentation rather than implying otherwise. The pattern is the one
Grafana (`secret_key`), Nextcloud (`secret`) and Gitea (`SECRET_KEY`) use: a key in the
configuration, ciphertext in the database.

### 4. Backups and restores

- **A database backup does not contain the key.** `VACUUM INTO`, `orpheum backup` and D181's
  migration snapshots all carry ciphertext only.
- **A backup of the whole state directory contains the key.** That is a copy of the machine,
  and restoring it is moving the machine.
- **Moving to a new machine:** `orpheum backup --include-key` writes the key beside the database
  file, and the command's output says what that means.
- **Restoring without the key is not an error.** It is Grafana's commonest migration trap made
  visible:
  - everything restores;
  - every sealed secret shows **"needs re-entering"** on the settings page and in `doctor`;
  - the features that need a secret say which one is missing (TMDB fetches pause, subtitle
    fetching asks the user to sign in again).

  Nothing else is lost. The same applies when `secret.key` is deleted or replaced.
- **Rotating the key:** `orpheum secrets rotate` writes a new key, re-seals every row in one
  transaction, and only then removes the old key. The key id in each row makes a half-finished
  rotation recoverable.

### 5. Nothing reads a secret back out

- **Write-only over the API.** `PUT` sets a secret and `DELETE` clears it. `GET` returns
  `{set, hint, set_by, set_at, needs_reentry}`, never the value. A user's own OpenSubtitles
  password is write-only to that user too. An admin can clear another user's secret but cannot
  read it.
- **A type that will not print.** In Go a secret is a `secrets.Value`. Its `String`,
  `GoString`, `Format`, `MarshalJSON`, `MarshalText` and `LogValue` all emit `[redacted]`. The
  only accessor is `Reveal()`, and the linter permits it only in the provider clients that send
  the secret to its owner's service. This is the mechanical form of
  [D74](#d74--bug-reports-pseudonymise-rather-than-redact-and-fan-in-across-components)'s rule
  that bug reports carry no secrets.
- **The canary test.** M1 sets every secret to a known canary string, then drives the API,
  `doctor`, a bug report, a backup and the logs, and asserts that the canary appears in none of
  them except as ciphertext. It must first be seen to fail against a deliberately leaking
  handler ([D190](#d190--the-testing-strategy-devices-report-on-themselves-against-numbers-a-missing-capability-fails-every-check-first-shows-it-can-fail-and-the-lab-is-built-from-what-is-on-the-shelf)).

### 6. Not chosen

- **Plaintext, as Home Assistant's `.storage` and many self-hosted projects keep it.** Cheaper,
  but it turns every leaked backup into a leaked OpenSubtitles account.
- **Environment variables or systemd credentials as the store.** Useful on some hosts, absent in
  others, and a second way to set a value (principles §4). The setup wizard and settings page
  are the one way.
- **Envelope encryption with per-row data keys** (Grafana 9+). It exists to put the master key
  in a cloud KMS, which a household server has no use for.
- **Encrypting the whole database** (SQLCipher). That means cgo, it defeats `VACUUM INTO` as a
  readable backup, and the key still has to sit on the same machine.

**Status:** Decided. [schema.md](../design/plans/schema.md) gains the `secret` table;
[auth.md](../design/plans/auth.md)'s open item is closed; [cut-a.md](../design/plans/cut-a.md)
gains the secret endpoints, and M1 gains the argon2id measurement and the canary test.

---

## D195 — "Orpheum" is the provisional name

**Decided** (2026-09-23), by the project owner: *"save it as the current provisional name."*
Research: [name-orpheum.md](../design/research/name-orpheum.md).

- **The name is Orpheum**, and publicly **"Orpheum Media Server"**. It is provisional until a
  professional trademark clearance, which is due before any store listing or the paid relay.
  The screen found no live ORPHEUM mark for software, streaming or SaaS. Nearby marks exist for
  loudspeakers (probably Bose Professional), for audio-visual devices in Germany, and for
  theatres.
- **The name is used in these places:**
  - the binary is `orpheum`, the Go module `github.com/kstenerud/orpheum`;
  - the service user and directories are `/var/lib/orpheum`, `/var/cache/orpheum` and
    `/run/orpheum`;
  - environment and test variables take an `ORPHEUM_` prefix.
- **The placeholders `vp` and `mediaserver` in the live documents are renamed**, and so is D194
  (written the same day with `vp`). Older decisions and research keep whatever they said; they
  are history.
- **Renaming later is mechanical and cheap until the first public release.** It means one module
  path, one binary name and a sweep. After release, the costly part is the Android package ID,
  which can never change after the first Play upload. So the package ID is chosen at the first
  public beta, not now.
- **Steps for the owner when convenient:**
  - register `orpheum.dev` and `orpheum.tv`, which appeared free;
  - claim a GitHub organisation such as `orpheum-media`, and the npm name.
- **The name has two neighbours to stay clear of:**
  - theatre imagery;
  - the "Orpheus" music piracy tracker and download tool, which its close spelling invites.
    Given [D187](#d187--users-are-responsible-for-what-they-play-we-never-supply-locate-unlock-or-promote-it--and-the-store-and-legal-constraints-that-follow),
    nothing we publish should play on that resemblance.

**Status:** Decided, provisional.

## D196 — The standards are written, every rule names its enforcement, and the gates run by themselves before the first line of feature code

**Decided** (2026-09-23), by the project owner: *"build the standards documents before we start
coding. All code should follow the standards from the moment the LLM starts writing code. We
should have mechanical checks of the code and tests that gets triggered automatically, like we
do in yoloai. I want everything ready up to the point where I can start the agent writing the
actual code on the next prompt."* It carries out
[D192](#d192--built-in-a-private-repository-tested-at-home-released-through-public-betas-standards-follow-the-final-stack)
§3 and is milestone M0 of [cut-a.md](../design/plans/cut-a.md).
Research: [yoloai-lessons.md](../design/research/yoloai-lessons.md), and the audit's §7.

### 1. What exists

- **Standards** in [`standards/`](../standards/README.md): `go.md`, `sql.md`, `typescript.md`,
  `testing.md`, `python.md`, `shell.md`, `makefile.md` and `markdown.md`. **Every rule names the
  compiler flag, lint rule, test, gate script or hook that enforces it, or says *review-only*.**
  yoloAI measured that prose rules were followed unreliably and mechanical gates were not.
- **Principles §17–§21**, adopted from yoloAI, each earned by a specimen:
  - §17: a rule nothing runs is a hope;
  - §18: a check never seen failing proves nothing;
  - §19: a defect is a sample;
  - §20: a gate changes on purpose;
  - §21: an owner's correction is written down, in
    [`agent-failures.md`](../agent-failures.md).
- **The skeleton:**
  - `cmd/orpheum` and one `doc.go` per package of cut-a §3, each with **Invariants** (naming
    their enforcement), **Read before changing** and **Where to change**;
  - the sanctioned clock and logger;
  - the web workspace: `sdk`, `player`, `web` and `cast-receiver`, each with the same three
    headings in its README.

  There is no feature code.
- **`make check` is the one gate.** On the skeleton it passes in about 9 s. It runs:
  - **docs:** links, anchors, decision IDs and the index;
  - **the gate scripts' own tests**, and shellcheck;
  - **SPDX headers** that match their directory, and a file-size limit (warn at 400 lines, fail
    at 800);
  - **the dependency allowlists;**
  - **claims:**
    - every cited `TestArch_` test exists and every one is cited;
    - every `D<n>` in code is a live decision;
    - every `ORPHEUM_TEST_` variable read is set by a job;
  - **Go:**
    - `gofumpt`/`gci`;
    - golangci-lint with depguard and forbidigo encoding the architecture;
    - `go vet` for Linux and macOS;
    - the tests, including eight `TestArch_` tests, each shown failing against a synthetic
      violation;
    - `go mod tidy`, and the speculative-API lint;
  - **generated code** regenerated and diffed;
  - **web:** `tsc`, strict ESLint with no warnings allowed, Prettier, dependency-cruiser,
    Vitest.

  **Seen failing end to end** on a core `os/exec` import, an `any`, a missing SPDX header and an
  invented decision ID.
- **Branch gates** (`make check-pr`):
  - **revert-and-require-red**, adapted from yoloAI. A `Verified-By:` trailer must name a
    ticked [`VQ<n>`](../verification-queue.md) (D190);
  - **test weakening:** a deleted test, a new skip, fewer assertions or a changed golden needs a
    `Test-Weakened:` trailer, and **a changed gate file needs the owner's `Gate-Changed:`
    trailer**;
  - **commit lint.**
- **Automatic triggers:**
  - **Claude Code hooks:**
    - the **Stop hook** runs `make check` at the end of any turn that changed a file, and blocks
      the turn on failure;
    - **pre-edit** refuses changes to gates, generated code and committed migrations;
    - **pre-bash** refuses dependency additions, `--no-verify` and force-pushes;
  - **git hooks**, installed by `make setup`, for pre-commit and the commit message;
  - **CI**, which runs `make check` on every push and the branch gates on every branch and pull
    request.

### 2. Choices made while building it, for the owner to know

- **SPDX identifier `GPL-3.0-or-later`** for the server tree; D80 said "GPLv3" without saying
  "only" or "or later". *Or later* is the common choice (the FSF's recommendation); changing it
  is a one-line sed until the first outside contribution.
- **npm workspaces, not pnpm.** npm ships with Node, so the build needs one tool fewer.
  cut-a.md is updated to match.
- **TypeScript is held at 6.0**, because typescript-eslint does not yet support 7.
  **`eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y-x`** replaces the unmaintained `jsx-a11y`.
- **Styling is plain CSS files with custom properties**, not CSS Modules, because themes (D138)
  need stable class names. **Named exports only; no `enum`.**
- **Go tests use the standard library only.** testify is banned outright, and go-cmp is used
  only once the owner allowlists it.
- **Spelling in code comments is British**, matching the docs (misspell's UK locale).
- **The store has one write connection and a read-only pool** ([sql.md](../standards/sql.md)).
- **`internal/node/bytes` is `internal/node/byteserver`**, so it does not shadow the standard
  `bytes` package.
- **The gate hooks refuse rather than ask.** Claude Code does not document that an *ask*
  prompts when a session bypasses permissions, which is how agents run in yoloAI sandboxes. A
  refusal always holds. Sessions for gate or dependency work start with
  `ORPHEUM_ALLOW_GATE_EDIT=1` or `ORPHEUM_ALLOW_DEPS=1`. The shell guard is a speed bump: it was
  shown bypassable by a Python one-liner while it was being built. The wall is the branch
  gate's `Gate-Changed:` trailer.

### 3. What M0 still lacks

- **CI has not run**, because the repository is not on GitHub yet. It will run on the first
  push to the private repository.
- **Tools on a new machine:** `make tools` installs the pinned golangci-lint, and
  `make tools-sqlc` installs sqlc, which needs cgo, before M1's first query.

**Status:** Decided. [cut-a.md](../design/plans/cut-a.md) marks M0 done except for CI's first
run. The next prompt starts M1.

---

## D197 — A development loop with opinionated, printed settings, and Makefile targets for the common debugging jobs

> **Amended by [D200](#d200--every-opinionated-value-is-a-setting-row-seeded-with-its-starting-value-nothing-has-a-default-in-code-the-config-file-holds-only-what-must-exist-before-the-database-opens-and-all-of-it-is-required):** `/debug/pprof` and `/metrics` are the `debug_pprof` and
> `debug_metrics` settings, not config keys.

**Decided** (2026-09-23), by the project owner: *"For the makefile, I want targets for common
debugging tasks, including spinning up the app with some opinionated config."*

### 1. What `make dev` does

It is one command that leaves a working app on the screen:
- **It fetches the pinned FFmpeg**, jellyfin-ffmpeg 8.1.2-5 (D193 §6), verifying its SHA-256.
- **It generates a synthetic dev library** in 17 s and about 20 MB. There is one file per Cut A
  playback path and per scanner filing, with NFO files so no TMDB key is needed. Nothing in it
  is copyrighted
  ([D187](#d187--users-are-responsible-for-what-they-play-we-never-supply-locate-unlock-or-promote-it--and-the-store-and-legal-constraints-that-follow)).
- **It builds with `-tags dev -race`**, seeds an empty database with Cut A's two users, and runs
  the server alongside Vite's hot-reloading dev server, which proxies to it.
- **It rebuilds the server whenever Go code or the dev config changes.**

It was run here: it builds, reports that the server is not implemented yet, keeps watching and
rebuilds on a change. Vite serves the app, and `/api` is proxied to the server.

### 2. The opinions, and why each one is visible

The owner's rule is that a default must be safe to be wrong and visible
([D183](#d183--an-override-is-an-override-wherever-its-value-came-from-a-librarys-source-is-asked-not-defaulted-a-default-must-be-safe-to-be-wrong-and-visible-where-it-acts)).
So every dev choice lives in two committed files, `dev/orpheum.dev.toml` and `dev/seed.toml`
(since 2026-10-01 they live in `deploy/dev/`, so that `./dev` can be the container launcher of
[D235](#d235--development-and-deployment-run-in-containers-one-image-family-one-command-each-built-by-goreleaser)),
and the loop prints them in a banner at start:

- **Loopback, plain HTTP.** Browsers treat localhost as a secure context, so the microphone
  works. `make dev-lan` opens the loop to the LAN for a phone or a TV, without the microphone.
- **Debug logs as text.** pprof and `/metrics` are on, on loopback only (D91 keeps them off in
  production).
- **Confinement is reported, not required**, so the loop runs on a machine without Landlock and
  says so. Production defaults to `require`.
- **The race detector is on** (`DEV_RACE=0` turns it off).
- **Users `owner`/`owner` and `partner`/`partner`.** These passwords are public. They are
  therefore creatable only by `orpheum dev`, which exists **only in `-tags dev` builds**, and a
  test guards that.
- **Libraries** take their metadata from NFO, watch for changes, and are never written to.
  Nothing reaches the network by itself.

### 3. The debugging targets

| Target | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `dev`, `dev-server`, `dev-web`, `dev-lan` | run the whole app, the server alone, Vite alone, or the server open to the LAN |
| `dev-config`, `dev-media`, `dev-seed` | print the effective config; generate the library (`FORCE=1` regenerates); seed again |
| `dev-reset`, `dev-clean` | drop the database and caches but keep the media; drop everything |
| `dev-logs`, `dev-db`, `dev-doctor` | follow the log; open the database in an SQL shell; run the doctor |
| `dev-debug`, `pprof`, `pprof-heap` | delve headless on `:2345` for an IDE to attach; CPU and heap profiles in the browser |
| `probe FILE=…` | what the node would record about a file |
| `test-one PKG=… RUN=…`, `test-web-watch`, `cover` | focused, uncached, race-checked Go tests; web tests in watch mode; a coverage report |
| `ffmpeg`, `tools-dlv` | the pinned FFmpeg; the pinned delve 1.27.2 |

**No new dependency.** The loop, the watcher and the generator are standard-library Python. The
Vite proxy reads its target through Vite's own `loadEnv`, not `@types/node`. `make check` now
also lints, vets and tests the dev build.

### 4. What it asks of the server

[cut-a.md](../design/plans/cut-a.md) §2a lists the contract:
- `orpheum run --config`, with the dev file's keys;
- `orpheum dev seed`: users and settings in M1, libraries in M2;
- `/debug/pprof` and `/metrics` behind their config keys.

**Status:** Decided. The Makefile, `scripts/dev.py`, `scripts/dev_media.py`,
`scripts/fetch_ffmpeg.py` and `dev/` land together, and cut-a gains §2a. This is a gate change
the owner asked for, so it carries `Gate-Changed:`.

## D198 — M1's four open points: `secret.key` lives in the state directory, `cache.db` waits for M2, the agent makes a golden the owner approves, and M1's API is setup, sessions, settings and secrets

**Decided** (2026-09-24), by the project owner, answering the questions the agent raised when M1
began ([cut-a.md](../design/plans/cut-a.md) §8). Each is where the plan was silent or said two
things.

1. **`secret.key` is `<data_dir>/secret.key`, mode 0600.**
   [D194](#d194--secrets-our-users-passwords-are-hashed-third-party-secrets-are-sealed-with-a-key-that-never-enters-the-database-and-nothing-reads-a-secret-back-out)
   said both "beside the configuration file" (§3) and "a backup of the whole state directory
   contains the key" (§4), and `internal/core/datadir` listed the key under the state directory.
   The state directory is the answer: it is what §4 describes, and the core touches files only
   in its state and cache directories. D194 §3 and [schema.md](../design/plans/schema.md) are
   corrected in place.
2. **`cache.db` is deferred to M2.** [schema.md](../design/plans/schema.md) puts `job`,
   `match_candidate` and `prepared_rendition` in a second file, but sqlc reads one migrations
   directory as the whole schema, and nothing in M1 uses those tables. Migration 0001 is
   `library.db` alone; `cache.db`'s layout, its "versioned by discard" rule and `sqlc.yaml`'s
   schema list are decided together when the job queue arrives.
3. **The agent makes the first schema golden; the owner approves it.** Goldens under
   `testdata/golden/` are the owner's
   ([standards/testing.md](../standards/testing.md) §8). The agent generates it with the test's
   `-update` flag and commits it alone, carrying `Gate-Changed:` that cites this decision.
4. **M1's API is setup, sessions, settings and secrets.** huma serves `/health`, `POST /setup`,
   `POST` and `DELETE /session`, `GET /me`, `GET`/`PUT /settings` and `/me/settings`, and the
   write-only `/secrets` and `/me/secrets` endpoints, so the canary test drives a real API. The
   OpenAPI document is generated and committed; the `make generate` and `check-generated` lines
   that regenerate and diff it are the owner's to add, because the Makefile is a gate.

**Status:** Decided.

## D199 — The core may reach `os/exec` through the SQLite driver's C runtime, and through nothing else

**Decided** (2026-09-24), by the project owner, when M1 found that `TestArch_CoreNeverExecs`
failed for every core package that uses the store.

- **What was found.** `modernc.org/libc`, the C runtime under the pure-Go SQLite driver
  ([D31](#d31--sqlite-with-a-pure-go-driver-supersedes-d5)), imports `os/exec` to implement C's `system()` and `popen()`. SQLite never calls them. No
  code of ours runs a process, but the transitive check cannot see that.
- **The decision.** The check exempts that one edge, `modernc.org/libc` → `os/exec`, with the
  reason beside it, and walks the real import graph so any other route to `os/exec` still fails
  and is named. The change is to the test only.
- **Not chosen.** Switching to `ncruces/go-sqlite3`, which reaches no `os/exec`, would add about
  ten modules to the allowlist, and the driver benchmark on devnas
  ([standards/sql.md](../standards/sql.md) §7) has not run. Checking direct imports only would
  duplicate depguard and stop catching a real indirect exec.

**Status:** Decided.

---

## D200 — Every opinionated value is a setting row, seeded with its starting value; nothing has a default in code; the config file holds only what must exist before the database opens, and all of it is required

> **Amended by [D202](#d202--missing-values-heal-themselves-and-say-so-unused-settings-are-listed-and-deleted-only-by-a-person-doctor-not-a-seed-command-is-where-to-find-what-needs-fixing):** a missing value heals — a setting row is rewritten with
> its starting value, a config key runs on its starting value — rather than refusing.

> **Refined by [D201](#d201--a-setting-a-person-set-stays-theirs-and-every-other-one-follows-its-starting-value-the-last-pre-database-values-are-config-keys-seeding-fills-both-places-and-reports-what-nothing-reads-new-goldens-have-standing-approval):** *modified* is a stored mark a manual set makes and
> "set to default" clears, and unmodified rows follow a changed starting value; the pre-database
> values below are config keys, not constants; seeding also fills the config file and reports
> keys nothing reads.

**Decided** (2026-09-24), by the project owner, reviewing the numbers M1 had compiled in: *"things
that take opinionated values should in general be configurable … stored in the database config
table, not necessarily directly accessible via the UI … in a similar spirit to how Firefox has
about:config"*, and *"I want to avoid default behaviors in code because they make things harder
to reason about."*

### 1. Settings

- **Every opinion the server acts on is a setting**: the failed sign-in limit and window, session
  idle expiry, how often a session's use is written, argon2id's costs, the API key hint length,
  doctor's backup-age warning, and the debug endpoints, beside the three M1 already had.
- **The registry in code says each key's type, bounds and starting value, and whether the
  settings page shows it.** On every start the server writes the starting value of any key that
  has no row — every key on a new server, and on an upgrade the keys the release introduced —
  and never changes a row that exists. The running server reads only rows.
- **A missing row is an error, never a fallback.** It names the key and its starting value and
  says how to fix it: set that one through `/config`, or write every missing one with
  `orpheum seed-settings` or `POST /config/seed`, which only fill gaps.
- **A question** — `update_check` (D184) — starts as JSON null and reads as unanswered.
  *(Since 2026-09-29, the key is `should_check_for_updates` ([D227](#d227--every-name-in-a-contract-that-a-reader-must-look-up-is-renamed-now-minor-ones-too-a-job-names-its-target-by-kind-and-a-sidecars-kind-has-its-own-column) §6). Noted 2026-09-30; the owner: "agreed" ([M3's closing audit](../design/research/audit-2026-09-29.md) §9 D).)*
- **The raw view is `/config`** (admin): every setting with its value, its starting value and
  whether it differs, with `?modified=true` for only the changed ones; `PUT` changes any setting,
  and `POST /config/{key}/reset` writes the starting value back. `/settings` shows and changes only
  what the settings page exposes. The page for the full list shows each value beside its starting
  value, and filters to the changed ones, when the web client is built. *(Since 2026-09-29, `?modified=true`
  is `?onlyModified=true` ([D227](#d227--every-name-in-a-contract-that-a-reader-must-look-up-is-renamed-now-minor-ones-too-a-job-names-its-target-by-kind-and-a-sidecars-kind-has-its-own-column)). Noted 2026-09-30; the owner: "agreed" ([M3's closing audit](../design/research/audit-2026-09-29.md) §9 D).)*
- **Values needed before the database opens cannot be settings**: ~~the HTTP read-header timeout,
  the free-space margin before migrating and the reader-pool minimum stay constants for now, as
  does the shutdown grace a failed start also needs~~ they are required config keys ([D201](#d201--a-setting-a-person-set-stays-theirs-and-every-other-one-follows-its-starting-value-the-last-pre-database-values-are-config-keys-seeding-fills-both-places-and-reports-what-nothing-reads-new-goldens-have-standing-approval)). Format and safety properties — pragmas, file
  modes, token length, the setup code's shape — stay constants because they are not opinions.

### 2. The config file

- **Every key is required**, and a missing one is refused by name. The dev loop and the installer
  write all of them.
- **What stays** is only what must be known before `library.db` opens, or must not be changeable
  by someone holding only an admin account: `server.listen`, `data_dir` and `cache_dir`;
  `node.roots` (D107), `ffmpeg_dir` and `confinement`; `log.level` and `log.format`.
  *(Since 2026-09-29, `node.roots` is `node.root_paths` and `confinement` is `confinement_policy`
  ([D227](#d227--every-name-in-a-contract-that-a-reader-must-look-up-is-renamed-now-minor-ones-too-a-job-names-its-target-by-kind-and-a-sidecars-kind-has-its-own-column)). Noted 2026-09-30; the owner: "agreed" ([M3's closing audit](../design/research/audit-2026-09-29.md) §9 D).)*
- **`[debug]` leaves the file** for the `debug_pprof` and `debug_metrics` settings. *(Since
  2026-09-29, they are `should_serve_debug_pprof` and `should_serve_debug_metrics` ([D227](#d227--every-name-in-a-contract-that-a-reader-must-look-up-is-renamed-now-minor-ones-too-a-job-names-its-target-by-kind-and-a-sidecars-kind-has-its-own-column) §6).
  Noted 2026-09-30; the owner: "agreed" ([M3's closing audit](../design/research/audit-2026-09-29.md) §9 D).)*

### 3. What it amends

- **[D183](#d183--an-override-is-an-override-wherever-its-value-came-from-a-librarys-source-is-asked-not-defaulted-a-default-must-be-safe-to-be-wrong-and-visible-where-it-acts)**: *"a row exists only when someone set a value"* is replaced. What D183
  wanted — an opinion visible where it acts — is kept more strongly: every opinion is a row, and
  its starting value is shown beside it.
- **[D182](#d182--metadata-is-a-stack-of-layers-with-one-fetched-layer-re-derivation-reads-only-stored-input-a-new-config-requirement-is-a-default-a-derivation-or-a-question) §3**: a config file key is never defaulted; a new one is a derivation, a question
  asked in the UI (and so a setting), or a refusal naming the key.
- **[D197](#d197--a-development-loop-with-opinionated-printed-settings-and-makefile-targets-for-the-common-debugging-jobs) §4**: pprof and metrics are settings, not config keys; `dev/seed.toml` turns them on.

**Status:** Decided.

---

## D201 — A setting a person set stays theirs, and every other one follows its starting value; the last pre-database values are config keys; seeding fills both places and reports what nothing reads; new goldens have standing approval

> **Amended by [D202](#d202--missing-values-heal-themselves-and-say-so-unused-settings-are-listed-and-deleted-only-by-a-person-doctor-not-a-seed-command-is-where-to-find-what-needs-fixing):** there is no seed command; missing values heal themselves,
> and doctor lists what needs fixing. §3 is struck.
>
> **Suspended in part by [D228](#d228--until-migrations-are-live-librarydbs-schema-is-a-baseline-and-one-step-and-a-schema-change-folds-the-last-step-into-the-baseline)** until migrations are live: the
> goldens are the baseline's and the current version's, and a fold rewrites them.

**Decided** (2026-09-24), by the project owner, refining [D200](#d200--every-opinionated-value-is-a-setting-row-seeded-with-its-starting-value-nothing-has-a-default-in-code-the-config-file-holds-only-what-must-exist-before-the-database-opens-and-all-of-it-is-required)
the same day.

### 1. Modified means a person set it

D200 computed *modified* as "differs from the starting value", so setting a value back to its
default made it unmodified, and a later release could not tell a choice from an untouched row.
Instead:

- **Any manual set marks a setting modified**, even to the value it starts with (migration 0002,
  `setting.is_modified`). *(Since 2026-09-29, migration 0002 is folded into the baseline, whose name and version move with each fold ([D228](#d228--until-migrations-are-live-librarydbs-schema-is-a-baseline-and-one-step-and-a-schema-change-folds-the-last-step-into-the-baseline) §3). Noted 2026-09-30; the owner: "agreed" ([M3's closing audit](../design/research/audit-2026-09-29.md) §9 D).)*
- **"Set to default"** (`POST /config/{key}/reset`) writes the starting value and clears the mark.
- **When a release changes a starting value** — to fix a bad choice — every unmodified row moves
  to the new one at the next start, and the start-up log, `seed-settings` and `POST /config/seed`
  say which. A modified row is never touched.
- **This is the database side only.** The config file is small enough to manage by hand.

### 2. The config file

- **The values needed before the database opens are required config keys**, with starting values:
  `server.read_header_timeout_s` and `server.shutdown_grace_s` (10), and a new `[database]` table
  with `readers_minimum` (4) and `migrate_space_factor` (3). Nothing about them is left in code.
  *(Since 2026-09-29, they are `read_connections_minimum` and `migrate_free_space_db_multiple`
  ([D227](#d227--every-name-in-a-contract-that-a-reader-must-look-up-is-renamed-now-minor-ones-too-a-job-names-its-target-by-kind-and-a-sidecars-kind-has-its-own-column)). Noted 2026-09-30; the owner: "agreed" ([M3's closing audit](../design/research/audit-2026-09-29.md) §9 D).)*
- **Every config key has a starting value, or is marked as having none** because it is specific to
  the machine (the listen address, the directories, the media roots, the FFmpeg path). A missing
  key's refusal gives its starting value, or says why it has none.

### 3. Seeding

~~- **`orpheum seed-settings` fills the config file first**: it adds every missing key that has a
  starting value, in its own table, keeping comments and order, after keeping a copy of the file
  as it was; and it names the missing keys only a person can fill. Then it seeds the database.
- **Keys nothing reads are listed, never deleted** — a typo, or a key a release removed — in the
  config file and in the database, by `seed-settings`, `POST /config/seed`, the start-up log and
  `doctor`. Deleting them is the person's choice.~~ Replaced by [D202](#d202--missing-values-heal-themselves-and-say-so-unused-settings-are-listed-and-deleted-only-by-a-person-doctor-not-a-seed-command-is-where-to-find-what-needs-fixing).

### 4. Goldens for new migrations

**Standing approval**: for each new migration the agent generates its golden with `-update` and
commits it on its own, with `Gate-Changed:` citing this decision. Changing an existing golden
still needs the owner.

**Status:** Decided.

---

## D202 — Missing values heal themselves and say so; unused settings are listed and deleted only by a person; doctor, not a seed command, is where to find what needs fixing

**Decided** (2026-09-24), by the project owner, resolving a contradiction in [D200](#d200--every-opinionated-value-is-a-setting-row-seeded-with-its-starting-value-nothing-has-a-default-in-code-the-config-file-holds-only-what-must-exist-before-the-database-opens-and-all-of-it-is-required)
and [D201](#d201--a-setting-a-person-set-stays-theirs-and-every-other-one-follows-its-starting-value-the-last-pre-database-values-are-config-keys-seeding-fills-both-places-and-reports-what-nothing-reads-new-goldens-have-standing-approval):
the server was to balk at a missing value, yet it seeds missing values so that a later release can
add one. *"I think it's probably fine to just auto-seed any missing values. It's technically hidden
behavior they didn't explicitly sign up for, but the settings page shows them what everything is."*

### 1. Missing values

- **A setting row that goes missing while the server runs heals**: reading it writes its starting
  value to the database and logs a warning. Every start already writes every missing row. The
  value is always a row, never held in memory, so the settings page shows it.
- **A config-file key that has a starting value runs on it when the file lacks it**, in memory; the
  file is never rewritten unasked (migrations.md, Files). The server logs a warning naming it, and
  doctor and `/config` show it read-only as "starting value, not in the file". A key with no
  starting value — the listen address, the directories, the media roots, the FFmpeg path — still
  refuses start, because there is nothing sensible to run on.

### 2. Unused settings: listed, never removed automatically

- **Never auto-removed.** A downgrade can run an older release on the same database
  ([D181](#d181--the-migration-policy-two-integers-our-own-small-runner-a-snapshot-that-outlives-success-refuse-what-we-cannot-read-and-re-derive-rather-than-transform)'s
  `compatible_version`), and it would find its setting gone and reseed it, losing the person's
  choice; and deleting a typo deletes the evidence of what was meant.
- **Listed and deletable by a person**: `GET /config/unused`, and `DELETE /config/unused/{key}`,
  which refuses a key this release reads — that one is set to default, not deleted. The start-up log
  and doctor list them too.
- **The registry keeps the retired keys**, each with the release that retired it and why, so an
  unused row says "retired in v1.3: replaced by X" or, when no release ever used it, "probably a
  typo".

### 3. No seed command

`orpheum seed-settings` and `POST /config/seed` are removed: every start sweeps the database, and
missing config keys heal as above. **doctor is the one list of what should be fixed**: config keys
running on their starting values, config keys nothing reads, unused setting rows, and a missing key
with no starting value.

**Status:** Decided.

## D203 — The audit between M1 and M2: what M2 builds first, how cache.db is versioned, and two standing practices, an audit between milestones and a plan-deviation log

**Decided** (2026-09-24), by the project owner, approving every recommendation of
[audit-2026-09-24.md](../design/research/audit-2026-09-24.md) §7. The audit's reasoning is there;
this entry records what was decided.

### 1. For M2

- **`cache.db` is versioned by discard.** Its schema is one file, `internal/store/cache/schema.sql`,
  with a version number; when the file on disk has another number it is deleted and recreated
  (migrations.md). `sqlc.yaml` gains a second entry generating a separate package, so a library
  query cannot name a cache table. The owner changes `sqlc.yaml`.
- **The SDK uses `openapi-typescript` and `openapi-fetch`** (cut-a §5); the owner adds them to the
  npm allowlist.
- **MKVToolNix is pinned as FFmpeg is**: a make target fetches a pinned release by checksum, and
  the test that needs `mkvpropedit` declares it as a prerequisite.
- **The "media root at mode 000" acceptance runs the core against a replaying node**, since a real
  node runs under the core's own user (cut-a §2). A second service user would be a design change.
- **Tier 1's recordings come from generated media only** — the dev library and the fixture tree,
  never the owner's library ([D187](#d187--users-are-responsible-for-what-they-play-we-never-supply-locate-unlock-or-promote-it--and-the-store-and-legal-constraints-that-follow): no commercial content in fixtures).
- **M2 builds `internal/testutil` and `ORPHEUM_TEST_UNCONTROLLED` first**, and a reference-scale
  database generator once the tables it fills exist; until then migrations.md's 10 s step budget
  is checked in review.

### 2. Gates and documents

The documentation fixes of audit §2 and the `err` idiom of §4.2 are made. Three gate changes are
the owner's to apply: the shell guard decides from write targets, query files are refused if not
ASCII, and the Makefile puts `$(go env GOPATH)/bin` on PATH. No mutation testing now (§4.4).

### 3. Two standing practices

- **An audit between every two milestones**, before the next one's first code: the finished
  milestone against its acceptance list, documents that no longer say what is true, mechanisms
  still missing, gates that fought correct work, and what the next milestone needs decided. It is
  written to `design/research/audit-<date>.md` and ends with a table of decisions for the owner.
- **A plan-deviation log**, [plan-deviations.md](../plan-deviations.md): each place where what
  happened differed from what was planned, with why the plan missed it and a lesson for planning
  any project. Each audit adds to it. *"Over time as I build more projects, it'll help give insight
  into how my general process for projects can be improved."*

**Status:** Decided.

## D204 — No ambient configuration: the shipped binary is configured by its config file, its flags and its database, and by nothing it inherits

**Decided** (2026-09-24), by the project owner: *"we should adopt a no ambient config policy
similar to what yoloai does. I'm fine with some specific configuration env vars for development,
but otherwise config must be explicit and contained."* The code-level half already held (only
`cmd/orpheum` reads the environment, go.md §12); this extends it to the product and closes the
places where the standard library reads the environment on our behalf.

### 1. What configures the shipped binary

Exactly three things: the `--config` file, which is required, has no default location and holds
only absolute paths; the subcommand's flags; and `library.db`'s settings
([D200](#d200--every-opinionated-value-is-a-setting-row-seeded-with-its-starting-value-nothing-has-a-default-in-code-the-config-file-holds-only-what-must-exist-before-the-database-opens-and-all-of-it-is-required)–[D202](#d202--missing-values-heal-themselves-and-say-so-unused-settings-are-listed-and-deleted-only-by-a-person-doctor-not-a-seed-command-is-where-to-find-what-needs-fixing)).
A release build hands its subcommands an empty environment; only a `-tags dev` build passes the
real one on.

### 2. What the standard library would otherwise read

| Variable | Would steer | Instead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY`, `NO_PROXY` | every outbound request through Go's default transport | `internal/platform/outbound.NewClient` takes no proxy; the defaults and `ProxyFromEnvironment` are banned. A proxy, if ever needed, becomes a config key. |
| `TZ` | every formatted time, logs and doctor included | `cmd/orpheum` sets `time.Local` to UTC at start; clients format for their viewer. `time.Local` is banned elsewhere. ([D246](#d246--what-a-person-may-do-is-their-roles-an-invite-names-who-it-is-for-and-a-watch-together-viewer-is-an-ephemeral-account-that-sees-only-the-hosts-playback) §7: TZ, else `/etc/localtime`, is read once at start as the default of the server's `time_zone` setting, and passed down explicitly; a release build lets TZ alone through.) |
| `TMPDIR` | `os.TempDir`, and SQLite's temporary files | `temp_store = MEMORY` on every connection; `os.TempDir` is banned. A temporary file goes in a directory the config names. |
| the working directory | `filepath.Abs` | banned outside `cmd/orpheum`; config paths are absolute already |

### 3. What may still be read, and by whom

- **Development:** `ORPHEUM_DEV_*` (the dev seed's secrets, the Vite dev server's address and
  allowed hosts) and the Make variables `DEV_LISTEN` and `DEV_RACE`. Vite reads the process
  environment only, never `.env` files, and refuses to serve without `ORPHEUM_DEV_SERVER` rather
  than guessing an address. The built web client reads no environment: `import.meta.env` is
  banned in its source.
- **Tests:** `ORPHEUM_TEST_*`, set per CI step or lab job (testing.md §3).
- **Not ours, left alone:** the Go runtime's own variables (`GOMAXPROCS`, `GOMEMLIMIT`,
  `GODEBUG`, `GOTRACEBACK`) and the operating system's trust store, including `SSL_CERT_FILE`.
- **Children** get an explicit environment from `internal/node/execx`, never the inherited one
  (go.md §13).

**Accepted cost:** the server cannot be put behind an HTTP proxy until a config key exists for
one.

**Status:** Decided.

## D205 — x86_64 is where Cut A is verified; arm64 is kept open, riscv64 is watched, and nothing may assume amd64

**Decided** (2026-09-24), by the project owner, on pinning MKVToolNix for x86_64 Linux only:
*"I'm fine with x86 now, but we need to keep arm open for the future."*

- **Verified on x86_64 Linux** in Cut A: the development VM and CI's runner.
- **Kept open for arm64 Linux:** the server builds and vets for `linux/arm64`, and code may not
  assume an architecture. Where something is x86-only today, it is written down here with the
  route to arm64, so it is a known gap rather than a discovery:

| x86-only today | Why | Route to arm64 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| MKVToolNix, the integration tier's Matroska editor | its only portable build is an x86_64 AppImage | pin distribution packages or a source build for `linux/arm64` in `scripts/fetch_mkvtoolnix.py`; until then an arm64 job lists `mkvtoolnix` in `ORPHEUM_TEST_UNCONTROLLED` |
| Quick Sync and NVENC (M3's hardware encoders) | Intel and NVIDIA hardware | the node reports its encoders in `hello` (cut-a §4), so an arm64 node reports what it has; profiles never assume one |
| The seccomp denylist (M3) | syscall numbers differ per architecture | written by syscall name for amd64 and arm64 (built 2026-09-27); the escape test has run on amd64 only, so arm64's filter is tested when the first arm64 machine is. Any other architecture reports seccomp not in force, cause `architecture_unwritten`, with no code of its own |
| CI | one `ubuntu-24.04` runner | an arm64 job (`ubuntu-24.04-arm`) when the first arm64 machine is in view |

The pinned FFmpeg is already pinned for `linux/arm64` and `darwin/arm64`.

### riscv64 is watched

The owner, the same day: *"We should also keep an eye on risc-v, with the expectation that
support in all of the parts we rely on will probably come slowly."* riscv64 is **watched**: not
a target, but its status is recorded and our own code must not be what blocks it. Checked
2026-09-24:

| Part | riscv64 today | What would change it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Go toolchain, our code, the pure-Go SQLite driver | **builds and vets** (`GOOS=linux GOARCH=riscv64`) | — |
| The pinned FFmpeg (jellyfin-ffmpeg 8.1.2-5) | **no build**: portable builds are linux64, linuxarm64, mac and Windows only | a riscv64 release from jellyfin-ffmpeg, or pinning a source or distribution build by hash. This is the blocker: the node cannot work without FFmpeg |
| MKVToolNix (tests only) | **no build** | as for arm64 above |
| Playwright's browsers (tests only, the browser tier `make test-browser`; added in M3 by D217 §4) | **no build**: Playwright downloads Chromium and Firefox for linux x86_64 and arm64 only | a riscv64 build from Playwright, or running the tier against browsers pinned from elsewhere |
| Hardware encoders | none expected | the node reports what it has |
| Landlock and seccomp (M3) | supported by the Linux kernel on riscv64 | the denylist by syscall name covers it |
| CI | no riscv64 runner | emulation (QEMU) or a lab board, when there is a reason |

**Revisit** at each between-milestone audit: re-check the FFmpeg and MKVToolNix rows, and
whether any new dependency lacks riscv64.

**Status:** Decided. `make check` vets `GOOS=linux GOARCH=arm64`. riscv64 stays out of the
code and the gates — no build tags, no vet line, no pins — until every part it relies on
supports it; the owner: *"Leave riscv out of our code until we know we have full support."*
Until then it lives only in this table.

## D206 — A symlink is followed only into a media root; golang.org/x/text normalises filenames and language tags

**Decided** (2026-09-24), by the project owner, answering two points the plan left open when the
scanner was built. (The question put to the owner said the node would normalise filenames; D49
puts that at the core's ingest boundary, and this entry follows D49.)

### 1. Symlinks inside a media root

The scanner follows a symlink **only when its target resolves inside a configured media root**.
Otherwise it reports a `skip` record with the rule `symlink_outside_roots`, naming the link. A
followed directory is walked once, however many links reach it, so a loop ends.

Why: ffprobe opens a file by its path, so a link to `/etc/shadow` in a media root would be read
by the node and its probe sent to the core. Following nowhere breaks the common practice of
building a library from symlinks into another (sharing-model.md); following everywhere turns
a media root into a read of anything the service user can see.

### 2. golang.org/x/text

Allowed, for two jobs:

- **Filenames** ([D49](#d49--unicode-discipline-at-the-boundaries-enforced-by-tests)): the node reports each path's bytes exactly as the
  filesystem gave them, and the core normalises to NFC at its ingest boundary with
  `unicode/norm`, keeping those bytes for opening the file.
- **Language tags** (scanner.md, Track facts): each track's raw tag (`ger`, `deu`) beside its
  BCP 47 form (`de`), with `language`, which knows ISO 639-2's bibliographic and terminological
  codes. The alternative was hand-maintaining FFmpeg's 695-entry table.

**Status:** Decided. `deps/go.allow` gains `golang.org/x/text`.

## D207 — execx starts the node child; the node's loop is internal/node/agent and the core's side internal/core/nodes; a node is known by its configured name

**Decided** (2026-09-24), by the project owner, answering three points cut-a left open when the
node process was built.

### 1. execx starts the node child

cut-a §2 has `orpheum run` start the node as a child, and only `execx` may start a process. So
`execx` runs one more program besides `ffmpeg` and `ffprobe`: **orpheum's own binary in `node`
mode**, long-lived, with an empty environment ([D204](#d204--no-ambient-configuration-the-shipped-binary-is-configured-by-its-config-file-its-flags-and-its-database-and-by-nothing-it-inherits)), in its own process group. The core's
supervisor receives it through an interface that `cmd/orpheum` wires in, so the core still never
reaches `os/exec` (`TestArch_CoreNeverExecs`). M3's confinement shim, also a re-execution of
orpheum, will live beside it.

### 2. Two packages cut-a §3 did not list

- **`internal/node/agent`** — the node's loop: dial the core's socket, say hello, long-poll for
  commands, run them, and stream the report.
- **`internal/core/nodes`** — the core's side: the node channel's handlers, the command queue,
  liveness, and supervising the child.

### 3. A node is known by its configured name

The `[node]` table gains `name`, starting value `local`. The core enrols a `node` row on the
first hello with a name it has not seen and matches by name after that; the socket's permissions
are the authentication ([D107](#d107--the-node-channel-is-mutually-authenticated-and-a-nodes-roots-are-local-and-never-remotely-settable)).

**Status:** Decided.

## D208 — The scenario walk's answers: re-identify on rename unless confirmed, a Title follows its files between libraries, withhold removals past half and twenty, and a returning payload revives its tombstone

> **Revised by [D277](#d277--a-scan-held-back-for-the-admin-leaves-its-root-playable-unless-it-saw-none-of-it-and-the-admin-is-told-what-waits-and-what-could-not-be-read-with-the-fix)** (2026-10-11): §3's held-back scan leaves its root playable unless it saw none of it.

> **Revised by [D276](#d276--a-scan-that-removes-nothing-never-waits-for-the-admin-though-its-root-moved-to-another-device)** (2026-10-11): §3's changed device or mount holds back only a scan that would remove something.

**Decided** (2026-09-24), by the project owner, answering the four questions of
[scenarios.md](../design/plans/scenarios.md)'s first walk, which the owner asked for: *"We
haven't done user story scenarios yet to test our model."*

1. **A renamed or moved file is re-identified from its new path, unless a person confirmed its
   match** (Q1; S1, S14). An automatic identification is derived from the path, so it is
   re-derived when the path changes, and fixing `Metropolis (1959)` to `Metropolis (1995)` lands the file on
   the right film. A confirmed match never moves ([D172](#d172--a-low-vote-count-is-shown-not-hidden-an-ambiguous-match-is-never-guessed-and-selecting-it-asks-rather-than-plays)).
2. **A Title follows its files between libraries** (Q2; S6, S19). When a newly identified Title
   has the provider id of a Title in another library that has no live files left, that Title —
   with its history — moves to the new library instead of a second one being made. Two libraries
   that both hold live files of one film (symlinked twins) keep a Title each.
3. **Removals are withheld, and the admin asked, when a scan would remove more than half of a
   root's files and more than twenty of them, or all of them, or when the root's device id or
   mount has changed** (Q3; S7). [D41](#d41--diagnose-the-failure-boundary-by-walking-up-and-guard-the-silent-case-which-is-worse)
   left the threshold open. Both numbers are settings with starting values (50% and 20).
4. **A payload that reappears in the library of a tombstoned file with that payload revives the
   tombstone**, with its history, position and subtitles, wherever it now is (Q4; S10). It is
   D41's "recovery restores; it does not re-add", applied to a file as well as a mount, and it
   makes D173's tombstone a reversible fact rather than an ending
   ([D173](#d173--a-replaced-file-is-a-deletion-and-an-addition-what-is-in-a-files-timeline-dies-with-the-file-and-what-is-about-the-work-survives-at-the-title)).

**Also recorded, from the same walk:** the node reports each root's device id, whether it is a
mount point and whether it is read-only at the start of every scan, and the core keeps each
root's last outcome, so a file on a root that could not be scanned shows as unavailable
([D42](#d42--nodes-are-sensors-the-core-is-the-only-thing-that-decides),
[D179](#d179--a-files-identity-is-a-hash-of-its-media-payload-not-its-bytes-a-rebuild-restores-the-identity-rows-and-runs-an-ordinary-scan-duplicates-are-surfaced)).
~~The per-directory "listed, empty" fact D42 lists is not reported yet: the core's comparison of a
root's counts against its last complete scan catches the same cases, and the fact returns when
the watcher needs it.~~ **Corrected the same day, by the owner's question** *"What if someone
uses /mnt as a root"*: counts do not catch it. With disks mounted inside a root, unplugging one
changes nothing about the root and leaves an empty directory that lists cleanly, so a small disk,
or one of several, would have its files removed. So the node reports every **mount boundary** its
walk crosses — a directory on another device than its parent — and the core keeps a complete
scan's boundaries (`root_mount`). A later scan that does not find one where it was, or finds it on
another device, reads nothing under it as removed: the subtree is unread, its files kept, and the
boundary marked missing until the disk returns or the admin says it is gone.

**Status:** Decided, and built: items 3 and 4 and the root facts with the ingest, items 1 and 2
with the identification pass.

## D209 — For shows, the series is what is identified; its episodes follow it by season and number

**Decided** (2026-09-24), by the project owner: *"yes, the series is the thing identified"*.

Identification was written per title: a title follows one source
([D170](#d170--one-source-per-title-fetched-once-a-users-correction-is-permanent-and-every-refetch-is-an-act-of-the-user)),
and an ambiguous match is never guessed
([D172](#d172--a-low-vote-count-is-shown-not-hidden-an-ambiguous-match-is-never-guessed-and-selecting-it-asks-rather-than-plays)).
That fits a film, which a provider can search for by name. It does not fit an episode: no
provider searches for "Episode 3"; it identifies the show, and an episode is then season 1,
episode 3 *of that show*. The library model made a series a Collection of its episodes
([D160](#d160--there-is-no-series-concept-a-sequence-is-what-a-collection-produces-and-next-up-is-a-query-over-any-of-them),
[D186](#d186--music-would-cost-one-reshape-and-it-is-made-now-things-that-are-not-titles-share-an-item-plus-four-cheap-renames))
but never gave that Collection a place in identification. Building TMDB matching for shows
found the gap.

1. **A series is matched, and may be ambiguous and chosen by a person**, exactly as D170 and
   D172 say of a title: one source, fetched once; a single result matching the name (and the
   year, where the folder or tvshow.nfo gives one) is accepted; anything else is ambiguous, with
   the results kept; a person's choice is permanent.
2. **An episode is not searched.** Once its series is matched, it takes its values from the
   series' source at its (season, number) in the aired ordering. An episode the source does not
   list stays on local data, unidentified, saying so.
3. **A new episode of a matched series is a first fetch** (D170): the listing it is missing from
   is fetched again; nothing else is.

**Status:** Decided, and built after the owner approved the schema and API it needs: migration
0007 gives a series the match state a title has and keys `provider_response` on `item` with a
`part` (a season listing is a part); the chooser endpoints moved from `/titles` to `/items`
(plan-deviations P16).

**Open, raised by the owner the same day:** *"How do we handle the situation where two sources
disagree on episode ordering?"* Two sources' orders are two orderings of one set of episodes
([D96](#d96--an-episodes-position-is-ordering-season-number-and-a-series-declares-its-orderings)),
not a conflict. What nothing records is **which ordering the files are numbered in**. What is
built assumes aired: an episode's S/E is looked up in its series' aired season listing, so a
series whose files follow DVD or absolute order would take the wrong names, flagged only where
a number is missing from the listing. **Answered by
[D210](#d210--a-series-has-an-on-disk-order-its-files-are-numbered-in-and-a-viewing-order-each-person-chooses-built-after-cut-a).**

## D210 — A series has an on-disk order its files are numbered in, and a viewing order each person chooses; built after Cut A

**Decided** (2026-09-25), by the project owner, answering D209's open question: *"for when
series are 'out of order', we could give them an 'on-disk order of the files' selector, and then
a 'viewing order' selector to select the order the user actually wants them to be displayed and
viewed in."*

1. **On-disk order** is a fact about a library's files: which of the series' orderings
   ([D96](#d96--an-episodes-position-is-ordering-season-number-and-a-series-declares-its-orderings))
   their S/E numbers are in — aired, DVD, absolute, or a provider's alternate. It is set per
   series, by an admin, for the household, and **defaults to aired**. Identification reads it:
   a file is looked up in that ordering's listing (at TMDB, the matching episode group), so its
   episode is named correctly. Changing it re-derives the series from stored listings.
2. **The files' numbering is trusted within that order.** The one failure left is a rip numbered
   wrongly by whoever made it, which the owner judges unlikely; nothing tries to detect it.
3. **Viewing order** is the preference
   [D159](#d159--d96-holds-under-the-new-lens-and-reaches-three-things-it-did-not-the-ordering-choice-is-a-preference-an-ordering-may-be-authored-and-a-multi-episode-file-is-a-boundary)
   already made: per person, at series scope, governing display, Next Up and play order. It is
   independent of the on-disk order: once an episode is identified, its provider id places it in
   every ordering the provider lists.
4. **Not in Cut A.** Aired is what Cut A assumes (D209). The owner was bitten by this before and
   is not sure the library still has such a show; if one is noticed before Cut A ships, this is
   built then. It is an addition — a series setting and reading a provider's episode groups — and
   needs no rework of what exists.

5. **A person's viewing order follows the series' on-disk order until they choose another**
   (the owner, the same day: *"viewing order would default to the same as on-disk order until
   the user specifies otherwise"*). It follows it: a person who has not chosen sees the new
   order when an admin changes the on-disk one.

**Status:** Decided; not built (after Cut A, unless a show in the owner's library needs it first).

## D211 — Text hygiene: a file is known by its bytes, display text goes through one sanitiser, subtitles are converted before they are shown, and usernames are compared by skeleton

**Decided** (2026-09-25), by the project owner, raising it: *"One thing we'll want to be careful
about is UTF-8 shenanigans. For filenames we'll probably want to keep raw bytes and then a
cleaned, normalized string version. For subtitles we'll want to make sure the text can't mess up
the display."* Extends [D49](#d49--unicode-discipline-at-the-boundaries-enforced-by-tests)'s rule
— keep the original for provenance, normalise for use — to every place text enters.

1. **A file is identified by the bytes its node reported**, not by its NFC text. Checking this
   found that two files whose names are different invalid UTF-8 (`a\xff.mkv`, `a\xfe.mkv`) both
   became `a�.mkv` and the library kept one of them; two names that differ only in Unicode
   normalisation, which a Linux filesystem holds as two files, did the same. The NFC text stays
   for display, search and D49's cross-node equality.
2. **Text shown to a person passes through one sanitiser** where it enters the library —
   filenames' display form, NFO and provider text, track titles, a person's overrides: bidi
   controls, invisible characters and C0/C1 controls are removed, runs of combining marks are
   capped and length is bounded. Identity and search keep their own forms. The web client also
   isolates the direction of every name it shows.
3. **Subtitles are converted by the node, never shown as found** (M3): encoding detected and
   converted to UTF-8, cue text never rendered as HTML, ASS sizes and drawing coordinates
   bounded, and embedded fonts parsed only inside the renderer's WASM sandbox.
4. **Usernames are compared by their Unicode confusable skeleton**, so a look-alike of an
   existing name is refused (M4, with invites).

**Status:** Decided. Items 1 and 2 built with this decision (`internal/core/textindex`'s
`Line`, `Prose` and `Path`, applied where text enters — a node's report at the ingest, an NFO
at its parse, a provider's answer through one wrapper, a person's text at the API — per
principles §22, which the owner stated the same day); items 3 and 4 with their milestones.

## D212 — Artwork: every image re-encoded by the node, a WebP base kept by the core, nine sizes, JPEG cut by the core, and a ceiling that evicts what can be remade

**Decided** (2026-09-25), by the project owner, over one exchange, with three studies behind it
([artwork-formats.md](../design/research/artwork-formats.md),
[artwork-sizes.md](../design/research/artwork-sizes.md),
[artwork-cache.md](../design/research/artwork-cache.md)). It settles artwork.md's three open
questions and narrows [D99](#d99--the-core-does-not-decode-an-image-either-and-community-uploaded-artwork-is-why).

1. **Every image is re-encoded, whatever it arrived as** — *"force all images through our webp
   conversion, even if the source already is webp"*. The node decodes the source under FFmpeg's
   confinement, refuses one over a pixel limit before decoding it, keeps the first frame, and
   encodes our own WebP; nothing a client decodes was written by anyone but our encoder
