   ([principles §22](../principles/22-untrusted-data-is-cleaned.md)). CVE-2023-4863 compromised the *clients* that
   decoded a crafted WebP; passing a provider's file through would put every screen in the house
   in its path. Metadata, extra chunks, trailing bytes and polyglots go with the re-encode.
2. **The core keeps a base**: our WebP encode at the largest size ever served (portrait-l,
   landscape-xl), from which every other size is cut. The original is discarded; a base that is
   lost is fetched again.
3. **Nine named sizes, a closed set, cropped to the exact shape** (a 27×40 one-sheet loses about
   1%): portrait 240×360, 480×720, 960×1440; landscape 480×270, 960×540, 1920×1080, 3840×2160;
   logo within 400×155 and 800×310. None larger than its source. The two largest are made on
   request; the rest when the image is fetched. *(Noted 2026-09-30: a stored size is keyed by
   its source's SHA-256 alone, not by the encoder's settings, so a change of
   `artwork_webp_quality` applies only to images made after it, and what is already stored is
   kept, as intended; evicting a size, or a base being lost, is what remakes it. The owner:
   "agreed" ([M3's closing audit](../design/research/audit-2026-09-29.md) §9 C).)*
4. **The format is in the URL, and the client chooses it.** WebP always; JPEG is cut by the core
   on the first request for it, from the base, and kept. No Cut A client needs JPEG.
5. **The core may decode its own base images, and nothing else** (narrowing D99): they are our
   encoder's output. It does so in `internal/core/artwork` only, with the node's pixel limit,
   using `golang.org/x/image` (allowlisted). It cuts JPEG there; it cannot encode lossy WebP in
   pure Go, so every WebP size is the node's. **The node is never on the request path:** a WebP
   size not yet made is answered with a temporary redirect to the nearest one there, and a job
   makes the real one.
6. **A ceiling, a setting starting at 20 GiB**, measured against a large library's 5–13 GiB.
   Evicted in this order, least recently served first within each step: a tombstoned item's
   images after a grace period; sizes made on request and JPEG; other large sizes; bases
   (fetched again when next needed). A live item's poster-wall size is never evicted. When it
   was last served is kept to the day, in memory, written hourly.
7. **High water:** when what is never evicted exceeds the ceiling, artwork keeps being served
   and fetched on demand, and the admin is warned, lastingly, with the size needed and a
   ceiling to set (the need plus 15%), shown again beside the setting.

8. **Only our encoder's images reach the core's store** (the owner, after a sweep of every way
   an image gets in: providers, files beside the media, images inside containers, image
   subtitles, frames we cut, and what people upload). The artwork store takes bytes from one
   place: the node's answer to an artwork command. A provider's download or a person's upload
   is held as an unsanitised value whose only use is being sent to the node; a file beside the
   media or inside a container is read and re-encoded by the node, and its bytes never reach the
   core. Past that, an image is as safe to pass around as a cleaned string
   ([principles §22](../principles/22-untrusted-data-is-cleaned.md)).
9. **URLs in NFO files are not fetched** — *"That's an easy way to DDOS someone using us as a
   naive relay. I'd leave that deferred until we get requests for it, and then only allow from a
   whitelisted set of image hosters."* The NFO reader does not read `<thumb>` or `<fanart>`.
10. **Direct play is the one stated exception to re-encoding**: it sends the file's own bytes to
    the client's decoders, which is what direct play is. A prepared rendition is our encoder's
    output; direct play is not, by design. Image subtitles (PGS, VobSub, DVB) are decided with
    M3's subtitle work: rendered by the node into our own bitmaps, or sent as found.

**Status:** Decided; built in M2 (2026-09-25 to 2026-09-27), the node re-encoding every image
and the core keeping its WebP base and cutting JPEG; the artwork service the one writer of
`artwork` since 2026-09-30 (architecture map F5).

## D213 — A good netizen: a dead image is checked once more, refresh rolls per provider, and nothing is deleted because a provider dropped it

**Decided** (2026-09-25), by the project owner, after the research in
[provider-etiquette.md](../design/research/provider-etiquette.md), which found that TMDB's terms
forbid keeping its data longer than six months and that we send no User-Agent of our own. The
owner's aim: *"I want us to be good netizens and not cause problems for these public
databases."* **Narrows [D170](#d170--one-source-per-title-fetched-once-a-users-correction-is-permanent-and-every-refetch-is-an-act-of-the-user)**:
its fetch-once model stands for first fetches and for everything a person wrote, but a record is
now refreshed on a schedule, and a dead image is looked into once.

1. **A dead image is checked once, then given up** — *"a 404 triggers one refetch after the
   CDN's timeout, then gives up."* When an image server answers 404, the record that named the
   image is fetched again once, after the time the CDN keeps its 404 (twelve hours for TMDB):
   the title's, the series', or an episode's season listing. A different image it names is
   fetched; the same one is tried once more; after that the image is recorded as missing and no
   longer asked for. An older image of the item stays shown meanwhile.
2. **A person may refresh a title whenever they like** — *"The user can manually try to
   refetch any time they want, as much as they want (per-movie, not per-library)."* Refreshing a
   film or a series fetches its record, and every image it has that is missing or was refused,
   again. There is no library-wide refresh; D170's bulk refresh is withdrawn.
3. **Records are refreshed on a rolling schedule, set per provider** — *"We make the rolling
   refresh values as configuration per-provider and populate with each provider's rules. If the
   user changes those that's their business."* Each provider's record for an item is fetched
   again once it is older than that provider's setting, starting at the provider's own rule:
   `tmdb_refresh_after_d`, 180, under TMDB's six months. Each item falls due somewhere in the
   last quarter of the period, spread by its id, so a library fetched in an afternoon is not
   refreshed in one. A refresh changes no field a person set (D183); it can change the others,
   which is what refreshing is.
   How often the server looks for what is due is a setting too, `refresh_check_every_h`,
   starting at a day, and it looks once when it starts — *"I don't care if a timeout goes beyond
   6 months by a few days. We could even make this configurable."* One look is one query; the
   interval decides only how late an item may be, a day at the start. *(Since 2026-09-29, the
   setting is `metadata_refresh_check_every_h` ([D227](#d227--every-name-in-a-contract-that-a-reader-must-look-up-is-renamed-now-minor-ones-too-a-job-names-its-target-by-kind-and-a-sidecars-kind-has-its-own-column)). Noted 2026-09-30; the owner: "agreed" ([M3's closing audit](../design/research/audit-2026-09-29.md) §9 D).)*
4. **A refresh that finds an item gone keeps our copy** — *"If on a refresh an item is no
   longer available, we do NOT delete our copy."* The stored record, the item's values and its
   images stay; the attempt is noted so the item is not asked for again before its next period.
5. **Failures that are not the item's back off, and a failing host is left alone.** An image
   that fails for any reason but a 404 is tried again after 1 minute, 5, 30, 2 hours, 12 hours,
   then daily for a week, then the job fails. After five failures in a row a host is paused and
   probed once per step, rather than tried for every image. `Retry-After` is honoured in both
   its forms, capped at an hour. Images are fetched one at a time.
6. **We say who we are.** Every request to another host carries `User-Agent: Orpheum/<version>`
   (TMDB's terms §1.C forbid concealing the application's identity).
7. **Every client has an About section that credits what we are built on** — *"we can have an
   about section and put all our acknowledgments there. I think it would be nice to acknowledge
   all of the major things we use, even if not required."* TMDB's terms (§3) and its developer
   FAQ ask for its logo, less prominent than ours, and the notice "This product uses the TMDB API
   but is not endorsed or certified by TMDB" in an "About" or "Credits" type section; a splash
   shown once is not that. The same section acknowledges the major projects we use — FFmpeg,
   SQLite, Go and the web client's frameworks among them — whether or not their licences ask
   for it, and is where the licence notices that ship with a binary are shown.

**Status:** Decided; built in M2. §5's retry and breaker were replaced by D231's parking (a host
that is down parks its destination), and §1's recheck is derived from the refused image since
2026-09-30 (G14).

## D214 — A later commercial service connects clients to a core without carrying content; the hosted relay stays deferred

> **§3 revised by [D297](#d297--a-household-is-found-by-its-realm-realm-name-and-password-together-proven-both-ways-by-a-key-the-password-makes-admin-only-from-the-cores-own-network) §2:** a core is also found by its realm, but only with a name and password that sign in.

> **Refined by [D273](#d273--clients-reach-a-core-through-apporpheum-appcom-or-the-owners-own-discovery-by-whatever-methods-work-with-no-traffic-relayed-by-us-a-node-without-landlock-runs-and-warns)** (2026-10-09): the service is discovery at app.orpheum-app.com, where a web client talks to its core with as much traffic as possible direct; a separate closed-source project.

**Recorded, not scheduled** (2026-09-25), by the project owner, after the study
[direct-reachability.md](../design/research/direct-reachability.md) found that no combination of
networks needs a relay we host: wherever a third party is needed, the owner's own VPS serves
every client. For Cut A, reachability stays as cut-a §2 has it (*"For my own purposes in this
initial cut it doesn't matter"*). **Revisits [D72](#d72--the-hosted-relay-has-no-free-tier-holds-no-data-and-has-no-accounts)**,
whose market — people who will not rent a VPS — is kept, and served another way first.

> *"Later in thinking of offering a commercial service that gives orpheum users a simple
> service to get their clients and core in contact, rather than a content relay (if possible).
> The target would be people who have their own libraries but don't want the hassle of
> maintaining their own vps, and end users who just want a qr code that does all of the set up
> once and for all."*

### 1. What a connection-only service can do, with no content passing through it

- **Where the core is now**: the core reports its current addresses (a DS-Lite prefix is often
  dynamic) and a paired client asks for them.
- **A real HTTPS name and certificate** for the core, issued through the service's own domain by
  DNS-01, as Plex does with `*.plex.direct`, so an owner needs no domain or DNS provider.
- **Set-up from a QR code**: it carries the core's identity (a key fingerprint) and a one-time
  pairing secret; the client asks the service where that core is and checks that it reached it.
- **Introductions for clients that can use UDP** — our native apps, and browsers through WebRTC
  data channels — which connect directly most of the time.

### 2. The gap it cannot close, and the owner's options for it

A TV browser or a Cast receiver on a network without IPv6, reaching a core with no public IPv4,
can only open an ordinary connection to an address; no introduction makes one. Something with a
public IPv4 must carry the bytes. The study puts this at roughly 2–10% of remote sessions after
one-time fixes, mostly televisions. The options, to be chosen when the service is built:

1. **A relay for that case only**, bounded to it — which brings back legal.md §4's duties for
   that part of the service (a conduit, a repeat-infringer policy, a DMCA agent, retention).
2. **Provisioning a VPS in the user's own account**: the service sets it up; the machine and its
   traffic are the user's, so we carry no content. Less hassle than running one, not none — the
   user needs a cloud account.
3. **Unsupported, and said plainly** on the set-up screen: this TV cannot reach your server from
   that network, and why.

### 3. What it must hold to

- **Private**: it answers *"where is this core"* only to a holder of that core's pairing secret,
  never *"what cores exist"* — [D187](#d187--users-are-responsible-for-what-they-play-we-never-supply-locate-unlock-or-promote-it--and-the-store-and-legal-constraints-that-follow) forbids a directory of servers.
- **Terms**: personal, non-commercial use of the user's own libraries; short retention of
  connection logs. A lawyer confirms what a content-blind service needs; it avoids the conduit
  questions a relay raises.
- **No free tier whose cost scales with use** (D72's rule); a connection service's cost barely
  does, which is part of its appeal.

### 4. What Cut A keeps open, at no cost

- The core has a **stable key identity** that a client can pin (D154's grants point that way).
- **Pairing is a step a client can complete from a scanned code**, not only from a typed
  address and password.
- **A device code typed at the service must name its core** ([D218](#d218--accounts-the-admin-creates-a-person-who-sets-a-password-from-a-one-time-link-a-signed-in-person-adds-a-tv-by-a-short-safe32-code)):
  either the core registers each live code with the service, or the code carries a prefix for
  the core. Decided when the service is designed.

**The hosted relay stays deferred** until all of these hold: a release aimed at owners who will
not run a VPS, measured drop-off at the VPS step, someone to carry legal.md §4's duties, and no
acceptable outside service — and even then, only if §2's first option is chosen.

**Status:** Recorded; not scheduled. Nothing is built for it in Cut A beyond §4.

## D215 — Local artwork: images beside the media follow the library's metadata source, named as Kodi and Jellyfin name them; embedded art waits

**Decided** (2026-09-25), by the project owner (*"follow your recommendations"*), when M2's
artwork turned to the images people keep beside their media.

1. **Images beside the media are taken in every library, at once; which one shows follows the
   library's metadata source** (amended the same day: *"make it so that the scanner grabs local
   images right away, and then if the user prefers them from a service, it updates the images as
   it fetches them"*). They cost no network, so the pass that follows a scan owes them straight
   away and the node re-encodes them. In a library that reads NFO files the image beside the
   media wins, and the provider's image of that kind is not fetched; in a library set to *"TMDB
   only"*, the image beside the media shows until the provider's is fetched, and then the
   provider's does ([D183](#d183--an-override-is-an-override-wherever-its-value-came-from-a-librarys-source-is-asked-not-defaulted-a-default-must-be-safe-to-be-wrong-and-visible-where-it-acts)).
   A person's own choice beats both.
2. **Names follow Kodi's and Jellyfin's conventions**: in a film's or a series' folder,
   `poster`, `folder` and `cover` for the poster, `fanart`, `backdrop` and `background` for the
   backdrop, `clearlogo` and `logo` for the logo; beside a video, `<name>-poster`,
   `<name>-fanart`, `<name>-clearlogo` for a film and `<name>-thumb` for an episode's still; in
   `.jpg`, `.jpeg`, `.png`, `.webp` or `.tbn`. A season's poster has no item to show it on yet,
   and is filed without being used.
3. **The node reads the image and re-encodes it; its bytes never reach the core**
   ([D212](#d212--artwork-every-image-re-encoded-by-the-node-a-webp-base-kept-by-the-core-nine-sizes-jpeg-cut-by-the-core-and-a-ceiling-that-evicts-what-can-be-remade) §8).
   A changed file (its size or modification time) is read again.
4. **Art embedded in a video file** (Matroska attachments, MP4 cover art) waits until after Cut
   A: image files beside the media are far more common, and embedded art needs its own
   extraction in the node.

**Status:** Decided; built in M2: images beside the media taken in every library, the shown one
following the library's metadata source. Embedded art still waits, as §4 says.

## D216 — Every byte path is under /api/v1/bytes/, the media cookie's one scope; the built web client is served by the binary from M3

**Decided** (2026-09-25), by the project owner, taking the recommendations of the audit after M2
([audit-2026-09-25.md](../design/research/audit-2026-09-25.md) §7): *"yes to all of your
recommendations"*. **Refines [D154](#d154--one-grant-table-opaque-and-revocable-the-session-credential-never-appears-in-a-url)**,
whose media cookie is scoped to the byte paths, and cut-a §5's paths.

1. **One prefix for everything a browser fetches as bytes**: images at
   `/api/v1/bytes/art/{hash}/{size}.{format}` (moved from `/api/v1/art/` while only our own client
   used it), and M3's direct play, HLS and subtitles at `/api/v1/bytes/media/…`. The media cookie
   is scoped to `/api/v1/bytes/`: one cookie, set at sign-in and cleared at sign-out, that the
   browser sends nowhere else, and that the API never reads.
2. **The built web client is served by the binary from M3**, embedded, at `/`, with the client's
   own addresses answered by its `index.html`; until then only the dev loop's Vite serves it. The
   release build builds the web client first.

**Status:** Decided; §1 built in M2, §2 in M3.

## D217 — M3's playback contract: the client sends ranked lists, the media token is a reference, every audio track is prepared, and hls.js, JASSUB and Playwright are allowed

> **§3 and §5 narrowed by [D344](#d344--the-whole-film-prepare-is-retired-every-playback-the-device-cannot-play-as-it-is-plays-from-its-ladder-cut-on-time-where-its-keyframes-cannot-be-had)** (2026-10-26): no prepare is made; a film's sounds keep §3's mixes as chunks, and the node's prepared directory holds its stores of chunks within §5's budget.

**Decided** (2026-09-25), by the project owner, over the gaps found in cut-a before M3
(*"1, 2, 4, 9: agreed"*, then *"ok, that all sounds good"* to §5–§8). What M3's accounts are is
[D218](#d218--accounts-the-admin-creates-a-person-who-sets-a-password-from-a-one-time-link-a-signed-in-person-adds-a-tv-by-a-short-safe32-code).

1. **The menu is ranked lists, one per axis, with no weights** (refines
   [D21](#d21--a-fixed-named-output-menu-negotiated-by-a-prioritised-client-list) and
   [D22](#d22--video-audio-and-subtitles-negotiate-as-independent-axes)): video, audio and
   subtitle names in the client's order of preference, and a fourth list, the containers the
   client can play as they are. The container list is used only to ask whether the original can
   be played directly, since a prepared rendition is always fMP4 (D21). A request whose lists
   lack the baselines `h264-sdr` and `aac-stereo` is refused. The core sorts a file's streams
   into menu names by a table in `internal/core/decide`, one test per row; a stream the table
   cannot place is prepared, never guessed playable.
2. **The single-playback media token is a reference, not a credential** (refines
   [D154](#d154--one-grant-table-opaque-and-revocable-the-session-credential-never-appears-in-a-url)
   and [D216](#d216--every-byte-path-is-under-apiv1bytes-the-media-cookies-one-scope-the-built-web-client-is-served-by-the-binary-from-m3)):
   it names a user, a file, a rendition and a device, and grants nothing. Every byte request
   still carries the media cookie or the Authorization header, so a URL that leaks plays for no
   one. Each `POST /playback` issues a new token; it ends with the session or after an idle
   period, a setting starting at 4 hours.
3. **A prepare encodes every audio track of the source**, each as a standard and a boosted
   rendition, so switching language never needs a new job
   ([D23](#d23--axis-switching-is-mid-session-by-default-burn-in-is-the-one-thing-that-breaks-it)).
   A prepare job's subject is its rendition, and an extract job's is its stream, so one file
   can have several jobs open at once. **Segments are two seconds long** (the owner, 2026-09-26,
   choosing it over six-second segments and over carrying both mixes in one four-channel track):
   switching between the standard and boosted mix waits for the next segment, so it takes about
   a second rather than three. The length is the server setting `hls_segment_length_s` (the owner:
   *"would it make sense to make the segment length configurable? We probably need to do testing
   for various network conditions"*), starting at 2, from 1 to 10; a copy made with another
   length is made again the next time it is played.
4. **New dependencies:** `hls.js` (HLS in every browser but Safari), `jassub` (ASS subtitles),
   and `@playwright/test` (M3's playback timing in Chrome and Firefox, and M4's two-client
   tests). `golang.org/x/sys` is used directly, for seccomp and Landlock.
5. **A node owns its prepared renditions** (settles cut-a §2, §4 and §6, which disagreed): they
   live in a directory named by the node's own configuration, under a budget the same
   configuration sets, and the node is the only thing that deletes there. A rendition lives on
   the node that holds its source, so there is never a choice of where to put one. The node
   evicts by last use, which it knows because it serves the bytes; a rendition is kept while
   someone is partway through its title, or for a short grace after its last play, within the
   budget. The core's record of a rendition is a note of what the node said it has: when the
   node answers that one is gone, the core prepares it again. `/doctor` shows each node's use.
   The byte path is `/bytes/v1/prepared/<file_id>/<profile>/<run_id>/<name>`, and eviction by the
   core is not needed. `<run_id>` is new each time a rendition is made (a random name, 2026-09-26):
   a copy made again never writes where an earlier making's files are, so no request can reach
   a copy half overwritten, and the earlier making's directory is left for eviction. **The starting values** (the owner, 2026-09-25: *"ok sounds good"*, then *"Maybe
   the cache should be default 200gb but also check that disk usage on that device isn't above
   95%"*): a budget of 200 GiB, a grace of 3 days after the last play, and a second limit on the
   filesystem that holds the directory: past 95% full, renditions are evicted as they are past
   the budget, whatever the budget says, because a fixed budget cannot know what else shares
   the disk. When nothing can be evicted and the disk is past it, a new prepare is refused with
   a reason rather than filling the disk.
6. **Subtitles are extracted when it is cheap to** (settles the gap in cut-a §4 and §6): a
   subtitle file beside the media is converted at scan; an embedded track, which means reading
   the whole file because its packets are spread through it, is extracted when the file is first
   played, whatever the decision. The node sends the converted text to the core, as it does
   artwork, and the core keeps it by payload hash; one job makes both ASS and VTT.
7. **A play position moves only for a report about a later moment of watching** (settles cut-a
   §5 and schema.md, which named three different guards): the moment is the device's
   monotonic time anchored to true time as
   [D165](#d165--a-heartbeat-is-not-an-event-the-log-records-state-changes-and-watched-spans-there-is-no-retention-horizon-and-an-offline-device-must-not-be-able-to-rewind-you)
   describes, so two devices reporting out of order never rewind a position. A device's own
   sequence number only drops a repeated report from the same device, and a report that cannot
   be anchored never moves a position.
8. **A device is created at sign-in**: the client names itself and its platform, and the server
   makes the device row and ties the session to it. How it makes sound (`audio_output`) is asked
   the first time it plays, then kept
   ([D184](#d184--the-defaults-audit-four-become-questions-seven-must-be-made-visible-the-rest-pass)).

9. **Fetching subtitles automatically is deferred** (the owner, 2026-09-25: *"this would be a
   feature that the user must activate. So it can be added later, low priority"*): a person who
   turns it on would have a missing subtitle in their chosen language fetched when a file is
   played, once per file and language, kept, and labelled unverified. Cut A keeps fetch on
   request (cut-a §1); neither is built in M3.

**Status:** Decided; built in M3. §5's budget and eviction, which the M3 audit found unbuilt
(audit-2026-09-27 §3), are built in `internal/node/prepared`: a rendition played within the grace
stands for "someone is partway through it", since only the core knows who is. §4's Playwright
timing test is built (`web/e2e/play-timing.spec.ts`, Chromium and Firefox). §6 is amended by D223 §5:
a subtitle file beside the media is converted at first play. §6's job is revised by
[D340](#d340--a-videos-text-subtitle-tracks-are-extracted-by-one-job-from-one-read-of-it-and-a-failed-track-alone-is-tried-again-when-next-played):
one job per file, a video's text tracks all from one read of it.

## D218 — Accounts: the admin creates a person, who sets a password from a one-time link; a signed-in person adds a TV by a short safe32 code

> **Replaced in part by [D288](#d288--a-device-is-activated-by-the-code-it-shows-entered-on-a-device-already-signed-in-and-a-check-code-both-show)** (2026-10-12): §3–§4 no longer hold; a device not signed in asks for a code, a signed-in person enters it, and a check code both show confirms it.
>
> **Refined by [D320](#d320--a-device-signed-out-on-itself-leaves-the-persons-devices-one-signed-out-another-way-stays)** (2026-10-20): a device signed out on itself is removed, so §1 resumes only one signed out another way.

> **Revised by [D273](#d273--clients-reach-a-core-through-apporpheum-appcom-or-the-owners-own-discovery-by-whatever-methods-work-with-no-traffic-relayed-by-us-a-node-without-landlock-runs-and-warns)** §10 (2026-10-09): a TV shows a code the core gave it, a signed-in device enters it, and a check code shown on both confirms the pairing; not built yet.

**Decided** (2026-09-25), by the project owner, who set the flow out: *"Admin creates account,
sends url / qr to user. User clicks / opens link from a phone or computer ... to complete
registration (selects a new password). User then uses phone/computer's browser/app to ask for a
code to log in via their TV ... User browses to the server in their TV and types in the code, and
it gets added as one of their devices"*, and *"A logged in user should be able to register as
many devices as they like."* **Refines [D93](#d93--device-pairing-is-rfc-8628-shaped)**, whose
code runs the other way (the TV shows it and a signed-in device approves), and moves signing in a
TV into Cut A, as part of M3's accounts. The admin is the technical person in a household;
everyone else should need nothing but a link and, on a TV, eight characters.

1. **The admin creates the account** (name and role) in the admin panel and receives a one-time
   registration link, shown as a URL and a QR code. Its secret travels after `#`, so the browser
   never sends it to the server's logs or to another site: the one deliberate exception to
   [D154](#d154--one-grant-table-opaque-and-revocable-the-session-credential-never-appears-in-a-url)'s
   rule, because a QR code needs it. It is single use and lasts 7 days.
2. **The person opens it on a phone or computer and chooses a password**, and that device becomes
   their first.
3. **A signed-in person adds a device** by asking for a code, naming the device ("Living room
   TV"), as many times and for as many devices as they like. An admin can make one for any
   person, which covers someone with no other device. The code is 8 characters of
   [safe32](https://github.com/kstenerud/safe-encoding/blob/master/safe32-specification.md), one
   full 40-bit group, shown as `xxxx-xxxx`: decoders accept either case, `o` for `0`, `l` or `i`
   for `1`, `u` for `v`, and ignore dashes and spaces, so it survives a TV remote. It lasts 10
   minutes and works once.
4. **On the TV**, the person opens the server's address, chooses "I have a code" and types it; the
   TV becomes one of their devices, listed and revocable like any other. A wrong code counts
   against the sign-in rate limit.
5. **A forgotten password**: the admin makes a new registration link. The old password works
   until the new one is set, and a reset signs no one out; "sign out everywhere" is a separate
   act.
6. **People change their own password** in their settings.

   **Amended 2026-10-13** after the second security audit (K1): a password reset left whoever held
   the old one signed in. A new password set by a registration link now ends every session of the
   person's, and one a person changes ends every other session of theirs, the asking one staying;
   "sign out everywhere else" ends every session but the asking one, not every session of the
   asking device. The owner approved the fixes to what is exploitable today: *"yes go ahead with
   those"*.

**Why this direction rather than D93's:** the TV is an ordinary page that sends one request
instead of waiting to be approved, and the code can be made by an admin on someone else's behalf.
Phishing risk is about equal either way; the ten-minute life and single use bound it.

**Status:** Decided; built in M3.

## D219 — A subtitle choice is kept per file; choosing one carries it to the work's other files that have none of their own

**Decided** (2026-09-26), by the project owner, answering where M3 keeps a chosen subtitle track:
*"why can't it be attached to the lowest id level (the hash or whatever uniquely identifies the
file)? If one subtitle file in a series is broken, we don't want them to be stuck. We can set all
unset ones when they select subtitles, but otherwise they need to be individually selectable."*
**Refines [D24](#d24--language-is-a-preference-axis-and-track-selections-stick-to-the-series)**,
whose sticky scope was the series for an episode and the title for a film; its three rules about
what a choice is still hold.

1. **The choice is kept per person and per file**, as the subtitle offset is (preference scope
   `file`): the track chosen in that file, or *off*. Within one file a track is a stable thing,
   a stream row whose id holds while the file does, so D24's warning against remembering a track
   index, which is about carrying one to another file, does not apply to the file itself.
2. **Choosing carries the choice to the work's other files that have none of their own**: every
   episode of the series, or every other copy of the film. In each, it takes the track of the
   same language and kind (forced, for the deaf and hard of hearing), preferring the same title;
   *off* carries as *off*. A file with no such track is left without a choice: a fallback is not
   a choice (D24, rule 1).
3. **A choice made in a file is that file's own; a carried one is not.** A later choice elsewhere
   carries over carried choices, never over a file's own, so one broken subtitle file chosen
   around stays chosen around, and a person who switches from English to Spanish at episode 5
   gets Spanish in episode 6. (The owner's words say "unset"; this reading, that a carried choice
   still counts as unset for the next carry, was put to the owner with the implementation.)
4. **An episode added after the choice has none**, and plays with subtitles off until one is
   chosen, since nothing carries a choice to a file that did not exist when it was made.

**Status:** Decided; built in M3. *(Since 2026-09-30, §2 to §4 are replaced by
[D230](#d230--the-last-subtitle-and-audio-language-chosen-in-a-series-follows-its-unwatched-episodes-worked-out-at-play-time),
built the same day: nothing is carried, and a work's last language is matched when a file plays.)*

## D220 — Before a public release, every dependency, direct and transitive, is pinned to an audited commit, and a bump is an audit of the changes

**Decided** (2026-09-26), by the project owner, for when the project prepares a public release:
*"record the commit sha of the exact version of the libraries we ingest, as well as those of the
full tree of dependencies. We do a full security audit of the libraries we use, and whenever
we're about to bump versions, we do an audit of the changes leading up to the new sha of each.
This will also detect rewritten histories."*

1. **A record of every dependency's source commit**: each Go module and npm package the release
   builds with, direct and transitive, with the commit its release was built from. A version
   number and a checksum of the published archive (go.sum, package-lock.json) say what was
   downloaded, not which history it came from; the commit does.
2. **A full security audit of each** before the first public release.
3. **A bump is an audit of the history between the recorded commit and the new one**, library by
   library. If the recorded commit is not an ancestor of the new one, the history was rewritten,
   and that stops the bump until someone has seen why.

It extends [deps/](../../../deps/) allowlisting (AGENTS.md rule 3), which says what may be used,
with what exactly is used. The mechanism (where the record lives, how a gate checks it, and how a
package whose published archive has no commit in it is traced) is designed with the release work.

**Status:** Decided; to be built before the first public release.

## D221 — A device keeps its identity across sign-ins, and a signed-out device is signed back in with a code made for it

> **Replaced in part by [D288](#d288--a-device-is-activated-by-the-code-it-shows-entered-on-a-device-already-signed-in-and-a-check-code-both-show)** (2026-10-12): §3–§4 no longer hold; a device not signed in asks for a code, a signed-in person enters it, and a check code both show confirms it.
>
> **Refined by [D320](#d320--a-device-signed-out-on-itself-leaves-the-persons-devices-one-signed-out-another-way-stays)** (2026-10-20): a device signed out on itself is removed, so §1 resumes only one signed out another way.

**Decided** (2026-09-27), by the project owner, after trying D218's devices on a phone: every
sign-in made a new device, so a signed-out device could never come back and a browser signed in
twice showed as two. The owner: *"that's fine for devices to be able to come back, but then we
need a way to regenerate a new sign-in code for that device."* **Refines
[D218](#d218--accounts-the-admin-creates-a-person-who-sets-a-password-from-a-one-time-link-a-signed-in-person-adds-a-tv-by-a-short-safe32-code)
§3–§5 and
[D217](#d217--m3s-playback-contract-the-client-sends-ranked-lists-the-media-token-is-a-reference-every-audio-track-is-prepared-and-hlsjs-jassub-and-playwright-are-allowed) §8.**

1. **A client remembers the device it was signed in as**, and a sign-in, by password or by a
   registration link, resumes that device when it is the same person's and has not been removed,
   rather than making a new one. What the device carries (its name, how it makes sound, its
   history) stays with it.
2. **A device code is for a new device or for one already listed**: a person, or an admin for
   them, can make a code for a signed-out device, and signing in with it resumes that device.
3. **One code is outstanding per person at a time** (the owner, 2026-09-27): making a new one
   withdraws the last, whichever device it was for. The client can ask whether its code is still
   waiting, so it stops showing a code once it is used.
4. **A registration link is not held back by the failed-sign-in limit**: its 256 bits cannot be
   guessed, and it is the admin's answer to a person locked out. Making one clears the person's
   account from the limit.

**Status:** Decided; built in M3.

## D222 — On stereo output, a multichannel sound always plays through our prepared copy, and headphones are stereo

**Decided** (2026-09-27), by the project owner, when the sound question on first playback
([D184](#d184--the-defaults-audit-four-become-questions-seven-must-be-made-visible-the-rest-pass), [D217](#d217--m3s-playback-contract-the-client-sends-ranked-lists-the-media-token-is-a-reference-every-audio-track-is-prepared-and-hlsjs-jassub-and-playwright-are-allowed) §8) was built. cut-a §6
played the original directly while the boost was off, and audio-presentation.md's *Done when*
played a 5.1 film on television speakers through a prepared copy either way; the two could not
both hold. The owner: *"I'm fine with always copying"*, and *"headphones count as stereo"*.
**Refines [D83](#d83--loudness-is-measured-at-scan-and-applied-as-gain-downmix-has-one-default-and-a-dialogue-control-drc-is-per-device) and cut-a §6.**

1. **A device's sound is one of three answers**: TV speakers, soundbar or receiver, headphones.
   It is asked the first time the device plays and kept on the device, and the person can change
   it in the player and in their devices. *(2026-09-29, the owner: "TV speakers" is renamed
   **built-in speakers**, `built_in_speakers` on the wire and in library.db (migration 0020), as
   it is not a name that describes the purpose well: it covers a laptop's and a phone's speakers
   as much as a television's.)* *(Since 2026-09-29, migration 0020 is folded into the baseline, whose name and version move with each fold ([D228](#d228--until-migrations-are-live-librarydbs-schema-is-a-baseline-and-one-step-and-a-schema-change-folds-the-last-step-into-the-baseline) §3). Noted 2026-09-30; the owner: "agreed" ([M3's closing audit](../design/research/audit-2026-09-29.md) §9 D).)*
2. **TV speakers and headphones are stereo output**: we fold a sound with more than two channels
   down ourselves, so the dialogue boost can act. On such a device a file whose main sound has
   more than two channels is always prepared (reason `dialogue_boost`), whether the boost is on or
   off, so switching it mid-film never needs a new job. A soundbar or receiver takes the sound as
   it is when the browser plays the original, and a device not yet asked is treated the same until
   it answers. A file prepared for another reason (its container, its codec) carries stereo mixes
   only in M3, standard and boosted, so on a receiver too the boost is offered there and works
   (the owner, 2026-09-27: *"That's fine with me"*); a surround track in prepared copies, so a
   receiver keeps its channels, is a later decision. *(Revised 2026-10-25 by
   [D336](#d336--a-films-sound-plays-as-it-is-unless-the-device-cannot-play-it-or-the-person-asks-for-a-feature-that-needs-it-made-no-one-is-asked-how-their-device-makes-sound):
   no one is asked how their device makes sound, and a surround sound is prepared only while the
   person's boost is on.)*
3. **Whether the boost is on is the person's** ([D83](#d83--loudness-is-measured-at-scan-and-applied-as-gain-downmix-has-one-default-and-a-dialogue-control-drc-is-per-device)): one choice that follows them
   from film to film, off until they turn it on, and the player starts with it.
4. **The boost's strength stays one fixed level in M3.** The owner asked whether it should be
   adjustable; the answer waits on the listening test on a television with a title whose
   background drowns the dialogue: *The Dark Knight* first (the owner: *"one really bad one for
   me"*), others later. If +6 dB is not enough, a stronger third mix (the centre raised
   further, the surrounds and LFE lowered) is the proposal, chosen per person like the boost
   itself.

**Status:** Decided; built in M3.

## D223 — The M3 audit's decisions: contract names are made clear now, subtitles start off, and fetching a subtitle on request is in Cut A

**Decided** (2026-09-27), by the project owner, answering the M3 audit's questions
([audit-2026-09-27.md](../design/research/audit-2026-09-27.md) §10): *"1, 2, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10,
11: Go with your recommendations."*

1. **The names in contracts that a reader has to look up are renamed now**, while one household
   uses the server: the API's JSON, the node protocol, database columns (by migration) and setting
   keys the audit marked unclear. The ones marked minor stay.
2. **The setup code is safe32**, as the device code is (D218 §3): one way to make a code a person
   types.
3. **Subtitles start off** (the owner: *"We shouldn't have subtitles on by default. The user can
   select them when they want them."*). A file with no choice plays without subtitles; cut-a §1's
   "on by default as a preference" is withdrawn. `subtitles_on_by_default` and
   `dialogue_boost_on_by_default`, read by nothing, are removed; the boost starts off (D222 §3).
4. **Fetching a subtitle on request is in Cut A** (the owner: *"I'll want subtitle fetching for cut
   A, but it doesn't have to be automatic. As long as I can from the play screen request subtitles
   and it tells me what it can download."*): from the play screen a person asks for subtitles in a
   language, is shown what can be downloaded, and chooses one; it is labelled unverified (cut-a
   §1, §5). Automatic fetching stays deferred (D217 §9).
5. **D217 §6 is amended:** a subtitle file beside the media is converted when its video is first
   played, as built, not at scan.
6. **Scans and backups become jobs in M4**, so the job view shows them, and scheduled backups
   come with them.
7. **Overriding an ambiguous item's name or year searches its candidates again.**
8. **When a file's subtitle tracks change, the work's choice is carried to it again** (extends
   D219 §4, which covered only new files).
9. **A rematch drops the old work's artwork of kinds the new work lacks.**
10. **The person's dialogue boost has its own endpoint, `PUT /me/prefs`**, not the file's (D222 §3).
    *(Since 2026-09-29, the endpoint is `PUT /me/preferences` ([D227](#d227--every-name-in-a-contract-that-a-reader-must-look-up-is-renamed-now-minor-ones-too-a-job-names-its-target-by-kind-and-a-sidecars-kind-has-its-own-column) §6). Noted 2026-09-30; the owner: "agreed" ([M3's closing audit](../design/research/audit-2026-09-29.md) §9 D).)*
11. **M4's nine open questions** (the audit's §8) are asked one at a time before M4's first line.

**Status:** Decided; built in M3 except three parts. §6 (scans and backups as jobs) is M4's, and
§11's questions come before M4. §8 is built for a file that has a stored choice, which is found
again when a rescan rewrites its tracks; it is **not built** for a file with no stored choice whose
rescan adds a track matching the work's choice, which still gets no choice. *(Since 2026-09-30,
§8 is replaced by
[D230](#d230--the-last-subtitle-and-audio-language-chosen-in-a-series-follows-its-unwatched-episodes-worked-out-at-play-time),
built the same day: a file whose tracks change is matched against the work's language when it
plays, so the case §8 left unbuilt follows too.)*

## D224 — A fetched subtitle uses the server's OpenSubtitles login, finds the file by its identity and its provider hash, shows the provider's own count, and is converted by the node

**Decided** (2026-09-27), by the project owner, answering the questions that building
[D223](#d223--the-m3-audits-decisions-contract-names-are-made-clear-now-subtitles-start-off-and-fetching-a-subtitle-on-request-is-in-cut-a)
§4 raised. **Amends [D194](#d194--secrets-our-users-passwords-are-hashed-third-party-secrets-are-sealed-with-a-key-that-never-enters-the-database-and-nothing-reads-a-secret-back-out)
§1 and subtitle-acquisition.md §4 and §8**, which made the OpenSubtitles credentials each user's
and a download a capability on the role.

1. **The login is the server's** (the owner: *"This is a trusted relationship with an admin. The
   admin puts in their credentials and any user may trigger the download."*). An admin enters
   the OpenSubtitles username and password once, as server secrets; every signed-in person may
   fetch with them, and no role capability guards it in Cut A. A rebroadcast server
   ([D177](#d177--a-rebroadcaster-is-a-user-whose-core-treats-our-server-as-a-node-and-his-household-plays-on-derived-grants-that-only-his-core-can-mint)),
   when it comes, fetches with the credentials of the admin of the server it shares to.
2. **The API key is the application's** (the owner: *"Wouldn't we register the app, and the
   admins each use their logins?"*). OpenSubtitles issues a key per registered application, so
   Orpheum is registered once and its key ships with it; each server's admin supplies only a
   login. *(Corrected 2026-09-28: this said an admin could set a key of their own, which
   OpenSubtitles forbids: "don't allow users to insert their API key". The key is the
   application's alone; [opensubtitles-api.md](../design/research/opensubtitles-api.md) §1.)*
3. **A candidate is found by what the file is, not by guessing** (the owner: *"if the NFO had an
   ID just directly use it. Let's implement something non-hacky for cut A."*). The search sends
   the work's IMDb or TMDB id when identification has one, from the NFO or from TMDB, and the
   file's OpenSubtitles `moviehash`, which the node computes when it hashes the file and the
   core stores with it. A candidate whose hash matches is listed first.
4. **The count of downloads left is the provider's** (the owner: *"sounds good"*): the one
   OpenSubtitles reports, which also counts downloads made on its site or in other programs.
   Nothing counts them here; `subtitle_quota` is removed.
5. **The node converts a fetched subtitle** as it converts a subtitle file beside the media (the
   owner: *"sounds good"*): it is hostile input, and the node is where hostile input is parsed
   (threat-model.md). The core sends the text in an `extract_subtitle` command, a third form
   beside a track in a video and a file beside it. *(Noted 2026-09-30: the node converts it while
   the person who fetched it waits, and it is kept (§6) and made their choice only once the node
   has converted it, so nothing unparsed becomes a choice; one the node cannot read is kept
   nowhere. A download's link is kept for its three hours, so fetching the same subtitle again
   within them spends no second download. The owner: "agreed"
   ([M3's closing audit](../design/research/audit-2026-09-29.md) §9 A7).)*

6. **A fetched subtitle is kept in `library.db`, compressed** (the owner, 2026-09-27: *"go with
   your recommendations"*), as schema.md has it. The owner asked whether it should go in
   `cache.db` instead, where the text extracted from the media already is. It stays in
   `library.db` because `cache.db` may be deleted at any time, and a lost fetch costs a download
   and a person's choice to get back. The size is small: a two-hour film's subtitle is 60–120 KB,
   20–40 KB compressed, and a free account fetches at most 20 a day, so a thousand fetches over
   years is about 30–40 MB.
7. **The application's API key is in the source** (the owner, 2026-09-28: *"yes put it in the
   source code"*), as the Jellyfin plugin's, Bazarr's and OpenSubtitles' own Kodi add-on's are;
   nothing asks that it be kept secret ([opensubtitles-api.md](../design/research/opensubtitles-api.md) §1).
8. **A free account's subtitles are shown as delivered** (the owner, 2026-09-28: *"option a"*),
   with any lines of advertising OpenSubtitles puts in them; a VIP account has none.
9. **Every secret is the server's** (the owner, 2026-09-28: *"Follow your recommendations"*).
   With the OpenSubtitles login the server's, no secret belonged to one user, so a user's secret,
   `/me/secrets` and its tests are gone rather than kept for a use nothing plans; a feature that
   needs one brings it back. Amends D194 §1. *(2026-09-30: the `secret` table keeps its `scope`
   and `user_id` columns until migrations are live ([D228](#d228--until-migrations-are-live-librarydbs-schema-is-a-baseline-and-one-step-and-a-schema-change-folds-the-last-step-into-the-baseline) §6). Each value is sealed
   with its scope, user and name as associated data, so dropping them would change what every
   stored value was sealed with, and each secret would have to be entered again. The owner:
   "agreed" ([M3's closing audit](../design/research/audit-2026-09-29.md) §9 D).)*

**Status:** Decided; built in M3. The core lists §3's hash-matching candidate first, whatever
order OpenSubtitles returns.

## D225 — One admin page, System, shows every fact about the server and each node, and M3's shows whether hardware encoding works

> **§3 narrowed by [D344](#d344--the-whole-film-prepare-is-retired-every-playback-the-device-cannot-play-as-it-is-plays-from-its-ladder-cut-on-time-where-its-keyframes-cannot-be-had)** (2026-10-26): there are no prepares to list; the encoder trials stay.

**Decided** (2026-09-27), by the project owner, asked how a person can tell whether the hardware
encoders of cut-a §6 work: *"Are things set up properly? Does it see the GPU? Does it have
access? Does it actually use the hardware when it transcodes? I have no idea! set-and-pray is
never fun."*

1. **One place** (the owner: *"We should put all of the server facts on this page rather than
   spread around other pages"*): an admin page, **System**, holds what the running server knows
   about itself, what `doctor` reports and anything else that helps diagnose a problem or shows
   what is under the hood. What other pages showed of it moves there; the Machines section of
   Libraries goes, and a library's creation still lists a node's roots.
2. **Per node** (the owner: *"We should also be presenting this information per-node"*): the
   server's own facts, then each node's.
3. **M3 builds enough to know that hardware encoding works** (the owner: *"We don't need all of
   that at M3, but I do want enough to know at least that the hardware encoding will work"*),
   answering the owner's four questions for each node:
   - **What it sees:** each GPU device, with the driver behind it.
   - **Whether it can reach it:** whether the node's user may open each device, and whether
     confinement grants it ([D112](#d112--the-node-probes-its-confinement-and-reports-it-the-escape-test-asserts-what-is-in-force)),
     which the next line's encoder trial answers: the trial runs confined, so a device
     confinement withholds shows as that trial's failure, in FFmpeg's words. *(Amended
     2026-09-30: this read as a fact reported for each device on its own; the confined trial is
     the answer, and nothing more is built. The owner: "agreed" ([M3's closing audit](../design/research/audit-2026-09-29.md) §9 D).)*
   - **What works:** each hardware encoder's trial at startup, with FFmpeg's own words when it
     failed, and the encoder chosen.
   - **What it did:** each prepare records the encoder it ran with and its speed against real
     time; the page lists a node's recent prepares with both.

   With them, M3's page shows the versions (the server's, each node's and its FFmpeg's), the
   confinement report, the disk each root and the prepared directory is on (used and free), the
   prepared directory against its budget, and doctor's findings. `doctor` warns when a node has
   a GPU but no hardware encoder works on it.
4. **Later:** CPU and GPU load over time, and whatever else shows the server's load (the owner:
   *"eventually even cpu/gpu graphs and other such things to understand server load"*).
5. **Each build and each machine's system are shown** (the owner, 2026-09-28, on the first
   page):
   - *"version should show tag if it matches one, otherwise "dev" + sha, and whether the tree was
     dirty when the binary was built."* The version is what Go records in every binary it builds,
     so the dev loop's, a test tier's and a release's all say it the same way; the Makefile no
     longer stamps its own.
   - *"each node's orpheum version info should also be in the info, so that we can catch
     version mismatch between them."* A node's hello carries its build, with its binary's hash,
     and doctor warns when it is not the server's.
   - *"put in the info we can get from lsb_release -a in each machine info."* The distributor,
     description, release and codename are read from `/etc/os-release`, the file lsb_release
     reads, with the kernel; the node runs no program but FFmpeg's (cut-a §7).

**Status:** Decided; built in M3 except §4, which is later by its own words. Of §3, whether
confinement grants each GPU is answered by the confined encoder trial, as §3 now says.

## D226 — Loudness is levelled in Cut A: the node measures each sound and its stereo mix, the core sets a gain towards -23 LUFS that no peak exceeds, and the player applies it after its volume

**Decided** (2026-09-28), by the project owner. Playing *Wing* (the director's cut) on the dev
loop, the owner found it *"so quiet that even when I put my speakers to maximum, it's hard to
hear"*. Measured, ten minutes of it were at -35.7 LUFS with a peak of -16.2 dBFS; the owner's
other films measured whole from -18.8 to -30.0 LUFS. The owner: *"this will be a problem for
when [we] are watching films, so it needs to be in cut A"*, and to the questions it raised, *"go
with your recommendations"*. **Brings [D83](#d83--loudness-is-measured-at-scan-and-applied-as-gain-downmix-has-one-default-and-a-dialogue-control-drc-is-per-device)'s loudness into Cut A, withdrawing cut-a §1's "loudness
measurement" from Out and [D178](#d178--the-first-release-is-for-two-people-the-owner-at-home-and-one-person-remote-watching-together-with-subtitles) §4's deferral, and settles what D83 left open.**

1. **What is measured.** Each audio track of a video file: its integrated loudness, loudness
   range and true peak, by FFmpeg's `ebur128` (ITU-R BS.1770). A track with more than two
   channels is also measured as the standard stereo mix the node prepares from it (D222 §2),
   because that mix renormalises its gains so it cannot clip and plays about 7 to 8 dB quieter
   than the original; a gain taken from the original would leave every downmixed film quiet.
   Both come from one read of the file. D83's limitation stands: this is programme loudness, not
   the dialogue-gated figure, and nothing says otherwise.
2. **Where it is kept, and when it is made.** In library.db, by the file's payload hash and the
   stream's index, so a rescan, a move or a second copy keeps a measurement that cost a read of
   the whole file. It is not part of the scan, which would take hours instead of minutes: a job
   per file (`measure_loudness`), queued for each file with sound whose payload has no
   measurement, runs one at a time on the node. Measured 2026-09-28 on the sandbox: 21 s for an
   81-minute film, most of it reading the file, about 230 times real time; the owner's 329 films
   take two to three hours, once. A track FFmpeg cannot measure is recorded as failed, with its
   words, and not tried again for the same bytes.
3. **The gain** is set by the core: towards **-23 LUFS** (EBU R128's target), chosen from the
   owner's films so that typical ones change little. It is capped so the track's true peak stays
   at or below -1 dBTP, and so no track is raised more than 20 dB into its own noise. **A film
   louder than the target is lowered**, so films sit at one level both ways. The gain for stereo
   output is the stereo mix's, and the dialogue boost's mix plays with the same gain, so turning
   the boost on raises the dialogue against the rest, not the whole film.
4. **The player applies it, after the volume control** (the owner asked whether the slider would
   then run past 100): the element's volume is still 0 to 100, and 100 now means the film at the
   level. The web player and the cast receiver route the sound through Web Audio's gain; a
   receiver's channels are kept. *(2026-09-30: the web player's is built in M3; the cast
   receiver's moves to M5, built with the receiver (cut-a §8's M5 row). The owner: "agreed"
   ([M3's closing audit](../design/research/audit-2026-09-29.md) §9 D).)* A prepared copy is made with its gain in its sound when the
   measurement exists as it is made, and the copy records the gain it carries; the player
   applies only the difference. Safari's own HLS, on an iPhone, cannot route through Web Audio,
   so there the sound is levelled only through a copy made after the measurement; a copy made
   before is not made again for it.
5. **Each person may turn it off** ("Level loudness"): one choice that follows them from film to
   film, like the dialogue boost (D222 §3), but **on** until they turn it off. On an iPhone, a
   copy's own gain cannot be undone, so turning it off does not reach the sound there.
6. **The player says what it did:** the gain applied to this film, or that its loudness is not
   measured yet, beside the switch. A film not yet measured plays as it is.

**Status:** Decided; built in M3 except §4's cast receiver, which moved to M5 with the receiver
(§4's note).

## D227 — Every name in a contract that a reader must look up is renamed now, minor ones too; a job names its target by kind, and a sidecar's kind has its own column

**Decided** (2026-09-29), by the project owner, shown the unclear names of the four contracts
and three calls. **Widens [D223](#d223--the-m3-audits-decisions-contract-names-are-made-clear-now-subtitles-start-off-and-fetching-a-subtitle-on-request-is-in-cut-a) §1**, which renamed only the unclear names and left the minor
ones.

1. **Every name is renamed, minor ones too** (the owner: *"Just fix everything now, including
   minor things. I'm not actually using the software yet so breakage is no big deal."*): the
   API's JSON and parameters, the node protocol, library.db's and cache.db's columns, and setting,
   configuration and stored keys. The names, with what each holds, are in
   [contract-names-2026-09-29.md](../design/research/contract-names-2026-09-29.md). Stored JSON
   (a file's probe and its error) is rewritten with the node's new names.
2. **A job names its target by kind** (agreed): an item, a rendition, a stream, a fetched subtitle
   or a file, each its own column in cache.db and its own field in the job view, not one
   `subject` whose table depends on the kind.
3. **A sidecar's kind has its own column** (agreed), `sidecar_kind`, and `filing_reason` holds
   only reasons.
4. **`file.path_raw` is dropped**: since D211 the reported bytes are always kept, in what is now
   `reported_path_bytes`, so it was a second copy. **`user_rating.rating` keeps its name**: its
   scale was never decided, and a name would decide it.
5. **Addendum (2026-09-29): one thing has one name in every layer** (the owner, shown what a
   second audit found: *"yes, align them all"*). Where the renames above left the same value
   under two names, in the API and the node protocol, in a column and its API field, or in
   stored JSON and the API, each takes the name that says more; a column holding JSON ends in
   `_json`; and the artwork and fetch jobs' stored arguments, which no table listed, say what they
   hold. The names are in the same research file's addendum; migration 0024 carries the
   columns and a stored subtitle choice's keys, and cache.db is discarded for its version.
   *(Since 2026-09-29, migration 0024 is folded into the baseline, whose name and version move with each fold ([D228](#d228--until-migrations-are-live-librarydbs-schema-is-a-baseline-and-one-step-and-a-schema-change-folds-the-last-step-into-the-baseline) §3). Noted 2026-09-30; the owner: "agreed" ([M3's closing audit](../design/research/audit-2026-09-29.md) §9 D).)*
6. **A second sweep, by data flow (2026-09-29)** (the owner: *"Do all of it. This is a housekeeping
   run so I don't mind churn. I want to start the next milestone with a very clean codebase."*).
   A sweep that traced each value from the node through the core to the database and the API
   found more values under two names, unclear names, and four values in the wrong form: a
   switch stored as `on`/`off` in a column that holds JSON, the quota error's reset time as a date
   while its field of the same name is milliseconds, a retry delay as a Go duration, and a file's
   error detail sent as JSON inside a string. Each value now has one name and one form; a
   language is `language` in every table; the artwork kind `thumb` is the `still` the API names;
   a column or JSON field spells out any unit but milliseconds (standards/sql.md); and the
   settings named as commands read as predicates. The names are in the research file's second
   addendum; migration 0025 carries library.db, cache.db goes to version 16. Two names stay two,
   on purpose: a series' `seasonNumber` and `episodeNumber` in the API are the group and the
   number in the group that `position` keeps for any ordering, not only a series'; and the
   error body's `detail` keeps its common name. *(Since 2026-09-29, migration 0025 is folded into the baseline, whose name and version move with each fold ([D228](#d228--until-migrations-are-live-librarydbs-schema-is-a-baseline-and-one-step-and-a-schema-change-folds-the-last-step-into-the-baseline) §3),
   and later changes have taken cache.db to version 18. Noted 2026-09-30; the owner: "agreed" ([M3's closing audit](../design/research/audit-2026-09-29.md) §9 D).)*
   *(Since 2026-09-30, a setting key spells out its unit too: standards/sql.md's allowance for a
   setting key's short `_s`, `_h` and `_d` is withdrawn (the owner: "keep spelled out names"), so
   `job_first_retry_delay_s` is `job_first_retry_delay_seconds` and so on, `_ms` staying; step
   0028 moves the stored rows, and [retired-names.md](../retired-names.md) lists the old keys.)*

**Status:** Decided; built before M3's closing audit.

**Addendum, 2026-09-30: M3's closing audit** (the owner, approving its §9 B: *"Yes, one form"*).
The audit found names that still held two things or read as something else, and values in two
forms. An error's `detail` is typed by its code, and the API document gives each code its form
(`ProblemBody`, which was `ErrorDetail`), so `retryAfterMs` and `downloadsResetAt` are numbers
there as everywhere; the registration invitation has one noun from its path to Go; the job kinds
`fetch` and `artwork` say what they do (`fetch_metadata`, `make_artwork_sizes`); a delivery is
`direct` or `hls` in the request and the answer; a session's last use is `last_used_at`; a
column or field holding a path's bytes is `…_raw`, since `_bytes` counts bytes; a subtitle
text's key, which also holds a fetched subtitle's body hash, is `source_hash`; a provider
response keeps `fetched_at` for its body's age and gains `last_asked_at`, which a refresh that
found nothing stamps; a subtitle track's `title` is `containerTitle` or `releaseName`; and
sqlc spells initialisms as hand-written Go does (SHA-256 is `Sha256` in both). The names are in
the research file's third addendum; step 0027 carries library.db (D228), and cache.db goes to
version 19.

## D228 — Until migrations are live, library.db's schema is a baseline and one step, and a schema change folds the last step into the baseline

> **Revised by [D272](#d272--production-runs-on-naslan-from-an-image-it-builds-and-migrations-keep-every-step-since-the-version-it-last-ran)** (2026-10-09): once production runs, the steps since the version nas.example last ran are all kept, and they fold into the baseline when the owner says nas.example has migrated; this replaces §3's one step behind, and stands in for §6 until the public beta.

**Decided** (2026-09-29), by the project owner. **Suspends, until migrations are live,
[D181](#d181--the-migration-policy-two-integers-our-own-small-runner-a-snapshot-that-outlives-success-refuse-what-we-cannot-read-and-re-derive-rather-than-transform) §2's *"every step kept, forever"*
and [D201](#d201--a-setting-a-person-set-stays-theirs-and-every-other-one-follows-its-starting-value-the-last-pre-database-values-are-config-keys-seeding-fills-both-places-and-reports-what-nothing-reads-new-goldens-have-standing-approval) §4's golden for every step**; the rest of D181 (the two integers, the runner and its checks, the
snapshot, the newer-database refusal) stands.

1. **Why.** Twenty-five steps had grown for no database but the owner's development one, each
   test database replayed them, and each had a test of its own. The owner: *"None of the
   migrations up until now actually matter. There are no actual systems out there to migrate. I
   only allowed the migration machinery so that the machinery itself would be tested and ready
   when we later have migrations we actually care about."* and *"yes to ... squashing the
   migrations. I'll give the word when we're finally at a point where migrations actually
   matter, and then we can go back to testing all migrations."*
2. **One step behind.** Revising a first design of one baseline at version 1, the same day:
   *"We should probably keep 1 version back so that it can migrate the dev db as we go. What I
   mean is: Squash everything up until the previous migration point, and keep only 1 migration
   to go from the previous one to the current one. That's the only migration we're actually
   going to do in a dev environment anyway."* Steps 0001 to 0024 are one baseline,
   `0024_baseline.sql`, which builds a new database at version 24 with the schema and the rows
   they built (the two built-in roles); 0025 stays as the one real step. Version numbers do not
   change: a database at 25 is current, and one at 24 migrates through 0025. *(Since 2026-09-29,
   §3's rolling rule has folded 0025 into the baseline too: the baseline's name and version move
   with each fold, and `internal/store/migrations/` holds the current baseline and its one step.
   Noted 2026-09-30; the owner: "agreed" ([M3's closing audit](../design/research/audit-2026-09-29.md) §9 D).)*
3. **The rolling rule.** A schema change folds the current last step into the baseline, which
   moves up to that step's version, and adds the change as the only step after it. A
   development database is only ever one step behind, and that step really runs on it. The
   baseline builds only a new file. It names the checksum of the last step it folded
   (`-- orpheum:baseline folds <sha256>`), so a database that reached the baseline's version
   through that step is as current as one the baseline built; any other text recorded at that
   version is refused as a changed step. A database below the baseline's version is refused,
   saying to start again (`make dev-reset`, then `make dev`); none exists.
4. **The machinery stays tested**, on synthetic steps: order, a data-transforming step, a
   rebuild keeping its id sequence, raising `compatible_version`, checksums, snapshots, free
   space, rollback, interruption, a newer database, and the baseline's rules. A test of a folded
   step's own rows goes with the step; the real step keeps its own. The reference-scale test
   fills the baseline's schema and times the real step and a rebuild of `file`.
5. **Goldens and gates.** There is a golden for the baseline's version and one for the current
   version, and their difference is what the step does. Until migrations are live, a fold
   rewrites or removes them without being listed as test weakening (they still need
   `Gate-Changed:`, with standing approval from this decision), and the pre-edit hook lets the
   baseline be edited; the step after it stays refused, because a development database has
   applied it.
6. **Going live.** The owner says when, and it is done by committing
   `internal/store/migrations/LIVE`. From then on the baseline is frozen like every step, steps
   append as D181 says, the pre-edit hook refuses every committed step, a changed golden needs
   the owner again (D201 §4), and `TestSteps_AreABaselineAndOneStepUntilMigrationsAreLive` no
   longer holds the steps to two.

**Status:** Decided; built 2026-09-29.

## D229 — Code that looks alike is merged only when it is the same thing; settled look-alikes are listed here, and doubtful ones are watched

**Decided** (2026-09-30), by the project owner, after M3's closing audit
([audit-2026-09-29](../design/research/audit-2026-09-29.md)) found CSS rules with identical
declarations in unrelated screens' stylesheets.

1. **The rule.** AGENTS.md rule 11 (one way to do each job) is about one *job* done twice, not
   about text that happens to match. The owner: *"If the CSS happens to match but the item is
   conceptually different, then it's a different component and shouldn't be consolidated."* Two
   pieces of code, style or markup are merged only when they are the same concept; matching
   declarations, shapes or lines are not evidence of that on their own. This holds in Go and
   TypeScript as in CSS.
2. **Settled look-alikes.** What an audit found alike and the owner or this decision judged *not*
   the same thing is listed here with why, so that later sweeps do not raise it again. A new
   settled pair is added here with its date; an audit (checklist item 10) reads this list first.

   | Look-alikes | Why they are different things |
   | --- | --- |
   | CSS `.series__episodes` and `.your-devices__list` | a series' episodes and a person's devices: two lists that share a spacing today, not one component |
   | CSS `.subtitles` and `.form-row` | the player's subtitle controls and a form's row of fields |
   | CSS `.subtitles__offset` and `.sound__switch` | the subtitle offset stepper and the sound question's switch |
   | Episode stills on the series list and on the title page | the series list keeps a blank box where there is no still so its rows line up; the title page shows nothing (2026-09-29) |
   | A title's year printed in four places | printing a number is not a job to share; a formatted year would gain a thousands separator |
   | The node's own segment-length default and the `hls_segment_length_s` setting | the node cannot read settings: its default is its guard against an out-of-range command, not a second copy of the setting |
   | `internal/core/providers/cloudflare` and `orpheum-connect`'s `internal/zone` Cloudflare client | one sets a household's ACME challenge through the household's own token; the other keeps the service's zone's records through the service's. They share only Cloudflare's answer envelope (the owner, 2026-10-14) |

3. **Doubtful look-alikes are watched, not merged.** The owner: *"If there's some ambiguity as to
   whether two components are actually the same thing, make a watch list so that we can revisit
   the question later."* They are in [the look-alike watch list](../look-alike-watch-list.md),
   each with the question that would settle it. When one is settled, it moves either into a merge
   or into §2's table.

**Status:** Decided 2026-09-30; §2's table and the watch list are kept by every audit.

## D230 — The last subtitle and audio language chosen in a series follows its unwatched episodes, worked out at play time

**Decided** (2026-09-30), by the project owner, after M3's closing audit found D223 §8 half built
(audit-2026-09-29 §9 A3). **Replaces D219 §2–§4 and D223 §8**; D219 §1 (a choice is kept per
person and per file) and D24's three rules about what a choice is still hold.

1. **Why.** The owner's scenario: watching *Dag* while adding its episodes one at a time, English
   subtitles chosen in episode 1, *"Now I binge watch eps 3-7 and I expect them all to show
   english subtitles, even though I only selected when watching ep1"*, including episodes added
   after the choice and a file swapped for one that gained the track. And on intent: *"If the
   track was broken and I chose another track (say, simplified english), there's no way to know
   my actual intent. Same goes if I'd chosen English subtitles while watching ep1 and then chose
   French on ep3. Maybe my grandma is over and so we use French subtitles that day. At best we
   can use the last chosen language (subtitle or audio track) for any unwatched episodes in a
   series."*
2. **The rule.** A person's last chosen subtitle language, and last chosen audio language, in a
   series (or among a film's copies) applies to its **unwatched** episodes (or copies). A
   **started** episode counts as watched (the owner: *"started counts as 'watched' for purposes
   of subtitles and audio"*) and plays again with what was last used in it.
3. **A language, not a track.** An unwatched episode plays the track of that language, preferring
   the same kind (forced, for the deaf and hard of hearing, plain) and then the same title. *Off*
   is a choice and follows as *off*. An episode with no track in that language plays without
   subtitles (or with its default audio) until it has one: a fallback is not a choice (D24).
4. **Worked out at play time, never copied.** What is stored is the person's last choice per work
   and what was last used in each started file; a file's tracks are matched when it plays. Nothing
   is carried between files, so an episode added later, or a file whose tracks change, follows
   without any refresh (the audit's derived-data class, agent-failures A4).
5. **Audio is new.** The audio language chosen was not remembered before; it now is, by the same
   rule.

**Status:** Decided 2026-09-30; built 2026-09-30 in `internal/core/preferences`, with the
architecture map's F2 (its preferences part) and F6. A person's last choice is kept per work
(preference scope `work`: the series, or the film's title) as `subtitle_language` and
`audio_language`, and what a started file last used as its `subtitle_used` and `audio_used`; a
file's tracks are matched when it plays (§2–§4). A file counts as started at its first play
report, which keeps what the playback started with; a choice made in it replaces that. A work's
language is matched by its normalised BCP 47 tag exactly first and, failing that, by its primary
language subtag: an `en-GB` choice finds an `en` track and an `en` choice an `en-GB` one (the
owner, 2026-09-30, deciding what the build left open); what a started file used is found again
by its tag exactly. Audio is
chosen from the play screen's Sound menu, and a chosen track other than the one the original
plays first is prepared, with the reason `audio_track`, since a browser plays the original's first
(§5). Step 0028 gave each work the most recent choice made in one of its files, and kept a
choice carried to a file only where the file was started; a started file with no stored choice
follows the work until its next play.

## D231 — Work is derived from state, the job queue is a regenerable cache, and a destination that is down parks its work

> **Revised by [D277](#d277--a-scan-held-back-for-the-admin-leaves-its-root-playable-unless-it-saw-none-of-it-and-the-admin-is-told-what-waits-and-what-could-not-be-read-with-the-fix)** (2026-10-11): §5's missing root is not one whose scan is merely held back for the admin.

**Decided** (2026-09-30), by the project owner, after M3's closing audit (audit-2026-09-29 §9 A4,
A8), research into how queues handle unreliable destinations and a survey of Go queue libraries
([queueing-2026-09-30](../design/research/queueing-2026-09-30.md)), and a scenario walk
([scenarios.md](../design/plans/scenarios.md) S22–S29, S70–S78). **Revises** D170's mechanism
(its intent, one fetch per answer and every refetch a person's act, stands), **replaces** D213 §5's
image breaker, and **amends** D41 and D208 with the retire actions of §7.

1. **Why.** The owner: *"for jobs we can't complete due to larger issues (server down, DNS not
   working, etc), it feels like we need to offload the jobs to another queue that waits for the
   issue at that layer to solve itself. There's no reason to hammer a server for 1000 things when
   1 alive check is enough to set those jobs aside until the machine comes back."* And: *"jobs
   that only get triggered once for a particular file, never to be brought up again in a sweep.
   If that job gets killed somehow, we'll never get what it was supposed to fetch, and there will
   be no way to ask."* And: *"If we can remove state from the queue, then that means the queue is
   100% regeneratable, and doesn't need to live in the main db."*
2. **Our own queue, in its own generic package.** No library does per-destination parking; the one
   candidate (River's SQLite driver) costs more than it saves (the survey). The owner: *"make this
   queue somewhat generic and in its own package so that we can re-use it for any future
   job-shaped things."* The package owns claiming, priority, back-off, parking, probing and
   merging, and knows no Orpheum kind, target or destination; its storage is an interface that
   `internal/store` implements on cache.db, so only store touches SQLite.
3. **Level-triggered work.** Every job is derived by a sweep from durable state in library.db;
   the queue is a cache of the work that state implies, and a request to enqueue is a hint to run
   sooner. **cache.db can be deleted at any moment and nothing is lost but timing**
   (`TestScenario_S78_DiscardingCacheDBLosesOnlyTiming`). Sweeps run at start, on their timers,
   after each pass and when a destination unparks. D170's "ever queued" lookup goes: a first match
   is owed until the item has an answer.
   *Since 2026-09-30 (the owner, "go with your recommendations" on the architecture map's F1):*
   expensive derived data does not live in cache.db. Small results (loudness, extracted subtitle
   text) are kept in library.db; large artefacts (prepared renditions, artwork sizes) are kept on
   the disk where they were made, which is their record, and the core's index of renditions is
   rebuilt from the node's inventory at hello (D233 §4). Only then does deleting cache.db lose
   nothing but timing.
4. **Facts, not job rows.** A failure that is the item's own (not its destination's) is a fact in
   library.db with its reason and time: the sweep skips it, the page shows it, and "try again"
   clears it. A person's request whose action cannot simply be redone is a fact too: in Cut A,
   refresh (requested-at, and whether to fetch images again). Play-driven work needs none; the
   next play asks again.
5. **Destinations.** A job names the destination it needs: `tmdb-api`, `tmdb-images`,
   `opensubtitles`, each node, each root or mount a scan found missing, and the core's own
   storage. A destination is **down** on a failure that says nothing about the item: connection
   refused, DNS, timeout, HTTP 502/503/504 (a plain 500 is the item's); a node not connected or
   silent; a root or mount missing; a write failing for want of space or with an I/O error. A
   missing or refused key parks `tmdb-api` with that reason, and it unparks when the secret
   changes. A node that answers "no room" parks prepares on its prepared directory until its status
   shows room. "Changed since the scan" is the item's failure: no attempt spent, the job ends, and
   the node is asked to rescan that path. A 429 keeps waiting for the time the server gave.
   *Since 2026-09-30 (the owner: "have data sources such as TMDB as a service, with assigned
   costs, limits, and quotas remaining etc, such that the caller can then make a more informed
   decision"; then "yes, fold it into phase 2 with those reservations"):* each outside host is a
   provider service owning its health, a request rate we keep to, its quota and reset, and its
