   credentials' state. A caller states how much its request matters and asks; the provider decides.
   Background work uses at most 80% of TMDB's rate and never spends the last 5 OpenSubtitles
   downloads of the day.
6. **Parking.** Work for a down destination is not claimed and spends no attempt; parked time
   counts against nothing. One probe checks an outside host, on a back-off from 30 s towards an
   hour; a failed probe costs nothing. A node's hello is its probe; a root returns when a scan
   finds it. A person's request for parked work probes at once (the owner: *"waking a job when a
   user needs something: We should also make an attempt then to unpark the queue"*), and a
   person's synchronous call to a parked host always tries and counts as the probe. When a
   destination returns, its work resumes in priority order. Parked state is in memory: after a
   restart, the first job probes again.
7. **Retiring.** A root, a node and a library each have a retire action (a library's is delete),
   which tombstones their files, keeping history on the Title (D173), and cancels their work. A
   deleted library's Titles are tombstoned, hidden with their history, so a film that reappears
   elsewhere brings it back (D208 §2); each person's watch history stays. Offline never ends
   without an admin (D41): the System page shows "offline since", and the admin is reminded after
   a week.
8. **One job per target, merged.** A target has at most one queued and one running job. A repeat
   request merges into the queued one: the higher priority, a job waiting to retry woken, and
   arguments merged where the kind allows; while one runs, a request it already covers is dropped
   and another becomes the one queued follow-up.
9. **Cancel stops a run, not the work.** The sweep may queue it again if the state still implies
   it; stopping for good is a change of state (retire, delete, a feature turned off).
10. **Back-off and giving up.** ±10% jitter on every retry. `job_attempt_limit` counts only the
    item's own failures; a job that exhausts it is recorded as the item's failure (§4).
11. **Nodes.** The node table says truthfully whether a node is connected, when it was last heard,
    and whether it is gone. A command to a node that is not connected parks its job instead of
    being dropped. A reconnecting node is not sent commands of jobs that have ended, and its hello
    returns the jobs that were running on it to the queue.
12. **What a person sees.** The job view shows parked work as "waiting for TMDB — unreachable since
    14:02, next check 14:10"; the System page lists each destination's state; play, subtitle and
    refresh answers can say "waiting for <destination> (since …)" beside "preparing".
    *Since 2026-09-30 (the owner: "we need feedback to the user about why we're balking", and "For
    host down (parked), aren't we triggering a host check when the user clicks? In this case we'd
    say 'TMDB hasn't been answering (since xxx). Checking the host now'"):* every time a person's
    request is held back they are told why and until when, in the provider's words where we have
    them, and a screen waits and retries on its own when a time is known. A host that asked us to
    wait shows a countdown and goes ahead when it ends; a parked host shows "hasn't been answering
    since … Checking now…", then either the result or "still isn't answering (since …); next check
    …" with a try-again; spent quota shows when it resets; our own pacing shows a spinner, and words
    past a couple of seconds; a missing or refused credential says who can fix it.

*Settled in the readiness audit's questions (2026-10-01; [audit-2026-09-30.md](../design/research/audit-2026-09-30.md)
§7 D7–D10, the owner: "Yes to your recommendations"):* §7's dismissal of the offline reminder stays
a preference (`offline_reminder_dismissed_at`), one value per person, not a table of its own; a
folder or disk that goes offline after an admin dismissed the reminder brings it back at once,
since a dismissal hides what the admin saw. §12's countdown holds for a person's own call to a
host that asked us to wait. Two names now say what they hold: the setting
`library_check_every_hours`, only a new library's starting interval, is
`new_library_scan_every_hours`, and the retire answers' `removedFileCount`, which counts
tombstoned files, is `tombstonedFileCount`.

**Status:** Decided 2026-09-30. Built by the jobs rebuild's Phases 1–3, and §12 by Phase 6
(2026-10-03), as D241 revised it for a play of what cannot be read
([jobs-rebuild.md](../design/plans/jobs-rebuild.md)). Read back at the pre-M4 audit (2026-10-04, [audit-2026-10-03](../design/research/audit-2026-10-03.md) §3): built; §5's "changed since the
scan" is built otherwise, a refused file retried with no rescan, which the owner accepted in 4b.

## D232 — What makes two names the same work is one identity fold, derived from the search fold

**Decided** (2026-09-30), by the project owner, answering M3's closing audit
([audit-2026-09-29](../design/research/audit-2026-09-29.md) §9 C1): *"agreed"*. **Extends**
[D48](#d48--two-fts5-tokenisers-routed-by-script-and-length-and-exactly-one-normaliser)'s one
normaliser from search to identity, and [D49](#d49--unicode-discipline-at-the-boundaries-enforced-by-tests)'s
rule that identity uses one normalised form.

1. **Why.** Nothing defined what makes two names name the same work, and four comparisons had
   grown: the matcher's own fold (NFC, lower case, punctuation dropped), the search fold (D48),
   `strings.ToLower` for the keys that file a film and a series, and SQLite's `NOCASE`. They
   disagreed: "Marvel's X" and "Marvels X" matched one TMDB work, yet were filed as two series,
   and a file named "Variety (1994)" did not match "Variety".
2. **One fold.** `textindex.SameWork` is the identity fold, and every comparison of a work's
   name goes through it: a provider's candidate against the file's name, a film's name with its
   year, a series' folder against the series already filed, and an extra's name against its
   folder's. It is D48's search fold (compatibility forms, lower case, combining marks removed,
   the atomic letters Ø Æ Œ ß Ð Ł Þ spelled out) keeping only letters, numbers and the spacing
   marks some scripts write vowels with. Punctuation, spacing, case, accents and width are what
   files, folders and providers each write their own way, and they say nothing about which work
   a name is: "Marvel's Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D." and "Marvels Agents of SHIELD", "Spider-Man" and
   "Spider Man", "Amélie" and "AMELIE" are one work.
3. **Where it does not fit.** Removing every combining mark is right for search, where finding
   too much is cheap, and costs identity little, because a name is never the whole of it: a film
   is its name and its year, a series its name in one library, and a provider id settles either
   first. Two works whose names differ only in their marks (in Devanagari, some vowels are marks)
   in the same year and library would be taken for one; the matcher's fold before this did the
   same. SQLite's `NOCASE` compares people's names at sign-in, not works, and is not this fold.
4. **Nothing is stored.** The fold keys only what a pass holds in memory, so a change to it
   takes effect at the next pass, and no stored key goes stale.

**Status:** Decided 2026-09-30; built the same day (`textindex.SameWork`, which identify's
matching uses).

## D233 — Work handed to a node survives restarts and lost messages: an outbox, reconciliation at hello, results known by what they are, and a watchdog on both sides

**Decided** (2026-09-30), by the project owner. Built with D231, which it extends from the queue
to the link between core and node. The research behind it is
[queueing-2026-09-30](../design/research/queueing-2026-09-30.md) and the domain pass on
coordinator and worker job systems recorded beside it; agent-failures A14 records why the first
pass missed it.

1. **Why.** The owner: *"What happens if the node that's supposed to do the job gets stuck? Does
   the core timeout on it? What happens then? What if the node actually did finish the job but we
   didn't get the result back? What about a restart? Does the node keep track of jobs it completed
   so that the core can get resolution?"* The code's answers were that a hung FFmpeg held its slot
   for ever, a result that failed to send was dropped and the work redone, and a core restart
   cancelled every encode.
2. **The node's lifetime is its own** (O1). The node on the core's machine runs as its own service
   (`orpheum-node`), always restarted; the core watches only that it is alive (D43's thin
   supervisor). A core restart does not touch node work.
3. **Results are delivered at least once and handled once.** A finished job's result waits in an
   outbox on the node's disk until the core acknowledges it, numbered as the report stream is (one
   mechanism). A result is identified by what it is (kind, target, source hash, run) and every
   command and answer carries an attempt token; the hello reply carries an id for this run of the
   core (O2). The core ignores a duplicate and accepts a still-valid result even for a job it gave
   up on.
4. **Reconciliation at hello.** A node job's state after a core restart is "awaiting hello" (O3):
   never re-sent blind. At hello the node lists what it is running and what finished unacknowledged,
   and its prepared renditions on disk; the core adopts, re-queues or parks each, rebuilds its
   rendition index from that inventory (D231 §3's note), and says what to stop. Commands of jobs
   that have ended are never sent.
5. **Stuck work is caught on both sides.** Stage 1 is built: every FFmpeg run on the node is
   watched for its position advancing, with a start grace, a stall window and a deadline per kind,
   and a stalled run is stopped (quit, then its process group killed) and answered as "stalled".
   Stage 2: the node classifies a stall from `/proc` (deadlocked, spinning, or waiting on a disk,
   which parks on that root as D231 §5 says) and watches output growth; loudness and extraction
   report progress; the core's lease on a running job is renewed only by movement, with waiting
   for a slot bounded on its own.
6. **Failure has three sources** (O4): the item's (a fact, D231 §4), the destination's (parking,
   D231 §5), and the tool's (a stall or a crash): free the first time, the item's failure the
   second. The core recovers from a panic in a job, and a claim checks the attempt count.
7. **Capacity and expiry.** Claiming respects each node's own slots, so one node's backlog never
   blocks another's plays, and a play-now prepare pauses background reads on its node (O6).
   Play-driven work carries a "wanted until"; past it, it falls to background priority or is
   dropped, since the next play asks again (O5).
8. **What is shown and kept** (O7). The System page shows, per kind, the number queued, the oldest
   queued age and the failures of the last 24 hours; per node, its slots in use and the time since
   its last progress. Finished job rows are pruned after 30 days.
9. **Compatibility** (O8, from M4). The hello carries a protocol number; a node whose number the
   core cannot serve is parked with that reason, and an unknown command is refused explicitly.

10. **A stall on the disk, as built** (the owner, 2026-10-03, *"agreed on both"*, to two questions
    asked before stage 2 was built):
    - **The root first, then the file.** A run that stalls waiting on the disk makes its root
      unavailable (D241 §2–§4: plays from it fail at once and say the disk is not answering), and a
      scan of the root is asked for, whose success brings it back (D231 §6). The same file stalling
      on the disk again after its root came back is the file's own failure, "the disk could not
      read this file", and the root stays available: one bad patch of a disk would otherwise make
      the whole root flicker forever.
    - **A process the kernel will not kill frees its slot.** A process waiting on a dead disk
      ignores even `SIGKILL` until the disk answers. The node answers its work as stalled and frees
      its slot, so one dead disk does not block a node's other work, and lists the process as stuck
      until it exits, which the System page shows.

**Status:** Decided 2026-09-30. Since 2026-09-30, §3, §5 and §7 are revised by D234. Built by the
jobs rebuild's Phases 4 and 5 (2026-10-03): §5's second stage and §10 by Phase 5; §8's System page
and pruning by Phase 6 ([jobs-rebuild.md](../design/plans/jobs-rebuild.md)). Read back at the pre-M4 audit (2026-10-04, [audit-2026-10-03](../design/research/audit-2026-10-03.md) §3): §8's queue
health was not on the System page, though this line said so; built 2026-10-04 by D244 §2: each
kind's queued count, its oldest and the day's failures, and each node's work.

## D234 — The core drives the node: the node keeps a durable journal of its jobs and schedules them, pushes progress and acknowledged results, and the core checks and reconciles

**Decided** (2026-09-30), by the project owner, from their own model of the link. It revises
D233 §3, §5 and §7 and keeps the rest. The discussion and the comparison with practice are
[node-link-2026-09-30](../design/research/node-link-2026-09-30.md).

1. **Why.** The owner, on how core and node talk today: *"Both the node and the core are
   spontaneously driving each other for various functions. It should be the core that drives the
   node."* The readiness audit ([audit-2026-09-30](../design/research/audit-2026-09-30.md)) found
   the round trip written five times, each a goroutine blocked on its answer, with everything in
   flight in memory on both sides.
2. **The node dials; the core decides.** The node opens and holds the connection (D127), so a node
   the core cannot reach still works, and says hello: who it is, its protocol number and
   capabilities, and a summary of its state. From then on the core sends requests over that
   connection and the node answers them, each matched by id.
3. **Jobs are the core's to give and the node's to schedule.** A job carries its id, an attempt
   number, a priority and its limits: a deadline, and for work a person waits for, a "wanted until"
   past which it falls to background priority (D233 §7). The core gives each node a window of work
   a little beyond its free slots and keeps global priority; the node keeps its jobs in a durable
   journal (`node.db`), orders them within their priorities, and takes updates, including a new
   priority, and cancels, each naming the attempt it applies to. The node's desired jobs carry a
   generation number the node echoes back.
4. **The node owns its jobs to the end.** It runs each to completion whether or not the core is
   there; its watchdog (D233 §5) keeps runs from getting stuck; it retries what it can and reports
   what it cannot as one of D233 §6's three failure sources. A job running when the node restarted
   is run again or reported interrupted. A node whose disk is full refuses new work, with its
   reason. Its own hang is the service manager's to restart.
   **It heals itself by design.** The owner: *"We must assume that eventually something will
   break, so it should be self-healing by design (but of course still report when invariants like
   this are violated)."* The core keeps its own model of what each node should hold; a job the node
   has lost, for whatever reason, shows as a difference at the next check, and the core issues a
   replacement to reach the state it wants. Each such difference is also reported as a broken
   invariant (logged, and counted where D233 §8's queue health shows it), never repaired silently.
5. **Progress is pushed, results are acknowledged.** While a job runs the node sends best-effort
   updates of where it is, throttled, the newest superseding the rest, no acknowledgement. When it
   ends the node sends its outcome: the result inline when small, a reference when large (always
   fetchable from the node's byte socket and checked by hash; readable on a shared mount when the
   core's shows the same content). An outcome is kept and resent until acknowledged, and after that
   for a retention period, bounded by the cache cleanup, oldest unacknowledged first under
   pressure. The core deduplicates by the result's identity and attempt.
6. **The core checks and reconciles.** The core expects updates from a node with assigned work; after
   a few update intervals of silence it asks the node what is happening, and a node that does not
   answer is unreachable and its work parks (D231 §5). At hello, and whenever it chooses, the core
   asks for the node's jobs and outcomes and squares them with its own: it adopts, re-issues or
   cancels, and tells the node to drop jobs it does not know. An idle node sends nothing; the
   core's periodic check is the liveness signal.
7. **The core never blocks on a node.** A job given to a node is a row in the assigned state, not a
   waiting goroutine; whatever depends on it waits with a timeout for its resolution: finished,
   failed, timed out, cancelled, or parked.
8. **A scan is a job.** Its result is a record stream the core reads from an offset, which retires
   the report stream as a mechanism of its own.
9. **Before a node is remote,** it is authenticated by a key or mutual TLS bound to its name.
10. **What it revises.** D233 §3's outbox becomes the journal with acknowledged outcomes; D233 §5's
    core lease becomes the expectation of updates; D233 §7's claiming by slots becomes the node's
    own scheduling within the core's window. D233 §2, §4, §6, §8 and §9 stand.

**Status:** Decided 2026-09-30; built as the jobs rebuild's Phase 4 (2026-10-01 to 2026-10-03).
Since 2026-10-02, §3, §4 and §5 are revised by D238: the node keeps no database; and §3's window
by D240: the core schedules. Read back at the pre-M4 audit (2026-10-04, [audit-2026-10-03](../design/research/audit-2026-10-03.md) §3): built; §4's broken invariants, counted but not shown, are on
the System page since 2026-10-04 (D244 §2).

## D235 — Development and deployment run in containers: one image family, one command each, built by GoReleaser

**Decided** (2026-09-30), by the project owner. It revises cut-a §2's "one binary, one systemd
unit" deployment and the core's supervision of a node child (D43's thin supervisor, D207's execx
start), which D233 §2 and D234 already ended.

1. **Why.** The owner wants a development environment on devnas (Debian trixie) that does not
   *"pollute the operating system with a bunch of stuff since it's supposed to just be a NAS"*, that
   does not accrete dependencies that make it *"harder to replicate on other machines"*, and
   end-user deployments that are *"easy to use"*: *"Ideally dev env setup, deployment packaging,
   and deployment use should be single-command if possible."* And: *"I think containers are going
   to keep things cleanest, so let's go with that."*
2. **One image family.** A runtime image holds the binary, the pinned FFmpeg and nothing else, runs
   as a non-root user, and is built for amd64 and arm64 (keeping arm64 open). A development image
   holds every tool the gates need (Go, Node, sqlc, the linters, Playwright and its browsers,
   Python), each pinned by version and checksum as `make ffmpeg` pins FFmpeg today; CI runs in the
   same image. Both share a base, so development and production differ only by the tools.
3. **Development is one command.** A host needs a container runtime and git. `./dev` builds or pulls
   the development image and runs it with the repository mounted, the media read-only, `/dev/dri`
   for Quick Sync, and the caches (Go's, npm's, the browsers') in named volumes, so nothing lands on
   the host; `./dev make check` runs a gate the same way. A new machine is a clone and `./dev`.
4. **Deployment is a compose file.** Two services, `orpheum-core` and `orpheum-node`, from the one
   runtime image. The runtime's restart policy and health checks are the service manager D234 §4
   asks for. Only the node mounts the media, read-only, and `/dev/dri`; library.db and the caches
   are volumes; the two sockets live on a volume both share. `docker compose up -d` installs and
   starts it.
5. **Packaging is one command.** `make release` runs GoReleaser: the binaries, the multi-arch
   images, checksums, a software bill of materials and signatures, in one pass that D220's audit
   can read. A `.deb` is deferred, not refused.
6. **Confinement holds inside the container.** FFmpeg's Landlock and seccomp confinement (D193 §7,
   D112) nests under the container's; the container's own seccomp profile must allow the Landlock
   system calls, and the escape test (VQ9) runs inside the container. No service runs privileged.
7. **Mac and Windows are deferred.** Both can run the development image through a desktop container
   runtime or WSL2, without Quick Sync; a native node there would be unconfined until its own
   confinement is designed.
8. **Settled in building it** (2026-10-01, the owner: *"agreed"*). The dev loop's templates moved
   from `dev/` to `deploy/dev/`, so the name `./dev` is the launcher's alone. The git pre-commit
   hook and the Stop hook run the gate where the tools are: directly inside the development image
   (it sets `ORPHEUM_IN_DEV_IMAGE=1`) or on a host with Go and Node on its PATH, through `./dev`
   otherwise, and fail saying how to fix the machine when neither works; the choice is made once,
   in `scripts/run_gate.py`. Go is pinned exactly by go.mod's `toolchain` line, which the image
   reads rather than keeping a copy of.

**Status:** Decided 2026-09-30.

## D236 — A scan shows itself and its count, a second request waits for it, and what it finds is playable before it ends

**Decided** (2026-10-01), by the project owner, after trying the dev loop on devnas: *"there's no
way to know from the UI that a library is currently scanning, so I ended up queuing multiple scan
requests"*, and *"it would be good to get rolling updates as the scan progresses, so that I can
start playing the already scanned movies while it's still scanning."*

1. **What a scan finds is identified while it runs.** A batch of records that stores a new file,
   or brings one back from its tombstone, asks for an identification pass; the sweeper runs one
   within a minute however many batches asked (D231 §3), off the path that takes the node's
   records. A film found early is browsable and playable before the scan ends; a series may show
   some episodes first and fill in. Removals still wait for a complete scan (D39): only a
   complete pass proves a file gone. For now, ahead of Phase 4.
2. **The library screen shows a scan as it runs:** beside the root, *"Scanning… 312 files found so
   far"*, updating as it goes. A percentage bar was refused: it needs a first pass to count the
   root's files. Built with the jobs rebuild's Phase 4, where a scan is a job whose progress is
   pushed (D234 §5, §8), not on the report stream Phase 4 retires: in Phase 4.
3. **A scan asked for while one runs does not start another** (D38's rule, which the code broke:
   each press queued a full scan behind the running one). The button reads *"Scan again when this
   one ends"*, and any number of presses during a scan schedule one rescan after it. In Phase 4,
   with §2.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-01. §1 built 2026-10-01, ahead of Phase 4; §2 and §3 built 2026-10-03 with the jobs rebuild's
4e: a scan's listing comes whole (D240 §8), so the root shows *"Scanning… listing the folders"* until
it is in, then *"Scanning… 312 files found, 12 of 40 new or changed read"*.

## D237 — A screen showing what the server changes in the background asks again, backing off while nothing changes, to 30 s

**Decided** (2026-10-02), by the project owner, watching a scan of the films on devnas fill the
library while the films list stayed as it was when opened: *"poll the server with a backoff when
nothing new is forthcoming, max 30s. This should be the general pattern for any pages that would
benefit from updated info."*

1. **One pattern for every such screen.** A screen whose content the server changes on its own (a
   scan, identification, artwork, jobs) asks again after 2 s, doubles the wait each time the answer
   is unchanged, up to 30 s, and asks again after 2 s once it changes. It keeps what it shows while
   it asks. It is the client's one way to poll (useResource, and usePages for a list read a page at
   a time, which asks again for every page it has shown).
2. **Which screens.** Those that show what the server changes in the background: the films and
   series lists, a title, a series, *Needs a match*, the libraries, the System page, the job view
   and the home page's rows. Not a form being edited, a search, the player or a sign-in, where an
   answer arriving would change what a person is in the middle of.
3. **Not a push channel.** The server tells no screen that something changed; a push channel can
   replace the polling later without changing what a screen shows.
4. **The waits are settings the server gives the client** (the owner, the same day: *"As per usual,
   the 30s max poll interval should be configurable, passed by the server to the client."*):
   `screen_refresh_first_wait_seconds` (2) and `screen_refresh_longest_wait_seconds` (30), read by
   every signed-in client from `GET /client-settings`; D237's waits until they are read.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-02; built the same day. Read back at the pre-M4 audit (2026-10-04, [audit-2026-10-03](../design/research/audit-2026-10-03.md) §3): §1's poller is tested
(polling.test.ts); §2's "each screen that shows background changes asks again" has no test that
each such screen does.

**Amended** (2026-10-06), when a films list opened while the dev server rebuilt stayed failed and
the home page took up to 30 s more to notice the server back: §1's "unchanged" is an answer, and a
failed read is none, and does not back off. After each failed read a screen asks again after
`screen_refresh_failed_wait_seconds`, a setting the server gives the client as §4's waits, starting
at 5 s (the owner: *"Make it every 5 seconds instead of 2"*), and a list whose first read, or whose
page more, failed is read again from the start (polling.test.ts, use-pages.test.ts).

## D238 — Each fact has one owner; the node keeps no database, holding its work in memory and its renditions' facts beside them

**Decided** (2026-10-02), by the project owner, when `node.db` met the gate that keeps the node
off the database: *"Let's step back and think about what the data requirements of the core and
nodes are, how to avoid duplication, and how to avoid one incorrectly storing data that belongs
to the other."* Then, on the proposal below: *"Agreed on both"*, *"Does the node need persistent
storage?"*, and *"Agreed"*. It revises D234 §3, §4 and §5.

1. **Each fact has one owner**: the side where it starts and where it must survive the other's
   loss. The other side keeps only what it needs to act, as a copy it can rebuild or as "what the
   other last said" (schema.md's class O).
   - **The core owns intent**: which work should happen, its priority, its "wanted until", a
     cancel. **The library's facts**, the node's findings among them once recorded. **A node's
     identity.**
   - **The node owns its configuration** (D107), which the core keeps as reported; **what is on its
     disks**, whose index the core keeps as a cache (`prepared_rendition`); and **the execution of
     the work it holds**: accepted, waiting, running, and how it ended, until the core acknowledges
     the outcome.
2. **Nothing is held twice by design.** The node keeps a command as it came, with its attempt token
   and priority, never broken into facts of its own, and drops it when the work ends or the core
   says so. An outcome becomes the core's when it is acknowledged, and the node then keeps only its
   identity (the token, the kind, when it ended) to know a repeated command, never its content: this
   replaces D234 §5's week of kept outcomes. Progress is never stored by the node. A rendition's
   facts (its profile, the source's identity, the gains, the run) live in a manifest beside it, so
   they go with its files.
3. **The node keeps no database.** Its work, its unacknowledged outcomes and the identities of
   ended work are held in memory; on disk it has its configuration and its prepared directory. A
   core that restarts finds them still held and resent. A node that restarts has lost them with the
   work its process ran, and the core's reconciliation (D234 §6) finds the difference and asks
   again: the hello carries an id for this start of the node, so the core knows the work was
   interrupted, the tool's failure source (D233 §6), free the first time and the item's the second.
   A prepare's outcome survives a restart as its rendition and manifest. What is lost is an
   unacknowledged measurement, subtitle or re-encode, redone. Reconciliation is the one way back.
4. **What it revises.** D234 §3's durable journal (`node.db`) becomes the node's memory; D234 §4's
   "run again or reported interrupted" is the core's, at reconciliation; D234 §5's retention keeps
   identities, not outcomes. The rule that the node never touches a database (D31, D42) stands.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-02; built with the jobs rebuild's 4.x (2026-10-02 to 2026-10-03):
the node keeps no database, its work in memory and its renditions' manifests beside them.

## D239 — `library.db` is `persistent.db`, named for how it is kept beside `cache.db`

**Decided** (2026-10-02), by the project owner: *"Would it make sense to call the persistent db
persistent.db? Then we have cache.db and it's easy to know which to back up from the file
alone."*

1. **The name says how the file is kept.** `persistent.db` is backed up and never discarded;
   `cache.db` is never backed up and may be deleted at any time. `library.db` also held users,
   devices, grants, settings, secrets and play state, which the name hid.
2. **The data directory is still the unit of backup**: `secret.key`, which opens the secrets,
   lives beside `persistent.db`.
3. Decisions before this one, and research, keep `library.db` as written: history, not
   specification.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-02; built the same day.

## D240 — The core keeps the smarts: a scan is a listing the core compares, the work it implies is the core's to schedule, and the node enforces its devices' limits and pauses background work for play

> **§8's extension lists revised by [D360](#d360--the-extensions-a-scan-reads-are-the-codes-each-container-proven-to-play-and-realmedia-is-one)** (2026-10-27): they are constants in the core's code, not settings, each container proven to play.

> **§5 and §6 revised by [D329](#d329--work-is-scheduled-from-wants-each-resource-is-decided-next-to-it-playback-is-admitted-and-long-work-is-cut-into-pieces)** (2026-10-22): the node decides its disks and encoders from the wants the core sends, and play is admitted rather than exempted from limits.

> **§5 revised by [D255](#d255--work-has-three-priorities-a-persons-a-fast-operations-and-a-slow-ones-and-a-higher-one-bumps-the-lowest-when-nothing-is-free)** (2026-10-07): work has three priorities, a person's, a fast operation's and a slow one's, and a higher one bumps a running job of the lowest when nothing is free.

**Decided** (2026-10-02), by the project owner, on the proposal for the jobs rebuild's 4d: *"Let's
step back and think about how we're doing jobs. [...] it seems to me that we're best off keeping
most of the smarts in the core."* Then, on the proposal below: *"yes, all of that makes sense"*,
*"Is there any way to put a task to sleep?"*, and *"ok, all of that sounds good"*. It revises D234
§3, D207's scan as the node's walk with its report stream, and the jobs rebuild's 4d and 4e.

1. **The node knows no library.** It knows the roots it is configured with (D107), which its hello
   names, and the core may ask for them again. A scan of a root no library covers is never asked
   for: a path is scanned only once it is a library's root, whose kind says what it holds (the
   owner, 2026-10-02).
2. **A listing, not a walk that reads.** The core asks a node to list under a path to a depth: one
   level for a person choosing a library's folder, the whole tree for a scan. Each entry is its raw
   path (D49, D211), its kind, size, modified time, device and inode, or the error that kept it
   from being read (D163); the root's filesystem facts come with it, so an unplugged disk is still
   told from an empty folder (D41, D208). A large tree arrives in pages, which the core compares as
   they come.
3. **The core compares; only the new and changed cost work.** A file whose size and modified time
   are as stored needs nothing. A new or changed one is examined. One at a new path with the same
   device, inode and size is a move, kept without reading it again. One gone is a removal, under
   D208's rules. The skip rules (D40) are the core's, which knows the library's kind. With the
   smarts in the core it can also ask again for what an older probe or rule left, without a scan.
4. **Work names operations, not library kinds.** The node probes and hashes a video (D179), reads an
   NFO's bytes (D182), hashes a subtitle; which of them a file needs is the core's choice from the
   library's kind. **One folder per command**, a title's video with its sidecars, bounded in files:
   the node answers each file as it is done, the core acknowledges each answer, and a node that goes
   down costs only the files of that folder not yet answered, which the core asks for again. That
   is neither a command per file, too chatty, nor one per root, too costly to redo.
5. **The core schedules.** It decides what each node does, in which order and how much it holds,
   by global priority, as D234 §3's window gave the node to decide within. A node's resources are
   its devices, not its roots, since several roots can share a disk, and its CPU and GPU slots
   (cut-a §5.3); a job needs a device, and some a slot too. Each device has a concurrency limit:
   one reader on a spinning disk, in path order, several on an SSD, its own on a network mount. The
   limit is a setting per device, whose starting value is what the node detects, one where it
   cannot tell. Detection follows a pool, array or volume to its member disks and reads each disk's
   `rotational` flag, spinning if any data disk spins, or the drive's rotation rate where udev read
   one; a disk behind USB whose flag says it spins is unknown, since most bridges hide the drive and
   the kernel guesses (the owner's USB SSD on devnas, 2026-10-03): an md array or LVM volume through
   `/sys/block/<device>/slaves`, btrfs through `/sys/fs/btrfs`, a ZFS dataset through the mount
   table to its pool and udev's database to the pool's disks, which the node's container reads
   from the host's `/run/udev`, mounted read-only (the owner, 2026-10-02: *"Are you sure we can't
   detect zfs?"*). A smarter scheduler for SSDs has room to come.
6. **The node enforces the limits and yields to play at once.** What a round trip to the core
   cannot do in time is the node's: when play-driven work arrives for a device, the node pauses the
   background work reading it (the owner: *"if a background task is allowed to finish first, that
   can take awhile"*), each FFmpeg's process group stopped with `SIGSTOP` and continued with
   `SIGCONT` when the play-driven work on that device ends, a hash in the node's own process at its
   next chunk. Paused time is neither a stall nor spent deadline (D233 §5). The node says what it
   paused, and the core shows it. Running both is a device's limit of two, for those who want it.
   Past its "wanted until" (D234 §3), play-driven work is background and pauses nothing.
   **Play-driven work never waits for another's** (the owner's choice, 2026-10-05, and for slots
   2026-10-06): two people's play-driven work read a device at once, past its limit, and run in a
   slot at once, past its count, the encodes sharing the machine; the limits bind background work
   alone. A lower quality made for one viewer had waited the whole of another's prepare on the
   same disk, and in the node's one encode slot.
7. **What it revises.** D234 §3's window within which the node schedules becomes the core's
   scheduling; the node keeps D238's memory of what it was given and the limits of §6. D207's scan,
   the node walking a root and reading every file into the report stream, becomes the listing and
   the examining (§2–§4). D234 §8's record stream is the listing's and the answers'. D233 and D234's
   other sections, and D238, stand.
8. **As built, the owner's four answers** (2026-10-03, *"agreed on all four"*):
   - **One answer per batch, not per file.** A command examines a folder's files in a batch: up to a
     setting's count of videos, each with the sidecars named for it. The batch is answered whole and
     acknowledged as every result is, so a lost node redoes one batch. A folder of loose videos, such
     as a movies folder holding a few dozen bare files, is several batches (the owner: *"those would
     all get swept up in one call to the base movies dir, right?"*). This revises §4's per-file
     answer.
   - ~~**The extension lists are settings.**~~ *(Since 2026-10-27, constants in the core's code, D360.)*
     Which files are videos and which subtitles is a skip rule, the core's by §3, so they leave the
     node's configuration.
   - **A move is still told by its payload hash** (D179). A file at a new path is examined like a new
     one, and the ingest finds the row it moved from. Telling a move by device and inode, which
     saves that one read, waits; §3's move by inode is not built.
   - **The listing comes whole.** It is fetched from the node's byte socket as large results are, not
     in pages; paging waits for a library large enough to need it.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-02; built as the jobs rebuild's re-cut 4d and 4e (2026-10-03),
except what §8 defers and §6's pause, which pauses between files rather than within one; §5's
System-page control of a device's reader limit was built 2026-10-04 (D244 §2). Until it is
in use the protocol and both databases change freely: their one user is the owner, testing (the
owner, 2026-10-02: *"I don't care about protocol changes or format changes or anything that causes
incompatibilities or requires migrations at this point"*).

## D241 — What goes missing stays listed as unavailable until an admin says it is gone, and a play of it fails at once

**Decided** (2026-10-03), by the project owner, after asking what happens when a node reconnects
naming a different set of roots. **Amends** D231 §5, §6 and §12 for play-driven work, and D231 §7
with a per-file retire and a root's repoint.

1. **Why.** A root the node stops naming in its hello is never scanned, so nothing marks it missing:
   its films look playable, a play fails with the node's bare "not under my roots", and the library
   screen shows nothing wrong, so the admin is never led to retire it. The owner: *"it should still
   show up, but marked as unavailable. This would be a general pattern for things that go
   transiently missing until the admin marks something permanently gone (either one at a time, or
   bulk through a 'this root is now gone')."*
2. **A root the hello does not name is missing.** At a node's hello, each of its library roots the
   hello does not name is marked missing from that moment, as a scan marks one whose folder or disk
   is gone (D41, D208). Nothing is removed on an absence. When a hello names it again, its scan
   runs and finds it.
3. **Unavailable is shown, not hidden.** A Title whose every live copy is under a missing root or
   disk, or on a node that is not connected, stays in every list and on its page, marked
   unavailable with the reason and since when. This is the one pattern for whatever goes missing
   for a while: it lasts until the admin says it is gone.
4. **A play of what is known unavailable fails at once and queues nothing.** The owner: *"If a
   request comes in to play something that's already known unavailable, it should fail immediately
   with appropriate messaging, and NOT queue any jobs. The user can't see the video, so the
   priority and even necessity of such a job is gone."* The answer names what is missing (the
   folder or disk and its node, or the node) and since when. This replaces, for play-driven work,
   D231 §12's "waiting for <destination>": a person is not kept waiting on a source known to be
   gone. A play-driven job already queued when its source goes missing is cancelled, as nobody can
   be waiting for it. Background work (loudness, artwork from the file, extraction for the sweep)
   still parks under D231 §5–§6, and the job view says why.
5. **Gone is the admin's word, one at a time or in bulk.** Retiring a root (D231 §7) is the bulk
   "this root is now gone". A file marked unavailable can also be retired by itself: its file is
   tombstoned, keeping the Title's history (D173). Unless that or a scan's confirmed removal happens,
   an unavailable file stays unavailable.
6. **A moved root is repointed, not recreated.** The admin can tell the core that a root, missing
   or reported moved, is now at another path on the same or another node. The root and its files'
   paths move with their history. The next scan confirms each file by its payload hash (D179) before
   it counts as present again, and treats one it cannot confirm as a removal under D208.
7. **A film already playing says why it stops.** When a fetch fails during play, the player asks
   the server why, as a new play would, and §4's answer names what is missing and since when. The
   film plays what the browser already holds, and the reason is shown when the picture stops; an
   answer that the source is there means a passing failure, and the player tries again. The order
   is the preferred one, not the requirement. The owner: *"If that turns out to not be feasible I'm
   flexible on the specific ordering. All that matters is that the user knows why playback failed
   (or is about to)."* Whether a browser plays out its buffer after a failed fetch, above all in
   direct play, only a device can confirm.
8. **Later.** "Rescan to find missing media": the core asks a node for the full tree of each of its
   roots and matches missing files by name, then confirms candidates by payload hash. It is not in
   Cut A.

§2–§6's details that the owner's words left open were proposed and confirmed (2026-10-03, *"yes to
the things you filled in"*): a node that is not connected counts as known unavailable (§3, §4); a
play-driven job is cancelled when its source goes missing (§4); background work parks (§4); a root
can be repointed to another node (§6).

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-03; built in the jobs rebuild's Phase 6 (2026-10-03), beside D231 §12's
other answers to a person. Read back at the pre-M4 audit (2026-10-04, [audit-2026-10-03](../design/research/audit-2026-10-03.md) §3): built; §6's repoint to another node, and the scan that
confirms each file after a repoint, have no test.

## D242 — An Orpheum instance is one directory: a small top-level config pointing at persistent, cache, backups and run, and a backup is a tarball of persistent

**Decided** (2026-10-03), by the project owner, after seeing the development data directory: *"It's
not clear which things need to be kept when I want to back up orpheum."* **Amends** D204 §1 (what
`--config` names) and D198's state directory, which becomes `persistent/`; D194 §4 stands.

1. **Why.** The owner: *"backing up is simply making a tarball of persistent. It could even be a
   function via the admin interface (put them in the backups dir)."*
2. **Orpheum is started with the instance directory, and with nothing else that says where things
   are.** The owner: *"orpheum must be started with a pointer to the dir containing the minimal
   top-level config. Everything else gets configured from there."* Every subcommand that needs an
   instance takes its directory as a flag, which is required and has no default. *"We make no
   assumptions about where anything lives, or any env variables. That's for the distribution to
   choose."* D204's rule of no ambient configuration stands.
3. **The top-level config is small.** `orpheum.toml` in the instance directory says the Orpheum
   version that wrote it and where each of the four directories is, as absolute paths:
   - `persistent/`: `persistent.db`, `secret.key`, and the full config file, which holds every
     other key that must exist before the database opens (D200);
   - `cache/`: `cache.db`, prepared renditions and artwork, all of which can be rebuilt (D238);
   - `backups/`: the backups, outside `persistent/` so a backup holds no earlier ones;
   - `run/`: what only a running instance needs, never backed up: the node sockets, the server
     lock and the one-time setup code.
   The pointers let a distribution put the cache on another disk. Where the log is written is a key
   of the full config: standard error, where the log has always gone, or a file the admin names
   (the owner, 2026-10-03: *"I also want to support specifying where the log should be written
   to"*); `default-config` writes standard error.
4. **`orpheum default-config <dir>` makes an instance.** The owner: *"The user should be able to
   generate a default config with something like 'orpheum default-config /path/to/dir' (config must
   not exist yet)."* It writes the top-level config and the full config with every key's starting
   value, creates the four directories, and refuses a directory that already holds an
   `orpheum.toml`.
5. **A backup is the server's: a tarball of `persistent/` in `backups/`.** A live `persistent.db`
   can be copied half-written, so the server takes the database's snapshot with `VACUUM INTO`
   (backup-restore.md) and tars it with the rest of `persistent/`. An admin makes one from the
   admin interface or the command line, and M4's scheduled backups make them too. Copying
   `persistent/` by hand is safe only with the server stopped. `secret.key` is left out unless the
   admin asks for it, for moving to another machine, as D194 §4 says: a backup with the key
   decrypts the sealed secrets, and a restore without it loses only those.

The owner agreed (2026-10-03, *"Agreed"*) to points 3's `run/`, 5's snapshot and the
key left out by default, and one instance directory over separate system directories; points 2 and
4 are the owner's stipulation.

6. **A node is an instance of its own** (the owner, 2026-10-03: *"The node should use its own
   instance"*). The top-level `orpheum.toml` says which kind an instance is, `core` or `node`;
   `orpheum core` refuses a node instance and `orpheum node` a core one. A node keeps no database,
   so its instance has `persistent/` (its full config), `cache/` (its prepared renditions, in
   `cache/prepared/`) and `run/` (its byte socket), and no `backups/`. `orpheum default-config
   <dir>` makes a core instance and `orpheum default-config --node <dir>` a node instance. The
   flag every subcommand takes is `--instance <dir>`.
7. **A core and a node find each other's sockets without sharing a directory.** The node's full
   config names the core's socket (`node.core_socket`, an absolute path): the node is the side
   that calls in. The node says where its byte socket is in its hello, as it says its roots, so
   the core needs no key per node. The keys the instance directories replace go:
   `server.data_dir`, `server.cache_dir`, `server.socket_dir` and `node.prepared_dir`. (Both
   agreed by the owner, 2026-10-03: *"Yes, go ahead"*.)

8. **A socket's path is short, so the run directory may live elsewhere.** A Unix socket's path is
   at most 103 bytes, which a deep instance directory can pass. `default-config` refuses such an
   instance before it makes anything, and `--run-dir <dir>` puts its run directory elsewhere, as
   the top-level config already allows. Not `/tmp`, which the owner suggested (*"maybe we should
   put them in tmp and use the config to point to them"*): anyone on the machine can create a
   file there, so another user could take the socket's path first. The owner agreed (2026-10-03,
   *"Ok go with your recommendation"*).

**Status:** Built 2026-10-03: the instance directory, `--instance` and `default-config`, the
node's own instance and its byte socket named in its hello (protocol 19), and `log.destination`
; the backup as a tarball of `persistent/`, restored from one, and made from the System
page. M4's scheduled backups make them too, when M4 builds them.

## D243 — M4's nine questions answered: a guest's cookie covers one film, invites are registration links under roles that choose libraries, the name's certificate comes by DNS-01 through Cloudflare, and a VPS carries every route in

> **Revised by [D263](#d263--the-acceptances-networks-are-realistic-links-emulated-without-artefacts-its-bounds-are-per-client-pair-and-the-server-sends-media-with-bbr)** (2026-10-07): §9's netem profiles are now home, mobile, congested and lossy as experts would build them, with bounds per client pair.

> **Revised by [D261](#d261--the-m4-audits-questions-answered)** (2026-10-07): §9's voice bounds are best effort on the congested profile;
> **and by [D263](#d263--the-acceptances-networks-are-realistic-links-emulated-without-artefacts-its-bounds-are-per-client-pair-and-the-server-sends-media-with-bbr)
> §2** (2026-10-07, confirmed by D270 §3): they hold on every profile again.

**Decided** (2026-10-04), by the project owner, answering D223 §11's nine questions as the audit
before M4 put them ([audit-2026-10-03.md](../design/research/audit-2026-10-03.md) §8):
*"Agreed on most of your recommendations"*, with notes on A4, A5, A7, A10 and B4, then
*"Everything except A4 sounds good"* and A4's shape set out below.

1. **An anonymous Watch Together guest** gets, on joining, a media cookie limited to the one film
   the session plays, for as long as the membership lasts: it moves when the film changes, and an
   ejection or the session's end revokes it at the next request. A guest never reaches the
   library (D122, D125).
2. **A signed-in guest's viewing** (D191): a device sends its membership credential in its first
   WebSocket `hello`, never in a header or a URL. A membership is a person's when any of its
   devices joined signed in, and the playing device's `state` reports are recorded as that
   person's spans. An anonymous membership records nothing.
3. **A join link's and an invite's secret travel after `#`**, as D218's registration link does:
   the page reads it, sends it in a body or the `hello`, and takes it out of the address bar.
4. **Library access is a role's** (D130), and an invite is a registration link (D218) for an
   outsider account (D174 §1) with a role. The owner: *"I'd want (b) right away before sharing
   with other households. I have personal stuff that I don't want shared."*
   - A role lists the libraries its members may browse and play, and the admin changes the list
     at any time.
   - **A library taken back is gone, not unavailable** (the owner: *"I want it to stop showing at
     all for them, immediately"*): every list, search, title, play and byte request checks
     access when it is made, and answers as if the library did not exist. A play from it stops
     at its next byte request. A Watch Together session still shows its guest the one film it
     plays, whatever the guest may browse (D122).
   - The check is one function of who is asking, so a later kind of caller (§5) is one more
     input, not a second mechanism.
   - A person has one role (D130), which is their whole access: the libraries they browse and
     play, and those ticked for rebroadcast (§5). The owner: *"I'm fine with only one role per user
     if it serves our purposes."* A mix of access no role has is a role of its own.
5. **Rebroadcasting is designed now and built later** (D174 §2; the owner: *"I don't need this
   functionality any time soon … I just want the design in place in case this affects how we
   structure the data architecture"*). A role's library may also be ticked *may rebroadcast*.
   Someone with that role may add the ticked libraries to their own Orpheum core, whose accounts
   then browse and play them beside its own libraries; they choose which and change it later.
   One hop only: a library a core got from another server can never be ticked on it. What it
   asks of the architecture, checked against the schema on 2026-10-04:
   - **Ids the API exposes are never reused and never hard-deleted.** True today (items, titles,
     files, editions and libraries use AUTOINCREMENT and tombstones, a merge leaves
     `merged_into`); `TestArch_IDsAreNeverGivenTwice` keeps it true (built 2026-10-04).
   - The other server is one more caller of §4's check: a `grant` of a new kind (D154), its scope
     the ticked libraries, with a ceiling on streams and bandwidth (F31), since its household
     shares this server's uplink.
   - On the rebroadcasting core, a file's location is either a path on one of its nodes or a
     file on another server, so its household's play state and overlay (its own tags and
     corrections, D174 §2) point at its own rows. Its bytes and prepared copies come from the
     source server's endpoints, made by the source's nodes.
   - Keeping its copy current needs a per-library feed of what changed; it is new protocol, not
     a change to the data. Taking a library back removes it there at the next sync.
6. **The HTTPS name** is `media.orpheum-app.com` (the owner registered `orpheum-app.com` at
   Cloudflare). Its certificate comes by ACME DNS-01: the core sets the TXT record through a
   Cloudflare API token scoped to *Zone → DNS → Edit* on that zone, kept as a sealed secret
   (D194). `golang.org/x/crypto/acme` (allowed) speaks ACME; the two Cloudflare calls are written
   on the standard library. The record is DNS only, never proxied: proxying would decrypt the
   traffic, carries no UDP, and Cloudflare's terms restrict video through it. The domain, the
   ACME contact and the HTTPS and TURN listen addresses are config keys.
7. **Reachability is a VPS** (the owner: *"I'll set up a VPS"*), Hetzner Cloud's smallest plan in
   Nuremberg or Falkenstein. The core's machine dials out to it over WireGuard, which works on
   DS-Lite and carries UDP; the VPS forwards TCP 443, TCP and UDP 3478 and the relay range into
   the tunnel, with replies routed back through it so the core sees each client's address. The
   name's A and AAAA records point at the VPS, so the home's changing IPv6 prefix does not matter.
8. **Embedded TURN**: port 3478, relay ports 49160–49199, credentials per membership that end
   with it, and the VPS's address as the relay's public address.
9. **Watch Together's numbers:** two clients within 200 ms of each other 95% of the time; voice
   one-way under 300 ms and audible loss under 2%; netem profiles *home* (20 ms, no loss),
   *mobile* (80 ± 30 ms, 1%) and *congested* (150 ± 50 ms, 3%, 5 Mbit/s); a session's cap two
   people by default, raised by its creator (D119). Now playing's stop reaches a player in the
   answer to its next play report, within one report interval (10 s).
10. **Dependencies:** `github.com/pion/turn` for the relay and `github.com/coder/websocket` for
    Watch Together, each to be added to `deps/go.allow` with its job; no certificate library.
11. **Backups are jobs:** one every 24 hours at a quiet hour and the last 14 kept, both settings;
    pre-restore and pre-migration copies are kept apart and never pruned. A scheduled backup never
    holds `secret.key`; the System page's *Back up now* keeps its checkbox for the key (the owner:
    *"I'd prefer to have a checkbox to include secret.key for the 'back up now' in the system
    page"*), and starts a job shown in the job view.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-04; built in M4, except §5, which waits for its own milestone, §2's recording, which waits with D246 §4, and §9's cap, which D246 removed ([M4's audit](../design/research/audit-2026-10-06.md)).

## D244 — The audit before M4's other questions: a kept failure is FFmpeg's alone, the System page shows what it promised, contract names are fixed now, and every request a click sends is safe to repeat

**Decided** (2026-10-04), by the project owner, on the audit before M4's remaining questions
([audit-2026-10-03.md](../design/research/audit-2026-10-03.md) §8): *"Agreed on most of your
recommendations"*, *"Everything except A4 sounds good"*.

1. **A loudness measurement that gave up is kept for good only when FFmpeg could not measure the
   file.** A refusal, a stall or a disk that went away is tried again by the next sweep, as a
   subtitle is by the next play (corrects D226 §2's built form and loudness's doc.go).
2. **The System page shows** D233 §8's queue health (per kind: queued, the oldest wait, failures in
   the last 24 hours; per node: slots in use and time since its last progress), D240 §5's reader
   limit for each device with its control, and D234 §4's broken invariants. Built before M4.
3. **The contract names the audit flagged are renamed now**, while formats change freely:
   `examineCount` → `toExamineCount`, `isScanAgain` → `isAnotherScanQueued`, the API's three
   `since` → `gaveUpAt`, `unavailableAt`, `notAnsweringAt`; config `node.min_free_mib` →
   `prepared_disk_min_free_mib`; settings `play_wanted_seconds` → `play_priority_kept_seconds`,
   `node_work_window_extra` → `node_jobs_beyond_free_slots`, `device_readers_*` →
   `*_reader_limit`, `scan_examine_batch_videos` → `scan_videos_per_examine_batch`,
   `new_library_scan_every_hours` → `new_library_default_scan_every_hours`; package `datadir` →
   `instancedir`.
4. **A request a click sends is safe to repeat** (the owner: *"we should have as many buttons
   debounced as is feasible. Idempotency is the ideal."*):
   - In the browser, every button that sends a request is disabled while it runs, through the one
     hook that runs requests (`useRequest`), with a check that none goes round it.
   - On the server, a request that sets a value is already idempotent. A request that creates
     something carries an `Idempotency-Key` the browser makes per click; the server keeps each
     key's first answer for some minutes and gives it to a repeat. Where the data allows, a
     unique index holds it as well: S90, one download per file and subtitle.
5. **M3's last device checks** (VQ9, VQ14, VQ15) are carried into M4; none changes M4's design.
6. **Phases 5 and 6's open deviations:** a stall on the prepared directory's disk is blamed on
   that disk, not the media root, and a job failed by `assigned_job_limit_hours` tells its node
   to stop: both fixed before M4. A prepare on a node gone silent parks, and a repointed root's
   parked work is asked for again when needed: both accepted.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-04; built before M4's first feature.

## D245 — Cut A ends with a polished, skinned web UI built on research, and the remote TV comes right after it

**Decided** (2026-10-05), by the project owner, while M4 was being built: *"I no longer need the
TV playback (M5) so soon. She can just watch from her laptop at first while we work the kinks
out, so cut A will be us on proper web browsers."* And: *"The big thing we need before she starts
using it is proper UX, with a skinned UI."* **Revises** cut-a's milestones: the remote TV, M5,
leaves Cut A, and a polished UI takes its place.

1. **Cut A is two households on proper web browsers.** The remote person watches on her laptop's
   browser. Voice is still tested as Watch Together's companion: her phone's browser carries
   voice while the computer's browser plays (watch-together.md's voice companion, D120). The
   remote TV (D188's table, the cast receiver, "Get this ready") comes right after Cut A; the
   owner still wants it.
2. **Cut A is not finished until the UI is polished**, with one skin: *"I don't need multiple
   skins (only one is fine)."* It is the new M5; the remote TV becomes the first milestone after
   Cut A.
3. **Research comes first**, and it covers:
   - best practices for user interfaces, above all a media server's;
   - what our competitors do, and what people say about their interfaces;
   - what the web ecosystem does now, contrasted with the practices that served maintainability
     and ease of development before it: the owner, *"It used to be that you'd make a number of
     common components and then re-use them, with the UI subsystem making sure layout flowed
     consistently, so that you didn't have to manually fiddle with one part of the UI just to make
     another unrelated part look right. And then that was all thrown out as JS and HTML became
     popular, and we lost over a decade re-learning those lessons (and I'm not sure if we've
     re-learned them all yet)"*; and the lessons to take wherever today's practice still falls
     short.
4. **Then a UI principles document**, and every standard that touches the UI is revisited
   against it.
5. **The design is iterative, so the UI's architecture stays supple**, at least at first: the
   look is changed often, and a change to one part must not need fiddling with another.
6. **When:** whenever it is convenient; it does not wait for M4 to end, and Cut A does not end
   without it.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-05; the research is the next step, then the principles, then the build.

## D246 — What a person may do is their role's, an invite names who it is for, and a Watch Together viewer is an ephemeral account that sees only the host's playback

> **Revised by [D271](#d271--m5s-first-questions-answered-four-browsers-no-user-facing-theming-or-light-palette-and-guests-who-may-pause-and-seek-unless-the-host-withholds-it)** (2026-10-09): §8's host-only control is revised: a guest may play and pause and change the position unless the host withholds it in the invite.

> **Revised by [D261](#d261--the-m4-audits-questions-answered)** (2026-10-07): §4's signed-in guest history is deferred as a nice-to-have, no longer in M4's acceptance.

> **§3–§5 refined by [D267](#d267--a-watch-together-membership-is-kept-by-the-browser-that-joined-or-by-the-account-of-whoever-is-signed-in-and-one-member-may-be-on-several-devices)** (2026-10-08): a guest's membership is kept by their browser, a signed-in person's follows their account, one member may be on several devices, and §4's signed-in recipient is brought forward for the session alone.

**Decided** (2026-10-05), by the project owner, reviewing M4's Phases A, B and E as built, and
answering the three questions that review left (§7–§9). **Revises**
[D121](#d121--an-ability-is-a-row-in-a-closed-table-with-a-two-valued-grant-chosen-at-session-creation),
[D174](#d174--sharing-is-an-account-from-outside-the-house-a-household-behind-a-grantee-is-a-rebroadcast-grant-deferred-and-it-makes-another-server-a-source)
§1, [D218](#d218--accounts-the-admin-creates-a-person-who-sets-a-password-from-a-one-time-link-a-signed-in-person-adds-a-tv-by-a-short-safe32-code)
§1–§2, [D119](#d119--a-join-link-admits-membership-is-what-persists-rotation-is-seamless-ejection-is-owner-only-and-a-cap-bounds-the-leak),
[D125](#d125--access-is-role-based-with-two-roles-a-watch-together-guest-is-not-a-principal)'s
"a guest is not a principal", and
[D243](#d243--m4s-nine-questions-answered-a-guests-cookie-covers-one-film-invites-are-registration-links-under-roles-that-choose-libraries-the-names-certificate-comes-by-dns-01-through-cloudflare-and-a-vps-carries-every-route-in)
§1, §2, §4, §9's session cap and §11.

1. **No "outsider" kind of account.** The owner: *"Can't the capabilities (see other members,
   downloads, etc) be attached to a role so that the admin can choose his own granularity? We
   could provide templates later (family, extended family, friends, guest, etc) if the number of
   knobs grows too much. I see this as more of the same kinds of questions that guard access to
   the family videos."* Everything D174 §1's table set apart for an outsider is a capability of
   a role, added with the feature it governs: seeing other members and their activity, a
   download's lease, a ceiling. `is_outsider` goes. Nothing in Cut A shows one person's activity
   to another but the admin's pages, so no new capability is needed yet. Role templates are
   later.
2. **How an account is made does not depend on who it is for.** For anyone, the admin either
   sets the account up in full (a name, a password and a role) or issues an **invite link** for
   the person to fill in their own name and password, under a role the admin chose. An invite
   carries a **note only the admin sees**, which the admin must write, saying who it was meant
   for (*"Uncle Joe", "Grandma", "The creepy guy from the bus station"*), so that once the person
   has filled in their own details the admin can tell who is who. The note stays with the
   account. A forgotten password is still a new registration link (D218 §5).
3. **A Watch Together viewer is an ephemeral account**, the one place a link alone admits
   someone. It shares much with a full account, but its hidden built-in role, which cannot be
   edited, is restricted to the playback screen: no browsing, no library, and no control of
   playback. It lasts as long as the session. The admin writes a note for each link, seen only
   by the admin; the viewer chooses a name or handle that the others see.
4. **A link's recipient already signed in on the server** may later be pre-filled with their own
   details and have their viewing recorded (D243 §2 waits for this). Later too: avatars; and
   inviting registered members directly, the invitation an in-app notification and a button on
   their home page, with no link.
5. **The session is the host's.** The host starts and stops it. While it is active the host
   browses the library as usual, and the viewers see none of it. When the host plays a video it
   plays on every participant's screen; when the host stops it, their screens go black again.
   The host can play a film, let it end, browse to another and play that, or watch a series and
   go on to the next episode as usual (auto-next too, once it exists). A viewer sees only the
   playback screen and the session's own controls: their own volume, the text chat once it
   exists, and **Leave**.
6. **A viewer chooses their speaker setup as soon as they join**, unless they already have one
   (D184), not when a video is about to start, and **no one waits for it**: once a viewer is
   ready, they start wherever the group's playback is; until something plays, the viewing area
   is black.
7. **Backups are every *x* days at *y* o'clock** (D243 §11 had hours), *y* in the server's time
   zone: a setting, an IANA name such as `Europe/Berlin`, so a change of clocks for summer time is
   followed. Anything else the server schedules by the clock uses it too, and a setting in it says
   so in its key (`backup_hour_local_tz`; the owner: *"so that we know the units and offset"*).
   Until the admin chooses one it is the machine's own (the owner: *"it's OK to default to the ENV
   timezone if the user hasn't selected one. That's an acceptable use of ambient config because
   it's only affecting the default, in a way that favors user friendliness"*), the one exception
   to [D204](#d204--no-ambient-configuration-the-shipped-binary-is-configured-by-its-config-file-its-flags-and-its-database-and-by-nothing-it-inherits):
   `cmd/orpheum` reads TZ, else `/etc/localtime`, once at start, and passes the zone down
   explicitly (the owner: *"ENV vars are taken at the EDGE of our system. Once inside our system
   everything gets passed explicitly, not via ENV (unless it's impossible to do otherwise)"*). The
   process's own zone stays UTC whatever
   the setting says, so nothing in the standard library that reads it gives a "works for me"
   bug: the owner, *"keep the official env time zone UTC so that ambient config doesn't pollute
   parts of the go stdlib that rely on it."* Wall-clock time is reached only through a
   `localtime.Zone`, each conversion explicit and its result a type of its own (the owner:
   *"make the conversion points between them explicit. Perhaps even enlisting the type system"*).
8. **In Cut A only the host controls playback**; D121's choice between the host and the group
   goes. Later the rights become granular, given per invite link: play and pause, seek, next and
   previous, and the like. The rights of the last link issued are the next one's defaults, and
   the first link's are every right.
9. *(Superseded by D250 §2: the group never stops for one member.)* **When a viewer stalls, everyone waits** for them in Cut A, as watch-together.md's Sync
   already has it. What is best for more people is open; the owner: *"The problem comes when one
   member stalls and the rest move on, and then the one member missed a crucial point. But then
   again someone could just rewind..."*

> **Revised by [D364](#d364--casting-is-a-session-with-a-device-while-it-lasts-whatever-the-person-plays-plays-there-and-the-sending-device-shows-it-in-the-tray)** (2026-10-27): leaving the film no longer stops it for the group (§5's stop on leaving is withdrawn): Stop on the session's page, or the host playing another film, ends it; the session's page holds the film's controls.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-05; built in M4 in place of what it revises, except §4, later by decision.
