## D247 — A slow link gets a lower version made at its first stall and played from its second, and a group waits for a stalled viewer once, then lets them catch up alone

> **§4's group wait superseded by [D371](#d371--a-session-has-a-leader-that-plays-as-a-device-plays-alone-everyone-else-catches-up-to-it-and-a-cast-takes-its-senders-part)** (2026-10-28): no group waits for anyone but its leader; a stalled follower catches up to the leader.

> **§9 amended by [D352](#d352--the-chunked-player-trusts-its-link-as-far-as-the-evidence-goes-its-first-seconds-latch-nothing-it-climbs-as-far-as-consistent-samples-carry-and-it-grows-steadier-when-it-swings-or-its-link-flakes)** (2026-10-27): the hold before a step up is 30 s on a steady link, doubling with each swing to 240 s, and the climb goes as far as consistent samples carry.

> **§10 revised by [D309](#d309--a-player-says-which-quality-it-wants-and-from-where-and-a-run-no-player-wants-stops)** (2026-10-17): a run goes on while a player says it wants its quality from where it plays, not while asks arrive.

> **Revised by [D260](#d260--a-film-plays-from-its-ladder-of-qualities-from-the-start-filled-on-its-page-and-its-player-keeps-choosing-as-it-plays)** (2026-10-07): **a film that can be cut plays from its ladder from the start**, at its top unless its link is remembered slow; §2's original-first and stall-made version remain for a film not cut yet.

> **Superseded in part by [D253](#d253--a-stalled-player-is-told-of-its-lower-version-at-its-first-stall-and-moves-to-it-once-it-is-ready-if-it-still-cannot-keep-up)** (2026-10-07): **the version is played from when it is ready, not from a second stall.** The first stall still makes it, and its answer now offers it; a player moves once it is ready if it still cannot keep up (§2, §10 below).

**Decided** (2026-10-05), by the project owner, after the first Watch Together test and the
research it prompted ([slow-links.md](../design/research/slow-links.md)). **Revises**
[D246](#d246--what-a-person-may-do-is-their-roles-an-invite-names-who-it-is-for-and-a-watch-together-viewer-is-an-ephemeral-account-that-sees-only-the-hosts-playback)
§9, and Cut A's "no ladder" in
[D86](#d86--adaptation-is-the-client-re-picking-on-a-buffer-signal-and-it-puts-bandwidth-transcoding-on-remote-accesss-critical-path)
and [D193](#d193--the-audits-proposals-are-accepted-the-node-does-all-media-work-prepare-is-the-one-path-besides-direct-play-the-machinery-is-cut-and-cut-as-design-freezes)
§2. The owner: *"Cut A was just a guess at what we'd need for my gf and I to use this for real.
The design was not intended to become inflexible in the face of reality."*

The test: the host on mobile data, the film 2.4 Mbps, the only rendition the remux. Alone it
paused often; in the group it played a frame and froze, over and over.

1. **No separate speed test.** The owner asked for one before playback. No production player runs
   one; the servers that do (Jellyfin, Emby) have had bugs in theirs for years and their
   maintainers advise turning them off (slow-links.md §2). The player measures the film's own
   segments as they arrive, which hls.js already does, and starts cautiously.
2. **The original plays first; a lower version is made at a viewer's first stall, and played from
   their second** (its mechanism is §10). The owner: *"It should try the original version first"*, and *"The moment a
   client stalls for the first time, we begin preparing the alternative streams in case it stalls
   again."* At the first stall, prepare starts a lower version in the background from where the
   film is, at a bitrate the player's own measurement of the original's download says the link
   carries (§1). It is encoded faster than the film plays, so it is ahead of the viewer within
   seconds. At a second stall the player changes over to it at its position. **A stall is also a
   load, the first or a seek's, that leaves the player unable to play for 15 s, once for each 15 s,
   and a Watch Together player that falls behind its group and seeks to catch up** (the owner's
   choice, 2026-10-05): a player on a link too slow to start never stalled while playing, and a
   follower catching up only ever loads, so neither was offered a lower version. The changeover is
   not seamless (a plain file and a segmented stream cannot be swapped without rebuilding the
   player), but it falls inside a stall that is happening anyway. The version is kept as a cache
   ([D169](#d169--a-lease-is-indefinite-by-default-expiry-is-a-property-of-a-conditional-relationship-and-the-servers-prepared-rendition-is-a-cache-rather-than-a-referent)),
   so a later play has it ready. A film already playing as a prepared rendition (its sound or
   container needed one) gets the same: a lower version at the first stall, the change at the
   second.
3. **The change is automatic, and the player shows which quality is playing.** Variants aligned on
   the source's keyframes in one playlist, switched by hls.js without a pause
   ([transcoding.md](../design/plans/transcoding.md) §(b)), remain the later refinement.
4. *(Superseded by D250 §2–§5: the group never stops for one member, and a catch-up aims at an 80%
   full buffer from the run already making its quality.)* **A stalled viewer holds the group once, then catches up alone** (Silo-Server's design,
   slow-links.md §5). A stall pauses the group only if that viewer has not stalled in the last
   5 minutes and the group has not waited for anyone in the last minute. Otherwise the others play
   on and the viewer catches up by itself, its seek aimed ahead by its last load time. A wait
   ends after 10 s for a re-buffer, or 60 s for a first load, and the group is told who it is
   continuing without. A viewer still loading gets no corrections. This answers the owner's worry
   in D246 §9, that a viewer who falls behind misses a crucial point, in the way that fits two
   people: a single hiccup costs no one anything, and only someone who stalls again and again
   skips ahead, by then usually on a lower variant (§2). The numbers are Silo's, to be measured.
   **The host's own seek is waited for as long as a first load, for the host** (the owner's
   choice, 2026-10-05, after a forward jump on a slow link left the host behind): the host chose
   where to go, so the others wait up to 60 s for the host's player to load there, and 10 s for
   anyone else's. A seek is the group's as the host makes it, not once it has loaded; each player
   is ready again only once it says so from the new place, its loading there is no stall, and one
   catching up is waited for again.
   **Amended** (2026-10-06), by the owner, watching a viewer on a 3 Mb/s link through Apple's
   Private Relay see one still frame every few seconds while she caught up alone: *"What about
   making her side jump slightly ahead of the group and wait so that her buffer has more time to
   fill by the time it has to play again?"* A viewer catching up alone jumps further ahead than
   its last load time: far enough that, at its link's measured speed, it can load refillAheadMs
   (§5) before the group gets there, up to what its player buffers ahead. It waits there, paused
   and loading, without holding anyone up, and plays when the group reaches it, with a full buffer
   rather than a thin one. The host's player does the same when it falls behind: the owner, *"I
   think that the host should also jump ahead if he's having those kinds of difficulties."* Its
   pause to wait there is not a command, and the group plays on.
5. **A stalled player is ready again only with 10 s loaded ahead** (built on 2026-10-05,
   `refillAheadMs`), not at its first frame, which was the loop.

   **Refined by D283 §1** (2026-10-12): after a seek, on a link that carries the film well faster than
   it plays, 3 s.

6. **The lower versions are a fixed set of standard qualities**, about 3 Mbps at 720p, 2 Mbps at
   540p, 1.2 Mbps at 480p and 0.7 Mbps at 432p (Apple's authoring spec's low rungs, to be tuned on
   the owner's films). A stall chooses the highest one within about 70% of the speed the player
   measured. The owner: *"Have a set of standard bitrates that can be chosen. When a client fails,
   we use the bandwidth situation to choose from those bitrates and begin transcoding."* Our own
   encodes cap their peaks, which the original's do not. **The list is a setting**, each quality
   its bit rate and picture height, which the admin can change; the numbers above are its starting
   value. The owner: *"Those standard qualities should be a list in config rather than
   hard-coded."*
   **Amended** (2026-10-06), by the owner, after a viewer on an airplane's Wi-Fi measured 0.6 Mb/s
   against a lowest quality that needed 0.9 Mb/s with its sound: a fifth quality, 0.4 Mbps at 360p,
   is added to the starting list, and the sound of a film cut into chunks is 96 kb/s, a setting
   (`chunk_sound_kbps`), where it was 192 kb/s, a quarter of her link.
7. **A version is the film at a quality, shared by every viewer.** One another viewer's stall
   already started is used if it is within the viewer's measured speed and not far from what would
   have been chosen: the same quality, or the one below it. The owner: *"If a client stalls, and
   another client has already stalled and triggered a lower bitrate transcode, we just use that if
   it's within bandwidth capability and not too far off from what we would have chosen
   otherwise."*
8. **A stall on a lower version steps down again**, chosen afresh from the measured speed, not one
   step at a time. **At the bottom, the person is told it will not work**: a stall at the lowest
   quality, or a measured speed below what it needs, says so with both numbers, and in Watch
   Together the group is told too. The owner: *"At a certain point the quality will be so bad that
   we're probably better off telling the user this won't work."*
   **Amended** (2026-10-06), by the owner, after a player on a 98 Mb/s link was told it could not
   keep up with the 892 kb/s quality: a stall at the lowest quality says so only when the link was
   not measured, or was measured below 1.5× what that quality needs, the margin a step up needs
   (§9). A stall on a link well above it is something else's doing, such as falling behind a
   group that held, and no quality answers it; the player's stall reports carry the link's speed.
9. **A viewer steps back up when the link has recovered with confidence**: the speed measured
   while chunks download (never across the pauses between them, which read slow) stays at about
   1.5× the next quality's rate for a couple of minutes, with a healthy buffer, and the step is one
   quality at a time. The owner asked: *"Is there a way to detect that the network situation has
   improved (with good confidence) and then step them back up?"*
10. **Every quality, the original's own picture among them, is cut into chunks at the source's
    keyframes and listed in one playlist**, so hls.js switches between them without a pause
    ([transcoding.md](../design/plans/transcoding.md) §(b), Kyoo's design in slow-links.md §4). A
    chunk is made when a player first asks for it and kept, so a seek, a viewer joining mid-film
    and a stall all start encoding where they are. A film still starts from the original file
    (§2); the first stall starts the chosen quality where the viewer is, and the second moves the
    player into the chunked playlist, once, with a short pause; every step after it is seamless.
    This replaces §3's "later refinement". The build plan is
    [chunks.md](../design/plans/chunks.md).
11. **Nothing detects whether a viewer is at home or away.** The owner: *"I'd avoid detecting a
    home network or lan. If it's a high bandwidth local network, none of this machinery should
    trigger unless there's a real problem (such as flaky wifi)."* The playback request's
    `network` goes, and with it the remote bitrate ceiling that chose `h264-8m` for a large file
    played away (cut-a.md §6); the only signals are the speed a player measures and its stalls.
    A slow film over flaky Wi-Fi at home is treated as one away.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-05; built in M4, §4 superseded by D250.

## D248 — Lost work never counts against a film, a crash in one job ends only that job, and a person's play tries again whatever failed before

**Decided** (2026-10-05 and 06), by the project owner, after films on devnas were marked failed
for good because the dev loop restarted the node while it read them through ("the tool failed on
two attempts in a row: node 1 does not hold read_through job 12"), and the owner asked whether
FFmpeg could crash the node and have other crashes blamed on the film.

1. **Lost work is never the file's failure.** A node that no longer holds work it was given
   (it started again, or its status no longer lists the work) says nothing of the file: an update,
   a power cut, the machine's memory running out and a bug in the node's own code lose work as
   surely as a file does, and FFmpeg failing on a file is reported as FFmpeg's failure, never as
   work lost. Lost work is an attempt like any other's failure, tried again after the retry delay;
   a job its node loses on every attempt fails at the end of its attempts as the job's alone, kept
   as no file's failure, and a sweep queues it again. This revises D233 §6 and D238 §3, under
   which a second tool failure in a row was the target's.
2. **A crash in one job ends that job, not the node.** The node recovers a panic in any job's work,
   logs it with its stack, and says so to the core (`Result.Crashed`); the core takes it as a
   failed attempt, tried again, never the file's. The work's FFmpeg is stopped with it.
3. **FFmpeg is the first the kernel kills when memory runs out.** The shim raises the tool's
   `oom_score_adj` to 1000 before it becomes FFmpeg, so a film that drives FFmpeg's memory up fails
   FFmpeg on that film, which is kept as FFmpeg's failure, and the node and every other job go on.
   No hard limit: FFmpeg's threads reserve address space a limit would refuse.
4. **A person's play tries again whatever failed before they pressed play** (the owner: *"If the
   user has an option to play a video, we should be making every attempt to make that happen"*).
   A kept failure stops background work from trying a file again; a play is the highest priority
   there is, and tries once more: a prepared copy that failed is prepared again, a subtitle track
   that could not be made is made again (both did already), and a picture whose read-through failed
   is read through again for a lower quality (D247). Only a failure on the attempt the play made is
   the one the person sees.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-06; built in M4.


## D249 — Three ways to run: dev as it is, staging from the checkout beside it, and release from a tagged image; the tunnel is a container of the deployment's own

> **Built out by [D272](#d272--production-runs-on-naslan-from-an-image-it-builds-and-migrations-keep-every-step-since-the-version-it-last-ran)** (2026-10-09): release mode runs on nas.example from an image built there, set up by the image's own command; the name swaps between staging and nas.example.

**Decided** (2026-10-06), by the project owner, setting up the VPS of D243 §7 and finding the
deployment it fronts unbuilt: *"Yes. I want to test deployment. Ideally we'd have dev mode, staging
mode (which I'll test as soon as it's ready), and release mode. There are no real users yet, and
won't be until I give the go ahead."* Then, on the proposal: staging beside dev on devnas, starting
fresh when the schema changed, built from the checkout; release designed now and built later; and
*"Should wireguard be done on my host, or is it better inside of the container?"*, answered: in a
container. It builds D235 §2 and §4, and revises D243 §7's core end of the tunnel.

1. **Dev** is the dev loop as it is: `./dev make dev`, the development image, Vite, the seed, plain
   HTTP, no tunnel.
2. **Staging and release are one deployment**, D235 §4's: a runtime image (D235 §2's base: Debian
   and the pinned FFmpeg, plus the binary with the web client in it, run as a non-root user) and one
   compose file with three services from it:
   - `orpheum-tunnel`: the core's end of the WireGuard tunnel to the VPS, with Debian's
     wireguard-tools in the runtime image (no third-party image), `CAP_NET_ADMIN` and nothing more.
     Nothing is installed or configured on the host: its kernel's WireGuard is all it needs.
   - `orpheum-core`: shares the tunnel's network, so what came in through the tunnel is answered
     back through it with no routing rules on the host. The tunnel is not that network's default
     route: the core's own requests, and its answers to the house's network, leave the house's own
     way; only what leaves from the tunnel's addresses goes back through it, as D243 §7 routes it.
     *(Amended the same day, in building it: the first text sent the core's outbound requests
     through the VPS too, which would have sent its answers to the house's network into the tunnel.)* HTTPS on :443 and TURN on the tunnel's address, as D243 §6 and §8 say, and plain HTTP
     on a port published to the house's network, for the LAN.
   - `orpheum-node`: the media read-only and `/dev/dri`; the core's socket on a volume both share
     (D235 §4).
3. **Staging is built from the checkout, beside dev.** One command on devnas, `./staging`, builds the
   binary in the development image, builds the runtime image from it, and starts or restarts the
   compose stack; after `yoloai apply`, it is run again. Its data is a directory of its own, apart
   from `.dev/`, and its ports never clash with dev's (8432, 5173). Its configs are rendered on
   every start from templates and one file of the owner's values (the name, the contact address,
   the VPS's address and key, the media), as dev's are. It is set up as a person meets a new server:
   the first-run setup with the code in its log, then libraries by hand.
4. **Staging starts fresh when its database cannot be brought forward.** Until migrations are live
   (D228), a schema change folds the last step into the baseline, and a staging database that missed
   two changes is below it, which the core refuses. Staging's core config says to start over then:
   it sets the old database aside, starts with an empty one, and says so in its log. Release's says
   to refuse, as D228 and D181 do.
5. **Release is designed, not built.** The same image and compose file, the image built by
   GoReleaser from a tagged version and pulled from a registry (D235 §5), the config written once by
   the admin, migrations live, and refusing what it cannot migrate. Built when the owner nears the
   go-ahead for real users; until then there are none.

**Amended** (2026-10-06, the same day), by the project owner, once Watch Together had kept up on
devnas: *"what if we just made media.orpheum-app.com point to you for now during early development
and left staging.orpheum-app.com for later?"* Until there is a staging server, the staging stack
runs in the agent's sandbox, the VPS's one peer, behind `media.orpheum-app.com`, so a change is
tried on the real name without the owner applying it first; devnas leaves the tunnel. One VPS
address can front only one machine's TURN, so a second name waits for a second address or VPS. The
agent does the first-run setup and sets the DNS token, which the owner hands over through the
sandbox's shared files and the agent deletes once set; the admin's password goes back the same way.
§3's "beside dev on devnas" holds for running staging on a machine of the owner's later.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-06; staging built the same day (deploy/staging, ./staging), release later.

## D250 — A Watch Together group stops only at its own sync points: a member's trouble is theirs to catch up on, from what is already being made

> **§2 and §3, with §2's amendments of 2026-10-12 and 2026-10-28, superseded by [D371](#d371--a-session-has-a-leader-that-plays-as-a-device-plays-alone-everyone-else-catches-up-to-it-and-a-cast-takes-its-senders-part)** (2026-10-28): the group waits for no one but its leader, the screen that is the film, whose position is the group's; there are no sync waits, no `together_sync_wait_seconds` (retired), and a player's stall or drop is a follower's to catch up on, or, the leader's, holds the group where the leader stands. §1, §4 and §5 stand: how a follower corrects and catches up.

> **§5 and §6 revised by [D309](#d309--a-player-says-which-quality-it-wants-and-from-where-and-a-run-no-player-wants-stops)** (2026-10-17): a run no player wants stops at once, with no rule of distance; under load a player moves down a quality, and only one at the lowest is stopped.

> **Revised by [D261](#d261--the-m4-audits-questions-answered)** (2026-10-07): the drift left alone is 150 ms by default, not 500 (§1).

> **§1 refined by [D268](#d268--a-watch-together-player-corrects-drift-as-its-device-measures-it-places-its-group-by-recent-pongs-starts-at-a-moment-the-server-names-and-its-hosts-moves-are-taken-at-the-controls) §2** (2026-10-08): a player whose rate's returns cost it more than the drift left alone corrects by seeks alone, beyond `together_seek_only_drift_left_alone_ms` (400 ms by default).

**Decided** (2026-10-06), by the project owner, after a viewer on an iPhone at an airport found the
film unwatchable on a link fast enough for her quality, and after the research of
[playback-in-practice.md](../design/research/playback-in-practice.md): *"I don't think we should be
stopping the group at all when someone has problems. Let their client try to catch up by whatever
means. We only do a full pause+sync up when the movie starts, when the host pauses then plays, and
when the host jumps playback to a new position using the scrubber."* It supersedes D246 §9 and
D247 §4 and its amendment, and revises D247 §8 and §10.

1. **Drift is corrected gently, by numbers kept in the database.** Drift up to 500 ms is left
   alone (it was 60 ms); beyond it, the rate is nudged by at most 10% of the group's (it was 0.5× to
   2×); beyond the seek threshold (3 s, unchanged), the player seeks. All three are settings, sent
   to every device of a session, so they are tuned while testing. The owner: *"I'm fine with
   loosening the drift numbers. 10% max speed drift also sounds fine. Make them db values so we can
   tweak as we're testing."*
2. **The group never stops for one member.** A stall, a slow link or a dropped connection is that
   member's alone: the group plays on, and their player catches up by itself (§4). The host's
   player is a member's here too. The group waits for its players only at its three sync points:
   a film put on (or started over), the host's play after a pause, and the host's seek.

   **Amended 2026-10-12**, after the owner, watching alone in a session, lost 40 s of link to
   staging: the group played on without their player, the only one, and when the link came back
   it jumped 75 s ahead to catch up. Told so, the owner: *"Fix the bugs."* When no other player
   plays along, a player's stall or drop holds the group where it was, waiting (event
   `waitingFor`) until a player is ready, past the sync wait; a waiting group never starts to no
   one. With another player along, the group plays on as above.

   **Amended 2026-10-28**, for a session of one (a cast, D364): asked *"Should a session whose only
   player never gets ready start anyway once its deadline passes?"*, the owner: *"yes"*. When the
   session's only player is not ready as its wait's time (§3) is up, the group plays all the same
   (event `continuedWithout`), the player catching up as it plays, and the group follows that
   player, catching up or not, as it follows a session's only player while it plays (D88), so it
   never runs on ahead of the one watching. A session with more than one player keeps the rule
   above: with none ready, it waits on past its time.
3. **A sync point waits at most 20 s**, a setting: then the group plays, and whoever is not ready
   catches up alone. The owner: *"30 seconds is too long. Let's start at 20."*
4. **A member catching up jumps ahead and waits there**, as D247 §4's amendment had it, aiming to
   have its buffer 80% full by the time the group reaches it: far enough ahead that, at the speed
   it measured itself loading, it loads 80% of what its player buffers ahead before the group
   arrives. The fraction is a setting. The owner: *"Ideally adaptable based on how much the client
   is ready to buffer [...] We just want to target an 80% full buffer by the time the group's
   playback catches up."*
5. **Catching up never starts an encode.** A member who jumps ahead waits for the run already
   making its quality to get there, and fills from there. Only a seek starts a run where it lands:
   the host's in a session, or a person's own when watching alone. The owner: *"Otherwise if we
   have multiple people needing to drop down, and start playing catch up, we could quickly end up
   with a lot of transcodes."* A chunk not made yet is answered at once with "ask again", not held:
   a held request is counted by hls.js as a slow download (playback-in-practice.md §3).

   **Refined by D284 §2** (2026-10-12): a request a player says a jump took it to starts a run
   20 s past where one makes; a catch-up's still waits.

   **Amended 2026-10-12**, after the owner's jump back in a three-device session stuck everyone: a
   seek far back from a store's run cancels it, as one far past it did, since the run a seek left
   ran on and took the node's room; and a run is in use (§6) when a player asks for its own chunks
   or those a minute before them, not for any of its quality's, so a quality still played elsewhere
   no longer keeps a run no one follows from being the one evicted.
6. **A run must stay faster than playback.** *"If 480p runs at 0.8×, it's by definition an
   impossible situation. Live transcoding only works when it's faster than playback."* The core
   watches each run's speed. When one more run brings any below 1.1× (a setting), it evicts a run:
   the oldest no one is playing from, or, when every one is in use, the newest. Whoever is left
   without their chunks by that is told why their playback stops.
7. **Older Safari** is supported according to market share, researched before it is built: where
   native HLS can be made to follow the group, it is used; else the non-native player is made to
   work. The owner: *"depending on the market share we may simply opt to not support them, pending
   an ios app."*

   **Amended 2026-10-06**, after [safari-versions.md](../design/research/safari-versions.md): the
   floor is **iOS and iPadOS 17.1**, the first an iPhone runs hls.js on (ManagedMediaSource), about
   95.6% of iPhone traffic. Native HLS is not made to follow the group. A browser that cannot run
   hls.js is told, before it joins or starts a session, that it cannot keep in step and to update.
   The test is the player's own (`Hls.isSupported()`), never the User-Agent; watching alone still
   falls back to native HLS. Every supported Apple device then runs the same player, so the
   follower's Safari care (a frozen `currentTime` after play, seek and rate changes) is one set of
   rules. The owner: *"I'll have her update her phone when she lands, so we can set the floor to
   ios 17.1."*

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-06; §7 amended the same day; §2 and §5 amended 2026-10-12; §2 amended
again 2026-10-28.

## D251 — The web client's first skin is dark, with one coral accent, the system typeface and slightly rounded corners

> **Revised by [D271](#d271--m5s-first-questions-answered-four-browsers-no-user-facing-theming-or-light-palette-and-guests-who-may-pause-and-seek-unless-the-host-withholds-it)** (2026-10-09): §1's later light palette is dropped; the app is dark throughout.

**Decided** (2026-10-06), by the project owner, ahead of a week of demonstrating Orpheum one to
one, mostly on a phone, Watch Together above all (a guest scans the host's QR code and joins). It
answers four of the open questions of
[ui-design-practice-2026-10-05.md](../design/research/ui-design-practice-2026-10-05.md) §5.3 and
starts D245's skin without its restructuring: *"Let's start with tier 1 and see what it looks like
before deciding to go further. Dark theme, pick an accent color that looks nice, use the system
font, and use slightly rounded corners."*

1. **Dark only, for now** (§5.3 question 1): near-black (now the logo's `#0e0f14`, item 6), surfaces lighter as they rise,
   true black only behind video. A light palette is a later set of token values, not a redesign.
2. **One accent, coral** (`#ffa891`, question 2, chosen by the owner from six shown side by side,
   then a lighter shade of it, from five, so links and the dark text on buttons read easily):
   the primary action, the current place in the menu, progress and range controls. Text on it is
   near-black. Amber came first and was dropped as *"too close to Plex"*; teal next, as *"ugly"*;
   then the owner: *"I like coral."* A problem is crimson (`#ff4d6d`), a hue apart, so it never
   reads as the accent.
3. **The system typeface** (question 3), on one type scale with two weights.
4. **Slightly rounded** (question 7): 6 pixels for cards and art, 4 for controls.
5. **What it covers ("tier 1")**: the tokens (palette, a 4-pixel spacing scale, type scale,
   radii, shadows), the look of plain elements everywhere (`base.css`: buttons, fields, tables,
   fieldsets, a form's submit as the primary button), the poster grid, the title page, the sign-in
   and join card, the Watch Together screens and the jobs list; and on a phone, the menu as one
   row that scrolls sideways. Then, the same day, the menu split: the places for watching in view,
   an admin's pages under Manage, the person's under their name. Home, layout primitives and the
   one-pass migration (ui-architecture-2026-10-05.md R1–R9) stay M5's.
6. **The owner's logo is the product's mark** (2026-10-06): the wordmark, its laurel standing in
   for the O, heads the banner, the sign-in and join card and a guest's session page; the laurel is
   the favicon, the home-screen icon and the web manifest's icon. The page takes the logo's own
   colours: its dark ground `#0e0f14` as the background, its ivory `#f3eee4` as the text, its coral
   laurel as the accent. The wordmark is outlined Poiret One, under the SIL Open Font License,
   whose text travels with it (`web/apps/web/src/assets/orpheum-logo-FONT-LICENSE-OFL.txt`).
7. **A title with no poster** shows a subdued, open clapperboard (the owner: *"Maybe a subdued
   clapboard?"*), and a file's path and streams are under a closed File details: *"Details like the
   full path to the filename should be in a normally collapsed view."*

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-06.

## D252 — M4's acceptance shapes each client's network with the kernel's netem, in a run of its own at the milestone's end

> **Revised by [D263](#d263--the-acceptances-networks-are-realistic-links-emulated-without-artefacts-its-bounds-are-per-client-pair-and-the-server-sends-media-with-bbr)** (2026-10-07): each profile is netem plus a tbf bottleneck on a 1500-byte loopback, in-order jitter, and competing traffic under congested.

> **Revised by [D261](#d261--the-m4-audits-questions-answered)** (2026-10-07): §2's short home run is in every branch check, CI's container allowed NET_ADMIN.

**Decided** (2026-10-06), by the project owner, building M4's acceptance (m4.md Phase H; cut-a's
M4 row; D243 §9). The development container had no `tc` and no right to shape its network, so
the three netem profiles needed a way to run. Offered the kernel's netem or a proxy of our own
that delays and drops, and a separate run against one inside every branch gate, the owner:
*"agreed. Go ahead with that"*, to the recommendation below.

1. **The kernel's netem, not a proxy of our own.** A proxy approximates a network and would prove
   less than the sync bound claims. The development image gains `iproute2`, and the container the
   acceptance runs in the right to shape its network (`NET_ADMIN`); each client's traffic is
   shaped by its own profile (D243 §9: *home* 20 ms, no loss; *mobile* 80 ± 30 ms, 1%;
   *congested* 150 ± 50 ms, 3%, 5 Mbit/s).
2. **`make test-acceptance`**, run once at a milestone's end, not in every branch gate: two
   Playwright clients for 30 minutes under each profile, an hour and a half. The branch gate's
   browser tier keeps a short run under *home*. The owner's remote-household VM on nuc13
   (device-lab.md) confirms the profiles as a verification-queue item, as m4.md planned.
3. **Voice is measured from the browsers' own WebRTC statistics** between two clients with fake
   microphones: one-way delay as half the round trip plus the jitter buffer's delay, under 300 ms;
   audible loss as the concealed share of the samples received, under 2%.
4. **A signed-in guest's history** waits with D246 §4, which leaves recording a signed-in
   recipient's viewing for later; the acceptance checks the half that is built, that an anonymous
   guest records nothing, and the milestone audit lists the rest as a deviation.
5. **An invitation is spent by joining, not by opening it** (the owner, the same day: *"It only
   invalidates once the user actually selects a name and starts. If they reload the page before
   doing so, the link must still work"*), which is how it was built; the acceptance reloads the
   page before joining to keep it so.

**As built** (2026-10-06): one profile per run, applied by netem to the development container's
loopback, which every packet between the two browsers and the server crosses, so host and guest
share it (§1 said each client its own). The short *home* run inside the branch gate (§2) waits on
`NET_ADMIN` in CI's container, and the nuc13 confirmation is VQ24 (M4's audit, Q2).

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-06.

## D253 — A stalled player is told of its lower version at its first stall, and moves to it once it is ready if it still cannot keep up

**Decided** (2026-10-07), by the project owner, after a Watch Together guest on a 2.2 Mbit/s link
joined a 9.9 Mbit/s film and saw one still picture: her first stall started a 1.2 Mbit/s version,
as [D247](#d247--a-slow-link-gets-a-lower-version-made-at-its-first-stall-and-played-from-its-second-and-a-group-waits-for-a-stalled-viewer-once-then-lets-them-catch-up-alone)
§2 says, but her catch-up then left her paused ahead of the group, waiting, where she could not
stall again, so the second stall that would have moved her never came. **Revises** D247 §2 and
§10: a version is still made at the first stall, but it is played from when it is ready, not from
a second stall. The owner: *"the moment the first stall happens, start producing a suitable low
bandwidth steam and tell the client. When the stream is ready the client decides if it's still
going to have trouble and switches over."*

1. **The first stall's answer offers the version**, and every report's answer after it, saying
   whether it is ready: made from where the player is for as far ahead as a stalled player loads
   before it plays again (D247 §5, 10 s). A player told of a version not yet ready asks again
   every few seconds.
2. **A ready version is moved to if the player still cannot keep up**: it stalled again since the
   offer, its link is not measured, or the film's own picture's average rate, which the offer
   carries as the server measured it, is more than the share of the measured link a quality may
   take (D247 §6, 70%). Otherwise it stays on the original, and its next stall moves it.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-07.

## D254 — In the browser's own fullscreen, the chosen subtitle track is shown as the browser's captions

**Decided** (2026-10-07), by the project owner, after subtitles on Love, Guaranteed vanished as
his phone went fullscreen: *"they stop showing when I switch to full screen mode"*. **Revises**
cut-a §1's "text tracks via JASSUB" for fullscreen alone. JASSUB draws on a layer over the
video; the fullscreen of a video's own controls, and the iPhone's player, which is always
fullscreen, show the `<video>` element by itself, and the layer is left behind.

1. **The chosen track is also given to the browser as captions**, its WebVTT form, which the
   server already serves beside the ASS (D217 §6), as the video's text track. It is hidden on the
   page, where the drawn layer shows the track as its author styled it, and shown only while the
   video is in the browser's own fullscreen: `fullscreenchange` with the video as the fullscreen
   element, and the iPhone's `webkitbeginfullscreen` and `webkitendfullscreen`.
2. **In fullscreen the styling is plain**: the browser's own captions, without the track's fonts,
   positions or effects. The offset moves the captions as it moves the drawn layer.
3. **A fullscreen of our own**, the player area with its drawn layer, which would keep the styling
   in fullscreen on Android and a computer but not on an iPhone, is left for later. The owner chose
   this, the option that works on every device.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-07.

---

## D255 — Work has three priorities, a person's, a fast operation's and a slow one's, and a higher one bumps the lowest when nothing is free

> **§2 and §3 revised by [D329](#d329--work-is-scheduled-from-wants-each-resource-is-decided-next-to-it-playback-is-admitted-and-long-work-is-cut-into-pieces)** (2026-10-22): tiers replace the three priorities; preemption happens at a piece boundary and throws no work away; the quick pass goes.

**Decided** (2026-10-07), by the project owner, watching a new library of films on the NAS take
minutes to list a dozen: *"It should be doing a quick scan first and then fill in with the more
detailed scan after."* Each film the scan found was identified at once and queued its read-through,
which reads the whole file; the read-through and the scan's examining were both background work on
the one reader the NAS's disk was allowed, so each batch of the scan waited behind a film read end
to end. **Revises**
[D240](#d240--the-core-keeps-the-smarts-a-scan-is-a-listing-the-core-compares-the-work-it-implies-is-the-cores-to-schedule-and-the-node-enforces-its-devices-limits-and-pauses-background-work-for-play)
§5, which scheduled background work by priority alone, with no running job ever displaced.

1. **Three priorities**, highest first: **work a person asked for** (to play, a scan they pressed);
   **an operation expected to be fast** (a scan's listing and examining, identification, artwork);
   **an operation expected to be slow** (a read-through, a subtitle extracted from inside a video,
   anything that reads a whole film). The owner: *"heavy operations are lowest priority"*, and *"We
   now have 3 priorities: triggered by user request, expected fast operation, and expected slow
   operation."*
2. **A higher priority bumps the lowest when nothing is free.** Work that finds no slot or reader
   free evicts a running job of the lowest priority below its own: that job's work is thrown away
   and it goes back to the head of its priority's queue, to start again when there is room. The
   owner: *"it should be the general pattern of the queue: higher priority job bumps lowest priority
   job, throws out its work, and reschedules it."* D240 §6's pause of background work for play
   stays as it is until this replaces it.
3. **A scan's quick pass comes first on its disk**, built first, for the demos (2026-10-07).
   While a scan lists a root and reads the files it found new or changed, background work that
   reads whole films on the root's disk waits, on the disk's quick pass rather than its readers,
   which the scan's own work needs, asking again every half minute. Work a person waits for never
   waits for it. It stays beside §2: without it, each batch of a scan would bump a read-through that
   started again behind it, throwing its reading away each time.
4. **Slow work leaves a disk's last reader to faster work that came for it in the last five
   seconds** (added 2026-10-23, until D329's node-side disk scheduler replaces bumping). Each kind's
   jobs are claimed by its own runner, so when a piece of fast work ended and freed a reader, a
   read-through could take it first and be bumped by the next piece moments later, its reading
   thrown away: on staging's first scan of 12,000 files, 2,654 times in half an hour, beside the
   index reads and artwork, each 50 to 400 ms after a reader freed. Slow work now waits on the
   disk's last reader, a destination of its own, until the faster work has been quiet five
   seconds, which holds a read-through back no longer than that once it ends; while a reader stays free after it, it
   starts as before. Work a person asked for is never held.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-07; §4 added 2026-10-23, after the owner asked for the churn's fix.

## D256 — An encode is made no heavier than its picture needs or its original is

**Decided** (2026-10-07), by the project owner, after *Born Brisk*, a 640×272 DVD rip of 1.6 Mb/s,
was prepared at the h264-8m profile's fixed 8 Mb/s into a 5.3 GB copy that stalled every two
seconds on a 3 Mb/s link: *"Ideally we shouldn't be increasing the bit rate higher than the
original (with sanity checks). The whole point is a lower bit rate stream that it can choose."*
**Revises** cut-a §6's h264-8m, *"`h264-sdr` at ~8 Mbps"*, which became its most.

1. **An encode's average rate is the top of Apple's HLS authoring ladder for its picture's height**
   (1 Mb/s to 288 lines, 1.1 to 360, 1.6 to 480, 2 to 576, 4.5 to 720, 8 above), **and never above
   the original's own rate**: its picture's, or the whole file's where the container gives none.
   Its peak is at most a quarter more.
2. **The sanity check:** an original rate under a quarter of its height's rate is taken for a wrong
   figure, as a file cut short reports, and ignored; an unknown height gets 8 Mb/s.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-07.

---

## D257 — A player starts on the version its link can carry, chosen before play from the speed remembered for that device on that network

> **Revised by [D260](#d260--a-film-plays-from-its-ladder-of-qualities-from-the-start-filled-on-its-page-and-its-player-keeps-choosing-as-it-plays)** (2026-10-07): the remembered link now chooses where on the ladder every cut film starts; a link not remembered starts at the top.

**Decided** (2026-10-07), by the project owner, after starts of a minute or more: a player on a
slow link started on the original, and only after 15 s of loading (D247 §2's slow load) moved to a
lower version. **Revises** D247 §2, *"The original plays first"*, for a link known to be too slow.

1. **The speed a device measures on real video is remembered, per device and per network**: the
   network is the address the server sees it come from, its IPv6 prefix or its public IPv4
   address. A phone that moves from Wi-Fi to LTE comes from another address, so the speed measured
   on one is never taken for the other (the owner: *"When network conditions have changed, the old
   measurements are now stale"*). A speed fades with age, counting for less after a day, and each
   measurement replaces it.
2. **The start is chosen before play.** Where the remembered speed is too slow for the original, by
   D247 §6's share of 70%, the player starts on the lower version that fits, made as at a stall, and
   that version is listed first in its playlist, since Safari starts with the first. Where nothing
   is remembered, the original starts first, as before, and the warm-up (D258) measures.
3. **This detects no place.** Nothing behaves differently at home or away (D247 §11); a network only
   keeps one measurement from standing for another.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-07.

---

## D258 — Opening a film's page warms it up, and the warm-up's download is the speed test

> **Revised by [D260](#d260--a-film-plays-from-its-ladder-of-qualities-from-the-start-filled-on-its-page-and-its-player-keeps-choosing-as-it-plays)** (2026-10-07): the warm-up is the player itself, built on the film's page on the film's ladder, and its first buffer's fill is the measurement (§1, §3).

**Decided** (2026-10-07), by the project owner: *"I wonder if we can preemptively check connectivity
situation and pre buffer the best matched steam (generating it if necessary)?"*, and *"the preload
would make a good speed test, wouldn't it? If the client struggles to preload, it already knows it
needs a lower bit rate stream."* Netflix's predictive caching and Apple's advice to start network
work once a title is likely are the precedent ([cold-start.md](../design/research/cold-start.md), 2026-10-07).

1. **Opening a film's page, or pressing play, starts a warm-up**: the server prepares the first
   minute of the version D257 would start on, or its first chunks, and the page loads its first
   segments. A tab warms up one film, the one it is on; the Play page plays on the decision its
   page made. A warm-up is fast work in D255's tiers.
2. **The client says when the person moves on to another film**, so the server knows a warm-up,
   or the making of what it played, is no longer wanted (the owner, the same day: *"we should record
   when a client moves out of a video details or play screen, so that we know that the pre fill jobs
   are no longer needed"*, then, of going from the player back to the film's page: *"Until the user
   signals intent to watch a different video, we should keep data"*). Opening another film's page,
   or playing another film, lets go of the last one's playbacks (`DELETE /playback/{token}`); going
   back to the film's page, or anywhere else, keeps them. A playback let go of keeps its token until
   it idles out; its jobs fall to background at the next demotion.
3. **The warm-up's download is the speed test.** How fast its segments arrive is a measurement as
   D257 §1 keeps; one that struggles moves the start lower before play is pressed.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-07.

## D259 — A film's cut points come from where each one falls, from the file's own index, or from reading ahead of the player, never only from a whole read

> **§3 replaced by [D269](#d269--a-film-with-no-keyframe-index-is-cut-on-time-and-plays-encoded-at-once-its-original-picture-is-copied-once-a-read-through-has-found-its-keyframes)**
> (2026-10-08): a file with no index is cut on time and played encoded at once, not read ahead of
> the player.

**Decided** (2026-10-06, confirmed 2026-10-07), by the project owner: chunks.md §6, agreed when the
read-through of every film over a network mount took minutes and a film whose read-through failed
could never be offered a lower quality; confirmed when films added from the NAS stalled with
nothing offered while their read-throughs waited: *"Even if the index isn't available, can't the
encoding start already when you know where enough key frames are?"* **Revises** D247 §10's grid,
which came only from reading the whole file through.

1. **A local rule for the grid.** A chunk starts at the first keyframe at or after each multiple of
   `hls_segment_length_seconds`, so each boundary depends only on the keyframes near it: a stretch
   of the film cut alone agrees with the whole film's grid. A last chunk shorter than the length is
   merged into the one before it, as before.
2. **The keyframes from the file's own index**: an MP4's sync-sample table, a Matroska file's cues,
   read in a fraction of a second; the read-through stays the fallback. A sound's chunks do not wait
   for its loudness: unlevelled until it is measured.
3. **Read ahead of the player for a file with no index** (AVI, MPEG-TS, Matroska without cues): the
   node reads a few minutes ahead of the player's position, saying each keyframe as it reads, and
   the playlists grow from there. Required before a public release (the owner, 2026-10-06).

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-07.

## D260 — A film plays from its ladder of qualities from the start, filled on its page, and its player keeps choosing as it plays

> **§1 revised by [D344](#d344--the-whole-film-prepare-is-retired-every-playback-the-device-cannot-play-as-it-is-plays-from-its-ladder-cut-on-time-where-its-keyframes-cannot-be-had)** (2026-10-26): a film not cut on its keyframes in time, or that cannot be, is cut on time and plays from its ladder; no prepared copy is made.

> **Refined by [D265](#d265--the-chunked-player-chooses-its-quality-with-a-bitrate-controller-of-its-own-inside-hlsjs)** (2026-10-07): its player chooses with a bitrate controller of its own, which steps down while filling and playing alike (§3).

> **§3 revised** (2026-10-28, below): no preload where the page's media go over WebRTC, which keeps none of it for the Play page.

**Decided** (2026-10-07), by the project owner: *"If the client has an idea of what its network
situation is when opening the summary page, it asks the server for a bit rate no higher than X.
Server sends it video data and it measures how well it's handling it. If it can't, it reassesses its
capability and asks for an even lower bit rate. This continues until it can handle the initial
buffer fill. When the user presses play, this process continues if it wasn't settled yet, and while
playing back, the client continues to monitor its network conditions, asking for different bitrates
when necessary"*; and, of the three questions that followed, *"Go with your recommendations"*.
**Revises** D247 §2 (the original plays first, a lower version only after a stall), D257 §2 (only a
link remembered slow starts lower) and D258 §1 and §3 (the warm-up prepared a version and measured
a separate download). D247 §1 stands: no separate speed test, the film's own data measures the
link.

1. **Every film that can be cut plays from its ladder** (D247 §10): the film cut into chunks, its
   own picture copied as the top quality where the player decodes it, the qualities of
   `chunk_qualities` below it, one master playlist. The player moves between them by itself, down
   when its link cannot fill its buffer and back up with care, from the first segment to the last.
   No prepared copy is made for it. A film not cut yet, its keyframes not known, plays as before (the
   original or a prepared copy, D253 at a stall) while its keyframes are read, and from its ladder
   the next time it is asked for; one that cannot be cut always plays as before.
2. **It starts at the top**, the film's own picture, unless its device's link on its network is
   remembered (D257 §1): then at the highest quality within the link's share (D247 §6). Stepping
   down from too high happens on the film's page, where nobody is watching yet.
3. **The film's page fills the first buffer.** Opening it builds the player on a hidden video and
   loads the film's first seconds from where it resumes, stepping down as it measures; Play shows
   that player, already filled, and the stepping goes on if it had not settled. A browser that loads
   nothing before a tap (Safari on iPhone) starts its chunks on the server only.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-07.

**Revised 2026-10-28** by the owner ("go with your recommendations", approving the web client
efficiency audit's cheap fixes for the batch): **§3's preload is not made where the page's media go
over WebRTC.** §3 counted on the browser keeping the chunks the hidden player loaded for the Play
page's player (chunks are `private, max-age=86400`); on WebRTC the service worker builds every
chunk's answer from the page's transport, the HTTP cache never sees one, and the Play page loaded
the preload's ~10 s again over the same link while the person waited
([web-client-efficiency-audit-2026-10-28.md](../design/research/web-client-efficiency-audit-2026-10-28.md),
finding 1). There the film page still takes the warm-up's decision (D258 §1), so the server starts
its chunks, and the Play page's player starts at the quality offered. On HTTP, a core's name or its
own origin, §3 stands. Whether a preload on WebRTC should be kept for the Play page (its player
handed over, or its chunks kept by the service worker) is a question for later, not built. Which
path the media take, the loader says (`pathInUse`, its interface's minor 2,
`web/apps/web/src/loader-interface.ts`); on the core's own origin, where `?transport=webrtc` moves a
tab to WebRTC for testing, nothing says it yet, and the preload is made as before.

## D261 — The M4 audit's questions, answered

> **§7 revised by [D263](#d263--the-acceptances-networks-are-realistic-links-emulated-without-artefacts-its-bounds-are-per-client-pair-and-the-server-sends-media-with-bbr)
> §2, confirmed by D270 §3** (2026-10-08): voice on the congested profile is held to its bounds.

> **§1 refined by [D268](#d268--a-watch-together-player-corrects-drift-as-its-device-measures-it-places-its-group-by-recent-pongs-starts-at-a-moment-the-server-names-and-its-hosts-moves-are-taken-at-the-controls) §2** (2026-10-08): the 150 ms left alone holds for players that nudge; a pair with a player that corrects by seeks alone is held to 500 ms apart 95% of the time.

**Decided** (2026-10-07), by the project owner, answering §8 of the M4 audit
(design/research/audit-2026-10-06.md): *"1: yes, 2: yes, 3: defer as a nice to have in future, 4:
yes, 5: yes, 6: rewrite it, 7: best effort, but we really need to look into how apps like signal and
WhatsApp handle voice, because they had no problems with the same bad connection where orpheum
failed"*.

1. **The drift a Watch Together player leaves alone is 150 ms by default**, so D243 §9's bound of
   200 ms apart 95% of the time holds. **Revises** D250 §1's 500 ms; it stays the setting
   `together_drift_left_alone_ms`.
2. **A short netem run, the home profile, is part of every branch check** (D252 §2): CI's container
   is allowed to shape its own network (`NET_ADMIN`).
3. **A signed-in guest's watch history is deferred**, a nice-to-have for later (D246 §4). M4's
   acceptance no longer asks for it.
4. **A Watch Together link's note is the host's: `hostNote`**, not `adminNote`, which stays the
   admin's note on an account.
5. **The ACME directory is a config key**, `https.acme_directory`, Let's Encrypt's production one by
   default, so staging can use Let's Encrypt's staging CA.
6. **watch-together.md is rewritten** to say the design as D246 and D250 made it.
7. **Voice on a congested link is best effort**: D243 §9's voice bounds hold for the home and mobile
   profiles, not the congested one. How Signal and WhatsApp keep voice working on links where
   ours failed is researched next (the owner: they "had no problems with the same bad connection").

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-07.

## D262 — Voice keeps working on a bad link: measured honestly, sent to survive loss, and the film gives way to it

> **Refined by [D265](#d265--the-chunked-player-chooses-its-quality-with-a-bitrate-controller-of-its-own-inside-hlsjs)** (2026-10-07): the film's half of the link is the link as measured, never the pace its paced downloads arrive at (§2).

> **Corrected by [D263](#d263--the-acceptances-networks-are-realistic-links-emulated-without-artefacts-its-bounds-are-per-client-pair-and-the-server-sends-media-with-bbr)** (2026-10-07): correlated jitter does not stop netem reordering; in-order jitter does (§1).

**Decided** (2026-10-07), by the project owner, on the research into how Signal and WhatsApp keep
voice working on links where ours failed ([voice-bad-links.md](../design/research/voice-bad-links.md);
D261 §7): *"Do all of them if it will help"*. Voice on a congested link stays best effort
(D261 §7); these are what make it likely to work there.

1. **Measure before tuning.** Each voice call reports its receiver's own statistics every ten
   seconds, logged by the core: the jitter buffer's target delay, samples concealed apart from
   silence, packets lost and packets that arrived too late, packets recovered by FEC, the round
   trip, and whether the relay carries it over UDP or TCP. The acceptance's emulation is made
   realistic: a 1500-byte MTU on the loopback, a queue of about a quarter of a second under the
   congested profile's rate, and jitter that is correlated rather than independent per packet. A
   voice-only run under each profile is the fair comparison with another app's call.
2. **The film gives way to voice.** While a person's voice is live, their player caps the film's
   quality at half the link it measures, and asks the server to pace each chunk's download to a
   little above the rate the quality plays at, so the film's download never fills the link's
   queue in bursts; the server also marks those downloads as lower than best effort (DSCP LE).
3. **Voice is sent to survive loss.** Opus with its in-band FEC, DTX and an explicit average
   bitrate; RED, each packet carrying the one before, where the browser offers it (Chrome, Safari);
   the voice marked high priority (DSCP EF) where the browser can.
4. **The relay prefers UDP**, TCP only as a fallback, and the log says which carried a call.

Not done, and why (the research's §7 and §8): the browser's jitter-buffer target only adds delay,
and no standard API caps it; Opus DRED, low-bitrate FEC codecs and neural concealment ship in no
browser.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-07.

---

## D263 — The acceptance's networks are realistic links, emulated without artefacts, its bounds are per client pair, and the server sends media with BBR

**Decided** (2026-10-07), by the project owner: *"My definition before was based on a guess, so I'd
rather go with what the experts advise. Do some research to make sure your information is current
and correct before proceeding"*; then *"I'm okay with browser-specific policies. Browsers will never
reach parity"*. On [network-profiles.md](../design/research/network-profiles.md). **Revises** D243
§9's profiles and D252 §1's shaping; **corrects** D262 §1, whose correlated jitter still reordered
packets.

1. **Four profiles, each a netem stage for delay, in-order jitter and loss, and a tbf bottleneck
   with its own tail-drop queue** (network-profiles.md §0, after RFC 8867 and 8869 and measurement
   studies):
   - *home*: 20 ms one way, a 100 Mbit/s bottleneck, no loss;
   - *mobile*: 40 ± 10 ms, 0.2% loss, 20 Mbit/s with a 300 ms queue;
   - *congested*: 40 ± 5 ms, 0.5% loss, 5 Mbit/s with a 200 ms queue, shared with a long-lived
     bulk download for the whole run, the household's other traffic;
   - *lossy*: 40 ± 10 ms, 3% loss each way, 20 Mbit/s with a 100 ms queue, a bad radio link.
2. **The bounds are per client pair** (D243 §9's numbers: 200 ms apart 95% of the time; voice
   one-way under 300 ms and under 2% audible loss). Film sync is held on home, mobile and
   congested. Voice is held on home, mobile and congested for every pair, and on *lossy* for a
   pair whose browsers both send RED (Chrome, Safari); a pair with Firefox is best effort there. The
   film was best effort on *lossy* until a run with BBR (§3) showed it holds; the first run did
   (100% in step, 2026-10-07), so it is held on every profile.
3. **The server sends media with BBR**: its listeners ask the kernel for BBR, which their
   connections inherit, and keep the default with one log line where the kernel has none; the host
   loads `tcp_bbr`. Only the sender's congestion control counts, and BBR does not read random loss
   as congestion: at 3% loss it carried 17.7 of 20 Mbit/s where CUBIC carried 1.0.
4. **Not yet**: each browser on its own network namespace and link, as D252 §1 first intended; on
   the loopback both browsers share one bottleneck.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-07.

## D264 — A follower places its group by the pong with the shortest round trip, which carries where the group is

> **§1–§2 refined by [D268](#d268--a-watch-together-player-corrects-drift-as-its-device-measures-it-places-its-group-by-recent-pongs-starts-at-a-moment-the-server-names-and-its-hosts-moves-are-taken-at-the-controls) §1** (2026-10-08): a placing ages by 50 parts per million of its age, so a later pong with a somewhat longer round trip may place the group anew; a device pings each second three times after a new timeline, then every 15 s.

**Decided** (2026-10-07), by the project owner, on the congested profile's failed run (D263):
asked whether to find and fix the guest's steady offset or accept it, *"yes"* to finding and
fixing it. **Refines** [D66](#d66--no-clock-synchronisation-monotonic-local-time-and-bounded-round-trips),
whose minimum-round-trip sample now places the group as well as bounding it.

The first run of D263's profiles held the film on *home*, *mobile* and *lossy*, and failed on
*congested*: 93% of samples within 200 ms, against 95%, with the guest a steady ~180 ms behind
(median 182 ms, p95 201 ms) rather than wandering. A follower took the group's position from the
group message that announced it, aged by half the shortest round trip any ping had measured. A
message that waited in a full queue, 200 ms on *congested*, behind the household's download, was
older than that by however long it waited, and the follower stayed behind by the difference for
as long as the timeline lasted: each later message of the same timeline is ignored, so that one
message's delay does not nudge every player (2026-10-06). No follower can know how long one
message waited. A ping can: its round trip is measured.

1. **The pong carries the group as the server has it when it answers.** A pong that answers the
   current timeline places the group anew when its round trip is shorter than that of the pong
   that placed it last: where the pong says, aged by half its own round trip. The group message's
   own placing, whose wait is unknown, gives way to the first such pong. The error left is half
   the difference between the two ways' waits on the shortest round trip seen, where it was the
   whole of one message's wait.
2. **A device pings as soon as a new timeline arrives**, besides every 15 s, so the first placing
   by a measured round trip comes within one round trip of a play or a seek.
3. **A follower notes each new placing**: the pong's round trip, and how far it moved where the
   group is expected (`placed`, logged at info), so a steady offset on a person's link is read
   from the log, not guessed.

Still no clock is shared (D66): the pong's position is the server's, extrapolated by the
follower's own monotonic clock from the moment it arrived.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-07.

## D265 — The chunked player chooses its quality with a bitrate controller of its own, inside hls.js

> **Amended by [D352](#d352--the-chunked-player-trusts-its-link-as-far-as-the-evidence-goes-its-first-seconds-latch-nothing-it-climbs-as-far-as-consistent-samples-carry-and-it-grows-steadier-when-it-swings-or-its-link-flakes)** (2026-10-27): every choice reads the controller's own estimate of the link, not hls.js's (§1), and the step-up (§5) climbs as far as consistent samples carry, at a hold and headroom set by how steady the link has been.

> **Refined by [D266](#d266--a-quality-whose-video-stands-still-while-its-chunks-arrive-is-one-the-device-cannot-play-and-is-given-up)** (2026-10-07): a quality whose video stands still while its chunks arrive is given up as one the device cannot play.

**Decided** (2026-10-07), by the project owner: asked for a bitrate controller of our own in place
of the patches on hls.js's, then, on [abr-controller.md](../design/research/abr-controller.md)'s
four new rules, *"Approve all three"* and the fourth, the cache-hit filter, approved. **Refines**
[D260](#d260--a-film-plays-from-its-ladder-of-qualities-from-the-start-filled-on-its-page-and-its-player-keeps-choosing-as-it-plays)
§3 and
[D262](#d262--voice-keeps-working-on-a-bad-link-measured-honestly-sent-to-survive-loss-and-the-film-gives-way-to-it)
§2; keeps
[D247](#d247--a-slow-link-gets-a-lower-version-made-at-its-first-stall-and-played-from-its-second-and-a-group-waits-for-a-stalled-viewer-once-then-lets-them-catch-up-alone)
§6 and §9 as written.

The player chose with hls.js's own controller and patched around it four times: a step-down while
filling, since hls.js gives up on a slow chunk only while the video plays; the start and step-up
held through `autoLevelCapping`; a voice cap reading an estimate the pacing had made the pace's;
and a speed known only once a chunk loaded. Each patch fought the controller underneath it, and
the voice cap ratcheted the film to its lowest quality.

1. **A subclass of hls.js's `AbrController` makes every choice**, keeping hls.js's estimator,
   which its other controllers read. It replaces the fill step-down, the start and step-up
   through `autoLevelCapping`, and the voice cap's own look.
2. **The start** is the highest quality within the offer's `startAtBps` (D247 §6, D260 §3).
3. **A chunk in flight is looked at twice a second, playing or not.** Once it has loaded for half
   the time it plays, it is given up when it arrives slower than its quality plays, what is left
   of it would take longer than the buffer ahead lasts, and a lower quality's whole chunk would
   arrive sooner; for the highest quality within 0.7 of the speed it arrived at, **the lowest
   included**, which hls.js never gives up for.
4. **As it plays**, the next chunk is of the highest quality, no higher than the step-up allows,
   within a share of the measured link: **0.7 with 10 s or less loaded ahead, rising evenly to
   0.95 at 25 s or more**. A step down lowers what the step-up allows.
5. **The step-up** is D247 §9's: one quality at a time, after 120 s with 20 s ahead and a link 1.5
   times the next quality's rate.
6. **While voice is live** the film takes at most half the link (D262 §2), the link as measured,
   never the pace.
7. **What counts as a measurement:** a chunk that loaded in under 10 ms came from the browser's
   cache, as the film page's chunks do when Play reads them again, and is not counted; a paced
   chunk counts only when it arrived at no more than 0.9 of its pace, where the link, not the
   pace, held it back. *Amended 2026-10-08 (owner):* where the browser says, its Resource Timing
   entry for the chunk decides instead: a chunk that transferred nothing for its body came from
   the cache, and one that transferred came over the link however fast it was; the 10 ms guess is
   kept for a browser that does not say (`web/packages/player/src/cache-hit.ts`).
8. **hls.js's own forcing**, a switch down after a load error, is obeyed until a chunk of that
   quality loads.

hls.js's checks of what the browser decodes and its penalty for a quality that failed are not
kept: the core offers only what the player decodes (D260 §1), and a quality that fails forces a
switch down (§8).

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-07.

## D266 — A quality whose video stands still while its chunks arrive is one the device cannot play, and is given up

**Decided** (2026-10-07), by the project owner: *"yes"*, on Flow freezing in Firefox on macOS at
any start but the film's beginning. **Refines**
[D265](#d265--the-chunked-player-chooses-its-quality-with-a-bitrate-controller-of-its-own-inside-hlsjs).

Flow's own picture is 10-bit HEVC by x265, whose keyframes are CRA after the first, an IDR; every
chunk of its picture but the first starts on a CRA. Firefox on macOS decodes HEVC through the
system and froze at the first frame of any such chunk, spinning while its chunks kept arriving;
Safari played it, and so did Firefox from the start (the owner's test). No browser says so before
it tries: it says it plays HEVC, and does, from an IDR. Branching on the browser's name is not
done (the User-Agent is logged only).

1. **A quality is unplayable on this device** when its video, waiting to play, has stood still for
   6 s while at least two chunks of picture arrived: the link carries them, and the decoder does
   not play them. A slow link brings fewer, and a chunk being made none. **Waiting to play** is
   playing, or paused short of the data to play on (readyState below HAVE_FUTURE_DATA): an
   autoplaying video stays paused until it can play, so Flow's, resumed part-way, sat paused at
   readyState 1 and the first form of this rule, which counted only a video not paused, never
   fired (the owner's retest, 2026-10-08). A video a person paused, its data there, is not
   waiting. Each stall report carries the video's readyState, whether it was paused, what its
   picture's and sound's buffers held, and the player's last error. **Sooner:** two chunks of the
   picture the browser took and held nothing of (hls.js's `bufferAppendNoProgress`, which hls.js
   reports and ignores) give the quality up at once. That was Firefox on macOS with Flow: captured
   when the quality was given up, the picture's buffer was empty, the sound's held, and every
   chunk's append added nothing (the owner's test, 2026-10-08). The report of a quality given up
   carries the video as it was, before the rebuild empties it.
2. **It is given up for the rest of the playback**, with every quality above it, and the video's
   decoding is built anew, a new MediaSource (hls.js's `recoverMediaError`), loading again from
   where it stood at the highest quality below it; neither the step-up nor hls.js's own forcing
   chooses it again. Dropping the buffer alone left Firefox on macOS stuck after Flow's HEVC, every
   lower quality frozen too, for about two minutes (the owner's retest, 2026-10-08).
3. **The play report tells the core**, which logs the quality and where it stood.
4. **The film's own picture, given up, is offered to none of the device's later playbacks of the
   film, for the server's life** (amended 2026-10-12): the report says whether the quality was the
   film's own picture, and the core remembers it by player (a device, or a session with none) and
   film. Firefox on a Mac gave Flow's up anew at every playback, 1.5 to 5 s each; the owner, asked
   whether a device should remember it for the film until the server restarts: *"yes, do fix 2
   also."*

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-07; §4 decided 2026-10-12.

## D267 — A Watch Together membership is kept by the browser that joined, or by the account of whoever is signed in, and one member may be on several devices

**Decided** (2026-10-08), by the project owner, after testing with two guests on iPhones: *"(a)
agreed"*; on several devices, *"whatever makes this easier in future"* for voice and controls on a
phone with playback on a TV, the host avoiding playing in two places for now; *"(c) Yes let's make
sessions follow them. If they're not logged in, they need to get a regenerated invite link to switch
devices (which cuts off the current one and any device that connected with it)."* **Refines**
[D246](#d246--what-a-person-may-do-is-their-roles-an-invite-names-who-it-is-for-and-a-watch-together-viewer-is-an-ephemeral-account-that-sees-only-the-hosts-playback) §3–§5; **brings forward** its §4's signed-in recipient, for the session
alone (their viewing recorded as their own stays later).

A guest who closed the page could not come back: the link is single use and the membership lived in
the tab. A host who opened the session on a laptop saw nothing of it on their phone, signed in as
the same person, and having it back on one device replaced the credential of the other.

1. **A guest's membership is kept by their browser**, not the tab: the same browser opening the page
   or the link again comes back as the same member. The link stays single use, and no other browser
   can use it.
2. **A signed-in person's membership follows their account.** Joining by a link while signed in
   makes the member that person; the host is one already. Any device they are signed in on has the
   session back without a link, the Watch Together page and the player asking the server which
   sessions they are in.
3. **One member may be on several devices at once**, each with a credential of its own: having the
   session back on one device cuts off no other. Each device keeps its role (playback or voice), the
   seam for voice and controls on a phone while a TV plays ([D245](working-notes.md#d245--cut-a-ends-with-a-polished-skinned-web-ui-built-on-research-and-the-remote-tv-comes-right-after-it)). The host plays in one
   place at a time; whichever device the host plays on leads.
4. **Someone not signed in moves to another device by a new link**: the host makes one for that
   member, which removes the member, cutting off every device that came in with them, and admits
   whoever opens it, under the same note. *Amended 2026-10-19, the owner ("go with 2"), settling
   D311 §5 against D312 §3 for Watch Together:* the new link no longer removes the member as it is
   made. They stay in on every device until it is used; whoever joins by it then takes their place,
   with its note and rights and the name they give, and the devices they came in on are cut off and
   told why. Removing them still cuts them off at once, and ends every link to their place.
5. **The host can show any link again**, waiting or used (*"I need a way to view the link (even if
   it's been used, since the guest can now use it to connect back using the same device)"*, the
   owner, the same day, after a reload lost one before it was shared). The server keeps each link's
   secret with its hash, in memory, for the session's life, as it keeps the session itself: someone
   who could read the server's memory could read a live link, a cost of the same order as reading
   its sessions.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-08.

## D268 — A Watch Together player corrects drift as its device measures it, places its group by recent pongs, starts at a moment the server names, and its host's moves are taken at the controls

> **§3 superseded by [D371](#d371--a-session-has-a-leader-that-plays-as-a-device-plays-alone-everyone-else-catches-up-to-it-and-a-cast-takes-its-senders-part)** (2026-10-28): a group names no moment to start at; it plays at once as its leader plays, or, with none, as it is told, and each follower plays as it hears it and is corrected into step (§2). `together_start_lead_ms` is retired. §1, §2, §4 and §5 stand.

> **§3 extended by [D282](#d282--a-watch-together-player-presses-play-early-by-how-late-it-has-learned-it-starts-kept-by-its-device-one-that-has-not-learned-it-runs-up-two-seconds)** (2026-10-12): each player presses play early by how late it has learned it starts; one that has not runs up two seconds, the group's lead lengthened to it.

> **Revised by [D271](#d271--m5s-first-questions-answered-four-browsers-no-user-facing-theming-or-light-palette-and-guests-who-may-pause-and-seek-unless-the-host-withholds-it)** (2026-10-09): §5's later guest rights are decided: play and pause, and changing the position, chosen per invite, each invite starting with the last one's.

**Decided** (2026-10-08), by the project owner, on the review of Watch Together's synchronisation
(design/research/sync-review-2026-10-08.md): *"ok, agreed"*, to its four recommendations that
change the design; and *"at a future time I want to be able to grant guests play/pause rights, and
possibly seek as well."* **Refines** [D264](#d264--a-follower-places-its-group-by-the-pong-with-the-shortest-round-trip-which-carries-where-the-group-is)
§1–§2, [D250](#d250--a-watch-together-group-stops-only-at-its-own-sync-points-a-members-trouble-is-theirs-to-catch-up-on-from-what-is-already-being-made)
§1 and [D261](#d261--the-m4-audits-questions-answered) §1; **amends** cut-a §5.1's group message;
**narrows** [D62](#d62--watch-together-is-a-first-class-feature-and-the-per-client-surface-is-six-methods)'s
per-client surface for the M5 player.

The review found the design sound and three things wrong with how it was built: a 150 ms allowance
tighter than anyone ships, on a browser whose rate changes cost 220 ms each; a group placed once and
then extrapolated for a whole film on each device's own clock, so two devices' clocks, tens of parts
per million apart, open hundreds of milliseconds between them over two hours; and a host's moves read
from the player's events with one-shot marks, where most of a week's bugs lived.

1. **A placing ages.** A pong of the timeline followed places the group anew when it is better now
   than the placing it has: half its round trip, against half the placing's round trip plus the
   placing's age times an assumed difference of 50 parts per million between the two clocks (BBC's
   figure for DVB-CSS). A placing a few minutes old gives way to a pong whose round trip is a little
   longer. A device pings each second three times after a new timeline, then every 15 s. Each pong
   is noted with its residual: where it says the group is, against where the follower expected it,
   so a pair of devices' skew is read from the log. A re-placing's step is the drift correction's
   to absorb. Still no clock is shared ([D66](#d66--no-clock-synchronisation-monotonic-local-time-and-bounded-round-trips)).
2. **A player corrects its drift as its device measures it**, never by its User-Agent (D250 §7). A
   player that learns its rate going back to the group's costs it more than the drift left alone
   corrects by seeks alone from then on: beyond `together_seek_only_drift_left_alone_ms` (400 ms by
   default), a small seek past the group by what its seeks have learned to lose, as MediaSync does
   on Safari. Every other player nudges as before. A pair with a player that corrects by seeks is
   held to 500 ms apart 95% of the time, its pair's bound in D263's bounds per client pair; D243
   §9's 200 ms holds for players that nudge, as the acceptance's Chrome and Firefox do.
3. **A group starts at a moment the server names.** The end of a sync point's wait announces
   Playing from a position, starting `startsInMs` later: `together_start_lead_ms`, 500 ms by
   default. The server's group stands at that position until then. Each follower holds its player
   there, and plays at the message's arrival plus what was left of the lead, less half its round
   trip. A pong or a later group message says what is left of the lead. Every player then starts at
   once, rather than each as the message reaches it and then nudged.
4. **A host's moves are taken at the controls.** In M5, the skinned player's play, pause and seek,
   and the Media Session's handlers (lock screen, media keys, the iPhone's own fullscreen), send the
   command, and the follower moves the player itself, as its own move. The player's events are a
   person's moves only where no control of ours was used: then by comparing the player's state with
   both what the follower last asked of it and the group's, as Syncplay does, not by one-shot marks.
   Until then, an own move's mark lasts at most 2 s, and its expiry is noted.
5. **Guests may later be given play and pause, and perhaps seek.** Not in Cut A, where the host
   alone controls playback (D246 §8). Kept open: a command carries no privilege of its own; the hub
   asks whether the member who sent it may give it, and answers yes for the host alone. §4 is what
   makes the rest possible: a guest's player, like the host's, would send commands from its controls,
   not events.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-08.

## D269 — A film with no keyframe index is cut on time and plays encoded at once; its original picture is copied once a read-through has found its keyframes
