> **§1 revised by [D344](#d344--the-whole-film-prepare-is-retired-every-playback-the-device-cannot-play-as-it-is-plays-from-its-ladder-cut-on-time-where-its-keyframes-cannot-be-had)** (2026-10-26): a film whose keyframes are not read in time, that cannot be read through, or that has no keyframe before its end is cut on time too, and on time the top of its ladder is the twin.

**Decided** (2026-10-08), by the project owner, on the question of what matching the original's
keyframes buys the viewer: *"Ok, go with your recommendations on the key frames issue"*; and, on
knowing a file's keyframes before it is played, *"is it possible as a future enhancement to scan
and save the index of a video so that we know up front what we're dealing with?"* **Replaces**
[D259](#d259--a-films-cut-points-come-from-where-each-one-falls-from-the-files-own-index-or-from-reading-ahead-of-the-player-never-only-from-a-whole-read)
§3's reading ahead of the player.

Only the original picture, copied, needs the film's own keyframes: HLS has a video segment start
on one (Apple's authoring specification 7.4), and every other stream is encoded, its keyframes
placed where it is cut. Most files with no index cannot be copied to a browser at all (Xvid and
DivX in AVI, MPEG-2 in a TV recording's MPEG-TS), so waiting for their keyframes bought their
viewers nothing, and reading ahead of the player would have made a seek past what it read wait.

1. **A file with no index of its keyframes is cut on time**: a chunk starts at each multiple of
   `hls_segment_length_seconds`, a last chunk shorter than that merged into the one before. Its
   playback is offered the encoded qualities and the sounds at once, from any point, and not the
   picture copied.
2. **The node says a file has no index at once.** A read-through a player waits on asks for the
   index alone, and a file with none answers so in a fraction of a second, rather than being read
   through while the player waits.
3. **A playback keeps the grid it started on.** One that began on time stays on time to its end,
   though a read-through finds the keyframes meanwhile; a playback after that is offered the picture
   copied, on the keyframes, when its player decodes it.
4. **Files with no index are read through first** by the sweep that reads every film through, so
   most are known before anyone plays them; what a read-through learns is kept by the file's bytes,
   and the file itself is never changed.

A file with an index keeps D259 §1–§2: its keyframes from the index, its picture copied.

5. **Every file's index is read first, then every file is read through** (the owner, the same
   day: *"As we do the scan, we keep the 'scan fast stuff first, slow stuff later' approach"* and
   *"yes add the fast tier"*). The sweep after a scan reads the index alone of each film that has no
   timeline, milliseconds each, ahead of any full read, so most films are cut on their keyframes
   before anyone plays them; each index read is followed by the film's full read, for its loudness
   and its bytes in each second, a file with no index ahead of the others. Every film ends with its
   keyframes known: the eventual state.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-08.

## D270 — M4's closing audit's questions, answered

**Decided** (2026-10-08), by the project owner, on §10 of M4's closing audit
(design/research/audit-2026-10-08.md): *"1-4: agreed"*. Questions 5 (M5's) and 6 (the acceptance
run) wait for the owner.

1. **A failed full read of a film whose keyframes came from its index is kept**, in a column of its
   own on the picture's timeline, `read_failure`, not in `failure`, which would make the film
   uncuttable: the sweep stops reading it through every hour; a read through that succeeds later
   clears it. No one waits on a full read, so a person's play does not try it again.
2. **Names that reach a setting key or the wire are renamed**, each old name retired:
   - `should_together_voice_level_microphone` → `should_together_voice_browser_level_microphone`,
     and the tuning's `shouldLevelMicrophone` → `shouldBrowserLevelMicrophone`: it governs only the
     browser's own gain control, Orpheum's levelling being on when it is off;
   - the note kind `led` → `leaderCommand`, and its `events` → `recentEvents`;
   - the ponged note's `residualMs` → `aheadOfExpectedMs`;
   - the startup report's `decisionMs`, `firstDataMs` and `playingMs` → `decidedAfterMs`,
     `firstDataAfterMs` and `playingAfterMs`, durations from the request that started it;
   - the prepare profile `h264-8m` → `h264`, its rate the picture's own up to a ceiling (D256);
   - the chunkLoaded note's `kbps` → `loadedKbps`, and the qualitySwitched note's `estimateKbps`
     → `linkEstimateKbps`;
   - the diagnosis's `streaming` → `mediaSourceState`.
3. **Voice on the congested profile is held to its bounds**, as D263 §2 and the acceptance hold
   it: D263 §2 revises D261 §7's best effort.
4. **The commit-msg hook runs the test-weakening check on the commit it records**, so a
   `Test-Weakened`, `Test-Renamed` or `Gate-Changed` trailer is written with the change it
   explains, not on a later commit.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-08.

## D271 — M5's first questions answered: four browsers, no user-facing theming or light palette, and guests who may pause and seek unless the host withholds it

**Decided** (2026-10-09), by the project owner, on M5's questions (design/plans/m5.md) and the
research made for them (design/research/browser-support-2026-10-09.md, theming-2026-10-09.md):
*"Browsers: Agree on the four with those floors."* *"Theming: Drop it. I'm also not sure that a
light palette would be a good idea in a media player, since you're almost certainly going to be
using it in a darkened room."* On guests' controls, from the owner's first tests of Watch Together
with five guests, two of whom asked why they could not pause: *"I think we need to allow it."*

1. **Four browsers are supported, from these versions:** Chrome and Edge 120, Firefox 140, and
   Safari 17.1 on macOS, iOS and iPadOS, the iPhone's floor D250 already set. Browsers on the
   same engines (Brave, Opera, Vivaldi, every iOS browser) come with them; Samsung Internet is
   best effort. Nothing more is supported without a compelling reason, as each adds to the test
   cycle. `@scope` is not used: it needs Safari 26.4 and Firefox 146. The Cast receiver's engine
   is checked on a device and gets a floor of its own when M6 builds it.
2. **There is no user-facing theming:** no third-party themes, no custom CSS, and no promise that
   class names or tokens stay stable, which stay free to change as M5 iterates. What themes are
   used for is built in instead and tested: the system's reduced-motion and contrast settings,
   forced colours, density and poster size as a person's settings, sizes that follow the
   browser's zoom. This revises D138 §4.
3. **There is no light palette.** The player is watched in a darkened room; the app is dark
   throughout. This revises D251 §1's later light palette.
4. **A guest may play and pause, and may change the position, unless the host withholds it.**
   - The rights are granular: play and pause is one, changing the position the other.
   - The host chooses them with a checkbox each when creating the invite. The first invite starts
     with both; each later one starts with the rights of the last one issued (the owner, on
     D246 §8: *"Actually, yeah it should copy the previous invite's rights."*).
   - A right granted lasts as long as the invite. The host already removes a person during
     playback.

   This revises D246 §8 and D268 §5, which kept control with the host alone in Cut A. D246 §8's
   later form is kept as it was: granular rights given per invite, each invite starting with the
   last one's. D268 §5's shape
   holds: a command carries no privilege of its own, and the hub asks whether the member who sent
   it may give it, now by the rights of that member's invite. It rides on D268 §4, a guest's
   player sending commands from its controls.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-09. §4 built 2026-10-11: a checkbox each in the invite, the server's check of each command, and a guest's player that offers the controls its link gives and full screen always.

## D272 — Production runs on nas.example from an image it builds, and migrations keep every step since the version it last ran

**Decided** (2026-10-09), by the project owner, before M5: *"at some point I'll want to actually use
this software to watch TV and movies with my gf, so before we begin the new dev cycle style on m5,
I want to make sure the production deployment procedure for the core and nodes is simple and
painless (which it will have to be anyway once I open up the first public beta)."* Then: *"I'd want
to run it on nas.example, since that's where the files are. While it's just me and my gf, I don't mind
swapping between media.orpheum-app.com pointing things to your staging server or nas.example."* And:
*"Once I start using this for real, we'll need to support migrations in a sliding window: keep
migration fully intact from the last checkpoint until I say that I've migrated nas, then make that
the new checkpoint. I don't mind if nas has to build the image itself, so whatever's easiest."* It
builds D249 §5's release mode and revises D228 §3 and §6.

1. **Production runs on nas.example**, where the media is: a Proxmox VE host on Debian trixie, with the
   core and its node on one machine (there are no remote nodes yet), in an LXC container (the
   owner: *"I'll go with lxc"*), so the media is bind-mounted and the kernel is the host's.
   Landlock is switched on in the host's kernel, since the node runs no FFmpeg unconfined (D112).
   - **The GPU is passed through**: the machine is a TerraMaster F4-424, whose Intel N95 encodes
     and decodes by Quick Sync, its render node given to the container.
   - **New files in `/tank/media/video` (ZFS) are noticed as they arrive** (the owner: *"it
     should be able to monitor the fs ... for catching new file additions"*): D27's native
     filesystem watching, built for production, with the periodic scan kept beneath it, as D27
     asks, since a watcher fails silently.
2. **`media.orpheum-app.com` is swapped** between staging, in the agent's sandbox, and nas.example
   while the owner and one other person are the only users: one VPS address fronts one machine's
   voice relay (D249).
3. **Release mode is built before M5's live iteration**, as D249 §5 designed it: the same runtime
   image and compose file as staging, with no source tree, Python or build needed by the
   deployment beyond the image. Installing is the image's setup command, which writes the
   deployment's directory (the compose file, a short values file, the tunnel's keys), then
   `docker compose up -d`; updating is a new image, then `docker compose up -d`. The tunnel is
   optional, for a host reached without the VPS. Staging is set up the same way, so the one path
   stays tested.
4. **The image is built on nas.example** from a tagged checkout, by one command. Publishing it to a
   registry waits for the public beta (D235 §5).
5. **Migrations keep a sliding window.** The checkpoint is the schema version nas.example last ran.
   Every step after it is kept as committed and never edited; a schema change appends a step. When
   the owner says nas.example has migrated to a version, the steps up to it fold into the baseline,
   which becomes the new checkpoint. This revises D228 §3's rule of one step behind, and stands
   in for D228 §6's going live until the public beta, when every step is kept for good (D181).
   D228 §5's standing approval for a fold's goldens holds at each new checkpoint.

**Added** (2026-10-09, the same day), by the project owner, choosing among the build's options:

6. **The checkpoint is a file**, `internal/store/migrations/CHECKPOINT`, holding the version nas.example
   last ran. A test holds the baseline at that version, so no fold happens before the owner moves
   it; it is a gate file, moved with the owner's `Gate-Changed:`. It is committed when nas.example
   first runs.
7. **The build re-renders.** The one build command of §4 builds the tag's image and then runs that
   image's setup over the deployment's directory, which renders the compose file and the configs
   from the image's templates and the values file and points them at the new image; then
   `docker compose up -d`. Going back is the same with an older tag.
8. **Staging and nas.example share one tunnel key pair**, so the VPS is never touched by a swap: a swap
   stops one deployment's tunnel and starts the other's. Only one may run its tunnel at a time.
9. **A change the watcher sees is a scoped scan, after a quiet spell.** The node tells the core which
   directory changed once events under it have stopped for a while, so a copy in progress settles
   first; the core lists that directory alone, by the listing that already goes only as deep as
   asked, from where asked (D240). An overflowed event queue asks for the whole root. The library
   page says of each root whether it is watched, or why it is scanned only. The periodic scan
   stays beneath it (§1).

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-09.

## D273 — Clients reach a core through app.orpheum-app.com or the owner's own discovery, by whatever methods work, with no traffic relayed by us; a node without Landlock runs and warns

> **Built by [D288](#d288--a-device-is-activated-by-the-code-it-shows-entered-on-a-device-already-signed-in-and-a-check-code-both-show)** (2026-10-12): §10, with the owner's refinements.

**Decided** (2026-10-09), by the project owner, planning a closed beta in two weeks. It revisits
D214, D249 and D272 §1–§2, and D112's refusal.

1. **The goal, not a mechanism.** *"We don't need to be stuck in our ways for how to connect a
   host to a discovery service. I'm fine with offering multiple methods. The method we have now is
   just something that happened so that we could start testing. In the end, all that matters is
   that clients can talk to servers, stream video, and users can voice chat (and eventually text
   chat as well)."* The WireGuard tunnel to a VPS (D243 §7, D249) is one method among several, not
   the design. The methods are compared in
   [reachability-approaches-2026-10-09.md](../design/research/reachability-approaches-2026-10-09.md).
2. **The paid tier is discovery at app.orpheum-app.com, with no relay** (refining D214): *"owners
   connect to app.orpheum-app.com, not their own subdomain of orpheum-app.com, and not a custom
   domain. If they're using web, they go to orpheum-app.com (our homepage) and then click login,
   which takes them to app.orpheum-app.com, where they are now talking to their core, with as much
   traffic as possible going direct between them and the core (i.e. I don't want to be relaying
   traffic)."* It is a separate, closed-source project, specified first in the sandbox's shared
   files; the agent keeps both projects in step.
3. **The free alternative is the owner's own discovery, single-target.** *"owners can set up their
   own discovery service, which we'll make easy for single-target (one VPS points to one core) so
   that they don't try to set up a competing service to app.orpheum-app.com. This will be
   expensive (minimum $5 per month), so it will be more economical for them to pay me $3 and just
   use app.orpheum-app.com."*
4. **Native clients** will connect through app.orpheum-app.com by default, with a custom domain
   for those who host it themselves.
5. **Landlock is a hardening, not a requirement** (revising D112's refusal): *"Landlock is just an
   enhanced security measure. We don't need to block them if they don't have it, but we should at
   least warn."* A node runs FFmpeg with what confinement the kernel offers and says what is
   missing, as the System page already shows; `node.confinement_policy` starts at `"report"`, and
   `"require"` stays for an admin who wants the refusal.

**Added** (2026-10-09, the same day), by the project owner:

6. **The protocol between a core and its discovery is stable and simple, so the two never upgrade
   in lockstep.** *"Ideally we should be able to survive multiple updates without having to make an
   incompatible change that requires them to upgrade. When that does eventually happen, we should
   support the previous 2-3 versions (negotiable here, not sure what number would be ideal) as
   well, with a deprecation warning that the next change could make them unsupported if they
   haven't upgraded."* Changes are additive wherever they can be; a breaking one raises the
   protocol's major version, the service keeps answering the previous ones for a deprecation
   window, and a core on a deprecated version tells its admin. The window's size is still open.
7. **The owner's answers to the follow-ups** (*"Agreed with your other recommendations"*), on
   [reachability-approaches-2026-10-09.md](../design/research/reachability-approaches-2026-10-09.md) §9:
   - The window of §6: the service answers the previous two major versions, each for at least six
     months after it is superseded, whichever is longer; a core on a deprecated one says so, with
     the date its support ends, on the System page.
   - A client reaches its core by racing every way it has (its IPv6 address, a LAN name, the public
     IPv4, WebRTC) (§9.1). The owner, the same day: *"first to succeed wins, but if a better method
     comes back successfully a short while later, we switch to that"*: the client uses the first
     path that answers, keeps the others trying for a short while, and moves to a better one that
     answers in that time (better: on the LAN over across the internet, plain HTTPS over WebRTC).

     **Amended 2026-10-13** by the owner: moving to a better path as it answers *"is moving the
     original problem one rung down rather than solving it. We should be taking the first one that
     succeeds as a control connection, then giving a few seconds for the other attempts to work or
     fail, and then out of all that succeeded, pick which one will work best."* The first path to
     answer carries the page at once; the others get a few seconds; then the client moves to the
     best of all that succeeded, by what it measured of each as well as by kind
     ([discovery-protocol.md](../design/discovery-protocol.md) §3.3).
   - Hidden per-core names live under a dedicated domain of the service's, not under
     orpheum-app.com, with one wildcard certificate per core (*"a separate domain for the hidden
     cores is acceptable (if it still makes sense to go this route)"*).
   - The core maps its ports automatically by UPnP, NAT-PMP or PCP by default, says what it
     mapped and whether the service's outside test passed, and can be told not to (§9.3).
   - WebRTC data channels are the direct path for a core behind carrier NAT whose client lacks
     IPv6; *"I approve trying pion/webrtc"*: its throughput and set-up time are measured first,
     and the module joins the allowlist when the owner accepts the result (AGENTS.md rule 3).
8. **pion/webrtc joins the dependencies.** On the measurement (reachability-approaches §9.4: one
   connection window-bound, four with faster window growth enough for 1080p at every round trip
   measured and 4K to about 100 ms), the owner: *"Ok let's add webrtc"*. The transport is planned
   in [webrtc-transport.md](../design/plans/webrtc-transport.md).
9. **The closed beta, the names' domain, and how a device finds its core**, the owner's answers to
   the discovery spec's questions:
   - *"invite only for the closed beta"*; billing comes after it.
   - The hidden per-core names' domain: *"maybe something like orpheum-core.com? I'll see what I can
     register"*.
   - A new device finds its core *"similar to what we do now: invite links and qr codes to create
     an account, and tv codes for an account holder to add a device like a tv"* (D218), each
     carrying where the core is. *"Another option for device registration would be to have the
     device itself get a qr code from the core, the logged in user scans with his phone to complete
     registration."* No search by name or e-mail: that would be a list of cores (D214 §3).
10. **A TV joins by a code it shows, and a check code both screens show** (revising D218 §3–§4,
    whose code a signed-in person makes and types on the TV). The owner: *"For the TV code, there
    have been multiple approaches tried. I prefer this way: unregistered device connects to the
    core (though vps or paid), gets a code, the user enters it into a registered device, then the
    core sends a new check code to both, which the user verifies are the same before accepting the
    pairing."*
    - The unregistered device reaches its core by whichever path it has (the owner's VPS, or the
      discovery) and is given a code, which it shows.
    - The person types it on a device already signed in.
    - The core then sends a new check code to both devices; the person sees they match, and only
      then accepts. A code shown by someone else's device fails at the check.
    - D218's safe32 shape, single use and short life hold for both codes. Not built: M3 built
      D218's direction, which this replaces.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-09; §7's choice among paths amended 2026-10-13; §5's default revised 2026-10-20 (the owner, the Plex-chain review's N2): a release node requires confinement, and `"report"` is the knowing choice to run unconfined.

## D274 — A core is reached first by what needs nothing from its owner, WebRTC through the discovery; direct paths are upgrades, and a relay waits for demand

**Decided** (2026-10-10), by the project owner, after the homelab network research
([homelab-networks-2026-10-10.md](../design/research/homelab-networks-2026-10-10.md)). It orders
D273 §7's methods; it revisits nothing D273 decided.

1. **The aim.** *"Ultimately what I want is maximum coverage for typical homelab setups. The idea
   is for this system to be very easy to set up when using our discovery server, and not
   unnecessarily complex when setting up their own. I'm not too hung up on which ports are
   open."*
2. **Three layers.** The owner: *"That sounds good."*
   - **The baseline needs nothing from the owner:** the core holds its connection out to the
     discovery, which passes on clients' WebRTC offers and runs STUN, and the client and the core
     punch through their NATs (W4). Nothing is opened inbound, so carrier NAT, DS-Lite, double NAT
     and a container on a bridge network do not stop it.
   - **Direct paths are upgrades, found by themselves:** an open IPv6 address, a port the router
     mapped, the LAN at home. D273 §7's race takes them when they answer; none is required. Port
     mapping may therefore use a high port of the core's choosing.
   - **A relay is the last resort:** the self-hoster's own TURN or VPS. For the paid tier, a relay
     of only the connections that fail, through TURN, encrypted end to end, with credentials the
     discovery issues per session, is open in principle but not built: *"I'm open to the idea of a
     relay, but I'd want to see how much demand there is before trying it."* A WireGuard tunnel
     from every customer's home through the service, relaying everything, is not the way: its cost
     scales with all streaming, it puts a path into every home on the service's machines, and it
     makes the service the carrier of every stream.
3. **Measure before deciding the relay.** Every connection records which path it took (direct
   over IPv6, direct over IPv4, punched, relayed, failed) and what the client's network was, for
   the System page and the log, so the closed beta says how often direct fails, mobile carriers
   above all. The owner's mobile tests so far went through the VPS, a relay, and measured nothing
   about punching.
4. **IPv6 first.** Over IPv6 there is no translation, only stateful firewalls, so punching between
   two IPv6 ends almost always works; mobile carriers mostly give phones IPv6. Cores are steered to
   IPv6 (a router mode that delegates a prefix, not NAT6), and the System page says when a core has
   none.

**Added** (2026-10-11), by the project owner (*"ok, agree with those recommendations"*):

5. **The self-hoster's discovery is the paid tier's shape** (`orpheum discovery`, W4b):
   - **It serves the web app**, as app.orpheum-app.com does for the paid tier, its files taken
     from the core over the core's own outbound connection, so their version is always the core's.
     Nothing has to come through a tunnel for a visitor to load the app.
   - **It claims its one core by the paid tier's flow**: the core shows a claim code, and the owner
     runs `orpheum discovery claim <code>` on the VPS.
   - **Direct HTTPS names under the owner's own domain wait**: W4b is WebRTC first.
   - **Its relay is TURN on the VPS**, as voice already has. The WireGuard tunnel (D243 §7, D249)
     becomes optional, and later goes: self-hosting becomes one VPS running one `orpheum
     discovery`.
6. **The paid discovery service's development starts** in its own repository,
   `/home/karl/orpheum-discovery`, closed-source (D273 §2), from the spec in the shared files; the
   agent works on both and keeps the protocol in step.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-10; §5–§6 added 2026-10-11.

## D275 — Orpheum's discovery is public building blocks that a closed multi-core service imports, and the server moves to the AGPL with a contributor agreement

**Decided** (2026-10-11), by the project owner, while the paid discovery service started (D274
§6). It replaces the paid-service spec's §9.2 recommendation (a third, permissively licensed
protocol module) and revises
[D80](#d80--licence-by-artefact-gplv3-for-the-server-mpl-20-for-the-clients-and-the-sdk) for the
server.

1. **The seam.** The owner: *"My paid discovery service talks the same protocol to an individual
   host's core, but itself has the ability to talk to multiple cores. We'd need some code in
   orpheum itself to support the host logging in to the paid service at app.orpheum-app.com, but
   otherwise it would be pretty clean. So orpheum is public, and orpheum-discovery is my
   proprietary discovery server that talks the same language to each core under its purview."*
   - Orpheum's discovery is **building blocks in public (not `internal/`) packages**: the wire
     types, signature checks, the signalling relay for one core's connection, STUN. `orpheum
     discovery` (W4b) assembles them for one core.
   - **The closed service imports them** and assembles them for many cores, with its own
     accounts, billing and names. It is run, never distributed.
   - **Orpheum carries nothing it does not use itself** (the owner: *"I don't see why orpheum
     would need to have hooks it doesn't use"*). What it adds for the paid tier is the host's
     sign-in to app.orpheum-app.com, beside the discovery client C1–C5 built.
   - The public packages' interfaces are a dependency of the closed service, so a change to them is
     made in step with it (D274 §6: the agent works on both).
2. **The server moves to AGPL-3.0-or-later; the clients and the SDK stay MPL-2.0.** The owner
   asked for *"a license that requires derivatives to publish"*, then *"OK, agreed on the
   licensing."* Under GPLv3 a fork run as a service, a multi-core discovery among them, keeps its
   changes private; under the AGPL it offers its users their source. Running an unmodified
   Orpheum asks nothing of a self-hoster: its source is already public. D80's *Why not AGPL*
   overstated that burden.
   - **Contributions come under a contributor licence agreement** that grants the owner rights
     beyond the AGPL, so the closed service may import public packages others have contributed to
     without falling under the AGPL's network clause. The owner's own code needs none.
   - The agreement is the owner's choice, *"go with the one that google uses"*: `CLA.md`, the
     Apache Individual CLA v2.2 adapted as Google's is, accepted by a sentence in the first
     contribution; a corporate agreement is asked of the owner when an employer owns the work.
   - Done 2026-10-11: `LICENSE`, every server file's SPDX header, `scripts/check_source.py` and
     goheader. The two migration steps committed before keep their GPL header, since a database
     records each step's checksum (rule 8); the next baseline fold carries the AGPL.
3. **The licence is not the defence against competitors.** The owner: *"we are also entering into
   a new era with AI able to clone existing services with ease ... licensing might make for a poor
   defense against competition. I'll need to use price and first mover advantage."* The AGPL's
   job is that improvements to Orpheum come back to it; the paid tier competes on price and on
   being first.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-11. §1 shapes W4b; §2's relicensing built 2026-10-11.

## D276 — A scan that removes nothing never waits for the admin, though its root moved to another device

**Decided** (2026-10-11), by the project owner (*"yes"*), after the rebuilt sandbox's staging
showed both its library folders "offline": the bind mounts it reads came back on another
filesystem device, every file still in them.
[D208](#d208--the-scenario-walks-answers-re-identify-on-rename-unless-confirmed-a-title-follows-its-files-between-libraries-withhold-removals-past-half-and-twenty-and-a-returning-payload-revives-its-tombstone) §3 held back any scan whose root's device or mount had changed since its last
complete scan, as an unmounted disk leaves its empty mount point behind. A scan that finds every
file it knew is not that, so:

1. **A scan that would remove nothing completes**, whatever its root's device: nothing waits for
   the admin, the root is not offline, and the new device and mount are recorded, so a later
   unplugging is judged against them.
2. A changed device or mount still holds back a scan that would remove anything, as before; one
   that would remove all of a root's files waits in any case.

**Status:** Decided and built 2026-10-11 (`library.withholdReason`;
`TestScenario_ARootOnANewDeviceWithEveryFileCompletesAndKeepsTheNewDevice`).

## D277 — A scan held back for the admin leaves its root playable unless it saw none of it, and the admin is told what waits and what could not be read, with the fix

**Decided** (2026-10-11), by the project owner (*"yes to all of those"*), after a replaced season
on the NAS, its new folder unreadable to the node, held back staging's Series library: the whole
library showed as offline and its files as unavailable, the banner led to a page with no action on
it, and that the node could not read the new folder was said only deep in the Libraries page. The
owner: *"We need a mechanism in place to deal with this kind of situation."*

1. **A held-back scan is not a missing root.** A scan whose removals wait for the admin
   ([D208](#d208--the-scenario-walks-answers-re-identify-on-rename-unless-confirmed-a-title-follows-its-files-between-libraries-withhold-removals-past-half-and-twenty-and-a-returning-payload-revives-its-tombstone) §3) leaves its root available: what the scan saw plays, and only
   the removals wait. A scan that saw none of the root's files still makes it unavailable, as a lost
   disk does ([D231](#d231--work-is-derived-from-state-the-job-queue-is-a-regenerable-cache-and-a-destination-that-is-down-parks-its-work) §5), and a scan that could not read the root at all
   still does.
2. **What waits is said where the admin is sent.** The System page, and the reminder above every
   page, say for each held-back root how many files its scan would remove, name the first of them,
   say why it waits, and carry the button that removes them (D208 §3's approval, which scans again).
   Putting the files back and scanning again is the other answer; nothing else is offered.
3. **What could not be read is said, with the fix.** The node reports which user and group it
   reads as. The System page, and the reminder, list each file or folder a scan could not read,
   with the library, the platform's error, its owner, group and mode (D163 §8), and what to do:
   make it readable by the node's user.

**Status:** Decided and built 2026-10-11 (`library.Admin.Waiting`, `UnreadPaths`; the System
page's *Waiting for you* and *Could not be read*; the reminder's counts). The node already
reported its user and group in its hello.

## D278 — A problem is shown beside what it affects, by a yellow warning sign that opens what is wrong; yellow means something needs fixing, bright red that an action cannot be undone

**Decided** (2026-10-11), by the project owner, as a general UI principle ahead of the UI revamp.

1. **Beside what it affects.** *"When there's something wrong (files missing, unmounted
   filesystem, corruption, whatever), any affected user-selectable part in the UI should have a
   yellow warning icon (the triangular one with an exclamation point inside) beside it to indicate
   that it has issues that will affect its functionality."* A problem is said as close to the
   affected item as possible: a title, a library, a folder, a person, a device.
2. **The sign opens the detail.** *"Selecting that icon will bring up a detail view to say what's
   wrong, and hopefully how to fix it."* Shortcuts to where it is fixed, or a button that fixes it,
   may come later; not before the UI revamp.
3. **A non-admin sees the generic words.** *"For a non-admin user, the view will only display
   generic information and ask them to tell the administrator."*
4. **Two colours with one meaning each.** *"Yellow means something's wrong that needs to be fixed,
   or something couldn't be accomplished because of a problem. Bright red means the action the user
   is about to take is irreversible."* The exact shades are the owner's choice, from samples. Today's
   crimson `--color-problem` gives way to the yellow.
5. **Not perfect yet.** *"We don't have to make this perfect yet, as we haven't done the full UI
   revamp sweep yet (i.e. there can be gaps if it's too much trouble, but the principle should be
   there for when we do the new UI)."*

6. **The shades**, the owner's choices from samples (*"Y3 looks good"*, then *"I like D1 and T5"*,
   then *"Adopt this color scheme"*): the warning yellow `#ffcc00` with a near-black mark; the
   irreversible red `#b91c1c` to fill a button under white words, and `#ff4d4d` for its words and
   outlines. The coral accent stays the ordinary action's.

**Status:** Decided and built 2026-10-11, with gaps the UI revamp closes: the tokens
(`--color-warning`, `--color-irreversible`, `--color-irreversible-text`), the warning sign that
opens its detail (`warning-sign.tsx`), beside a title, a Continue Watching row and a film that
cannot be played now, a library folder whose scan could not read it, waits for the admin or misses
a disk, and a role that reaches no library; the plain sign beside the System page's offline,
waiting and unread entries and the reminder; and the red on every confirming button and the System
page's removal. Not yet: a role's deletion asks nothing first, and an episode, a person and a device
carry no sign.

## D279 — Test runs are proportionate to the change: a 30-second spot check while working, make check at a commit, check-pr for a batch

**Decided** (2026-10-11), by the project owner, after a day on which the agent ran `make check-pr`
after each small fix, six runs of 139 to 1133 seconds against a 300-second budget:

1. *"Running check-pr after every little change is slowing down the dev cycle (plus it's blown way
   past the 5 minute limit). We should be running quicker tests for small changes, and run
   check-pr only after extensive, or accumulated changes. Test runs should be proportionate to the
   changes."*
2. *"Ideally a 'spot check' from a small change shouldn't exceed 30 seconds."*
3. **Restructuring the tests to fit is allowed:** *"If that means refactoring/rearchitecting the
   tests to support this, I'm fine with that."*
4. **Written into the principles**, not only the agent's memory: *"put it in the testing
   principles since your memory could get erased if the sandbox goes down"*: principles §23 and
   testing.md §10.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-11; the rule is written. Restructuring the tiers so each fits its
budget, and measuring them, is the next piece of work.

## D280 — A status tray at the banner's end shows what is on, in a light blue; Watch Together's opens its controls over the screen; the admin's yellow sign leads to a page of what needs them

**Decided** (2026-10-11), by the project owner, for using Watch Together the next day:

1. **What is on is in view on every screen.** *"When a 'watch together' session is active, I think
   it would be good for some kind of status to show up as I navigate around the app so that it's
   clear I'm in that mode. Often when demoing this I forgot I was in watch together mode. Maybe an
   icon on the top-right? A silhouette of two heads facing each other."*
2. **Its controls without leaving the film.** *"Clicking on it brings up pop-up controls so that I
   can do all of the watch together management without navigating away from the movie (which stops
   it for everyone I think, requiring me to navigate back to the same movie/show to restart it)."*
   It does stop it: leaving the player stops the film for everyone (D246 §5).
3. **A status tray, in a status colour.** *"We'll probably have other statuses to show at some
   point, so a status tray might be in order, with a standard status tray icon color (maybe some
   kind of light blue?)"*: `--color-status` `#7cc8ff`, provisional until the owner chooses.
4. **The admin's warning sign, yellow, leads to a page.** *"We could even have a top-level warning
   icon when something's wrong somewhere, although that one should buck the trend and be yellow.
   Clicking on it would bring you to a summary page of everything that's wrong (not a pop-up). The
   page can just be a placeholder for now until we design it properly."*

**Status:** Decided and built 2026-10-11 (`status-tray.tsx`, `needs-attention.tsx`): the tray shows
the host's Watch Together sign and, for an admin, the warning sign while the reminder counts
anything. Not yet: a signed-in viewer's sign, and a designed summary page.

**Revised 2026-10-12** by the owner: *"Since we have the warning icon in the top right now, we
don't need the other alert box under the top bar anymore."* The reminder under the banner (D231 §7,
P39) is gone; the tray's warning sign alone tells the admin. The owner, the same day: *"Remove the
other parts for the reminder box."* Its dismissal (`POST /offline-reminder/dismissal`), the
`offline_reminder_interval_days` setting, the kept dismissal and `isShown` went too, and the
counts the tray shows moved to `GET /needs-attention`.


## D281 — Everyone in a session hears voice from the start; Talk only opens the microphone, and Mute only stops one's own sending; the host's pop-up runs voice, each person's volume and the film's, with invites and people in dialogs of their own

**Decided** (2026-10-11), by the project owner, from using Watch Together through D280's pop-up:
*"There's no voice controls or per-user + video volume controls in the pop-up. Voice should work
even if the other people haven't turned on talk yet. Mute should only stop you from transmitting
voice, not prevent others from talking. Invite shouldn't be ever-present on the pop-up. It should
be a button, with pops up a sub-dialogue. Similarly, clicking on a user in the pop-up should bring
up a dialog for what to do with them."* It revises the plan's Voice (watch-together.md): Talk no
longer attaches the voice device.

1. **Everyone hears voice without pressing anything.** Each member's voice device attaches as their
   page opens, with no microphone, and keeps a call with every other person's voice device, able to
   receive from the start. A call sends nothing until its person talks.
2. **Talk opens the microphone and sends it on the calls already up**, by putting the microphone's
   track on each call's sender: no call is made again. **Stop talking** closes the microphone and
   sends nothing again, still hearing everyone; on an iPhone that gives the sound back to the
   speaker (WebKit 230902).
3. **Mute stops only one's own sending**: the microphone's track switched off. Nothing anyone else
   sends is touched.
4. **Each person's voice has a volume of its own**, from silent to four times as loud as it came
   (`partnerGainMost`), kept per member across their devices' calls, beside the film's own volume.
5. **The host's pop-up runs the session during the film**: voice (Talk, Mute, Stop talking), each
   person's voice volume, and the film's volume. Inviting is a button that opens a dialog of its
   own; a person in the list opens a dialog of what may be done with them (show their link again,
   a new link, remove them, their voice's volume).
6. **A call that fails reconnects by itself** (the owner, later the same day, after a locked phone
   and a sleeping iPhone each left voice off until someone pressed a button: *"Yes, auto-reconnect
   until the user turns off the voice button. We should probably have some kind of animation to show
   that it's connecting."*). A call that fails, or does not connect within a while, is made again,
   waiting a little longer each time up to a few seconds, for as long as the other's voice device
   is in the session; a microphone that was talking stays on until its person turns Talk off. The
   status line moves while any call connects. This revises the owner's 2026-10-06 rule, kept here
   until then, that a failed call turned voice off with a button to try again.
7. **Talk is one toggle, and §2's Mute and Stop talking are one press** (the owner, later the same
   day): *"Rather than having stop talking and mute as separate buttons, let's simplify: A talk
   toggle button. They press it to turn on their microphone, and then press it again to stop
   talking. How we make it "stop talking" is implementation defined. If we can easily just turn off
   the microphone and then restart it when they turn talk back on, do that. If we encounter problems
   and need to mute instead, do that. Prefer turning the microphone off."* The second press closes
   the microphone; muting (§3) is kept in the SDK as the fallback, not offered. Its look is the
   owner's choice B of five samples (`talk-toggle-options.html`, shared files): *"B looks good for
   the toggle."* A round microphone button, struck through while off; in the status blue while on,
   with a ring that grows with the voice going out.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-11.


## D282 — A Watch Together player presses play early by how late it has learned it starts, kept by its device; one that has not learned it runs up two seconds

> **Superseded by [D371](#d371--a-session-has-a-leader-that-plays-as-a-device-plays-alone-everyone-else-catches-up-to-it-and-a-cast-takes-its-senders-part)** (2026-10-28): with no moment named to start at (D268 §3 gone), there is nothing to press play early for or run up to; the leader plays as it would alone, and a follower plays as it hears the group play and is corrected into step. The start lag is no longer learned or kept (`orpheum.together.startLag` is cleared), and `together_run_up_ms` is retired. D371 §2 allows a follower's run-up where it would help it land in step; none is built.

> **§4 refined by [D283](#d283--after-a-seek-a-player-is-ready-on-3-s-of-film-when-its-link-carries-the-film-well-faster-than-it-plays-ready-players-hold-their-loading-while-their-group-waits-and-a-run-up-starts-no-earlier-than-what-was-loaded) §3** (2026-10-12): a run-up starts no earlier than what its player loaded where the group starts.

**Decided** (2026-10-12), by the project owner, after a four-device test in which every player
started within 60 ms of the moment the server named (D268 §3), and the iPhone and the Android phone,
whose pictures moved some 170 ms later, were then nudged into step for about six seconds. The owner
first asked whether players could start from before where the group starts, *"so we could set the
target to that. Then all participants aim to catch up to the same 'future' point rather than having
a lot of back-and-forth"*; then, given the choice: *"we can have it remember how late it was last
time and use that, but if it hasn't run yet, we do the 2s run-up time. I expect that the most
common scenario for watch together will be: everyone connects, watches one show, then disconnects.
The second most common would be: Everyone connects, watches a series of shows, then disconnects.
The rare situation would be: Everyone connects, a show starts, then someone gets added via invite
halfway through."* It extends D268 §3.

1. **A player learns how late it starts.** At each start it presses play for before the moment, it
   measures, once its position settles after its player says it plays, how far it lost from where
   the group runs: learned as D268 §2's losses are, the first whole and each after averaged with it.
2. **The device keeps it, for every session.** One show a session is the commonest case, so a lag
   kept only for the session would rarely be used: the web client keeps it in the browser's
   storage (`orpheum.together.startLag`). The player says it in its state while it has one.
3. **A player that has learned it presses play that much early**, held where the group starts
   until then.
4. **A player that has not runs up.** While any player along has not learned its lag, the group's
   start lead is `together_run_up_ms` (2000) instead of `together_start_lead_ms` (500). Such a
   player seeks back to where the group would be had it already started, plays at once, and is
   judged on the way by where the group runs, so it makes its lag up before the moment. A group
   starting in the film's first two seconds starts at two seconds, so there is film to run up
   through: *"If the video is at the very start, losing a second or two isn't bad."*
5. **Every start of the group is one**: a film put on, the host's play after a pause, and the
   host's seek (D250 §2's sync points). Someone joining mid-film catches up as before.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-12.


## D283 — After a seek a player is ready on 3 s of film when its link carries the film well faster than it plays, ready players hold their loading while their group waits, and a run-up starts no earlier than what was loaded

> **§3 superseded, and §2 narrowed, by [D371](#d371--a-session-has-a-leader-that-plays-as-a-device-plays-alone-everyone-else-catches-up-to-it-and-a-cast-takes-its-senders-part)** (2026-10-28): there is no run-up (D282 superseded); a group waits only for its leader, so a ready follower holds its loading while the group stands for its leader, the leader never holding its own.

**Decided** (2026-10-12), by the project owner, on
[seek-resync-2026-10-12.md](../design/research/seek-resync-2026-10-12.md), after a group took 10 to
20 s to play again after the host's jumps: *"Those sound good"*, of its options 1 to 3, and,
asked to build them, *"yes go ahead"*. Its option 4, a seek snapped back to its chunk's start, is
not taken: it saves at most a chunk's unused head and lands up to a chunk before where the person
aimed. It refines D247 §5 and D282 §4.

1. **After a seek, ready on 3 s, when the link keeps up well.** A player sought by its group or its
   person is ready again with `seekReadyAheadMs` (3 s) loaded ahead when its last chunk of picture
   loaded at least `seekReadyLoadsAtLeast` (1.5) times faster than it plays; else, and after any
   stall or a catch-up's seek, with D247 §5's 10 s. Every player researched starts on a second or two
   after a seek.
2. **A ready player holds its loading while its group waits** at a sync point, and goes on as the
   group plays, so the players not yet ready have the server's upload to themselves.
3. **A run-up starts no earlier than what its player loaded where the group starts**: an earlier
   chunk is one more to load, and on an encoded quality one more to encode (a run-up of 2 s asked
   for a whole chunk for 12 ms of it, 2026-10-12). A shortened run-up starts once the group's run
   reaches it.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-12.


## D284 — Encoded qualities carry a keyframe every 2 s, each its own fragment, and a chunk is served as it is made; a player says when a jump took it where it loads, and a jump starts a run there

**Decided** (2026-10-12), by the project owner, on [seek-resync-2026-10-12.md](../design/research/seek-resync-2026-10-12.md)
§6 and the owner's group jumps of the same day, where an iPhone on an encoded 720p was ready 7 to 26 s
after a jump while the others were ready in 3 to 7: *"yes go ahead with both."* On how a server tells
a jump from a catch-up: *"We should be able to tell from the controlling client whether it's a jump
or not. The user interaction would tell you what happened."* It refines D250 §5.

1. **Encoded qualities carry a keyframe every 2 s**, inside chunks that stay on the copied picture's
   grid, each keyframe beginning its own fragment, and **a chunk is served as it is made**, so a
   player on an encoded quality starts on the first 2 s of a chunk rather than its whole 10 s: about
   9 s to 2 or 3 after a jump. (The 3 to 5% more bits first given for it was a guess; measured, a
   2 s keyframe costs 8.5 to 23% at 720p: fast-start-2026-10-12.md §0.)
2. **A jump says it is one.** A player loading where its person's seek, or its group's, took it
   says so on each request (`Orpheum-Sought`) until it can play there; a catch-up's seek
   (`catchUpSeekEvent`) and hls.js's own steps over a gap never do. Such a request more than
   `chunk_seek_new_run_beyond_seconds` (20 s) of film past where a run is making starts a run there,
   cancelling that one; any other keeps `chunk_new_run_beyond_seconds` (90 s), so a catch-up still
   waits for the run already making its quality. A run made at playback's speed reached a jump 70 s
   ahead some 50 s later.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-12.


## D285 — A long jump is snapped back to its keyframe and starts the run-up after it, and while anyone in a group is still loading, the rest hold a short runway

> **§1 revised by [D371](#d371--a-session-has-a-leader-that-plays-as-a-device-plays-alone-everyone-else-catches-up-to-it-and-a-cast-takes-its-senders-part)** (2026-10-28): a long jump is snapped to its keyframe itself, with no run-up after it, and the leader's own jump is not snapped: it is already where it went.

**Decided** (2026-10-12), by the project owner, on [fast-start-2026-10-12.md](../design/research/fast-start-2026-10-12.md)
and the group jumps of the same day. On snapping: *"What if seeking snapped to the first keyframe
leading up to that point? Using the scroll bar to jump is by nature imprecise, so I doubt anyone would
notice."* and *"if we, on the server side, snapped to a keyframe, and then set the target playback
point to a comfortable margin in the future (i.e. a bit beyond the keyframe) such that all clients
have enough time to synchronize playback"*; on the runway: *"if the clients play cooperatively (only
grab enough that they have runway to continue once everyone's caught up), then this should reduce
contention for the bandwidth"*; to both, and to making a jump's first chunk sooner: *"yes. I'm also
fine if it turns out we get better responsiveness from presenting a common, lower quality stream
before settling on what each device can handle."* It refines D250 §2 and D283 §2.

1. **A group's jump of more than 30 s is snapped** by the server back to the keyframe at or before
   where it was asked, the start of the chunk holding it, and the group starts the run-up
   (`together_run_up_ms`, D282) after it. Every player loads from a chunk's start, the encoded
   qualities' runs too; none needs a second chunk for the film a player is ready on past where it
   aimed; a run-up runs on what is loaded. A shorter skip, by a key or a button, lands where asked:
   snapped back, a skip of 10 s at a chunk's start would never move on.
2. **While any player along a group is still loading or catching up, the others load no more than a
   short runway ahead**, and fill as far as they would once all play, so the one behind has the
   server's upload.
3. **A jump's first chunk sooner** on an encoded quality, by whichever of a faster encode, a lower
   common quality first, or the node putting it first measures best. *Measured the same day, none
   is worth building now:* a 10 s chunk of Conan at 720p took 4.5 to 5.8 s whatever the preset,
   x264 zones of lesser effort for the first chunk, scaling filter or number of cores (3 or 8): its
   10-bit AV1 picture's decoding, 2.2 to 2.7 s, and the scaling and the encode follow one another;
   480p at ultrafast was 3.3 s. With §1, a device on an encoded quality waits for one chunk after a
   jump, never two; shorter encoded chunks (fast-start-2026-10-12.md, option C) are what would go
   further.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-12; §1 and §2 built the same day, §3 measured and set aside.


## D286 — A jump cuts every run of a quality it does not land in, a group's player keeps the film's own picture while its link carries it, encoded devices start a jump on a common quality, and an overloaded server moves a player onto a quality it already makes

> **§1 and §4 revised by [D309](#d309--a-player-says-which-quality-it-wants-and-from-where-and-a-run-no-player-wants-stops)** (2026-10-17): a jump's player says where it now wants its quality, which ends the runs it left; moving a player down is the rule under load.

**Decided** (2026-10-12), by the project owner, after a group test in which a Mac stepped down from
the film's own picture to a 720p encode, two 720p runs and a 540p one ran beside the sound's, each
at 0.6 to 1.2× playback, and the Mac and an iPhone took 70 and 85 s to play again. To cancelling a
jump's old runs and keeping a computer on the film's own picture: *"yes that sounds good."* On a
common start: *"My common low encoding start was more for preventing the server from getting
overloaded when 3 devices each want a different encoding. Starting them all off at a
likely-achievable middle-ground encoding, and then letting them settle to higher or lower after
that, should help. When a network connection is too constrained, I'm not that worried about
degraded performance if the happy path gives the better experience. So if a common 720p would work
in most cases, fine."* And: *"If the proliferation of encodings starts to tax the server too much,
we should allow it to forcibly drop a client down to a lower quality encoding already being used
by another."* It refines D284 §2, D265 and D250 §6.

1. **A jump's ask cuts every run of its quality ahead of where it lands, at any distance**, and
   one past it beyond D284 §2's 20 s: its group left where the run was going. Any other ask keeps
   the reach of a run made a minute ahead.
2. **A player in a Watch Together group keeps the film's own picture while its link, as measured,
   carries the picture's average rate**, whatever share the controller keeps back for voice
   (D262 §2) or a growing buffer: such a step down adds an encode, on a link only crowded by the
   group sharing the server's upload.
3. **After a jump, every device that needs an encoded quality starts on one common quality**, the
   one most likely to work on a real link (720p unless measurement says otherwise), and settles
   higher or lower from there; one encode for all of them, not one each.
4. **An overloaded server moves a player onto a quality it already makes** for another, lower,
   rather than dropping the run the player needs (D250 §6's eviction).
5. **When its clients saturate its upload, the server consolidates their qualities**, moving
   players onto fewer and lower common ones, **and as a last resort removes the member who joined
   most recently**. The owner: *"If the clients are saturating the network pipe, we should allow the
   server to consolidate playback quality among the clients, and ultimately to boot the most recent
   member if it still doesn't help enough."* The upload it can spare is **a setting the owner
   gives**, how fast their link is or how much of it they allow, with a button to measure it
   by a speed test site left for later: *"Let's allow the user to specify what his bandwidth is (or
   what he'll allow). We can also in future offer a button to auto-detect using one of those speed
   test sites."* Removing the newest member: *"yes, booting the newest member is ok."*

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-12.

## D287 — A film's player keeps the screen awake while the film plays

**Decided** (2026-10-12), by the project owner, after an iPhone and an Android phone left on a table
during group tests locked their screens mid-film, iOS pausing its video as it did: *"Is it possible
to prevent screen lock when a video is playing?"*, and to the Screen Wake Lock API, held while the
film plays: *"go ahead"*.

1. **Every film's player holds a screen wake lock while its video plays on a shown page**, solo or
   in a group, and lets it go when the video pauses or ends or the player closes; a paused film lets
   the device lock as it would.
2. **The browser lets the lock go when the page is hidden; it is asked for again when the page is
   shown** and the video plays.
3. **Where there is no lock, it plays on as before**: a browser without the API, a page not served
   over HTTPS, a request refused (as in low-power mode), asked again at the next change.
4. **A film whose page is hidden pauses**, as YouTube's page does, unless it is in
   picture-in-picture (amended 2026-10-12): an iPhone's page told it plays as a video app's, so the
   silent switch does not mute it, played its sound on in the background with the picture gone. The
   owner, asked: *"yes"*. In a Watch Together group the pause is the browser's, and the player
   rejoins the group as the page is shown again.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-12.

## D288 — A device is activated by the code it shows, entered on a device already signed in, and a check code both show

**Decided** (2026-10-12), by the project owner, building D273 §10's direction, which was not built:
*"For the device activation code, we should do it this way for maximum security: On the login
screen on the untrusted device, you can either log in via username/password, or you can request a
code ... Requesting a code asks the core to issue a code, which the device then shows to the user.
On an already logged in device, the user goes to their account page. At the top of that, there's a
box to enter activation codes. The user enters the code there and clicks "Activate". The device is
now activated and connected to their account."* Why: *"The way it works right now requires a logged
in user to generate the code on a trusted device and then input it on an untrusted device, meaning
that any untrusted source can spam codes from distributed IPs in the hopes of harvesting devices as
users try to set them up. With the above method, no code spamming can happen because you have to
enter it from a trusted device."* Asked about D273 §10's check code and an admin activating a device
for someone else: *"Yes to both. Also, when the check code shows, we should have a big, easy to
understand warning that they need to verify visually, not take some stranger's word for it."*
**Replaces D218 §3–§4** (a signed-in person makes a code and types it on the TV) and D221 §2's code
for a listed device; **refines D273 §10**.

1. **A device not signed in asks the server for a code** from its sign-in page, beside the name and
   password: eight characters of safe32 shown as `xxxx-xxxx` (D218 §3's shape), for ten minutes,
   once, with a secret of its own the device alone holds, by which it asks every couple of seconds
   how its pairing stands; asking again returns the same code until it is used or expires. The core
   limits nothing here: on its owner's server and VPS it needs no protection, and limiting how often
   strangers ask for codes is the paid discovery's, which faces them for many cores (the owner:
   *"Such a rate limiter would need to be enforced from the paid discovery tier. Otherwise it's just
   the admin's own server and VPS, which needs no protection"*).
2. **A person signed in enters it** in "Activate a device" at the top of their account page, with
   the name the device is listed by; an admin enters it on another person's page, for someone with
   no other device. A code that is no one's counts against the account entering it, as a wrong
   password does.
3. **The server then gives both devices a check code**, and the device being activated shows it.
   The person compares the two with their own eyes, on the device in front of them; a big, plain
   warning says so, and never to take someone's word for it, on a call or in a message. Only their
   "Yes, they match" activates the device; "They don't match" ends the pairing.
4. **The device is then signed in as the person**, listed and removable as any other. One that was
   signed in before and remembers which device it was resumes as that device (D221).
5. **A device with no link first opens the address of the discovery it means**: the admin's own
   VPS, which fronts their one core and passes the request for a code to it, or the paid discovery,
   which an app opens by default and which, fronting many cores, issues the code itself for the core
   of whoever types it to claim (the owner, 2026-10-12; the discovery service's spec). The core's
   side is built here; the paid discovery's is its own.
6. **Pairings are kept in memory**: a restart ends those under way, which the device shows, and it
   asks for a new code. At most a hundred wait at once, the oldest not yet entered giving way: not a
   limit on who asks, but a bound on the memory strangers' asking can take.

   **Amended 2026-10-13** after the security audit (S13) showed the oldest giving way let a stranger
   push a television's code out before it was typed, on the owner's own discovery as on the core:
   past a hundred waiting, or five not yet entered from one network (an IPv4 address, or an IPv6
   /64), a new code is refused and none waiting is dropped (the owner: *"D: Take your
   recommendation"*).

   **Amended again 2026-10-13** after the second security audit (K5): twenty networks' five codes
   each filled the hundred, and no television could get a code. A thousand may wait, and twenty not
   yet entered from one site (an IPv6 /48, which a provider gives one customer, or an IPv4
   address).

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-12.

## D289 — The paid discovery's questions answered: accounts for payers only, the identity key backed up as the secret key is, byte paths by header, one client build per core API major

**Decided** (2026-10-13), by the project owner, on the paid service's open questions (its
specification, draft 4, §11), the ones that bind Orpheum recorded here: *"Q8, Q11, Q12, Q16, Q17:
Follow your recommendation"*, then *"Q5, Q6, Q13, Q14, Q18: Agreed"*. The protocol is
[discovery-protocol.md](../design/discovery-protocol.md).

1. **Only the paying owner has an account with the paid service** (Q5). Household users never do:
   they sign in to their core, which their device found once by a link, a QR code or its code
   (D288) and remembers by a locator. **Refines [D72](#d72--the-hosted-relay-has-no-free-tier-holds-no-data-and-has-no-accounts)**
   for a service that relays nothing: one account per paying household, granting nothing on any core.
2. **The core's identity key is backed up as `secret.key` is** (Q12, D243 §11): out of scheduled
   backups, in *Back up now* when its box is ticked; losing it costs a re-key.
3. **A page served by a discovery authenticates byte paths by the header on every request** (Q17):
   hls.js's loader, `fetch` and blob URLs for images and subtitles; no credential in a URL (D154,
   D217 §2), since the media cookie is not sent cross-site.
4. **A discovery serves one web client build per supported core API major**, chosen by the major the
   core reports (Q18), so the central client never speaks every old API at once; the window is
   D273 §7's.
5. **The rest is the paid service's**, recorded in its specification: its customers with their own
   VPS are served (Q11); its dashboard has its own origin (Q16); payment stopping runs 14 days'
   grace, 60 frozen, then the core's id retired, the core working on its LAN throughout and the
   exit path tested in Orpheum (Q8, D25); aggregate counts only, no identifiers (Q13); two
   repositories and two machines (Q14); code shared as D275 decided (Q6). Q7, the business and tax
   questions, waits for a session of its own.
6. **Replaced by D290 §1** (2026-10-13): claiming is done from the core instead.
   **Claiming a core on the paid dashboard ends with a check code** (Q19, the owner: *"Q19:
   Agreed"*): the dashboard and the core's System page both show it, with the core's name and
   fingerprint, and only the customer's "they match" binds the core, as D288 §3 ends a device's
   activation. The core's System page shows it, so this is Orpheum's to build too.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-13.

## D290 — The discovery audits' findings taken: claiming on the core, paths ranked by kind, re-keying signed by the old key, computed DNS behind Cloudflare, and WebRTC in the beta

> **Revised by D310 §13** (2026-10-18): the paid service's accounts sign in with a username and a
> password, not §16's e-mailed link; §16's invitations stand.

**Decided** (2026-10-13), by the project owner, on the four reports of
[the security audit](../design/research/discovery-audit-security-2026-10-13.md),
[the ease-of-use audit](../design/research/discovery-audit-ux-2026-10-13.md),
[the correctness audit](../design/research/discovery-audit-correctness-2026-10-13.md) and
the DDoS and availability research (kept with the paid service, in its own repository),
which the owner asked for before any development: *"A1, A3, B1, B2, B3, B4, B5, B6, B7, B8, B9,
B10, B12, D: Take your recommendation"*, and *"C: Yes, we'll need webrtc during the beta. It needs
to be as seamless UX as possible for the user or else adoption will suffer."* Each item names the
finding it answers. They revise [discovery-protocol.md](../design/discovery-protocol.md) and the
paid service's specification, which are brought in line before development starts.

1. **Claiming is done from the core** (A1; security S7, ease of use U5). The customer claims from
   the core's own System page, in the same browser, the core's admin approving the claim and the
   core showing which account holds it; this replaces D289 §6's check code compared on two screens,
   which protects little when the person comparing is the one being deceived.
2. **The paths are ranked by kind once the race ends** (A3; correctness C5, ease of use U1), within
   D273 §7 as amended: of the paths that succeeded, the LAN first, then IPv6 or IPv4, then WebRTC,
   round-trip time breaking ties; the client moves later only when its path fails or the network
   changes. Throughput is not measured in the race. The LAN name is tried only when the device
   seems to be at home, so Chrome's local-network prompt does not meet every first visit.
3. **Re-keying is signed by the old key** (B1; security S1). A lost key's recovery waits about 72
   hours and tells the customer by mail; the web client remembers a core's identity key on first
   contact; the core watches Certificate Transparency for its own names.
4. **The central web client is built reproducibly, its hashes published**, and served with
   integrity and content-security policies (B2; security S2). Sessions made through it keep their
   admin rights for now.
5. **Device codes on the paid tier** (B3; security S3, S4): the session is sealed to a key the
   device makes, so the service never holds it; the person entering a code sees where the device
   asking is; a device activated by a code may start with a narrower role.
6. **Signalling** (B4; security S5, S6): the core checks a device's locator itself, idle WebRTC
   connections close, offers are limited per locator, and the core signs its DTLS fingerprint with
   its identity key, so no discovery can sit between a client and its core.
7. **DNS and certificates** (B5; correctness C1, C2; security S12; availability): names answered by
   computing them from the name from the start, not a record each; DNS treated as on the playback
   path and kept available; Let's Encrypt's DNS-PERSIST-01 and renewal information (ARI), and a
   limit increase asked for early; CAA records naming the core's ACME account.
8. **Hosting for the beta** (B6; availability): Cloudflare's free plan in front of the service's
   HTTPS, the static client on Cloudflare Pages, and a second small machine at another provider
   holding a live copy of the database.
9. **Port mapping maps TCP 443 only** (B7; availability: Plex servers were used to amplify attacks
   through a port UPnP opened).
10. **A way back to one's core** (B8; ease of use U2): a reusable link per person that finds the
    core and grants nothing; a page for a device that knows no core; "Add to Home Screen" offered on
    iPhones, whose Safari erases a site's storage after seven days unvisited.
11. **Recovery** (B9; ease of use U6): after a backup restored without the identity key, the core
    guides its admin to re-key rather than enrol anew; the same key reclaims its old id after a
    lapse.
12. **The message when nothing reaches the core** is written for whoever reads it, suggests a
    phone's hotspot, and the beta counts how often it is shown (B10; ease of use U3).
13. **The document is brought in line with the code**, but for a core's id, which is 130 bits as
    the document says, not the 40 the code makes (B12; correctness).
14. **WebRTC through the discovery is in the beta** (C), so a household behind carrier NAT and a
    phone on IPv4-only Wi-Fi reach their core from the start; it must be seamless to the person.
15. **Two flaws in built code are to be fixed** (D; security S13): the single-target discovery's
    nonces carry their own expiry and MAC, and device codes are refused past their caps rather than
    pushing a waiting one out (D288 §6 as amended).

16. ~~**The customer's sign-in link follows current practice** (A2; security S8): at most 24 hours,
    spent only by the click on its page, never by opening it (mail scanners open links), tied to
    the browser that asked or confirmed when opened in another, cancelled by the next asked for.~~
    (Superseded by D310 §13: a username and a password.)
    The owner: *"if these are different things then just go with best practices. I'd mistakenly
    thought that the magic link was for invites."* Invitations are separate and keep their own
    lives: a household member's registration link on the core, 7 days by its setting
    (`registration_invitation_life_days`, D246 §2); a beta tester's invitation to the paid service,
    about 14 days, whose opening sends a fresh sign-in link then.
17. **A Watch Together link finds its core while it lives** (B11; correctness C3): finding the core
    by a link grants nothing, so it works again and again, as long as the link is live on the core;
    admission stays the core's, an unused link admitting its one person and a used one only the
    device holding the membership credential its first use gave (D267 §2). The owner: *"I want
    'watch together' links to be re-usable on the same device, so that if they accidentally close
    the page they can get back in."*
18. **One core per paying account in the beta** (B11), the account and its cores kept apart in the
    data, so more is a matter of price and dashboard later; and **two cores sharing one identity
    key**, a backup restored onto a second machine, are detected and refused (correctness C4). The
    owner: *"OK, go with your recommendations."* The rest of the correctness findings are taken as
    the audit recommends.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-13; design to fold into the protocol before development.

## D291 — What the discovery audits raised and D290 left open: taken as the audits recommend, the probe on a machine of its own, DNS on Bunny, IPv6 before IPv4

**Decided** (2026-10-13), by the project owner, on the questions
[discovery-protocol.md](../design/discovery-protocol.md) §7 and the paid service's specification
§11.3 listed after D290, and on the places where D290 and the four audit reports pulled apart. The
owner: *"All of this looks good"*, then, on the second machine, *"Go with your recommendations"*.

1. **The outside probe runs on a machine of its own** (S10), the smallest instance at any provider,
   holding no database and no secret but a token that can only post probe results; the spare of
   D290 §8 holds the database's copy and the service's secrets and runs nothing that talks to
   strangers until it takes over. The probe refuses private, shared, documentation and the cloud's
   internal addresses and the service's own, tests only what a core listed, and is rate-limited per
   core and per target. About €4 a month more.
2. **The zone's DNS is on Bunny DNS**, whose scripted records compute answers from the name, answering
   only for core ids that exist (C2, S12); Cloudflare stays in front of the service's own HTTPS
   (D290 §8), whose DNS cannot compute answers.
3. **IPv6 ranks before IPv4**, and a path whose round trip is far worse than the best (more than three
   times and 50 ms over) is demoted (C5), refining D290 §2.
4. **No Public Suffix List entry now** (S12, C1): the zone's own domain already isolates the service;
   it is revisited if the list's rules change.
5. **A device activated by a code gets ordinary rights** (S4): playback and its own settings, never
   admin, even when an admin entered the code; admin rights only once the person also signs in with
   their password on that device. Refines D290 §5.
6. **The rest of the open list is taken as the audits recommend** (protocol §7, the spec §11.3), but
   for a switcher for a person on two cores (U8), which waits until after the beta. Where an audit
   named no recommendation, a client that remembered a core's old identity key accepts the new one
   when the old key signed it, and after a key recovered without it (D290 §3) shows a plain notice
   that the server's identity changed, naming the date the owner confirmed it.

7. **The router is asked for outside port 443 first**, and whatever port it grants is taken when 443
   is held (S14 weighed against reach): a random high port keeps mass scanners off, but networks
   that allow only ports 80 and 443 cannot reach it, and a scanner finding 443 meets only a sign-in
   page with its limits. The owner: *"ok, go with your recommendation"*.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-13; design to fold into the protocol before development.

## D292 — The third audit round taken: no admin through a discovery, a thin path first, two machines, staging inside the owner's own names, the household zone at orpheum-core.com

**Decided** (2026-10-13), by the project owner, on the consolidated plan
(`orpheum-connect`'s `docs/plans/beta-bring-up.md`) built from the third round's four reports
([security](../design/research/discovery-audit3-security-2026-10-13.md),
[coherence](../design/research/discovery-audit3-coherence-2026-10-13.md),
[development loop](../design/research/discovery-devloop-2026-10-13.md),
[infrastructure, the core's part](../design/research/discovery-infra-core-2026-10-13.md)). The owner
took its 28 recommendations (*"agreed on the rest of the stuff"*) and changed two after asking:

1. **The household zone is `orpheum-core.com`**, registered and served at Cloudflare, replacing the
   `.app` domain and Bunny DNS (D291 §2). For the beta the service writes an A or AAAA record per
   published address, no computed answers (200 records a free zone); a script, at Bunny or elsewhere,
   is weighed again when the beta's count or a tested script calls for it. The isolation from
   `orpheum-app.com` is the separate registered domain; the HSTS preload `.app` gave is had by
   submitting `orpheum-core.com` to the list. Its apex holds `issue ";"` and `issuewild ";"`; each
   claimed core's own name allows Let's Encrypt for that core's ACME account by DNS-01 only.
2. **Staging has no domains or accounts of its own.** Its client and API are `app-staging.` and
   `api-staging.orpheum-app.com` (one level, which the free certificates cover), reached through a
   Cloudflare Tunnel whose token edits no DNS; its cores sit under a subzone of `orpheum-core.com`.
   Staging is used by the owner alone, so the rule that matters is that **no credential able to touch
   production enters the agent's sandbox**; and production's cookies are `__Host-` prefixed so no
   other subdomain can set them.
3. **The closed beta is scoped down:** a thin path working end to end on staging before any step is
   thickened; no customer accounts, sign-in links or mail (the operator claims each core by its
   code); two production machines (`prod-api`, which serves the client too, and `prod-probe`), the
   spare and Cloudflare Pages at the public launch; mailbox recovery, re-keying, CT watching, the NAT
   measurement, HPKE device codes, ARI and DNS-PERSIST-01 deferred; the version window promised from
   the public launch, a security floor from the first day. Revises D290 §8 and D289.
4. **Security** (audit3 A1–A12): a session minted through a discovery's client never carries admin;
   in the beta admin only from the core's own origin on its own network, a passkey later (revises
   D290 §4). Offers through a discovery are checked and bounded, and `discovery/single`'s K13–K15 are
   closed, before any signalling connection opens. A recovery code is made at claiming and seals the
   identity key in scheduled backups (revises D289 §2's leaving it out). A key change the old key did
   not sign blocks the client until a fresh link from the core (revises D291 §6). The identity key's
   fingerprint is in every link and QR, and answers are signed over the exact SDP. One "device" scope
   for every code-activated device (refines D291 §5). A used registration link becomes the person's
   own, revocable and bounded.
5. **No relay in the beta**; a relay for connections that fail waits on the beta's count (restates
   D274 §2 over "no relay, ever").
6. **Every household is told its core's home address** (link and QR), replacing D291 §6's last good
   LAN address, which an HTTPS page could not call.
7. **The edge VPS gains a Floating IPv4 and a WireGuard peer per deployment**, so staging runs beside
   nas.example (revises D272 §8's one shared key), and becomes the staging server once `media.` retires.
8. **Repositories:** `orpheum-connect` (the paid service, renamed from `orpheum-discovery`),
   `orpheum-ops` and `orpheum-site`, all private.
9. **The development loop:** check-pr back under its budget first; the service imports Orpheum by
   `replace` and a pin file; its own gates and Stop hook; Pebble pinned; a netlab tier on demand;
   two cores in the dev loop; `pion/transport/v5` and `golang.org/x/net` direct.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-13; to fold into the protocol, the plans and the specification in one
pass before development. *§4 narrowed 2026-10-20* (the owner, taking the device code audit's fixes,
docs/contributors/design/research/device-code-audit-2026-10-20.md): the device scope also leaves
out editing metadata and reading the person's own link, and the person's account page names each
