device a code activated in the past week.

## D293 — The discovery's open questions answered: a live instance is pinged before it is replaced, device codes through the service sealed by HPKE on P-256 in the beta, staging's DNS token in the sandbox until production

**Decided** (2026-10-13), by the project owner, on the questions the D292 pass left open
([discovery-protocol.md](../design/discovery-protocol.md) §9, `discovery-core.md`'s and the
specification's lists). The owner proposed §1 and asked for §2; the rest were taken as recommended
(*"all as recommended"*).

1. **A second instance pings the first.** When a core enrols with a new `instanceId` while another
   holds a signalling connection for the same `coreId`, the discovery pings the old instance on that
   connection and waits about 10 seconds: no answer, or no connection, and the newcomer replaces it;
   an answer, and the newcomer is refused as another copy, which says so in its log and on its System
   page and retries every few minutes. A crash-restart is accepted in seconds, a real second copy
   never displaces the one serving, and a stolen key cannot knock a live core off. Replaces both
   "the newest wins" (coherence decision 7) and waiting out missed heartbeats (T14).
2. **Device codes through the paid service are in the closed beta**, sealed with HPKE (RFC 9180)
   using DHKEM(P-256, HKDF-SHA256), not X25519: P-256 has been in Web Crypto for a decade and
   television browsers run old engines, so no minimum browser rises and no library is needed. Go's
   `crypto/hpke` seals on the core; the client opens with Web Crypto, checked against RFC 9180's
   vectors. The sealed blob carries the session, the core's id, its identity key's fingerprint and
   a device locator; nothing the device needs crosses the service readable. The page entering a
   code warns "only enter a code shown on a screen in front of you"; the line naming where the
   asking device is (D290 §5, S4) waits until after the beta, since it needs an IP-location
   database. Revises D292 §3's deferral of HPKE device codes; answers protocol §9 item 5.
3. **Staging's DNS token sits in the sandbox until production.** A Cloudflare token cannot be
   scoped below a zone, so staging's zone writer holds a token for `orpheum-core.com` while the zone
   holds nothing of value; before the first production core enrols, staging's writes move behind the
   production zone writer, accepting only staging's subzone, and the token is revoked, on M-S7's list
   beside the legacy token's. Staging's subzone is `staging.orpheum-core.com`. A narrow exception to
   D292 §2, bounded by that date.
4. **The core learns its discovery's client origin from the discovery**: a field in `GET /status`,
   accepted only as an `https` origin with no path and shown on the System page. It gives the
   discovery no power it lacks, since it already serves the client's code.
5. **A lost identity key in the beta** is re-keyed by the operator by hand, after checking with the
   household; recovery when built waits on its own design (protocol §9 item 3, after the beta).
6. **The core's state reaches a household member** as a `state` field in the `paths` answer.
7. **Failed connections are counted by the service:** the client reports a dead end to the
   discovery, which keeps a weekly count per core with no device identifier, and the core reads it
   with its heartbeat for the System page (D290 §12).
8. **The `paths` answer carries the client's network prefix** as the discovery sees it, the key the
   client's remembered paths need (§3.3 item 7).
9. **The account lock-out (audit3 A13) is fixed in Phase 1:** a device that proves an earlier
   sign-in (A8's device secret) passes the account-wide limit, networks are keyed by IPv6 /48, and
   the account-wide limit delays rather than refuses.
10. **The zone's apex serves no HTTPS:** Universal SSL stays off so its CAA stays `issue ";"`, and
    the HSTS preload of `orpheum-core.com` is not sought (revises D292 §1); each core's name sends
    its own HSTS.
11. **The reports' lesser items** (B1 items 5–6, B4, B7–B11, B13–B17, I9, the infrastructure
    report's §5.2 secrets rules) are taken as the reports recommend.

Left for when their features are built, after the beta: sign-in across browsers and mailbox
recovery's wait, the claim page's address, the NAT measurement, CT watching, the ACME library, and
the self-hosted discovery's questions (`discovery-mode.md`).

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-13; folded into the protocol, the plans and the specification.

## D294 — Admin from anywhere in the beta, and an operator's reset of who administers from the server's machine

> **Revised by [D297](#d297--a-household-is-found-by-its-realm-realm-name-and-password-together-proven-both-ways-by-a-key-the-password-makes-admin-only-from-the-cores-own-network) §6:** admin only from the core's own network, until passkeys.

**Decided** (2026-10-13), by the project owner, answering whether admin should come only from the
core's own network (D292 §4's second point; the security audit's A1), which in a container would
have ended admin on nas.example: *"Compromising a home server isn't the end of the world during beta.
The owner is deploying on his own homelab."*

1. **Admin works from anywhere.** No rule ties an admin session to the core's own network; D292
   §4's "in the beta admin only from the core's own origin on its own network" is withdrawn.
2. **The operator's way back in is a command on the server's machine**: `orpheum reset-admin
   --instance <dir> --name <person>` demotes everyone whose role administers to the user role, makes
   the person named the admin with a password read from standard input (asked twice without echo
   at a terminal), making the account when no one has the name, and ends that person's sessions. No
   account is removed. It runs beside a running server.
3. **Passkeys come later, as an option the owner turns on**, never required (revises D292 §4's
   "a passkey later" as the admin factor).
4. **A password sign-in carries the whole role wherever it comes from**, a discovery's page and
   WebRTC included, withdrawing D292 §4's "a session minted through a discovery's client never
   carries admin". The owner: *"If I'm remote, I still want to be able to administer my server ...
   the public facing login is what absolutely needs to be secure in the first place."* Without §1's
   withdrawn rule the restriction bought little: a password a compromised page harvested signs in
   directly at the core's own name wherever one is reachable, so it stopped only page script holding
   a session, and it left a core reachable only by WebRTC with no admin away from home. A device a
   code activated keeps the device scope (D292 §4; A11), and the core still believes nothing a
   WebRTC request's head says of where it came from.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-13.

## D295 — The security model: what a compromise costs decides what is hardened, the paid service most of all

**Decided** (2026-10-13), by the project owner: *"all we have to protect on the per-host level is a
video library."*

1. **What a compromise costs.** The paid service's would be catastrophic: it reaches every
   household. A core's, or a node's, is bad only where it can write: it could delete files or the
   metadata kept with them. One that cannot write costs little. A core's own database (accounts,
   watch history, identification) is restored from its backups.
2. **Nodes read the media only, by default.** A node's config file (TOML, as every config, D197)
   may allow writing metadata beside the media (NFO files, artwork) or full writing (deleting,
   moving), read at the node's start and settable by no other means: not by the core, the API, the
   node channel or a setting. Until a feature needs writing, there is no such key; what exists today
   is read-only three times over (the deployment's read-only mounts, `confine.MediaRoot`, and the
   forbidigo rule against removing and renaming). When a mode that writes is built, its key, the
   mount and the node's confinement change together, and the default stays read-only.
3. **Passkeys are each server's own choice**, never required (as D294 §3).
4. **The paid service follows best practice throughout** and is built to withstand penetration:
   its security work comes first in its plan, and what limits the harm a compromised service can do
   to households (the fingerprints in links, signed answers, sealed device codes) is kept.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-13.

## D296 — Staging's households move to their own domain, orpheum-test.com, so no sandbox token reaches production's zone

**Decided** (2026-10-14), by the project owner, revising D293 §3: *"OK, I'll get orpheum-test.com."*

1. **Why.** A Cloudflare token reaches a whole zone, and whoever can write a zone's records can
   have certificates issued for its names. While staging's cores lived under
   `staging.orpheum-core.com`, the sandbox's token could have rewritten production's households'
   records and taken certificates for them. D293 §3 answered that by moving staging's writes behind
   production's zone writer once the first production core enrolled; nas.example is about to be that
   core, and that route put production code on staging's path and days of security work before it.
2. **Staging's households live in `orpheum-test.com`**, a registered domain of their own, at
   Cloudflare beside `orpheum-core.com` and set up as it is: DNSSEC on, Universal SSL off, the apex
   holding only `issue ";"` and `issuewild ";"`, each core's name its own CAA. A staging core's names
   are `<address>.<core id>.orpheum-test.com`. The sandbox's token reaches `orpheum-test.com` alone,
   and the token for `orpheum-core.com` is revoked; production's is made later and never enters the
   sandbox. Production and staging share no zone, and no Let's Encrypt limit counted per registered
   domain: staging's re-issuing no longer spends production's.
3. **Staging's front names stay** `app-staging.` and `api-staging.orpheum-app.com` (D292 §2): their
   tunnel's token edits no DNS. Staging mirrors production: front names under `orpheum-app.com`, the
   households in a domain of their own. `orpheum-test.com` may later hold other test names.
4. **How others do it** (the owner asked): a separate registered domain for test environments is the
   common answer (Mozilla's `allizom.org`), since the registered domain is where cookies, DNS
   permissions and certificate limits stop. Delegating `staging.orpheum-core.com` to a second DNS
   provider would have kept two domains, at the cost of a second DNS client in the service.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-14. Revises D293 §3.

## D297 — A household is found by its realm: realm, name and password together, proven both ways by a key the password makes; admin only from the core's own network

> **Refined by [D298](#d298--a-realm-is-the-hosts-accounts-a-master-realm-chosen-once-a-subrealm-per-further-core-none-when-self-hosting):** the realm is the host's account's at the discovery, not the core admin's choice; the key is salted by the master realm.

**Decided** (2026-10-15), by the project owner, after the first production test, where a guest's
page lost its way and the owner could not tell staging from production: *"What if we did some kind
of realm system, where the admin chooses a realm name, and then his own users have realm, username,
pw?"*; then *"they must get all 3 correct or else the entire login fails"*. Revises D214 §3 and
D294 §1 and §4.

1. **A realm names a household at a discovery.** The admin chooses it on the System page; the
   discovery keeps it unique. Lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, 3 to 32 characters. A person
   with no link signs in at the discovery's page by realm, name and password together.
2. **All three, or nothing.** The sign-in answers only that it worked or that it did not, never
   which part was wrong, so no one learns which realms exist: there is no directory to harvest, and
   D214 §3's "never *what cores exist*" holds. The owner: *"It's actually more secure than
   username/pw because there's a third piece of information you have to get correct."* A guessed
   person's sign-in costs viewing, history and that person's account (D295); admin is what is
   dangerous, and §6 keeps it at home.
3. **The page proves its offer by a key the password makes, and the core proves its answer by the
   same key.** The page derives the key from realm, name and password with PBKDF2-SHA256 at 600,000
   rounds (OWASP's figure; built into browsers and Go, so no dependency); the offer goes to the
   discovery under the realm and a hash of realm and name, which tells the core whose key to use and
   tells the discovery no name. The core keeps each person's key, derived whenever it sees their
   password (sign-in, registration, a password set); an offer whose proof does not hold is refused
   before ICE, as every offer through a discovery is (A2). The core's answer carries, beside its
   identity signature, a tag under the person's key, which only the core can make: a discovery
   cannot answer in the core's place to harvest the password that the sign-in then sends, so the
   identity needs no trust on first use, and the page pins it for later visits. The discovery sees
   proofs, never passwords; turning a proof back into a password costs it 600,000 rounds a guess.
4. **Links stay** for what has no password: a Watch Together guest, a first invitation.
5. **The page shows the realm a person is signed in to**, beside their name. It stands in for a
   banner telling staging from production (the owner: *"show the realm a user is logged into (which
   will effectively serve the same purpose)"*). **"This is my own device: remember my realm"**, a
   box on the sign-in form, keeps the realm in the browser for next time; unticked, nothing is kept.
6. **Admin only from the core's own network**, until passkeys: the admin role takes effect only on
   a request that reached the core directly from an address on its own network, so `app.` at home,
   which reaches the core at its LAN name, administers, and the same page away from home, or any
   request over WebRTC, whose source the core cannot know, does not. Revises D294 §1 and §4 (*"keep
   it restricted to LAN-only for now"*); passkeys for admin away from home come later, as D294 §3
   has them.
7. **Staging and nas.example are two households of production's discovery**, the realms `staging` and
   `nas`, so one site reaches either and the realm says which (the owner: *"can't we just set up two
   realms now: staging and nas? Basically treat them as two hosts"*). The staging core enrols as any
   household does: its credential reaches only its own records, so D296's rule holds. `app-staging.`
   and its discovery stay for testing the discovery itself.
8. **Not decided here:** a realm's renaming re-keys every person (the key's salt names the realm),
   so each signs in once more by another way after one; whether to keep the old keys meanwhile is
   left until renaming is built.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-15.

## D298 — A realm is the host's account's: a master realm chosen once, a subrealm per further core, none when self-hosting

**Decided** (2026-10-15), by the project owner, refining D297 while it was being built: *"A host who
is self-hosting has no realm, and we don't show anything realm-related in that case. A host who
decides to do the paid service creates an account with us, and then can define which master realm
he wants."* Revises D297 §1, §7 and §8.

1. **Self-hosting has no realm.** An owner's own discovery (`discovery/single`) offers no realm
   sign-in, and the page shows nothing of realms unless its discovery says it has them (a meta tag,
   as it names its client API). A development or test discovery may name one, to test it.
2. **The master realm is the host's account's**, chosen when the account is made, first come first
   served, unique at the paid discovery, and never changed (*"If enough users complain we can
   revisit changing it, but it avoids complications with existing logged in users"*): 5 to 32
   lowercase letters, digits and inner hyphens, few enough to guess.
3. **A core takes the master realm, or the master and a subrealm**: one core alone takes the
   master realm by default; each further one takes a subrealm, `<master>.<subrealm>`, 1 to 32 of the
   same characters, unique within the account, and the first core may be given one later
   (`karlnas`, then `karlnas.test` beside it, then the first renamed `karlnas.live`). No part holds a
   dot, so none is mistaken for another's. The discovery gives the core its realm; the core only shows
   it (D297 §1's admin choosing it on the System page is withdrawn).
4. **A person's realm key is salted by the master realm alone** (revising D297 §3's salt and §8):
   a subrealm given or changed later leaves every key as it was, and the core finds the person a
   sign-in names by the whole realm and their name, which needs no password. A person renamed signs in
   once with their password before their realm sign-in works again, since the key names them.
5. **Connecting a core to the paid service is by a code the service shows**, which the admin enters
   on the core over the house's network, as the core's other codes are entered; until customer
   accounts exist, the operator gives realms on `prod-api` (`up.sh realm <core> <realm>`), and the
   claim stays as it is.

6. **Cancelling keeps every account and password.** A host who leaves the paid service runs a VPS
   with an address per core, their own concern; each core's people sign in at its own address with
   the names and passwords they had, which the core alone ever held, and that page has no realm
   field, its discovery having none (the owner: *"All that changes is the login URL"*). A core that
   leaves its discovery forgets its realm keys, which serve nothing after.
7. **At most five subrealms per account** to start, one tier of subscription, until the owner weighs
   tiers by the number of cores (*"$3 a month for one core, $4 a month for up to 5 cores or something
   like that. But for now we just have one tier"*); the discovery holds the count.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-15. The code-entry connection, subrealm management and the count wait for
customer accounts; the realm's shape, its key and its sign-in come with D297's work.

## D299 — A core that leaves its discovery keeps its people's realm keys

**Decided** (2026-10-15), by the project owner (*"OK to keep the keys"*), revising D298 §6's last
sentence. Staging left one discovery and joined another under the same master realm, and every realm
sign-in was refused until each person signed in once on the core's own page: the keys had gone with
the Leave. A person who only ever reaches the core from away, as a Watch Together partner does, has
no such page, and would be locked out of realm sign-in after any move.

1. **Leaving forgets no realm key.** A key is salted by its master realm (D298 §4), so a kept key
   serves nothing but that realm; a core that comes back under it is found by its people at once, and
   one given another master realm makes new keys at their next sign-in, as before.
2. **Passwords stay as D298 §6 says**; only its forgetting of the keys is withdrawn.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-15.

## D300 — A WebRTC connection made inside the house counts as home; the core offers WebRTC on its LAN address

**Decided** (2026-10-15), by the project owner (*"option A sounds good"*, *"I don't mind taking longer
to do it properly"*), revising D297 §6's "any request over WebRTC … does not". Firefox fails every
request a page at a discovery's origin makes to a LAN address once the page's service worker controls
it, even with its local-network permission granted (idiosyncrasies.md), so `app.` at home could not
administer in Firefox; WebRTC is not subject to that check. A core in a container offered no address
a device at home could reach over WebRTC, so a page at home went out through the VPS and back.

1. **The core takes WebRTC on its LAN address.** A deployment that names the house's address
   (`[lan] address`) has the core gather its host candidates on one UDP port (`[webrtc] udp_port`),
   published at that address on the same port, and add that address, at that port, to every answer
   as a host candidate. A core with no LAN address gathers as before.
2. **The audit's A2 holds, sharpened.** An offer through a discovery still never makes the core send
   a check into its own networks: a candidate the offer names in them is dropped before the offer
   is answered. The core answers a check that reaches it from an address in its home networks
   (`server.home_networks`), and only the address that sent it: a device in the house had to send
   it, and nothing a discovery passes on chooses it.
3. **A request over WebRTC is from home** when its connection's selected pair is not relayed and the
   client's end of it is in the home networks, as the core's own end of the pair says; anything else
   over WebRTC is not. The core alone decides it, from its end of the connection: nothing a page
   sends counts, and every admin operation refuses a request that is not from home (D297 §6).
4. **A page tries WebRTC next when its LAN name fails after answering**: it is in the house, so
   WebRTC finds the LAN pair there, where the core's public names would take it out through the VPS
   and away from admin.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-15.

## D301 — An unsettled match takes the oldest candidate, the most voted within a year, and an admin corrects it from the title's page

**Decided** (2026-10-15), by the project owner, revising D172 §3's "anything else is not guessed".
nas.example's "Needs a match" held about 85 titles, many the owner saw as obvious (*"Some are indeed
ambiguous, but others (like The Thief of Bagdad with an identified year of 1992) should be pretty obvious. I
think that when something has no date and there are multiple versions available, we should choose
the oldest one by default, and then offer a 'this is identified incorrectly' button on the details
page so that the admin can correct it"*), and for two works of one name in one year (Disney's
*The Thief of Bagdad* and a lesser one, both 1992) the agent's proposal of the vote count (*"Yes that sounds
good"*).

1. **Among the candidates whose names match**, as D172's tiers find them, where more than one
   remains: with no year in the name, the **oldest** is taken (a series by its first air date);
   with a year, the one with the **most votes** at the source among those of that year. A
   provider ID in hand, and a single clear winner, are taken as before.
2. **A taken guess is corrected from the title's page**: an admin's "Identified incorrectly" opens
   the chooser over the candidates kept for it (D172 §3 item 3), and their choice is final as any
   person's choice is (D170).
3. **Nothing whose name matches no candidate is guessed**: "No match" stays as it is.
4. **A guess is marked as one where its title is shown**, until an admin confirms or corrects it,
   which keeps D172's "nothing says it is a guess" from coming back: the owner's uncertain-match icon
   (a question mark on a caution yellow, ringed over art) in a **tray of status cues** down from the
   poster's top-right corner, under the warning sign of one that cannot play (D278), opening what it
   means as that sign does; and on the film's or series' page the same icon with an explanation
   suited to its reader, an admin told how to correct it (*"a vertical icon tray going down from the
   top right corner to display status cues. On the info page for the video we can display the same
   icons when relevant, with an explanation (suitable to the audience)"*).

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-15.

## D302 — An admin may administer from away from home, by their own setting, off by default

**Decided** (2026-10-15), by the project owner, beside D297 §6 and D300 §3: *"an admin user should
have a field they can set for their user to give them admin from outside anyway, default disabled.
Later we can add another enum to it: only with passkey."*

1. **Each admin has a setting, "Administer from away from home"**, one of `never` (the default)
   and `always`; `with_passkey` comes with passkeys (D294 §3). It is set by the admin for
   themselves, from home.
2. **The server decides it**, at every request, as it decides home (D297 §6): an admin whose
   setting is `always` administers from any network; one whose setting is `never`, only from home.
   Nothing a page sends changes it.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-15; scheduled after D301 and the tiered gate.

## D303 — The data layer is rebuilt to written principles: short writes that re-check what they decided, a fresh baseline, committed statistics, hourly backups

**Decided** (2026-10-15), by the project owner, after nas.example's requests waited 3–47 s behind an
identification pass that held SQLite's one writer for 25–30 s. The evidence is three research
documents: the [access audit](../design/research/database-access-audit-2026-10-15.md), the
[practice research](../design/research/data-layer-practice-2026-10-15.md) (principles DL1–DL17),
and an [independent DBA's audit](../design/research/data-layer-independent-audit-2026-10-15.md)
(amendments, and principles M1–M13). The owner: *"These look good to me"*, then, on the
independent audit's amendments and additions, *"Agreed"*.

1. **The principles are standard.** DL1–DL17 as amended by the independent audit §2, and M1–M13
   from its §3, become rules in [sql.md](../standards/sql.md) and the
   [audit checklist](../audit-checklist.md), each with what enforces it. In short:
   - **Correctness first (M1–M4).** A write that depends on a read made outside its transaction
     re-checks it inside, by compare-and-set; rows people edit carry a `revision`. A read built
     from several queries uses one read transaction. Every identity is a unique constraint.
     A write transaction covers one consistency unit (a title with its versions and text, a
     series with its episodes), within a budget of milliseconds, and a chunked job resumes.
   - **Access paths (DL1–DL5).** Each query's path and the index serving it are written down and
     checked. A column with few values never leads an index unless every query binds the next.
     A foreign key whose parent can be deleted, or that cascades, has a child index. A partial
     index is used only by queries that repeat its condition literally; the tombstoned side has
     its own.
   - **Requests (DL6, DL10).** Nothing a request does grows with the library; counts are SQL;
     reading never writes.
   - **Writes (DL7–DL9, DL11).** A write that changes nothing writes nothing (guarded upserts and
     triggers, stamps excluded). People's writes go before background work through a writer
     service with aging and group commit.
   - **Derived data (DL12–DL14).** Grouping files into titles and resolving one title's values
     are separate derivations; a change re-derives what it touched; inputs carry a fingerprint
     and a rules version; bursts coalesce. The whole-library run is a backstop that compares.
   - **Integrity in the engine (M5).** `STRICT` tables (sqlc 1.31.1 parses them), cross-column
     `CHECK`s, subtypes tied to their supertype's kind.
   - **Operations and tests (DL16–DL17, M6–M11).** Connection settings by measurement; slow work
     names itself; invariants as zero-row SQL run after tests and nightly; data split by
     volatility and width; random-operation and crash-injection tests; a retention policy per
     growing table; a stated protocol between `persistent.db` and `cache.db`.
2. **No migration: the current database is discarded** (*"Agreed on not doing a migration for
   this step. We toss out the current db."*). The redesign is a fresh baseline; staging and
   nas.example start empty and scan and match again. This ends D272 §5's window for this change.
3. **Planner statistics are committed** (DL15): a `sqlite_stat1` generated from the reference
   library, loaded into every database, with a test that fails when it is stale. Nothing runs
   `ANALYZE` or `PRAGMA optimize`; plans are tested over several library shapes.
4. **A session's last use is kept in memory** (DL10) and written in a batch about once a minute
   and at shutdown, never earlier than the stored value; the idle check, Your devices and the
   live locators read the later of the stored and the remembered time.
5. **Deleting a person pseudonymises** (M12): *"Probably fine to pseudonymise and keep."* Their
   name and personal fields are cleared; their history stays under their id.
6. **Edits keep no history** (M13): *"I doubt that a record of changes would be very useful."*
   The last write wins, as now.
7. **Backups are hourly** (M6), revisiting D243 §11's daily one: *"would it hurt anything to make
   it an hourly backup?"* — it does not, once a backup reads a snapshot on its own connection
   instead of holding the writer. A backup is skipped when nothing changed (`data_version`),
   older copies thin out (24 hourly, 7 daily, 4 weekly), and each copy passes `integrity_check`.
   The recovery point is an hour.
8. **The gates are built first** and fail on today's code; their gate-file changes are approved
   (*"#4 sounds good"*): every foreign key whose parent can go has an index; every query's plan,
   both databases', is read; a GET writes nothing; a second pass writes nothing; every table is
   `STRICT`; nothing runs `ANALYZE`; the invariants pass.
9. **Phases:** A, the store's foundation (read transactions, the writer service, a maintenance
   connection, settings, last use in memory, the first gates); B, the fresh baseline schema; C,
   the derivation split; D, operations (integrity checks, metrics, runbook, restore drill,
   retention).

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-15. Revisits D243 §11 (backup schedule) and D272 §5 (this change
starts a new baseline). Phase A next. §1's M4, DL13 and DL14 amended by D304; §5 and §7 revised by D305.

## D304 — A library is filed in stages by weight: titles show from the listing, still reading, and fill in by whole units

**Decided** (2026-10-16), by the project owner, on the
[staged identification proposal](../design/research/staged-identification-2026-10-16.md), after
the owner's: *"We should be able to trickle in the lightest data, then progressively build out the
higher level data in small batches + jobs. We're aiming for eventual consistency (good enough for a
nice UX), not a perfect view at every single moment."* It amends D303 §1 (M4, DL13, DL14) and
revises D240 §3, §4 and §8.

1. **Five stages, by weight**: the listing stores every file, a new video unread; filing from the
   path; the small files beside a video (NFO, images, subtitles) in their own fast read; the
   provider's match; and the video's read (probe and payload hash, D179), at the slow priority
   (D255).
2. **The unit of work is a filing unit**: a film's folder, or loose files sharing one name and
   year; in a series library, one series. A unit is never split across writes, and a write holds
   as many whole units as a budget allows (M4). Each stage finds its work from stored state (D231
   §3); a change marks its unit as owing filing again, in memory (DL14), and the whole-library
   comparison on a reader, writing in batches, is the backstop.
3. **DL13 is amended**: compare before writing, with the whole-library run as the backstop; no
   fingerprints (*"Agreed"*).
4. **Every title shows straight from the listing, marked "still reading"** until its video is
   read, and cannot play until then (*"Yes, Show every title straight from the listing, marked
   'still reading'"*). Play asks for that video's read at a person's priority.
5. **A move is told by device and inode** at the listing, D240 §3's move that §8 deferred, so a
   renamed folder does not show its films twice before they are read (*"Yes."*). A file whose
   read later shows the payload a tombstone holds brings that title back, which absorbs the one
   filed from the path, keeping what a person set on it.
6. **Each retention limit of D303 §1's retention policy is a config value** with a sane default and bounds
   (*"Sane limits for each, stored as a config value."*).

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-16; to be built in the proposal's §7 order.

## D305 — Removing a person deletes what was theirs; backups are hourly, thinned by counts the config holds

**Decided** (2026-10-16), by the project owner, on two of D303's open questions. It revises D303
§5 and §7.

1. **Removing a person deletes what was theirs, not pseudonymises it** (D303 §5, M12). The owner,
   asked what removal should keep: *"I've already said that I don't need an audit trail (who set
   what when) because the most likely setup will have a single admin, and even two admins wouldn't
   need it. [...] What data do we have that wouldn't be an easily purged leaf table off a user (and
   that we really would want to keep around for other reasons)?"*; and to the proposal below,
   *"yes"*. Each table of the person's alone is emptied of their rows by the package that writes it
   (their watching, preferences, credentials, devices and realm key); the columns that record who
   set something everyone shares (an override, a setting, a key) are cleared; and the person's row
   stays only as a nameless tombstone (no name, password or note), so ids are never reused and a
   subtitle fetched for everyone still names a row. Watch counts, should they matter one day, are
   a counter on the title.
2. **Backups are hourly with no quiet hour** (D303 §7): *"what is a quiet hour?"*, then *"yes"* to
   dropping it. A backup runs each hour, is skipped when nothing changed, and old ones thin to so
   many hourly, daily and weekly, each count a config value with a sane default (24, 7, 4) and
   bounds, as D304 §6's retention limits are.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-16.

## D306 — The scanner is tested on names of our own, places an unnumbered episode by a guessed title match, and keeps watching by title and edition

**Decided** (2026-10-16), by the project owner, on the questions of the scanner research
(`design/research/library-scanner-practice-2026-10-16.md`), the data-delivery review and D304 §6's
retention. It revises D172 for episodes and D304 §6 for plays.

1. **Test names are our own.** *"I'd prefer not to get into licensing issues. How about we use
   those as inspiration and generate our own test data that has similar issues?"* No file name is
   copied from another project's tests, whatever its licence. Ours are written in the same shapes
   and with the same difficulties.
2. **An episode whose name has no number may be placed by its title, fuzzily, as a guess.**
   *"We can do a fuzzy match and mark it as guessed."* The file's title text is matched against
   the provider's episode list of its series. A match places the file and is marked guessed, as
   D301's unsettled match is, so an admin can see and correct it. The path still decides when it
   holds a number. This revises D172's "never guessed" for this one case.
3. **A "filed wrongly" report is a Markdown file on the server's disk.** *"We could make it save
   the report to the disk somewhere, and then the admin can view it (probably markdown is best)
   and decide if he wants to tweak personal info before posting it as a github issue."* Nothing
   leaves the server by itself. The admin reads it on the System page too, with a copy button
   (the owner chose "On disk and on the System page").
4. **Daily and date-numbered shows are out of the beta's scope.** *"Out of scope for beta. Make
   sure the architecture can handle adding it later."* A position stays a group and a number, and
   the parser's result keeps room for a date.
5. **Disc folders, ISOs and `cd1`/`cd2` films are out of the beta.** *"We'll keep them out of beta
   for now, unless people start asking for it."* One is listed as skipped, "disc image, not
   supported yet", rather than ignored in silence.
   *Revisited by [D350](#d350--a-disc-image-plays-its-main-title-read-by-the-node-from-the-images-own-structure-and-served-to-ffmpeg-through-fdproxy)
   (2026-10-26): an `.iso` image is read, its main title played; disc folders stay skipped.*
6. **Absurd data is a health signal.** To "should a series with far more specials than its files
   or listing could explain appear in Needs attention?": *"Yes"*.
7. **Off-screen rows may go stale while a library is filed.** To "may rows off screen go stale
   until scrolled back to?": *"yes"*. A poll reads the window in view, and pages scrolled past are
   read again when they come back into view.
8. **Watching follows the title and its edition, not the file.** *"Plays should match name +
   edition (so if someone gets the director's cut dvd rip of XYZ, deletes that because the file
   is defective, then gets another copy, it still has the play count)."* A removed file can then
   be purged by D304 §6's limits without taking what was watched of it. An unknown cut matches
   any cut, and two different known cuts keep their own history (the owner chose "Carry if either
   is unknown"). What carries is whether it was watched and how often, not the resume position:
   a new copy starts from its beginning (the owner chose "No, keep only watched/play count").

9. **Reads follow series → season.** A series is read with its seasons and their counts and the
   season it opens on; a season is read with its episodes, paged. No response grows with a
   library's damage.
10. **The client cache and list windowing are our own code**, grown from `useResource` and
    `Remembered`, with no new dependency.

The owner, to the recommendations on disc images, series → season reads and the client cache:
*"ok, I agree with your recommendations."*

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-16.

## D307 — A work released under another name is guessed from the provider's search; a series with unplaced episodes has every season fetched

**Decided** (2026-10-17), by the project owner, on the agent's two questions after the first full
scan of the owner's NAS. It revises D301 §3 and builds D306 §2.

1. **A candidate whose name differs may still be guessed** (D301 §3 said none was). The owner, to
   "When TMDB returns exactly one series in the folder's year but under a different name (Kaito Kumo
   (1971) is TMDB's "Kaito the 3rd", 1971), should it be accepted as a guess?": *"Yes. There are
   some series that had different names depending on the country they were destined for. Kaito Kumo
   in Japan was released as Kaito the 3rd in America. Many Japanese titles had similar treatment.
   "Kaze no Mamoribito", also called "Keeper of the Quiet Wind" was later released as
   "Moribito: Keeper of the Quiet Wind"."* When no candidate's name matches: with a year in the
   name, the one candidate of that year is the guess; with none, a search that found one or two
   candidates takes the oldest, as D301 §1 does. A search that found more found the words, not the
   work under another name (staging, 2026-10-16: "Harbor Lights" found eight works with the word in
   them), and is a person's choice. Each such guess is marked and corrected as D301's are. The
   bound of two is the agent's, from the owner's examples, and the owner's to move.
2. **An unnumbered episode is placed by its name across every season** (D306 §2), the owner to
   "Should I build the guessed episode placement next, including fetching every season of an
   affected series?": *"Yes"*. A series with episodes that have no number outside a specials or
   extras folder has every season's listing its provider lists fetched, and such an episode whose
   name matches one episode of them is placed there, marked as a guess.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-17.

## D308 — app.orpheum-app.com serves a small loader, and each core serves its own client

> **Revised by [D319](#d319--stagings-client-origins-are-orpheum-client-testcom-behind-one-wildcard-on-stagings-tunnel)** (2026-10-19): staging's client origins are `<core id>.orpheum-client-test.com`, behind one wildcard on staging's tunnel.

**Decided** (2026-10-17), by the project owner, after the update to v0.2.0-nas.8 needed prod-api
repackaged for a change in the core's API alone. It refines D273, whose §6 keeps the protocol
between a core and its discovery stable but says nothing of the one between a client and its core.

1. **The client a browser runs is its core's.** The page at the discovery's origin today is the
   whole web client, built into the discovery's package, so the client of every household is the
   one the discovery last shipped, whatever its core runs: one API change, and every core on the
   older version breaks. The owner asked: *"Shouldn't the web client details come from the
   core?"* Of three ways (the agent's): a small, stable loader that fetches its core's client over
   whichever path reached it; the discovery hosting each version, with the core naming its own;
   or a client-to-core API kept compatible across a window as §6 keeps the discovery's. The owner:
   *"Go with 1"*.
2. **The loader is the discovery's; the client is the core's.** The discovery's page signs in by
   realm, finds the core and races its paths (D273 §7), and then runs the client the core serves
   over the path that won, checked before it runs. The discovery's package then changes only when
   the loader or the discovery does, never for a core's release, and a core built by anyone runs
   with the client it was built with. On the core's own address (at home) nothing changes: the core
   serves its client there already.

3. **Each core's client has an origin of its own, under a new registered domain**, after an
   independent audit ([client-from-core-security-audit-2026-10-17.md](../design/research/client-from-core-security-audit-2026-10-17.md))
   found that a core's code on `app.`'s shared origin could take other households' sessions and
   their admin from home, and that Cloudflare's free certificate on `orpheum-core.com` would likely
   cancel the per-core CAA of D292 §1. The owner: *"I'll register a new domain."* `app.` keeps no
   core's session.
4. **A realm sign-in hands over by a single-use code**, the owner choosing it over a second password
   (*"Typing the password twice is annoying. We go with (a)."*): `app.`'s loader signs in with the
   password, asks the core for a code of one use and a short life bound to the device, keeps
   nothing, and the client's origin exchanges the code for its own session.
5. **No sessions are carried over.** The owner: *"The only deployments so far are your staging, and
   nas.example. Both are expendable, and nobody but you and me have logged into either."*

6. **The owner's answers to the rest** (2026-10-17):
   - The domain is **`orpheum-client.com`** (*"I'll use orpheum-client.com"*), and staging's client
     origins are in it too (*"use the same domain for staging"*), one level down as the free
     certificate covers.
   - A core **signs a list of its client's file hashes**, which the loader checks before any of it
     runs, and the discovery publishes **a floor of client versions it refuses** (*"yes"*).
   - The browser **keeps each core's client by its hashed file names**, checked against the signed
     list each time (*"yes"*).
   - The audit's finding that a core's media cookie reaches another core's pages is **fixed apart
     from D308** (*"fix it"*).
   - Opened by itself, `app.` **sends the browser to the last core it reached, with links to the
     others it is signed in to** (*"Send to the last one, with links to any others the browser is
     logged into"*); refined by §8.

7. **No Public Suffix List entry for now; disciplines instead** (the agent's proposal; the owner:
   *"agreed. Proceed."*). The owner, having bought both
   domains for a year: *"Aren't there other methods or disciplines we can apply to mitigate the
   worst? Consider the actual threat model we face."* Separate origins already stop a core's code
   taking other households' sessions, their service workers or their admin; what being one site
   leaves is a nuisance in one browser, so instead:
   - no client origin sets or reads a cookie: connectd sends no `Set-Cookie` there and the client
     never writes `document.cookie`, each held by a test;
   - the loader deletes every cookie it can see at its start, and its page is kept by its service
     worker, so a cookie bomb from another core's code can only stop a browser's first visit;
     *amended 2026-10-19, the owner:* the kept page is opened only when the origin fails (a cookie
     bomb's refusal included), not first: opened first, the visit after an update ran the page
     before it, and a household whose server was replaced read "This link no longer finds its
     server" until a reload (*"I don't mind a short wait on initial load"*);
   - every client origin sends `Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1` and `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy:
     same-origin`;
   - the entry is weighed again at the public launch, when the registration can be extended past
     the list's two years.
8. **The household list is `app.`'s alone** (the owner: *"We shouldn't make core aware of how many
   cores app knows of, because the situation could change while I'm navigating around in core"*).
   `app.` remembers each core it handed a browser to (its id, fingerprint, realm and name, nothing
   secret). Opened by itself it sends the browser to that core when it knows one, and lists them,
   last used first, when it knows several. A client's menu always offers to switch household, which
   goes back to `app.` with a mark asking for the list however many there are, one included. The
   list also leads to the sign-in by realm, to join another core (*"This page should also have a
   button to bring the user to the login screen so they can join a new core"*), and each entry can
   be forgotten. Whether a browser is still signed in to a core is not shown: only that core's own
   origin knows.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-17.

## D309 — A player says which quality it wants and from where, and a run no player wants stops

> **§1 amended by [D355](#d355--a-playbacks-picture-and-sound-are-each-wanted-from-a-position-of-their-own-moved-by-their-own-asks-and-together-by-a-seek-a-pause-a-resume-and-the-start)** (2026-10-27): a playback's picture and sound are each wanted from a position of their own, moved by their own asks; its word, a seek, a pause, a resume and its start move both.

**Decided** (2026-10-17), by the project owner, after Wings on nas.example stopped for minutes after a
small seek. The node was making four runs: two of 720p, left from before the player moved to 360p,
and two of 360p. One 720p run measured just under 1.1x, so the newest run, a 360p one 3.5 s old that
the player needed, was evicted (D250 §6). Every rule that chose it guessed: a run was in use when a
player had asked for any of its chunks in the last 30 s, a seek was told from how far apart two asks
were (D250 §5, D286 §1), and a player moved onto another quality needed a rule of its own (D286 §4).
The owner: *"What if we had clients express interest and disinterest? Then we'd know if there's
actually any reason to keep chunks around or even continue them. Each client can only express
interest in one quality at a time."* It revises D247 §10, D250 §5 and §6, and D286 §1 and §4.

1. **A player says what it wants: one picture quality, from a position, and its sound.** It says so
   as it starts, and again whenever its quality-switching (D265) moves it or a seek moves where it
   plays: each saying replaces the last. Leaving the film withdraws it.
2. **A run no player wants is stopped at once**, with no grace period and no rule of distance: a
   run of a quality its players left, or of a place they sought away from. A Watch Together group's
   run goes on while any member wants it; members on different qualities each keep their own.
3. **Interest lapses when a player falls silent.** Its play reports renew it, so a closed tab, a
   crash or a lost link lets it end; the player's own word is the signal, the lapse only the backstop.
4. **A paused player wants only the minute ahead of it** (the agent's proposal; the owner:
   *"agreed on all points"*): its run makes that minute and stops, so a tab paused for an hour holds
   no encoder, and playing again starts at once.
5. **Chunks no one wants are kept, within the disk budget**: interest decides what a node encodes;
   what is made costs only disk, and a rewind or a second viewer plays it again.
6. **When the runs players want cannot all keep up, a player moves down a quality** (D286 §4's move,
   made the rule): the run that gives way is one a player wants, moved to the quality below; only a
   player already at the lowest is stopped and told why (D250 §6).
7. **A player that stops says why, and the reason decides what is finished and what is kept**
   (the owner, 2026-10-17: *"When a client stops, it gives a reason … The reason determines how
   strongly we keep the 1 minute of data in cache, and whether we cancel the filling of that 1
   minute"*). The reasons: **paused**; **left its page** (navigated away, closed the tab, the page
   hidden for good); **played another film**; and, unsaid, **silent** (a crash, a lost link). Paused
   and left both finish what is made ahead of where they stopped, then stop; another film stops the
   old film's runs at once; a quality switched from is not wanted again (§2). A paused player
   replaces §4's minute: what is finished ahead is **`chunk_kept_ahead_seconds`**, 30 by default
   (*"Is 1 minute of pre-generated data too much? Would 30 seconds be better? Should we make this a
   config value?"*, the agent's proposal: the player's own buffer already holds about 30 s; the owner:
   *"yes"*).
8. **What is made is kept by tier, the highest any player gives it** (the owner's tiers; *"The
   highest priority demanded by any client determines the resulting cache priority"*). The
   playbacks are the list of who wants what, so a store's tier is read from them, never kept beside
   it. From when its player was last heard (the owner: *"5 minutes, 10 minutes, 20 minutes. After 20
   minutes they might as well start the process anew"*):
   - **in use**: a playing player's, heard within §3's lapse;
   - **likely**: a paused or silent player's, for 5 minutes;
   - **maybe**: theirs to 20 minutes, and a player's that left its page, for 10;
   - **unlikely**: a quality switched from, a film another replaced, and everything after.
   The node removes the lowest tier first, the least lately used within one, and only when it needs
   the room: an unlikely store is first to go, not deleted at once (*"4: yes"*). The times are
   settings.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-17; §7 and §8 the same evening.

## D310 — The closed beta runs on the paid service, free: an account gives one key for one core, the core's admin enters it at home, and the household then uses the service's app

**Decided** (2026-10-18), by the project owner, at the milestone reassessment
([milestone-reassessment-2026-10-18.md](../design/research/milestone-reassessment-2026-10-18.md)),
after it found that the discovery run today matches neither outcome the owner wants: a discovery a
household runs on its own VPS, and the paid service with accounts and registration. The owner:
*"For closed beta, we build an easy, free-for-now version of the paid service so that people don't
need to set up their own VPS. People who participate in the closed beta will get a free-for-life
account, so we can build out the account service, and then I'll test account termination and such
myself while everyone else has a permanent subscription. For open beta we can have the self-host
version. The key is to make the core registration process incredibly easy … Actually, we should
probably limit them to one key (one core) for now, and decide later if multi-core support is
something we really want to open up yet."* It brings the paid service's accounts (P2) into the
closed beta, replaces the operator's claim from the console (P4, D292 §3) for customers, and gives
D290 §1's claim from the core its form.

1. **The closed beta runs on the paid service, free.** No beta household sets up a VPS. The
   discovery a household runs itself (discovery-mode W4b.5, W4b.8) comes with the open beta.
2. **A closed-beta household's account is free for life**: a permanent subscription, which no
   lapse reaches. The account service is built whole all the same, and the owner tests lapse,
   termination and the exit path (D289 §5) on the owner's own accounts.
3. **Registration is the person's own, and it is easy**: they make an account (free in the beta)
   and it gives them a key for their core.
4. **One key, for one core, per account, for now.** Whether an account may hold several cores is
   decided later.
5. **The core is claimed from the core** (D290 §1): its admin, signed in to it at home, enters the
   key, and the core joins the account. Setting up a core must be very simple: an install a
   household follows without help is part of this decision, not an extra.
6. **Then the household reaches it through the service's app** (app.orpheum-app.com, D308), from
   anywhere.
7. **A discovery a household runs itself enrols its core the same way** (the owner, the same day:
   *"The admin creates the discovery service on their VPS, and gets a core key via the cmdline on
   their VPS, points their core to their domain and enters the key to enrol."*): the discovery's
   command line gives the key, the core is pointed at the household's own domain, and its admin
   enters the key at home. One way to enrol, whichever discovery holds the core; it replaces the
   claim by the core's code that W4b.8 planned (`orpheum discovery claim <code>`).

The owner answered §1–§7's open questions the same day: *"A key is one-time-use. If they fuck
something up, they can request a new key, which invalidates the old key. A user is invited via
invite URL, which I generate via an admin panel on the paid discovery server (with a note field so
I know which invite is for whom - similar to the watch together link we have now). These can also
be removed from the admin panel. A user can see their server from an admin panel in the paid
discovery server app (different login from the core login, different username, completely
unrelated except that it entitles them to enrol a core). They click generate key for this core, and
have 1h to use it. If they click generate key again, the old key is invalidated, and any core
enroled via that key is kicked out (no matter how long it's been enroled). By "do everything" I
mean in the same sense that it works now (they can admin from remote only if they opt in)."*

8. **A key is used once, within an hour of being made.** The account's panel has *Generate key*
   for its server.
9. **Generating a key again invalidates the last one, and removes any core enrolled with it**,
   however long ago it enrolled. A household that got something wrong starts over with a new key;
   with §4's one core per account, the new key's core is the account's only one.
10. **A person joins by an invitation URL** the operator makes in the paid service's own admin
    panel, each with a note saying whom it is for, as Watch Together's links have (D246); the
    operator can remove one there.
11. **The service's account is apart from every core's accounts**: its own sign-in and its own
    username, related to nothing on the core, granting only that it may enrol a core (D289 §1).
    Its panel shows the account its server.
12. **"Do everything" from the app is what the app does now**: admin away from home only where the
    core's admin opted in (D292, D302, unchanged).
13. **The service's account signs in with its username and a password; a second factor such as a
    passkey comes later** (the owner, the same day: *"The link is only an entitlement to create an
    account. Once the account is created, they log in with username/password (and eventually we will
    also support 2fa such as passkeys)"*). The invitation (§10) only entitles its redeemer to make
    the account (D311 §1). It replaces D290 §16's e-mailed sign-in link for the service's accounts.
    The passkey comes in the closed beta after all (D312 §7).

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-18; §7, §8–§12 and §13 the same day.

## D311 — A code establishes an entitlement: it expires, its issuer sees it and what it made, and a new code for the same entitlement moves it to whoever redeems it

**Decided** (2026-10-18), by the project owner, on D310's keys and invitations, as the rule for
every kind. Restated the same day: the first record read "revoking a link ends what it granted",
and the owner corrected it (agent-failures A35): *"A "code" (key code or invite code) is a means to
establishing entitlements (setting up an account, enroling a core, joining a watch together
session, etc). Codes expire after a certain time (the timeout depends on what we are setting up).
While codes are outstanding (have not been redeemed), the issuer must be able to see the codes,
plus their private notes, and be able to revoke or regenerate them. Once a code is redeemed, the
issuer needs a way to see the result of that redemption (e.g. I can see registered users, users can
see their enroled core, hosts can see their watch together guests, etc). As an escape hatch,
issuers can generate a new code for that entitlement, which invalidates the entitlements associated
with the old code, and allows the person redeeming the code to gain those entitlements. So, I can
re-issue an invite link for someone who's locked themselves out of their account. A user can
re-issue a core key if something goes wrong or they need to rebuild their VPS. A watch together
guest couldn't get things to work with brave browser and wants to try with chrome or safari, etc.
So the way things get manifested in the UI may appear different, but the mechanics are mostly the
same."* Earlier the same day: *"The general pattern when using links (invites, watch together,
etc) is: URL + QR code, private note."* It holds for the core's registration invitations, Watch
Together's links (D246), device codes (D218, D288), and the paid service's invitations and core
keys (D310 §8–§10).

1. **A code is a means of establishing an entitlement**: an account made, a core enrolled, a place
   in a Watch Together session. Each kind is one mechanism, however its screens show it.
2. **A code expires**, after a time that depends on what it sets up (a core key's hour, D310 §8).
3. **While a code is outstanding, its issuer sees it with its private note, and may revoke or
   regenerate it.** A code a person follows is given as a URL and a QR code; one a person types,
   as a core's enrolment key is, is a `discovery/safe32code` code (the owner: *"because it has to
   be entered by a human"*).
4. **Once a code is redeemed, its issuer sees what it made**: the owner the registered people, a
   household its enrolled core, a host the session's guests.
5. **The escape hatch: a new code for the same entitlement.** Issuing it invalidates what the old
   code granted, and whoever redeems the new one takes the entitlement over: the person locked out
   of their account has it back, the rebuilt VPS's core replaces the old one (D310 §9), the guest
   moves from one browser to another. The entitlement is kept and passed on, not made afresh.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-18, restated the same day. Each kind of code is to be checked against
it: today the core's invitations and Watch Together's links can be withdrawn while outstanding, but
none can be issued again for an entitlement already made.

## D312 — The accounts' security for the closed beta: the account steers a household's sign-ins, so it is guarded as the household's own key

**Decided** (2026-10-18), by the project owner, on the agent's review of D310 and D311 for security
issues and best practice: *"We should do all of those for closed beta. Also, the login screen should
defend against timing attacks that can be used to map out valid usernames & realms."* The review's
finding: a service account grants nothing on a core (D289 §1), but it decides which core
app.orpheum-app.com sends a household to, and so where realm sign-ins (D297) carry its people's
passwords; whoever takes an account, steals a fresh key or is handed a re-issued invitation can
remove the real core (D310 §9), enrol their own, and collect passwords from devices that do not
yet know the core's fingerprint (D308). It brings D310 §13's second factor into the closed beta.

1. **What moves a household is confirmed and recorded.** Generating a key, re-issuing an
   invitation and changing the password ask for the password or passkey again; every enrolment
   and every core removed is recorded where the account sees it: when, the core's name and
   fingerprint, where it came from.
2. **A household is told when its core changed.** After a new key, the core's pages and the app
   say the household's server changed, and when; a device that remembers the old core's
   fingerprint stops with a warning instead of following the new one.
3. **Re-issuing an entitlement is recovery, and is done as recovery** (D311 §5). The issuer
   confirms who asks by a channel already trusted; the new code's redemption ends every session
   and removes the old password and passkeys, on the paid service as on the core and in Watch
   Together, so the one it was taken from keeps nothing.
4. **The operator's panel is guarded most**: a passkey or second factor from its first day,
   reached over the WireGuard network only, as SSH is (edge VPS runbook), with no sign-in shared
   with customers.
5. **A core's enrolment key is 16 safe32 characters** (`xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx`, 80 bits), not a
   device code's 8: kept as its hash, compared in constant time, failures limited by source and in
   all, spent by its first attempt, right or wrong.
6. **Passwords follow NIST SP 800-63B-4**: at least 15 characters while the password stands alone
   and 8 with a second factor, no composition rules, pasting and password managers welcome, every
   new password checked against breached ones (k-anonymity, as Have I Been Pwned offers), no
   forced change, argon2id as the core's (D193).
7. **Passkeys (WebAuthn) in the closed beta**, not later.
8. **Guessing is slowed, never locked out**: growing delays per account and per source, so no one
   can lock a household out by guessing; a wrong username and a wrong password are answered alike.
9. **Sessions**: P2's `__Host-` cookies, CSRF token and cross-origin protection, an idle limit
   beside the 30-day absolute one, the account's sessions listed, and signing out everywhere.
10. **Opening a link redeems nothing**: redemption is an action on its page (D290 §16's rule, kept
    for invitations), so a messenger's or mail scanner's preview spends nothing.
11. **A link's secret rides in its fragment**, never its path or query, so no log or Referer holds
    it, as Watch Together's links do (D154).
12. **A QR code is a link like any other**: short-lived, used once, and invalidated with its link
    when the entitlement is issued again.
13. **The free-for-life mark is the operator's alone**, set in the panel, never from what a
    customer sends; the owner's tests of lapse and termination run on accounts marked as tests,
    which reach no household.
14. **Generating keys is rate-limited**, so a taken account cannot keep a household's core off the
    service; §1's re-confirmation stands in front of it.
15. **A removed core is removed at once**: its service sessions revoked, its names withdrawn, its
    connections closed, its System page saying it was removed from the account; its identity key
    enrols again only with a new key.
16. **Issuing and redeeming are a durable record**: who issued a code, when and from where it was
    redeemed, what it replaced; the record is D311 §4's view of what a code made, and answers
    "was this me?".
17. **Sign-in reveals nothing by its timing**, on the service's account sign-in, the realm sign-in
    at the discovery's page (D297) and the core's own: an unknown username costs the same password
    work as a known one (a hash against a stand-in), and the discovery answers a realm sign-in no
    sooner than a time that covers a core's round trip, so an unknown realm's quick refusal does
    not tell it from a known one's. Every failed sign-in is answered no sooner than that one time,
    whatever failed, and a success as soon as it is done (the owner, the same day: *"A failed login
    is the rare path, so it's fine if it's a bit inconvenient."*): the wait falls only on failures,
    which an unknown name and a wrong password both are.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-18, §17's last sentence the same day. All of it before the closed
beta's first outside household.

## D313 — The closed beta's milestones: joining, between episodes, the library and its people, every file plays well, the UI revamp, then the living room

**Decided** (2026-10-18), by the project owner, from the marks the owner gave every feature in the
reassessment's ledger ([milestone-reassessment-2026-10-18.md](../design/research/milestone-reassessment-2026-10-18.md)):
*"This looks good."* With D310–D312 it replaces cut-a.md's M5 (the polished UI, D245) and M6 (the
remote TV) as what comes next. The owner, before the marks: the UI revamp waits until the features
are in, "doing the ui revamp would risk handcuffing us"; *"We'll do TVs last, once we have the other
features in and can test properly"*; all of B0 before the first outside household, though *"I may
decide to open to other people before we are feature complete for B0, but that's a decision I'll
make in the moment"*; music left out of the closed beta and revisited after it.

1. **B0, joining the beta:** the simple core install (D310 §5); the paid service's accounts with
   passkeys, the operator's panel and invitations, enrolment keys and the accounts' safeguards
   (D310, D312); every code to D311's pattern; the identity key's recovery code; connections that
   heal on network changes; the System page in plain words; the paid service made whole; bug reports;
   log levels changeable while running; terms and privacy.
2. **B1, between episodes:** Next Up; intros and credits detected (D82); skip intro, recap and
   credits; the next-episode countdown with a setting to turn it off; scrub-bar thumbnails; a Watch
   Together group carried from episode to episode; the host's media keys moving the group (D268 §4);
   chapters if they come easily, else the open beta.
3. **B2, the library and its people:** genres first (cast, crew and ratings later); filters and
   sorts; watched marks, shown in the poster's tray; the watchlist; episode orderings; missing
   episodes; disc images; profiles with a PIN; a second factor on the core's own accounts.
4. **B3, every file plays well:** the playback survey first; HDR tone mapping, scoped before it is
   committed to; VAAPI and AMD encoding; caption styles; language defaults; night mode; HEVC played
   as it is where the browser can, prepares staying H.264 (the owner: *"for transcoding we stick to
   h264 for beta"*).
5. **B4, the UI revamp** (D245's M5), over the features above.
6. **B5, the living room:** TV mode for a TV's own browser, TV sign-in by a code the TV shows,
   through the paid service too, Google Cast, AirPlay, "Get this ready", voice on a second device.
7. **Not placed:** the owner's maybes (OIDC or LDAP, recommendations, trailers, Trakt, Watch
   Together's text chat, each viewer's own tracks, our own relay); everything marked later; music,
   after the closed beta; the discovery a household runs itself (D310 §7), before the open beta and
   possibly during the closed one. **Not wanted:** the API's compatibility gate for now (the owner:
   *"First we build out the functionality, then we can think about making an API"*), live TV,
   photos.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-18. cut-a.md §8 and the plans behind the code follow it in one change.

## D314 — A core is installed from a public image, on any machine that runs Docker with the hardware it needs, and with no tunnel; a connection that needs a relay fails, and is counted

**Decided** (2026-10-18), by the project owner, on B0's phase A questions ([b0.md](../design/plans/b0.md)):
*"1: A container registry. I don't mind if it's public from the start (it will be public eventually
anyway). 2: Ideally any platform that supports docker and the hardware passthrough we need. 3: That's
acceptable, and we record when it happens."* It revises D272 §4 (the image built from a tag on the
machine that runs it) and builds D272 §3's optional tunnel.

1. **A household installs a core from a prebuilt image on a public container registry**, from the
   start: no source and no build on the household's machine. The registry is GitHub's, beside the
   repository, and the image is published when a version is tagged, unless the owner names another.
   The owner's own machines may still build from a tag.
2. **The closed beta supports any machine that runs Docker** and passes through the hardware the
   node needs (the media's disks, and a GPU where it has one): the install names what it needs and
   reports what it finds, rather than listing supported brands. Images for amd64 and, as
   keep-arm64-open intends, arm64 where every piece builds (D205's rows say which do not yet).
3. **The deployment needs no tunnel.** A core is reached through its discovery over WebRTC and at
   home by its LAN names (D300); the tunnel stays as an option for a household with a VPS.
4. **With no tunnel there is no public relay for WebRTC, and that is accepted for the closed beta:**
   two devices that can meet only through a relay do not connect. **Each such failure is recorded**,
   so the beta shows how often it happens (D274 §3's count, which decides whether a relay is built).
5. **Windows is not a closed-beta host** (the owner, the same day, on the agent's research: *"yes"*).
   Under WSL 2 and Docker Desktop, changes made from Windows never reach the node's watching, Intel
   Quick Sync is unavailable, Docker Desktop rewrites every client's address so no device is at home
   (D297 §6, D300), and nothing runs before a person logs in. A native Windows build, about six to
   ten weeks of its own by the research's estimate, comes later if testers ask for it. A technical
   tester may run it unsupported under Docker Engine inside WSL with mirrored networking.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-18; §5 the same day.

## D315 — The service's accounts: a passkey signs in alone, verified by our own code; an unchecked password is refused; the operator's panel is opened at localhost; no e-mail in the closed beta

**Decided** (2026-10-18), by the project owner, on the accounts' design (orpheum-connect's
`docs/plans/accounts.md` §14), which b0.md's phase B wrote first, each answer as recommended.

1. **A passkey signs in alone** (*Sign in with a passkey*), not as a second step after the
   password: with user verification it is two factors and resists phishing; the password stays for
   a device without one, and is always at least 15 characters (D312 §6).
2. **WebAuthn is verified by our own minimal code, with no library**: attestation `none` only;
   ES256, EdDSA and RS256; a small CBOR reader for the COSE key; tested against WebAuthn Level 3's
   published vectors. `go-webauthn/webauthn` would have brought about eight modules, mostly for
   attestation formats and metadata the service does not ask for, each to audit (D220).
3. **A password the breached-password check could not reach is refused for now** (*"try again in a
   minute"*), never accepted unchecked: setting a password is rare, and an unchecked one is what
   D312 §6's check exists to prevent.
4. **The operator's panel listens on `prod-api`'s loopback and is opened at
   `http://localhost:<port>` through an SSH forward over WireGuard**, since WebAuthn accepts no IP
   address as its relying party, which the WireGuard address is; `localhost` is a secure context
   and needs no certificate or name (D312 §4).
5. *(Replaced by D316 the next day.)* **An account holds no e-mail address in the closed beta**: nothing in the beta sends mail, a
   person locked out asks the operator for a new invitation (D312 §3), and a household learns its
   core changed on the core's pages and in the app (D312 §2). The address, mail on each new
   sign-in and recovery by mail come with the open beta.

6. **The service account's session ends after 7 days unused or 30 days in all, and a
   re-confirmation counts for 5 minutes** (accounts.md §7, §8), each a setting: the panel is opened a
   few times a year and grants nothing on a core, and what moves a household always asks the
   password or a passkey again (D312 §1), so AAL1's limits stand for the session and the
   re-confirmation in front of what matters.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-18; §6 the same day, after the owner asked what a session is here.

## D316 — The service's accounts hold a verified e-mail address: sign in by it or the username, and a forgotten password or username is sent to it; a reset restores the account at once

**Decided** (2026-10-19), by the project owner, replacing D315 §5. The owner, on the failed sign-in
limits: *"A user who has forgotten their password will likely try 5 times and then get locked out
for 15 minutes, and also be very aggravated already. I think 5 minutes is better. They're also going
to forget their usernames. I think it would be good if they could also be able to log in with their
email address."* On the agent's proposal that a reset by e-mail hold back a new core key for days
(itself corrected the same day, agent-failures A36): *"I think we may be getting a little too
paranoid. If an attacker has compromised someone's email account, a home video collection is the
least of their worries. … The more likely situation will be: Someone's core dies in a fire, and they
want to set up a new one, but they don't remember their password … only to discover they now have to
wait days just to get their core attached so that their kids can watch videos again."*

1. *(Revised by D317 the same day: there is no username.)* **An account holds an e-mail address,
   verified before it signs in or resets anything**, and the sign-in form takes the username or the
   address. The failed sign-in counts run over five
   minutes, not fifteen (orpheum-connect).
2. **A forgotten password or username is sent to the address**: "forgot password" sends a link
   (once, about 30 minutes, its secret in the fragment, spent only by a button on its page, D312
   §10, §11), and its answer never says whether an account matched; "forgot username" sends the
   username. *Every link sent stays live for its thirty minutes until one of them is used, which ends them
   all* (the owner, the same day: *"to deal with the situation where mail is slow and the user does
   another request, and then an old one comes to their email and doesn't work because another one
   had been issued, creating chaos and confusion as they try again and it keeps failing"*).
3. **A reset restores the account at once**: no wait before a new core key, which D310 §9 makes
   at once as before. Setting the new password ends every other session. A notice of the reset and
   of each core change goes to the address. A device that knew the old core still stops with a
   warning at a new one (D312 §2).
4. **No sign-in with Google, Apple, Amazon or others** for now: it adds those companies to every
   sign-in and a second identity per person, and passkeys and the e-mail reset already answer a
   forgotten password.
5. **Passkeys stay in the closed beta** (D312 §7, D315 §1), offered right after the first sign-in.
6. **The mail provider is chosen by the owner** from a current comparison, before the e-mail is
   built; SPF, DKIM and DMARC on `orpheum-app.com`, and a mail catcher on staging so no test sends
   real mail.

7. **The provider is Scaleway Transactional Email** (the owner, the same day, from orpheum-connect's
   `docs/research/mail-providers-2026-10-19.md`): French, its data in the EU, no open or click
   tracking at all, so no link is rewritten.
8. **An account holds as many passkeys as its person adds** (the owner, the same day: *"we should
   support multiple passkeys per account"*), each named, listed and removable, as accounts.md §6
   had it.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-19; §7 and §8 the same day.

## D317 — The service's accounts have no username: an e-mail address and a password make one, it signs in unverified, does nothing until verified, and is deleted after seven days unverified

**Decided** (2026-10-19), by the project owner, revising D310 §11, §13 and D316 §1, §2: *"I don't
think we need usernames for orpheum-connect. They can make usernames for their own core but we
don't need them at this elevation because nobody but the user himself would ever see it, and it's
just something that he would forget. An unverified account is purged after 7 days if unverified.
The address/password CAN be used to sign in during this time (in case they switch browsers), but
the account can't do anything until verified."* Earlier the same day: *"A new user who uses an
invite link to create an account can set up an email address and password, which gives them an
account. However, they can't do anything with that account (i.e. enrol a core) until they verify
their email. Once verified, the account becomes fully active. If they change email providers, they
can change their email on account, but the old account still works for 24 hours and a warning
email is sent there so that the user can cancel the migration to the new email (this part can be
done after closed beta)."*

1. **No username on the service.** An invitation's redemption asks for an e-mail address and a
   password; the address is what the account signs in by, compared without regard to case. A
   core's own accounts keep their usernames (D218); the two are unrelated, as D310 §11 has it.
2. **An unverified account signs in, and does nothing else**: no core key, no passkey, no change
   but resending its verification link and signing out. Verifying the address makes it fully
   active.
3. **An account unverified after seven days is deleted**, its address freed; its invitation's
   record says so, for the operator to issue another (D311 §5).
4. **A verification link** lasts 24 hours, is used once, carries its secret in the fragment and is
   spent by a button on its page (D312 §10, §11); a new one replaces it.
5. **Changing the address comes after the closed beta**: the new one verified, the old one still
   signing in for 24 hours and told, with a way to cancel the change from it. Until then the address
   is not changed; one lost is recovered by a new invitation for the account (D312 §3).
6. **"Forgot username" goes**, there being none; "forgot password" sends its link to the address
   (D316 §2), which an unverified account cannot use.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-19.

## D318 — Several codes may be outstanding for one entitlement, and redeeming any one of them ends them all

**Decided** (2026-10-19), by the project owner, extending D311 to every kind of code, after
D316 §2's reset links: *"Yes, for any invite type link, multiple can be issued, and redeeming one of
them invalidates all of them. This ties into the "same shape for link/key based entitlements"
design. We shape everything this way at the core even if it's not going to be technically possible
with our UI flow."*
