1. **An entitlement may have several codes outstanding at once**: a new code for it leaves the
   others live, each for its own life. Mail is slow, a person asks twice, a host sends a link to two
   addresses: every code that was sent still works.
2. **Redeeming any one ends every other code for that entitlement**, in the same step.
3. **Revoking ends every outstanding code for it**; D311 §3's regenerate is that revocation and a
   new code, one after the other.
4. **One mechanism holds every kind**, whatever its screens show (D311 §1): the service's
   verification links, password-reset links, invitations and, with phase C, core keys; the core's
   registration invitations, Watch Together links and device codes in B0's phase D. The model allows
   several codes even where a flow never issues a second.
5. **D310 §9 is read through it**: a new core key does not end the last; whichever key is redeemed
   first enrols its core, ends every other key, and removes the core enrolled before (D311 §5), so
   a household that generated two keys while rebuilding is not stranded by the order mail arrives.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-19. The service's verification and reset links and invitations take it
at once (orpheum-connect); core keys with phase C; the core's codes with phase D.

## D319 — Staging's client origins are `<core id>.orpheum-client-test.com`, behind one wildcard on staging's tunnel

**Decided** (2026-10-19), by the project owner, who registered `orpheum-client-test.com` for it.
Revises D308 §6's staging names.

1. **Why.** Staging's client origins were `<core id>-staging.orpheum-client.com`, each a public
   hostname on staging's tunnel made by hand, since a wildcard leads to one tunnel and
   `orpheum-client.com`'s is production's. Every wipe of staging gives its core a new id, and the
   owner's fresh setup met Cloudflare's 404 at the new one. Staging's household zone,
   `orpheum-test.com`, cannot carry them: its apex forbids every CA and Universal SSL stays off there
   (D296 §2), which a Cloudflare-certified name would undo (agent-failures A37). The first choice,
   `orpheum-site.com`, was no domain: `orpheum-site` is the landing page's Pages project.
2. **`orpheum-client-test.com`** is staging's `orpheum-client.com`, as `orpheum-test.com` is its
   `orpheum-core.com`: a zone at Cloudflare with Universal SSL on and no CAA, one wildcard public
   hostname on staging's tunnel to connectd, and a staging core's client origin
   `https://<core id>.orpheum-client-test.com`, one level down, as the free certificate covers.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-19; staging's connectd takes it at once, the route by the owner
(orpheum-ops production/README.md §6c).
## D320 — A device signed out on itself leaves the person's devices; one signed out another way stays

**Decided** (2026-10-20), by the project owner. Refines
[D221](#d221--a-device-keeps-its-identity-across-sign-ins-and-a-signed-out-device-is-signed-back-in-with-a-code-made-for-it)
§1.

1. **Signing out on the device itself removes it.** Sign out on a device ends every session of that
   device and its device secret, and the device leaves Your devices, as Remove does (D218 §4). A
   sign-in there afterwards makes a new device. A person who signs out of a browser means to be done
   with it, and the list kept every browser they had ever left.
2. **A device signed out another way stays**, so it comes back as itself (D221 §1): one whose
   session expired, one ended by Sign out everywhere else, a hand-off's temporary session.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-20; built 2026-10-20: §1 by `DELETE /session` through
`auth.SignOutHere`, §2 by every other ending, which leaves the device as it was.

## D321 — A TV shows a QR code carrying its key's hash, which activates it with one tap; the typed code's check code is committed

**Decided** (2026-10-20), by the project owner, from the device code audit's options (b) and M2
([device-code-audit-2026-10-20.md](../design/research/device-code-audit-2026-10-20.md) §2, §3).
Refines [D293](#d293--the-discoverys-open-questions-answered-a-live-instance-is-pinged-before-it-is-replaced-device-codes-through-the-service-sealed-by-hpke-on-p-256-in-the-beta-stagings-dns-token-in-the-sandbox-until-production)
§2's device codes through the paid service; the core's own codes (D288) are unchanged.

1. **The TV shows a QR code beside its typed code.** It is a link to the loader,
   `https://app.orpheum-app.com/activate?code=<code>&key=<hash>`, whose hash is 128 bits of the
   SHA-256 of the TV's key (`proof.DeviceKeyHash`). The key's hash reaches the phone by camera,
   past the service, which can then drop or delay an activation but not substitute its own key.
2. **The QR path needs no check code.** The loader opens the realm's client at Activate a device,
   the code filled in; the phone names the device and how long ago it asked, with the warning, and
   one tap on **Activate** activates it. The core claims the code with no nonce and activates only a
   key whose hash is the QR code's; any other is refused. The TV then asks its own question,
   "Sign this TV in to the household ‹realm› as ‹person›?" (the audit's M1).
3. **The typed path's check code is committed**, as Bluetooth's numeric comparison does (the audit's
   M2):
   1. The TV commits to `H(key ‖ n_t)` when it asks for its code.
   2. The core claims the code with a random `n_c`.
   3. The TV, told `n_c`, reveals `n_t`; the service and the core check it against the commitment.
   4. Both show `H(key ‖ n_t ‖ n_c)`'s first 40 bits.

   No one knows the check code before the code is entered, so a fixed phishing message cannot name
   one (the audit's M3), and a service swapping in a key gets one try in 2⁴⁰, not a search. A TV that
   sends no commitment is refused.
4. **The loader chooses by realm** (the owner: *"access should be by realm, which right now is
   already one core"*): with one realm it goes there; with several it asks which; with none it shows
   a page to **Copy link** to a phone that is signed in, or **Sign in here** and carry on to
   Activate a device. On an iPhone a home-screen app cannot be opened from a link, so Safari's
   sign-in is the practical way.
5. **Activating needs a session that manages the account**, one signed in with a password, never a
   device a code activated (D292 §4).

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-20; built 2026-10-20: §1 and the TV's side of §2–§3 in an earlier commit, the core's
claims in an earlier commit, the service's commitment and reveal in orpheum-connect, §2's one tap and
§4 in an earlier commit, §5 by Activate a device's existing need of a session that manages the account. On a
real TV: VQ48.

## D322 — Activating a device names the country it asks from, as Cloudflare names it; the network's name waits

**Decided** (2026-10-20), by the project owner (*"Put that as a decision so that it doesn't get
lost"*), for the device code audit's M3 and the protocol's deferred line naming where the asking device
is (D290 §5, S4). Refines D321's Activate a device.

1. **The service names the country a device asks for its code from**, by the two-letter code
   Cloudflare's `CF-IPCountry` header gives each request reaching connectd through its tunnel: no
   location database, no dependency, and only a header read, as `CF-Connecting-IP` already is. It is
   kept with the code and passed to the core in the claim's answer as an optional field; a discovery
   that has none, as a self-hosted one, sends none.
2. **Activate a device shows it**: "A TV in Germany asked 12 s ago", and, when it differs from the
   country the phone's own request comes from, says so plainly, the case a code someone sent the person
   is. It is a hint, never proof (a VPN or a carrier's NAT names its exit), so the warning stays as it is.
3. **No city, and nothing stored**: Cloudflare's city headers guess wrong too often (DS-Lite and mobile
   networks), and the country lives only as long as the code. The privacy page says the service reads it.
4. **The network's name** ("on Vodafone") **waits**: it needs an IP-to-network database (IPinfo Lite or
   DB-IP Lite), a dependency for the owner to approve (AGENTS rule 3).

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-20; to be built after the closed beta's current work.

## D323 — A picture the device cannot play is converted at its own size first, and the ladder follows the encoder

**Decided** (2026-10-20), by the project owner: *"When we hit encoding issues like the HEVC one on ff,
or an encoding the client can't handle at all, we try converting it directly to a compatible encoding
at the same size and quality, and then step down as necessary much like today if we hit bandwidth
problems. If the encoder can't keep up (for example we're software encoding), we step down. The
quality ladder is different depending on whether hardware acceleration is available."* On Firefox on
macOS giving up The Big Parade's HEVC picture after a jump and dropping to 540p and 360p, though the
film's node encodes on Quick Sync. **Refines** [D266](#d266--a-quality-whose-video-stands-still-while-its-chunks-arrive-is-one-the-device-cannot-play-and-is-given-up)
§2 and [D247](#d247--a-slow-link-gets-a-lower-version-made-at-its-first-stall-and-played-from-its-second-and-a-group-waits-for-a-stalled-viewer-once-then-lets-them-catch-up-alone) §6.

1. **The twin.** When the film's own picture is not for this player, because the decision says the
   device cannot decode it or the player gave it up (D266), its ladder's top quality is an H.264
   copy at the picture's own height, its width following, at the rate that height takes, raised
   from the original's own for a codec that packs more into a bit (HEVC and VP9 by half, AV1 by
   twice), and at most the height's rate on Apple's HLS authoring ladder. It is the one quality that
   may carry more than the original. **The qualities below it step down from the twin**: each is
   offered below the twin's rate and the picture's height, since they are H.264 as the twin is, so an
   HEVC original of 2.2 Mb/s whose twin takes 4 Mb/s steps down to a 3 Mb/s quality, not past it to
   2 Mb/s (the owner: *"it should act as if it were originally playing the h264 twin when deciding
   [...] we haven't actually figured out the pipe's bandwidth yet since the movie has only just
   started playing"*).
2. **A picture given up mid-film is played again from where it stood**, the page asking for the
   playback afresh once its player has told the core, so the new ladder starts at the twin rather than
   at the quality below the original (D266 §2's fall, for the film's own picture alone).
3. **The ladder follows the film's node's encoder**: `chunk_qualities` where it encodes in software,
   and `chunk_qualities_hardware`, starting at 1080p, where it encodes on a GPU (Quick Sync, NVENC).
   Each quality is still offered only below the original in rate, or below the twin where it plays
   in the original's place (§1), and below the picture in height.
4. **An encoder that cannot keep up steps its players down**, the twin included, as D286 §4 already
   does for any quality.

**Status:** Built 2026-10-20: §1 and §3 in internal/core/chunks (`topOf`, `twinOf`, `ladderOf`) and
`decide.TwinKbps`; §2 on the Play page. A Watch Together guest's page still
falls to the quality below the picture given up, as before §2; §4 is D286 §4's move, which goes by
stream and so moves a twin's players too.

## D324 — Work follows interest: what is played comes first, then what is being looked at, then everything else; work in the way is stopped, and what waits says how long

> **§2 and §4 revised by [D329](#d329--work-is-scheduled-from-wants-each-resource-is-decided-next-to-it-playback-is-admitted-and-long-work-is-cut-into-pieces)** (2026-10-22): interest is a source of wants whose tier the core gives; numbers are no longer raised, and work in the way yields at its next piece.

**Decided** (2026-10-21), by the project owner: *"When a user opens a film or series page, he
expresses interest in it, which should shift all priorities for that item. For a series, it starts
going through the episodes, starting with the one after the last one watched. When a user starts
playing a video, it gets the highest priority over all. If jobs for it are not done yet, we should
give an estimate of how long until it's done. If a user goes away from a page or stops playing and
goes to another page, his interest has shifted, and we switch priorities even if it means throwing
out work. [...] We allow processing while a video is playing so long as it doesn't starve the CPU for
the playing video (if the video is using hardware codecs or direct play, that changes the
equation)."* Then, to the proposal: *"Go with your recommendations. 1: next 3 eps. 2: kill only
what's in the way. 3: those two are fine."* On the owner's staging, where every film said its
loudness was not measured: 3,412 read-throughs waited in id order, and 41 of 324 films were measured.
**Revises** [D234](#d234--the-core-drives-the-node-the-node-keeps-a-durable-journal-of-its-jobs-and-schedules-them-pushes-progress-and-acknowledged-results-and-the-core-checks-and-reconciles) §3's play priority, [D240](#d240--the-core-keeps-the-smarts-a-scan-is-a-listing-the-core-compares-the-work-it-implies-is-the-cores-to-schedule-and-the-node-enforces-its-devices-limits-and-pauses-background-work-for-play) §6's pause, and the order of
[D226](#d226--loudness-is-levelled-in-cut-a-the-node-measures-each-sound-and-its-stereo-mix-the-core-sets-a-gain-towards--23-lufs-that-no-peak-exceeds-and-the-player-applies-it-after-its-volume)'s measuring; **generalises** [D309](#d309--a-player-says-which-quality-it-wants-and-from-where-and-a-run-no-player-wants-stops)'s interest.

1. **Interest is what people play and look at, now.** The core keeps each session's playback and
   the film or series page it shows. A page says it is shown while it is, and a playback is shown
   by its reports; either lapses within seconds of the page left or the playing stopped.
2. **Interest orders the work.** Anything played comes first; then what is looked at, the latest
   look first; then a person's own request, such as Look again; then the work of anything anyone
   has shown interest in, played, looked at or partly watched, once that interest is past ("user
   has shown interest", a rung above the background: the owner, *"Anything that a user has signaled
   any level of interest in goes to the just-above-bg priority if it would otherwise drop to bg
   priority"*); then the background, whose sweeps keep their order. Everyone's interest counts, and
   anyone's playing comes before anyone's looking.
3. **What interest raises.** For a film, every job its playing needs or shows: its read-through
   (loudness and timeline), its prepared copy where it needs one, its artwork, its subtitles and its
   metadata. For a series, the same for three episodes in its order, from the one its person is
   partway through, the latest played when several are; or else the one after the last they
   finished; or else the first (the owner: *"'last one watched' means the last one completed. If
   they're in the middle of an episode, it counts as the first of 3. If no other videos of the series
   has been completed, it's the first episode, or the most recent one they're partway through"*).
4. **Work in the way is stopped.** When raised work needs what other work holds, a device's only
   reader or an encoder slot, the other work is stopped, even part done, and queued again at its own
   priority. Work not in the way runs on, and work that can resume resumes. Interest that lapses
   gives its work back its own priority; nothing is thrown out for it.
5. **Playing is not starved.** A film played as it is, or encoded on a GPU, leaves the CPU free:
   work runs beside it within its devices' reader limits. A film encoded in software keeps the CPU:
   other encodes wait, and lighter work runs while the playing encode stays faster than playback.
6. **What waits says how long.** The film's page, where it says the loudness is not measured, and
   the player, where it waits for a prepared copy, say what is being done and about how long it
   will take, from the file's size and the device's measured speed, the encoder's measured speed, and
   what is ahead of it.

**Status:** Planned: [interest-priority.md](../design/plans/interest-priority.md).

## D325 — A page pulls what it needs to know; the server never pushes it

**Decided** (2026-10-21), by the project owner: *"we should make this a general policy: Avoid server
push and keep it client pull in order to avoid adding yet another queueing problem."* Asked whether
the server should tell a player at once that its film can be read again, rather than the page asking
every ten seconds, the risks were a message lost to a connection severed as it was sent, which leaves
the page waiting for ever (the wedged player of the dead-share tests that day), the page's
re-subscribing after every reconnection, and the server's keeping who listens. **Generalises**
[D168](#d168--entitlement-is-resolved-at-the-point-of-use-never-pushed-revocation-needs-no-message-and-the-notification-is-a-latency-optimisation-that-may-always-be-lost), whose notification may always be lost, from entitlements to everything a page shows.

1. **A page asks for the state it shows; the server never sends it unasked.** Each ask carries the
   whole current state, so a lost or late answer costs only the time until the next ask, and there
   is no event to miss, no subscription to restore and no listener to keep.
2. **Where waiting matters, the ask may be held.** A long poll, answered at once when the state
   changes and otherwise after a bound, is still a pull: it fails as an ask fails, and the page asks
   again.
3. **The node is not a page.** The node's reports to the core ([D234](#d234--the-core-drives-the-node-the-node-keeps-a-durable-journal-of-its-jobs-and-schedules-them-pushes-progress-and-acknowledged-results-and-the-core-checks-and-reconciles))
   are outside this decision.

**Status:** Holds: the player's check whether its film can be read again (`mediaBackAskEveryMs`) asks.

## D326 — A root whose disk answers again as its last complete scan read it is available at once

**Decided** (2026-10-21), by the project owner, choosing it over only ordering the scans: after the
dead-share test, a share back took about a minute and a half to bring its film back, because only a
complete scan of the root made it available, and the scans of every root on the disk ran one at a
time behind its one reader. **Extends** [D233 §10](#d233--work-handed-to-a-node-survives-restarts-and-lost-messages-an-outbox-reconciliation-at-hello-results-known-by-what-they-are-and-a-watchdog-on-both-sides).

1. **The node's status measures each root and says its facts:** the device it is on and whether it is
   a mount point, as a scan's first record says them (D42, D208).
2. **A root whose disk the previous status said was not answering, and this one measures, comes back
   at once** when its facts are those of its last complete scan: the work parked on it resumes, and
   a page waiting on its film sees it playable at its next ask (D325).
3. **Other facts are the empty directory an unmounted disk leaves**, and the root stays unavailable
   until a scan reads it, as before.
4. **A scan of the root follows in the background** for what changed while it was away.

**Status:** Decided.

## D327 — Whoever needs to know whether a root can be read asks, and the node answers at once, outside every queue

**Decided** (2026-10-21), by the project owner: *"Pull is usually better (and far less complex)
because then the interested party is in charge of getting the information it wants, rather than
hoping the machinery from the other side works to inform it in a timely manner. But pull has the
problem that we have concurrency limits on disks. So what we need is a special queue that side-steps
all limitations, but is restricted to quick status checks that don't tax any resources."* After the
dead-share tests, the core learnt a share was back only from the node's next status (D326), and a
listing asked for to bring a root back waited 163 s on the node behind a viewer's read-through for
the disk's one reader. **Extends** [D325](#d325--a-page-pulls-what-it-needs-to-know-the-server-never-pushes-it)
to the core asking its node, and [D326](#d326--a-root-whose-disk-answers-again-as-its-last-complete-scan-read-it-is-available-at-once).

1. **A probe is a question, not work.** The core asks a node whether one of its roots can be read
   now, on the node's byte socket, the core's one way to ask a node directly. The node answers it
   without a slot, a reader or a queue: a probe measures the root's filesystem and its facts (its
   device, and whether it is a mount point), and opens and reads nothing under it.
2. **A probe is bounded, and shared, not retried.** A read on a share that is gone waits in the
   kernel, and no asking again makes it answer sooner; each try left waiting is one more thread held.
   So the node runs at most one probe of a root at a time, every ask meanwhile sharing its answer; it
   answers within a probe window, from the disk gate
   ([D233 §10](#d233--work-handed-to-a-node-survives-restarts-and-lost-messages-an-outbox-reconciliation-at-hello-results-known-by-what-they-are-and-a-watchdog-on-both-sides)):
   readable, with the root's facts; not answering, since when and on what; or missing. A probe that
   outlives its window leaves the root held stuck, as any reading does, later probes answered at
   once from that, and its return is the news the disk answers again.
3. **The core asks when someone is waiting.** A page asking whether its file can be read again is
   held (D325 §2) while the core probes the file's root, one probe of a root at a time however many
   pages wait, and answered as soon as a probe finds it readable with its last complete scan's facts,
   which brings the root back (D326 §2–4), or else at the hold's bound. The sweep of unavailable
   roots probes them, and a scan follows only once one is back.
4. **The status stays the background signal.** A node's status still measures its disks and brings
   a root back by itself (D326); the probe is how a waiting party need not wait for it.
5. **Outside this decision:** how the core's queue and the node's work list share a disk's capacity
   between work a person waits for and maintenance (the 163 s wait), a design of its own; and what
   the mount of a network share should be, which research settles.

**Status:** Decided.

## D328 — Availability is kept per place, a root or a disk mounted inside one, in one table with one writer and one reader

**Decided** (2026-10-21), by the project owner, from their proposal: *"What if we used a tree
structure for availability like the directory tree structure the actual files exist in? If a file
becomes unavailable, we check its parent, and keep going back until we find something readable.
Then we mark unavailable at that level, so that when it becomes available again, you don't need to
scan everything under it to make them available again."* Answered with the tree's levels being
filesystems, not every directory, the level found from what the scans know of the mounts rather
than by reading up a dead share, and one store; approved (*"yes"*). The day's tests had found
availability kept four ways: a root's `unavailable_since`, a mount's `is_present` and
`missing_since`, the queue's parked destinations, and the node's connection; written by scans,
stalls, hellos, statuses and probes each its own way; and read by one query that also counted a
scan's outcome, which held a root a probe had brought back unavailable. A disk dead
inside a root made the whole root unavailable, and only roots could be probed and brought back.
**Extends** [D41](#d41--diagnose-the-failure-boundary-by-walking-up-and-guard-the-silent-case-which-is-worse),
[D208](#d208--the-scenario-walks-answers-re-identify-on-rename-unless-confirmed-a-title-follows-its-files-between-libraries-withhold-removals-past-half-and-twenty-and-a-returning-payload-revives-its-tombstone),
[D231 §5](#d231--work-is-derived-from-state-the-job-queue-is-a-regenerable-cache-and-a-destination-that-is-down-parks-its-work),
D326 and D327.

1. **A place is where availability fails: a node, a root, or a disk mounted inside a root.** Below
   a mount point every directory of a dead disk is dead alike, and one that vanishes or turns
   unreadable while its disk answers is content, which scans judge. A file can be read when its node
   is connected and no place above it is unavailable; the deepest one that is says why. The places
   a node has are few, so the check is a match of the file's path against them. D41's walk up to a
   broken subtree stays the scanner's, within one scan; what lasts between scans is a place.
2. **One table holds the unavailable places**, each with since when, and why: its disk did not
   answer, a scan could not read it, a scan found its disk gone from its mount point, or its node's
   hello no longer names it. What a place's disk should be (its device, and whether it is a mount
   point) stays the last complete scan's fact, where the scans keep it. A root's scan outcome and a
   mount's boundary are the scans' facts, and say nothing of availability.
3. **One writer.** Every change of a place's availability, from any cause, goes through one place
   in the core, which also unparks the work waiting on the place. Nothing else writes the table.
4. **One reader.** Whether a file can be read, which places the System page shows offline and
   since when, and which the sweep probes are all read from the table through one function.
5. **Work that stalls marks the deepest known place holding what it read:** a disk mounted inside
   the root when the read was under one the scans know, else the root. It is found from the
   scans' record of the mounts, so nothing on the dead disk is read to find it.
6. **Every place can be probed and brought back** (D327): a probe of a mount inside a root is
   answered as a root's is, and a place comes back when its disk answers with the facts its last
   complete scan recorded; a scan follows in the background.

**Status:** Decided.


## D329 — Work is scheduled from wants, each resource is decided next to it, playback is admitted, and long work is cut into pieces

**Decided** (2026-10-22), by the project owner, on the design
[work-scheduling.md](../design/plans/work-scheduling.md), which answers the scenarios of
[data-timeliness.md](../design/plans/data-timeliness.md). The owner had asked for the redesign:
*"This is starting to feel like an architectural problem with how we queue and prioritize jobs"*;
then *"a data system relying on a single dimension only is doomed to fail (which is why our numeric
priority system became a mess) … I don't care even if we have to rip all the pieces out and
greenfield them"*. To the design's questions: *"1: Yes. 2: Yes, test this and then we decide based on
the results. 3: I'm fine with whichever ordering is more efficient."* **Revises** [D240](#d240--the-core-keeps-the-smarts-a-scan-is-a-listing-the-core-compares-the-work-it-implies-is-the-cores-to-schedule-and-the-node-enforces-its-devices-limits-and-pauses-background-work-for-play) §5 and §6,
[D255](#d255--work-has-three-priorities-a-persons-a-fast-operations-and-a-slow-ones-and-a-higher-one-bumps-the-lowest-when-nothing-is-free) §2 and §3, and [D324](#d324--work-follows-interest-what-is-played-comes-first-then-what-is-being-looked-at-then-everything-else-work-in-the-way-is-stopped-and-what-waits-says-how-long) §2 and §4's ordering by raised numbers; **keeps** D231, D233, D234,
D238, D309, D324's interest register, and D325–D328.

1. **Wants, not priorities.** A want is someone's need for data by a deadline: ephemeral (a lease a
   session holds, declared again on reconnecting) or durable (a fact the server keeps until done).
   Its tier comes from a table in the core, from what the want is, never from a client. Deadlines
   travel as remaining budgets. Numeric priorities and the play-driven flag go.
2. **Work is keyed by its content** (kind, content, parameters); wants for the same data meet on
   it; its tier is its wants' highest and its deadline their earliest; with no live want it is
   cancelled at its next piece. Background work keeps D231's standing wants, derived by sweeps.
3. **Each resource has one decider, next to it.** The node decides its disks and its encoders; the
   core derives work, values it and sends it with its attributes. The core decides the uplink, the
   providers and the database writer. The core's window, bump and quick pass go.
4. **Playback is admitted, not prioritised**: all or nothing across disk, encoder and uplink, then
   protected by feedback. No running playback is lowered to admit a newcomer; below a floor the
   newcomer chooses to play now at less or to wait. When capacity itself shrinks, the most
   recently started playback yields first (*"seniority wins if someone has to suffer"*).
5. **Four tiers order the rest inside each decider**: interactive, attended, predicted (spare
   capacity only, never waking a disk), background (Due by latest start; Eventually by value over
   cost, shared between kinds with a minimum share).
6. **Long work is made of pieces** of about two seconds of a resource, with progress kept between
   them; preemption happens only at a piece boundary and throws nothing away.
7. **FFmpeg's reads, for the closed beta: a pipe the node feeds where FFmpeg reads straight through,
   the file itself where it must seek.** The byte path over HTTP was tested and works
   ([ffmpeg-http-input-2026-10-22](../design/research/ffmpeg-http-input-2026-10-22.md)), but it
   needs FFmpeg to open a socket, which its confinement forbids (the Plex-chain review's N1), and a
   pipe cannot seek. So a whole-film read of a container that streams (Matroska, MPEG-TS, an MP4
   with its index first) reads a pipe the node feeds through its disk scheduler: in pieces, paced,
   its stuck reads the node's and not FFmpeg's. A run that seeks (a chunk run, a probe, an MP4 with
   its index at the end) reads the file as today, and the scheduler counts it as a reader it cannot
   see. A run is judged by whether its source was read to the end and by the demuxer's I/O error,
   never by FFmpeg's exit status alone. The owner: *"I don't like the fuse idea. Rust is sounding
   better, but for the closed beta it sounds like we can still do the easier hybrid approach"*: after
   the beta, our own media program in Rust, reading through the node by offset with no socket, gives
   the scheduler every read.
8. **Quiet hours, idleness and sleeping disks** govern background work as data-timeliness A8 says.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-22; §7 on its tests the same day. Phases in
[work-scheduling.md](../design/plans/work-scheduling.md) §16.

## D330 — FFmpeg reads its input through the node, over a protocol of our own patched into jellyfin-ffmpeg

**Decided** (2026-10-22), by the project owner, after the media-access scenarios, the own-binary
research and the interposer wargame: *"OK, let's take the wide view of the ffmpeg thing... two viable
options now: A small LD_PRELOAD library, or maintaining our own patches"*, choosing the patches, kept
in a repository of their own, with our own media program in Rust kept as the way out *"if we hit a
blocker"*. **Revises** [D329 §7](#d329--work-is-scheduled-from-wants-each-resource-is-decided-next-to-it-playback-is-admitted-and-long-work-is-cut-into-pieces),
whose hybrid (a pipe where FFmpeg reads straight through, the file where it seeks) it replaces, and
[D193 §6](#d193--the-audits-proposals-are-accepted-the-node-does-all-media-work-prepare-is-the-one-path-besides-direct-play-the-machinery-is-cut-and-cut-as-design-freezes),
whose pinned FFmpeg becomes jellyfin-ffmpeg with our patches.

1. **Every run that reads a film from storage reads it through the node,** by offset, over two
   inherited pipes per input: the protocol *ffstreamer* (its specification, after five
   audits). FFmpeg is given no path to the film, opens no socket, and never waits in the kernel on a
   dead share; the node's disk scheduler serves, paces, holds or refuses every read.
2. **The patches live in their own repository** (ffmpeg-ffstreamer, first named orpheum-ffmpeg), applied after jellyfin-ffmpeg's own
   series and moved with each of its releases: the protocol in libavformat, and fftools exiting
   non-zero when an input's reads failed. They know nothing of Orpheum.
3. **The node kills; FFmpeg is never told to stop.** No message aborts, pauses or reports a read
   error: the node holds reads and stops the process to pause it, and kills it, the process itself
   by pidfd, to end it. A run's verdict is FFmpeg's exit status, the channel's DONE, and the node's
   own account of its reads.
4. **A confined run starts no process and leaves neither its session nor its process group**
  , so a kill reaches everything it is.
5. **Runs that read bytes the node holds in memory** (artwork, subtitle text) keep reading stdin.

**Status:** Decided. The patches are in ffmpeg-ffstreamer, tested on amd64 and arm64. The node's side is
built (internal/node/ffstreamer; every run's film from execx.Runner's FilmOf, a scan's probe too) and
streams a film only when its FFmpeg has the protocol, so it waits on two things: published patched
builds to pin (ffmpeg-ffstreamer's release workflow), and FFmpeg's block cache, which thrashes on a film
whose tracks are stored one after another (ffmpeg-ffstreamer's bench/RESULTS.md).

**Renamed** (2026-10-24), by the project owner: *"OK, let's call it ffmpeg-fdproxy. I want to rename it
now so that we don't have to retool things around a different name later."* The protocol is
*fdproxy* and its repository ffmpeg-fdproxy (the package internal/node/fdproxy), after research found
that an "ff" prefix in FFmpeg marks a format FFmpeg owns or an internal helper, never an outside
protocol users name (ffmpeg-fdproxy's docs/research/ff-prefix-names.md). The names above are those of
their day. Nothing keeps the old names (the owner: *"Backwards compatibility is not an issue"*): until
the next pin, the pinned build, which knows only ffstreamer, lacks the protocol by its new name, and
its node reads each film by its path, as a node whose FFmpeg has no fdproxy does.

## D331 — The node proves itself on both sockets, so a GPU encode may open a Unix socket

**Decided** (2026-10-22), by the project owner (*"go with your recommendations"*), after a confined
NVENC encode was found never to have worked: CUDA's initialisation needs a Unix socket (it asks
NVIDIA's multi-process daemon, and listens on an abstract socket of its own), a few files under
`/proc`, and to name its threads, and the node's encoder trial fell back to x264 on every NVIDIA
machine. The Plex-chain review's N1 had refused FFmpeg every socket because the core took any
process on its node socket as the node, by name alone; its second remedy, that the node prove
itself, was never built. **Revises** N1's socket rule for GPU runs; **extends**
[D242 §7](#d242--an-orpheum-instance-is-one-directory-a-small-top-level-config-pointing-at-persistent-cache-backups-and-run-and-a-backup-is-a-tarball-of-persistent).

1. **Each socket asks for a key FFmpeg cannot read.** Each listener, the core's node socket and the
   node's byte socket, makes a random key at every start and keeps it beside its socket
   (`core.sock.key`, mode 0600), and serves nothing to a request that does not present it; whoever
   dials a socket reads the key beside it, as it finds the socket (D242 §7). The two sides run as one
   user, as FFmpeg does, so the file's mode keeps out other users and Landlock keeps out every run:
   no key is in any place a run is granted.
2. **A GPU run may create a Unix socket, and no other kind;** every other run still creates none. A
   run's network stays refused by seccomp and Landlock alike.
3. **A GPU run is granted what its driver reads to start:** `/proc/devices`, `/proc/cpuinfo`,
   `/proc/sys/vm/mmap_min_addr`, its own `/proc/self/maps` and `status`, and to write its own
   threads' names. Without `/proc/devices`, CUDA starts `nvidia-modprobe`, which a run may not.
4. **What a hijacked GPU run can still reach** is any other named Unix socket on its machine that its
   user may open. In the container image there is little; on a bare install, a private mount
   namespace would close it, and is not built.
5. **The encoder trial's failure stays visible**: the doctor warns of a node with a GPU that encodes
   on the processor, and the System page shows each trial's error.

**Status:** Decided.

## D332 — The node encodes on an AMD card through VAAPI, tried after Quick Sync and NVENC

**Decided** (2026-10-23), by the project owner (*"yes"*), after VQ52 on the owner's machine with a
Radeon RX 6600 XT: a VAAPI encode there worked confined and through ffstreamer, but the node never
tried one, since its encoders were Quick Sync, then NVENC, then x264, and it encoded on the
processor beside an idle card. **Revises** [cut-a §6](../design/plans/cut-a.md#6-prepare)'s encoder
order; **extends** [D331](#d331--the-node-proves-itself-on-both-sockets-so-a-gpu-encode-may-open-a-unix-socket)
§3, a GPU run's grants, to VAAPI.

1. **The node tries `h264_qsv`, then `h264_nvenc`, then `h264_vaapi`, then falls back to x264,**
   each trial confined as a real encode runs, and the System page shows each (D225 §3). VAAPI covers
   AMD cards through Mesa's `radeonsi` driver, and any card with a VA driver.
2. **A VAAPI encode opens FFmpeg's own device for the run** (`-init_hw_device vaapi`, the first
   render node), uploads each picture as NV12, and takes the same rate, profile and keyframes as the
   other encoders. It has no preset. Forced keyframes are IDR pictures, at exactly the times asked,
   for a prepare's segments and a chunk's times alike (measured on the RX 6600 XT).
3. **The release image carries Mesa's VA drivers** (`mesa-va-drivers`) beside Intel's, so an AMD
   card works in it. A bare install needs libva 2.21 or later, which Ubuntu 24.04 and Linux Mint 22
   don't have (idiosyncrasies: jellyfin-ffmpeg's portable build needs libva 2.21).
4. **Not built:** choosing among several cards. FFmpeg's default device is the first render node, so
   on a machine with an Intel and an AMD card VAAPI uses whichever that is; Quick Sync, tried first,
   already takes an Intel card that has it.

**Status:** Built. Read back against the code: the node tries Quick Sync,
NVENC, then VAAPI, each confined (`prepare.hardwareEncoders`); a VAAPI encode's arguments open the
device and upload, with the others' rates and keyframes and no preset (`Encoder.encodeArguments`,
`QualityArguments`); the image carries `mesa-va-drivers` on amd64. On the RX 6600 XT a node from
main chose `h264_vaapi` (VQ52).

## D333 — The container is given an NVIDIA card's GPU when Docker can hand it over

**Decided** (2026-10-23), by the project owner (*"do the rest as well before we deploy to nas.example,
including #7"*, #7 being NVIDIA in the release container). An install gives the node the machine's
`/dev/dri` and its render group, which is all an Intel or AMD card needs, since the image carries
their VA drivers ([D332](#d332--the-node-encodes-on-an-amd-card-through-vaapi-tried-after-quick-sync-and-nvenc)
§3). An NVIDIA card's encoder also needs the driver's own libraries, which must match the host's
kernel driver exactly, so no image can carry them: NVIDIA's container toolkit puts them into a
container as it starts, but only when the container asks. None did, so on an NVIDIA machine the
node found no NVENC and encoded on the processor. **Extends**
[D314](#d314--a-core-is-installed-from-a-public-image-on-any-machine-that-runs-docker-with-the-hardware-it-needs-and-with-no-tunnel-a-connection-that-needs-a-relay-fails-and-is-counted)'s
install.

1. **The install script asks Docker for the GPU the two ways the toolkit offers, on the image
   itself, and writes whichever worked into the node's compose override:** a CDI device,
   `nvidia.com/gpu=all`, as the toolkit describes the cards since 1.18 or after
   `nvidia-ctk cdi generate`, which rootless Docker also takes; else Docker's `nvidia` device
   driver, which the toolkit's hook provides, asking for the compute, video and utility
   capabilities NVENC needs. It tries only where the host has `/dev/nvidiactl`, so a machine without
   an NVIDIA driver runs no trial.
2. **A machine with an NVIDIA driver whose Docker can do neither is told so** in the install's
   report, with the toolkit to install, and installs without the GPU, encoding in software, as before.
3. **Nothing else changes:** the node's own detection and confinement already handle NVIDIA's
   devices (D331 §3), and its trials choose NVENC when it works.

**Status:** Built. Read back against the code: the install script tries CDI, then the
driver, on the image, only where `/dev/nvidiactl` exists (`nvidiaAccess`), passes
`--nvidia cdi|driver` to write-deployment, and reports either way; the override names
`nvidia.com/gpu=all` or reserves the `nvidia` driver with the four capabilities
(`mediaOverride`). On gpuhost (rootless Docker, CDI) the node chose `h264_nvenc` confined. The
driver's route waits on VQ53.

## D337 — Casting starts with a person's own signed-in devices: one chosen from those connected now plays the film, the one that cast becomes its remote, and either may take control back

**Decided** (2026-10-25), by the project owner, choosing the first casting route after the casting
research ([casting-2026-10-25.md](../design/research/casting-2026-10-25.md),
[casting-review-2026-10-25.md](../design/research/casting-review-2026-10-25.md)), which proposed the
remote page and a playback-only credential first, then a Google Cast receiver, and the split-device
sketch's code at `orpheum.cc`
([watch-together-split-devices-2026-10-24.md](../design/research/watch-together-split-devices-2026-10-24.md)
§4) for TVs with no Cast:

> *"The user can select 'cast to other device' from one of their devices. Orpheum brings up a page
> listing devices that are currently connected and active. The user selects one of them. That
> device enters casting receiver mode. The casting sender device now controls the casting receiver
> device. The casting receiver device would also have an escape mode to take back control. This
> would require the device to be logged in as that user. We can sort out the 'takeover for this
> session only' functionality later."*

The owner then agreed the answers below the same day, and changed two of them: a second cast by
the same person takes over without asking (*"a cast session should be last-one-wins"*), and the
receiver's own media controls go on working (*"the controlled device's media controls should also
work"*). The route needs no Cast or AirPlay receiver, no code typed on a TV and no new credential:
a TV whose browser plays our client (Fire TV's Silk, a TCL's TV Bro; closed-beta B5) is signed in
once, as any device is
([D288](#d288--a-device-is-activated-by-the-code-it-shows-entered-on-a-device-already-signed-in-and-a-check-code-both-show),
[D321](#d321--a-tv-shows-a-qr-code-carrying-its-keys-hash-which-activates-it-with-one-tap-the-typed-codes-check-code-is-committed)),
and is then a device a person can cast to, at home or away. **Narrows**
[D135](#d135--casting-on-your-own-is-a-device-delegation-not-an-invitation-the-credential-is-the-session-and-the-queue-is-next-up)
and
[D136](#d136--control-belongs-to-the-cast-session-not-to-the-sender-and-an-externally-paused-receiver-must-say-so);
keeps
[D88](#d88--casting-is-remote-control-of-another-client-which-is-watch-together-with-a-group-of-one),
[D120](#d120--a-participant-is-a-person-devices-attach-to-them-with-roles-and-the-cap-counts-people)
and
[D124](#d124--the-playback-role-may-be-a-cast-receiver-and-for-a-guest-that-is-the-best-path-the-phone-controls-it-does-not-relay).
The build plan is [cast-to-device.md](../design/plans/cast-to-device.md).

1. **Only a device signed in as the same person can receive.** A receiver is signed in to one
   account, so only that person's devices can cast to it, and nothing new is minted for it: it
   plays under its own sign-in, by its own playback decision (D2, D124: the receiver probes and
   picks; [D103](#d103--a-device-scoped-preference-is-stored-a-device-capability-never-is)). This
   narrows D135, whose casting to one's own TV was a delegation to a device that is *not* signed
   in, with a `cast` grant
   ([D154](#d154--one-grant-table-opaque-and-revocable-the-session-credential-never-appears-in-a-url)
   §3): that grant is not needed for this route and waits for §8.
2. **A device is active when Orpheum is open and connected on it now, on any page.** The list of
   devices to cast to holds the person's other devices that are connected at that moment, each
   with its name and when it was last used, as the person's own list of devices shows them. A device signed in but not open is
   not on it.
3. **The receiver shows the film full screen and nothing else**, with a brief "Controlled from
   ‹sender device›" that fades.
4. **Taking control back is two presses.** Any key or tap on the receiver shows "Take back
   control"; one more press confirms it, so a bumped remote does not end the cast. On Fire TV,
   Back reaches the page only as a history step, one per press and never a key (the owner's lab
   results `Q5JAAP2N`, `HSH4M2QQ`, `BHJ6AJ7I`), which the page can catch, so Back also brings up
   the prompt. Taken back, the receiver is an ordinary player again, its own controls on screen,
   and the sender is told.
5. **The sender becomes a remote:** play and pause, the timeline and seeking, subtitles, sound
   and the dialogue boost
   ([D336](#d336--a-films-sound-plays-as-it-is-unless-the-device-cannot-play-it-or-the-person-asks-for-a-feature-that-needs-it-made-no-one-is-asked-how-their-device-makes-sound)
   §2), and volume. It plays nothing itself. In Watch Together the sender keeps the voice call
   while the receiver plays the film: the split-device arrangement D120 and
   [D188](#d188--the-interface-is-designed-against-the-fields-recorded-failures-accessibility-shapes-the-design-but-does-not-gate-cut-a-her-television-plays-and-her-phone-talks)
   §3 describe (*"her television plays and her phone talks"*), with the person's subtitles,
   audio track and volume theirs alone (D188 §4).
6. **One controller at a time; the last cast wins.** If the same person casts to the receiver
   from a second device, the newest cast takes over at once and the earlier sender is told; no
   one is asked. This replaces the proposal of asking before replacing, and narrows D136, under
   which any authorised device could attach to a cast session and control it beside the others:
   here a device that casts replaces the controller. D136's purpose holds, since a sender that
   left is never a stuck receiver (§7, §6's next cast).
7. **The receiver goes on by itself.** If the sender goes away (a phone locked, a browser closed),
   the receiver keeps playing and shows its own controls at a key press. **Its own media controls
   work throughout**, receiving or not: play, pause, seek and volume from its own remote, keyboard
   or media keys act on the playback, and the sender's remote shows the change. A change made on
   the receiver is reported upward as D136 requires, never inferred from a position standing
   still.
8. **Later, not now:** a "takeover for this session only" for a device not signed in as the person
   (D135's delegation, under D154's grants; the split-device sketch's `orpheum.cc` code and
   playback-only credential, which serves a Watch Together guest's TV); and Google Cast and AirPlay
   receivers (D124, D135–D137), which can later appear as further entries in the same "Cast to"
   list.

**Consequences.**

- **Presence is new.** Nothing in the core knows which devices are open now: a device's
  `last_used_at` says when it last made a request, and Watch Together's socket holds only a
  session's members. "Connected now" needs a live connection per open device of a signed-in
  person, carried over WebRTC when away as the session socket already is.
- **In Watch Together only someone signed in on the host's core can cast.** A guest who came by a
  link is an ephemeral account
  ([D246](#d246--what-a-person-may-do-is-their-roles-an-invite-names-who-it-is-for-and-a-watch-together-viewer-is-an-ephemeral-account-that-sees-only-the-hosts-playback)
  §3) with one device, and a guest's own TV is signed in to their own household, so their TV waits
  for §8. The host and a signed-in member, whose sessions follow them to every device
  ([D267](#d267--a-watch-together-membership-is-kept-by-the-browser-that-joined-or-by-the-account-of-whoever-is-signed-in-and-one-member-may-be-on-several-devices)
  §2, §3), can cast; a host's receiver leads, as *"whichever device the host plays on leads"*
  (D267 §3).
- **D88 is kept.** The remote's commands travel through Watch Together's hub, a cast being a
  session of one (D88), the owner chose on 2026-10-25 between that and a channel of the person's
  own ([cast-to-device.md](../design/plans/cast-to-device.md) §3).
- **The research's build order changes:** its remote page (casting-2026-10-25.md §5.2 step 1) is
  built first for this route, and its playback-only credential, Cast receiver and `orpheum.cc`
  steps wait for §8.

**Answered by the owner** (2026-10-25), accepting every recommendation of
[cast-to-device.md](../design/plans/cast-to-device.md) §9: "Cast to another device" is offered
from the player first and a title's page next; the receiver reports the viewing and the sender
leaves its playback at the hand-off; a sender that plays another film while casting sends it to
its receiver; at a film's end the receiver plays the next episode as the sender would, else goes
to its home page and the remote is told; a sender whose control was taken back or replaced shows a
note with "Play here from ‹position›"; a background tab counts while its socket lives, with no
opt-out; the fading "Controlled from" line is enough; and the remote's commands travel through
Watch Together's hub (a cast is a session of one, D88), with a presence socket for presence and
the hand-off (the plan's §3, A).

> **Revised by [D364](#d364--casting-is-a-session-with-a-device-while-it-lasts-whatever-the-person-plays-plays-there-and-the-sending-device-shows-it-in-the-tray)** (2026-10-27): a cast is a session with a device, not one film: started from the status tray's Cast, asked once, and while it lasts whatever the person plays plays there, ended by Stop, taking control back, another cast or the receiver gone two minutes.

**Status:** Decided; its §9 questions answered 2026-10-25; being built.

## D336 — A film's sound plays as it is unless the device cannot play it or the person asks for a feature that needs it made; no one is asked how their device makes sound

**Decided** (2026-10-25), by the project owner. People were confused by the question of how their
device makes sound, asked before their first playback (*"people get confused by the sound device
selector"*), and the owner asked which answer taxes the server least, then:

> *"I wonder if there's even any point in asking them the question. We could default to passthrough
> unless the device can't handle it, in which case we transcode. If the user wants dialogue boost or
> any feature that requires transcoding, we transcode. We'd also need transcode for 'night mode'."*

**Revises**
[D222](#d222--on-stereo-output-a-multichannel-sound-always-plays-through-our-prepared-copy-and-headphones-are-stereo),
which had a multichannel sound on stereo output always played through our prepared copy so the
dialogue boost could be switched mid-film.

1. **The sound plays as it is by default.** The decision keeps a film's own sound wherever the
   browser says it can play it (its playable formats: codec and channels); the device mixes it down
   for its speakers itself. This is the least work for the server.
2. **The server makes the sound only when it must:** the device cannot play the codec or the
   channels; or the person turns on a feature that needs it made: the **dialogue boost**, or **night
   mode** (the loud passages compressed, a new mix beside the standard and boosted ones).
3. **Turning a feature on mid-film.** On the ladder it switches to that mix (as the boost already
   does). A film playing directly moves onto its ladder at the same position.
4. **No question is asked.** How a device makes sound (built-in speakers, receiver, headphones) no
   longer changes a decision, so it is not asked before a first playback, nor of a Watch Together
   guest; the sound button holds the features instead.
5. **Night mode is made on the server,** not in the browser: a sound routed through Web Audio plays
   late on an Android TV by the context's latency (the owner's TCL TV, 2026-10-24; research
   youtube-tv-browser-av-sync-2026-10-24.md).

**Status:** Built: part 1: the decision keeps a film's own sound wherever the playable
formats list its codec and channels (aac-multi apart from aac-stereo, so a browser without
multichannel AAC still has it made, for audio_codec), and only the dialogue boost, on, over a sound
of more than two channels prepares it (§1, §2); the boost turned on over the original keeps the
choice and asks for the film again from where it stands (cause `boostChosen`), answered by its
ladder or a prepared copy with the boosted mix, and turned off on the ladder or a prepared copy it
stays there on the standard mix (§3); the question is gone from the first playback, the player, the
device pages and a Watch Together guest's join, with its `choosingSound` standing, and
`device.audio_output` is read and written by nothing, kept unmigrated (§4). Night mode (§2, §5) is
not built. On the ladder, whose sounds are the server's stereo mixes, a film's sound is made as
before.

## D335 — What should have been fetched and was not is filled in by the sweeps; a refetch that replaces is the person's deliberate act

**Decided** (2026-10-25), by the project owner, answering the episode-orderings sketch's question on
when a series' orderings are fetched ([episode-orderings.md](../design/plans/episode-orderings.md)):

> *"for any data that should have been populated, there will come edge cases where it wasn't
> populated for some reason. Our regular sweeps should be checking for what's not populated and then
> try to do so (with the usual back-off and give-up logic). This also solves the migration issue
> where we add more metadata fields to a type but the existing data doesn't have it filled. There
> should be two variants of this operation: (1) fill it in if it's missing (passive). (2) a
> deliberate rescan order: fetch the metadata anew and replace (with an option to also replace
> things manually set by the user)."*

**Revisits**
[D170](#d170--one-source-per-title-fetched-once-a-users-correction-is-permanent-and-every-refetch-is-an-act-of-the-user)
("every refetch is an act of the user") and
[D213](#d213--a-good-netizen-a-dead-image-is-checked-once-more-refresh-rolls-per-provider-and-nothing-is-deleted-because-a-provider-dropped-it)'s
rolling refresh: a fetch that only fills what is missing is not a refetch, and the sweeps do it.

1. **Fill in what is missing, passively.** The regular sweeps look for data an item should have and
   does not: a field a fetch left empty, a part a failed fetch never stored, or a field added to a
   type after its items were fetched (so a schema that grows needs no backfill of its own). Each is
   fetched as the first fetch would have been, with the queue's usual back-off and its giving up
   (D231), at the background's priority unless interest raises it (D324). It fills only what is
   empty: nothing present is replaced.
2. **Fetch anew and replace, deliberately.** A person's order, on an item or a library, fetches its
   metadata again and replaces what was fetched before. By default what a person set by hand stays
   (D170: a correction is permanent); an option replaces that too.
3. **Etiquette holds.** Both go through the providers' limits as every fetch does (D213); a sweep
   asks for what is missing a little at a time, never as a flood at startup.

**Status:** Decided; not built.

## D334 — A tester sets up a core from one command at a terminal, which asks for its admin and, if they have one, its key

**Decided** (2026-10-23), by the project owner, for the closed beta (*"Yes this makes sense"*, to
the flow below; *"(d) agreed"*, to the realm rules). The first-time experience was found while
bringing staging back that day: the one-time setup code, a browser at home to type it, the core's
key pasted on a System page afterwards, and an admin refused on the server's own machine. **Extends**
[D314](#d314--a-core-is-installed-from-a-public-image-on-any-machine-that-runs-docker-with-the-hardware-it-needs-and-with-no-tunnel-a-connection-that-needs-a-relay-fails-and-is-counted)'s install and [D297](#d297--a-household-is-found-by-its-realm-realm-name-and-password-together-proven-both-ways-by-a-key-the-password-makes-admin-only-from-the-cores-own-network)'s admin-at-home rule.

1. **The core works at home first, the discovery service never required.** The install command
   carries what the core cannot find for itself (the folders it may serve). Everyone in the house
   can reach it directly; over plain HTTP the browser withholds the microphone, the clipboard and
   service workers, which the client says rather than leaves silently broken. A self-hosted
   discovery service, a mode of the same binary, gives HTTPS without ours; it is for the open beta.
2. **The install asks for the admin at its terminal**, read from `/dev/tty`, never a flag, which
   would land in shell history and `ps`. With no terminal (a NAS's web panel, Portainer, a script)
   it prints the one-time setup code as now, and the first admin is made in the browser.
3. **Then, optionally, for the core's key**, which it enters with the password just given, so the
   core is paired and the admin's realm key made in the same sitting; it ends by saying where to
   sign in, at home and from away. A key can still be entered later in the browser.
4. **The server's own machine is home, by a port only it reaches.** A browser there reaches the
   core through Docker's published port, which hands the request on from Docker's gateway, never
   home. The gateway itself is not made home: wherever Docker's own proxy carries outside connections
   (rootless, or IPv6 without its firewall rules) the internet arrives from it too. The deployment
   publishes a second port, `http.this_machine_port` (8441), on the host's loopback alone, and a
   request on it is from home; the install names both addresses, the house's and
   `http://localhost:8441`, and an admin refused away from home is told to open the latter on the
   server's own computer (the owner, *"OK that sounds good"*). The core's own loopback is home too,
   which only a command run in its container reaches, as §2 and §3's do.
5. **Through the paid discovery service:** the owner sends an invitation (a link and a QR code); the
   person makes an account (name, password, e-mail confirmation; free for life in the closed beta),
   chooses a realm, then makes a key for a core (password or passkey) and gives it to the core. A
   realm is 5 to 32 lowercase letters and digits with hyphens inside, chosen once and never changed
   ([D298](#d298--a-realm-is-the-hosts-accounts-a-master-realm-chosen-once-a-subrealm-per-further-core-none-when-self-hosting)), and names that would mislead, such as `admin`, `orpheum`, `support`,
   `api`, `app`, `account` and `www`, are reserved. A rename, if complaints come, costs every member
   one sign-in with their password, since each realm key is derived from the realm.
6. **The rest of the household is invited by the admin, with no e-mail:** the core's invitation link
   leads to a page that makes a name and a password ([D246](#d246--what-a-person-may-do-is-their-roles-an-invite-names-who-it-is-for-and-a-watch-together-viewer-is-an-ephemeral-account-that-sees-only-the-hosts-playback), [D311](#d311--a-code-establishes-an-entitlement-it-expires-its-issuer-sees-it-and-what-it-made-and-a-new-code-for-the-same-entitlement-moves-it-to-whoever-redeems-it)). An
   admin can still make a person directly, which a home with no discovery service needs.

**Status:** Built (earlier commits; orpheum-connect),
but the self-hosted discovery mode, which waits for the open beta. Read back against the code: the
install script asks at `/dev/tty` for the admin, makes them with `orpheum reset-admin`, then for
the key, which `orpheum pair` enters with the same password, both on standard input, and prints the
setup code instead with no terminal (§2, §3); the deployment publishes `http.this_machine_port` on
`127.0.0.1` alone, the core marks a request on it as home and names it when it refuses an admin,
and its home networks hold its own loopback (§4); connect refuses the reserved realms when one is
chosen (§5); a page over plain HTTP says what is off (§1); the core's invitations and admin-made
accounts are D246's and D311's (§6). On the amd box, 2026-10-23: installed at a terminal as a
tester would, administered from `localhost:8441` and from another machine at home, refused at
`localhost:8440` with the hint, paired by a staging key, and signed in to from away through its
realm in 3.5 s.

## D338 — A cast goes to the device's tab in front, its receiver keeps a television's controls and leaves by Back or a double OK, and Stop casting returns it to the page it was on

**Decided** (2026-10-26), by the project owner, after trying the first build of
[D337](#d337--casting-starts-with-a-persons-own-signed-in-devices-one-chosen-from-those-connected-now-plays-the-film-the-one-that-cast-becomes-its-remote-and-either-may-take-control-back) ([cast-to-device.md](../design/plans/cast-to-device.md) §11). **Amends** D337 §3,
§4 and the §11 assumptions it was built on; keeps D337 §1, §2, §5–§8, and
[D120](#d120--a-participant-is-a-person-devices-attach-to-them-with-roles-and-the-cap-counts-people)
as it names its roles.

1. **Stop casting returns the receiver to where it was.** *"Ideally, I want stop casting to return
   the TV to its previous state, so whatever page it happened to be on before being taken over."*
   And: *"Leaving cast mode should return the controlled device back to whatever page it was
   showing before being taken over."* The first build paused the receiver and left it a player
   (§11's assumption 5). Leaving by the receiver's own exit (§6) is not this: there the film plays
   on, there, as D337 §4 has it.
2. **The tab in front receives.** *"The currently visible tab. If no tab is visible, it should give
   the user an error that they need to bring an orpheum tab to the front."* The first build handed
   the cast to the device's newest connection (§11's assumption 3). Each page's live connection
   says whether its tab is in front, and the "Cast to" list says of a device that it has no
   Orpheum tab in front.
3. **Casting stays hidden while hosting Watch Together**, *"fine for now"* (§11's assumption 11).
4. **A member is the person; their devices fill roles.** *"A remote session member is the human.
   They can have multiple devices connected to that session (one per role it fulfills) but that's
   still one 'member'. For now we will have two device roles: control panel + voice, and video
   viewer."* Watch Together's hub already counts a member as a person with devices attached in
   roles (D120); its roles are named for these two: `video`, the video viewer, and `panel`, the
   control panel with voice, with `both` for one device that is both (they were `playback`,
   `voice` and `both`). A cast is one member: the remote attaches as the panel, the receiver as
   the video viewer.
5. **Both devices have controls.** *"Both devices should have controls (the controlled device would
   have only the fullscreen controls)."* The receiver shows a television's player controls, the
   overlay over the film, rather than nothing (D337 §3 had it show the film and nothing else).
6. **Back, or OK pressed twice, leaves controlled mode.** *"pressing back or double-pressing select
   inside the controlled device's view exits controlled mode. I believe this should cover all
   cases so that you can exit from the controlled device regardless of the local tools
   available."* This replaces D337 §4's two presses, any key raising Take back control and one
   more confirming it. Every other press works the receiver's own controls. Leaving gives the
   receiver back its own playback, which plays on there, and the remote is told.

> **Revised by [D364](#d364--casting-is-a-session-with-a-device-while-it-lasts-whatever-the-person-plays-plays-there-and-the-sending-device-shows-it-in-the-tray)** (2026-10-27): between videos the receiver waits full screen and ready; taking control back with nothing playing goes to its home page; Stop casting returns it to the page it was on before the session.

**Status:** Decided, and built (cast-to-device.md §11, its assumptions 2, 3, 5, 7, 11–13). Device checks: VQ64–VQ66 and VQ68 as revised, and VQ71.

## D339 — Up next keeps its 30 s lead until credits are detected, a run of three autoplays with no press asks Still watching, and a host's autoplay moves their group on

**Decided** (2026-10-26), by the project owner, answering what
[up-next.md](../design/plans/up-next.md) §2 and §9 left open:

> *"accept 30 seconds for now"*

1. **The offer keeps its fixed lead**, 30 s before the end, until credits are detected
   ([D82](#d82--media-segments-are-typed-attach-at-the-version-and-carry-provenance)), when
   it moves to the credits' start (D139).
2. **"Still watching?"** After three episodes autoplayed in a row with no press between, the next
   autoplay does not count down: the film's end shows a *Still watching?* card, **Continue** (focused,
   so OK presses it), which plays the next episode, and **Stop**, which leaves the film. Any press
   on the page, a remote's, a key, a tap or a click, starts the run again. Three is a justified
   constant (`stillWatchingAfterAutoplays`): the field's number, so a person asleep is not played a
   season, and a press resets it, so no one awake meets it. The run is the tab's.
3. **In Watch Together the host's autoplay moves the whole group on.** The host's player moving on
   to the next episode, by autoplay or by a press of Up next, does not stop the session as leaving
   the player does (D246 §5): the next episode's player puts its film on for everyone, so every
   screen follows the host's player into it without going black between.

**Proven by:**
- 1: web/apps/web/src/up-next.test.tsx (the fixed lead: "shows within its lead of the end and on the end screen, and not before")
- 2: web/apps/web/src/up-next.test.tsx (the three D339 tests), web/apps/web/src/still-watching.browser.test.tsx
- 3: web/apps/web/src/together-host.test.ts

**Status:** Decided, and built (2026-10-26, an earlier commit; point 3's test 2026-10-27). Point 1's move to the
credits' start waits on credits detection, which nothing makes yet
([D82](#d82--media-segments-are-typed-attach-at-the-version-and-carry-provenance),
[media-segments.md](../design/plans/media-segments.md)); until then the fixed 30 s lead is the
whole of it.

## D340 — A video's text subtitle tracks are extracted by one job from one read of it, and a failed track alone is tried again when next played

**Decided** (2026-10-26), by the project owner (*"build it"*), on finding N3 of the
[2026-10-25 audit](../design/research/audit-2026-10-25.md): each embedded text track was its own job
and its own read of the whole file, one at a time, so a film with N text tracks cost N reads of
20–60 GB on the disk its playback used. **Revises**
[D217](#d217--m3s-playback-contract-the-client-sends-ranked-lists-the-media-token-is-a-reference-every-audio-track-is-prepared-and-hlsjs-jassub-and-playwright-are-allowed)
§6's job, which made one track's ASS and WebVTT.

1. **A subtitle job is a file's.** `extract_subtitle` works on the file a track's bytes are in, no
   longer on the stream: a video, for its own text tracks, or a subtitle file beside it, for its one.
   A play queues one job per such file that holds a track with no text kept; run, the job asks the
   node for every text track in the file that has neither a text nor a failure kept.
2. **A video is read once for all its tracks.** The command names the video and its tracks
   (`streamIndexes`, node protocol 44). The node's FFmpeg reads the film once and writes every
   track as ASS into one Matroska on stdout; each track is taken out of that in memory and converted
   to WebVTT, as before. Its watchdog gives the run the whole file's read. Matroska on the one stdout
   rather than a pipe or a temporary file per track: it changes neither the runner's descriptors nor
   what a confined run may write.
3. **A track fails alone.** The answer carries each track's text or its own failure. A track that
   cannot be taken out of the Matroska or converted fails alone. FFmpeg fails the whole read for one
   track it cannot convert, so then the node reads each track on its own, and only that track fails:
   N reads, in that case alone. A refusal or a stall still says nothing of the bytes and is the whole
   command's: not kept, the job tried again, and a second stall in a row the failure of every track
   it named (D233 §6).
4. **The retry rule.** A failed track is kept as its own failure and shows `prepare_failed`; the
   others' texts are kept, and the job fails naming the tracks that failed. The next play forgets the
   failure and queues the file's job, which then asks for that track alone. A job given up (D231 §4,
   §10) is the failure of each of its tracks with nothing kept, never of one already made or failed.
5. **The subtitles package's first invariant** now reads: every text subtitle track of a played
   video, its own and its subtitle files', is extracted, whatever the decision, once per payload hash
   of the file it is in, by one job per file that makes every track in it not yet made, a video's
   from one read of it; a track not yet extracted is 425 with Retry-After, a failed one is
   `prepare_failed` on its own, the others kept, and it alone is extracted again when next played; a
   node's refusal or a stall is the whole job's, not kept, and its job is tried again; and a playback
   reaches only its own file's tracks.
6. **Out of scope.** Making the text from the playback's own read of the film
   ([data-timeliness.md](../design/plans/data-timeliness.md) §4.4) stays open. A job that works on a
   file is raised by a person's interest in that file, as a read-through is (D324 §3).

**Status:** Decided.

## D341 — Reserved: A hidden tab's interest

**Reserved** (2026-10-26) for a branch being built from the owner's answers of 2026-10-26; the branch replaces this entry with the decision.

## D342 — API answers that carry no credential are gzipped; an answer that carries one never is

**Decided** (2026-10-26), by the project owner, answering the 2026-10-25 audit's R1, whose API half
was left for BREACH ([audit-2026-10-25.md](../design/research/audit-2026-10-25.md)): compress the
API's JSON answers that carry no secret beside text a request chose (lists, titles, search results,
browse pages), with the standard library's gzip, and never the session, sign-in, device, pairing,
link or token answers. The owner asked whether zstd is better; it is not taken.

1. **An allowlist of operations.** `compressedOperations` (internal/core/api) names the operations
   whose answers are gzipped: browsing, identification, the scanner's view and the admin's views.
   A new operation is not compressed until it is added there.
2. **No compressed answer carries a credential, and a test says so.**
   `TestArch_NoCompressedOperationAnswersWithACredential` walks each listed operation's success
   answer through the API document and fails on any field named as a token, secret, password,
   session, link, code, key, nonce, signature or locator, unless the test's table names it as
   holding none (a setting's key, a scan's error code). BREACH needs a secret and request-chosen text
   in one compressed answer; with no secret in any, there is nothing to recover.
3. **When.** A success whose JSON is at least 1 KiB, to a client whose Accept-Encoding takes gzip,
   at gzip's fastest level; every listed answer varies by Accept-Encoding. A byte path (films,
   images, subtitles) is never one of them.
4. **No zstd.** Browsers decode zstd (Chrome and Edge since 123, Firefox since 126; Safari only recently,
   and older iPhones and televisions not at all),
   but Go's standard library has no zstd encoder, so it would be a new dependency for a few percent
   on answers of a few kilobytes; gzip is in every browser and television's.
5. **Over WebRTC, not yet.** A request over a data channel carries only the headers the page's SDK
   sends, which name no Accept-Encoding, so its answers stay as they are until the SDK asks for gzip
   and unzips (DecompressionStream) — a later change.

**Status:** Built.

## D343 — The replay nonce is one public building block, discovery/proof's Nonces, which both discoveries use

**Decided** (2026-10-26), by the project owner, choosing option (a) of the 2026-10-25 audit's R4
([audit-2026-10-25.md](../design/research/audit-2026-10-25.md)): the MAC'd stateless nonce that
guards every signed core call against replay (the security audit's S13) was written twice, in
`discovery/single` and in orpheum-connect's `internal/cores`, and a fix to one would not have
reached the other.

1. **One public type.** `discovery/proof` holds `Nonces`: `NewNonces` makes its key, `Issue` makes
   a nonce (8 bytes of expiry, 16 random, a 16-byte HMAC-SHA256, keeping nothing) and `Spend` takes
   a `SignedNonce`, checks the MAC, the expiry and the signature for its purpose, discovery and core
   (`Verify`), and spends it once, kept until it expires.
2. **Both use it.** `discovery/single`'s discovery and orpheum-connect's cores service hold one
   each; their own copies are deleted. Connect takes it through its pin of Orpheum's `discovery/`
   (D275 §1: the paid service assembles the public building blocks).
3. **Revises the copy-don't-publish habit for this one piece:** a security check that both
   discoveries must apply alike is published, not twinned.

**Status:** Built.

## D344 — The whole-film prepare is retired: every playback the device cannot play as it is plays from its ladder, cut on time where its keyframes cannot be had

**Decided** (2026-10-26), by the project owner, on C9/N6 of the audit of 2026-10-25
(design/research/audit-2026-10-25.md): *"agreed"*, to deciding whether the on-time grid
([D269](#d269--a-film-with-no-keyframe-index-is-cut-on-time-and-plays-encoded-at-once-its-original-picture-is-copied-once-a-read-through-has-found-its-keyframes))
can carry the playbacks that still fell back to a prepared copy, then retiring prepare, or
recording why it stays. The check is design/plans/retire-prepare.md §1: it can. **Narrows**
[D193](#d193--the-audits-proposals-are-accepted-the-node-does-all-media-work-prepare-is-the-one-path-besides-direct-play-the-machinery-is-cut-and-cut-as-design-freezes)
§2, [D217](#d217--m3s-playback-contract-the-client-sends-ranked-lists-the-media-token-is-a-reference-every-audio-track-is-prepared-and-hlsjs-jassub-and-playwright-are-allowed)
§3 and §5 and [D225](#d225--one-admin-page-system-shows-every-fact-about-the-server-and-each-node-and-m3s-shows-whether-hardware-encoding-works)
§3; **revises** [D260](#d260--a-film-plays-from-its-ladder-of-qualities-from-the-start-filled-on-its-page-and-its-player-keeps-choosing-as-it-plays)
§1 and D269 §1.

1. **There is one path besides direct play: the ladder** (D247 §10, D260). No whole-film copy is
   made: the prepare job, its renditions, their index in cache.db, their files on the node, and
   what showed or waited on them (a prepared playback's playlists, the System page's finished
   prepares, a file's prepare wait) are removed. A film's sounds keep D217 §3's mixes, each track's
   standard and, with a centre, its boosted one, as chunks; the node's prepared directory keeps
   the stores of chunks within the same budget (D217 §5).
2. **A film whose keyframes cannot be had in time is cut on time** (D269 §1): one whose
   keyframes were not read within `play_ladder_wait_ms`, one FFmpeg could not read through, and
   one with no keyframe before its end. Its playback keeps that grid to its end (D269 §3); the
   next is cut on the keyframes once they are known. A run asked for on the time grid is made on
   it.
3. **On time, the top of the ladder is the twin** (D323 §1), H.264 at the picture's own height,
   whether or not the player decodes the original, so a playback that would have had its picture
   copied by a prepare is not held below the film's own height.
4. **A picture too small for a twin, which the player cannot decode, is offered the one quality**
   an on-time film is offered when none is below it, so its playback has a picture.
5. **A playback that still cannot start on its ladder is refused** as one that cannot be
   converted: a file with no picture, or with neither a known length nor keyframes. A prepare
   could not carry those either.
6. **Offline download** ([D87](#d87--a-download-is-a-rendition-plus-a-lease-and-it-is-self-contained),
   not built) was designed as a prepared rendition plus a lease; what a download's rendition is
   becomes its own question when it is built.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-26; built the same day (design/plans/retire-prepare.md). Not yet watched on a
device: a converted film whose keyframes come late now starts on time, its twin at the top.
