## D346 — A Watch Together invitation is short-term: a link admits for an hour, ending the session ends every link and membership, and a session idle for six hours is ended

**Decided** (2026-10-26), by the project owner:

> *"watch together should be a short-term invitation. Invitations are good for an hour, and once
> the host ends the session, all invitations and session links are invalidated. A host who forgets
> to close the session has it closed after 6h of inactivity."*

This revises [D246](#d246--what-a-person-may-do-is-their-roles-an-invite-names-who-it-is-for-and-a-watch-together-viewer-is-an-ephemeral-account-that-sees-only-the-hosts-playback)
§3, under which a link waited until it was used or withdrawn, and a session lasted until its host
ended it or the server restarted.

1. **A link admits its person for an hour from when it was made**, then no one: it leaves the
   host's list and the discovery's links, and a join by it is refused as a used or withdrawn one is.
   Whoever joined by it in time stays in; their membership is not the link. A new link for a
   guest's place (D267 §4 as amended) is a link like any other. The host's list says until when each waiting link
   admits (*good until 21:40*).
2. **Ending the session ends everything of it at once**: every link, every membership's credential
   and every viewer's cookie admit nothing from then on (as built since Cut A; D119, D246 §5).
3. **A session idle for six hours is ended as the host's end would**, each device told why
   (`idle`). **Idle** is neither playback nor anything a member does. Playback is the group playing
   with a player attached; a group left "playing" with every player gone plays to no one. What a
   member does is a command (play, pause, seek, a film put on or stopped), a join, a leave, a link
   made or withdrawn, a member removed, or the host opening their session's page. What a device's
   page sends by itself is not: its state reports and pings each second, its notes, what it waits
   on, a reconnect, and voice signalling, since a call set up again after a drop is the page's, not
   a person's. Two people only talking for six hours with nothing on are ended; they open a new one.
4. **Both are settings, not constants:** `together_link_lifetime_seconds` (3600) and
   `together_idle_session_end_hours` (6). They are a household's policy, the owner's numbers a
   start: another household may send an invitation earlier in the day or want a long pause kept, and
   nothing in the code depends on their values. They are read each minute, the bound on how late an
   idle session is ended; a link is refused from the moment its hour is up whatever the look's time.
5. **A guest holding a link that no longer works is told so plainly**: invitations are
   short-lived, this one has expired, was used or withdrawn, or the session is over, and to ask the
   sender for a new one. A guest whose session the server closed is told it was closed because
   nothing had happened in it for hours.

**Status:** Decided; not built.

## D347 — The core's log level is a setting an admin changes while it runs, and every API request carries an ID into its log lines and its answer

**Decided** (2026-10-26), by the project owner, answering the 2026-10-25 audit's G11
([audit-2026-10-25.md](../design/research/audit-2026-10-25.md)), which the owner asked for on
2026-10-15 (runtime-changeable log depth): an admin changes the log's level with no restart, and
every API request gets an ID carried in its context, on every line it causes, and returned to the
client.

1. **A setting, log_level.** `debug`, `info`, `warn` or `error`, or `file`, its starting value,
   which is the config file's `log.level`, so a deployment's own level holds until an admin chooses
   another. A change takes effect at once (the settings service's OnChange sets the logger's
   `slog.LevelVar`), and the change itself is logged. It is the core's alone; a node's level stays
   its config file's.
2. **A request ID, the core's own.** Every request the API answers, over TCP or a WebRTC data
   channel, is given 16 random base32 characters, never an ID the client sent (a client cannot write
   into the log's correlation). The answer names it in `X-Request-ID`, which a page on the
   discovery's origin may read, so a person reporting a failure can quote it.
3. **On every line it causes.** The ID rides in the request's context, and the process's logger
   (`internal/platform/slogx`) adds it as `requestId` to every line logged with that context, the
   form nearly every log call in the core takes.
4. **Not in this:** per-component levels and the `component` attribute on every service (G11's
   mechanical part) are later work.

**Status:** Built.

## D348 — The most WebRTC connections a core holds is a config key, webrtc.max_connections

**Decided** (2026-10-26), by the project owner, answering the 2026-10-25 audit's R10
([audit-2026-10-25.md](../design/research/audit-2026-10-25.md)): *"make webrtc max connections a
config value."*

1. **A config key, not a setting.** `[webrtc] max_connections` in the core's config file bounds the
   peer connections the core holds at once, of every network. It is the machine owner's, beside the
   UDP port and the STUN servers, not an admin's in the database: it sizes what the machine carries.
   Each network's share under it stays the `webrtc_connections_per_network` setting.
2. **Its starting value is 64,** the constant it replaces (`rtcapi.DefaultMaxConnections`): a client
   opens up to four connections, so 64 holds 16 remote devices. A file without the key runs on 64
   and says so (D202); a value under 1 is refused at start.
3. **Read at start.** A change takes effect when the core restarts; connections held are kept.

The audit's other half of R10, a verdict code for an offer refused at the limit, is not part of
this.

**Status:** Built.

## D349 — Libraries are browsed on a page of their own, which replaces Search; a kind, other, holds the videos that are never identified; Films and Series gather every library of theirs but those a person leaves out

**Decided** (2026-10-26), by the project owner, answering the ten questions of
[library-browsing.md](../design/plans/library-browsing.md) §8, which the owner asked for on
2026-10-25 (*"I want to have the ability to browse individual libraries … This will be important
when we add support for other kinds of videos, like home movies, which won't fit under series or
films"*). The answers depart from the plan's recommendations in two places: a library is a place,
on a page of its own, not a filter on the Films page (Q1, Q9), and Films and Series gather their
libraries with a per-person way to leave one out (Q8). **Extends** D243 §4 (the libraries a role
reaches are still the only way in), D163 (the folder view is the file tree as the scanner saw it)
and D149 §7 (folder browsing); **keeps** D160 (a folder is not a collection) and D170 (a correction
is a person's override).

1. **A page of libraries replaces Search** (Q1, Q9). *"Replace the search page with a 'Libraries'
   page. On that page you can select libraries (or 'all'). The dropdown shows the libraries in
   alphabetical order and auto-selects the first one when visiting the page. Eventually all
   listing view pages will include a search field, and other things like the sorting, genre
   selection and such along the top row next to the library name."* and *"Libraries goes to a
   separate page."* The top bar is Films, Series, Libraries, Watch Together. The page's top row holds
   the library chooser, its views and sorts, and a search field, so search stays one press away
   until every list carries its own; a search there searches the library chosen, or every one.
2. **The page starts afresh on every visit, and Back restores it** (Q2): *"the other page resets on
   every visit, except when using the back button to return to it."* What it shows (the library,
   the view, the folder, the sort, the search) is in its address, so the top bar's link opens it at
   its start and Back, a reload and a bookmark return to where it was; focus comes back as on every
   page (the focus memory of each history entry).
3. **One kind, `other`, for every video that is neither a film nor a series** (Q3): home movies,
   concerts, lectures, clips. The library's name, which its admin gives it, says what it holds. A
   library of the kind files every video it lists as a title of the kind `other`, one title a file,
   never an extra, an episode or a version of another, with the file's name as its name unless an
   NFO file beside it names it.
4. **Dated, and sorted more ways than by date** (Q4, Q5): *"For dates, yes (recorded-time tag, else
   a date in the name/folder, else the file's time; show where it came from; admin can correct it).
   However we should be able to sort by things other than date (such as extracted name, file name,
   etc)."* An other video's recorded date is the container's recorded-time tag as the node's probe
   reads it, else a date in its file's or folders' names, else the file's modified time, kept with
   where it came from, which its page shows; an admin's correction is an override (D170) and shows
   as theirs. Its list sorts by recorded date (newest first, the default), by name, by file name and
   by date added.
5. **An other library's page has no genres; it has a View, All or Folders** (Q5): *"'other'
   libraries won't show things like genre (which wouldn't make sense), but will have a View ['All',
   'Folders']. For now it will only show video files (all kinds, even really old ones like
   realmedia), with drill-down into folders."* Folders is the library's folders as the scanner saw
   them, each opening into its own folders and videos; every video the scanner reads is listed,
   whatever its container. A disc image is the ISO work's to list; nothing here excludes one.
6. **A folder is only a view** (Q6): *"Viewing a folder should prioritize its contents. We can save
   that for later if it's a lot of work."* The videos of a folder in view are the page's interest
   (D324), as a list's posters are.
7. **Other videos are videos like any other** (Q7): *"'Other' videos get treated the same as any
   video. It's just that we can't classify them like movies and series (e.g. no genre). So I may
   want to view wedding videos with the family using watch together."* They play, resume, appear in
   Continue Watching and in search, and are watched together, as a film is.
8. **Films and Series gather every library of their kind, and a person may leave one out** (Q8):
   *"The 'Film' and 'Series' links from the top menu are aggregated from all libraries of those
   types. The user can exclude a library from that aggregated view."* The choice is the person's,
   kept on their account and made on their own settings; a library left out is still on the
   Libraries page.
9. **The alphabet rail shows only where it means something, and only letters that lead somewhere.**
   The owner, the same day: *"When sorting by anything other than alphabetical, the alphabet rail
   doesn't make sense so it shouldn't be shown. The rail should also follow the alphabetical sort
   order selected (when sorting alphabetically)."* and *"The alphabet rail shouldn't show letters
   that won't map to a starting movie. This also means that it will have to update itself if a
   movie is found that has a letter not present currently."* The server says which letters the list
   in its order begins its titles with, by name or by file name, in a handful of index seeks, and the
   rail asks again with the list's own background poll (D237).
10. **Nothing about an other video leaves the server unless its owner chooses** (Q10): *"Owners can
    opt-in on a per-report basis (default no) whether to include 'other' library information. The
    bug report will be in markdown so they can verify."* An other library is never identified
    online: it takes NFO files only, which the schema holds it to, so no name of it reaches TMDB. A
    filing report of an other video withholds its name and paths unless the admin asks for them in
    that report, and says which it did, in the Markdown they read before posting it.

**Rejected:** a chooser on the Films and Series pages (the plan's §5.2), for a page of libraries
(the owner, Q1); remembering a chosen library per person or device (Q2); `home_videos` and further
kinds as they come (Q3); an other video filed as a film in a library that says so, which would have
spared the title table its new kind and made every list of films ask the library's kind.

**Status:** Built (library-browsing.md): the Libraries page itself, §8's setting of which
libraries Films and Series gather (the person's own account, `left-out-libraries.tsx`; honoured
server-side since the page that called for it was built), and §9's alphabet-rail letter-filtering
on Films and Series too (2026-10-26). The picture of an other video is an image beside it where
there is one; a frame the node takes from the video waits for its own step.

## D350 — A disc image plays its main title, read by the node from the image's own structure and served to FFmpeg through fdproxy

**Decided** (2026-10-26): the owner, *"I also want iso support now."*, which revisits
[D306](#d306--the-scanner-is-tested-on-names-of-our-own-places-an-unnumbered-episode-by-a-guessed-title-match-and-keeps-watching-by-title-and-edition)
§5 for `.iso` images; how, by the agent's recommendation in
[iso-support.md](../design/research/iso-support.md) (option A), for the owner to confirm.

1. **A DVD or Blu-ray image (`.iso`) in any library is read as a video**, its film being its
   **main title**: the longest title of a DVD (by its program chains' playing time) or the longest
   playlist of a Blu-ray. Menus are never played. Disc folders (`VIDEO_TS`, `BDMV`) stay skipped as
   D306 §5 has them.
2. **The node reads the image's structure itself**, in Go with no new dependency (UDF with its
   metadata partition, the DVD's IFOs, the Blu-ray's playlists), bounded as every hostile input is
   ([D126](#d126--hostile-bytes-never-reach-the-core-hostile-strings-reach-it-constantly-and-that-is-the-design)),
   and turns the main title into byte ranges of the image.
3. **FFmpeg is served those ranges, joined, through fdproxy**
   ([D330](#d330--ffmpeg-reads-its-input-through-the-node-over-a-protocol-of-our-own-patched-into-jellyfin-ffmpeg)):
   to FFmpeg the title is a program stream (DVD) or an M2TS transport stream (Blu-ray), demuxed as
   such a file is. No FFmpeg change: FFmpeg's own disc readers (`dvdvideo`, absent from the pinned
   build, and `bluray:`, present) open their input by path, which would give up D330 for discs. A
   node whose FFmpeg cannot be streamed a film refuses a disc, saying so.
4. **The probe record says it is a disc** (its kind and title), with the title's duration, chapters
   and its streams' languages from the disc, which neither stream carries. **A disc never plays
   direct**, even when a person prefers it: its bytes are the image's.
5. **What is refused, with its reason, until a later step lifts it:** an encrypted image (CSS,
   AACS; decrypting is not proposed); a DVD title with interleaved cells (angles, seamless
   branching). A Blu-ray playlist of several play items is served as its whole clips in order,
   in and out points inside a clip not cut.

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-26; not built.

## D351 — The core's services are assembled in one package, internal/core/assembly, which serve and the tests share; cmd/orpheum reads the outside world and runs the lifecycle

**Decided** (2026-10-26), by the project owner, choosing option A for the test-architecture
review's finding 9 ([test-architecture-2026-10-26.md](../design/research/test-architecture-2026-10-26.md)):
the server was wired by hand in three places, production's `serve`, the API tests' harness and the
metadata scenarios' `jobsWorld`, so a constructor's change edited all three and the harnesses
drifted from production. A test inside package `api` cannot import anything that imports `api`,
and the wiring builds `api.Dependencies`, which is what kept the wiring in `cmd/orpheum`.

1. **One package assembles the core's services: `internal/core/assembly`.** `assembly.Build` makes
   every service the core runs over its stores and wires them to each other, and returns them with
   the API's dependencies and the jobs table (each kind's runner, each sweep). `serve` calls it, and
   so do the API's test harness and the metadata scenarios: tests run production's wiring.
2. **`cmd/orpheum` stays the composition root.** It reads argv, the environment, the config and the
   instance's files, opens and migrates the databases, seeds the settings, makes what the config
   alone configures (the HTTPS certificates, the discovery, port mapping, the reachability check,
   the voice relay, WebRTC, diagnostics) and runs the lifecycle: the listeners, the node channel,
   the runners and loops on their tickers, the shutdown.
3. **The assembly is given what it cannot make itself, and a test's fakes in its place.** Its parts
   are the stores, the settings, the secret key, where the setup code is kept, the clock, the
   randomness, the log, the outbound client and the outside hosts' addresses; and, where a test
   fakes what reaches a node or another host, the fake, nil being production's own. The node
   connection is an interface, the union of what each service already asks of `nodes.Service` and
   the setters through which they are wired to it, which the API harness's fake node implements;
   faking the node at the wire would change how three hundred tests observe its commands.
4. **The API's tests are an external test package, `api_test`,** which may import the assembly;
   `export_test.go` exposes what they read of the package's internals. The metadata scenarios
   (S25, S70, S73, S78) are the assembly's tests.
5. **The assembly is core code under every core rule:** no file but through `instancedir`, no root
   context, no environment, no logger of its own.

**Rejected:** faking the node at the wire level (above); a dependency-injection framework (the
one-way rules); keeping the harnesses' own wiring beside production's.

**As built** (the agent's choices on the points the owner left open):

- **The name says what it holds,** read at the use site: `assembly.Build(ctx, assembly.Parts{...})`
  returns `*assembly.Services`, whose `API` is the API's dependencies.
- **The node connection is one interface, `assembly.Nodes`,** made of the interfaces each service's
  own package already declares of `nodes.Service` (the exchanges' Sender and Rooms, artwork's,
  readthrough's, subtitles', chunks' Encoders, waits', the library admin's and the API's
  NodeReports) and four setters (SetResultSink, SetScans, SetChanges, SetStoreTiers): 23 methods in
  all, of which the API harness's fake node lacked six, which it now implements, four as no-ops.
  The byte socket's setter is not in it: only the core's own node channel has a byte socket, so a
  test that fakes the channel fakes its bytes too, and Build refuses one that does not.
- **The seams are six,** each nil in production: the node channel, its bytes, the scan requests, the
  file reads, OpenSubtitles and the metadata providers; and the job queue's jitter, which a test
  makes exact. Everything else the harness has is production's: the logger, the job queue's
  argument merges, the node work's silence limit, the scans, the artwork service and its hand-overs,
  Watch Together's seeks snapped to keyframes, the interest raiser, every hook a pass and a secret
  run. The API's 311 tests passed on it with no assertion changed.
- **The jobs table moved with the services:** each kind's runner (`KindRunners`, the assembly giving
  the exchanges each node kind's assignee) and each sweep (`AddSweeps`); the runners' tickers and
  goroutines, the sweeping loop and the loops beside them stay `cmd/orpheum`'s.
- **Eight of the API's test files stay internal** (package `api`): they test internals alone and
  need no harness.
- **No architecture test changed:** none says that only `cmd/orpheum` composes; the forbidigo rules
  that exempt `cmd/` (`[ambient]`, `[context]`, `[print]`, `[panic]`) hold the assembly as
  any core package, and it needs none of them.

**Status:** Decided, and built (2026-10-26).

## D352 — The chunked player trusts its link as far as the evidence goes: its first seconds latch nothing, it climbs as far as consistent samples carry, and it grows steadier when it swings or its link flakes

**Decided** (2026-10-27), by the project owner, agreeing an agent's proposal and answering its
questions as it recommended (below), made at the owner's direction after The Unknown sat on its
lowest quality for minutes on staging (2026-10-26): *"We're going to have transient network issues in
the real world, so we should be more adaptable to the changing environment, and more intelligent
about how we recover from it (such as jumping multiple rungs when it's obvious that we can). We do,
however, want to switch to a more conservative approach if it starts to feel like we've started
thrashing (jump down too far, then jump up too far, repeat). Also, if network conditions keep flaking
out, the network itself is too unreliable at higher rates and we're better off staying on a lower
rung longer."* **Amends** [D265](#d265--the-chunked-player-chooses-its-quality-with-a-bitrate-controller-of-its-own-inside-hlsjs)
§4–§5 and [D247](#d247--a-slow-link-gets-a-lower-version-made-at-its-first-stall-and-played-from-its-second-and-a-group-waits-for-a-stalled-viewer-once-then-lets-them-catch-up-alone)
§9. The research is [abr-adaptation-2026-10-27.md](../design/research/abr-adaptation-2026-10-27.md).

The measurement itself was fixed first (a chunk is timed from its first byte to its last, the
`arrivalMs` fix of 2026-10-27). What remains is the controller's response: one sample lowered the
ceiling at once, and D247 §9's step-up, one quality per 120 s held, took eight minutes to climb four
qualities back while its link measured 2.8–5.6 Mb/s within the first minute. The controller has one
speed of caution for every link; this gives it a measure of how far to trust its estimate, and of how
steady its link has been.

1. **The first seconds latch nothing.** Until the playback has **four chunks that measured the
   link** (D265 §7) *and* has played **20 s**, it is *starting*: each chunk's quality is chosen as
   D265 §4 chooses it, from the link's estimate (§2) as it stands, but a choice below the ceiling
   does not lower the ceiling, so the next chunk may be chosen higher again as soon as the estimate
   recovers. Only
   a chunk given up on its way (D265 §3) or a stall lowers the ceiling while starting: each is a
   chunk that did not arrive in time, not a reading of one. When starting ends, the ceiling becomes
   the highest quality the *confident estimate* (§2) carries, by D265 §4's share, no higher than the
   start (D260 §2). A start's samples are the least reliable a playback takes: the first request
   on a WebRTC connection opened seconds before waits for its channel and its transport's queue,
   and a fresh connection's congestion window is still opening (the research, §2), so a single one
   must not decide minutes of playback. **The speed remembered for the device's next start (D257
   §1) is the confident estimate**, never a lone first sample. *Why four and 20 s:* four samples
   are the fewest whose spread says anything (§2), and by 20 s played the player has filled its
   first buffer, a dozen chunks or more, so a bad first sample has left §2's five; both are
   constants, to be measured. In the owner's report, the first chunk's 1008 kb/s would have chosen
   the lowest quality for the next chunk alone; the chunks after it, measuring 2.8–5.6 Mb/s, would have
   chosen higher again within seconds. *As built (2026-10-27):* a stall is D247 §2's, as the
   player counts it (`watchStalls`), a first load slow to play and a group's player falling behind
   among them; it lowers the ceiling to what the estimate then chooses.
2. **The step-up climbs as far as consistent samples carry.** The controller keeps the **last five
   chunks that measured the link**, each counted once whatever its length, and from them **the
   link's estimate**, their harmonic mean, which every choice of D265 §4 reads in place of hls.js's
   (hls.js's estimator is still fed, for hls.js's own readers, D265 §1). hls.js's weighs each sample
   by the seconds it took to load, so one slow sample outweighs dozens of quick ones: after the
   owner's 1008 kb/s, 30 to 80 chunks at the lowest quality would have passed before its estimate
   came within a tenth of 12 Mb/s (the research, §1.4). The harmonic mean of five falls as fast at
   one slow sample and is rid of it five chunks later. From the estimate comes the **confident
   estimate**: the estimate divided by one plus the largest error of its own recent predictions
   (how far each of the five fell from the estimate before it, as a share of the sample;
   RobustMPC's discount, the research §3).
   At each look (every 10 s, as now), once the quality has been held for the hold (§3) with
   **20 s loaded ahead** (as now), the ceiling rises to the **highest quality whose average rate
   times the headroom (§3) the confident estimate carries**. When the samples **agree**, their
   largest prediction error at most **20%**, the rise may be several qualities at once; when they do
   not, it is one quality, as D247 §9 has it. A link that falls is still followed at once: one
   slow sample pulls the harmonic mean of five down by most of the way, and a chunk on its way is
   given up as now (D265 §3). *Why the harmonic mean of five:* it is the average a chunk's download
   time follows, pessimistic about a slow sample without remembering it long, and five is
   RobustMPC's window and FESTIVE's down to a quarter (FESTIVE keeps 20); *why 20%:* about one
   rung's gap on the ladder (0.7 → 1.2 → 2 → 3 Mb/s), so samples that agree within it name one
   rung, not two.
3. **A swing makes it steadier.** The controller has a **steadiness level** from 0 to 3, 0 at a
   playback's start. A **swing** is a step down, by the link, a chunk given up or a stall, within
   **twice the hold after a step up**: the climb did not hold. A swing raises the level by one. The
   level sets the **hold before a step up: 30 s, 60 s, 120 s, 240 s**, and the **headroom: 1.5×
   the quality's rate at levels 0 and 1, 1.75× at 2, 2× at 3**; at level 1 and above the step-up is
   one quality at a time. **It relaxes by one level for each 10 minutes with no swing and no drop
   (§4).** A link that settles is back at level 0, the 30 s hold and multi-quality climbs, within
   half an hour; one that swings twice in a film's first ten minutes is held for four minutes per
   step. *Why 30 s at level 0:* five to eight chunks of evidence (our chunks are 4–10 s), where
   Shaka waits 8 s between switches and Media3 10 s of buffer; 120 s at level 2 is D247 §9's hold, so
   a link that has swung twice is treated as today's every link. *Why doubling:* each swing says the
   last hold was too short by an unknown factor; doubling reaches the slow end in three swings.
4. **A link that flakes is trusted less.** A **drop** is a chunk given up or a stall, at any
   quality. A second drop within **10 minutes** of the first raises the steadiness level by one, as
   a swing does, and each drop after it within those 10 minutes raises it again (to 3 at most). The
   confident estimate (§2) already falls on a link whose samples vary, since its divisor is the
   largest recent error: a link whose chunks arrive at 4, 12, 3 and 11 Mb/s is targeted near its
   slowest, not its mean. A link that holds steady earns back its trust by §3's relaxing, and its
   divisor shrinks as varying samples leave the five. *As built (2026-10-27):* one event raises
   the level once, though it is both a swing and a second drop, and a climb swings once, at its
   first step down or drop.
5. **The log explains each choice.** Each change of the ceiling is noted (D265's steps, the play
   report) with why, the confident estimate and its parts (harmonic mean, error), how many samples
   it rests on, what is loaded ahead, the steadiness level and the hold; each change of the level
   is noted with what raised or relaxed it; the end of starting is noted with its samples. The last
   five samples, each its quality, bytes, time to arrive and wait for its first byte, go with every
   stall and seek report beside the steps, and the core logs them. *Why:* the owner's report needed
   a day's reading of code to explain one number (memory: "if explaining a report needs digging,
   the fix adds the logging that would have said it").

**Values:** every number above is a **constant** in the player (`web/packages/player/src`), beside
D265's: they tune one algorithm against the others and no admin can judge them, and each is to be
measured on the acceptance's emulated links (D252, D263) and the owner's devices before it is
trusted. The share a quality may take stays the setting `link_share_for_quality_percent`
(D247 §6). No new setting.

**Rejected:** BOLA or (Robust)MPC as the controller, a learned controller, a buffer-only
controller, the median, a probe, and a memory of the rung that failed (each with why in the
research, §5); keeping one hold for every link (the owner's report).

**The owner's answers** (2026-10-27), each as recommended:

- Q1. *A hold of 30 s at level 0, against D247 §9's "a couple of minutes"?* Yes, 30 s at level 0:
  confidence is now the samples' agreement (§2).
- Q2. *Should a playback start at the steadiness level its device last ended at on that network,
  remembered as D257 §1 remembers its speed?* Yes. D257 §1's network is the address the core sees a
  request come from, which the player never learns, so the owner chose (2026-10-27) to keep it in
  the core. *As built (2026-10-27):* every play report carries the chunked player's level
  (`steadiness`), which the core keeps beside the speed, by the same player and network and for the
  same `link_speed_fresh_hours`, in memory as the speed is; every offer (`LadderBody.steadiness`, at a
  start and for a stall's lower quality) hands it back, and the controller starts at it and relaxes
  from there as §3 says. Between playbacks the core relaxes it by one for each hour since it was
  reported, six times slower than §3's ten calm minutes while playing, since nothing is watched
  between them: a film started again within the hour starts as steady as the last ended, and a bad
  evening is forgotten by the next morning, well inside the day the speed is kept. The hour is the
  setting `link_steadiness_relaxes_seconds` (3600 to start, 600 to 86400; the owner, 2026-10-27).
- Q3. *§5's samples in the stall and seek reports?* Yes, always, not only at debug level. *As built
  (2026-10-27):* each stall's and seek's `linkSamples`, a field of its own beside the steps, which
  the core logs (`stallLinkSamples`, `linkSamples`).
- Q4. *Should a swing or a drop of a Watch Together player raise its level?* Yes: swings and drops
  count per viewer, each Watch Together player its own, the film's own picture kept or not.
- Q5. *Is replacing hls.js's estimator for our choices acceptable?* Yes: the controller chooses by
  its own estimate (§2); hls.js's is still fed, for hls.js's own readers.
- Q6. *A floor for small chunks?* No, not for now: the 128 KB rule (D265 §7) stands, and each
  sample's size is logged (§5) so the question can be revisited from data.

**Proven by:**
- 1: web/packages/player/src/abr-trust.test.ts ("a low first sample does not hold the playback low once its next chunks arrive fast"; "a chunk given up while starting lowers the ceiling"; "a stall while starting lowers the ceiling to what the estimate chooses"; "ends after four samples and 20 s played, the ceiling no higher than the start"; "reports its confident estimate as the link's speed, remembered for the device's next start"), web/packages/player/src/chunked.test.ts (a stall told to the controller)
- 2: web/packages/player/src/link-estimate.test.ts (the estimate and the confident estimate), web/packages/player/src/step-up.test.ts ("climbs to the highest quality consistent samples carry"; "climbs one quality when its samples disagree"), web/packages/player/src/abr-trust.test.ts (the step-up in the controller), web/packages/player/src/abr-measure.test.ts (hls.js's estimator still fed)
- 3: web/packages/player/src/steadiness.test.ts ("a climb that falls back within twice its hold raises the level and doubles the hold"; "relaxes one level for each ten minutes without a swing or a drop"), web/packages/player/src/abr-trust.test.ts ("a climb that falls back within twice its hold raises the level, and the next climb waits twice as long, one quality")
- 4: web/packages/player/src/steadiness.test.ts ("a second drop within ten minutes raises the level"), web/packages/player/src/link-estimate.test.ts ("a varying link is targeted near its slowest samples"), web/packages/player/src/abr-trust.test.ts ("counts each Watch Together player's drops as its own")
- 5: web/packages/player/src/abr.test.ts ("notes each change of its ceiling with why and what it rests on"; "tells the page its last samples"), web/packages/player/src/diagnosis.test.ts ("keeps the link's last samples apart from its steps"), web/packages/player/src/report.test.ts ("tells a stall the link's last samples apart from its steps"), web/apps/web/src/play-state.test.ts ("sends the link's last samples with a seek apart from its steps"), internal/core/api/stall_report_test.go (TestReport_TheLinksSamplesAreLoggedApartFromTheSteps)
- Q2: internal/core/playback/speeds_test.go (TestLinkSteadiness_IsKeptBesideTheSpeedAndRelaxesAnHourAtATime, TestLinkSteadiness_RelaxesAsOftenAsItsSettingSays), internal/core/playback/playback_timing_test.go (TestRefreshTiming_IsTheSettingsAndInterestLapsesByIt), internal/core/api/start_lower_test.go (TestPlayback_ADeviceStartsAtTheSteadinessItsLastPlaybackOnTheNetworkReported), web/packages/player/src/steadiness.test.ts ("starts at the level its device last ended at"), web/packages/player/src/abr-trust.test.ts ("starts at the level its device last ended at, told as it starts and at each change"), web/packages/player/src/chunked.test.ts ("is the one its offer says"), web/packages/player/src/report.test.ts ("sends the steadiness level with every report"), web/apps/web/src/play-state.test.ts ("tells, with each report, the steadiness level"), web/apps/web/src/moving-down.test.ts ("starts at the steadiness level the offer says")

**Status:** Built 2026-10-27, in the player (`web/packages/player/src`: `abr.ts`, `link-estimate.ts`,
`steadiness.ts`, `step-up.ts`); Q2's remembered level and Q3's own field built the same day, in the
core (`internal/core/playback/speeds.go`) and the play report. Every value is a constant, to
be measured on the acceptance's emulated links (D252, D263) and the owner's devices.

**Revised 2026-10-28** by the owner ("yes", agreeing the lead's two fixes for the batch), after a
Fire TV playing Nosferatu (staging, file 5671, device 60) stepped down on one slow sample: 20 s in, its
five samples were 191842 B in 159 ms, 895044 in 393, 555018 in 349, **376471 in 1200** and 801491 in
284; the one slow sample made §2's largest error 460%, the confident estimate 1315 kb/s (mean 7362),
and starting's end (§1) lowered the ceiling from the film's own picture to q700k432p with 37.3 s
loaded ahead. The step down changed the sound too (D368), which threw the loaded sound away and
stalled the TV 1172 ms. Two changes:

1. **Plenty loaded holds the quality.** A step down exists so the player does not run dry. While
   **20 s** is loaded ahead (`holdsQualityAheadS`, the step-up's own `stepUpBufferMs`: what is
   enough to climb on is enough to stay on), no reading of the link lowers the quality loading,
   neither the next chunk's choice (D265 §4) nor the ceiling, at starting's end or after; once less
   is loaded, the link decides on the evidence then. A chunk given up (D265 §3, already weighed
   against what is loaded), a stall, a force by hls.js and a quality found unplayable (D266) still
   lower it. The note says so: `started, ceiling 3 kept, held at 3: link carries 1, 37.3 s loaded
   ahead (holds from 20 s); …`, and after starting `ceiling 3 held at 3: link carries 1, …`, once
   until the link decides again (§5). A constant, as every value here is.
2. **One sample of five sets no spread.** Once five samples are kept, the confident estimate's
   divisor (§2) is the largest prediction error after the single most extreme is set aside
   (`predictionError`, `trimsErrorFromSamples`): the Fire TV's five give 69% (with one sample before
   them) where they gave 404–460%. Two slow samples of five still count, so §4's varying link is
   still targeted near its slowest; with fewer than five kept every error counts, and a lone first
   sample still decides nothing (§1). The harmonic mean is unchanged, so a link that falls is still
   followed at once.

*Proven by:* web/packages/player/src/abr-trust.test.ts ("keeps its quality at starting's end with
37.3 s loaded, and decides once less is loaded"; "holds the quality loading against a slow link
while the hold is loaded, and says so once"), web/packages/player/src/link-estimate.test.ts ("is not
ruled by one slow sample of five: the most extreme error is set aside"); VQ116.

**Revised 2026-10-29** by the owner, accepting P1–P6 of
[bandwidth-sampling-2026-10-29.md](../design/research/bandwidth-sampling-2026-10-29.md) ("1: yes",
and "put it in this batch because it will affect some of the VQs we're trying to confirm"), except
P3's fourth point: a chunk stuck on one WebRTC connection is **not** asked again on another; its
log says which connection carried it instead (6 below). The research explains the three staging
failures of 2026-10-28 (Nosferatu's 69 kb/s from a given-up chunk, a start that waited on 753 kb/s ten
minutes after a 17 Mb/s film, one slow sample of five cutting the ceiling) and proposes the estimator
below. It replaces §2's harmonic mean and RobustMPC's divisor, and the divisor's trimming of this
decision's revision of 2026-10-28 (its 2) with it; §2's agreement of samples, the hold, the
steadiness levels and every other number stand. Six changes:

1. **The estimate is a robust centre in log space (P1).** Of the last five samples' natural logs,
   Huber's centre, a sample further than 2 spreads from it counted as if that far; the spread their
   median absolute deviation as a standard deviation, at least 0.3, and 0.38 assumed until three
   are kept. A fall is followed once most of the five say it; a chunk given up and a stall still act
   at once.
2. **The remembered link is a prior (P2).** It counts as 2 samples while under an hour old, fewer in
   step with its age, none at `link_speed_fresh_hours`; it lends its spread until three samples are
   kept; two of the playback's own samples more than 2 spreads from it on the same side and within 4
   of each other drop it, and the playback's own samples retire it once they leave the window. The
   speed reported, and remembered, is the estimate (the prior's centre), with its spread; the core
   keeps both, with the steadiness level, in the store (`link_memory`, step 0063), so a restart
   keeps them, and hands a start the speed, its spread and how many samples it counts as.
3. **A chunk given up is censored (P3, 1–3).** Arriving (bytes within the last second, and 128 KB
   of them), it is a sample over its first byte to the give-up; stuck, it is no sample, still a
   drop, and while starting lowers the ceiling only as far as the estimate carries.
4. **Choices read a quantile (P4).** The confident estimate is e^(centre − z × spread / √n), and a
   single chunk's bound e^(centre − z × spread × √(1 + 1/n)), n the samples counted with the
   prior's; z is 1.28 with nothing loaded ahead, 0.84 at 10 s, 0 from 20 s, straight between.
   D265's share stays the headroom over a quality's rate.
5. **The start gate reads the one-chunk bound, and starting can end on evidence (P5).** A next
   chunk's load is the median first-byte wait plus its bits over the bound, from the prior alone
   before any chunk, so it waits `refillAheadMs` only with nothing remembered and nothing measured.
   Starting ends once 20 s have played and the samples settle the ceiling, the same with any one left
   out; *as built*, four samples also end it however they disagree, where P5 would have
   disagreeing samples take more, since a playback still starting never steps up — for the owner to
   confirm.
6. **The log says how well the estimate predicts (P6).** Every play report carries the player's
   notes on its link, which the core logs: its prior; each sample with the time the estimate before
   it expected and its bound's, "below" when slower than the bound; and each chunk given up, or
   stuck where it cannot be, with the transport and WebRTC connection that carried it, how long that
   connection has been up, what it carries and how long since it last delivered bytes.

*Values:* constants, as the decision's own are (its Values): the clip 2, the spread floor 0.3 and assumed
0.38, three samples to measure a spread, the prior's 2 samples and its hour, the drop's 2 and 4
spreads, the second of arriving, and z's 1.28/0.84/0 at 0/10/20 s. They are textbook starting values,
measured on no link of ours; the notes of 6 are to tune them.

*Proven by:*
- 1: web/packages/player/src/link-estimate.test.ts ("is not ruled by one sample that is not the link's: Nosferatu's four near 15 Mb/s and one at 14 kb/s"; "follows a fall once most of its samples say it")

## D353 — A player that jumps ahead of a run stops it when waiting for the run would cost more than starting a new one

**Decided** (2026-10-27), by the project owner, replacing the fixed minute the fix for the owner's
The Unknown (staging, 2026-10-26) gave D309 §2: a run was no longer a player's once the first chunk
the player needed lay more than the look-ahead (`chunk_lookahead_seconds`, 60 s) past what the run
made next. A minute is a guess: a fast run gets there in seconds, and a slow one makes the player
wait the whole minute of film. It amends D309 §2 (a place a player sought away from), and follows
Jellyfin's rule for a run not yet measured (`segmentGapRequiringTranscodingChange = 24 /
state.SegmentLength`, Jellyfin.Api/Controllers/DynamicHlsController.cs).

1. **A run is stopped for a jump when waiting for it costs more than restarting.** Waiting costs the
   film between what the run makes next and the first chunk the player needs not made (the gap)
   over the run's speed, film made per wall time; restarting costs the time a new run takes to make
   its first chunk (the startup). The run is no longer the player's when gap / speed > startup, and
   the player's ask then stops it and starts a run where it landed; a run planned for an ask is
   refused by the same rule, so an init asked for from where the playback last reported, far behind
   the player, starts nothing there.
2. **Both are measured from what the core already sees,** on the sanctioned clock, with no change to
   the node. The speed is the run's own, from its progress over the last
   `chunk_run_speed_window_seconds`, as soon as two chunks made span any time (the capacity watch,
   D250 §6, still waits for half the window): it is the run being judged that the player would wait
   for. The startup is its store's (one film's stream on one grid) most recent run's, from the core
   giving the run to its node to its first chunk made: a new run at the jump is of that same source,
   recipe and node, as loaded as now, so the last one says best what it costs. A run the core learned
   from its progress, after a restart, has no start the core saw and gives none.
3. **Until a run is measured,** no speed yet or its store no startup, the gap past which the player
   jumped away is Jellyfin's 24 s of film.
4. **A player's own nearby asks never stop its run.** The threshold, measured or not, is never under
   two chunks past what the run makes next: a player's picture and sound, loaded apart, each move its
   one position (D309 §1), and hls.js loads a sound at most one fragment past the picture it is
   loading (audio-stream-controller.ts, "up to one fragment ahead of main"); one chunk for that and
   one of slack. And a run making within those two chunks of the chunk last asked for of its store is
   never one its player jumped away from, wherever the other stream moved the position: hls.js loads
   a picture without waiting for its sound, so a picture 30 s ahead of a late sound (its buffer)
   moved the position past the sound's run by more than 24 s, cut the run the sound waited on, and
   refused the sound's ask its run (the restart loop the minute had kept off). A sound made alongside
   a sought picture, made from where the picture landed, is asked for there.
5. **Each stop for a jump is logged, at debug,** with the chunk the run made next, the chunk the
   player needed, the gap, the speed, the startup, the threshold and whether it was measured or
   Jellyfin's 24 s, so a report is explained from the log alone.

**Values:** the 24 s and the two chunks are constants (`unmeasuredJumpGapMs`, `jumpFloorChunks` in
internal/core/chunks): the first governs only a run's first seconds, before its second chunk, and
the second follows hls.js, not the server; no admin could judge either. No new setting.

**In the code:** the test of a run its player will reach within a minute had its player move forward
40 s into a run that made nothing yet, kept by the minute; by §3 that run now restarts, so its jump
is 20 s, within the 24 s, and the 40 s jump is the measured tests' (a run of 10x that started in 5 s
is waited for; one that started in 1 s is not).

**Open question for the owner:** §4's second half, the store's last ask, is the agent's: the two
chunks alone did not cover a picture loaded ahead of a late sound. The cleaner answer is a position
per stream in the playback (each stream's own asks move its own, a seek or a pause moves both), which
changes D309 §1's one position; is that wanted instead? *(Answered 2026-10-27: yes. §4 amended by
[D355](#d355--a-playbacks-picture-and-sound-are-each-wanted-from-a-position-of-their-own-moved-by-their-own-asks-and-together-by-a-seek-a-pause-a-resume-and-the-start): each stream has its own position, and §4's second half, the store's last
ask, is removed; the two chunks stay.)*

**Proven by:**
- 1: TestStopUnwanted_AJumpAheadOfAMeasuredRunWaitsWhileWaitingCostsLessThanRestarting, TestStopUnwanted_APlayerThatSeeksFarIntoARunStopsItAndStartsItsOwn, TestWant_AnInitAskedForFarBehindWhereThePlayerIsStartsNoRunThere
- 2: TestStopUnwanted_AJumpIsJudgedByTheStartOfItsStoresLastRun, TestStopUnwanted_ARunLearnedFromItsProgressIsJudgedByJellyfinsGap
- 3: TestStopUnwanted_ARunLearnedFromItsProgressIsJudgedByJellyfinsGap, TestStopUnwanted_ARunItsPlayerWillReachWithinAMinuteGoesOn
- 4: TestStopUnwanted_ARunIsNeverStoppedForAPlayerTwoChunksPastIt, TestStopUnwanted_ARunItsOwnStreamWaitsOnGoesOnWhereverTheOtherStreamIs, TestWantAlongside_ASoughtPicturesSoundStopsTheSoundsRunWhereThePlayerWas
- 5: TestStopUnwanted_SaysTheNumbersAJumpWasJudgedBy

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-27.

## D354 — A WebRTC pair that goes out to the NAT both ends share and back is named a hairpin, warned of to the admin, and never counts as home

**Decided** (2026-10-27), by the project owner, approving recommendations B and C of
[local-path-2026-10-27.md](../design/research/local-path-2026-10-27.md), which found why the owner's
playback from a laptop in the house went out through the carrier and back (2026-10-26): the laptop's
checks to the core's LAN UDP port never arrived, so ICE settled on a pair whose two ends were the
carrier's one DS-Lite address, which every log line called an ordinary `punched_ipv4`. **Amends**
[D274](#d274--a-core-is-reached-first-by-what-needs-nothing-from-its-owner-webrtc-through-the-discovery-direct-paths-are-upgrades-and-a-relay-waits-for-demand)
§3 (the paths counted) and sharpens
[D300](#d300--a-webrtc-connection-made-inside-the-house-counts-as-home-the-core-offers-webrtc-on-its-lan-address)
§3 (home over WebRTC).

1. **A hairpin is its own path.** A selected pair that is neither direct nor relayed, over IPv4, whose
   core's end (server- or peer-reflexive) has the client's address, is `hairpinned_ipv4`, not
   `punched_ipv4`: the core's public address is the client's, so the pair goes out to the NAT both sit
   behind and back. It is counted with the others on the System page, and its log line is a warning
   naming both ends by type and address.
2. **The admin is warned.** While a hairpin stands, the doctor's finding *WebRTC from devices at home*
   (on /doctor and the System page) warns: *"devices at home reach this server through your provider,
   not your network: UDP port <port> at <LAN address> is not reachable"*, with how many connections
   hairpinned, from which address and when last, and the action: publish the UDP port from the
   server's machine and let it through its firewall. A core taking WebRTC at no LAN port is told to set
   `webrtc.udp_port` and `discovery.lan_addresses` instead.
3. **The warning clears** on the first direct pair (`direct_ipv4` or `direct_ipv6`) whose client's end
   is in the home networks after the last hairpin, or **a week after the last hairpin** with none
   since, and with the core's restart, as the path counts do. A direct pair from the house is the
   proof the warning asks for: a device in the house reached the core across its network. A week
   without one says whoever hairpinned has gone: a household whose port is unreachable hairpins every
   time it plays, so it renews the warning daily, while a visitor, or another household behind the same
   carrier address, does not. A shorter wait would hide a standing fault between evenings of use; no
   wait at all would keep a stranger's one hairpin up for good. The week is a constant
   (`HairpinWarningLasts`), not a setting: no admin could judge it better.
4. **A hairpin never counts as home** (D297 §6, D300 §3): its client's address is a NAT's public one,
   and a carrier's shared address is many households. It is not a direct path, so a request over it
   carries no admin even when its address is named in `server.home_networks`.
5. **The page and the core say why a path was taken** (the research's §4 items 1–3 and 7). A page at a
   discovery's origin tells the core's log once per reach (`POST /client-paths`, signed in, bounded,
   only logged): the browser's family, whether it uses the LAN name, its local-network permission, how
   many names and LAN names the discovery offered, what came of each in the first race (answered,
   failed and how, not waited for, or left out and why), the path taken, and over WebRTC its first
   connection's candidate pairs as the browser's `getStats()` gives them, read 5 s after reaching so
   the pair to the core's LAN address has had time to fail: the selected pair, then those to the core's
   host candidates, each end by type, protocol and address. The core's connection line names its own
   end too, by type and address, and a request over WebRTC carries the browser's user agent in its
   head, so a playback over it names the browser and the device, not `userAgent=""`.

**Not decided here:** the research's option D (the discovery judging "at home" for an IPv4-only core)
is the owner's design question, and its option E (an ICE restart aimed at the host pair) waits for
these reports to show a house's LAN pair losing races it could have won.

**Proven by:**
- 1: TestPathOf_IsToldByTheCoresEndOfThePair, TestHairpinWarning_StandsUntilADirectConnectionFromTheHouse, web/apps/web/src/system-discovery.test.tsx
- 2: TestHairpinFinding_WarnsThatDevicesAtHomeReachTheServerThroughTheProvider, TestHairpinWarning_StandsUntilADirectConnectionFromTheHouse
- 3: TestHairpinWarning_StandsUntilADirectConnectionFromTheHouse, TestHairpinWarning_LapsesAWeekAfterTheLastHairpin
- 4: TestIsDirectPath_CountsNoRelayedOrFailedPath, TestIsHomeOverWebRTC_CountsTheCoresOwnIPv6NetworkAsTheHouses
- 5: TestClientPaths_APagesChoiceOfPathIsLoggedWithItsReasonsAndItsPairs, TestRecordPath_NamesBothEndsOfThePairByTypeAndAddress, TestRTCOffer_ASignedInClientReachesTheAPIOverDataChannels, web/apps/web/src/path-choice.test.ts, web/apps/web/src/kept-path.test.ts, web/packages/sdk/src/rtc-pairs.test.ts, web/packages/sdk/src/direct-path.test.ts, web/packages/sdk/src/rtc-transport.test.ts

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-27.

## D355 — A playback's picture and sound are each wanted from a position of their own, moved by their own asks, and together by a seek, a pause, a resume and the start

**Decided** (2026-10-27), by the project owner, answering D353's open question. A playback had one
position (D309 §1), which the picture's and the sound's chunk asks each moved; hls.js loads the
picture up to its buffer, about 30 s, ahead of a late sound, so the position jumped back and forth
between them, and the sound's run was judged from where the picture was. D353 §4 guarded the run with
its store's last ask. It amends D309 §1 and D353 §4.

1. **Each stream of a playback has its own position.** Its picture's and its sound's chunk asks each
   move only their own stream's position. Subtitles have no runs of chunks (internal/core/subtitles
   serves each track whole), so they have none.
2. **A seek, a pause, a resume and the start move every stream's position together:** the player's
   word (`PUT /playback/{token}/interest`, said as it seeks, pauses and plays again), a picture's
   chunk asked for where a seek took the player (`Orpheum-Sought`, D284 §2), as hls.js asks for the
   seek's sound only once the picture's first chunk has come and the sound is made alongside it from
   there, and its start on its ladder. A picture asked for while its player said it is paused moves
   nothing, as before.
3. **Interest is judged per stream from that stream's own position**: whether a run is wanted, a
   run planned for an ask, a stop for want of a player and D353's jump rule each read only the
   interests in the run's own stream, as internal/core/chunks already did; the playback now gives
   each its own position.
4. **D353 §4's second half, a run making within two chunks of its store's last ask is never one its
   player jumped away from, is removed.** Its case, a picture loaded ahead of a late sound moving the
   sound's position past its run, cannot happen: the picture's ask moves the picture alone. The guard
   was also wrong where it outlived the ask: the store's last ask, kept per store and not per player,
   kept a run its player had sought away from by its word until its first ask where it landed, and
   kept a run for a player that had left. The two-chunk floor of §4's first half stays: a chunk
   served is known made at once, and the run's progress, which says what it makes next, follows on
   the node's next word, so a player's next ask may read a chunk past what the run makes.
5. **The position a playback resumes from is neither stream's.** It is where its player reports it
   plays (the play report's position, D217 §7, D165), kept and stored as before: a stream's position
   is where its loading is, up to the buffer ahead of what was watched, and the picture's, the
   earliest's or any stream's would resume the person past what they saw. An init asked for is still
   made from the reported position.
6. **The logs of interest say each stream's position**: a run stopped as no player wants it, and an
   ask that planned no run, say where every player of the film wants each stream from, beside what
   the players of the run's own stream want.

**Values:** none new.

**Proven by:**
- 1: TestInterestsIn_EachStreamIsWhereItsOwnAsksPutItAndASeekMovesBoth, TestInterestsIn_AreWhatEachPlayerLastAskedFor
- 2: TestInterestsIn_EachStreamIsWhereItsOwnAsksPutItAndASeekMovesBoth, TestSayInterest_ReplacesWhatThePlayerWantedAndLeavingSaysWhy, TestWantAlongside_ASoughtPicturesSoundStopsTheSoundsRunWhereThePlayerWas
- 3: TestStopUnwanted_ARunItsOwnStreamWaitsOnGoesOnWhereverTheOtherStreamIs
- 4: TestStopUnwanted_AWordOfASeekStopsTheRunItLeftThoughTheStoresLastAskWasNearIt, TestStopUnwanted_ARunIsNeverStoppedForAPlayerTwoChunksPastIt
- 5: TestInterestsIn_EachStreamIsWhereItsOwnAsksPutItAndASeekMovesBoth, TestPlayState_TwoDevicesReportingOutOfOrderNeverRewindThePosition
- 6: TestStopUnwanted_SaysWhereEachStreamOfTheFilmIsWanted

**Status:** Decided 2026-10-27.

## D356 — An IPv4-only core's devices at home are recognised by the house's IPv6 networks, which the core learns from devices that reached it directly in the house and tells its discovery

**Decided** (2026-10-27), by the project owner, who approved the direction the same day in
[local-path-2026-10-27.md](../design/research/local-path-2026-10-27.md) option D (*"the core tells the
discovery the house's IPv6 network so an IPv4-only core can recognise devices at home"*), then agreed
this proposal and answered its five questions as recommended (below). The evidence,
the mechanisms weighed and how Plex, Jellyfin and Tailscale judge "local" are in
[house-ipv6-2026-10-27.md](../design/research/house-ipv6-2026-10-27.md). A core whose heartbeat
leaves over IPv4 behind DS-Lite or carrier NAT (staging; a host without IPv6; a Docker install on the
default bridge) reports from the carrier's shared address, which the discovery rightly never trusts,
while the house's devices ask over the house's IPv6 /64: none is ever judged at home, so none is
offered the LAN name. **Amends**
[D290](#d290--the-discovery-audits-findings-taken-claiming-on-the-core-paths-ranked-by-kind-re-keying-signed-by-the-old-key-computed-dns-behind-cloudflare-and-webrtc-in-the-beta)
§2 (what "seems to be at home" is judged by, and what the discovery is told of a household), and the
discovery protocol's §2.4 (the heartbeat) and §3.2 (the `lan` path).

1. **A house network is learnt from a device the core has proven at home.** When a WebRTC
   connection made through a discovery is from home by
   [D300](#d300--a-webrtc-connection-made-inside-the-house-counts-as-home-the-core-offers-webrtc-on-its-lan-address)
   §3 (its selected pair direct, the client's end in the home networks or the core's own IPv6
   networks), the core keeps the network that device's offer came from (§2) as a house network. A
   relayed, punched or hairpinned connection (D354 §4) teaches nothing, and nothing a page sends
   counts. A device in the house is the strongest evidence the core trusts; the network is the
   discovery's own observation of the same device.
2. **The discovery passes each offer's source network to the core with the offer**:
   `clientNetwork` on the signalling message, the offer request's source address as the discovery
   saw it (`CF-Connecting-IP` behind Cloudflare), as its /64, and only when it is a public IPv6
   address: a shared IPv4 says nothing of a household. Both the paid service and `discovery/single`
   pass it. The core learns nothing new of a device by it: an offer's candidates already carry the
   device's public addresses.
3. **The core tells its discovery its house networks in each heartbeat** (`houseNetworks` beside
   `candidates`), each a public IPv6 /64 with how it was had, `learnt` or `configured` (§6), at most
   four, the most recently witnessed first. A network newly learnt sends a heartbeat at once rather
   than at the next interval.
4. **A house network is kept 30 days after it was last witnessed**, and a fifth pushes out the one
   least recently witnessed. They are kept in the core's discovery state (`discovery.json`), so a
   restart keeps them, and a Leave forgets them with the enrolment. A provider's new prefix (Deutsche
   Telekom's moves every night) is learnt from the first device that reaches the core from home
   after the move; every first reach is WebRTC through the discovery (D274), so that is its first
   use. Until then the house's devices get no LAN name, as before this decision.
5. **The discovery judges a device at home also when its address is in one of the heartbeat's house
   networks.** The match is `discovery/discoveryproto`'s, which both discoveries and Orpheum's tests
   share, and counts only a public IPv6 /64: a shorter prefix, a private or IPv4 one, or a fifth,
   counts for nothing. The existing matches (the heartbeat's source /64, a public IPv6 candidate's
   /64, the household's own reached IPv4) stand.
6. **The admin may name the house's networks** (`discovery.house_ipv6_networks`, public /64s, sent
   as `configured`), for a house whose devices cannot make a direct pair, as staging cannot until its
   UDP port is published (the research's option A1). The System page says a configured network goes
   stale when the provider moves the prefix.
7. **A house network grants nothing but the LAN name's place among the paths** (D290 §2). The core
   never counts one as home, for admin or anything else (D297 §6, D300 §3, D302): a learnt network is
   the discovery's word, and a stale one may be another household's once the provider reuses it.
8. **No stranger can name a household's network.** The heartbeat carries only what the core, under
   its own credential, sends; a learnt network needs a direct pair into the house's networks, which an
   offer through a discovery cannot make the core send (D300 §2). A household's own device can teach
   a wrong one, a VPN's exit network when the VPN keeps LAN access; the harm is that the household's
   own link holders in that network are offered the LAN name and may meet Chrome's local-network
   prompt, until it ages out (§4).
9. **What the discovery keeps, and for how long.** The house networks are part of the core's
   heartbeat and kept as it is: the current value only, replaced by each heartbeat, past values in
   backups for their period, deleted when the core is released (the paid service's spec §6, "Current
   addresses"). They are never written to the zone and never returned to a client, who is told only
   its own `clientPrefix` (D293 §8). For a dual-stack core this adds nothing the heartbeat's source
   did not already say; for a DS-Lite or carrier-NAT household it is new, tying the core to the
   household's current connection, where the discovery held only a carrier's shared address.
10. **The judgement says why.** The discovery's `a core's paths were asked for` line names what
    judged the device at home (`heartbeat`, `candidate`, `houseNetwork`, `ownIPv4`) or `none`; and a
    core whose heartbeat comes over a shared IPv4 with no house network is logged once as one whose
    devices at home cannot be recognised (local-path §4 item 6). The core's System page lists its
    house networks, how each was had, and for a learnt one by which device, named by its address in
    the house (the client's end of the direct pair), and when.
11. **The core logs whether the device's own address agrees** (Q5): when a network is learnt, its
    line says whether the public IPv6 addresses the device's offer names are in it (`yes`), are all
    elsewhere (`no`, a VPN's or a relay's sign), or are none (`unknown`, a browser hiding them), with
    the /64s they are in. Nothing acts on it.

**Rejected** (the research's §3): the install script reading the host's prefix and a STUN helper in
the host's network (each works only where the host has IPv6, where Orpheum's compose already sends the
heartbeat over IPv6, and the first goes stale); listening for router advertisements (the host's
network and a raw socket, for the same case); the page's own word (D300 §3); a hairpin as evidence
(D354 §4).

**The owner's answers** (2026-10-27, each as recommended):
- Q1: **one proven connection teaches a network**, with no two-device or two-day rule: a new
  prefix's first LAN name is not delayed, and a VPN's network is bounded by §4 and §8.
- Q2: **keep the configured networks** (§6) as the fallback, for a house whose devices make no
  direct WebRTC pair.
- Q3: **30 days and four networks are constants** (`HouseNetworkKeptFor`,
  `discoveryproto.MaxHouseNetworks`), not settings.
- Q4: **the System page shows the house's public /64s** to the admin (§10).
- Q5: **the core logs, without acting, whether the device's own IPv6 address in its offer agrees**
  with the network the discovery saw (§11).

**Values:** `HouseNetworkKeptFor` = 30 days and `discoveryproto.MaxHouseNetworks` = 4, constants
(Q3); `discovery.house_ipv6_networks`, a config key, empty by default (§6).

**Proven by:**
- 1: TestProvenAtHome_ADirectConnectionFromTheHouseProvesItself, TestProvenAtHome_ARelayedPunchedOrHairpinnedConnectionProvesNothing, TestAnswerRelayed_TellsAConnectionProvenAtHome, TestHouseNetworks_ADirectConnectionFromTheHouseTeachesItsOffersNetwork
- 2: TestSignal_AnOfferCarriesItsSourcesIPv6NetworkAndNoIPv4, TestHouseNetworkOf_IsAPublicIPv6SourcesSlash64AndNothingElse, TestHouseNetworks_AnOfferFromNoIPv6NetworkTeachesNothing
- 3: TestHeartbeat_CarriesTheHouseNetworksMostRecentFirst, TestHouseNetworks_ANewNetworkSendsAHeartbeatAtOnce
- 4: TestHouseNetworks_ANetworkUnwitnessedForThirtyDaysIsDropped, TestHouseNetworks_AFifthPushesOutTheLeastRecent, TestHouseNetworks_SurviveARestartAndGoWithALeave
- 5: TestInHouseNetworks_ADeviceInAPublicSlash64IsAtHome, TestInHouseNetworks_AShorterPrivateOrIPv4NetworkCountsForNothing
- 6: TestDiscoveryConfig_HouseIPv6NetworksArePublicSlash64s, TestHeartbeat_CarriesTheHouseNetworksMostRecentFirst, web/apps/web/src/system-discovery.test.tsx
- 7: TestMarkingHome_AHouseNetworkGrantsNoAdmin
- 8: TestIsFromOutside_RefusesEveryAddressOfTheCoresOwnNetworks, TestProvenAtHome_ARelayedPunchedOrHairpinnedConnectionProvesNothing
- 9: TestHeartbeat_CarriesTheHouseNetworksMostRecentFirst
- 10: TestDiscoveryStatusBody_CarriesTheHouseNetworks, web/apps/web/src/system-discovery.test.tsx
- 11: TestHouseNetworks_ADirectConnectionFromTheHouseTeachesItsOffersNetwork, TestOfferedIPv6Addresses_AreTheOffersPublicIPv6Candidates

The paid service's side is tested in orpheum-connect, which `make check-claims` cannot see: its
offer's `clientNetwork` (§2) by TestOffers_CarryTheIPv6NetworkTheyCameFromAndNoIPv4 and
TestRegistry_EachCoreHasItsOwnConnection; its `isAtHome` calling §5's match by
TestPaths_ADeviceInAHouseNetworkTheHeartbeatNamesIsAtHome; and its log lines (§10) by
TestAtHomeBy_NamesWhatJudgedTheDeviceAtHome and
TestWarnIfHomeUnrecognisable_LogsACoreOverASharedIPv4OnceWhileItStaysSo.

**Build note** (2026-10-27): the core, `discovery/discoveryproto`, `discovery/single` and the System
page are done here, and the paid service's side in orpheum-connect; not yet on staging or nas.example.
